# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Holy Age (An Aois Naomh)

# Part One: The Cord

# Chapter One: Of Ìomhar Dearg and the Bier of Spears

*FE 1*


> *Cha do leag aon duine e; leag an sluagh uile e.*
> No one man brought him down; the whole host brought him down.
>
> — said on the east bank at Àth na Fala, the night the king fell

## I. Of the Fires on the East Bank

*The people of Dùn dhearg tell this, and they tell it low, for it is their own shame and their own lord's pride together.*

On the night the king fell the host of the east did not sleep. It stood a long while in the water where he had gone down, and then it came out of the river by twos and threes, as men come away from a barrow of their own dead, and lit its fires again along the east bank. Nobody gave the order. The fires were lit because it was dark and the men were wet to the breast and the river had turned cold all at once.

There was a lad at one of those fires, a lad of the eastern hills who had been in the river on the second day and had come out alive. He sat with his knees drawn up and his spear across them, and the older men about him kept asking what the king had been like, close to. He told them the king had been warm. After that they let him alone.

Nobody went back across the ford that night to take the body up out of the river. They had drawn it onto the west bank, where the stone was, and there they had left it; and nobody on the east bank would say why he did not go and stand over it, or strip it, or cut the grey head off to carry home as the old wars were said to have done. The lad thought afterward that it was fear. He thought also, when he was old, that it was something else that has no plain name, the thing a man feels in a hall when the fire has gone out and the house is still warm from it.

The greybeard who had given the counsel for the third day walked up and down behind the fires until near dawn. At every fire he stopped and said, "It is done. We have done it." At the lad's fire a man threw a stone at him, and he went on.

Before first light the saying had gone the length of the bank: *no one man brought him down; the whole host brought him down.* The households of Dùn dhearg meant it as a boast when they first said it, and by morning it had become an excuse, and before a year was out it was the only thing any of them would say at all.

## II. Of the Son Who Came Late

Ìomhar Dearg left the valley under Dùn ìseal at noon on the third day of the fighting, which was the day his father fell, and he left it in a temper.

He had been three days in the gathering-house arguing for a stretch of river-grazing below the Red Hill that a nephew of his claimed by his mother. He was fourteen hundred years old, near enough; he had been a grown man when the stones were first raised at Tobar dhìreach round the slab, and there was not a cattle-path in the east he had not ridden. On the first day word had come that the spears of Dùn dhearg were out and that the king had gone down to the ford. He had heard it as they all heard it, with half his mind, as one hears that a neighbour's roof is being mended. The king had gone down to fords before. He had come back from all of them.

On the second day a man of his household came in from the eastern road and said that the host was greater than anyone had thought, and that the king had sent the handful of his own people back up the road and held the ford alone. Ìomhar said that he would go when the grazing was settled. He remembered afterward that he had said it standing up, with his hand on the post of the gathering-house door, and that his nephew had laughed.

On the third morning the grazing was still not settled, and he found that he could not sit still. He went out into the valley and looked east. From the lip of the valley on a clear day a man can see the smoke of Dùn dhearg over the shoulder of the hill, and that morning there was smoke all along the low ground where the river runs, the smoke of many fires, and none of it moving. He stood there a long time. Then he went down to his own camp and told his steward to call up the household, every man who could carry a spear, and the steward asked him whether the grazing was settled.

"It will keep," said Ìomhar Dearg.

"Your nephew will have it by tonight."

"Then he will have it," said Ìomhar, and the steward looked at him, and went.

He rode east with a little over two hundred at his back, and he did not hurry them, which he never forgave himself. The road from the valley to the ford is a few miles, no more than a morning's walk for a carrier with a basket. He could have been at the water by the middle of the afternoon. But the host held the road beyond the second rise, and his scouts came back and told him so; and he turned his people north over the hill-grazing to come down on the ford from above, out of the heather, where the host would not look for them; and the hill was wet and steep and the light went. They lay that night in a fold of the hill a mile above the river. From there they could hear the fighting, and then, toward midnight, they could not.

Ìomhar did not sleep. He sat against a stone with his cloak over his knees and listened to the silence come up out of the valley, and he knew what it was. His steward came and sat by him in the dark and said nothing for a while.

"Maybe he has driven them off," the steward said at last.

"Then we would hear them running," said Ìomhar Dearg.

## III. Of the Ford in the Morning

They came down out of the heather in the grey light.

What he saw first was the water. The river below the ford had spread out over the meadow in a sheet, brown and still, with the grass standing up through it, and it did not look like a river at all. It looked like a field in a wet spring. Then he saw why. At the shallows below the ford the dead lay across the whole width of the stream, piled on one another, thrown up against the gravel as the current had rolled them, so thick that the water came over them in a low fall and made a sound like a mill-lade. The ford itself lay above the dam, wide and slow and dark. Crows were already walking on it.

On the west bank, by a grey stone at the head of the ford, there was one body lying by itself on its back, with nothing near it.

He knew it from the hillside. He knew it by the length of it and by the grey hair, which was the only grey on that bank. Ìomhar did not go to it. He said afterward that he could not have gone to it then and done what came next, and that he chose what came next.

On the east bank the host of Dùn dhearg lay in the heather where it had dropped. It had come out of the river in the night and lit its fires, and the fires had burned down, and the men had gone to sleep where they sat, three thousand of them or what was left of three thousand, wet and bloodied and spent, some with their spears still in their hands and many without. A few were awake. They saw the spears come down out of the hill on the far side of the ford, and they stood up and shouted, and the shout went along the bank; and the men who heard it got up slowly, like men in a dream, and looked for their spears and did not find them.

"They are finished," said the steward, at Ìomhar's elbow. "Look at them. They can't lift their arms."

"Neither could he," said Ìomhar Dearg. "At the last."

He took his household across the ford at a run, over the stones his father had held for three days, through water that was still red at the edges and stank, and up the east bank into the host. It was a slaughter, and the tellers of Dùn dhearg, who have never had much to say about that morning, say at least that much. The men of the east had spent everything they had on the king and had nothing left for his son. Some stood and fought and died. More ran, up the valley toward Dùn dhearg, and Ìomhar's people ran after them and killed them in the heather. Some sat down where they were and put their hands over their heads.

Ìomhar himself fought at the head of it until noon, and then he stopped. He found that he had come to the end of wanting to. He stood on the east bank above the dam of the dead and looked across at the grey stone and the body beside it, and his steward, coming up, found him weeping, and waited a while before he spoke.

By evening he held the ford. It was the thing his father had held, and he had it now; and none of the host who were left alive could have taken it from a child.

## IV. Of the Double Bank of Dùn dhearg

Dùn dhearg stands on its hill above the river a few miles from the ford, and in those days it was a fort of the old kind, with two banks of earth about its crown and a ditch between them, and timber halls within where the households of the east met to swear that they owed nothing to Dùn ìseal or its king. It had never been taken. It had not often needed to be.

Ìomhar Dearg came up to it on the second morning after the ford with his household and some hundreds of the host who had surrendered to him and had nowhere else to go. The gate in the outer bank stood open. There was nobody on the bank at all. The women and the old men of the households had heard what had happened at the ford, and many of them had gone up into the eastern hills with the cattle, and those who had not gone stood in the doors of the halls within the inner bank and watched him come.

He walked in through both gates. He did not draw. In the middle of the inner ground, where the households had sworn their oath against his father, he stood and asked who among them had given the counsel of the third day, that every spear should go into the river together and keep going in.

Nobody answered. Nobody had to; the greybeard was not among them. He had been found at dawn of that same morning lying face down in the shallows at the head of the ford, below the grey stone, and whether he had fallen or gone in of his own will, nobody on the east bank would say.

Then Ìomhar asked who had struck the blow that brought the king down in the dark. Nobody answered that either, and this time it was not from fear. He went from face to face, and every face he looked into told him the truth, which was that no one knew, and that no household there would own it if it could. He understood then what the saying on the east bank meant. The whole host had brought him down. It was the only boast they had, and it was also the only thing they could bear to have done.

He burned the halls. He had the people carry out what they wanted first: cloaks, pots, the old men's stools, a loom with the web still on it. Then his household set fire to the thatch, and the halls within the double bank burned through the afternoon, and the smoke went up over the hill and was seen in the valley under Dùn ìseal, where some of the heirs took it to be the host of the east coming on, and armed themselves at last.

When it was done Ìomhar Dearg stood on the inner bank with the hot ash blowing past him and said, loudly enough for the whole ground to hear, that the households of Dùn dhearg had sworn they owed nothing to Dùn ìseal, and he would hold them to it. They owed nothing to Dùn ìseal. They owed everything to him.

Among the people who came in from the hills in the following days there was a lad who had been in the river on the second day and had lived. Ìomhar's steward brought him forward, because the lad had said to someone that he had been close to the king, and the steward thought his lord would want to hear it. Ìomhar asked him what his father had been like at the end.

"He was warm," the lad said.

Ìomhar Dearg looked at him a long time, and then sent him back to his mother, and gave orders that nobody was to touch him. The lad lived to be old, and he never went back to the ford, and it is his telling of the ford that the east keeps.

## V. Of the Bier of Spears

On the fifth day after the ford Ìomhar had the body brought up from the west bank.

He went down to it himself at last, alone, with the rest held back on the east side. He had expected to find the face changed, as the faces of the dead are changed. What he found was a young man's face, with no line on it, and the grey hair lying wet across the brow as if he had only that moment come up out of the river. The eyes were open. The wounds were all in front, many of them, and none of them seemed to be enough. He knelt by the stone, where his father had sat between the rushes of the host and drunk from the river and washed his hands, and he closed the eyes. Then he did what his father had done on those evenings. He went down to the edge of the ford and washed his hands in the water, which was clean now above the dam, and cold.

He sent for spears. There were more than enough; they lay in the ford and along both banks and in the heather where the host had dropped them, ash shafts and hazel shafts and a few of old dark oak, and his people gathered them by the armful. The wrights of his household lashed them into a bier with thongs cut from the host's own belts, two long spears for the poles and a lattice of shorter ones across them, and over the lattice they laid the cloaks of the east. Then they set the king on it.

It took twelve men to carry him. The bier was heavy with the spears, and he had been a big man, bigger than anyone living. Ìomhar chose the twelve from among the host of Dùn dhearg: twelve who had been in the river. He told them that they had brought the king down between them, and between them they would bring him home.

Some of his own household thought that a hard thing to ask. Some thought it a mercy. The twelve went without a word.

Ìomhar Dearg did not go with the bier. He said that he had the east to settle, which was true. He said also, to his steward only, that he would not walk up the valley road behind his father's body among the fires of his brothers and sisters and nephews and cousins who had not come, and be looked at by them as one who had come and been too late; and that when he went up to Dùn ìseal he would go as what he was, and not as a mourner who had been at the wrong gathering.

So the bier went up the valley road without him. It went slowly, with the twelve changing their grip at every stream, and a few of Ìomhar's household walking before it with green branches, as the old custom was for a death on the road. At the lip of the valley two of the king's sons came down to meet it. They had seen the smoke from Dùn dhearg and heard the herd-boy's news, and had ridden out at last, with the spears of their households behind them, and met the bier coming up instead. They got down and walked behind it. Both of them were grey.

## VI. Of the Twelve Who Came Back

The twelve came back to Dùn dhearg on the evening of the eighth day, walking, with the two long poles of the bier over their shoulders and nothing on them. The heirs had kept the lattice of short spears and the cloaks, and sent the poles home. Nobody in the valley had wanted to burn them, and nobody had known what else to do with them.

Ìomhar had them brought to him where he sat by the new posts on the inner bank. They stood in a row in the dusk and would not sit, though he told them to. The eldest of them was a man of the barley-fields named in no telling, grey-bearded, with a cut across one hand from the second day of the ford that had gone bad and smelled. He did the talking.

He said that the bier had gone up the valley road slow, as it had been ordered, and that the two grey sons of the king had walked behind it all the way. He said that the heirs had come out of their tents on both sides of the road to see it go by, more of them than he could have counted, the old and the young together, in good cloaks, and that none of them had said a word to the bearers, good or bad, but only looked at the king.

"And they looked at you," said Ìomhar Dearg.

"Some did," said the man. "Most did not. We were only the bier."

He said that a woman of the valley had come down from the spring with a pail and given each of the twelve water as the bier passed, and had not asked who they were, though she must have known. He said that the keening had started up again as the king went by, at the upper camps first, and run down the valley from fire to fire until it reached the bottom of the road, and that he had heard nothing like it in his life and did not want to again. He said that they had carried the king as far as the long house below the hill, and that there the old men of the slab had taken him from them, and the twelve had been given bread and sent away.

"Was anything said of me?" said Ìomhar.

The man thought about it. "One of them asked where you were," he said. "A young one, laughing. He asked whether you had come up with the bier, and when he heard you had not, he said, 'He has found something to hold, then,' and some of them laughed with him and some did not."

Ìomhar Dearg was silent a long while. Then he asked the man's name, and the man gave it, and the telling has let it go. Ìomhar gave each of the twelve a cow from the herds of the east that had come down out of the hills, and a place on the new ground within the bank, and told them that they were his people now, first of all his people, and that if any man of Dùn dhearg ever threw the ford at them he was to answer for it to him.

The poles of the bier he had set up on either side of the inner gate, where they stood for many years, bleaching, until the weather had them.

## VII. Of What Ìomhar Kept

For nine days Ìomhar Dearg stayed at Dùn dhearg.

In those nine days he had the dead of the ford drawn out of the river and buried on the meadow in long trenches, the host of the east all together, because there was no telling them apart. He had the bank of the ford cleared and the grey stone left standing, and he forbade anybody to move it. He sent riders round the eastern hills to the households who had gone up with the cattle and told them to come down, and that they would keep their cattle and their lives if they came down to him and to nobody else. Most of them came. Those who did not were hunted, and the tellers of Dùn dhearg do not say how those hunts ended.

He counted what he had. It was a hill with a double bank and a burned crown, and the valley under it, and the lowland fields toward the south where the eastern households had their barley, and some thousands of people who had come against his father and now had nobody to answer to but him. It was more than any share he had been arguing for in the gathering-house. He had not been given it. He had taken it with a sword, on the morning after the king fell, from men who could not lift their arms, and he knew very well what his kin would say of that, and he did not greatly care.

On the ninth day word came from the valley that the king was laid in the earth, and that the heirs were sending to every coast of the island for the kin who had not come in, so that the whole of the king's blood might sit down together at Dùn ìseal to part what he had left.

"Part it," said Ìomhar Dearg. He was standing on the inner bank where the halls had been. The ash had been cleared and the first new posts were in the ground. "Let them part it. They will not part this."

He went up the valley road the next morning, riding, with his household behind him in the cloaks of the east. The heirs came out of their tents to watch him pass as they had come out to watch the bier. He did not look at any of them. He went up past the fires of the valley to the long gathering-house below the hill, and got down, and stood in the door with the light behind him, and the people inside stopped talking.

His holding was called afterward *an Earrann Dhearg*, the Red Share, for the hill and for the blood. It was the one share on the island that was won with a sword before the parting and never given in it; and the heirs who sat down to part the rest had to part it around him, as a river parts round a stone it cannot move.

# Chapter Two: Of the Runner at the Spring

*FE 1*

## I. Of Sìne and the Cord of the Households

*At Dùn ìseal the knot-keepers tell this, and they tell it with a cord across their knees.*

Sìne nan Snaidhm kept the cord at Dùn ìseal in the year the king fell. It was the cord of the households, of the kind Catrìona Mhòr's people had first made: a long rope of twisted flax, grey with handling, with a knot in it for every hearth in the valleys about the hill. A birth was a small knot tied beside its hearth's knot, a death was a small knot untied, and a household that went away over the hills was cut out and the two ends spliced. Sìne could run it through her fingers in the dark and tell you who lived at the head of every glen from the slab to the salt road, and how many mouths they fed, and which of them had burned their measure early the winter before.

She was of no one's blood that mattered. Her mother had kept the cord before her, and her mother's mother, and nobody could remember why it had gone down that way and not through some better family. She had the tying of it because her fingers were quick, her memory was good, and she could not be bribed, having nothing that she wanted. She had a house of turf and stone below the spring, a husband who cut peat, two daughters who were learning the knots, a goat, and the cord. The cord lived in a basket by the hearth with a lid on it, and when there was news in the valley people came to her door to see it written.

That summer the valley was full of the king's kin. They had been coming in since the spring, from every coast of the island, to wait about the king for their shares, and there were so many of them now that the cord of the households had nothing to say about them. Each of them was a fire and no household: there was a fire for every son and daughter of the king who had come, and every grandchild, and every great-grandchild, and all the fires down the length of the valley had stewards to argue for them and servants to fetch their water and grievances against the fire next door. Sìne fetched her own water, and on most evenings she was the only woman at the spring who did.

The king had gone down to the ford seven days before the runner came. Everybody knew he had gone. The talk at the spring was that the spears of Dùn dhearg were out, and that the old man had taken a handful of his own people and gone to meet them, and that the kin would follow him in a day or two when the grazing and the salt and the shore-rights were settled. Sìne had heard it every evening. On the second day the smoke of many fires had stood over the low ground to the east, and nobody moved. Two days after the fighting stopped, a great smoke went up over Dùn dhearg itself, a black smoke that leaned north in the wind, and the fires in the valley took it for the host of the east coming on at last, and there was a great running about and arming, and stewards shouting at each other about whose spears should stand at the head of the road. Then nothing came, and the smoke thinned, and the kin put their spears away again and went back to arguing.

## II. Of the Herd-Boy

She was at the spring with her pails on the fourth evening after the battle when the runner came up the valley road.

He was a herd-boy of the eastern hills, barefoot, in a shirt that had been white at some time and was now the colour of the heather. He came up the road at a run that had gone past running, the run of a body that has forgotten how to do anything else, and he had run so far that he could not stop when he reached the spring. He went on past it three or four steps, and then his legs folded and he sat down in the mud with a grunt, as if someone had pushed him.

Sìne put her pail down beside him and gave him water in her cupped hands, because the pail was too heavy for him to lift. He drank half and was sick, and drank the rest.

"Where is the camp of the king's son?" he said. "Any of them. I was told to tell the king's sons."

She looked down the valley at the fires, which were being lit for the evening, one after another, all the way to the bend of the road and past it.

"There are sixty camps in this valley that call themselves the king's sons," said Sìne. "Tell me, and I'll tell them."

His name was Donnan, and he came from the high grazings north of the ford, where his people had summer shielings. He had been with the cattle on the ridge above the river when the host of Dùn dhearg came down the valley, and he had stayed there, because the cattle could not be left and because he wanted to see. He had seen all of it. For three days he had lain in the heather on the ridge with a crust in his shirt and watched.

He told her, sitting in the mud, in the plain words of a herd-boy, with his teeth going. The king had held the ford alone, three days and three nights. The host had come at him through the water and across the deep channel above it, all the first day and all the second, and the dead had piled at the shallows until the river backed up behind them and spread out over the meadow. On the third day every spear of the east had gone into the river together, and had kept going in, and there had been a light round the king in the afternoon that the boy could not describe, and did not try to twice. On the third night the king went down. No one man had done it. They had come at him until there were no more of him to come at.

"I would have come the straight road," he said, "but they are all over it. The host. Those that are left of them. And then there were other spears coming down off the hill in the morning, the day after, and I didn't know whose they were, so I went round. Over the tops. I have been two days coming over the tops."

"Whose were they?" said Sìne. "The spears in the morning?"

"I don't know. They came from this side. They killed the rest." He looked past her at the tents, all down the valley, and the smoke of the cooking fires going up straight in the still evening, and a woman laughing somewhere, and a dog. He had come a long way. "Where were his kin?" he said. "The king's kin. Where were they?"

Sìne did not answer that. She picked up the boy by the arm, and left her pails at the spring, and took him up to the tents.

## III. Of the Question in the Valley

She remembered afterward, and told it to her daughters, and they to theirs, that the first thing said when the news went into the camps was a question about the hill.

The nearest fire-circle was where she took him, because it was the nearest, and because she did not know which of the sixty was the right one and did not believe that any of them was. A steward in a blue cloak came out to see what the knot-woman wanted, and she told him to hear the boy, and he heard him through. He was a man of middle years, clean-shaven, with good shoes, and he heard the whole of it without a word, looking at the boy's feet. When it was finished he turned round to the men behind him at the fire, and he said:

"Who holds the hill now?"

Sìne watched that question go down the valley faster than the grief did. It went from fire to fire as a spark goes along dry heather. She saw men get up from their suppers and walk quickly to the next fire, and men come out from the next fire to meet them; she saw stewards running, and a boy sent up the slope toward the upper camps at a gallop on a pony; she heard the question asked at a dozen fires before she heard anybody weep. For a while nobody keened at all. The valley was full of voices, and all the voices were talking about the hill.

Then a woman in one of the upper camps began to keen alone.

She was a daughter of the king, and her name was Mairsile. She was so old that her hair had gone white and then gone thin, and she had come in from the north coast in a litter that spring because she could no longer ride, and she had sat all summer at her fire in the upper valley with a blanket over her knees and taken no part in the arguing. Her keen was thin and cracked, like the voice of a very old bird, and at first it only made the voices below it louder. But it did not stop. After a while the fire nearest hers took it up, and then the next; and it came down the valley from fire to fire as the question had gone up it, slowly, until the whole of the valley was crying in the dark, the old and the young, the stewards and the servants, the sons and daughters and grandchildren of the king; and the herd-boy with it, sitting on the ground by the fire of the blue-cloaked steward with his face in his arms.

Sìne did not keen. She stood a while and listened, and then she went back down to the spring, where her pails were still standing in the dark, and carried them home, and put the lid more firmly on the basket where the cord was. Her husband asked her from the bed what the noise was. She told him the king was dead, and that the kin were asking who had the hill. He said nothing for a while, and then he said that the peat would want cutting the same, whoever had it; and she lay down beside him and did not sleep.

## IV. Of the Bier Coming Up

The bier came up the valley road three days after the boy.

Sìne was at the spring again, because the water had to be fetched whatever happened, and she saw it come round the bend of the road below, slowly, with the evening sun behind it. It was a strange long thing, black and bristling, and at first she did not know what it was. Then she saw that it was made of spears: two long spears for the poles and a lattice of shorter ones lashed across them, with cloaks laid over the lattice, and on the cloaks a man lying.

Twelve men carried it, men of the east and none of the valley, in the rough brown cloaks of the eastern barley-country, and some of them had cuts on their arms and faces that had not healed. Before them walked a few men with green branches, as the old custom was for a death on the road, and behind them walked two old men, tall, with grey heads, who she knew were sons of the king because she had seen them at the gathering-house door; and behind those came the spears of their households, who had ridden out that morning to meet the bier and were now walking home behind it.

The heirs came out of the tents on both sides of the road to see it pass. Sìne stood among them with her pail.

She had seen the king three times in her life, and each time far off: a tall man on a horse at the edge of a gathering, with people falling back from him on either side. She saw him now close to, for the first time and the last. He had not grown old. His hair was grey, as it had been since before anyone in the valley could remember, but his face was a young man's face, and his eyes had been closed. The wounds were all in front. There were a great many of them, and none of them, to look at, seemed enough.

The bearers were thirsty. She could see it in their mouths. None of the heirs had thought to give them anything, and the bearers would not ask. When the bier came level with the spring she stepped out into the road and gave each of the twelve water from her pail, in a cup she carried at her belt, one after another as they walked, without stopping them. None of them looked at her. The last of them, a grey-bearded man with a bad hand, said "Thank you," very low, in the speech of the east. She did not ask who they were. She thought that she knew.

The keening began again as the king went by, at the upper camps first, where Mairsile's fire was, and ran down the valley to the bottom of the road. Sìne walked beside the bier as far as the long gathering-house below the hill. There the old keepers of the slab were waiting, nine of them, on the bench before the door, and they stood up and took the king from the twelve men of the east, and the twelve were given bread and sent away.

As they went a young man of the kin, standing at the gathering-house door with his thumbs in his belt, asked loudly whether Ìomhar Dearg had come up with the bier. When he heard that Ìomhar had not, he said, "He has found something to hold, then," and laughed. Some of the kin about him laughed too. Sìne knew him. He was a grandson of the king, some nine hundred years old, who laughed at most things, and whom the kin called Niall Òg, Niall the Young; and she saw that when the others had stopped laughing he went on looking after the twelve men of the east, down the road, and did not laugh any more.

## V. Of the Two Mounds

Where they laid the king, the tellers of Dùn ìseal and the tellers of the Mason's line do not agree, and each has a mound to show.

This much all agree on. He lay for three nights in the gathering-house, on the lattice of spears, with the keepers of the slab sitting by him in turn and the kin coming in to look at him and going out again. On the fourth morning he was carried out before dawn, with the nine keepers walking before and his two grey sons behind, and a few of the eldest of the kin; and he was laid in the earth that same day, and a mound raised over him, and nobody who was not there saw it done.

The tellers of Dùn ìseal say that they laid him on the slope of the hill, on the side that faces the vein, with his face toward the mountain, as the keepers of the slab were laid. There is a long low mound on that slope, grown over with heather, and the knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal will take you to it if you ask.

The tellers of the Mason's line say otherwise. There was a man of Clann na Ceiste in the valley that year, a reciter from Tobar dhìreach named Seathan Crom, who had walked down to Dùn ìseal at midsummer to see the king once more before he died, for he was an old man and the king had been kind to his father. He was lame in one leg, which is why they called him Crom, and he was at the gathering-house when the bier came in. The reciters of the Mason's line say that it was Seathan who went to the grey sons on the third night and reminded them of what the king was: that he had been crowned in a grove by the gods themselves and was the heir of the mason's fire, and that he should lie where the fire had first come to his people, and not on a hillside among keepers. They say the grey sons heard him, and that the bier went out before dawn by the north road and not by the slope; and the reciters of the Mason's line have a mound of their own to show, older-looking, in a place they will name only to their own.

Sìne was not there, and she said so to her daughters. She said that she had seen the bier go out of the gathering-house in the dark, and the lamps go with it, and she had not followed. She said that when the grey sons came back in the evening they were very tired and their shoes were wet, and that the shoes might have got wet on either road.

The knot-keepers who tell this tale after her leave the matter there.

## VI. Of the Lord of Dùn dhearg

On the day after the burial, Ìomhar Dearg came up the valley road.

He came riding, which nobody did in that valley any more except the king, and he came with his household behind him, two hundred spears or more, all in the rough brown cloaks of the east. The valley had heard by then whose spears had come down off the hill on the morning after the ford, and what they had done, and what they had done after that at Dùn dhearg. The heirs came out of their tents to see him pass as they had come out to see the bier, and they did not keen this time. They stood in silence on both sides of the road, and Ìomhar Dearg rode up between them, looking at nobody, a big red-bearded man on a big horse, and got down at the gathering-house door.

Sìne was inside, because she had been sent for. The keepers of the slab had asked her to sit at the back of the house with the cord of the households, in case there was need to say who lived where. She saw him stand in the door with the evening light behind him, and she saw the talk in the house stop as if a knife had cut it.

"I have come," said Ìomhar Dearg, "as the lord of Dùn dhearg."

Nobody said anything. It was the eldest of the keepers of the slab, an old bent man named Aodh Crom, who stood up at last from the bench by the hearth and said that the lord of Dùn dhearg was welcome under that roof, as anyone of the king's blood was welcome, and that he might sit.

Ìomhar Dearg sat. He did not take off his cloak. He sat a little apart from his brothers and sisters, on a stool his own steward carried in for him, and he said nothing more that evening. But Sìne, who watched him from the back of the house with the cord in her lap, saw that the others kept looking at him when they thought he did not see; and that when they spoke of the shares, as they were already speaking of them, they spoke of them around him, as a stream goes round a stone.

## VII. Of the Runners to Every Coast

That night the heirs sent to every coast.

There were kin of the king who had not come in that summer: some who were too old, some who had quarrelled with the others, some who had held that there was no hurry, since the king had lived four thousand years and would plainly live four thousand more. Now there was a hurry. Runners went out of the valley before dawn by every road, north over the high passes, west toward the lake shore and the salt, south to the barley-country and the southern sea. They went in pairs, one from each of two fires that did not trust each other, so that neither fire could send a message the other had not heard. There were so many pairs of runners on the roads in the week after that the carriers coming up from the coast to the slab with their baskets of fish thought there had been a war.

The kin who had come in waited. They buried nobody else, and they did not go home. They sat at their fires and argued about who held the hill, and who should, and by what rule, and they began to count one another.

The counting was the trouble. Every fire in the valley had its own reckoning of how many of the king's blood there were, and every reckoning left out somebody that another fire said was owed, and put in somebody that another fire said was nobody. The stewards went from fire to fire with notched sticks and came back with different numbers. Nobody believed anybody else's sticks. A steward of the salt shore came to blows with a steward of the western lake over a great-grandchild whom one of them counted twice and the other not at all, and the child's mother, when they asked her, said that she had four sons and had not come all this way to be counted as half of one.

Three nights after Ìomhar Dearg came up, there was a knock at Sìne's door, late, when the fire was banked and the children asleep. She opened it and found Aodh Crom there, the eldest of the keepers of the slab, leaning on his staff in the dark, with the rain running off his hood.

He was older than any keeper of the slab had been before him, and he looked it. His people said that there was a thin strain of the king's long years in them somewhere far back, through some marriage in the old days that nobody would name, and he had outlived three wives and most of his grandchildren. He had sat on the bench by the slab at Tobar dhìreach for longer than Sìne's mother had been alive. She had never had him at her door before.

"I want a new cord," he said.

"The households are counted," said Sìne. "I have them all. You saw them tonight."

"Not the households," said the keeper. "The heirs. They will want to know how many there are before they start. And they will not believe each other."

She looked at him a long time in the dark doorway, with the rain coming down between them. Then she said that she would need flax, a good deal of it, and a place to sit where every one of them would have to come to her, and not she to them.

"The door of the gathering-house," said Aodh Crom. "They will all come through that."

"And who will they believe," said Sìne, "when they won't believe each other?"

"You," said the old man. "Because you want nothing." He pulled his hood forward over his face. "And because none of them will have thought yet that you are worth the trouble of buying."

He went away up the path in the rain. Sìne shut the door and stood a while in the dark by the banked fire. Then she took the lid off the basket, and took out the cord of the households, and began to run it through her fingers, knot by knot, from the slab to the salt road; and she was still at it when the grey came into the smoke-hole at dawn.

# Chapter Three: Of the Binding of the First Flame

*FE 1*

> *Cha tèid an fhèith a roinn. Gearr i, agus silidh i fuil.*
> The vein will not be parted. Cut it, and it bleeds.

## I. Of the Keepers of the Slab

*This is told at Tobar dhìreach, where the slab lies, by the households whose turn it is to sit by it.*

Under the king the hill-folk of Dia-thìr had burned the coloured coal by the handful and shared their grain before the storms, and at every gathering they said that they had always been on the island and had come from nowhere. Nine keepers, one drawn by lot for each district of the hills, watched the slab over the crack at Tobar dhìreach where the mason had broken the vein at the beginning of the count. All of it was custom. None of it was law, for there had been no law but the king's word, and the king was in the earth.

Aodh Crom had been drawn for his district so many times that the households had stopped drawing and simply sent him. He was the eldest of the nine that year, and the eldest keeper there had ever been. His people said that some grandmother of his, far back in the long reign, had married a grandson of the king whose name the family did not say, and that a little of the long years had come down to them in the blood, thinned out like a dye in a great vat of water. Aodh had lived a hundred and eighty years and walked with a stick. He had buried three wives and four of his seven children. He was older than any keeper had been before him, and younger than the youngest of the king's sons in the valley, who were none of them less than some centuries old; and he knew both things about himself, and thought about the second more than the first.

When the runners had gone out to every coast, the nine keepers came down from Tobar dhìreach to Dùn ìseal together, walking, with the fire of their hut carried before them in a covered pot.

That fire was the only thing in their charge besides the slab. It had burned in the keepers' hut beside the slab for as long as anyone could remember, fed with a little of the coloured coal each night and never let go out, and the keepers passed it from hand to hand at the change of the lot as they passed the slab. The reciters of the Mason's line held that it had been lit from the mason's own fire, the fire the lightning had kindled in the broken vein, and carried from hearth to hearth down all the generations until it came to the keepers. The keepers did not say that. They said only that it was old, and that it was not allowed to go out, and they did not quarrel with the reciters, who were welcome to their telling.

They brought it down to Dùn ìseal in the pot because Aodh Crom had told them to. The others had asked him why.

"Because they are going to fight over the hill," he had said, "and I want something in the room that is older than they are."

On the road down the nine keepers passed a great many carriers going up and down between the slab country and the coast, as they always did at that season, with their baskets on their backs; and every carrier stopped and asked them the same thing: whether the handful would still be given out at Samhain. None of them asked who would hold the hill. Aodh Crom told each of them that it would. He did not know it. He said afterward that it was the first promise he made in the matter of the Binding, and that he made it to people who had no knot on anyone's cord and no voice in the gathering-house, and that it was the one he minded most about keeping.

## II. Of the First Quarrel

The heirs' first quarrel was over the hill, and it came before any other, because the hill stands over the vein.

They met for it in the long gathering-house below Dùn ìseal on the twentieth day of the month, when the nearer coasts had come in and the farther were on the roads. The house was built for the gatherings of the valley and held some hundreds at a pinch, and that day it held more than it could, and the rest stood outside the doors in the drizzle and passed back what was said. The kin sat on the benches along the walls by the age of their lines, as near as they could agree on it, which was not near. The nine keepers of the slab sat at the back of the house on a bench of their own by the hearth, with their covered pot on the floor between their feet, and nobody paid them any heed.

The king had held the hill of Dùn ìseal in his own hand at the last, and had given it to no one. Every line in the house claimed it, and every line by a different rule.

Murchadh Mòr claimed it by the rule of the eldest. He was the king's eldest living son, close on two thousand nine hundred years old, a heavy slow man with a white beard to his belt and a voice like a door on a cold hinge, and he did not argue his claim so much as stand in it. He said that the eldest son took the father's hearth, as every household in the hills knew, and that the hill was the king's hearth, and he was the eldest son, and there was an end of it.

Eithne nic Ailein rose before he had sat down. She was a daughter of the king, some nineteen hundred years old, small and quick, with a sharp chin and a sharper tongue, and she held the lowland barley-country toward the south sea in all but name. She said that if the hill went to the eldest, then the eldest had only to die for the hill to be parted among his eleven sons, and each of those among his, and that she for one would sooner not live to see it.

"You are not likely to," said Murchadh Mòr.

Eithne's hand went to her belt, and so did the hands of the men behind her; and the men behind Murchadh stood up; and there was very nearly blood on the floor of the gathering-house on the first day. It was Niall Òg, the laughing grandson, who got between them, with his hands open and spread, saying that he had not come all this way to see his aunt and his uncle kill each other before he had been given anything to be killed for. Some laughed. Enough of them sat down.

Then the others began. There were those who claimed the hill by the rule of the living: that the king's children who were alive, and there were more than a score of them, stood before the children of his dead children, whose lines were only grandchildren. The lines of the dead answered that the king had loved their fathers and mothers as well as he had loved anyone in the house, and better than some, and that a grandson of a firstborn stood higher than a fifth daughter. There were those who said that the hill should go to whoever the king would have chosen, and each of those had a different notion of whom the king would have chosen, and a story to prove it. A cousin from the western shore, whose name the tellers have let go, stood up and said that there was no call for all this. The hill could be cut like any other ground. Give each of the great lines a gallery, he said, and let each dig its own, and the one that dug deepest would be the one the vein loved best.

There was a noise in the house at that, half laughter and half a growl. Aodh Crom, on the keepers' bench at the back, looked down at the pot between his feet.

## III. Of What the Old Keeper Said

The heirs argued through that day and into the night, and on the second day, and into the third.

Aodh Crom listened to all of it. He heard the rule of the eldest put twenty times and the rule of the living thirty. He heard the western cousin's galleries taken up by a dozen young heirs who liked the sound of digging for themselves, and heard their fathers shout them down. Once a great-grandson of the king explained at length that he had a better claim than anybody present through a marriage in the second millennium of the reign, and the whole house groaned. Once, late on the second night, when the lamps were low and most of the old heirs were asleep on their benches, he heard a young woman near the door say quite quietly to her neighbour that the king had been dead eighteen days and nobody in the house had yet said his name.

On the third day, toward evening, he got up.

He did it slowly, because of his knees and his stick, and at first nobody noticed. Then the keepers on either side of him stood up too, to help him, and then the whole bench stood, and the heirs nearest the back turned round to see what the old men were doing, and so it went up the house, until the house was looking at him and had fallen quiet, more from surprise than respect.

He was a small man, bent almost double, and his voice was thin. He did not raise it. The heirs at the far end of the house had to lean forward, and they did.

"Cut the vein," he said, "and it bleeds."

He waited, and then he said the rest of it. "You will be parting it for as long as there is any of it left to part. Every one of your children will want a gallery, and every one of theirs. You will be cutting the mountain into slices for the rest of your lives, and your lives are long. And when there is nothing left in it you will part the hole."

Nobody laughed.

Then he reminded them what the keepers of the slab had asked of Catrìona Mhòr in her time, when she held the hill under the king: that the keepers' charge be declared before a whole gathering, so that it should stand on something firmer than custom. Catrìona Mhòr had told them to ask again when the king was gone, since while he lived his word was all the declaring anyone needed. The king was gone. He was asking again.

"And I ask more," said Aodh Crom. "I ask that the vein, and the hill over it, be put into no share at all. Let no one of the king's blood hold it. Not the eldest, not the living, not the dead. Give it to the keepers, who are nobody's, and let the keepers answer for it to the gods."

He sat down. The keepers on either side of him sat down with him.

The heirs were quiet a long while. It was the longest quiet in the gathering-house in three days, and Aodh Crom said afterward that he had counted his own breaths through it, and got to forty.

Then Eithne nic Ailein laughed. It was a short laugh, and not a kind one. "I would sooner nobody had it," she said, "than Murchadh."

Murchadh Mòr turned his great head and looked at her. "I would sooner nobody had it," he said, "than Eithne."

So it went down the house, line by line. The lines of the living would sooner nobody had it than the lines of the dead, and the lines of the dead than the lines of the living. The western cousin would sooner nobody had it than whichever of his uncles would have taken it from him. Ìomhar Dearg, who had sat three days on his stool apart from the others and said nothing, stood up when it came near him and said that he held Dùn dhearg, and that the hill was nothing to him either way; but that he would sooner it went to the old man's pot than to any of his brothers; and sat down. Niall Òg said he would sooner nobody had it than anybody, since he was plainly never going to be given it himself, and at least this way he would not have to watch someone else enjoy it.

Each of them was willing to give the thing away sooner than see a cousin get it. The tellers of Dùn ìseal, who love the Binding more than any other tale they tell, admit that this is how it was won.

## IV. Of Murchadh at the Hut

That night, the night between the old keeper's words and the swearing, Murchadh Mòr came up the slope to the keepers' hut alone.

Aodh Crom was sitting by the pot with the lid off, feeding the fire. He heard the heavy step outside and the door-skin pushed aside, and the king's eldest son came in stooping, for the door was low and he was a very big man, and stood a moment getting his breath. Then he sat down on the ground across the fire from the keeper, as a carrier sits, with his knees up.

"You'll not have the hill for yourself," said Murchadh Mòr. "You understand that. None of you. It goes to the fire and not to the man who feeds the fire."

"I understand it," said Aodh Crom.

"Then what do you want?"

The old keeper thought about it. "To die before I see you cut the mountain," he said. "And I am a hundred and eighty, and you are nearly three thousand, so I have the better chance."

Murchadh looked at him. Then, to Aodh's surprise, he laughed, a short creaking laugh like a gate, and put out his hands to the fire.

They sat so a long while. The king's son said nothing for a time, and then he began to talk about his father: how he had ridden with him to the salt shore in the first thousand years of the reign, when the salt-folk would not kneel, and how the king had gone down alone to the edge of the water and stood there until they came out to him. He said that his father had never told him anything he did not need to know, in two thousand nine hundred years, and that he had thought there would be time.

"I was on my way," he said. "I want you to know it. I was on my way to the ford. I had the spears called up. I was going in the morning, when I had the salt-rights settled with my sister." He looked into the fire. "They are still not settled."

Aodh Crom said nothing, because there was nothing to say that would help, and the king's eldest son knew it. After a while Murchadh got up, stooping, and went to the door, and turned there.

"Tomorrow I swear first," he said. "Because I am the eldest. You will see to it."

"You will swear first," said Aodh Crom.

When he had gone the old keeper sat a long while looking at the door-skin, which was still swinging. The young woman by the gathering-house door had been wrong, he thought. Somebody in the valley had said the king's name at last. It had taken eighteen days, and it had been said in the dark to an old man of no account, where no one else would hear it.

## V. Of the Swearing

They swore it the next day, the twenty-third of the month, three weeks after the king fell. It was the first oath the heirs took, before they had agreed on anything else; and it was the one oath all of them could take, then or afterward.

The keepers had asked for it to be done out of doors, on the slope above the gathering-house where the ground runs up toward the mountain, and the heirs had agreed, since the house would not hold them all and nobody wanted to swear in a room where somebody else had been given the best seat. They stood on the wet slope in the order of their lines, as near as they could agree on it, with their households below them, and the valley people below the households, and the carriers who had come up from the coast with fish and found the whole kingdom on a hillside standing among the valley people with their baskets on their backs.

The nine keepers stood at the top of the slope with the pot. Aodh Crom took the lid off it with his own hands, and lifted out the fire in its dish of clay, and held it up so that the whole slope could see it: a small red fire of the coloured coal, burning low, with a thread of smoke going straight up in the still air.

He said whose it was from then on. He said it was Brìde's, who keeps the hearth and the undying flame, and that it would not be let go out while there was anyone on the island to feed it. He said that the vein under the mountain, and the slab over the first break in it, belonged from that day to Crom Cruaich, the bent one of the mound, whose price is measured, and that what was taken from the vein would be answered for to Crom. He said that the keepers of the slab would keep both, the flame for Brìde and the vein for Crom, and that they would keep them for no one's share and in no one's name; and that no one of the king's blood would ever hold either, though every one of the king's blood might warm his hands.

The reciters of the Mason's line, standing among the valley people, say that the flame Aodh Crom held up that day had come down from the mason's fire. The keepers never said so, and they kept the two apart after, as the reciters did too, at the last. The mason's fire is the first fire, which the lightning lit in the broken vein at the beginning of the count. The First Flame is the flame that was sworn to on the slope below Dùn ìseal, and it is from that swearing that the Holy Age has its name.

Then the heirs came up the slope one by one to swear, and it took until dark.

Murchadh Mòr came first, as the eldest, and he put his great hand over the fire in the dish and held it there till the heat made him take it away, and said that he would never hold the vein, and went down again without looking at anyone. Eithne came after him and did the same, quickly, and said something to Aodh Crom under her breath that the old man would never repeat. Ìomhar Dearg came in his brown cloak of the east and swore with his left hand, since his right was cut, and nobody asked how. Niall Òg swore, and grinned at the old keeper, and said, "There. Now I've given away something."

The last of the king's blood to come up the slope that day was nobody the heirs knew.

He was a man of middle height, weathered, in a plain hill cloak, and he had walked down out of the high valleys to the west of Tobar dhìreach when he heard the king was dead. His name was Gille-Brìde. He was of the line of Somhairle, the king's son who had lived among Clann na Ceiste by the slab and died long before his father, and who had taken no share of anything, and whose children had kept to the high valleys ever since and asked for nothing. Gille-Brìde was a man of a hundred and seventy-two, which was young for a man of the king's blood and old for anyone else, and he had the long years in him, though they were running out.

He put his hand over the fire and swore that he would never hold the vein. Then he asked Aodh Crom, very courteously, whether he might take a coal of it home.

The keepers looked at one another. Nobody had asked that. Aodh Crom said that he might, since the flame was sworn to no one and so was the one thing on the island that anyone might have a little of. Gille-Brìde took a coal from the dish on the end of a stick, and dropped it into a small clay pot he had carried at his belt for the purpose, and put the lid on it, and went down the slope past the heirs, who stared at him.

"And your share?" said one of them. "You're of the blood. You'll want your knot."

"I've got what I came for," said Gille-Brìde, and he walked back up into the high valleys with the pot under his arm that same night; and no knot was ever tied for him on anyone's cord.

## VI. Of the Night after the Binding

Aodh Crom sat that night in the keepers' hut on the slope above the gathering-house, where they had carried the dish, and fed the flame.

It was a small hut, of stone and turf, with one low door. The flame burned on a flat stone in the middle of it, in its dish, and the old man sat on the ground beside it with a basket of coal and put a little on from time to time with his fingers, as the keepers had always done, and listened to the valley.

The valley was loud. The heirs had gone back to their fires in a good humour for the first time since the king fell, pleased with themselves for having given a thing away, and they were drinking to it. He could hear singing from the upper camps. He could hear Niall Òg's laugh, which carried. Below all of it, down on the valley floor, he could hear the carriers, who had stood all day on the slope with their baskets and now had to go back down to the coast in the dark with them, calling to one another on the road.

After a while another of the keepers came in and sat down across the flame from him. She was the youngest of the nine that year, a woman of the southern districts named in no telling, and she had not said a word all day.

"They'll go back to the hill tomorrow," she said.

"They will," said Aodh Crom. "Tomorrow they'll start on the rest of it. The shares. And they'll count each other, and they'll cut each other, and they'll hate each other for a thousand years, some of them, for they have the years to do it in." He put a coal on the flame. "But not over this."

"And who holds this?" said the woman. "When you are gone? And the rest of us?"

For a while he gave her no answer. He was thinking of the young woman by the door of the gathering-house, on the second night, who had said that the king was eighteen days dead and nobody had said his name.

"Somebody of nobody's blood," he said at last. "They will need to find somebody of nobody's blood. That will be the hardest thing they ever do." And he put another coal on, and the flame took it, and the smoke went up straight through the hole in the roof into the dark over Dùn ìseal.

# Chapter Four: Of the Knots

*FE 1*

## I. Of the Flax and the Door

*At Dùn ìseal the knot-keepers tell this, and they tell it with a cord across their knees.*

Sìne nan Snaidhm sat down at the door of the long gathering-house below Dùn ìseal on the second day of an Dàmhair, in the morning, with a basket of flax beside her and a stool under her and a new cord in her lap.

She had spent the days since the old keeper's knock making the cord. It had taken the flax of three households, bought with the keepers' coal, and she and her two daughters had twisted it on the long walk behind her house, the elder girl turning the hook and the younger walking backward down the walk with the strands, until they had a rope as thick as a thumb and longer than the gathering-house, coiled in the basket like a sleeping snake. It was pale and new and smelled of the retting pond, and she had never had one so long in her hands.

She had worked out the knots at night, by the fire, on a spare length. The cord of the households had one knot to a hearth, and small knots beside it for the mouths the hearth fed. That would not do for the heirs. The heirs had no hearths that mattered; they had lines. So she had taken threads of dyed wool, one colour for each child of the king who had living heirs in the valley, as near as the keepers could tell her how many that was, and she meant to tie each heir's knot with a turn of his line's thread caught in it, so that a knot could be traced back by its colour to the child of the king it came down from. It was not a new thing. The households did something like it for marriages. But nobody had ever done it with so many colours, and she had had to send to the dyers of the lowlands for some of them; and by the first morning she had twenty-three colours of wool in a bag at her belt, and knew she would want more.

The keepers had chosen the door because every heir had to come through it. Aodh Crom had said to the heads of the lines that no one would be heard in the gathering-house on the matter of the shares who had not first been knotted at the door. The heads of the lines had agreed, each thinking that it would keep out somebody else. So when the doors were opened that morning there was a crowd outside them that went back down the path and round the side of the house and out onto the grass, all in their good cloaks, all watching the woman on the stool.

"Say your line," said Sìne nan Snaidhm to the first of them, "and I'll tie your knot."

## II. Of Murchadh Mòr

The eldest came first. That had been agreed without argument, because none of the others could think how to argue it, and because nobody wanted to stand in front of him.

Murchadh Mòr stood over her in the doorway so that his shadow fell across the cord, and he gave his line in two words.

"Ailean's son."

Then he looked down the valley to see who would argue. Nobody did.

Sìne took the thread of his colour, which was a dark blue, and caught it into the cord, and tied the knot. She tied it slowly and hard, because she could feel him watching her fingers, and she did not look up. He stood over her the whole time she tied it, as if she might tie it loose. When it was done she ran her thumb over it and said, "That is you," and he bent down, a very long way, and felt the knot himself between his great fingers, and then straightened up and went in without another word.

After him came his sons, eleven of them, all old men, and each gave his line in three words, "Murchadh's son, Ailean's grandson," or near enough; and after the sons their sons, and theirs. The blue went into the cord at every knot, and the cord began to come out of the basket and lie across Sìne's lap and over her knees and down onto the step, and the elder daughter, who sat behind her, began to coil it into a second basket as it came.

It took the whole of the first day to knot the line of Murchadh.

## III. Of Eithne's Knot-Keeper

Eithne nic Ailein came on the second morning, and she did not come alone.

She had brought a knot-keeper of her own from the lowlands, a thin young man with long clever fingers and a face like a heron, named Fionn Beag. Why she had brought him she did not say, and had no need to. She set him on the step beside Sìne, close enough that their elbows touched, and told him to count the count after her.

Sìne said nothing. She gave Eithne her knot, with green for her line, and Eithne gave her line crisply, "Ailean's daughter," and stood back and watched Fionn Beag bend over the cord and run the knot through his fingers and nod.

After that Fionn Beag counted every knot. He counted Eithne's children and grandchildren, and he counted the lines that came after them, the grey of the line of Fionnghal of the western shore, the brown of Artair's line of the salt shore, the yellow of Cormac's in the east. He counted them all day. When Sìne tied a knot he reached across and felt it; when she caught a colour into it he checked it against the bag; when an heir gave a line he listened with his head on one side, and more than once he stopped an heir and asked him to say it again. Sìne let him. She did not hurry and she did not slow down.

On the evening of the fourth day he went to Eithne at her fire and told her that the knot-keeper of Dùn ìseal had made no mistake. He said it had been four days and near two hundred knots, and that he had never in his life seen fingers like hers, and that he did not think he could have kept up with her if she had not been letting him.

Eithne sent him home in the morning.

Before he went he came to the door of the gathering-house and stood a moment on the step, looking at the cord coiled in its baskets, and then at Sìne.

"How do you do it?" he said. "Four days, and your hands aren't tired."

"They are tired," said Sìne. "It isn't my hands that are doing it."

He did not understand her, and she did not explain, and he went back down to the lowlands, where he kept the cord of Eithne's households for the rest of his life and was reckoned the best knot-keeper in the south. But he told his own children that there was a woman at Dùn ìseal who could hold seven hundred people in her head at once and tie them in the right order, and that the heirs of the king did not know what they had sitting on their doorstep.

## IV. Of Niall Òg and the Knot Tied Once

Niall Òg came on the fifth day, laughing.

He was a grandson of the king, nine hundred years old, and at nine hundred he was a boy beside his uncles and his aunts. So they had called him the Young since before he could remember, and he had never got rid of it and had long since stopped trying. He had a round face and quick brown eyes and a mouth that was always about to smile, and he had been in the valley all summer at a small fire of his own on the edge of the upper camps, where he argued for nothing in particular and listened to everyone.

He gave his line through his mother, who was a daughter of the king, dead these two thousand years; and Sìne took the colour of that line, which was a pale red, and began to catch it in. Then he gave his line again through his father, who was a son of a son of the king, of another line altogether, the grey line of Fionnghal; and when Sìne looked up at the second he grinned at her and said, "I'm owed twice."

She tied the knot once.

She tied it with the pale red of his mother's line, since he had given that first, and left the grey out; and when it was done she ran her thumb over it and said, "That is you."

"And my father?" said Niall.

"Your father has a knot of his own," said Sìne. "Two, if you like. His own, and his line's. You are one man."

Niall Òg looked at her. For a moment she thought he would argue, and she saw the men of the lines standing behind him lean in to hear it. Then he laughed again, differently, and put his hand on the cord for a moment, over his knot, and said, "So I am," and went in.

He told it for the rest of his life. He told it at inn tables and by hearths and in the halls of three great shares, and he always told it against himself. His saying was that he had been nine hundred years in the world and had never been told so plainly what he was, and that it had been done by a woman on a stool who had nothing she wanted. And once, when he was very old and had had a good deal of heather ale, he said that he had gone into the gathering-house that morning and sat on his bench and cried for his grandfather for the first time since the ford, and that he did not know why it was the knot that had done it.

## V. Of the Cow That Was Not Taken

By the sixth day the heirs had learned that a knot on the cord was worth something, and had begun to think about what it was worth.

It was then that the stewards began coming to Sìne's house at night.

The first was a steward of one of the lines of the dead, a line that came down from a son of the king who had died in the second millennium of the reign and had left a great many grandchildren. He came to her door after dark with a boy leading a cow behind him, a good red cow in milk, and he said that his lord's line had some great-grandchildren who might be hard to place, and some cousins by marriage whose claim was not quite clear, and that it would be a kindness if the knot-keeper could see her way to tying them close in to the line, and tightly, so that they could not be picked out afterward; and that the cow was hers in any case, for her trouble, since he could see she had only a goat.

Sìne looked at the cow, and at the steward, and at the boy.

"Take it home," she said. "I have a goat."

The steward said that he did not think she understood him.

"I understand you," said Sìne. "Tell your lord's great-grandchildren to come to the door and say their lines. If they are his, I'll tie them to him. If they aren't, I won't. And if you come to my house again with a cow I'll tell Aodh Crom, and he'll tell the gathering-house, and then every line in the valley will know that yours has cousins it needs to buy knots for."

The steward went away with the cow. Two more came in the nights after that, one with a pin of carved bone and one with the promise of a stretch of summer grazing for her husband's sheep, which he did not have. She sent them both away. Word went round the fires that the knot-woman could not be bought, and after that the stewards left her alone, and began instead to watch each other's lines at the door, very closely, for anyone the knot-woman might be tying close in who had no business being tied at all.

Sìne said to her daughters that this was the best thing that had happened. She said that a cord that no one could buy was a cord everyone would watch; and that a cord everyone was watching was a cord that would be believed.

## VI. Of the Knots of the Dead

On the eighth day the lines of the dead began to come to the door, and Sìne had to decide what to do with them.

The king had been having children for four thousand years, and a great many of them had died before him: some in the long wars of the reign, some of accidents, some of the slow thinning that came even to the long-lived in the end, and a few, the eldest, simply of years, having been born before the long years were in the king's blood at all. They were more than the living. Their children and grandchildren were in the valley in hundreds, and every one of them came to the door and gave a line that began with a name nobody living had seen.

Sìne could not tie a knot for a dead man in the heirs' cord. The dead were not heirs. But she could not tie his grandchildren to nothing, either, and have them hang loose in the cord between the living lines with no colour to say whose they were. The lines of the dead watched her at the door that morning to see what she would do, and so did the lines of the living, more closely.

She tied a knot of the dead.

She took a length of black wool, and tied it round nothing, in the old way the households tied a knot for a child who had died at birth, so that there was a small hard ring in the cord with a hole through the middle where a knot should be. Then she tied the grandchildren's knots after it, each with a turn of the black in it and a turn of the dead child's own colour beside, so that anyone running the cord through his fingers could feel the hollow and then the knots that hung from it.

There was a murmur in the crowd at that. A grandson of a dead daughter of the king, an old man with a stick, came up and felt the hollow knot for a long time.

"That's my mother," he said.

"That's where she would be," said Sìne.

He nodded, and gave his line, and she tied him after the hollow knot. After him came the rest of that line, eleven of them, and each of them stopped before giving the line and put a finger on the hollow knot first, as one touches a door-post on coming home; and the custom stayed, so that for the rest of the gathering nobody of the lines of the dead was knotted without first touching the black ring of the parent they came down from. When he went in he said to the lines of the dead who were waiting that the knot-woman had put their fathers and mothers in the cord, and after that they gave her no trouble. But the lines of the living went in muttering that the dead were being given places in the cord; and Aodh Crom, when he heard of it, went and looked at the hollow knots a long while and said nothing, and Sìne thought afterward that he had seen before any of the heirs did that the dead would have to be given a place in the shares as well.

By the eleventh day there were more hollow knots in the cord than there were knots for living children of the king. The heirs walking the cord on the last night felt them under their fingers in the lamplight and counted them too.

## VII. Of Ìomhar's Knot and the Child in Arms

Ìomhar Dearg came on the seventh day. He came at the head of his line, which was the line of a living son of the king, and gave it plainly, "Ailean's son, and lord of Dùn dhearg." Sìne tied the knot with his colour, a rust red, and did not tie in the lordship, because there was no colour for it.

Behind him in the crowd four men of four different lines began to mutter, and one of them said out loud that the cord ought to have a knot for what Ìomhar had taken as well as for what he was owed. Ìomhar turned round and looked at him. The man stopped. But the muttering did not stop; it went back through the crowd and round the side of the house, and the next day four lines sent their stewards to Aodh Crom to say that when the shares came to be cut, they would not agree to Dùn dhearg being counted as one.

Most of the knots were not like that. Most of them were people Sìne had never seen before and would never see again: sons and daughters of the king's great-grandchildren, come in from the far coasts in the last days before the gathering closed, who had never been in the valley and stood blinking at the door in their travelling cloaks and gave their lines slowly, as if they were not sure of them. Many of them were not sure. Sìne helped them. She knew the lines by then better than most of the people in them.

There were old men and women, grandchildren of the king, who had been born in his second thousand years and looked it. There were young ones, great-great-grandchildren, who were the age of her own daughters and had the long years in them so faintly that they might live no longer than anyone. And on the ninth day there was a child in arms.

The child was the youngest of all of them: a great-great-grandchild of the king, some months old, of the salt-shore line. The mother came to the door with the child wrapped in a shawl and held it up in both hands for Sìne to see, and gave its line for it, one name after another, back to the king. The crowd behind her went quiet to hear it. It was the longest line anybody gave at the door, and the child slept through all of it.

Sìne tied the smallest knot she tied in those eleven days, with a turn of the brown in it. Then she put out her finger, and the child woke and took hold of it, and the mother laughed, and some of the crowd laughed with her; and for the only time in eleven days Sìne found that she had to stop, and wait, before she could tie the next.

## VIII. Of the Cord on the Floor

The cord took eleven days. On the evening of the eleventh the last heir came through the door, a great-grandson of the king who had walked from the far north-west and arrived with his shoes in his hands; and Sìne tied his knot, and put her hands flat on the cord in her lap, and sat a while without moving.

Then she told Aodh Crom the count. She had not counted as she went. She had not needed to. The cord went through her fingers from the beginning, knot by knot, from Murchadh Mòr's dark blue to the tired man of the north-west, while the old keeper stood over her, and the count came to seven hundred and twelve.

That night the keepers had the cord laid out on the floor of the gathering-house. It ran from the hearth at the upper end all the way down the length of the floor to the door, and turned there, and came back up the other side to the hearth again, and still there was some left over, coiled at the hearthstone. Lamps were set along it. The heirs were let in.

They walked along it in their good cloaks, slowly, bending down with the lamps. Each of them was looking for his own knot, and when he found it he stopped, and knelt, and felt it with his fingers, as Murchadh had done on the first day; and then he stood up and looked at the knots on either side of it, and counted them.

Sìne watched from the door. She watched them all evening. She saw an old grandson of the king find his knot and kneel by it for a long time, and then get up and walk three knots down to where his brother's knot was, and kneel by that, and look back at his own, and frown. Eithne nic Ailein walked the whole length of the cord twice without stopping at her own knot at all, and Sìne saw it. She saw two cousins of the western shore stand on either side of the cord at the turn by the door and argue across it about a knot that lay between them. She saw Ìomhar Dearg stand over the rust-red knots of his line with his arms folded, and the four lines who had muttered at him standing at the far wall, watching him.

She saw Niall Òg find his own knot and sit down on the floor beside it and look at it for a long time, and then look up and catch her eye across the house, and nod.

She said to her daughters afterward that the heirs had not come to see their own knots. They had come to see everybody else's. She said that she had tied seven hundred and twelve people to a rope, and that every one of them had walked the length of it that night to see who was tied too near.

On the next day, the thirteenth of an Dàmhair, the keepers of the slab declared to the whole valley that the heirs of Ailean Mòr were counted, and that there were seven hundred and twelve of them; and the heirs agreed, because every one of them had watched every knot being tied, and none of them could say otherwise. It was the first thing they had agreed on since the Binding, and the last for a long while.
