That evening Aodh Crom came down to Sìne's house for the second time, and this time he came in and sat by the fire. He had brought her a basket of the keepers' coal, a season's handful and more, and he set it down by the hearth without a word. She kept it. It was the only thing she took for the cord, and she said afterward that she took it because it came after the work and asked nothing of her. The old man sat a while and watched her daughters coiling the spare flax. Then he asked her whether she thought the heirs would keep to what the cord said, when it came to the cutting.

"They'll keep to the knots," said Sìne. "It's what lies between the knots that they'll fight over."

Aodh Crom laughed, which she had not heard him do before, and said that she should have been a keeper of the slab, and she said that she had enough to keep.

That gathering is called *Cruinneachadh nan Oighrean*, the Gathering of the Heirs; and the cord Sìne tied at the door of it was kept in the gathering-house in a chest of its own, and was called *Sreang nan Oighrean*, the cord of the heirs, and was not cut until the night of the handful.

# Chapter Five: Of the Four Rules

*FE 1 – 2*

## I. Of the Grass That Did Not Come Back

Seven hundred and twelve knots had been counted, and not one thing settled by the counting. That was what Niall Òg came to understand in the days after the cord was carried out of the gathering-house and put by, and he was slower to understand it than most, because he had gone about the valley all that autumn in the good humour of a man who has just watched something enormous be done, and it took the first frost to teach him that the doing was only the naming of the trouble, not the end of it.

The camps did not break up. He had thought they would: that the heirs, having stood up and given their lines and had them tied, would scatter back to whatever hall or headland or hill-farm they called their own and wait to be sent for. A handful did. Most did not. Word went about the fires that the shares could not be cut until it was agreed how they were to be cut, and that this could not be agreed in a day, and the heirs, who had waited weeks for the tying of a cord, found that they could wait a good deal longer for the cutting of it, so long as they were near enough to have a voice in how it went. By the turn of the month there were more tents in the valley than there had been at the king's death, because every heir who could afford to had sent home for more household, more baggage, more argument.

The valley could not carry it. It had fed the king's own following for a season and the host of the ford for three days and the whole gathering for a fortnight of knotting, and each of those had left a mark on it that the next one found still raw. The grass along the river, which had been grazed to the earth by the second week of the gathering, did not come up green again that spring; it came up thin and grey and was grazed to the earth again before midsummer, and it did not come up at all the spring after that, or the spring after that. Sìne's daughters said afterward that it was three years before a beast could get a full belly on that ground, and that carriers coming down from the north for the first time after the Roinn asked what blight had struck the valley, not knowing that the blight had been seven hundred and twelve households and their horses camped on it through two winters running.

Niall walked the camps most days, because he had nothing else to do that anyone would let him do, and because he found that people would say things to him on a walk that they would not say sitting down. He was not one of the great lines. His mother had been a daughter of the king who died two thousand years before the ford, and his father, a grandson of Fionnghal's line, had died a hundred years back of a fever that a longer-lived man might have thrown off; so Niall stood in the cord as a small knot in a small line, owed twice over as he liked to say, and owed little enough by either half. It left him free to walk where the greater heirs could not, because nobody thought his good opinion worth buying and nobody feared his bad one. He carried word between fires that would not otherwise have spoken, and he came, before that year was out, to know the shape of every quarrel in the valley better than any of the men who were having it.

There were four shapes to it, when he had walked enough camps to see them clear. Four rules, and each one had a hundred heirs standing behind it, and every heir standing behind one thought the other three so plainly wrong that he could not understand how a grown man came to hold them.

## II. Of the Eldest and the Living

The first rule was Murchadh Mòr's, though he did not call it a rule; he called it the way it had always been done, in the households he knew, when a man died and left more than one child. The eldest took the whole and owed the others a living out of it. Murchadh was himself the eldest of all the king's living children, near three thousand years old and built like a doorway, and he put the case the way a man puts a case he has never had to argue before because everyone around him has always agreed with it: the eldest holds, because the eldest is closest to the blood and was longest at the king's side, and the rest are fed from the eldest's hand as they always were. He did not trouble to say what this would mean for himself. Every heir in the valley could count that it would mean Murchadh Mòr holding the whole of Ailean Mòr's kingdom and everyone else in it standing at his table for their supper, and this was, as Niall said to Eithne one evening, a reason Murchadh liked the rule a good deal better than most people did.

The second rule was harder to fix on one mouth, because half the lowland heirs held it and none of them had thought it out past the shape of their own complaint. It said that the living should hold, in the order of their nearness and no further back than that: sons and daughters first, if any lived, and their children after, but no weight given to a man's place in the birth order, only to whether he still drew breath. Eithne, who was herself the youngest living child of the king and stood to gain a good deal by it, argued it hardest and argued it well, because she had the wit to see that a rule of pure age would leave her with nothing at all, being the youngest, while a rule of nearness to the living blood put her on a level with Murchadh whatever the years between them. Niall did not think the less of her for arguing her own good; he had never met an heir in that valley who was arguing anything else, under whatever coat of principle he wore over it, and he thought Eithne wore hers more honestly than most, because she never once pretended the rule was fair to the dead.

It was over the dead that the third rule stood or fell, and it was the hardest fought of the four, because it was fought less between the living heirs than between the living and a silence. Ailean Mòr had been having children for four thousand years, and a great many of them had died before him, in wars and by accident and by the slow thinning that came even to the long-lived at the last, and their children and grandchildren stood in the valley in their hundreds, wearing black wool at the throat as Sìne had knotted it, and they said, through whichever of their number could speak loudest, that a line did not end because the man at its head had died before his father; that the dead's children stood in his place exactly as they would have stood in it had he lived one day longer than the king; and that any rule which forgot the dead was a rule made by people who found it convenient to forget them, which was true, and said so plainly that even the heirs who found it convenient did not much enjoy hearing it.

The fourth rule Niall heard first from a boy of perhaps four hundred years, a great-great-grandson of the king who could not have told you the name of his own great-grandfather, who said to him at a fire one night that the whole of the argument was foolish, because the fairest thing, the only thing that could not be quarrelled with afterward, was to throw lots for the shares and let the ancestors decide it as they decided everything else worth deciding. Niall asked him whose idea this was, and the boy said it was his own, and Niall believed him, because he heard the same idea independently from a dozen more of the youngest heirs before the winter was out, always from someone with the least claim and the least to lose by chance, and never once from anyone with an old man's memory of exactly how many grandchildren stood ahead of him.

"You want the lot," Niall said to one of them, "because you're young enough that anything is better than what the other three rules would give you."

The boy said that was so, and did not seem ashamed of it, and Niall found he liked him rather better for saying so than he liked most of the older heirs, who wanted exactly the same thing and dressed it up as justice.

## III. Of the Words Niall Carried

He did not mean to become a carrier of words between the two loudest voices in the valley, Eithne and Murchadh, and he told it afterward as though it had happened to him rather than by his own doing; but the truth, which he told less often, was that he had gone to Murchadh's fire of his own will in the second week of the sitting, to ask a question about grazing on his own account, and had found himself asked in turn what Eithne had said of the eldest's rule that morning, because word had come to Murchadh's fire garbled, and Murchadh wanted it straight. Niall told him straight. He had heard Eithne say it herself, at her own fire, not an hour before: that a man's eldest right to his father's cattle did not make him fit to hold nine hundred grandchildren's worth of a kingdom, and that the day the eldest rule was sworn, half the lines in the valley would begin quietly arming, because no one under the age of a thousand years would sit still under it. Murchadh heard this without moving his face, which Niall came to know was how the old man showed that a thing had gone home.

After that it became a habit. He went from Eithne's fire to Murchadh's and back several times a week, carrying nothing that either of them could not have sent by a steward, except that a steward would have softened it, and Niall did not. He found, to his own surprise, that both of them preferred it that way. Murchadh told him once, gruffly, over the head of the fire, that Niall was the only man in the valley he could be sure was repeating the words and not the meaning some go-between had decided to give them; and Eithne told him much the same thing in her own way, which was to say nothing and simply begin, when he arrived, "Tell him this," without wasting breath on why she trusted him to carry it straight.

He did not always enjoy it. There were nights he came away from Murchadh's fire with words in his mouth that he knew would put Eithne into a rage before he had finished the sentence, and he carried them anyway, because a message half-told was worse than one told whole, whatever it cost the teller. He watched the two of them, over that winter, come to understand each other's positions better than either understood any of the smaller lines, and hate each other's positions no less for the understanding; and he thought, though he did not say it to either of them, that this was very likely the nearest thing to peace that the eldest rule and the rule of the living were ever going to manage, two people who despised each other's case and had stopped mistaking the other for a fool.

The lines of the dead he did not carry for, not at first, because no single mouth spoke for them the way Murchadh spoke for the eldest or Eithne for the living; they spoke through whichever grandson had the readiest tongue that week, and the readiest tongue changed. But by midwinter one voice had risen above the rest among them, an old man with a stick who had felt the hollow knot at the door and said, "That's my mother," and who now stood at the gathering-house steps most mornings and told anyone who would listen that the dead's children were being asked to disappear twice, once by their fathers' early deaths and once by a rule that would not count them; and Niall began carrying his words too, to Murchadh and to Eithne both, because he saw that neither of the two great voices had troubled to hear the old man out in full, each being too busy answering the other.

## IV. Of Mairsile in the Cold

The first winter of the sitting was hard on the valley's ground, and harder on some of the people in it than on the ground.

Mairsile nic Ailein, the king's white-haired daughter who had begun the keening in the valley on the night the herd-boy's news came, was old even among the king's children, older than Murchadh, and the long years in her were nearly spent; and she had outlived a husband and two of her own children already before that autumn. She had sat through the knotting with her women about her, near the upper fires, and had said little in the councils of the four rules, being past the age of the kingdom mattering to her the way it mattered to the younger heirs. What she wanted, she told her women, was to go home before the snow; and she did not go home, because there was always one more day's argument that her line's steward thought she ought to hear, one more vote of the assembled dead that could not be taken without an elder of her age to lend it weight.

She died in the cold, in the second month of the new year, in a tent on the upper slope with her women about her and a brazier that had run low in the night because the wood had run short in the whole valley that winter, every hearth burning the same short ration as every other. Niall was not there. He heard of it in the morning from a woman of her household who came down to the lower fires white in the face, and he went up with her, because there seemed nothing else to do, and stood at the tent door while Mairsile's women wound her in her own cloak, and thought, not for the first time that winter, that the argument over who should hold the kingdom had already begun to cost the kingdom people who had never asked to be part of it.

She was carried down to the river two days after and laid in the ground there, near enough the ford that the carriers passing with their baskets could see the mound from the road; and for once in that whole long sitting there was no quarrel over where she should lie, because she had asked for the place herself before she died, plainly, to her women, and nobody thought it worth their trouble to dispute a dying woman's one wish when there were nine hundred living wishes still to be fought over. Niall stood at the graveside with Eithne on one side of him and, a little apart, Murchadh on the other, and neither of them spoke to the other across it, but neither of them left before the mound was closed, and Niall thought that this too, in its way, was a kind of agreement, the only one the valley had managed since the cord went on the floor.

He carried the word of her death to every fire in the valley himself, that day and the next, because he found he could not sit still with it; and at more than one fire he heard the same thing said, in different words, by people who had never met her: that the sitting had already killed one of the king's own children, and that whatever else the shares came to, they had better come to it before the next winter found another.

## V. Of the Share That Could Not Be Taken

Through all of it there was one line in the valley that argued for none of the four rules, because none of the four rules touched what it already held.

Ìomhar Dearg sat that winter much as he had sat through the knotting, apart from the loudest fires, with his own household about him and little enough said. He had held Dùn dhearg since before the cord was ever tied, taken it by the sword in the days after the ford, and he had made no claim on the four rules at all, because he did not need one; what he had, he had, and the argument of the valley was over what the rest of them were to have. This did not sit well with everyone. Four lines in particular, none of them close enough kin to Ìomhar to have any hope of the fort themselves, took to saying at their own fires, and then at other people's, that a kingdom parted by rule ought to be parted by rule entire, and that Dùn dhearg with its double bank and its burned halls and its living taken under one man's hand was as much a part of Ailean Mòr's kingdom as any acre still standing green, and ought to come into whatever settlement the rest came into rather than sitting outside it as a thing already decided.

Niall carried this to Murchadh, who said only that he did not see how it was to be done; and he carried it to Eithne, who said the same in fewer words; and when he pressed her on why, since she plainly agreed the complaint was just, she told him something he thought about for a long while after. "Ask any of the four how they mean to take it from him," she said. "Ask them who is to stand in that gap in the bank and tell Ìomhar's household that they answer to somebody else now. He didn't win it by a rule. He won it because he was there and the rest of us weren't, and a rule made after the fact can't put us there instead of him. You can make a hundred rules for dividing what nobody has taken yet. You can't make one that takes back what's already held."

He put this to the four lines himself, more than once, in something like her own words, and none of them had an answer for it beyond repeating the complaint louder, which told him, as much as anything did that winter, that the complaint and the remedy were two different things, and that a valley could go on being angry about a wrong for a very long time without ever finding a hand strong enough to put it right.

## VI. Of the Word Nobody Would Wear

There was one more thing that came up at every fire that winter, sooner or later, and it came up so often, and was refused so often, that by spring it had stopped being argued at all and had simply become understood: that whatever the shares came to, and whoever held the largest of them, no one of the nine was to be called what their father had been called. Niall heard it first from an old steward of Murchadh's line, half as a joke, that the great share of the north would want a rìgh over it the way the whole island had once had one, and heard Murchadh himself answer, not laughing, that he would sooner burn the share to the ground than sit in his father's seat and be called by his father's name for it, because he had seen what the name had cost the man who bore it and had no wish to invite his own kin to come and try to take it from him the same way.

It was Eithne who put the clause first in words that could be sworn to, at a fire late in the summer when the heirs of the nine strongest lines had begun, almost without anyone declaring it so, to meet apart from the rest: that none of the nine, whatever they held and however they came to hold it, should ever be called rìgh, or take the word for themselves, or suffer it to be given them by their own households; that the kingdom Ailean Mòr had made was ended with him, and what came after it was shares, held by heirs, and not a kingdom held by a king. Murchadh swore to it first, and swore it hardest, because he above all of them had spent a winter watching what the shape of a single crown could still do to men three thousand years old who ought to have known better. Ìomhar Dearg swore to it from his own fire, sending word rather than coming himself, which some of the others remarked on and none of them pressed. Every one of the nine swore it in the end, and Niall, standing near enough at more than one of the swearings to see the faces as well as hear the words, thought that a good half of them swore it the way a man swears off a thing he still wants, with the private thought that the word might yet come to one of their own children or grandchildren, once enough years had passed that nobody living could object; and he judged, rightly as it turned out, that this reservation would trouble nobody at all so long as the nine kept it out of their own mouths in their own lifetimes.

## VII. Of the Settlement

It was Aodh Crom, in the end, who put the four rules together, though it was not his place to put anything together, being no heir and holding no share; but he had sat through enough of the councils that summer, at the edge of the gathering-house with the flame's business finished for the day, that the heirs had come to ask his opinion the way men ask the opinion of someone who has nothing to gain by giving it.

He did not choose between the four rules. He told the assembled heads of the strongest lines, one evening in the last days of summer, that he did not think any one of the four could be sworn alone without half the valley taking up arms against it before the winter turned again, because each rule left out a claim that a great many people in that valley were not going to consent to seeing left out; and that the only settlement he could see holding was one that gave each rule enough to keep its people quiet, though none of them all it asked. Let the eldest lines hold the great shares, since the living heirs of most substance were, in the main, the eldest surviving of their branches in any case; let the shares run to nine, since nine lines could be found among the living with claim enough and following enough to hold a share and defend it; let a portion be set aside out of all nine together for the lines of the dead, so that no line vanished from the reckoning because its head had died a day too soon; and let the youngest, who wanted the lot, take some comfort in this much of it, that within each of the nine shares the parting among the living children and grandchildren should still be settled by drawing, where an equal claim could not otherwise be told apart.

It satisfied nobody entirely, and Niall came to think that this was very likely why it held. Murchadh had the great share of the north, which was the largest thing on the table and more than answered the eldest's rule so far as he was concerned; Eithne and her allies among the living heirs had shares of their own, proof that nearness of blood counted for something whatever a man's place in the birth order; the lines of the dead had their portion, grudging and smaller than they had asked for, but a portion, and a name for it, *Cuid nam Marbh*, so that it could never afterward be said the dead had been forgotten; and the youngest, muttering, had their throw of the lot within whatever share they fell under, which was not the throw across the whole kingdom that the boy at the fire had wanted, but was a throw, and kept a few hundred of the youngest and least-landed heirs from making trouble that autumn over having nothing at all.

Ìomhar Dearg's share was let stand where it stood, Dùn dhearg and the ground he had already taken, let stand beside the nine as a tenth that no rule had made, won by the sword and not by any of the four rules; the four lines who had argued against it argued once more, at the council itself, and were heard, and were not answered beyond Eithne's old words given back to them in Aodh Crom's mouth, that no rule made that day could put them where Ìomhar already stood; and they gave way in the end: nine of the strongest lines in the valley had already agreed among themselves, and there was no tenth strong enough to stand against the nine.

## VIII. Of the Agreement to Cut the Cord

They settled it, in the shape it would keep, in the last days before the turn of the year, at a council that ran two days and a night without the heads of the nine lines leaving the gathering-house floor; and Niall, who had carried words between them all that year and stood at more firesides than any other man in the valley, was let in to hear the end of it because Eithne asked for him by name, saying she wanted one honest ear in the room besides her own.

It was agreed, when it was agreed, without much ceremony. There was no swearing that night; the clause against the crown had already been sworn separately, at a dozen fires, over the summer, and needed no repeating. What was agreed was simpler and, to Niall's mind, colder than anything that had gone before it: that the cord Sìne had tied, seven hundred and twelve knots long, should be carried back into the gathering-house and laid on the floor again as it had been laid before, from the hearth to the door and back; and that on the night of the handful, when every hearth in the hills burned its measure together, as it always had, the heads of the nine lines should each take a knife to it in turn, and cut it into nine lengths where the shares fell, each length carrying the knots of the heirs who stood under that share; and that whatever oaths needed swearing over the cutting, the clause against the crown and the peace of the Hall's own ground among them, should be sworn that same night, once, in front of the whole valley, so that no line could say afterward it had not heard.

Murchadh Mòr agreed to it first, with the same still face he had shown all that winter. Eithne agreed after him, and looked once at Niall across the fire as she did, which he took, and told her afterward he had taken, for something between thanks and warning: thanks for a year's carrying, warning that the carrying was not finished, only changed. Word went out that night from line to line, fire to fire, down through the valley and up into the hills where the smaller households were camped, that the cord would be cut at the handful, and that every heir who meant to hold anything under the nine great shares had better be at Dùn ìseal to see it done.

Niall walked the camps a last time before the year turned, as he had walked them at the start, and found the valley much changed from the one he had walked with a light heart the autumn before: the grass gone from the riverbank, three winters before it would come green again though none of them yet knew that; the mound by the ford with Mairsile under it; Ìomhar's fires apart from the rest as they had always been; and at every hearth, instead of the seven hundred and twelve separate quarrels he had carried between all that year, one single date now, the night of the handful, that every line in the valley was waiting on together, for the first time since the cord went first upon the floor.

He came back down to the lower fires as the light went, and found Eithne's steward waiting for him with a message, which was, he said afterward, the last one he ever carried that winter, and the shortest: that she wanted him at her own fire that night, to hear how the cutting was to be done, so that when it came he would know, better than most of the valley, exactly what he was watching.

# Chapter Six: Of the Night of the Handful

*FE 2*

> *Aon oidhche, aon teine, aon scian.*
> One night, one fire, one knife.
>
> — said afterward of Oidhche an Dòrlaich at Dùn ìseal

## I. Of the Telling

*Niall Òg told this in his old age to whoever would sit and hear it, and by then he had told it so many times that the households of the salt shore could say the ending with him. He always began the same way.*

There is one night in the valley below Dùn ìseal, Niall Òg would say, that every hearth on the island still keeps some memory of, though not one hearth in a hundred could tell you why. It is kept without being understood, the way a child keeps a game its grandmother taught it and never asks what the game was for. On the night of the handful every household burns its whole season's measure at once, though the Small-Burning Law was not yet made and would not be made for six generations, and no household then owed the Hall a handful of anything. They did it because the heirs did it. The heirs did it because there was a night in the second year of the Holy Age when every fire in the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal burned at once, and by morning the kingdom of Ailean Mòr had nine lords and one that would not be sworn to any of them.

Niall was there. He was some nine hundred years old, a grandson of the king in one of the lesser lines, and he had spent the year since the ford carrying words between his aunt Eithne and his uncle Murchadh because he was the only one of the family either of them would let into a room with the other. He used to say that this made him, of all the king's grandchildren, the one who least wanted the cutting of the cord to come, because a peace was a thing he could carry messages about, and a division was a thing that was simply done, after which there would be nothing left for him to do at all. He was wrong about that, as it turned out, but on that night he did not know he was wrong, and he watched the whole of it the way a boy watches a house being pulled down that he has played in all his life.

The year between the agreement of the four rules and the cutting had been a long, watchful one. The grass of the valley, trodden by seven hundred and twelve heirs and their households and their stewards' households besides, had not come back green that spring, and the summer after it had been worse, so that a man riding down from the passes that autumn said the valley looked less like the floor of a kingdom than the yard of a fair that had gone on three years too long. The nine who would cut the cord spent that year each in his own tent or hall, sending stewards to argue small points that had been thought settled and were not, and Niall carried more words in those twelve months than he had carried in the nine centuries before them. He grew, he said, very tired of being trusted by everyone and believed by no one, which he came in time to think was most of what it meant to be neither eldest nor first.

## II. Of the Waiting Out the Year

The stewards of the nine lines spent that year haggling over things the four rules had left unsaid, and most of what they haggled over came down, in the end, to boundaries: whether a line drawn "from the ford to the hill" meant the near hill or the far one, whether a wood belonged with the pasture beside it or the stream beyond it, whether a fishing-weir built by a household now claimed by two lines paid its catch to one or split it. None of it could be settled before the cutting, because none of the nine would agree to a line on the ground before they had agreed to a line on the cord, and so the small quarrels piled up outside the gathering-house all that year like unswept snow, waiting for the one night that would let them all be argued at once, by daylight, with a boundary-stone instead of a steward's word.

Aodh Crom aged visibly in that year, more than a man of his hundred and eighty-odd years by rights should. He had carried the asking of the Binding and the counting of the knots and now the setting of this last night, and he told Sìne, when she asked him once at her own door whether he slept, that he did not think a man his age was owed sleep on top of everything else the valley wanted of him. The eight other keepers of the slab watched the hill and kept the flame and let the old man carry the heirs' business, because none of them wanted it and he had never once refused it.

By the time autumn came round again and the heirs began riding back down into the valley for the second time in two years, the grass under their feet had given up trying to grow back at all, and the gathering-house, which had stood through the knotting with its thatch still new, wore the black smudge of eleven days' smoke over every door. Niall rode down with his uncle's household, as he had the year before, and found the valley smaller than he remembered it, though nothing in it had shrunk; only the crowd in it had grown used to being crowded, the way a room grows smaller the longer a family sits in it.

## III. Of the Cord Laid Twice Round the Floor

They chose Oidhche an Dòrlaich for it, the night of the handful, because it was already the one night of the year on which no household in the hills held anything back. Whatever coal a family had put by against the winter it burned that single night, all together, so that the dark half of the year should begin with every hearth in the valley alight at once and none of them alone in the cold. It was an old custom and older than the king, and Aodh Crom said, when the heirs asked him to set the night, that it was fitting the kingdom should be cut on the one night when nobody kept anything back.

The keepers had the cord of the heirs brought down from its chest and laid along the floor of the gathering-house as it had been laid on the last night of the knotting, from the hearth to the door and back to the hearth again, with the length that was left over coiled at the hearthstone. Lamps stood along it the whole way, one every few paces, so that a man walking beside it in the smoke could see his own feet and not much else. There were more people in the house that night than there had been on any night of the eleven days of knotting: every heir who had given a line to Sìne nan Snaidhm was there, or had sent someone in his place, and the nine who would cut the cord stood each at the place along it where his own colour began, with a household's worth of kin crowded behind him against the wall.

The hearths outside were doing what the gathering-house's own hearth was doing, burning the whole valley's measure at once, and the smoke of it lay over the roof and came in under the eaves and hung along the beams until a man's eyes stung with it before the night was an hour old. Niall said afterward that he had never in his life, before or since, been in a house so full of smoke and lamplight and people that he could not see across it, and that the cord itself, when he first looked for it on the floor, seemed to swim.

Nine knives were laid out on a cloth by the hearth, plain knives, none of them marked, because no one wanted it remembered afterward which knife had been whose. Aodh Crom stood over them. He had grown old fast that year, faster than a man of his years should, and he leaned on a stick he had not needed at the Binding. He said only one thing before the cutting began, and Niall remembered it word for word because it was so short: that the cord had been laid once for the whole kingdom, and would now be laid nine times for nine lines of it, and that whoever cut wrong would have to live with his own hand and no other's to blame.

Each of the nine walked the cord first with a lamp, bent low, before he was let touch a knife. Murchadh Mòr went first because he was eldest, and the house went quiet enough to hear the cord's fibres creak under his hand as he ran it through his fingers, counting. Then Eithne went, and after her the rest in the order they had agreed among themselves that summer, an order none of the tellers give the same way twice, because none of the nine were there afterward to be asked and cared to be remembered as having gone last. Each of them walked the whole length twice: once toward the door, once back. By the time the last of the nine had walked it the lamps had burned low enough that servants came along the wall refilling them, and the night was not young any longer.

## IV. Of Murchadh's Cut

Murchadh Mòr was near two thousand nine hundred years old that night, the eldest living son of the king by more than seven hundred years over the next, and he had known for a summer exactly where along the cord he meant to cut. He did not walk it twice out of doubt. He walked it twice because the keepers had told the nine to walk it twice, and Murchadh did what he was told when he had already decided to do it.

Murchadh knelt at the place, took up his knife, and cut. It went through clean, one stroke, and the two ends of the cord lay apart on the floor with the lamp between them, and he stood up without looking at either end again. A murmur went along the wall, the first sound the house had made since the cutting began, because everyone there had been waiting to see whether the eldest of them would flinch at doing with a knife what he had spent a summer arguing for with his tongue, and he had not flinched at all.

"There," he said, to no one, and went to stand by the hearth with his length of the cord already gathered over his arm, and did not speak again that night, though he watched everything.

His length ran from the hearth almost to the turn by the door, the longest of the nine, for it held more knots than any other line: the great share of the north, from Baile Mòr mhòr to the high passes, with eleven sons of his own body already knotted into it and their children's children besides. He had asked for nothing more than the rule of the eldest gave him and had got exactly that, and Niall, watching him stand at the hearth with the whole length of the north over his arm, thought that this was the last time in his life he would see Murchadh want for nothing.

## V. Of Eithne and the Woman Who Would Take Both

Eithne nic Ailein was the youngest of the nine, not yet two thousand years old, and she had argued harder for the lowland plain than anyone had argued for anything else that summer, on the plain grounds that it was flat, it was rich, and it was hers by right of being loudest about it longest. She knelt at her place a long while before she cut, longer than Murchadh had, running her thumb back and forth over a single knot as if she were counting it more than once.

When she cut, her knife went through the knot itself.

The house went silent in a different way than it had for Murchadh, a silence with an edge on it. Aodh Crom, who had been standing by the hearth with his stick, came forward at once and looked at the cut end, and asked, in a voice that carried the length of the house because every other voice in it had stopped, whose knot that had been.

A woman came out from the wall with her hand over her mouth. She was a cousin of Niall's own generation, of the line of the salt shore, and her name was Ciorstaidh; Niall had known her since they were children together at the spring below Dùn ìseal, before either of them had learned to count the years in their blood, and he said afterward that he had never seen anyone go so white so fast in a room already full of firelight.

"That is mine," said Eithne, looking at the cut end in her own hand.

"That is mine," said the man who held the length beyond it, the head of the next share down the cord, and he was not smiling either.

Ciorstaidh stood between the two ends with the whole house looking at her, and for a moment she said nothing at all. Then she took her hand away from her mouth.

"I'll take both," she said.

Nobody had thought to ask her whether she wanted to be part of the argument at all, and it was the first time in the whole of Roinn na Rìoghachd that anyone had answered a question no one had put to her. Eithne looked at her for a long moment, and then laughed, short and without much warmth in it, and said that the girl had more sense than either of the two lords quarrelling over her knot, which was not a kind thing to say in front of both of them, and was also true. The man beside Eithne did not laugh. But neither of them wanted, on the first night of the Roinn, to be seen arguing over one knot in front of seven hundred witnesses, and so it was let stand: Ciorstaidh of the salt shore swore to both lines that night, the first of the double oaths, and carried both colours in the wool she kept afterward, and her children after her carried both, until the lands under each grew so far apart that no one family could ride between them in a season and the two oaths quietly went their own ways.

## VI. Of the Rest of the Nine

After Eithne the cutting went on, and it did not go cleanly again. Some of the nine had chosen their places with as much care as Murchadh, and their knives went through the cord and nothing else; some had not, and where the cord ran thick with the knots of the portion of the dead, thick enough that no eye could be sure which knot lay exactly under a knife in that light and that smoke, more than one blade went through wool that had a name tied into it. By the time the ninth of them had cut, eleven knots along the whole length of the cord had been cut through and not between, and ten households besides Ciorstaidh's found themselves sworn that night to two lords at once, though none of the others made so short and plain an answer to it as she had. Some quarrelled for a season over which oath should stand and which should lapse; most simply paid both, the way a man pays two tolls on a road he cannot avoid, and grumbled about it at both ends.

Fionnghal nic Ailein cut her length clean, and it ran west to Ros dhomhain and its harbour, and she was some twenty-five hundred years old that night and had wanted the sea more than she had wanted the plain or the hills, and got it. Artair mac Ailein took the salt shore, with its seat at the western Baile ghorm, a little more than twenty-three hundred years old and the quietest of the nine, who had said less in the whole summer of argument than any of his brothers and sisters and had ended, all the same, with a coast the length of two days' sail. Cormac mac Ailein cut through to the eastern share, seated at Caol shean, a little over two thousand years old, and did not yet know, and could not have known, that a seam of silver lay under a hill in his own share that no one then living had found.

The last four cuts went quicker, because the smoke was thick by then and the lamps were burning down and everyone in the house wanted the night over. Ùna nic Ailein took the north-west, with her seat at Muileann àrsaidh; Coll mac Ailein took the hills east of the Red Hill, along the Abhainn fhionn, with his seat at Ceann àrsaidh; Gormlaith nic Ailein took the south-east, seated at Tobar dhearg; and Tadhg mac Ailein took the Abhainn ìseal and the bay the hawks fished, with his seat at Cnoc bheag. The tellers who came after did not agree on the order in which these four cut, and Niall himself, asked about it in his old age, said only that he had been watching Ciorstaidh at the time and could not swear to it either, which the tellers took as leave to put the four in whatever order suited the telling.

When the ninth cut was made the cord of the heirs no longer ran the length of the floor. It lay in nine pieces, each gathered over the arm of the lord who had cut it, with the loose ends of the eleven double knots hanging free where two lords held the same knot between them; and the Red Share of Ìomhar Dearg, which no knife had cut that night because it had never been tied into the cord with any colour of its own, stood as it had stood since the summer after the ford, needing no cutting because it had already been taken.

## VII. Of the Red Hill Sworn to Nobody

There was one length of the old kingdom that no knife touched that night, because no line of the nine could say it was theirs to cut.

The Red Hill was not the Red Share. The Red Share was Dùn dhearg and the ground about it, which Ìomhar Dearg had taken with his own hand at the ford and no one had found a way to take back. Far to the west, above the lake shore, lay the Red Hill, another place entirely, where a settlement had stood since before the king's grandfather's time, and its holders had sworn to Ailean Mòr and to no one else in all the years of his reign; not to Dùn ìseal, not to any lord of a share, only to the king himself, man to man, in a way that no other holding on the island had sworn.

On the night of the handful the Red Hill's holder stood up in the smoke and the lamplight, when the nine had finished their cutting and the house had begun to think itself done, and said what everyone in the house had known he would have to say sooner or later: that his oath had been to Ailean Mòr, and Ailean Mòr was in the ground beside his stone, and there was no man now living he had ever sworn to. He did not ask to be released. He said only that he was already free, and that the Red Hill was, as it stood that night, sworn to nobody at all.

It was the quietest claim made in the whole gathering, and it caused the loudest argument. Before he had well finished speaking three of the nine had crossed the floor toward him at once, Murchadh from the hearth end and two others from nearer the door, each saying that a holding sworn to nobody could not simply remain so, and each meaning, though none of them said it so plainly that first night, that it ought to be sworn to him. The Red Hill's holder said nothing further. He had said his piece, and the three lords could argue over an empty answer as long as they liked; it changed nothing that he had said. They argued a good while, there on the floor among the cut ends of the cord, with the fires burning low outside and the smoke thinning at last through the roof, and came to no settlement that night or for a long while after. The Red Hill stayed as its holder had left it, claimed by three and kept by none, a small stubborn place that grew no faster than a place claimed by three lords and served by not one of them ever does.

Aodh Crom, who had watched the argument from the hearth without joining it, said one more thing before the house began to empty. He reminded the nine, in the same short way he had reminded them of everything else that night, that the ground on which they stood, the whole hill of the slab and the gathering-house and the valley below it as far as the boundary the keepers themselves had walked, was in no share and never would be; that this had been sworn at the Binding and was not to be argued afresh on a night when everything else in the kingdom was being cut apart. No one answered him. No one, that night, had the appetite left to argue with the one thing in the valley that nobody wanted for himself.

## VIII. Of the Grey Light and the Lengths of Cord

Dawn found the gathering-house half empty and the fires outside burned to grey ash, the whole valley's measure spent in one night as it was spent every year at the turning, though this year it had lit a division that would run for centuries where every other year it had only lit the dark. The nine lords went out through the door one after another, each with his length of the cord folded or coiled over his arm, and their people went with them, carrying baskets and rolled hides and children still asleep against a shoulder, so that the road out of the valley by full light looked less like the end of a gathering than the start of nine journeys that all happened to begin at the same door.

Niall stood by the door a long while and watched them go. He had no length of cord of his own to carry; his knot hung in the portion of the dead, after his mother's hollow knot, for Niall held no share and would hold none, being neither eldest nor first among the living children of the eldest line, only "owed twice," as he put it himself, by two different accountings that had never yet paid him anything. He watched Ciorstaidh go last of all, with two colours of wool wound together over her wrist where the others each carried one, and she caught his eye at the door the way she had caught it across the house the night before, and neither of them said anything, because there was nothing yet to say that the whole valley had not already seen.

He told it afterward, in his old age, always ending the same way: that he had stood at that door and thought the division was finished, the cord cut, the kingdom parted, the worst of the year's work done, and that he had been a young fool of nine hundred to think so, because a cord, once cut, does not stay cut in the same nine pieces forever, any more than a family, once parted, stays parted along the lines its parting first drew. The Red Hill alone, he would say, sworn to nobody on that grey morning, outlived every one of the nine who had argued over it, and was still sworn to nobody when he himself was an old man; and of all the things cut and given and sworn on the night of the handful, it was the one piece of the old kingdom that belonged, in the end, to no one at all.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Stones and the First Blood

*FE 2 – 4*

> *Mharbh mi mìle bliadhna.*
> I have killed a thousand years.
>
> — said by Ruairidh Glas of the line of Ìomhar, kneeling in the mud at Dùn thais

## I. Of the Stone on Each Bank

Ruairidh Glas was a grandson of Ìomhar Dearg, some three hundred years old that autumn, and he had never in his life killed a man.

He had not been at the ford the autumn his grandfather took Dùn dhearg; he had been in the western grazings with the Red Share's cattle, and what he knew of that morning he knew from other men's mouths. Since then he had grown up in the granaries and the cattle-yards of the Red Share, learning what a grandson of the man who held it by the sword was supposed to know, which was mostly where the boundary of a thing ran and how to hold it, and he had come to think of himself, without ever quite saying so, as a man who held ground rather than a man who fought for it. He was wrong about that, though he did not yet know it, any more than Niall Òg on the night of the handful had known he was wrong to think the cutting of the cord was the end of the trouble rather than its beginning.

The cord was cut, and had been cut for a year by the time the boundary stones went up. It had taken that long for the nine lines to agree even roughly where their shares began and ended on the ground, because a line drawn on a cord with a knot is one thing and a line drawn across a hillside with cattle on it is another, and the two did not always answer to each other as neatly as the heirs at the gathering-house had supposed they would. Through the winter after the handful the stewards of the nine lines rode the boundaries with the reciters who had carried the tale of the cutting in their heads, arguing over fords and ridgelines and the exact course of streams that moved their own banks between one flood and the next, and where they could agree a mason cut a stone with the sign of the share that looked into it and set it up on the line.

They called them *clachan-crìche*, the boundary stones, and there came to be a great many of them before the winter was out, more than the stewards themselves could always account for, because a lord's man who did not like where a stone stood would sometimes move it in the night, a hand's breadth or a field's width, and set it again facing the same way as before, so that in the morning it looked as though it had always stood there. The keepers of the slab, who had no share and wanted none, said nothing about this, because it was no business of the Hall's what the heirs did with their own boundaries, so long as none of it came near the ground under the mountain. Aodh Crom, when a steward once asked him to witness where a stone had truly stood the week before, said only that he had not been watching, and that he did not think any man alive had, which was as near as the old keeper ever came to naming what everyone already knew.

Dùn thais stood on its hill north of Dùn dhearg, the first fort the island's people had ever banked away from the mountain and the Red Hill both, in years so far back that the reciters could put no king's name to the raising of it. It sat close by the line the cord had drawn between the great share of the north, which was Murchadh Mòr's, and the Red Share of Ìomhar Dearg, and it sat close enough that nobody could say with any confidence on which side of the line it truly fell. The stewards who rode that stretch that winter argued it for the better part of a month and came away no nearer agreement than when they had started, and in the end, because neither side would give way and neither side would let the fort stand for the other, the masons of both lines did the one thing that let each of them go home believing he had lost nothing: they set a stone on the north bank of the burn below the hill, cut with the sign of Murchadh's share, and another on the south bank, cut with the sign of the Red Share, and left the fort, and the slope above it, lying between the two.

Ruairidh had ridden that ground twice that winter with his grandfather's steward, an old man named Lachlann Glas who had held the same office under Ìomhar since before the ford and had grown grey in it, and both times Lachlann had stood a long while looking at the two stones and said nothing worth remembering. The third time Ruairidh rode it, in the wet spring of the third year of the Holy Age, he rode it alone, with twenty men of the Red Share behind him and the cattle of the northern slope in front, because his grandfather had said, over supper the week before, in the flat voice he used for things he did not expect to be argued with, that the grazing above Dùn thais was theirs and had always been theirs, whatever a stone on the wrong bank of a burn might say, and that it was time somebody drove the beasts down off it before another season's grass went to a share that had never paid for it.

## II. Of the Rain at Dùn thais

It rained the whole of that day, the low, steady rain of early summer that does not so much fall as hang in the air and soak a man through by evening whether he has stood still or ridden hard, and by the time Ruairidh came up under the hill of Dùn thais the ground on the northern slope had gone to mud past the fetlock, and the cattle he had come to move were bawling and slipping and turning back on themselves faster than his twenty men could turn them again.

Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh was on the bank above with twenty men of his own, and Ruairidh did not at first know why. He had ridden that slope twice before without meeting a soul of the northern share on it, and it did not occur to him, coming up through the rain with his mind on the cattle, that word of his grandfather's supper-table decision could have crossed the boundary faster than he had. It had. Somebody in Ruairidh's own household, or in Lachlann's, had said something to somebody who ought not to have heard it, the way such things always went in a country that had nine great households and every one of them full of cousins married into every other, and Aonghas Bàn, a grandson of Murchadh Mòr some four hundred years old, had come up with his own herdsmen the night before to hold the ground his own grandfather had said was theirs.

He stood above the beasts with a herding-stick in his hand, not a spear, because he had come to move cattle, not to fight for them, and Ruairidh saw him first as a shape on the bank in the rain, grey against grey, and did not know for a moment whose man he was. Then Aonghas Bàn called down, not unkindly, that the grass under Ruairidh's cattle belonged to the north, and that he would be glad to help drive them back across the burn if Ruairidh's men were finding the going hard in the wet.

It might have ended there. Ruairidh said afterward, many times, to anyone who asked him and to a good many who did not, that it might have ended exactly there, with two grandsons of two brothers standing in the rain arguing amiably enough over a hillside neither of them had ever slept on, and going home each to tell his own household that the other side had been reasonable, for northerners, or for the Red Share, whichever way the telling ran. It did not end there, and the reason it did not, as near as Ruairidh could ever afterward make out, had less to do with the grass than with the twenty men behind each of them, none of whom had ridden up that hill expecting to be reasonable, all of whom had grown, in the year and a half since the cutting of the cord, thoroughly used to hearing that the other lines were thieves and liars and worse, and none of whom, when the shouting started somewhere down among the cattle, over whose beast had trodden whose man's foot, waited to hear whether their own lord meant to answer it with words.

Ruairidh's spear was up before he had decided to raise it. He said that afterward too, more than once, in the years he had left to say it in: that his hand had done it before the rest of him had caught up, the way a man's hand closes on a hot stone before his mind has finished telling him it is hot. He did not remember aiming. What stayed with him was the shape on the bank turning toward the shouting below, the herding-stick still in his hand and not a weapon raised anywhere near him, and the spear going, and then, after it had gone, the knowledge that there was nothing in the world he wanted less than to have thrown it.

Aonghas Bàn went down into the mud without a sound that carried over the rain and the cattle and the shouting, and for a moment neither side seemed to understand what had happened, so that the noise of the quarrel went on a little while over his body before it died away into something worse than quiet, a kind of ragged stillness broken by the bawling of beasts that did not know or care what the men around them had just done.

Ruairidh came down off his own horse and knelt by him in the mud. Aonghas Bàn had the face of a man of thirty, though he was four hundred years old and had, by the long years of his own line, perhaps a thousand more before him that he would never now come to; and Ruairidh, kneeling there with the rain running down both their faces, one living and one not, said the same six words over and over to the men who came to lift the body, because it was the only true thing he could find in himself to say and no other words would come in its place.

"I have killed a thousand years," he said. "I have killed a thousand years."

## III. Of Eachann Ruadh's Oath

They carried Aonghas Bàn down off the hill in a cloak between two spear-shafts, the rain not yet finished with them, and word went ahead of the party faster than the men carrying him could travel, the way it always does when a man dies who was not expected to, so that by the time they came within sight of his own hall the household was already out at the gate, and his brother Eachann Ruadh was already standing at the front of it, having heard, and not yet having been told, and already knowing from the shape of the party coming down the road what he was about to be told.

Eachann Ruadh was a year or two the younger of the two brothers, red-haired where Aonghas had been fair, and he had been, until that afternoon, the quieter of the pair by a wide margin, the one who let Aonghas do the talking at councils and the deciding at boundaries and was glad enough to let him, having, as he said of himself more than once, no great appetite for either. He stood at the gate while the party came up, and he did not go to meet it, and he did not ask the question everyone standing near him could see forming on his face, because by the time the two spear-shafts were near enough for him to see what lay between them, there was no longer any question left to ask.

He knelt by his brother's body in the yard of their own hall, in front of the whole household and in front of Ruairidh's men, who had carried it down themselves and would not have trusted the carrying to anyone else, and he put his hand flat on the dead man's chest, over the wound the spear had made, and swore an oath there that the reciters of both lines kept afterward, word for word, though they never agreed between them on quite what it meant to keep an oath of that kind. The blood on the grass at Dùn thais, he swore, would be answered, blood for blood, by his own hand or his sons' or theirs after them, for as long as there was a man of Murchadh's line living to remember whose spear had thrown it; and he did not name Ruairidh Glas in the oath, though everyone standing in that yard understood well enough whom it was aimed at, because to name a man in a blood-oath was, by the old custom of the households, to close the door on any settling of it that did not end in a second death, and Eachann Ruadh, red-haired and quiet and not yet altogether sure, in that first grey hour, what kind of man his brother's dying had made of him, left the door open that far and no further.

Ruairidh did not go back to Dùn thais. He rode home to his grandfather's hall with his twenty men in a silence none of them broke the whole way, and he told Ìomhar Dearg what had happened in as few words as Eachann Ruadh had used to swear his oath, and his grandfather, who had taken a fort by the sword and burned the halls inside its double bank and thought little enough of a single death on a wet hillside, told him only that he had done what a man does when his own are threatened and that he was not to trouble himself with an oath sworn by a boy over his brother's body. Ruairidh did not answer that either way. He was three hundred years old and had, by his own line's long blood, some centuries yet before him in which to find out what it meant to have killed a man with a thousand more coming to him than Ruairidh himself was ever likely to see, and he spent a good many of the years he did have turning the six words he had said in the mud over in his mind, and found, each time he turned them, that they had not worn any smoother.

With that death began *Aimhreit nan Oighrean*, the strife of the heirs. It was a feud first between the line of Murchadh and the line of Ìomhar only, a matter of raided byres and burned haystacks and the odd broken head at a boundary market, the kind of quarrel two great households might, in another age, have let cool over a generation or two. It did not cool. As the years went by and the lines married into each other, as they had married for a hundred years before the Roinn and went on marrying after it because there was no one else on the island of a rank fit to marry, the quarrel married too, carried into new households on both sides by every wedding that was meant to end it, until there was scarcely a line of the nine great shares that did not, sooner or later, find some grievance of its own tangled into the old one from Dùn thais, and the strife that had begun with one spear on one wet hillside went on, by fits and lulls and fresh grievances, for the better part of five hundred and fifty years. Every man who had stood on that slope in the rain was dead and past caring who had thrown first before it burned itself out.

## IV. Of the Shares of Shares

The stewards who had ridden the boundaries that winter had done the easy half of the work, and knew it. Nine great shares, agreed on a cord and marked, more or less, with stone, were the whole of what the Roinn had settled; but under each of the nine lay the households that had knotted their own claims into it, some of them the direct line of an heir's own children, some of them cousins six times removed who had stood up at the gathering-house because a great-uncle's blood gave them a right to stand, and none of them, once the great sharing was done, willing to be governed as one undivided thing by a single lord when the cord had already recorded them as separate strands.

So the shares were parted again, and parted a second time under that, in the two years after the stones went up at Dùn thais, until what had been nine great shares on the cord had become countries under each of the nine, and provinces under the countries, and counties under the provinces, and under the counties holdings smaller than any of these, some no bigger than a single steading and its grazing, sworn by the household that held it to whichever county's steward stood nearest and could be bothered to ride out and take the oath. It was not done tidily, and it was not done once. A holding whose old boundary had run along a stream that changed its course in a wet winter was claimed the following spring by two counties at once, each steward certain the stream had always run where it now ran, and more than one such holding, rather than let the matter be settled by force, simply swore to both and paid both, and hoped the two counties would forget to compare their tallies, which for some years they generally did.

The mill on the Abhainn dhomhain, a little way below where three counties met at a bend in the river, came to be held by three lords at once in exactly this fashion, none of whom had ever laid a stone of it or ground a single sack of grain in it, and all three of whom claimed, with equal confidence and no writing at all to settle the matter, that the eels taken from the millpond in the autumn run were theirs by right of the ground the pond stood on. The miller, an old man who had built the wheel himself before the Roinn was so much as thought of and cared nothing for whose ground it stood on so long as the water kept turning it, took to paying each of the three lords a third of the eel-catch every autumn without being asked, on the plain reasoning that a third paid three times over cost him less in the end than a whole season's catch seized by whichever lord's steward arrived first and angriest, and the three lords, who might otherwise have come to blows over it the way Ruairidh and Aonghas Bàn had come to blows over a hillside, found that a miller who paid all three punctually and complained to none of them was a peace easier to keep than a war worth fighting, and let the matter stand at that for longer than any of them lived to see changed.

It went on so, boundary by boundary, holding by holding, all through the two summers after the stones went up at Dùn thais, and the boundary stones themselves went on being set up and moved in the night and set up again, until it was said, by carriers who came to know that stretch of country better than any lord's steward ever did, that a man could walk from the Red Share to the great share of the north in a single day and cross nine stones that all claimed to mark the same line.

## V. Of the Count That Gave Up

The knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal, who had counted the seven hundred and twelve knots of the Roinn on Sìne's own cord and never once lost the tale of it, tried in those same two years to keep some count of what the shares had become underneath, because it seemed to them, as it seemed to Aodh Crom and the other keepers of the slab, a foolish thing for a kingdom to be cut so fine that no one living could say how many pieces it had been cut into.

They began well enough. Nine great shares, no one disputed; and by careful asking, county steward by county steward, riding the boundaries themselves with cords of their own to notch a knot for every claim they were shown, Sìne's daughters and the women who had learned the craft from them came, in the second summer, to a count of forty-four countries under the nine, which held for a season and was believed, and then had to be unmade and made again when two of the forty-four turned out, on a closer asking, to have quietly divided themselves into three apiece without troubling to send word to Dùn ìseal that they had done so. Under the countries they counted a hundred and thirty-one provinces, and were reasonably confident of that number for the better part of a year, though even as they counted it two provinces of the eastern share fell to quarrelling over a fishing-weir and split into three between them before the ink of the notches, had there been ink, could have dried.

Below the provinces lay the counties, and there the knot-keepers gave up.

It was not laziness, and none of the tellers who carried the story afterward ever said it was. There was, in those years, no writing on the whole of the island, no mark on hide or stone that could hold a name still while a man's memory went on to the next thing; the rolls of the kingdom lived nowhere but in the knotted cords and the notched sticks and the heads of the women who kept them, and a head, however well trained to the craft, could hold only so many counties before the eight hundredth or the nine hundredth began to crowd the first out. Anna nan Snaidhm, Sìne's eldest daughter, who had ridden more of those boundaries herself than any woman then living, told Aodh Crom plainly, the autumn the count of counties passed nine hundred and showed no sign of stopping, that she could keep the nine great shares in her head until she died and her daughter's daughter could keep them after her, but that the counties changed their own borders faster than any cord could be tied to hold them, and that a knot-keeper who tried to count them all would spend her whole life chasing a number that was never the same number twice.

Aodh Crom, when she told him this, said only that a kingdom too fine-cut to be counted was a kingdom that would have to be governed, in the end, by something other than counting, and that he did not envy whoever was given that task, because it had not yet been given to anyone, and would not be for a long while after his own death. He did not say what he thought that something might be. He was an old man by then, older than his years by rights should have made him, and he had carried the asking of the Binding and the counting of the first cord and now the setting of the stones, and he told Sìne once more, at her own door, much as he had told her once before, that he did not think a man his age was owed rest on top of everything else the valley wanted of him.

## VI. Of the Ground No Feud Might Follow

In the second summer after the stones went up, a household of the Red Share that had suffered a raid from across the boundary at Dùn thais, a matter of burned hay and two calves driven off in the night, brought its steward to the Hall's own ground under the central mountain to lay the complaint before the keepers, not because the keepers had any authority over a boundary quarrel between two lines of the king's blood, but because there was nowhere else on the whole of the island that both sides of the quarrel could be brought to stand together without one side or the other coming armed.

The steward of the northern line came too, when word reached him, and for a moment it seemed to the keepers watching from the door of their hut that the quarrel meant to follow the two men up the hill and finish on the very ground where the Binding had been sworn. Aodh Crom, old and slow on his stick by then but not too slow to see what was coming, came out and stood between the two stewards before either had raised a hand, and said what he had said once before on the night of the handful, in much the same short way: that the ground under the mountain, from the slab to the boundary the keepers themselves had walked at the Binding, was in no share and never would be, sworn so before any cord was cut, and that no man's spear, thrown or carried, was to come onto it in anger, whatever quarrel had brought him there.

It was not a new law. It was the same word Aodh Crom had spoken over the flame three summers before, said again because a new kind of trouble had come along to test whether the old word still held, and it held. The two stewards laid their complaint before the keepers instead of before each other's spears, and went away no more satisfied than men in a boundary quarrel generally go away, but they went away on their own feet, and the Hall's ground kept, that summer, the one thing it had always claimed: that whatever a man had done, or had had done to him, on the wrong side of whichever stone claimed to be the true one, he could stand under the mountain and not be answered for it there.

The heirs went home from the valley in the last of that summer, most of them for the first time in nearly two years without a boundary still open to argue, though a good many boundaries would open again before the strife of the heirs was done, and Ruairidh Glas went home to the Red Share with them, older than his three hundred years by more than the calendar could account for, and never, in all the centuries that were left to him, rode the ground above Dùn thais again. Carriers who came that way in the seasons after learned to walk the road between the two stones without troubling to read what was cut on either face, the way a man learns to step over a root in a path he has walked often enough not to need to look at it, and if any of them ever wondered, crossing the burn at the fort's foot, whose grass they were walking on that day, none of the tellers who carried their sayings afterward thought it worth setting down which of them asked, or what answer, if any, they were given.

# Part Two: The Flame without a Hand

# Chapter Eight: Of Beathag Bhàn

*FE 4–15*


## I. Of the Rush on the Slope

The mud was cold before it was anything else. Beathag Bhàn stood at the back of the crowd on the slope below the slab, and the wet of the path had climbed past her ankles and found her shins, and she thought, before she thought of anything grander, that she should have worn the other shoes. It was the twenty-eighth day of an t-Ògmhios, the fourth year since the fall of the old king, and half the valley had come up the hill to watch nine old men and women decide who would hold a fire that no one else was allowed to touch.

She had come for the barley, if she was honest with herself after, not for the choosing. Her mother's household sent her up with two others to trade a basket of it for salt, and the trading had not gone well, and she had stayed to watch because there was nothing better to do on the walk home. The keepers of the slab sat on their stones in a half-ring below the shoulder of the mountain, old people in undyed wool, and behind them stood the households who had sworn the Binding in the first weeks after the fall, smelling of wet fleece and peat-smoke and the black dust that does not wash out of a hill-woman's hands even after she has stopped mining. Further up the slope, apart from the rest and from each other both, stood the heirs who had sworn it first: men and women in good cloaks who did not look at the crowd, and did not much look at each other either.

A wind came down off the high passes and worried at every cloak on the hill, hers included, and she pulled it tighter and thought about her wet feet and did not hear her own name the first time it was said.

The second time she heard it because the woman beside her turned and stared, and then the man on the other side, and then the whole crowd around her seemed to draw its breath in together and step back, the way a field of standing barley parts when something runs low and fast through it. She had seen a hare do that once, seen the grain lean away on either side of a path the hare made and had not asked to make, closing again behind it as though nothing had passed. She understood, standing in the gap the crowd had opened for her, that she was the hare.

The walk down the lane the crowd had made left no mark on her memory at all. What she kept was the arriving: the bottom of it, in front of the nine, with mud on her shins and salt still owed to her mother's household, and the eldest of the keepers holding out a rush already lit, cupped in both his hands the way a man holds water he is afraid to spill.

His name was Aodh Crom, and she had seen him before at a distance, at the swearing that bound the flame to no one's blood, though she had not known his face up close until that morning: an old man bent sideways from some hurt long healed crooked, with eyes gone the pale grey of woodsmoke.

"Hold it for Brìde," he said, in a voice pitched to carry to the heirs on the slope above as much as to her. "And answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein."

She took the rush. It stank of tallow and the little flame bent sideways in the wind, away from her and toward the mountain, as though it too would rather be somewhere else. She found she had nothing to say. The silence went on long enough that she heard, behind her, one of the heirs shift his weight and someone's dog bark twice down in the valley, and still she said nothing, because nothing she could think to say seemed large enough for the size of what had just been put in her hands, and in the end she only stood there holding the flame steady against the wind with her whole body turned to block it, the way she would have sheltered a lamp carried across a dark yard.

The keepers counted that silence in her favour. She learned this only afterward, from one of them, an old woman named Beitris who had sat nearest the fire and had watched her rather than the flame. "A mouth that has nothing ready is a mouth that has not been planning," Beitris told her, months later, when the two of them knew each other well enough for the old woman to say such things plainly. "We had had enough, that spring, of mouths with something ready."

Of what Beathag Bhàn had been before that morning, little enough was thought worth keeping even by those who had known her. She was of no heir's line: her mother's household held no share and traced its blood to none of the seven hundred and twelve who had stood up to claim the old king's leavings, and no lord in the valley, however the shares fell out in the months after, could call her his by right of birth. That was the whole of why she had been chosen, and the keepers, whenever asked, gave no other reason and seemed to feel that none was wanting. She was six-and-twenty that summer, by her mother's counting of the winters, which made her younger than most of the keepers' own grandchildren and younger by some centuries than the least of the heirs standing above her on the slope, several of whom had outlived kingdoms she had never heard named.

The heirs did not come down from their place on the hill to speak to her. She stood at the bottom of the slope a long while after the keepers had risen and gone, still holding the rush, until someone from the households below came up and told her, not unkindly, that a fire held that long in the wind would want feeding soon, and showed her the way down to where they had made her a bed of dry heather in a turf hut at the mountain's foot, the nearest shelter anyone had thought to build before the choosing was done. She carried the flame in with her, set it on a flat stone in the hut's one room, and sat up with it through the first night telling herself, without much success, that she would think of the right words in the morning. The right words never came, that morning or any other. In time she came to believe that the keepers had been right, and that no words would have served her better than the silence had.

## II. Of the Slab and the Nine Households

The keepers of the slab were an old order and their own, older than the fall of the king and older, by their own telling, than the coming of Ailean's people to the mountain at all, and they kept a reverence that ran alongside the new Binding rather than under it: the ancestors, the sìth of the hollow hills, the vein itself, and the weather that ruled when a gallery might safely be opened. They had no wish to keep the flame themselves, and said so plainly to anyone who asked why they had chosen a girl of no line to do it rather than one of their own: a thing given to no one's blood, Aodh Crom said, could not afterward be claimed back into any blood, theirs included.

They taught her what they judged she needed and no more. In the first weeks it was the shape of the mountain from outside: which slope held snow longest and which shed it, where the galleries ran under which fields, which of the cairns above Cnoc ghlas the watchers climbed to read the cloud on the high passes before a gallery was let open for the season, for a coal cut when the weather above was wrong could bring the roof down on the cutters, and the watchers had died more than once proving it.
