Beitris took her up to the nearest cairn herself, on a morning cold enough to whiten their breath, and taught her to tell a cloud that meant rain from a cloud that meant only wind, a distinction Beathag never afterward managed with the old woman's certainty, though she learned to fake it well enough that no one below the cairn could tell the difference.

Of the galleries themselves she was told less, and told it slowly, a little at a time, as though the keepers were feeling out how much a stranger's mind could safely hold before it began to want too much. She went down once, in her second month, on Aodh Crom's arm, into a low black gallery lit by nothing but the lamp he carried, and heard the coal answer his pick with a sound she never found the word for afterward, a note somewhere between a knock and a sigh. He did not let her cut it herself. "The hand that holds the flame does not also cut the vein," he told her on the climb back up into daylight, sounding, for the only time she ever heard him, almost apologetic. "That was decided before either of us was born, and it will not be undecided for us."

He named the galleries for her one by one as they went, in a low even voice pitched for the dark rather than for teaching, as though he had said the names so many times to himself that saying them to another person cost him nothing extra: the first gallery, the low gallery, the gallery under the stone that fell, the gallery of the cold spring. She asked him once why none of them bore a person's name, as she had heard was the custom in the eastern hills, and he was a long while answering, long enough that she thought he had not heard the question over the drip of water somewhere ahead of them in the dark. "A gallery outlives the man who cut it," he said at last. "Name it for him and you've promised the mountain will remember a debt it never agreed to. Better it owes nothing to anybody, the same as the flame." She did not fully understand him that day. She came, over the years that followed, to think it the truest thing he ever told her, and to repeat it, in her own turn, to keepers who asked her the same question in the same dark.

That first winter taught her, too, what it was to be looked at rather than to look. Word of her went down the valley faster than she herself ever travelled, so that she came, in households she had never visited and among people she had never met, to be a figure fixed and finished in other people's mouths before she had finished becoming anything in her own eyes: the girl of no blood who had said nothing at the choosing, who fed the flame Brìde's fire and answered to Crom for the coal, who was already, by the second winter, being credited with a wisdom she did not feel she owned and a coldness she did not feel she deserved. She minded it less as the years went on, since a face seen only from a distance will always be simplified into whatever the distance requires, and she came to understand that the valley's Beathag Bhàn and her own were never going to be quite the same woman, and stopped trying to correct the gap between them.

Nine households stood about the mountain's foot, one for each of the old slab's districts, and it was settled among the keepers, in a summer of arguing she was not asked to sit through, that the tending of the flame through each season would pass among the nine in turn, a son or a daughter of each house sent up to sit with her and learn what she herself was only just learning. There was more argument in the settling of it than the keepers ever told her outright, though she pieced enough together over the years from things half said: two of the nine districts had wanted the office kept wholly among themselves, on the grounds that their people had sat nearest the old slab the longest, and had been outvoted by the other seven, who pointed out, not gently, that the whole reason for choosing a girl of no blood at all had been to keep exactly that kind of claim from ever taking root again. The two districts did not forget the vote, and their grudge over it outlasted every one of the keepers who had cast it, though it never once, in Beathag's own years, rose to more than a cold word at a gathering.

The first of the nine to come up the path was a broad quiet boy named Cailean, from the northern district, on the twenty-seventh of an t-Iuchar in the tenth year, who arrived expecting, he admitted to her much later, a shrine rather than a cold hut with one girl in it barely older than himself, and adjusted his expectations within the first evening. He turned out a poor hand at the fire and a good one at silence, which she came, over the season, to value rather more. After him came a sharp-tongued girl of the western district, then a widower's son who cried the first three nights and never once afterward, then in their turns the rest of the nine, each carrying up whatever their own household's gossip had made of the Hall before they arrived, and each, by the season's end, carrying something truer back down.

More households claimed some thread of blood back to one or another of the nine than nine hearths could ever truly have bred, and the keepers learned to let such claims stand unchallenged, since nothing was gained by disputing a thing that cost nothing to grant. In her own years the nine were still few enough, and near enough, that she knew every face that came up the path by name before it reached the top.

## III. Of Niall Òg's Gift

He came up alone, without the household guard that most heirs, even the least of them, thought beneath their dignity to travel without, in the twelfth year, on a morning when the mist had not yet lifted off the lower slope and the mountain above the mist looked, from where she stood, like an island in a grey sea. She knew him before he reached her only because Beitris, standing beside her, went very still and said his name under her breath as though it might carry uphill ahead of him and give warning.

Niall Òg was young among the heirs, as they reckoned it, and old by any other reckoning. He had stood among the heirs at the fall of the king and again at the cutting of the cord, though he held no share of his own and never would, and he carried his years the way some carried a limp, lightly enough that a stranger might not notice it until he moved wrong, and then would notice nothing else. What she noticed first, coming up out of the mist toward her, was that he was smiling, and that the smile did not look practised, which she had been told to expect of any heir who troubled himself to climb this far.

He had brought a cup of dark polished wood, small enough to sit in one palm, its rim carved into a pattern of running deer. She had never in her life held a worked thing so fine. "For the hut," he said, holding it out, "since a girl who feeds a fire for the whole valley ought to have one cup that is only hers."

She looked at it a long moment before she answered him, long enough that Beitris shifted beside her, and she understood, looking at the cup and at the man holding it, that whatever he meant by it, and she believed afterward that he meant it kindly and simply, the valley below would read it another way entirely: an heir's gift to the Keeper of the flame, a gift into the hand that was sworn to hold nothing of any blood but its own, and by evening every household on the mountain would have heard some version of it, most of them wrong.

"I have no cup that is only mine," she said, "and I am not to have one. Whatever I hold, I hold for all of them." She nodded down toward the households scattered below the slope, and did not name the heirs standing further off in their good cloaks, though both of them understood she meant them as much as the crofters. "If I take a gift from your hand, I must take one from every hand in the valley before winter, or answer for why yours was different. I'd rather answer for nothing."

He did not press it, which she had also been warned an heir would do, at length and with wounded dignity. He turned the cup over once in his own hand, looking at the running deer as though seeing them for the first time, and put it back inside his cloak. "That's a harder rule than the one I swore," he said, "and I swore it standing in the mud with everyone watching, and you're keeping yours alone on a hill with nobody watching at all." He looked at her a moment longer, not unkindly. "I think you'll keep it longer than I keep mine."

He left the way he had come, down into the mist, and she never heard that he tried the like again, with her or with any other Keeper. The keepers of the slab, when the story reached them, said it was the first proof they had that the choosing had been rightly made, since a girl of no line, offered a gift by one of the king's own blood, had known without being told what the gift was for. Beathag herself gave it less weight than they did, whenever the tale was told back to her. "I was afraid of the talk," she told Beitris once, "more than I was strong. A stronger woman might have kept the cup and answered the talk down. I only wanted the talk not to start."

## IV. Of the Raising of Talla na Lasrach

The turf hut held the flame for eleven years, and it was never meant to hold it longer, but a hall is not raised quickly by nine households who must also mine their vein and mind their sheep and pay their measure of coal at the season's end, and the work went forward the way such work goes, in a week here and a week there between the harvest and the first snow, so that it was the fifteenth year before the last stone went into the wall.

They built it of dry stone below and turf above, on ground a little higher than the hut, where the wind could not so easily find the door. Aodh Crom, older now and slower on the slope than he had been at the choosing, walked the ground with Beathag before the first stone was set and marked with his stick where the one door should stand.

"Toward the vein," he said, "and none toward the sea." He would not say more when she asked him why, only that the sea had no claim on the coal and ought not to be given one by a door left open to it, and she let the matter rest there, as she had learned to let most things rest that the old keeper judged better left unexplained. In the years after, other keepers gave other reasons for the same rule, none of them the same as each other's, and none of them, so far as anyone could later discover, the reason Aodh Crom had actually meant.

The masons were the nine households' own sons and daughters, taught as they built, and the walls show it: straight enough where the ninth hearth's people laid them, and less straight where the second hearth's did, and the keepers who came after Beathag Bhàn learned to tell one household's work from another's by the set of a stone as surely as by a face. She herself carried water up the slope for the mortar through two whole summers, since the flame could not be left untended long enough for her to do heavier work, and her arms, she said once to Beitris, learned more of the Hall's building than her hands ever did.

It stood finished by the last month of the fifteenth year: one long room of dry stone under a turf roof, a hearth-pit at its centre lined with the same grey stone the old slab was cut from, and the one door facing east along the line the vein ran under the mountain. No window looked toward the sea, or toward anything else; what light the hall had came in at the door, or from the flame itself.

## V. Of the Two Who Did Not Speak

Before the roof was finished the valley kept its Samhain at the foot of the new walls, since the ground below the Hall, unlike every other ground on the island by then, belonged to no lord and could be walked on by every lord without any of them owing thanks to another for the standing room. Beathag watched the fires lit that night from the door of her hut, the last Samhain she would keep there, and saw among the crowds below two men she had not seen stand near each other since the choosing.

One was Ruairidh Glas, of the line of Ìomhar, who twelve years before had put a spear through Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh at the stones of Dùn thais over a boundary neither of them, in the end, had been sure which side of the line it stood, and had not gone back to that ground since. The other was Aonghas Bàn's brother, Eachann Ruadh, who had sworn over the body that the debt would be paid, and had spent the years since finding no ground on which he was willing to be the first to speak and no ground on which Ruairidh Glas was willing to be found. Between the households sworn to each of them lay a dozen years of raids and reprisals that the tellers had already begun to call Aimhreit nan Oighrean, the strife of the heirs, and would go on calling it for five centuries more before either side found reason to stop.

They stood, that Samhain, on opposite sides of the same fire below the unfinished Hall, close enough that either could have crossed to the other in a dozen steps, and neither did, and neither, so far as anyone standing near enough to hear could report, said one word to the other across the flames the whole night through. But they stood. Every other ground on the island that year would have put a spear between them before the fire had burned an hour, and this one did not, and both of them, whatever they felt about it, seemed to understand that this was the one ground on which they could not afford to be the man who broke it first.

Beathag watched them from the hut door a long while, and told Beitris afterward that it was the first time she understood what the flame was actually for. The mountain would have gone on giving its coal whether anyone tended a hearth over it or not; the ground the Hall stood on was another matter, ground that could hold two men in the same firelight who would have killed each other anywhere else on the island, and ask nothing of either of them but that they stand there and not draw.

## VI. Of the Flame Carried In

The carrying was done at midwinter, on the shortest and coldest day of the fifteenth year, with the last frost of the old hut's floor still white on the heather when Beathag lifted the flame from the hearth-stone where it had burned, unmoved, for eleven years, and carried it out into the grey morning in a covered lamp that Cailean's own hands had made for the crossing.

The nine households came up for it, and the keepers of the slab, Aodh Crom leaning now on two sticks where one had served him at the choosing, and a scattering of the valley's crofting families who had no particular right to be there and came anyway, since a flame does not move house every day and a person likes to have seen a thing once that she can tell of afterward. Sìne nan Snaidhm came up from the gathering-house below with her cords, as she came to every gathering that seemed to her worth a knot, and she tied one that morning into the long record she kept of such days, a plain unmarked length beside the tangled record of the Roinn, and told anyone who asked that it was the first knot she had ever tied for good news alone. No heir came. None had been asked, and none, that morning, seemed to feel the lack.

Beathag walked the short distance from the old hut to the new door slowly, shielding the lamp with her body against a wind that had dropped, for once, to nothing worth shielding against, out of what she admitted afterward was pure habit and a little vanity, since a Keeper who let her flame gutter on the one morning everyone was watching earned no other name for the rest of her days. She set the lamp down inside the door, on the grey stone hearth cut to match the old slab, and opened it, and the flame that had burned eleven years in a turf hut at the mountain's foot burned that evening for the first time under a roof built to hold it, with its one door facing east along the vein, and no door at all toward the sea.

Aodh Crom stood at the door through it all, leaning on his two sticks, and said nothing while the flame was set, though Beathag, glancing once at his face across the new hearth, saw a look there she had not seen at the choosing eleven years before, on the slope in the mud and the wind: the particular stillness of a man watching a thing he had built with his own hands begin to stand on its own. He had never told her the reason for the door, and that evening, watching the flame settle into its new stone as though it had always meant to end up there, she found she no longer much minded not knowing it.

# Chapter Nine: Of the Cairns and the Unentered Temple

*FE 16 – 44*

> *Chan eil dia air a' bheinn; tha cuimhne.*
> There is no god on the mountain; there is memory.
>
> — said still among the nine hearths, of the reverence that took no priests

## I. Of the Name the Hearths Gave It

It is told at Dùn ìseal, by those who keep the memory of the nine hearths the way the knot-keepers keep the memory of the cord, that the reverence they practised about the mountain had gone a long while without any name at all, because a thing done by everyone from birth has no more need of a name than breathing does, until a stranger asks what it is called and there is, for the first time, nobody ready with an answer.

The stranger, when he came, was no stranger to the valley: a walker of the eastern share who had married into the ninth hearth and came to sit his season with the flame in the eighteenth year after the choosing of Beathag Bhàn, and who asked, on his first evening in the Hall, what the households called the thing they did at every dawn and every dusk and every turning of the moon, the small bowl of milk left on the sill for the dead, the coal-dust rubbed into a threshold before a birth, the silence kept on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas when the cloud came wrong. Beathag herself did not know the answer. She had grown up inside the doing of it, as everyone about the mountain had, and had never once needed a word for a thing that was simply what a morning was for.

It was Beitris, old by then and past climbing to the cairns herself, who gave it its name that winter, sitting by the Hall's own hearth with the flame between her and the stranger's question: *Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach*, the Old Spirits of the Dia-thìrich, and when the stranger asked what that meant, exactly, whether it was one spirit or many, whether it was the ancestors or the hills or the vein itself that a person honoured with the milk and the coal-dust, Beitris told him it was all of these and none of them separately, the way a man does not honour his own left hand more than his right, and that the reverence kept no priests because it needed none, having nothing to teach that every child did not already learn at its mother's knee: that the dead were owed remembering, that the sìth of the hollow hills were owed courtesy, that the vein was owed its season and its silence, and that the weather ruled all three and was owed the most careful watching of anybody's.

The name went down the valley faster than most things went, carried by carriers who had no carrying yet to speak of beyond their own two legs and the goods they could sling across them, and within a few years it was the name every household used for what it had always done without a name, so that a thing that had been nameless for the whole of living memory came, in the end, to seem as though it had always been called that, and the households who used the name forgot, within a generation, that anyone had ever needed to ask.

Beathag Bhàn heard the name from Beitris's own mouth, and turned it over for a long moment before she answered, the way she turned over most things that came to her fast. "It will do," she said at last. "It says what it needs to and claims nothing it shouldn't." She meant, though she did not say so plainly even to Beitris, that a reverence that kept no priests and claimed no single mouth to speak for it was of a piece with the flame she herself kept: a thing held by everyone's hands together and by no one's alone, which was, as near as she could tell, the whole of what the choosing on the slope had been for.

## II. Of Mòrag nan Càrn and the Watch on the Ridge

Above Cnoc ghlas the ground climbed in long grey shoulders to a ridge that caught every weather coming off the high passes before the valley below had so much as felt the first of the wind, and it was there, in the years after the Hall was raised, that the watching of the cloud was given its proper cairns, three of them at first and more after, built by hands that knew already, from a hundred years of losing coal to a bad reading, that a pile of stones on a height could save a season if a person only troubled to read it right.

Mòrag was of the fifth hearth, a quiet child who had shown, from the time she could walk the slope without being carried, an unaccountable gift for telling one grey sky from another that no one in her own household could match and no one much troubled to explain. She could stand at the door of her mother's house on a morning that looked, to every other eye in the yard, exactly like the morning before it, and say whether the day would hold or break by noon, and be right often enough that by the time she was grown the old watchers of the ridge had stopped asking her how she knew and started simply asking her.

She went up to the cairns for the first time in the tenth year, not yet twenty and sent, at first, only to carry water and turf for the watchers' fire, and stayed, by the end of that first season, because Aonghas Ruadh, the eldest watcher then living, told her plainly that he had watched that ridge for forty years and had never once seen a child read the western cloud as fast as she did, and that a man who did not use a gift like that when it stood in front of him was a fool twice over, once for having it wasted and once for knowing it was wasted and doing nothing. Within three years the elder watchers named her to the cairns in her own right, the youngest ever given them to keep, and she went on keeping them, by the end, longer than anyone before her.

The three cairns had not always stood where they stood. The first watchers, in the years before Mòrag's own grandmother was born, had kept no fixed mark at all, only a habit of climbing whatever height seemed nearest and trusting their own eye to the cloud, and it was a watcher of that older kind, an eastern woman named Sorcha whose grave no one now could point to, who first began piling stones at the three places on the ridge where she found she read the sky truest, so that a watcher coming after her would have the same three points to stand on rather than a fresh guess every morning. The households never troubled to hallow the cairns with any rite, and Mòrag herself thought that fitting, since a cairn's whole worth lay in standing exactly where the last watcher's eye had proved it useful, and a stone moved for the sake of ceremony was a stone moved for the worse.

The watch was simple to describe and hard to do well. Three cairns stood along the ridge, each built to a height a watcher's own eye could use as a mark against the sky, and from each of them, on any morning the galleries below were meant to open for the season's cutting, a watcher climbed before first light and read the cloud coming over the high passes: whether it carried only wind, which the coal-cutters could work under well enough with their cloaks drawn tight, or whether it carried the wet, low weight of rain that would find its way down through every crack the mountain had and turn a gallery's footing to mud before the cutters below had cut a single basket. A wrong reading either way cost something. A watcher too cautious kept the galleries shut on a day that would have given good coal, and the households went short for want of coal that was there for the taking; a watcher too bold sent the cutters down under a sky that broke by mid-morning, and more than once, in the years before Mòrag climbed the ridge, a gallery had come down on men working under rain they had been told would hold off.

"The sky doesn't lie," Mòrag told the two youths sent up to learn the watch from her in the twentieth year, standing with them at the first cairn in a wind that had already found every gap in their cloaks. "It only speaks a tongue most people never learn to hear right, and it doesn't repeat itself for the slow." She showed them the shape a cloud took when it meant only wind, high and torn and moving fast, and the shape it took when it meant the wet, lower and thicker and slower, though the difference, to the boy from the second hearth who had come up mostly because his household had nowhere else to send him that season, looked for the first two months like no difference at all, and he said so plainly, and she did not scold him for saying it, only told him to come back up the next morning and look again, and the one after that, until the difference stopped needing to be pointed out to him.

## III. Of the Season the Mountain Lost

It was in the twenty-ninth year, on a morning that Mòrag herself was not on the ridge to read, that the wrong reading came that the tellers still speak of, and it came, as the worst of such things generally do, from a watcher who had done the work long enough to trust himself past the point his own eyes deserved.

Fearchar Glas had watched the second cairn for six years by then and never once been badly wrong, and on the morning in question he read the cloud coming low and grey off the passes and judged it wind only, the kind a cutter could work under with a cloak drawn tight, and sent the word down to the Hall that the galleries might open. The cutters went down in good spirits, since the season had been slow to start and every household wanted its measure filled before the shorter days came, and they had not been at the coal three hours before the sky that Fearchar had judged wind-only opened into the heaviest rain the mountain had seen that year, water finding every seam and crack above the low gallery and running down into it faster than any hand could bail, so that the gallery had to be given up entirely, its footing gone soft and unsafe for the rest of the season, and with it the whole autumn's cutting that the households had been counting on.

Fearchar did not try to excuse it. He came down off the ridge himself that evening, before anyone had sent for him, and stood before the keepers of the slab and told them plainly that he had read the cloud wrong and knew it the moment the rain began, and that he would not watch the cairns again unless they told him to. They did not tell him to. The tellers say it was never spoken as punishment, and Fearchar himself never called it that; the keepers judged, plainly, after that season, that a watch on which a whole mountain's coal for a whole season could turn deserved a choosing at least as careful as the choosing that had once put a flame in a girl's hands on the slope below the slab, and from that year the cairns were given to no one who had not first stood a full season under an elder watcher's eye and been judged, by more than one pair of eyes, fit to read a sky alone.

Mòrag herself sat on the small council that judged the new watchers after that, and she was harder on the youths who came to her than Aonghas Ruadh had ever been on her, because she had watched a season lost from a mistake she herself might have made on a lazier morning, and she told anyone who asked why she pressed the young ones so hard that a watcher who had never once doubted himself had simply not yet met the morning that would teach him to. "Fearchar wasn't a fool," she said, more than once, in the years after. "He was only sure. Sureness is the one thing this work can't afford, and it's the one thing that comes free to anyone who does it long enough not to be careful."

## IV. Of the Cold on the Doire uaine Slopes

The Doire uaine hills lay north-west of the mountain, a low green country of birch and rowan where the old inscriptions on the standing stones, cut by hands nobody living could name, forbade any fire, of wood or of coal, to be lit within sight of them, and the keepers of the slab held to that prohibition as strictly as they held to anything the Binding itself demanded, though none of them could say, when asked, what the inscriptions meant by it or whose the hand had been that first cut the warning into the stone.

It fell hardest on the herders who wintered their flocks on those slopes, since a hillside with grazing enough for sheep through the cold months is not a hillside a household gives up lightly for want of a fire, and the households that held grazing rights on the Doire uaine slopes had held them since before the fall of the old king and were not about to move their flocks elsewhere on the strength of an inscription none of them could read. They wintered there instead as they always had, and ate cold, as they always had, boiling nothing, warming nothing, wrapping themselves in as much wool as a body could carry and moving enough, through the short grey days, to keep the blood working, and told their children, as their own parents had told them, that a fire lit within sight of those hills was a debt taken out against something none of them wanted to meet the collector of.

The thirty-third year was harder than most, a winter that came early and stayed late, with a wind off the western sea that found its way through wool the way water finds its way through unfired clay, and it was that winter the tellers remember best, because it was the winter a boy of nine, sent out from Doire uaine's northern steading to bring in a ewe caught in a drift, was himself caught by the same wind and found two days later, alive but barely, huddled in the lee of a boundary stone with no fire he had dared light to warm him, though he had carried flint enough to strike one and had chosen, even half out of his mind with cold, not to strike it within sight of those hills.

His mother carried him down to the Hall herself rather than risk the shorter road past the standing stones, and Beathag Bhàn sat with the boy through the night he was brought in, since a Keeper's hearth was the one fire on the mountain that had never asked anyone's leave to burn, and she asked him, once he was warm enough to speak, why he had not struck the flint, cold as he was and alone as he was and with no one there to see whether he broke the old rule or kept it. "Because it isn't only about being seen," the boy told her, through teeth that had not yet stopped chattering. "My grandmother says the hills know a fire whether anyone's watching for it or not." Beathag did not answer that at once. She had, by then, kept a flame for near thirty years that the whole valley had agreed to trust without watching over her shoulder every hour of it, and she found, turning the boy's words over, that she had no better account of her own reverence than his grandmother's, and did not try to find one.

The ban was never lifted in all the years after, and no herder of those slopes, so far as the tellers know, was ever proven to have broken it, though more than one household lost a beast, and once very nearly a child, to a winter they might have made easier with a fire they would not strike.

Beathag sent word to the northern steading that winter that any household of the Doire uaine slopes was welcome, whatever the hour, to bring a sick child or a frost-bitten hand up to the Hall's own hearth, since the ban spoke of fires lit in sight of those hills and said nothing at all of a fire kept a good many miles off at Dùn ìseal. Few households made the journey, the distance being what it was and a sick child a hard thing to carry so far in the cold, but the offer was remembered longer than it was used, and the boy who had chosen the drift over the flint told his own children, in his turn, that the Keeper's hearth had once been held open for his sake, and that he had never once needed to walk to it to know the offer had been meant.

## V. Of Beathag's Walk to the Ruin

There was a place, some way east of the mountain along a spur no gallery had ever been cut into, that the valley called Làrach an Teampaill, the temple ruin, and had called it that for longer than any household could account for, a low broken wall of dressed stone standing in bracken with an altar-slab at its centre that had clearly been shaped by hands and clearly, from the wear on it, had not been shaped recently.

It belonged, by every account the households gave, to nobody: not to the keepers of the slab, whose reverence had its slab at Dùn ìseal and no other; not to the Hall, whose flame was sworn to touch nothing outside its own hearth; not to any heir's line, since no share's boundary had ever been drawn to take it in, whether by accident or by the deliberate choice of stewards who wanted no part of a ruin nobody could explain. It sat in the bracken, uncounted and unclaimed, and every teller who spoke of it in those years said the same thing in more or less the same words: that it had stood before the Roinn, before the Binding, before, by the look of the moss on its oldest stones, the fall of the old king himself, and that nobody now living had ever heard a true account of who had raised it or for what.

Beathag walked out to it alone in the thirty-fourth year, on a morning she told no one she meant to keep, not even Beitris, though Beitris guessed something of it afterward from the mud on her shoes and said nothing until Beathag was ready to speak of it herself. She had heard, by then, every account the valley gave of the ruin, each one different from the last, and had come to feel, tending a flame she herself had been given by no explanation better than "hold it for Brìde, and answer to Crom", that a place so near her own mountain and so wholly unaccounted for was a thing she owed it to her own office to see with her own eyes rather than take entirely on other people's word.

The walk took the better part of a morning, over ground broken enough that she lost the path twice and found it again by the shape of the spur against the sky rather than by any mark on the ground itself, and she came on the ruin from the north, through bracken taller than her waist, before she quite expected to, so that the first stone of the old wall was almost under her hand before she saw it for what it was.

What she found inside the broken walls was less than she had braced herself for and stranger for being less. No image, no carved face, no sign she could read as belonging to any god or spirit the valley named by any name she knew: only the altar-slab, waist-high and long enough for a person to lie on, standing at the ruin's centre with its face turned, unmistakably and without any accident of the ground to explain it, toward the mountain, toward the very shoulder of rock under which she herself kept the flame. She stood before it a long while, in a stillness broken only by wind moving through bracken that had grown up through gaps in the old paving, and found, the longer she stood there, that she could not decide whether the turning troubled her or steadied her, since a thing that faced her own mountain might have been raised in reverence of it, or might, for all she could tell standing there with the wind pulling at her cloak, have been raised to keep some older watch on it that had nothing to do with reverence at all.

She came back down off the spur before the light went, and told the keepers of the slab what she had found, plainly and without adding to it what she could not swear to. "It is not Brìde's," she told them, "and it is not Crom's. Whatever hands turned that stone toward the mountain, they were not ours, and I would not have us claim a place we cannot account for, the same as I would not have any of the heirs claim the flame." Some of the keepers wanted to send masons out to clear the bracken and set a watch on the place, the way a watch was kept on the cairns; others wanted it left exactly as it stood, on the plain reasoning that a place three ages might have left alone was not a place four ages ought to disturb on a guess. Beathag herself, when the argument had gone on longer than she cared for, put an end to it the way she had learned to put an end to most arguments that could not be settled by evidence: she said that no keeper of the slab, and no Keeper of the flame after her, would set foot inside that ruin again, since a reverence built on remembering the dead and courtesy to the sìth was no reverence at all if it went stamping over ground it could not read.

The vow held. Whose place it truly was, the tellers say, the keepers never afterward claimed to know, and it seems, from everything that has come down of those years, that they did not know, and were, in the end, content not to.

## VI. Of the Flame Passed On

Beathag Bhàn kept the flame ten years more after her walk to the ruin, quieter years than the ones before them, in which the nine hearths came and went in their turns and the Hall's roof held against every winter it was given, and if she thought often of the altar turned toward her own mountain, she said little of it to anyone but Beitris, and Beitris, by the time the two of them were old women together, had learned not to press her on it.

She died in the forty-fourth year, at Dùn ìseal, within sight of the mountain she had answered to for forty years, and the manner of her dying was as plain as the manner of her choosing had been: no illness anyone could name, only a slowing, over one winter, of a body that had carried water up a slope for two summers and shielded a flame against every wind the high passes could send down, until one grey morning near the year's turn she did not rise from the bed Cailean's own children had built her, and Beitris, sitting with her as she had sat with so many others by then, understood before anyone told her that the watch had changed hands.

They laid her on the slope below the Hall, facing the vein under the mountain, with her back to the sea, though every teller in the valley knew, and said so plainly at the burial, that the dead of the Dia-thìrich went west over that same sea to whatever waited for them there, and more than one of the nine households wondered aloud, in the days after, whether a Keeper ought not to be laid the same way as everyone else who had ever died on the island. Beitris answered that question before it could grow into a quarrel, standing at the graveside with a certainty she had not always owned in her younger years: "She never once, in forty years, turned her back on the vein while she lived. I'll not have her do it the one day she can't choose for herself." No one argued the point further, and every Keeper after Beathag Bhàn was laid the same way, facing the mountain, though the reason given for it, in the generations that followed, slowly stopped being Beitris's grief and became simply the custom, the way the reverence itself had gone, in Beathag's own lifetime, from an unnamed thing everyone did to a name everyone used without asking why.

The nine hearths gathered within the week to choose who should hold the flame after her, as they had gathered once before to choose Beathag herself, though this time there was no slope crowded with heirs looking on, only the households and the keepers of the slab and Sìne nan Snaidhm's daughter come up with a fresh length of cord in case a knot should be wanted, which in the end it was not, since the choosing this time needed no long argument to settle it.

Beathag had a sister, long since married into a household of the fourth hearth, and that sister had a son named Muireach, quiet and grey-eyed even as a boy, who had come up to sit his own season with the flame twice already and had shown, both times, a stillness about the work that more than one of the keepers had already marked without saying so aloud. He was named that week, the nine hearths agreeing on him faster than any choosing the mountain had yet seen, and Beitris herself, old now and near the end of her own years, put the rush into his hands with words close enough to the ones Aodh Crom had once used that more than one person standing near enough to hear thought, for a moment, that the old keeper had somehow come back to say them himself.

"Hold it for Brìde," she told him, "and answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein." Muireach Liath took the flame the way his aunt had taken it before him, without much to say for himself, and carried it into the Hall that same evening, past the door that faced the vein and away from the sea, to keep it there through years the mountain had not yet begun to ask of him.

# Chapter Ten: Of Muireach Liath and the Luck-Stream

*FE 45 – 68*

> *Bheir an fhèith an gual; bheir an t-sruth an t-àgh.*
> The vein gives the coal; the stream gives the luck.
>
> — said of Muireach Liath's ruling on Allt an Àigh

## I. Of the Basket Once a Season

Muireach Liath had held the flame a year before he asked the nine hearths for anything, and what he asked for, when he asked it, was so small a thing that Beitris laughed when she heard it, and then stopped laughing, because he had not meant it as a jest.

"A basket," he said. "One to a household. Filled once a season, and not before."

He had watched, in that first year, what his aunt Beathag had watched for forty and never fixed: that a household near the mouth of a gallery sent its baskets down for coal whenever the weather turned, and a household two valleys off sent a boy with a creel only when the cold had already got into the old people's hands, and that the households near the mouth thought themselves no more favoured than anyone, because they had never once had cause to think about it at all. Muireach had grown up the son of no great house, in the fourth hearth, and he had carried a creel himself as a boy on more than one bad morning when the family nearer the gallery had already had theirs filled twice. He did not put it to the hearths as a grievance. He put it to them as a measure, the way Catrìona Mhòr's people had once measured a knot to a hearth, and let them argue over the size of the basket until they had argued themselves into agreeing on one, a lidded thing of plaited heather that a strong arm could carry full and an old woman could carry a quarter full, so that no basket asked more of a household than the household had to give, and none took more than its neighbour's.

There was grumbling. A household with six mouths said the same basket that fed six ought not to feed a widow and her one grandson at the same measure, and Muireach heard that out and answered that the basket measured coal, and a widow's hearth burned the same whether one sat by it or six. The grumbling thinned within the season and did not return. The weavers of the third hearth took the making of the baskets on themselves, since the weave wanted a particular closeness of plait to hold its shape under a full load, and it became, before Muireach had held the flame five years, a thing a household was almost proud to be known for, that its basket had lasted three winters unmended while a neighbour's had gone soft at the rim after one. Baskets of that weave are made at Dùn ìseal still, long after the cup took the measure from them, and are made now for no purpose the weavers themselves could tell you but the making.

Beitris, who had kept the slab since before the Binding and buried a Keeper, said of Muireach in those years that he ruled the way water finds a channel: patient, going round whatever stood in the way so quietly that the thing in the way did not notice it had been gone round until the water was already past. It was not entirely meant as praise. She had known keepers who pushed, in her time, and one or two who had needed to. But she said it to his face once, in the third year, sitting by the hut's fire with her hands gone stiff from thirty winters of carrying water up the slope, and Muireach only turned the question back on her, saying little, as he did most things.

"Would you rather I pushed?"

"I'd rather you knew when the water can't go round," she said, "because there'll come a stone in your channel one day that won't be gone round, however patient you are with it. I only hope you know the stone when you meet it."

He said nothing to that. In the third year of his keeping he did not yet think himself a man who had met such a stone, and Beitris, watching him carry the rush-lamp in through the door that faced the vein that evening, let the matter rest, being by then an old woman who had learned there was little use pressing a young one before the world had done it for her.

## II. Of the Stream Named for Luck

There was a stream that came down off the mountain's northern shoulder, no more than a stride wide at its narrowest and never dry even in the driest summers the valley had known, and it had no particular name in the years before Muireach's keeping beyond the plain one the households gave any small water, until a woman of Caol shean, whose boat had gone down twice in one season and come up both times with every man in it, said openly at a gathering that she had drunk of that stream on her way inland the week before each sinking, in what she swore was the right quarter of the moon, and had thought no more of it until the second boat came up whole as the first had. She was not believed at first, or not much, and the tellers say the households of the eastern share laughed at her more than they credited her, until a second man, and then a third, came forward with tales enough alike that the laughing thinned out.

By the time Muireach had held the flame ten years the stream had a name of its own, Allt an Àigh, the stream of the luck, and a season had not gone by without someone walking the long way up from the coast to drink of it under a moon they judged right, though no two households agreed entirely on which quarter that was, and the tellers of a later age would say only that the pilgrims never wholly ceased to come, without ever once agreeing among themselves on the reason.

The path they wore was walked mostly by night, since the right quarter more often than not fell in hours when a fisherman or a herder had no other business being anywhere but asleep, and it ran up from the river landing at Caol shean along the valley's eastern flank, worn deeper each year by feet that trusted the dark better than they trusted daylight questions about what exactly they were doing out in it. A boy of that landing, sent with his grandmother on the walk in his ninth year because she would not make it alone and would not be talked out of going, told Muireach himself, years later, that he had asked her on the way up what the stream would do for them, and she had told him she did not rightly know, only that her own mother had walked it and lost fewer nets in a lifetime of fishing than any other household on that stretch of coast, and that a woman did not need to know why a thing worked to know that it did.

Muireach heard a great many such tellings in those years, sitting outside the Hall on evenings when the pilgrims passed below on their way up, and he listened to all of them the same way, without correcting any and without endorsing any, a habit that more than one of the nine hearths took, in time, for wisdom, and that Beitris, who knew him better, took for what it more plainly was: a man keeping his own counsel until he had heard enough tellings to trust his own judgment over any single one of them.

## III. Of the Hall's Ruling

The stone under the mountain had never wanted for people willing to claim more of it than the Binding allowed them, and it was perhaps only a matter of years before someone thought to ask whether a stream that brought luck to those who drank of it might not, in some fashion, belong to the same reckoning as the vein it ran down from.

It was a keeper of the older reverence, one of the hearth-elders who had kept the ancestors' watch and the sìth's courtesy since before Beathag Bhàn had ever climbed the slope with a lit rush in her hand, who put the question to Muireach directly, on a morning when the mist still lay in the valley and the Hall's own hearth had not long been fed. She was old enough to remember Aodh Crom, or said she was, and she had walked up from the third hearth with a question she had turned over, by her own account, for the better part of a winter.

"The stream runs off the same mountain the vein runs under," she said. "If the vein is the Hall's to answer for, why not the stream?"

Muireach was quiet long enough that she thought, for a moment, that he meant not to answer her at all, which was a thing he had a name for among the nine hearths by then, though not always a kind one.

"Because the vein is stone that doesn't move," he said at last, "and coal that only comes out when a hand goes in and takes it. The stream moves on its own, the way weather moves on its own, and it was giving luck, if it gives it, long before any keeper stood on this mountain to answer for anything. I won't have the Hall claim what it never gave and can't take back."

"Then who does answer for it?"

"The same as answers for the wind, and for the dead under the ground it crosses. Not the vein. Not us."

It was said plainly, in a few sentences, on a morning no teller thought to mark as anything unusual while it was happening, and it was only afterward, looking back on it from years further on, that the households came to see it as the first time the Hall's own reckoning and the older reverence of the nine hearths, which up to then had run alongside each other without much need to define where one left off and the other began, had been made to stand apart and be named separately. The hearth-elders who kept the ancestors' watch took Muireach's ruling as the Hall admitting, plainly, that there were things on the mountain older than the vein and outside its claim, and said so with some satisfaction to anyone who would listen. The keepers of the slab, for their part, took it as proof that the Hall's flame answered only for what it had been sworn to answer for and reached for nothing beyond it, which they judged, on the whole, the more honest position, and said so with satisfaction of their own. Both sides have cited the same handful of sentences ever since as proof that Muireach Liath had been right, though they have never agreed on what, exactly, he had been right about.

Muireach himself, asked once late in his years whether he had known, standing in the mist that morning, that he was drawing a line the whole valley kept walking along in the years after, said only that he had not been thinking about lines at all, only about a stream and a question that deserved a true answer rather than a convenient one, and that anyone who found more in it than that was welcome to, so long as they did not ask him to agree with them.

## IV. Of the Carrying to Muileann ruadh

West of the mountain, where the ground broke into a shoulder of grey rock above a wooded glen, the warm springs of Muileann ruadh had run since before any teller could set a beginning to them, water that came up from some depth in the mountain's roots already heated, without fire and without any hand breaking the stone to make it so, and pooled in hollows a man could sit in to his chest.

The sick had been carried there in litters for longer than the Roinn itself, but it was in Muireach's years, when the roads down from the high valleys had worn a little smoother under the traffic of pilgrims going the other way to Allt an Àigh, that the carrying became a thing the households did as a matter of course rather than a last resort. A fevered child, a shoulder that would not set right, an old man whose joints had stiffened past what any winter fire could ease: the litters went up before dawn, so that whoever was carried could be bathed in the springs at first light, which the households held, without much argument among themselves, to be the hour the water worked best, though no one could say why that hour and not another.

Muireach let it stand without ruling on it at all, which was itself a kind of ruling, since more than one of the keepers of the slab thought the practice wanted the Hall's blessing, or its restraint, one or the other, and got neither. "The heat comes up from the mountain on its own," he told them, when they pressed him on it, "the same as the vein's coal sits in the mountain on its own until a hand goes in for it. No one breaks the stone for this water. I'll not break anything by speaking on it."

He went up himself once, in his fourth year, carrying nothing more than a walking-stick and a mind, by his own later account, to see what the households saw in the place before he let it run past him unquestioned as he had let the stream run past him. He found an old woman of the second hearth sitting waist-deep in the nearer pool with her granddaughter beside her, the girl's arm bound from wrist to elbow in a splint that had not set true the first time and was being given, the grandmother said, one more season in the warm water before anyone spoke of breaking it again to reset it. Muireach asked her, as he had asked no one about Allt an Àigh, whether she believed the water did the mending on its own, or only the rest that came with sitting in it a while each dawn.

"I believe my granddaughter's arm hurts her less after than before," the old woman said, "and I've stopped asking the water to explain itself, the same as I've stopped asking most things that help me to explain themselves. You might try it yourself, Keeper. It's restful, not knowing everything."

He did not answer that either, though Beitris, hearing the tale from him afterward, said it was the nearest thing to a joke she had ever heard him repeat against himself, and that she took it as a good sign in a man who did not, as a rule, find much in his own work to laugh at.

## V. Of Gille-Brìde in the High Valleys

Word came down from the high valleys in the ninth month of Muireach's ninth year that Gille-Brìde, of Somhairle's line, who had carried a coal of the First Flame home from the Binding and asked for nothing since, had died in his own bed among his own people, two hundred and twenty-four years old, in a winter that had come early to the passes west of Tobar dhìreach and stayed hard on the hill-folk who wintered there.

He had never come down to claim a share of anything in all the years since the Roinn, and the hearths at Dùn ìseal, who had grown used to seeing his sons and grandsons pass through on their way to trade wool for salt at the coast, had grown used also to thinking of Somhairle's line as a thing apart from the quarrelling of the nine great shares, a people who lived on the mountain's shoulders the way the sìth were said to live under its roots, wanting nothing from the valley below but leave to go on as they had always gone on.

It fell to his son Ceallach to keep the coal after him, on the same hearth it had burned on since the year it was carried up, and the tellers of the high valleys say that Ceallach did nothing on the day of his father's death that he had not already been doing for years, since Gille-Brìde had grown too frail, in his last seasons, to tend the fire himself, and Ceallach had been feeding it quietly on his behalf for longer than either of them had thought fit to remark on aloud. What changed, the day his father died, was only that Ceallach fed it now in his own name and not another's, and the hill-folk who came to sit by that hearth in the months after, as they had always come to sit by it, found the fire no different for the change, which was, Ceallach himself said once, the whole point of a coal kept so long: that it should not know, or seem to know, whose hand fed it.

Niall Òg, who by then had outlived more of his father's kin than he cared to count on any cord, heard the tidings at Dùn ìseal from a wool-trader come down off the passes, and went up himself, alone, without asking leave of anyone, to sit an evening by that hearth before the year turned. He had known Gille-Brìde only once, briefly, on the morning the Binding was sworn, a still man among heirs who none of them were still, and he had thought little of him since, in the way a man thinks little of a hill he has only once climbed. The fire he found there was small and steady, the household around it unhurried, Ceallach himself a grey-eyed man not unlike the father Niall dimly remembered, and Niall said afterward, to Muireach, that it was the first death of anyone of Ailean's whole scattered kin, in the fifty-odd years since the ford, that had left him with nothing at all to feel bitter about, only a stillness he did not much know what to do with.

"He never asked for anything," Niall said. "Not the flame, not a share, not a knot on Sìne's cord. I keep waiting to hear what it cost him, and nobody up there can tell me, because as far as they're concerned it cost him nothing at all."

Muireach, who had by then buried enough people of his own to have a settled answer for most things, offered none for that one, and Niall, who had not come up the mountain looking for an answer so much as somewhere to say the thing aloud, did not ask him for one twice.

## VI. Of the North Cut in Eleven

Murchadh Mòr, eldest of Ailean's living sons at the Roinn and the first of the seven hundred and twelve to be knotted on Sìne's cord, died at Baile Mòr mhòr in the eleventh year after Gille-Brìde, close on three thousand years old, the eldest of Ailean's children to the last, with a score of his brothers and sisters still living to hear of it.

Niall Òg went north for it, as he had gone north for little else in the years of calm that had settled over the great shares since the shares of shares were first counted, because Murchadh had been the first man's voice he remembered from the gathering-house floor, the door on a cold hinge that had given the line "Ailean's son" and dared anyone to argue it, and because Niall, whatever else he had become in nine hundred years of watching people die, had never entirely stopped being the boy who had grinned at Sìne nan Snaidhm and said he was owed twice.

He found Baile Mòr mhòr crowded with a different quarrel than the one he remembered from the Night of the Handful, though it wore the same shape. Murchadh had left eleven sons, none of them by the same mother, each with a household and a following and a grievance old enough to have outlasted the grievance's original cause, and none of them willing to let the north pass whole to any one of the eleven the way the old man himself had let no cousin near it in his lifetime. There was no cord for it this time, and no knot-keeper sent for, since the households of the north had long since stopped trusting a cord to settle anything a knife could settle faster; there were eleven knives instead, one to each hall of the north's chief holdings, and eleven nights of arguing over which hall went with which knife before a single cut was agreed on.

Niall stood at the edge of that hall on the night the cutting was finally done, an old man himself by the reckoning of anyone but the line he had been born into, and watched Murchadh's sons divide their father's great share the way he had once watched the nine eldest divide their father's kingdom, with lamps and cords and the same brittle courtesy men use when a wrong word might cost more than either side can afford. Lachlann Mòr, the eldest of the eleven, took the seat at Baile Mòr mhòr itself and the name that went with it, and was given it, in the end, with less argument than Niall had expected, since none of his ten brothers much wanted the burden of a hall their father had held so long that half the households under it remembered no other lord. Donnchadh Iar, the fourth of the eleven and the sharpest-tongued, took the western glens after an argument that ran two nights longer than any other, and made no secret, in the years after, that he judged the division unjust and Lachlann's seat too easily won.

"Eleven knives for one man's share," Niall said to Muireach, when he came back down to the mountain some weeks after, "where Ailean's whole kingdom took nine and a cord besides. I watched my grandfather's kingdom cut, and I've now watched my uncle's, and I'll tell you the only thing that's changed: nobody troubles now to call it holy."

"Does it need to be holy to hold?"

"I don't know yet," Niall said. "Ask me again once I've seen what eleven small lords do with a share too small to feed the quarrels their father used to feed on his own."

The north that came out of Baile Mòr mhòr's last division was a floor of counties smaller than any that had stood on the mountain's other flanks since the Roinn, each with its own hall and its own small lord and none of them, singly, able to raise so much as twenty spears, a fact the tellers already read as the plainest proof the long-lived blood was fading from that line faster than from any other, though at the time no one troubled to say it in so many words, being too occupied with the counting of glens to count anything so far off as a generation not yet born.

## VII. Of the Cattle Taken at the Ford

It was in the third year after Murchadh's dividing that Eachann Ruadh, of the line that had shed the first blood at Dùn thais and never wholly laid the feud down since, rode with a dozen men across the boundary stones into the Red Share's northern grazing and drove off near forty head of cattle before the herders of that ground had done more than raise the alarm.

No one on either side called it the opening of a new quarrel, since the old one between Eachann's line and Ìomhar's had never closed enough to need reopening; it was, by every account the tellers give, simply the feud finding, after some fallow years, a fresh grievance to spend itself on, the boundary stones at Dùn thais having stood long enough by then that a generation had grown up on each side of them who knew the stones only as a line to be tested rather than a wound to be remembered. The Red Share's steward sent word to the Hall asking whether the cattle, once recovered, might be driven onto the Hall's own ground for safekeeping until the matter was settled, on the reasoning that no feud had ever been permitted to follow a man onto that ground since the days of Aonghas Bàn's death, and Muireach refused him as plainly as he had refused the hearth-elder over the stream.

"The Hall's ground keeps a man safe from a knife," he said. "It was never sworn to keep cattle safe from a drover. Settle it the way the shares of shares are settled, or don't settle it at all, but don't ask me to make holy ground of every quarrel that finds its way to my door."

The cattle were never fully recovered, and the two lines went on, in the years after, much as they had gone on before, trading raids and grievances across a boundary that had cost one man his life already and would, before the long years finally ran out of that blood, cost more than one more. Niall Òg, hearing of it at Dùn ìseal, said only that he had stopped being surprised, some centuries back, by how little either side needed to remember why they were fighting so long as they still remembered that they were, and went back to whatever quieter business had occupied him before the news came, being by then a man who had learned, as Muireach had learned on his own mountain, which stones in the channel could be gone round and which could not, and who no longer troubled himself overmuch trying to move the ones that could not.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the Silver of Muileann chiar

*FE 69 – 96*

> *Chan eil fuil san airgead.*
> There is no blood in the silver.
>
> — Muireach Liath, of the seam apart from the vein

## I. Of the Furnace that Answered to Nobody

The smiths of Muileann chiar say still, when they tell the making of their own trade, that it began on a morning when three men stood about a wet fire and waited for a thing they had never made before to decide, on its own account, whether the fire held metal or only ash, and that no one among them could have told you, had you asked, what they meant to do if it chose ash. Fearchar Airgeadach was the youngest of the three, and it is his name the households kept, though he himself said, in old age, that the finding was none of his and the waiting that morning belonged as much to old Tormod who had fed the peat as to the seam, which had lain under the hill a great while before anyone troubled to ask what it was.

The seam was found in the sixty-ninth year of the Keepers' count, a few miles north of Dùn ìseal along a spur the mountain's own vein had never reached, where a shepherd looking for a ewe caught in bracken saw a grey stone with a bright wound in it where her stick had scraped the moss away, and carried the stone down to the Hall more out of curiosity than any thought that it might matter. It was the first thing dug from the ground of the island that was surely not coal: no household could name a use for it, no keeper could say whose it was, and it sat on a sill at Dùn ìseal for the better part of a season, turned over now and again by whoever passed, bright where the shepherd's stick had scraped it and dull everywhere else, until Fearchar, who carried baskets for the ninth hearth and had spent more hours than most men watching the fires that fed the vein, asked to take it away and see what a fire hot enough would do to it.

He was not a smith. There were no smiths on the island in those years in the sense the word later came to carry, only households that shaped bone and horn and wood, and heated stone for building, and Fearchar's whole claim to the work was that he had watched the vein's fires longer and more closely than most, banking them and starving them and coaxing them by turns through three winters of carrying baskets for keepers who trusted him with the watching precisely because he asked so few questions of it. He built his own fire apart from the Hall's, on the spur where the grey stone had been found, of wood first and then, when the wood alone would not answer, of peat cut and dried the way the vein's own peat was cut, and he fed it through most of a day and half a night before old Tormod, dozing against a rock with the second basket of peat still unopened beside him, woke to find Fearchar standing over the ashes with something in his hand that had not been there when the fire was lit: a bead of metal no larger than a thumbnail, soft enough to press a mark into with a fingernail, and brighter, where it caught the last of the firelight, than anything either man had ever pulled whole out of the ground.

It is told that Fearchar said nothing for a long while, turning the bead in his fingers the way the Hall's own keepers turned a coal to judge its burning, and that when he did speak it was only to ask Tormod whether the fire had answered to the Hall in any way that either of them could account for, since he himself had lit it on the spur and fed it with his own hands and asked leave of no one to do either. Tormod, who had spent thirty years of his life keeping fires that answered to nobody but the Hall, said that this one, so far as he could tell, answered to nobody at all, and the two men sat a while longer by the dying peat without either of them saying what they both plainly thought, which was that a fire owing nothing to the vein and nothing to the flame was a new thing on the island, whatever else it turned out to be.

Word of the bead reached Dùn ìseal within the week, carried by Tormod himself, who could not keep from telling it, and within the month Fearchar had built a proper furnace of clay and dry stone on the same spur, banked into the hillside the way the vein's own galleries were banked, and was smelting the grey stone by the basketful into beads and then into small ingots and then, once he had learned to hammer the soft metal without cracking it, into rings. The households of the ninth hearth called the place Muileann chiar, the dark mill, after the smoke that hung over it on a still morning, and the name held, though there was already another place of that name far to the east, near a holy wood, and the two were never once mistaken for each other by anyone who had walked to both.

## II. Of the Ring that Showed No Colour

The seam lay apart from the mountain's own vein by a distance no gallery had ever crossed, and it was not long before someone asked, as someone always asked of anything new on the island in those years, whether the new metal fell under the flame the way the coal did, and whether Fearchar's furnace, answering to nobody, ought in fact to be made to answer to the Hall the same as every other fire that burned near Dùn ìseal.

Muireach Liath heard the question at the Hall's own hearth, from two of the ninth household who put it to him plainly enough, and it is said that he asked first to see the metal before he answered anything, and sat a long while with one of Fearchar's rings turned in his fingers by the light of the flame he himself kept, much as Fearchar had turned the first bead by the light of his own fire on the spur. Whatever he was looking for in the ring, the Hall's own coal never showed it to anyone: a coal, cracked open at the vein's own edge, showed its colours in the break, now one of the seven and now another, to any eye of the island that looked, and it was that colour and nothing else that the flame answered to and the households paid dues on. The ring showed nothing of the kind. It broke, when Muireach pressed a thumbnail hard enough into the softest part of it, with no colour at all beneath the break, only the same pale sheen the whole ring already wore, and Muireach set it down on the hearth-stone between himself and the two who had asked and said the thing that every teller of the Hall's history repeats afterward in nearly the same words.

"Chan eil fuil san airgead," he said. *There is no blood in the silver.* He meant, and said so plainly when one of the two asked him to say more, that the coal of the vein bled a colour when it broke that every keeper since the first had sworn to answer for, and that this new metal showed nothing of the kind under any breaking he could give it, and so belonged, so far as the flame's own oath reached, to nobody at all. "Fearchar dug it, and Fearchar may dig on," he told them, "and whatever comes of the digging is his to keep or give as he sees fit, since the Hall has no claim on a thing that shows no colour when it breaks." He gave the ruling once, at the Hall's own hearth, and never troubled to give it again, though more than one household, watching the digging swell, muttered afterward that they wished the flame had claimed a share of it.

Muileann chiar dug on. Within two years the spur held four furnaces where Fearchar's one had stood, worked by his own kin and by a handful of households of the ninth hearth who had grown tired of carrying baskets for a vein that gave them coal and asked for their whole lives in return, and the place that had been a shepherd's path a few years before had a name of its own on every carrier's tongue between Dùn ìseal and the coast. Fearchar himself kept the first furnace and taught the others what he had learned of the fire's temper by trial and by the burns on his own hands, and it is remembered of him, by those who worked the spur in his own lifetime, that the first ring off every new furnace he raised was never sold nor worn nor traded but set instead, whole, on a flat stone at the mouth of the workings, an offering to Goibhniu, the smith beyond the smiths, before the second ring was so much as begun; and that no furnace of his ever failed in its first season, which the smiths of Muileann chiar took, for as long as the custom held, as proof enough that the god had taken the offering kindly.

## III. Of the Two Cousins and the Ground Between

The seam's freedom from the flame did not make it free of every other claim a household on the island knew how to press, and it was not two years before the ground the seam ran under was claimed, in the same season and with equal certainty, by two cousins of the eastern share who had never before had cause to trouble themselves over a stretch of hillside neither of them had thought worth a boundary stone.

The two were grandsons of one grandfather through different daughters, and the boundary between their households had run, since their grandfather's own day, along a burn that dried in most summers and was never once in living memory worth arguing over, since the ground either side of it was thin pasture that fed a scattering of goats and little else. The seam changed that reckoning inside a single season. Both cousins sent word to Dùn ìseal within days of each other, in the seventy-fifth year, each swearing that the spur where Fearchar's furnaces now stood lay on his own side of the dried burn and not his kinsman's, and each bringing, when the keepers of the slab asked for it, an account of the boundary that agreed with his own claim to the seam and disagreed with his cousin's in every particular that mattered.

It was not a matter the flame could rule on, the seam having already been ruled outside its reach, and the keepers of the slab, who had no more standing over a boundary between two heirs' households than the flame did, sent the two cousins back to settle it as households of their kin had always settled such things, by the word of elders both sides trusted and, failing that, by whatever each side could hold and defend. Neither cousin would yield the claim, and for the better part of a year the smiths of Muileann chiar worked their furnaces under the eyes of two households who watched each other across the dry burn more closely than either watched the fires, until a solution presented itself that satisfied neither man's pride and both men's purses at once: Fearchar himself, weary of digging under a dispute he had not started and could not settle, offered a ring to each cousin from the season's working, in the seventy-sixth year, on the plain condition that both let the digging go on undisturbed while their elders argued the boundary at their leisure.

Both cousins took the ring, neither gladly, since taking it looked, to anyone watching from the valley, a good deal like admitting that the ground in dispute was worth less to argue over than a season's silver was worth to hold; but neither man found, once the ring was in his hand, that he could think of a dignified way to give it back, and the digging went on. The burn's true course was settled at last by a boundary stone the two households raised together at the driest point of the burn's bed, cut with a mark on either face and set so that each cousin's flock could be seen from his own side of it, and the stone came to be known, to every household of the eastern share, simply as the silver stone, though not every household that used the name could have said why.

## IV. Of the Rings for Salt and Sealskin

It was carriers, not smiths, who first thought to take the new rings anywhere beyond the spur that made them, and it was to the river quays at Ros fhionn, a day and a half's walk north along the old path the pilgrims of Allt an Àigh had first worn, that the earliest of them were carried, in the same season that Fearchar's second furnace first began to answer as steadily as his own.

Ros fhionn stood where the river widened enough for boats out of the northern coast to come up on a rising tide and go down again on the next, and its households had long since learned to want more of everything than the land immediately about them could give: salt, which no household inland could make for itself in any quantity the winter's fish-curing wanted, and sealskin, which the boats brought down from the colder waters north of the cape and which no inland household had any way to come by at all except through a coast-dweller willing to trade it. What Muileann chiar's smiths had that Ros fhionn's boatmen wanted was less obvious to either side at first than it seems from this distance, since a ring of soft grey metal fed nobody and mended no net and kept out no weather, but a boatman who had carried salt fish up every river landing on that coast for twenty years put the two things together within a single evening's talk at the quay, reasoning that any household inland that wanted salt badly enough would find some way to want the rings too, once it was known that the coast would take them.

He was proved right within the season. The first exchange the quays remember plainly was a single ring for a full boatload of salted fish and sealskin together, struck between a carrier of the ninth hearth and a boatman whose name the tellers no longer agree on, and it stood, once it was known, as the measure every later trade was weighed against, so that for a long while afterward a boatman naming his price for a load of any size would say simply "a ring's worth" or "half a ring" and be understood by anyone on the quay without further reckoning. It was the first trade the island had ever struck in anything but food and shelter and labour owed, and the first whose price outlived the season it was struck in, carried in memory from one bargaining to the next the way a coal's colour was carried from one keeper to the next, and carriers who had grown old walking the path between Muileann chiar and Ros fhionn said, when they were old themselves, that they had watched a whole new kind of reckoning grow up on that path within their own lifetimes, though none of them, pressed to explain what the reckoning was for, could give an answer much better than that a ring bought what a ring bought, and everyone on both ends of the path had come, somehow, to agree on it.

The salt came back up the path in barrels lashed to poles carried two to a load, and the sealskin in bundles that smelled, more than one household said, of the whole northern sea at once, and Muileann chiar, which had been four furnaces and a scattering of turf huts a year before, grew a smokehouse and a salting shed within two more, until a traveller coming up from the coast could smell the place before the smoke of its furnaces ever came in sight of him. Fearchar himself went down to Ros fhionn only once, in the last years before his hands grew too stiff for the hammer, to see with his own eyes the place his rings had been going all that time, and is said to have stood a long while at the quay watching a boat unload salt he had never once thought, when he stood over his first bead of metal by a dying fire on the spur, to have any hand in bringing ashore.

## V. Of Ceallach's Long Years Ended

Not every household of that generation measured its years the way the smiths of Muileann chiar measured theirs, in furnaces raised and rings hammered, and it was in the seventy-ninth year of the Keepers' count, while the boundary stone between the two cousins was still new-set and the salt road to Ros fhionn still young enough that old men remembered walking it for the first time, that Ceallach mac Ghille-Bhrìde died in the high valleys at the age of a hundred and forty years, the last of Somhairle's line in whom the long years still showed.

He was Gille-Brìde's son, and had kept, since his father's death twenty-six years before, the coal of the First Flame on his own hearth in the high valleys where the air ran thin and cold and few households troubled to build above the tree line at all, tending it the way his father had tended it since the Binding, while his own line reached back through years that the valley itself could no longer count with any certainty, since every teller who tried gave a different tally.
