His own years had begun to fail him some seasons before his death, the way a slope fails under snow that has been building a good while before anyone marks the first crack in it, and by his last winter he no longer walked the high paths himself but sat by his own hearth and let his grandchildren carry word up and down to him, watching the flame he kept grow, in his own words to more than one of them, "no dimmer, though I am."

He died in his sleep on a night no household afterward could fix with certainty, since the valley learned of it only when a grandson came up at dawn with bread and found the old man cold and the hearth-coal, by some account or other, already grown ash, though other tellers of the same death swear the coal still glowed when the household gathered and was carried down, in a covered dish, to be given at last to the Hall's own flame, the line of Somhairle's long keeping ending where the line of Beathag Bhàn's shorter keeping had begun. His children, none of whom had inherited anything of his years beyond the ordinary span any household on the island by then expected of itself, did not stay in the high valleys once he was gone. They went down into the lower ground within the year, scattering among households of the ninth and the fourth hearths, and though the name of Somhairle's line was remembered a good while longer in the telling of Ceallach's own death, no household after him in that line was ever again spoken of as one that a stranger might mistake, meeting an old man on a slope, for someone who had watched the mountain since before the Roinn.

It is told, and no teller of the Hall's history has ever thought to doubt it, that word of Ceallach's death reached Fearchar at his furnace on the same day the last ring of that season was set out on the flat stone for Goibhniu, and that Fearchar, hearing it, set the tools down for the rest of the day, though the two men had never once met in life, on the plain reasoning, as he gave it to Tormod that evening, that the island had just grown a great deal younger all at once, and a man ought to mark that the same as he would mark anything else worth marking.

## VI. Of the Flame Passed to Gormshuil

Muireach Liath kept the flame ten years more after Ceallach's death, years in which the Hall's roof held and the nine hearths came and went in their turns much as they had under Beathag Bhàn before him, and if he thought often, in those years, of the ring he had once turned in his fingers and found to show no colour when it broke, he gave the Hall no further ruling on it, the first one having settled, so far as anyone could tell, every question the households afterward thought to ask him.

He died at Dùn ìseal in the eighty-ninth year, at eighty-one years of age, in much the same manner Beathag Bhàn had died before him: no illness the households could put a name to, only a slow failing of strength over one winter, until a morning came on which he did not rise, and the nine hearths were called together within the week to choose who should carry the flame after him, as they had been called to choose him after Beathag. Three of the households put forward candidates of their own that year, each with a claim the keepers of the slab judged sound enough to weigh seriously: a grandson of the sixth hearth who had already sat two seasons with the flame and shown, by every account, a steadiness the keepers valued; a daughter of the third hearth whose grandmother had been one of the nine who chose Beathag Bhàn herself, and who argued, through her own household, that the choosing owed something to that memory; and a nephew of Muireach's own, of the ninth hearth, whose chief claim, as more than one keeper noted privately, was blood and little more. The nine hearths heard all three argued for at length, over the better part of two days, and passed over all three in the end, choosing instead Muireach's own daughter Gormshuil, then forty-nine years of age, who had sat her own seasons with the flame without either household or grandmother's memory to speak for her beyond the work itself.

It is told that the three passed-over candidates took the choosing, each in his or her own fashion, better than the households behind them had expected: the grandson of the sixth hearth is remembered to have said only that the flame had chosen rightly before and would likely go on doing so without his help; the daughter of the third hearth kept her own grandmother's memory alive in another fashion, knotting at last, on a cord of her own, the names of every household that had sat a season with the flame since Beathag Bhàn, a cord the Hall kept and went on adding to; and Muireach's own nephew, who alone among the three might have pressed his claim further on the strength of blood, chose instead to go north to Muileann chiar within the year and take up work at one of Fearchar's furnaces, where it is said he prospered a good deal more than he might have as a Keeper who had come to the flame by kinship rather than by the households' own choosing.

Gormshuil nic Mhuirich took the flame from her father's own hands before he died, in the last days when he could still hold it steady enough to pass it on, and carried it into the Hall the evening the nine hearths' choosing was made known, past the same door that faced the vein and away from the sea that every Keeper before her had passed through. Seven years into her keeping, in the ninety-sixth year, when the smiths of Muileann chiar had grown from Fearchar's single furnace to a settlement the carriers named without needing to explain which Muileann chiar they meant, the kin of Gormshuil herself at Dùn ìseal began to be spoken of, by households up and down the valley, by a name of their own, and no longer by their hearth alone: Sliochd Mhuirich, the house of Muireach, the first house of the flame's keeping that the island had ever troubled to call by a name rather than a number. No account that has come down of those years tells of the other eight hearths raising any objection to it, whether because none was raised or because none thought worth remembering, and the name held, as the ring's silver had held against every argument brought to keep it from the smiths who first hammered it, and no household of the ninth hearth troubled any further to ask why a house needed a name at all when a hearth had always done well enough.

# Chapter Twelve: Of Sìleas and the Stag

*FE 97 – 125*

> *Carson a tha an fhèith a' freagairt aon làmh, is a' diùltadh làmh eile?*
> Why does the vein answer one hand, and refuse another?
>
> — asked first by Sìleas nic Coinnich in the grove at Muileann chiar

## I. Of the Coal that Would Not Answer Evenly

At the far-eastern Muileann chiar, where the seam ran shallower than under the mountain and a cutter could work standing instead of on her knees, Sìleas nic Coinnich had cut coal since she was twelve years old, and she had never once, in all that cutting, seen the thing she began to see in her twelfth year at the face.

It was a small thing to begin with, the kind of thing a tired woman notices and puts away with the rest of the day's noticing, meaning to look at it again when there is less to do. Two cutters worked the same wall that season, she and a broad, slow, good-natured man named Dòmhnall Beag, and where his pick broke the coal it came away dull, dark, honest coal that burned steady and gave no more light than coal ought to give; where hers broke it, now and again, some strokes and never quite all of them, often enough that she began to count, it came away threaded through with colour, a green and a blue and a deep red running in it like oil on water, and that coal, burned in the evening at the hearth, gave a light that made the women mending by it complain they could not tell their thread.

She said nothing of it for a year. The vein was the vein; it gave what it gave, and a cutter who asked too many questions of it, the older women said, was a cutter who would end by asking it for more than her handful, and no good had ever come of that. But she went on counting, in her head, at the face, which strokes broke bright and which broke dull, and she began to notice that it was not always her stroke and never Dòmhnall's; sometimes his pick broke bright too, on a day when hers broke dull the whole shift, and once, memorably, a boy new to the galleries who had never in his life given the coal a moment's reverent thought broke three bright pieces running before the overseer took the pick from him for wasting his strokes on show.

"It isn't the hand," she said to Dòmhnall one evening, over the ale that ended every shift at Muileann chiar. "I thought it was the hand. It isn't."

"What is it, then?"

"I don't know. That's the trouble of it." She turned her own hands over, looking at them as though the answer might be written on the palms and she had simply not held them to the light the right way. "Carson a tha an fhèith a' freagairt aon làmh, is a' diùltadh làmh eile? Why does the vein answer one hand and refuse another, if it isn't the hand at all?"

Dòmhnall, who was not a man for questions that could not be answered by supper, said only that she would wear herself thin asking a wall of rock why it did what it did, and went to his bed, and thought no more of it. Sìleas did not go to hers for a long while after. She sat by the last of the fire with a lump of the bright-veined coal in her lap, turning it in the light, and it was that night, though she did not know it yet, that the question took hold of her in a way it would not let go of again for the rest of her life.

She was twenty-six years old, cutting coal in the galleries of a mountain her whole family had cut coal in since before her grandmother's grandmother, and she had a question nobody at Muileann chiar could answer and, so far as she then knew, nobody anywhere on the island had ever thought to ask.

Her mother, who had cut the same wall before her and had never in her own long life seen anything in the coal but coal, told her plainly that a question like that one was better left where she had found it. "The vein gives what it gives," she said, "and it has given this house bread for four generations without being asked why. Ask it why, and the next thing it gives you may be nothing at all." Sìleas did not argue with her, having been raised to a proper respect for the vein and for her mother both, but she noticed that her mother, saying this, would not meet her eye, and that the coal her mother's own pick broke that season ran bright as often as dull, though her mother never once remarked on it herself. It was the first time Sìleas understood that the not-asking was a kind of answer in its own right, chosen by people who had looked at the same thing she looked at and decided, long before she was born, that looking was as far as a body ought to go.

## II. Of the Wood and the First Lesson

She stopped cutting, in the end, when she had run out of people at the face willing to be asked, and the galleries, whatever else they might still have taught her, had nothing left to say to a woman the overseer had learned to watch. A cutter who wanted to know whether the coal answered her better on a fast day or a slow one, on an empty stomach or a full one, standing or kneeling, singing or silent, was a cutter the overseer began to find reasons to move to another wall, and after the third such moving Sìleas understood that Muileann chiar's galleries would give her no more than they had already given, and that whatever came next would have to come from somewhere else.

There was a wood above the town that the town called holy without being able to say, if pressed, precisely why: Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, oak and rowan on the shoulder of the hill behind the workings, older than the cutting by anyone's reckoning, where a woman who had lost a child or a man whose luck had turned against him went sometimes to sit alone among the trees, and came down again saying only that it had done him good, without ever saying how. Sìleas went up into it one evening in the autumn of her thirty-third year with no more plan than to sit where it was quiet and think, and she found, when she got there, that three others from the galleries had followed her without being asked, having heard she meant to go and having questions of their own that the face had never answered either.

She did not set out to teach. She set out only to say aloud, among people who would not move her to another wall for the saying of it, the question that had kept her from her bed a year before, and to hear whether anyone else in the wood that evening had noticed the same thing at their own face and never spoken of it, for fear of being thought a woman who asked more of the coal than the coal owed her. Three had. By the second evening there were nine. By the spring there were near forty, cutters and basket-carriers and two of the overseer's own children, sitting on roots and fallen trunks in a clearing where the light came down thin and green through the oaks, and Sìleas, who had never meant to be anyone's teacher, found that she had become one without noticing the day it happened, in the same way she had noticed her own question without meaning to.

She taught them nothing she did not herself believe, which was very little, set against how much she did not know. To count as she counted, first: which strokes broke bright, which broke dull, on what day, by what hand, after what meal, in what temper. That the counting was worth doing even when it answered nothing, next, because a question said aloud and returned to was a question that might one day be answered, where a question only felt and never spoken sank back into the dark of the gallery and was lost. And, most of all, that revering the vein and asking a question of it were not the same act, whatever the old women at the hearth believed, so that a hand might do both in the same day without offence to either.

The clearing had grown too full for the old fallen trunk she liked to sit on by the eighth spring of the teaching, and it was that spring the stag came.

An ordinary stag, or so the tellers who came after always insisted on saying, a red stag such as any hunter on the eastern slopes might raise in a season and take without ceremony, came out of the trees at the clearing's edge on an evening in early summer while Sìleas was in the middle of setting out, for the fortieth time that spring, the question of the bright coal and the dull, and did not run. Its head up and its ears turned toward the clearing, it stood at the tree-line the whole length of the lesson, through the counting and the arguing that followed the counting and the long quiet in the middle where nobody spoke and Sìleas herself said afterwards she had not known what to say next; when the lesson broke up at dusk the beast turned and went back into the wood as though it had somewhere else to be, and was not seen again that season.

Nobody in the clearing that evening claimed it meant anything. Sìleas herself, asked about it many times over the years that followed, would say only that a stag had stood at the tree-line through a lesson once, and that she did not know why, and that she had never claimed to know why, whatever was made of it afterwards by people who had not been there. But the forty who had been there told it to others who had not, as tellers do, and by the autumn the school in the wood above Muileann chiar had given itself a name, claiming nothing about the stag's meaning, wanting only a name and taking the thing that had happened to them that nobody else's teaching could boast of: they called themselves the stag's people, and the wood's own name, Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, began to be spoken alongside the older reverences as somewhere a different kind of asking was done.

Sìleas let the name stand. She had never had much patience for naming things, holding that a name settled a question before the question had earned its settling, but she saw well enough that forty people needed something to call themselves besides Sìleas's people, which she liked less than any name they might have chosen instead, and the stag's people cost her nothing to allow.

What the name cost the school was harder to weigh, and came only later. A stag that stands still through one lesson and is never seen again is, to the forty who saw it, a fact and nothing more; told a second time, by someone who was not there, it becomes a wonder; told a third time, it wants a meaning, and Sìleas spent more evenings than she cared to count turning aside hearers new to the clearing who arrived already certain that the stag had been sent, and by whom, and for what purpose, none of which she had ever claimed and none of which she was willing to teach as though she had. "I saw a stag stand at the trees while I talked too long about coal," she told one such hearer, a girl down from the northern shore who had walked a fortnight to sit in the clearing on the strength of a story grown taller with every telling between her home and the wood. "That is the whole of what I know of it. If you have come for more than that, the wood will not give it to you, and neither will I."

The girl stayed anyway, and cut coal beside Dòmhnall within the year, and learned, as most of the forty learned in time, that the counting was the true teaching and the stag only the door that had brought her through it.

## III. Of the Ford

Word of the school in the wood travelled slowly east to west, the way most word travelled that was not carried by a runner with a reason, and it was two years and more before anyone at Dùn ìseal troubled to ask what the far-eastern Muileann chiar was teaching under its trees. What travelled faster, that same year, went the other way, west to east, carried by carriers who had it from other carriers at the waypoint houses and told it at every fire they stopped at from the Red Share to the last inn before the eastern wood, and it reached the clearing above Muileann chiar on an ordinary morning in the autumn of Sìleas's forty-fourth year, brought by a basket-carrier who had walked three days out of his way to be the one who told it.

Ìomhar Dearg was dead.

He had ridden out from Dùn dhearg that spring, old even by the reckoning of his own blood, fifteen hundred years and more behind him and not a grey hair to show for it, to see for himself a boundary stone on the Red Share's northern march that his stewards swore had been moved in the night, a small thing, the kind of thing that on any other share would have been settled by two men and a rope before noon. At a ford on the Red Share's northern march, which he had crossed with four riders a hundred times before, Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh, who had sworn over his brother's body six score years before that the blood spilt at Dùn thais would be answered by his own hand or his sons' after him, without naming the man he meant, had been waiting in the alders on the far bank with a spear he had carried, by his own account afterwards, every day of those six score years, though no one had ever seen him carry it before that morning.

He did not throw it from cover. That much was granted him, by friend and enemy both, in every telling that came after: Eachann Ruadh stepped out onto the ford in plain sight, called Ìomhar Dearg by name across the water, and said only that Aonghas Bàn had waited longer than a man ought to wait, and threw the spear when Ìomhar's own guard was already turning their horses toward him. It took Ìomhar Dearg in the throat. He was off his horse and into the water before his riders understood what they had seen, and Eachann Ruadh was back into the alders and gone north before they had him out of the current, and the fords of the east, which had taken the first king a hundred and twenty years before, took now a son of his, one more child of the king to die at another's hand as Iain Dubh had died, in a quarrel begun before either of the men who fought it that morning was born.

Sìleas heard it standing at the edge of the clearing with the basket-carrier still catching his breath from the last of his three days' walking, and she found, turning the news over as she had once turned the bright coal over in her lap, that she felt less for the dead man, whom she had never seen and whose quarrels were no quarrels of hers, than she did for the plain unfairness of a thing that had waited six score years to be paid, on a morning that began, for Ìomhar Dearg, with nothing more than a moved stone.

"They'll cut the Red Share now," Dòmhnall said, at her side. "Four lines have been waiting since the Roinn for an excuse to claim a piece of it."

The Red Share held whole. That was the second part of the news, arriving a season later and travelling more slowly, since it interested the carriers less than a king's son dead at a ford: Dùghall Dearg, Ìomhar's eldest son, eight hundred and twenty-three years old and already grey at the temple in the way his father had never been, took up the Red Share whole the week his father was buried, and told the four lines who came to Dùn dhearg with their old claims in hand that the share had been won with a sword once and would be kept with one again if it came to that, and none of the four, weighing what it had cost the last man who tried Ìomhar Dearg's household, thought the claim worth pressing. It was, the tellers said afterwards, the one wise thing the line of Ìomhar ever did in all its long history of feud and grazing-right and boundary stone, and it did it, as the same tellers were careful to add, for no better reason than that nobody wanted to fight for a piece of what a dead man's son had made plain he would defend to the last of his household.

Eachann Ruadh did not go home. He rode west through the night of the killing and the day after, past his own hall and past his own household, who would have hidden him gladly and been hunted for it, straight to the ground before the Hall of the Flame at Dùn ìseal, where he threw down the second spear he carried, the one he had not thrown, and sat on the bare earth within sight of Brìde's flame until the Keeper's cutters came out to him. The Hall's ground had been declared, in the first years after the Roinn, the one place on the island a feud might not follow a man, and it had never yet been tested by a killer walking onto it with the blood still on his hands. Gormshuil nic Mhuirich, who had held the flame thirty years by then and buried more of her own certainty than she cared to count in that time, came out herself to look at him.

"You have killed the king's son," she said.

"I have. Six score years late, and he never threw the first spear at Dùn thais. I have killed him all the same, and I'll not pretend to you or to Crom that I haven't." He did not raise his eyes to her. "I ask nothing of the flame. I ask only the ground."

"The ground was never yours to ask. It was sworn to every hand on the island, killer's and king's alike, or it was sworn to nothing." She looked at him a long while, an old woman by then, though not so old as the man she looked down at, and said at last, "No spear follows you past that boundary stone. What follows you past it, into whatever household still owns you, is not mine to answer for."

He lived out the rest of his life on the Hall's ground, in a hut the Keepers let him raise at its edge, cutting turf for the Hall's own fires and speaking to almost no one who came to the mountain, and when Sìleas heard the whole of it, months later and third-hand as she heard everything that happened west of the eastern wood, she thought less about the killing, which was an old story dressed in a new man's blood, than about the ground itself, sworn to hold a killer as safely as it held anyone else who stood on it, and what it meant that a place could be asked to be fair to a man in a way that no household, weighing six score years of a debt unpaid, had ever been asked to be.

## IV. Of the Shut Galleries

Gormshuil nic Mhuirich heard of the stag's people in the same season she heard of Eachann Ruadh's flight to the ground, though it came to her by a slower and quieter road: a cutter of her own galleries, home from a season working the far-eastern seam on loan to Muileann chiar's overseer, who mentioned at the Hall, without thinking much of it, that the eastern cutters had taken to counting their strokes and asking why the coal answered one hand and not another, as though the coal were a thing that owed an answer to anybody.

She did not act on it at once. Gormshuil had held the flame long enough to know that most things said of a season's loaned cutter came to nothing by the next, and she let two more years pass, hearing the same report grow a little each time it reached her, before she sent a cutter of her own east to see the wood above Muileann chiar with her own eyes and bring back a plain account of what was taught there.

The account she got back was plain enough to trouble her. The stag's people did not deny the flame, did not refuse the handful, did not set themselves against Brìde or Crom in word or in oath; what troubled Gormshuil, hearing the cutter's account by the light of the flame she alone was sworn to carry, was something harder to answer than a rival reverence would have been, because a rival reverence could be met with the flame's own claim and weighed against it before the council. The stag's people asked, beyond any question of whether the vein should be revered, why it behaved as it behaved, and a Keeper who had spent thirty years learning that the vein's behaviour was not hers to question, only to serve, found she had no ready word for a school that treated the asking as a kind of reverence, and a better one, some of its own hearers were beginning to say, than kneeling and asking nothing.

She summoned Sìleas to Dùn ìseal in the spring of Sìleas's forty-eighth year, and Sìleas came, because the mountain under the Hall was where the vein itself was thought to run truest, and she had never in her life had the chance to put her question to it directly.

They spoke in the keepers' hut, the two of them and no one else, on either side of the same fire Beathag Bhàn had once been given to hold, and neither afterwards ever gave a full account of what passed between them, holding, both of them, that some things said in that hut were said to each other and not to be carried further. What is known is only what followed. Gormshuil forbade the hearers of Sìleas nic Coinnich to cut in the galleries of Dùn ìseal, holding, when the ruling was given out at the Hall, that a question asked of the vein was a demand made of it, and that a Keeper who let a demand stand unanswered in her own galleries answered for it to every hand that trusted the flame after her. She did not forbid the school itself, having, whatever passed between them in the hut, no ground and no wish to forbid a woman from asking why a stone burned bright under her own hand and dull under her neighbour's; she forbade only the mountain to the asking, and left the wood above Muileann chiar to it entire.

Sìleas walked out of Dùn ìseal that same week and did not come back to it in the years that were left to her. She said little of the ruling to the forty and more who waited for her at the wood, beyond the plain fact of it, that the galleries under the mountain were shut to any hand that had sat in her clearing, and that the school would go on where it had always gone on, under its own trees, asking its own question of its own seam, and troubling the Hall's mountain no further.

"She is not wrong to be afraid of it," Sìleas said once, to Dòmhnall, who had never stopped asking her, all those years, what the coal would answer next. "A question, once it is let loose in a gallery, doesn't stop where the asker meant it to stop. I have never once pretended otherwise to her or to anyone."

"Are you afraid of it, then?"

"No," she said. "I only think it fair to be afraid of the thing you have started, if you mean to go on starting it."

The stag's people went on where they had always gone on, cutting their own seam in the far-eastern hills, counting their strokes, teaching a lesson that had once been interrupted by a stag and had, by then, grown too large for any single clearing to hold in comfort. In the last years of Sìleas's teaching a dozen of her oldest hearers walked east out of Muileann chiar altogether, following the wood where it thickened and the seam where it ran deeper, to raise a house of their own further from the mountain's shadow than the first clearing had ever stood, and it is that walking, the last of the mountain's cutters going east under their own trees with their own question still unanswered, that the tellers of the school still keep, in the years after Sìleas nic Coinnich, as the true beginning of all that came from her question: not the day the stag stood at the tree-line, which anyone might have seen and made nothing of, but the day forty of the eastern cutters chose to walk further from the flame than any reverence on the island had walked before, asking nothing of the mountain any longer but to be let alone with their own coal, and their own counting, and the question that had kept one woman from her bed on an ordinary evening a lifetime before.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of the Smoke and the Stone Cup

*FE 126 – 148*

> *Cha do dh'iarr mi mo shùilean air ais. Dh'iarr mi làmhan a b' fheàrr na sùilean.*
> I did not ask for my eyes back. I asked for hands better than eyes.
>
> — said of Fionnlagh Dall, called the Blind Keeper

## I. Of the Death of Gormshuil

Fionnlagh had been three days without sleep worth the name before anyone thought to tell him that Gormshuil nic Mhuirich was dying, and when the word came at last it came by a boy's hand on his sleeve rather than by any voice raised for him, since the household at Dùn ìseal had fallen into the habit, over the years of his sitting with the flame, of forgetting that a thing said across a room was no use to him at all unless someone thought to walk it over.

He had sat with the flame himself on and off since he was a boy of fourteen, one of a dozen or more the nine hearths sent up in their turns to learn the slab and the galleries under the Keeper's eye, and in all that time he had never once seen Gormshuil's face, having lost the last of his sight to a fever in his childhood, long before either of them came near Talla na Lasrach. What he had of her he had built the way he built everything, out of what came to him by other roads: the particular dryness of her voice when a household pressed her too hard for a ruling she had not yet made up her mind to give; the way she paused, always, a full breath before she said a hard thing, as if weighing whether it still wanted saying; the smell of the oil she rubbed into her hands against the cold of the galleries, which he could pick out of a crowded room before anyone spoke a word. He built her out of these the way a man born blind builds a mountain out of the wind that comes off it, and he had come, over eighty-seven years of her life and near forty of his own, to trust the picture he had built better than he trusted most things he was told he could see.

She died on the ninth night of the second month of the hundred and twenty-seventh year, in the small room off the Hall where the Keepers slept, with her cutter's daughter holding one hand and Fionnlagh, sent for late, holding the other, and the last thing she said to him, in a voice gone thin as the last of a coal's colour, was a complaint, plainly meant to be his last memory of her and, by every account he was given afterward, exactly the thing she would have wanted it to be: that the room had always been colder on his side of the bed than on hers, and no one in eighty-seven years had troubled to find out why.

He sat with her body until the household came to wash it, and when they had gone he sat a while longer with the empty bed, and it was there, by his own telling of it in the years that followed, that he first let himself think what half of Dùn ìseal had already begun to think for him, which was that the nine hearths would meet within the week to choose who carried the flame after her, and that his own name, sitter of more seasons than any man living who was not already too old to be chosen, could not honestly be left off whatever list the hearths drew up, blindness or no blindness.

## II. Of the Nine Hearths and the Boy who Led Him

The nine hearths met at Dùn ìseal on the appointed day, as they had met to choose Gormshuil after Muireach Liath and Beathag Bhàn before either of them, and heard the households argue for their own candidates through the better part of an afternoon: a strong young cutter of the fourth hearth who had never once, in six seasons, let a lamp gutter in a gallery; a niece of Gormshuil's own who carried her aunt's dry manner and, some said, a fair measure of her judgement besides; and Fionnlagh, put forward by three keepers of the slab together, no household of his own eager to claim him, on the plain ground that a man who has read the mountain by touch and hearing for twenty years knows it in ways a man who reads it by sight has never had cause to learn.

It was the niece's own household, in the end, that settled it, standing up before the hearths were done arguing to say that a Keeper's hands mattered more to the measure than a Keeper's eyes, and that they had watched Fionnlagh's hands fill a lamp steadier than any two of the other candidates' together, blind hands having no choice, as sighted hands sometimes did, but to feel exactly what they held. The nine hearths chose him before the light failed that day, the first blind man ever set to keep the flame, and it is told that when the choosing was carried to him where he sat waiting in the passage, he asked only one question of the elder who brought it, which was whether anyone had thought to ask who would walk him from the Hall to the slab and back on the mornings his own feet did not yet know the way, the galleries having grown, in Gormshuil's years, a good deal further than they had been in his own boyhood.

The answer to that came from an unlooked-for quarter within the week, in the shape of a boy of ten named Calum Beag, a grandson of one of the nine-hearth households who had taken to following Fionnlagh about the Hall since he was old enough to walk, out of nothing more than a child's plain curiosity about a man who moved through rooms he had never seen without once putting a hand wrong. The boy's own mother brought him to Fionnlagh on the third morning of his keeping and said, more or less, that the child would follow him whether she gave leave or not, and that she would rather he did it with her knowledge than without it. Fionnlagh, by his own later telling, asked the boy a single question before he agreed to anything, which was whether he could hold his tongue about what he saw in the galleries, since a Keeper's eyes, borrowed or his own, owed the vein the same silence either way; and Calum Beag, who had clearly given the matter no thought whatever before that moment, said yes so quickly and so solemnly that Fionnlagh laughed for the first time anyone at Dùn ìseal had heard him laugh since Gormshuil's death, and took the boy's shoulder in his hand, and from that day the two of them went about the Hall together, the blind Keeper and the boy who told him, in a voice pitched low enough for no one else to hear, what step came next and which face of which gallery he was standing before.

## III. Of the Smoke at Cnoc dhubh

The winter that came on within the year was harder than any the Hall's own memory reached back to plainly, and it fell hardest of all on the households of the high ground above Cnoc dhubh, a scatter of turf-roofed houses a few miles from Dùn ìseal where the wind off the mountain ran cold enough, in a bad season, to freeze the milk in the pail before a woman could carry it from byre to hearth. One household there, whose name the Hall's own roll kept afterward with a plainness that spared no one, had burned its measured handful through the early cold and found, by the turn of the year, that the handful had not been enough to keep three small children and an old woman through the worst of the nights, and so had begun, in the desperation of a house going cold around people it could not warm any other way, to burn the coal by the basketful instead, a measure no household on the island had ever burned before, since no household before that winter had ever needed to find out what a basketful would do.

What it did, over three nights of steady burning in a turf house with no chimney worth the name and a wind outside too fierce to let a door stand open, was lie down in the valley the way smoke from a green fire lies down on a still evening, thick and low and unwilling to lift, filling first the house that made it and then, before the wind changed, the two houses nearest it as well. Calum Beag was the one who brought Fionnlagh the word, three days after, having heard it first from a carrier who had smelled the valley from half a mile off and turned aside to see what burned; and it was Calum's own voice, cracking somewhere in the middle of the telling in a way that had nothing to do with a boy's changing years, that told Fionnlagh before the carrier's own account did that this was worse than any winter's ordinary grief. Five were dead of it in the end: three of the burning household, a grandmother of the house beside it who had gone in to see why no smoke rose properly from either chimney and never came out again on her own feet, and a neighbour's infant carried in its mother's arms through air that should have been safe a full house-length from the fire and was not.

Fionnlagh went up to Cnoc dhubh himself before the case was ever argued at Dùn ìseal, led by Calum Beag over ground neither of them knew well, and stood in the burned household's own doorway while a neighbour described to him, in the flat voice of a man too tired for grief to sound like grief any longer, what five bodies carried out of two houses in a single morning had looked like laid side by side on the frozen ground before anyone could dig a grave for them. He asked to touch the hearth before he left, and knelt with his hand flat against the cold stone a long while, Calum Beag said afterward, longer than seemed needed for any purpose the boy could name, until an old man of the third house, watching him, said aloud that a hearth-stone could tell a blind man nothing a burned house had not already told the whole valley. Fionnlagh, rising, answered that he had come to know what his own hands had been set over, and the stone was the surest way he had of learning it.

## IV. Of the Season of Argument

The case was carried to Dùn ìseal within the week and argued there, on and off, for the better part of the season that followed, and Fionnlagh, new to the flame and new to judgement of any kind that mattered beyond a lamp's filling, found himself sitting through arguments that circled the same ground again and again without ever quite landing on it. The dead household's kin said plainly that a house with three children and an old woman in it and only a handful of coal to warm them through the worst nights the Hall's own memory could name had no choice at all, and that a law which let people freeze rather than burn what the mountain held in more than enough for every household living was no law worth keeping. The households of the other eight hearths, frightened by what a single family's basketful had done to two houses that had burned nothing at all, said with equal plainness that the handful had held the island's peace since before any of them was born precisely because it was never argued with, and that the day a household could burn what it judged it needed rather than what the Hall measured out was the day the measure meant nothing to anyone.

Fionnlagh listened to both sides argued past each other for the better part of two months without once giving a ruling, which some of the households took, in those early days of his keeping, for a blind man's slowness and others, more rightly, for a new Keeper's unwillingness to answer a hard question before he had turned it over as many ways as it would turn. What he came to, sitting alone with it through the nights Calum Beag had gone home to his own mother's hearth, was neither of the two things argued at him: not that the measure should be loosened, since he had heard enough that season of what five deaths from too little coal could look like beside five deaths from too much of it to know the mountain's own patience was not the question, and not that the law needed no change at all, since a law no one could be certain of, held only by custom and the memory of what Beathag Bhàn and Muireach Liath had once ruled by word of mouth, had let one frightened household burn its way past the edge of what any hearth could survive before anyone stopped it.

What the mountain wanted, he came at last to think, turning the question over the way his own fingers turned a lamp's wick when he could not yet tell by touch alone whether it was trimmed even, was a measure no household could argue with, because no household could argue with its own two hands.

## V. Of the Grey Stone Re-cut

There had been a stone cup at Dùn ìseal since the Age of Ailean, a plain thing of soft pale rock that the earliest keepers of the slab had used, by tradition rather than by any law, to measure out the coal each household carried home from the galleries; but it had cracked across one side in Muireach Liath's day and been mended with clay so many times since that no two households, filling it in turn, ever quite agreed how full it ought to sit before the measure was met. Fionnlagh sent Calum Beag up into the hills above Dùn ìseal in the hundred and thirty-eighth year to find him a stone the boy judged hard and fine-grained and free of any crack a mason's eye could find, and when the boy came back three days later leading a cutter of the fourth hearth and a slab of grey stone slung between two poles, Fionnlagh spent the better part of a month with his own hands upon it before he would let the cutter's chisel near it at all.

He had the mason cut it hollow to the exact measure of his own two hands cupped together, palm to palm, the fingers curled just short of touching, since his own hands were the one instrument he trusted absolutely to be the same hands every time; and when the cutting was done he tested it himself, again and again, filling it by feel alone until he could say, blind, with his fingers alone against the stone's cold lip, whether a fill sat a hair short of the measure or a hair over it, the way another man might have tested it by eye. Calum Beag, watching him do this through most of an autumn, asked once why he did not simply mark a line on the stone's inner face for a sighted keeper to judge by, and Fionnlagh's answer, which the boy carried about the Hall afterward as though it were a thing worth keeping, was that a line could be read generously by a friend and meanly by an enemy, and a blind man's fingers, having no friends and no enemies among the coal, could not.

## VI. Of the Threshold Found by the Foot

He set the finished cup, when it was done, on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach, the worn stone slab between the Hall's own ground and the path that every household walked to reach it, rather than inside the Hall where the old one had always stood within reach of whichever keeper the council favoured that season. There any man or woman with a claim to the coal could see, or be told by a neighbour who could see, that the cup sat in the open where no keeper's favour could shield it from any eye.

He found the threshold's exact centre himself, on the day he set the cup, by walking the width of the doorway with his own bare feet until he felt the worn place where centuries of households had crossed it evenest, the stone smoothed to a hollow no deeper than a fingernail's width by feet that had none of them meant to wear it so, and it was there, kneeling with the cup before him and Calum Beag standing silent at his shoulder, that he filled it for the first council to come and ask.

The household of the fourth hearth that came first that morning was a poor one, its elder an old woman whose hands shook with a palsy the cold made worse, and Fionnlagh, hearing the shake in her own voice before he ever touched her hand to guide it, filled the cup by touch alone and held it out to her level, not favouring the low reach an old woman's trembling arms might have asked for nor demanding the steady one a young man's would have given without thought. "Give me the coal," he said, and she gave it into the cup's mouth handful by handful from the household's own store until his fingers, resting light along the stone's rim, told him the measure was met; and when it was met he said only "Enough," and closed his own hand over the cup's lip so that no more could follow, whether the old woman's shaking hand meant to give more or not. It is told, and the households of the fourth hearth kept the telling a long while, that she wept a little at the fairness of it, having gone to every council for three years certain that a sighted keeper favoured whichever household stood nearest his own eye, and having found in a blind one's hands the first measure she had ever trusted absolutely.

## VII. Of the Law Sworn at Samhain

Word of the cup on the threshold ran ahead of Fionnlagh through that autumn faster than any ruling he had yet given in council, and by the time the lords of the shares gathered at Dùn ìseal for the Samhain gathering of the hundred and forty-second year, most of the island's households had already heard, from a neighbour or a neighbour's neighbour, that a blind man's hands had found a measure no one could quarrel with. Fionnlagh put the custom to the lords plainly that Samhain, standing before the assembled council with Calum Beag's hand light at his elbow: that the measured handful, held till then by nothing firmer than a Keeper's word and the memory of two dead Keepers before him, should be sworn as a law binding on every share alike, north and south, the Red Share and the lowland plain together, so that no household anywhere on the island might burn more than the cup on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach would give it in a season.

The lords grumbled, as lords of every share had grumbled at every measure laid on them since the Roinn, several rising to say that a law was a poor thing to bind on people who had kept the custom faithfully enough without one, and that the Hall had never before told a share what it might or might not burn on its own hearths. But the five who had died at Cnoc dhubh were not so far behind any of them that the argument could be pressed very hard, and in the end it was not Fionnlagh's own words that carried the council so much as the memory, fresh in every lord's mind that autumn, of the old woman of the fourth hearth weeping over a cup that had measured her fairly for the first time in three years. The lords swore to the law that Samhain, one by one, each laying a hand on the stone cup where it sat on the threshold; and when the last of them had sworn, Fionnlagh, who could not see a single one of the hands that had touched the stone that day, said only that he trusted the measure to hold them to it better than any oath would, since a cup, unlike a lord, could not be argued out of its own fullness. So the custom of the handful hardened that day into the Small-Burning Law, the first law that ran the same in every share the island held, made by no lord of any share and grumbled at by all of them, and it held, unaltered by a word, for longer than any man living that Samhain would ever have thought to guess.

## VIII. Of the First Sentence

It was a household of Seann Tarr, a fishing town on the north-eastern coast that had never before troubled the Hall's roll for anything worse than a boundary dispute over drying-racks, that gave the new law its first sentence, in the hundred and forty-fifth year, having burned twice its measure in a single season against a run of wet weather that had kept its boats ashore and its store of dried fish thinner than any winter before it. The household's elder came to Dùn ìseal himself to argue the case before the council, laying out plainly that a fisher's household without fish to trade for grain had needed the extra coal to smoke what little catch the weather allowed rather than lose it to the damp entirely, and that a law meant to spare lives had very nearly cost his own.

Fionnlagh heard him out at length, and Calum Beag, a man of seven-and-twenty by then and still standing beside the Keeper through a whole council's sitting without his attention wandering, told him afterward that the old man's hands had shaken through the whole of his telling in a way that had nothing to do with cold. But the law Fionnlagh had sworn at Samhain three years before allowed no household's need, however honest, to loosen a measure sworn the same for every hearth on the island, and he ruled at last, with what Calum Beag remembered as real reluctance in the set of his shoulders, that the household of Seann Tarr should lose its right to the coal for the season following, its name set upon the roll with the offence beside it. It was the harshest thing Fionnlagh had yet done as Keeper, and the household's own descendants, the tellers of Seann Tarr say still, petitioned Dùn ìseal for generation after generation afterward to have the offence struck from the roll, and were refused every time, the roll itself having become, by then, a thing the Hall would sooner let stand unaltered than see loosened for any household's asking, however old the wrong or however honest the need that had first caused it.

## IX. Of the Fires that Answer to Nobody

The last question the law raised that Fionnlagh had to answer came from the headland at Tobar dhearg, from no household's own hearth, where a beacon had burned, time out of mind, to warn boats off the rocks on a black night, fed by whatever coal the households nearest it could spare from their own measured store. A fisherman of that coast asked the council, in the hundred and forty-eighth year, whether a beacon lit for the safety of strangers who might never set foot on the island at all ought to be counted against a household's handful the same as a fire lit for its own hearth, since a light that answered to no one household's need seemed to him a different thing from a fire that warmed a family's own children.

Fionnlagh turned the question over for the better part of a day, Calum Beag told it afterward, sitting alone with the stone cup at his own hand the way he had sat with it through the season of the smoke at Cnoc dhubh, and the ruling he gave in the end went further than the fisherman had asked for. No coal at all, he ruled, might feed a beacon meant to warn strangers off the rocks, since the vein's fire was the island's own and owed nothing to a boat that might never touch the shore it warned away from; and from that ruling the beacon at Tobar dhearg was kept after with driftwood gathered off the tideline and seal fat rendered down for the purpose, a poorer light than coal would have given and, by every account the fishermen of that coast kept afterward, a steadier one, since driftwood and seal fat answered to no measure at all and never once, in all the years that followed, ran short at the one hour a black night made it matter. Every sea-light raised on the island after Tobar dhearg's was kept the same way, on the same ruling, and the households of that coast, telling of it to their own children afterward, said that the blind Keeper had judged rightly what a fire owed to its own people and what it owed to no one at all, which was, they said, a harder thing to see plainly than it sounds, and a thing a man with his eyes about him might easily have judged the other way.

Fionnlagh himself, asked once in his old age by a stag's teacher passing through Dùn ìseal why he had ruled the beacon apart from every other fire on the island, gave an answer Calum Beag, by then long grown and still at the old man's side, remembered word for word to the end of his own life: that a man who cannot see a fire learns early to judge it only by what it is for, and that the coal under the mountain, whatever else it was, had never once in all the island's telling been for a stranger.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of the Carriers and the First Bridges

*FE 149 – 163*

> *Fìrinn nach do bhris i a rinn an drochaid làidir.*
> The truth it never broke made the bridge strong.
>
> — the masons' saying at the crossing of Ros fhionn

## I. Of the Carrier's Trade

Fionnlagh Dall was nine and fifty in the year the Small-Burning Law first bore hard on the households it bound, and Calum Beag, the boy who had led him about the Hall since his own choosing, was grown to a man who no longer needed telling which gallery he stood before, though he still told him anyway, out of a habit neither of them had ever troubled to break. The law that had hardened at Samhain three years before had made the Hall, for the first time in the mountain's memory, a giver-out rather than merely a keeper: a household came to the threshold of Talla na Lasrach with its claim, and the stone cup filled and emptied, and what the cup gave out had then to travel, on somebody's back, to every hearth of every share that had sworn to take no more than its measure and not a handful over it.

It had travelled, before that year, along whatever track a foot had worn first and every foot after had worn a little deeper, up over the mountain's shoulder and down through country that had never once been asked to bear a laden basket every week of every year, in whatever weather a year chose to send. A carrier's trade had grown up around the coal the way a trade grows up around any need that will not go away of its own accord, households of no land and little standing who carried for hire or for their own dues both, their baskets marked by hearth so that a household's own measure could be told from its neighbour's on the road, and it was a hard trade and a thankless one, praised by no one when the basket arrived whole and cursed roundly when it did not, and it was the carriers, more than any lord or Keeper, who came first to know exactly which miles of the island's paths a winter's rain could not be trusted to leave standing.

The southern households, whose dried fish came up the same tracks the coal went down by, felt the want of a proper road before any other share did, since the last mile above the harbour of Ceann chaol dropped so steep between two shoulders of bare rock that a carrier with a full basket went down it sideways, one shoulder to the stone, or did not go down it at all in wet weather, and more than one had gone down it faster than his own feet meant to and come up afterward with an ankle that never again carried a load the same way.

## II. Of Ailean Clachair and the Steps to Ceann chaol

Ailean Clachair was four and twenty that year, a cutter of the fourth hearth who had spent the better part of his growing years with a chisel in his hand rather than a basket on his back, the same boy, grown now to a man, who had gone up into the hills above Dùn ìseal eleven years before to help a child named Calum Beag carry down the grey stone the blind Keeper had wanted for his cup. He had cut stair-steps into a hillside before, for a byre that needed them and a well that needed them worse, and when the council at Dùn ìseal asked, in the hundred and forty-ninth year, whether anyone among the nine hearths' cutters would take on the steep mile above Ceann chaol, it was Ailean who stood forward first, more from a young man's wanting of a task worth his hands than from any thought of what the task would grow into.

He worked at it through the better part of two years with six others of the fourth hearth, cutting the steps where the rock allowed a step to be cut and setting fitted stone where it did not, a foot's width at a time down a fall that had killed no one outright but had turned more ankles than the Hall's own roll troubled to count. That work taught him what stone would hold a man's step wet and what stone would not, a different knowledge from the knowledge of a well-shaft or a byre wall, and a knowledge, though he did not know it yet, that the whole of the rest of his life would be built upon. The path was finished in the hundred and fifty-first year, steps enough that a carrier with a full basket could go down to Ceann chaol on a wet morning without once setting a hand to the rock, and the Hall's baskets went down it after that, and the dried fish of the south came up it, faster and drier than either had ever gone before.

## III. Of the Rising of the Abhainn dhomhain

It was the Abhainn dhomhain that took what the steps to Ceann chaol had spared, in the hundred and fifty-fourth year, on a night in the last days of an t-Samhain when a rain that had fallen steadily for three days turned, sometime past midnight, into a rain that fell as though the sky itself had broken open. The river ran deep in ordinary weather, deep enough that its name had never asked for any better reason, but it ran fordable at the one crossing the carriers' road used, a wide gravel shallow where a man could cross with a basket on his back and the water no higher than his knees on any day the Hall's own memory reached back to.

Eleven carriers crossed it that night, a party bound south with the Hall's baskets for the households beyond the ford, walking by the last light because the rain had already cost them half the day and a household waiting on its handful in a bad season was not a household a carrier liked to keep waiting past its need. They had crossed that ford a hundred times between them, in every season the mountain sent, and it is told that the leader of the party, a woman of many years on the road named Beathag nan Cliabh for the baskets she had carried since she was a girl, said only that the water looked no worse than a spring flood she remembered from her own youth, and led them into it on that word.

The river that had stood knee-deep at dusk stood chest-deep and rising by the time the last of them was halfway across, the current carrying down branches and, before long, whole trees torn out by their roots somewhere upstream in the dark, striking a man's legs from under him before he ever felt the water grow too strong to stand in. It stood over a tall man's head, by the account of the one carrier who turned back at the water's edge rather than follow the rest in, before the party on the far bank could so much as call a warning across it, the sound of the river by then too loud for any voice to carry over. Eleven were lost that night, baskets and all, and the one who had turned back, a young man new enough to the trade that his own fear had not yet learned shame, walked the two hours to the nearest hearth in the dark and the rain to say so, arriving with nothing in his own hands but the knowledge of what he had watched happen and had not been able to stop, and it is told that he did not carry the Hall's coal again for the better part of a year afterward, though no one at the Hall ever once asked it of him.

## IV. Of the Names of the Drowned

The bodies came down with the flood over the days that followed, most of them within a few miles of the ford, two of them not at all, taken out to the sea by a river running harder than any living carrier had seen it run before or would see it run again for the better part of a century. The Hall kept on its cords a tally of names it had never before had cause to keep in quite that shape, eleven names knotted together under one night, and it is told that Fionnlagh Dall asked to have each name said to him twice before he would let the tally be tied off, so that he might be certain he had heard each one and not merely the sound of a list.

Beathag nan Cliabh, who had led the party in on her own word that the water looked no worse than a flood she remembered from her girlhood, went into it near the last, having stood in the current a long while calling the others on before her own footing gave way beneath her; the households of the road kept her name afterward the way a trade keeps the name of one who is blamed by no one and forgiven by everyone, since a leader's word, honestly given from a life's worth of crossing, could fail a party as surely as a coward's could, and had failed no one before that night. Griogair mac Ailig went into the water early, by the turned-back carrier's account, having gone ahead to test the ford's depth as the party's habit was on a rising night, and Sìneag nighean Dhonnchaidh went in trying to reach a hand to him rather than let go of her own basket's strap, which the households afterward held against her not at all, though some said privately that a strap was a poor thing to die holding. A boy not yet come to his full growth, whose name the Hall's tally gives only as young Tormod of the salt shore, had asked to go on the crossing that night in place of an uncle whose knee had gone bad in the wet, and it was that uncle, whole and dry on the near bank, who lived after to tell what his own knee had cost.

It is told, and told still by the households of that stretch of road, that the carriers who came after made a joke of their own grief within the season, saying that the Hall mourned its coal along with its dead, since eleven baskets of the mountain's own coal had gone into the sea with the eleven who carried them, and that a joke told against oneself in that manner was the only kind of grief a carrier's trade had ever found room for. Fionnlagh, hearing the joke repeated to him by Calum Beag, did not rebuke it. He said only that a mountain that measured its coal so carefully against a household's need might, in fairness, be allowed to grieve a basketful lost the same way its people grieved a life, and that he saw no unkindness in a carrier who let both griefs sit in the one sentence, since both, that night, had gone into the water together.

## V. Of Fionnlagh's Asking

Fionnlagh brought the matter to the council himself within the fortnight, led to the Hall's own ground by Calum Beag as he was led everywhere, and asked the assembled lords and hearth-elders a question none of them, by the plain evidence of the silence that met it, had thought to ask in all the years the ford had served them. He asked for a crossing the river could not take, whatever weather might come against it, so that no household waiting on its handful should ever again cost a carrier's life for the waiting.

The lords who spoke first spoke of cost and of years, a ford having served well enough for longer than any of them had lived, and one of the elders of the southern hearths, a stout old man named Neacal who had buried two carriers of his own household to lesser fords in his own lifetime, said plainly that a river which rose once in a generation to kill eleven people was, taken across the whole of that generation, no worse a risk than a hill-track in winter or a boat on the western sea, and that the Hall could not build itself proof against every misfortune the mountain's own weather might send it. "You would have us throw stone at every ford on the island," he said, "against a flood that comes once in a man's life, and leave the coal the poorer for the labour spent on it." Fionnlagh heard him out, as he heard out every argument brought against him, sitting with his own hands folded in his lap the whole of the old man's speaking, and answered only that his question was whether the risk could be made smaller. "A cup that measures fair by the fill of two hands," he said, "asks no household to trust its fortune to luck. I see little reason a carrier's life should trust to luck what stone and labour might answer for instead." It is told that he asked, last of all, whether any man in the hall could name him a mason who had already proved his hand against water and weight, and that more than one voice answered him with the same name, which was Ailean Clachair's, the cutter of the fourth hearth whose steps above Ceann chaol a wet winter had not yet found a way to break.

## VI. Of the Forty of the Nine Hearths

Ailean was sent for the same week, and stood before the council a man of nine and twenty with stone-dust still under his nails from a well he had left half finished at another household's asking, and heard the Keeper's charge laid on him in fewer words than the council's own arguing about it had taken: a single crossing above Ros fhionn, where the Abhainn dhomhain ran narrower and its banks stood higher and firmer than anywhere else along its whole reach, built to stand against any flood the river might ever again choose to send it. He answered, by his own later telling of it, that he did not yet know whether such a thing could be built at all, a span of stone thrown clear across water that wide having been done nowhere on the island that any living mason could name him, but that he would rather try it and fail than tell a Keeper who had just buried eleven carriers that it could not be tried.

He went to Fionnlagh once more before the calling began, alone, without Calum Beag to hear it, and asked the Keeper plainly whether he understood that the thing might fail, that a mason of nine and twenty with nothing behind him but a stair of steps and a boyhood spent carrying a blind man's cup-stone might throw a season's labour and the Hall's own coal-dues into a river and have nothing to show for it but a heap of cut stone on either bank. Fionnlagh's answer, which Calum Beag had from Ailean's own mouth many years after and kept it word for word the rest of his life, was that he had asked no mason living for a certainty, having buried eleven carriers already on the strength of a ford everyone had called certain, and that he would rather trust a young man's honest doubt than an old man's easy promise, since a promise too easily given was, in his experience, the surest sign of a thing not properly thought through. Ailean carried that answer with him through the whole of the building that followed, and told the forty, more than once when the work went hard, that a Keeper who could not see the bridge at all had trusted it further than any of them yet trusted their own hands.

He drew from the nine hearths, over the winter that followed, every cutter and mason he judged worth the calling, forty in the end, men and women who had cut wells and byres and boundary-stones and the steps above Ceann chaol and had never, any of them, cut anything that had to hold a whole river rather than a roof. They quarried through the worst of the cold at a face of grey stone not far from Ros fhionn, close enough grained, Ailean judged, to bear the load without splitting, and spent the better part of a season only in learning how a stone cut to a wedge's shape would lean upon its neighbours and hold up its own weight by leaning, a thing none of the forty had understood in their bones before that winter taught it to them by the plain evidence of stones that fell when cut wrong and stones that stood when cut right.

## VII. Of the Single Span above Ros fhionn

The span went up through the spring and summer of the hundred and sixtieth year, one course of fitted stone above another, each stone cut and set and tested by hand before the next was laid, Ailean himself walking the scaffold at every hour of daylight and, by Calum Beag's telling of what he heard from the masons afterward, at a good many hours of dark besides, unwilling to trust any course to the morning that he had not first trusted to his own eye by lamplight the night before. The forty worked from both banks toward the river's middle, on wooden centring that carried the weight of each course until the arch could carry it itself, and it was on that centring, in the sixth week of the building, that a mason of the ninth hearth named Aonghas Beag put a foot wrong on a wet timber and went down toward the water with a half-cut stone still in his arms, caught at the very edge of the fall by two others who had his belt in their hands before his own mind had understood what his feet had already done. Ailean would not let the man back onto the scaffold that day nor the next. He told the forty plainly that he trusted Aonghas Beag as much as any of them; a mason frightened in his own body simply cut stone worse than a mason who had learned to steady his fright first, and a bridge meant to answer for other men's lives asked steadied hands before it asked anything else.

The arch closed at last on a morning in the height of summer when the keystone, the single wedge of stone that would hold every other stone in its place by the same leaning weight that held them all, was raised on ropes and levers by every hand the forty could spare and set into the gap the rest of the arch had left for it. Ailean himself guided it the last hand's-width into its place, kneeling astride the gap with the river running loud beneath him, and it is told that the whole forty stood silent on both banks while the ropes came free, since a keystone wrongly seated could bring the two half-arches down together before anyone standing near enough to help could do more than watch it happen.

It held. The scaffold came down within the week, board by board, until the arch stood alone over the water on nothing but its own weight and its own shape, a single span of fitted stone thrown clean across the Abhainn dhomhain where eleven carriers had gone into it four years before, and it is told that Ailean, standing beneath it on the gravel bank where the ford had been, wept without shame in front of the whole forty, having not, by his own account, believed with his whole heart until that morning that the thing would truly stand.

## VIII. Of the Hearth-Sign in the Keystone

Before the scaffold came down Ailean climbed back up to the keystone and cut into its face, with his own hand and no other's, a small mark that the fourth hearth had used among its own cutters for as long as any of them could remember, a sign no household outside the trade would have known to read but every mason of the nine hearths knew at a glance, meant to say, to any eye that troubled to look for it, that the stone above it had been raised by hands that answered for their own work. He had not been asked to cut it there, and told the forty afterward, when some asked why, that a bridge a man's own name might be forgotten from within a generation ought at least to carry some mark that said a living hand, and not chance, had set it standing.

The mark caught on faster than the bridge did, in the way of things a trade takes up before the wider Hall has quite noticed it happening. Every span the forty raised after Ros fhionn's carried the same sign cut somewhere into its keystone or its central course, and within a handful of years it was said, first among carriers and then more widely, that a crossing without the mark was a crossing built by hands that had not troubled to answer for their own work. That was an unfair thing to say of many an honest builder who had simply never learned the fourth hearth's sign, and it was said all the same, often enough that it became, before Ailean himself was an old man, very nearly as good as a law.

## IX. Of the Oath Sworn on the Stone Cup

It was in the winter following the bridge's raising that the forty, gathered at Dùn ìseal to be paid what the council had promised them for the season's labour, asked Fionnlagh whether they might swear something of their own before the Hall, a fellowship bound together the way the nine hearths were bound, so that a mason called to one crossing might trust a mason called to another to hold the same measure. Fionnlagh heard the asking with what Calum Beag remembered as a plain pleasure, and set the matter before them at the threshold of Talla na Lasrach, on the same worn stone where the cup that measured the coal sat open to any eye that cared to look.

They swore two things that day, each of the forty laying a hand on the stone cup in turn as the lords of the shares had laid their hands on it three years before, Aonghas Beag among them, his own hand steady on the stone though Calum Beag said afterward it had shaken through the whole of the walk to the threshold: that no span they raised would ever be closed to a traveller in the dark, a bridge shut against the night being, in a mason's own reckoning, no better than a bridge that had never been built at all; and that no span would ever be paid for in coal, since a crossing built to spare carriers' lives ought not be bought with the very coal those carriers' lives were spared to carry. Fionnlagh, who could not see a single hand laid on the stone that day any more than he had seen the lords' hands laid on it before, said to the forty what he had said to the council then, that he trusted the cup to hold them to an oath better than any spoken word would, and it is told that Ailean answered him, half in earnest and half in the plain wit of a young man still giddy with his own bridge standing, that a mason trusted stone before he trusted anything else living or dead, his own self not excepted, and saw no reason a Keeper should not do the same.

## X. Of the Lodge at the Western Ford

The forty did not scatter, once Ros fhionn's crossing was finished and paid for, the way a gathering of cutters called for one task commonly did, but kept themselves together under Ailean's leading and took on, over the two years that followed, three crossings more where the carriers' roads asked for them, the last and widest of the three above a ford in the country of Ros dhomhain that the western share's own herds had used, badly, for longer than any living herder's memory reached. They raised there, once the western span was finished, a plain stone lodge of their own beside the crossing, a hall no grander than any nine-hearth's own gathering-house, where a mason called from any share could find a roof and a fire and a fellow of the trade to hear what stone he had cut that season and how it had answered him.

It was at the western crossing, in the hundred and sixty-third year, not at Ros fhionn's own span, that the fourth hearth's mark was tested for the first time against a bridge that did not carry it. A wright of Ros dhomhain, impatient of the mason's slow season and the mason's higher wage, had thrown a lighter crossing of his own a half day's walk upriver, unmarked, over a narrower reach that his own eye judged safe enough for a laden carrier, and a carrier of the Hall's baskets, coming to it after dark on a night the western span lay a weary two hours further on, stood at its near end a long while by his fellow's account and would not cross it, saying only that he had sworn no oath himself, that he knew well enough whose oath a bridge without the sign had not been built under, and that he would rather sleep cold on the near bank than trust his basket, and his own neck besides, to a crossing no mason living would answer for. He slept cold that night, and carried word of it to Dùn ìseal within the week, and it is told that Fionnlagh, hearing it, asked Calum Beag to set the carrier's name on the same roll that had once held the names of the eleven drowned, this time among the living the fourth hearth's mark and the oath sworn upon the stone cup had kept that way.

The Hall had been, in the years before the Small-Burning Law, a keeper only, a thing a household went up to and came down from, its business finished at the threshold where the cup filled and emptied. It was a giver-out now, and a giver-out, Fionnlagh had come to understand before that ninth year was out, owed its people more than a fair measure at the door; it owed them a road the measure could travel by without asking a life for every basket lost to bad weather or bad stone. The forty of the nine hearths went on cutting spans across the shares for a long while after Ros fhionn's, under Ailean's leading and, when he was old, under the leading of masons he himself had taught the trade to, and it was said of every one of their crossings, long after the flood on the Abhainn dhomhain had passed out of any living carrier's own memory into the Hall's roll alone, that a bridge with the fourth hearth's mark in its keystone was a bridge a man might cross in the dark without once wondering whether the stone beneath his feet had been asked to answer for its own standing.

# Chapter Fifteen: Of Mòr nic Dhùghaill's House and the Blind Keeper's Last Road

*FE 164 – 189*

> *Cha tarraing lann fo mo mhullach.*
> No blade is drawn under my roof.
>
> — the carriers' word for the road-peace, kept first at the house of Mòr nic Dhùghaill of Doire shean

## I. Of the House at Doire shean

It is told at the long table still, by carriers who never knew her and never will, that Mòr nic Dhùghaill kept the first house on the mountain road for no better reason than that her husband had died leaving her a widow's third of a poor herd of buffalo and a worse third of a stony croft above Doire shean, and that a woman with more beasts than grass to feed them on had to find some use for the meat before the winter found it for her. The carriers' road had not long been cut then, the stepped path down to Ceann chaol still raw where the masons' picks had bitten it, and the baskets going west to the harbour households and the dried fish coming back passed within a stone's throw of her own door twice in every week the weather allowed it, which in the mountain's early seasons was not every week.

She began, the telling goes, by boiling a haunch for her own table on a night three carriers stopped to ask shelter from a rain that had turned the stepped path to a chute of mud, and by finding, the next morning, that word of a widow who fed a wet man hot meat and asked no payment for it travelled the road faster than any basket on it. Within the year she had built a second room onto the croft with her own hands and a neighbour's, and within two she had given up the herd's wool trade entirely and kept buffalo for the pot alone, jugged slow over a low fire the whole night through the way her mother had taught her against a lean season, until the smell of it, carriers said afterward, could be caught a quarter-mile off on a still evening and would turn a tired man's feet toward her door before his own head had properly decided to. The Hall at Dùn ìseal, which had built the road for its baskets and thought little else about it, gained thereby a waypoint it had not asked for and would not, in all the years after, have known how to do without; and it is because of that house, raised for no purpose grander than a widow's grass and a widow's grief, that every circuit-house on the island since has kept a name rather than a number, the way the Hall's own galleries never did.

Mòr herself, by the account carriers older than these ones gave of her, was a broad, plain-spoken woman of thirty-four when the first three men came in out of the rain, grey-eyed like half the households of that mountainside, with a laugh that came easily and a temper that came more easily still to any man who thought a widow's table was owed him for nothing.
