She fed every traveller the road sent her the same portion in the same pot regardless of what share he carried a token from, a lord's man and a smith's boy and a beggar off the coast road eating from the one ladle in the order they arrived rather than the order their blood might have claimed, and when a steward of the Red Share once objected, early on, to eating below a fisherman who had come to the door first, she told him, in words the carriers still repeat nearly word for word, that the pot did not know one man's blood from another's and neither, under her roof, would she trouble herself to. He ate below the fisherman, and came back the following season, and ate below whoever the road had sent ahead of him that time too.

## II. Of the Second House at the Meeting of the Roads

The road grew faster than any one widow's pot could feed it, and within a handful of years a second house stood where the carriers' way down from the mountain met the road running west to the harbours, raised by three families of the fourth hearth together, who had watched what a fed and rested carrier was worth to a basket's safe delivery and judged, rightly enough, that a second such house a day's walk from the first would lose them nothing and gain the road a great deal. They built it long and low of turf and timber both, a hearth burning at either end of the one room rather than the single hearth Mòr kept, so that carriers coming down off the mountain with the day's cold still in their bones might sit at one fire while carriers going up, dry and rested and dreading the climb ahead of them, sat at the other, the two fires never quite meeting in the middle of the room though the same roof covered both and the same door let a man choose which end he wanted before he had so much as shrugged off his pack.

It became the custom of that second house, within its own first year, that a man might cross from the down-fire to the up-fire and back as many times as he liked in an evening, trading news of the road behind him for news of the road ahead, and carriers who had never once spoken a word to each other on the mountain path, being strangers of different hearths with baskets to mind and no leisure for talk, found themselves, over a bowl at that long central table, telling each other things they had not troubled to tell their own households: where a ford had shifted since the spring flood, which of the lodgings kept a dog that bit and which kept one that only barked, whose basket had been light at the last weighing and whose scale a wise man watched. It was at that table, more than at any council held under the Hall's own roof, that the road first began to feel like one thing rather than a scatter of separate paths each household walked alone, and it is at that same table, the carriers say, laying a hand flat on the wood as they say it, that the custom which came to be sworn a law was first kept without anyone troubling to call it one.

## III. Of the Chase Stopped at the Door

The custom found its first true test in the hundred and seventy-fifth year, when a man of the eastern shares came pounding down the mountain road at a run in the last light of an autumn evening with three of his cousin's household not far behind him and a grievance between the two houses old enough that neither side troubled any longer to say aloud what had started it, only that a knife had been drawn somewhere upriver that morning and a man's arm opened to the bone, and that the arm's owner's kin meant to have the opening answered before the sun rose on a second day.

He came in at Mòr's own door, the telling has it, white to the lips and past speech for the first several breaths, and threw himself down on the bench nearest the fire with no more ceremony than a stranger begging shelter from rain, and Mòr, who by then had fed carriers and lords' men and beggars alike under that roof for near ten years and had learned to read a hunted man's face the way another woman read weather, did not ask him his business before she set a bowl in front of him, only told him, once the bowl was down, to eat it while it was hot, since a man eats slower with food in his mouth than with none, and a slower man was easier to talk sense to. His cousin's three came in not a quarter-hour behind him, knives still at their belts and their own faces set for whatever the door might hold, and found the man they had chased sitting at Mòr's own table with a bowl of her jugged buffalo half gone in front of him and Mòr herself standing between the table and the door with her arms folded and her feet planted as if she had grown there.

What passed between them the carriers tell several ways, and none of the ways quite agree on her exact words, but every telling keeps the shape of it the same: that she told the three men plainly there would be no blade drawn under her roof for any grievance whatever, old or new, hers or another's, because a house that fed every traveller from the one pot regardless of his blood could not, in the same breath, let one traveller's blood be spilled across the same floor, and that whatever the two houses owed each other could wait until both sides of it had walked back out through her door and off her own ground, at which point it was no longer any affair of hers what they did to each other on the open road. The three stood a long moment weighing a widow's word against a debt of honour older than most of them could properly account for, and then, the telling says, the eldest of the three sat down at the table's far end, a careful distance from the man he had chased, close enough to watch him and far enough to say nothing by it, and asked Mòr, in a voice gone suddenly and plainly tired, whether there was more of the pot for three hungry men who had run the best part of five miles for nothing they could now collect on. She served them, and the four of them ate in a silence that held the whole length of the meal, and when it was done the hunted man rose first and walked out into the dark without a word to any of them, and the three cousins gave him a full quarter-hour's start, by Mòr's own later telling of it, before they rose themselves and went out after him into the same dark, and what happened on the road that night beyond her door the house never learned, and did not, the tellers say, greatly wish to.

## IV. Of Niall Òg at the Long Table

Word of the chase stopped at Mòr's door ran the road faster than any basket that season, carried hearth to hearth and house to house the way the smell of her pot had once travelled it, and it reached, before the year was out, the ears of Niall Òg, who by then had outlived so many quarrels of blood that a new one seldom troubled him to cross a valley for, but who came anyway, on foot as he came everywhere, to see for himself the house where a widow's word had held two feuding houses to the one table.

He arrived unannounced on an evening much like the one that had made the house's name, and sat himself at the long table's middle without asking leave of anyone, an old man by the mountain's own reckoning though not so very old by the reckoning of his own kin, who ate what was set before him and said little for the better part of an hour, watching the room fill and empty around him the way a man watches a river he has crossed many times before. When Mòr herself came at last to see who the quiet stranger at her table was, he told her his name plainly, as he told it to whoever asked, and watched her face for the flicker of recognition that came to most faces at the hearing of it, the name of a grandson of Ailean Mòr being one that carried its own weight on any share of the island by then, whatever the man himself had done or not done to earn it.

She gave him no more and no less than she gave any other traveller, the same bowl and the same place at the same table, and it is told that he thanked her for it with more warmth than he had thanked a host in a long while, saying that he had sat at more tables in his life than he cared to number, heirs' tables and lords' tables and the Hall's own table more than once, and that most of them had given him a better seat than his neighbour's for no reason but his blood, which he had come, over the centuries, to find a wearying kind of courtesy rather than an honour. He asked her, before he left the next morning, whether she had ever turned a man from her door for the house he carried a token from rather than for anything he had done himself, and when she answered that she had not and could not see the sense in starting, he laughed, the carriers say, longer and more freely than the household had ever heard a stranger laugh at that table, and told her that she had managed, without ever once sitting at the gathering-house floor or hearing the cord counted, a trick the whole of Ailean's scattered kin had spent a hundred and seventy years failing at among themselves. He left a ring of silver behind him on the table when he went, worth more than the meal by any measure, and when Mòr sent a boy running after him to give it back, as she gave back every payment offered under that roof, he would not take it, saying only that a man who had outlived every one of his own quarrels could afford, once in a great while, to pay for a peace he had not made himself.

## V. Of the Names Kept at the Harbours

In those same years the road's reach carried households far past the mountain's own shoulder, down to two harbours on the western shore of Loch chrom that no one of the nine hearths had settled before, though both had stood, empty and roofless, since some earlier people's time the oldest tellers could not put a name to. Fishers of the nine hearths came first to the nearer of the two, finding a scatter of old house-footings above a good landing and a name for the place already fixed in the mouths of the few herders who grazed the ground nearby, a name not of their own tongue and not, so far as any of them could tell, of any tongue spoken on the island in their fathers' time either. They kept the name rather than giving it one of their own making, on the plain reasoning, passed down since in the carriers' own song of it, that a name found already standing on a place, like a house-footing found already dug, had more right to stay than any new one a stranger could invent to replace it; and Seann Mhorn it remained, the carriers still singing, on the road between the mountain and the sea, that the stones came with the name and the name came with the stones, and no one who settled there afterward had ever troubled to ask whose.

Families walking the same road a season or two later found the second harbour a short way along the same shore, house-footings there as well and a name of its own already fixed to it the same way, and settled it in the same spirit, building on the old footings without asking, the song has it, whose hands had first laid them. Seann Warr they kept it, as their neighbours up the shore had kept Seann Mhorn, and the two harbours grew together in the years after as two ends of one growing town might grow, sharing a landing and a market day and, before long, a single waypoint house of their own where the road from the mountain came down at last to meet the sea, so that a carrier walking the whole circuit from Dùn ìseal to the western shore and back again might sleep, by the century's end, under a roof at every day's remove of the journey and never once lie out in the open unless the weather denied him a door.

## VI. Of the Keeper's Last Asking

Fionnlagh Dall kept the flame at Dùn ìseal a full fifty-six years from the day the nine hearths first chose him, longer by a good margin than any Keeper before him, and it was in the hundred and eighty-fourth year, an old man of four-and-ninety with a body that had begun, in its last seasons, to fail him in ways his blindness never had, that he called Calum Beag to his own bedside in the small room off the Hall and told him, in a voice gone thin but not yet unsteady, what he wished done with him when the failing was finished.

He did not ask, he said, to be laid on the slope above Dùn ìseal with the Keepers who had gone before him, Beathag Bhàn and Muireach Liath and Gormshuil nic Mhuirich each in their own turn, though no one in the Hall would have thought it strange had he asked for exactly that. He asked instead to be carried south, to the old graves near Cnoc dhìreach that no household or share on the island had ever claimed for its own, a burying-ground older, by every account the mountain's oldest tellers could give, than any name the island now used for anything upon it. Calum Beag, who had led him by the elbow through the Hall's own galleries for more than fifty years and had grown, in that time, from a boy of ten who followed him out of plain curiosity into a man grey at the temples himself, asked him why, since a Keeper's own ground lay ready and waiting not a stone's throw from the Hall he had served his whole life. Fionnlagh's answer, which Calum carried afterward the whole rest of his own life and repeated to whoever asked though he never claimed to understand it fully himself, was that a man who had spent fifty-six years judging what belonged to whom, coal to household and household to share and share to the whole island besides, wished at the last to lie somewhere that belonged to no one, in ground that had never once been divided by any cord or counted by any hearth, and that if the Hall's own roll could not say who the old graves at Cnoc dhìreach belonged to, that was, to his own mind, the surest recommendation the ground could carry.

He died within the month, in the small room off the Hall with Calum Beag's hand in his own, and it is told that his last words were not a ruling of any kind, as some at Dùn ìseal had half expected of a man who had spent his whole life giving them, but a plain question to Calum about whether the boy — he called him that still, at the last, though the boy by then had grey in his own beard — had remembered to see the flame fed before he came to sit, since a Keeper's dying, Fionnlagh said, was no excuse for a household to go cold. Calum told him it had been fed, which was true, and Fionnlagh said only that he was glad of it, and closed his eyes, and did not open them again.

## VII. Of the Eleven Days' Road

Word of the asking went out from Dùn ìseal before the body was a day cold, and by the time the bearers set out southward with Fionnlagh Dall carried between them on a litter of plain wood, every hearth along the twenty miles between the Hall and Cnoc dhìreach had already heard, and every hearth along that road asked, when the bearers passed, to be allowed to carry him some part of the way themselves, so that what should by any ordinary reckoning have been a journey of three days at most, twenty miles being no great distance for men walking a road they knew, stretched instead to eleven, the litter passing from one household's shoulders to the next at every waypoint house and every crossroads shrine the road offered, each hearth keeping him a night and sending him on in the morning with fresh bearers and, more than once, with the whole household walking some distance alongside out of a wish to have been some small part of the carrying.

Calum Beag walked the whole eleven days at the litter's head, by every account the only man on the journey who never once handed his own share of the bearing to another pair of shoulders, though he was by then a man of six-and-sixty and the road no easier for him than for anyone half his years. He led the way, as he had led Fionnlagh through the Hall's own galleries for more than fifty years before, though there was nothing now for him to lead a blind man's feet around, only the road ahead and the growing weight, the carriers who told it afterward all agreed, of a grief he did not trouble to hide from anyone who cared to see it plainly on his face. At the first waypoint house on the southern road, one of the houses raised after the manner of Mòr nic Dhùghaill's, the whole household turned out at the door as the litter passed, and its keeper pressed a bowl on every bearer in turn whether he had asked for it or not, saying, when Calum tried to refuse his own portion out of some sense that grief should go hungry, that a man could not carry a Keeper's weight on an empty stomach any better than he could carry a basket of coal on one; and word came to them there that Mòr herself, too old now to walk the width of the island, had sent from Doire shean to say the same.

## VIII. Of the Grave at Cnoc dhìreach

They came to the old ground on the eleventh day, a scatter of grave-mounds and standing stones so ancient that no household living could say with any certainty which of them marked what or belonged to whom, the whole of it grown over with the same rough grass that covered the hillside around it, undisturbed, the tellers say, since some people's time so far back that even the mountain's own memory did not reach it plainly. Calum Beag chose the spot himself, a low rise near the ground's centre from which, on a clear day, a man could see the smoke of three separate hearths without turning his head, and the bearers dug there, and laid Fionnlagh Dall in ground that had never before, so far as any record the Hall kept could say, held a burial anyone had troubled to mark by name.

The Keepers who came after him, when the question was put to them why he had asked for that ground rather than his own, gave two different answers between them and would not choose which was truer: some said he had wished, at the last, to belong to something older and larger than any measure he himself had spent his life keeping, and others said he had simply wished, being a man who had judged every household's claim to every handful for fifty-six years, to lie at last somewhere no one could claim at all. Calum Beag, asked the same question more than once in the years that followed, would say only that he had asked Fionnlagh himself and been given an answer that satisfied him, though he never repeated it whole to anyone, holding, he said, to the same silence a Keeper's own eyes owed the galleries, borrowed eyes included.

The ground was hallowed five years afterward by Keepers who travelled down from Dùn ìseal to do it, the first burial the place had ever received that any living hand had set down by name, and from that hallowing the burying-ground that had belonged to no one at all became, within the year, a ground that belonged, by the Hall's own reckoning, to everyone. A handful of families from the households nearest Cnoc dhìreach settled by it after, to tend the grave and keep the ground from growing wild over it again, and the Hall paid them for the work one measured handful of coal each a season, the only payment the Small-Burning Law was ever known to allow in coal rather than in grain or kind, on the ruling that a service kept for a dead Keeper's own sake was owed the one payment a Keeper himself would have judged fitting.

## IX. Of the Stone Calum Beag Laid

Mòr nic Dhùghaill did not live to hear the whole of how the burying finished. She died at her own house above Doire shean in the hundred and eighty-sixth year, two years past sixty and grey as the buffalo she had jugged for near her whole adult life, found by her own daughter one morning sitting upright in the chair by the fire where she had sat every evening of the household's memory, gone as quietly, the telling has it, as she had lived loudly, and the road kept her house running without a single night's fire missed, the daughter and a niece taking up the pot the same week their mother was laid in the ground behind the croft, because a house that had never once in twenty years failed to feed a traveller was not, the household judged, going to begin failing on the strength of one woman's death, however dearly the road had loved her.

Calum Beag came to the funeral himself, walking the width of the island to Doire shean, two years after he had walked beside Fionnlagh's litter, and it is told that he stood longest of anyone at the grave's edge afterward, an old man himself by then, though he outlived her by a good many years still, and said to no one in particular that the island had lost, within two seasons of each other, the two people he had spent the better part of his own life walking beside, one who had taught him to see with another man's hands and one who had taught him, without ever once meaning to teach it, that a table with no blade drawn under it was as fine a law as any the Hall had ever sworn.

It was in the hundred and eighty-ninth year, some years past the burying, that Calum Beag went back to Cnoc dhìreach a last time, an old man now in truth, to finish a thing he had put off since the day of the burying, uncertain, he told the grave-keepers who met him at the ground, whether his own hand was the right one to do it. He had brought with him, carried the whole way on his own back rather than trusted to any carrier, a plain stone the size of two cupped hands, cut by a mason he had paid for out of his own purse and asked to carve nothing on its face but the shape of the stone cup Fionnlagh had set on the threshold at Dùn ìseal, since no name, Calum judged, could say what that shape already said of the man well enough to be worth the cutting. He knelt at the grave's head a long while, the grave-keepers standing back to give him the ground, and set the stone down with his own two hands, pressing it into the turf until it sat level and would not rock, and then rose, an old man's knees complaining of the kneeling, and stood looking at it a moment before he turned and walked back down the road toward the mountain, leaving the stone to mark, without a single word carved anywhere upon it, what the hands that had once filled a cup by touch alone had judged, by the last measure any of them ever needed, enough.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Unforgotten Wedding

*FE 190 – 380*

> *Cha do scuir an fhuil ged a scuir an sabaid.*
> The blood did not stop when the fighting stopped.
>
> — a saying of the road, of the long strife between the king's blood

## I. Of an Old Man's Telling

Niall Òg told this tale more often than any other he kept, and told it, by every account the carriers give of him, the same way each time, sitting at whatever hearth would have him with a bowl going cold in his hands and his eyes on the fire rather than on whoever sat across from him, so that a listener new to the man might have thought he spoke to the flame and not to them at all. He was well past a thousand years old before the tale's own ending caught up with him, and older still before he stopped telling it, and those who heard it from him more than once said he never shaved a detail from it nor added one, though the households he told it to grew, across those same centuries, from grandchildren to great-grandchildren who had not known the people in it and would not live to see how it came out.

It was not a tale of a battle, he would say first, by way of warning a listener not to expect one, and it was not much of a tale of a wedding either, whatever its name implied, but a tale of how little a household needs to begin a grudge that will outlive every soul who remembers what it was for. He had watched the whole of it from somewhere near enough to see faces, being kin himself to both sides of the quarrel and welcome, or near enough welcome, at either table, and it was this, he said, more than his years, that let him carry the story whole from one end to the other where a teller born to only one side of it would have carried only half.

The strife of the heirs was old by the year he set his telling in, older by then than the mountain's own carriers' road, and it had long since stopped being, in any single man's memory, a quarrel about anything a living man could name. It ran instead the way a river runs, from a source no one now living had seen, through banks it had cut for itself over generations, carrying forward whatever fell into it without much caring what that thing had originally been. Men who had begun feuds in their own youth lived, by the strange mercy or curse of the king's blood, to grow old inside them, to see their own grandchildren born into a hatred they themselves had once started for a reason that no longer signified to anyone but them, and some, Niall said, forgot the reason before they forgot the hatred, which he judged the saddest thing a long life could do to a man.

He would say, to any listener young enough to ask why he troubled to tell so long and so joyless a tale at all, that he told it because it was the truest thing he knew of his own people, truer than any account of a war won or a Hall built, and that a man who wished to understand why the island's governors spent so many centuries governing so little beyond their own grudges had first to understand how small a thing a grudge could be at its beginning, and how patiently, given long enough years to work in, it could grow into something neither side any longer knew how to set down. He had buried enough of his own kin by the year he first told it this way to know the shape of the thing from the inside, having lost cousins and great-nephews to quarrels he himself had never once raised a hand in, and he counted himself, more than once in the telling, luckier than most of his blood only in having been born to no share worth fighting over, a grandson twice removed and content to stay so.

Those who carried his sayings on after him, hearth to hearth, kept this tale nearer the front of their own tellings than its length alone would have earned it, on the plain reckoning that a people who forgot how their own quarrels began were in danger of repeating them exactly, and that Niall's own telling, however sad its shape, was meant less as an entertainment than as a warning kept warm at the hearth for whoever next felt a boast rising in him at a wedding table.

## II. Of the Wedding at Ros dhomhain

It began, so far as any beginning could be put to a thing so old, at a wedding held in the two hundred and fourteenth year of the age, at Ros dhomhain, in the western share that had come down by then, three generations removed, from Fionnghal nic Ailein, the king's own daughter, who had held it quietly from her own hall until that very year. The couple being married that day were of no great account in the quarrel to come, a daughter of one of Fionnghal's household stewards and a young mason of the fourth hearth, and it is one of the tale's own small cruelties, Niall would say, that neither of their names is now much remembered, though the day itself is remembered by everyone.

Among the guests, as was the custom at any wedding held on a share's own ground, sat a scattering of the wider kin: cousins of the bride's mistress, cousins of cousins, and among them a great-grandson of Fionnghal's own line named Griogair mac Lachlainn, a man of some five-and-forty years, quick-tempered by every account and quicker still with drink in him, who had come from the western share's own hall to stand for his kinswoman at her wedding. Across the same table, sent as guest by a marriage two generations back that had tied a thread of Baile ghorm's salt-shore blood into the mason's own family, sat Tormod mac Ruairidh, a great-grandson of Artair mac Ailein and near the same age as Griogair, a man no less proud of his own descent and no more patient with drink than his counterpart.

The two had never met before that day, and might, by every reasonable turn of chance, never have troubled to meet again, had the ale not run generous and the talk not turned, as talk at such tables will, to whose blood carried further in the island's reckoning. The hall at Ros dhomhain was hung that evening with rowan and late heather, the mason's own kin having brought down whatever the hillside above the town still offered so far into the season, and the long table had been set with three separate jugs of the western share's own brew, strong enough that a guest who drank steadily through the toasts might find, by the fourth or fifth, that his tongue moved somewhat ahead of his judgement. Niall himself sat near the door with a cousin of the bride's, an old habit of his at any gathering he had not been asked to lead, and watched, without much alarm at first, the talk at the middle of the table climb from the mason's own trade to the standing of the two families who had lent the wedding its wider guests.

Griogair said something of the western share's age and standing that Niall, questioned closely on it across the whole rest of his own life, would only repeat as "a boast no worse than any man makes drunk at a wedding": that Ros dhomhain had held its ground unbroken since the king's own daughter first claimed it, while other shares, he said, had passed through more hands than a common toll-stick. Tormod answered it with something sharper, a word about the salt shore's own dignity set against the west's, that carried, by the account of three separate guests who told it afterward and agreed on this much if nothing else, a plain slight against Fionnghal's own memory, dead scarcely a season by then, and the manner of her death, which he named, in front of her own great-grandson and half her own household, an old woman's slow going rather than the peaceful end the family itself preferred to speak of. Griogair struck him across the table with the flat of his own drinking-horn before a third word could be spoken, the horn's rim catching Tormod high on the cheekbone and drawing a line of blood that both families would remember, in later tellings, at very different lengths, and the wedding that had begun in a house garlanded for a mason's daughter ended with two great-grandsons of the king's own children dragged apart by six men apiece and sent home to their separate shares nursing separate grievances that neither, in the whole of his own life afterward, would consent to set down. The mason and his bride, by every account Niall gathered afterward, danced out the rest of their own wedding with as much cheer as they could summon, and are remembered, where they are remembered at all, only as the two people whose feast it had briefly, uselessly, been.

## III. Of How a Small Thing Grows

It would have ended there, Niall always insisted, any ordinary quarrel between two ordinary men ending, as such things do, in a season's coldness and a slow forgetting, had the two men in question been of no particular blood. But Griogair and Tormod were each, in his own share, a man whose word carried weight beyond his own person, and each carried the insult home as an insult offered to the whole of his line through him, and never once, in all the years after, as a private hurt he alone might have chosen to forgive, so that within the year the western share and the salt shore, which had traded fish for grain across that same stretch of coast for three generations without a cross word between them, found their carriers refused lodging at each other's waypoint houses and their tolls counted twice as carefully at each other's borders.

A raid followed within two years, a small thing as such things are first counted, a dozen head of cattle lifted from a salt-shore pasture by men who called it no more than payment owed for an insulted household, and answered within the season by a barn burned on the western share's own ground, and by the fifth year of the quarrel neither side could any longer say with certainty who had struck first, only that the other side had certainly struck since, and struck badly, and owed for it. Niall Òg, who had watched the wedding itself from a bench near the door and thought little of it at the time beyond the ordinary regret any man feels at a spoiled feast, told listeners across the centuries that he marked the moment the quarrel changed from a grudge between two drunk cousins into a strife between two households as the exact moment he understood, better than any lesson the Hall's own reciters had ever given him, how the whole vast tangle of the king's blood had come to hate its own kin so thoroughly for so long. A hundred small wrongs, each answered a little harder than it was given, had done the work no single great wrong could have managed alone, until the answering became the whole of what either side remembered wanting, and the wedding itself, the mason and his bride and the ale and the garlands, was forgotten by everyone but the two men it had made enemies.

## IV. Of Eimhir nic Mhuirich and the Flame

The Hall at Dùn ìseal kept its own business through these same years largely apart from the quarrels of the king's blood beyond it, as the Binding had always meant it to, though the Keeper who held the flame through the middle of this strife, a woman named Eimhir nic Mhuirich, of the hearth-line rather than the king's own, watched the widening feuds with a plainer eye than any heir could manage for want of a stake in either side of them. She was chosen by the nine hearths in the two hundred and thirty-sixth year, a woman then of six-and-twenty and thought young for the choosing, and she kept the flame four-and-fifty years after, longer than any Keeper since Fionnlagh Dall and calmer, the tellings say, than most before him.

Eimhir's own rule of the Hall, which she was heard to repeat to every heir who came to the threshold to plead one side of the quarrel or the other, was that the stone cup filled and emptied by measure and by nothing else, and that a household's dues were owed to whichever lord's stewards came first to the door in the season they fell due, whatever quarrel that lord's blood carried against his neighbour's. She would not judge between Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair, as the two lines had come by then to call themselves, nor take either's account of who had wronged whom first, and it is told that when Tormod mac Ruairidh himself came to Dùn ìseal some years into her keeping of the flame to ask the Hall's blessing on a raid he meant to call justice rather than vengeance, she heard him out in full, sitting the whole while on the low stool the Keepers kept beside the stone cup, and asked him, when he had finished, whether the salt shore's own measure had gone short that season. He said it had not. She told him then only that the Hall blessed no man's raids, being in the business of coal and not of grudges, and that he was welcome to as much of the one as his household's measure allowed and none of the other whatever his measure, and when he pressed her a second time, naming his great-grandfather's blood as a claim on her sympathy if not her blessing, she answered that the flame she kept had been lit before Artair mac Ailein was born and would, with any luck the Hall was owed, still be burning after every quarrel his blood had raised was as forgotten as the ash of it, which she judged a truer measure of what mattered than any grudge he cared to bring her.

He left without the blessing he had come for, and it is told, though not by Tormod's own household, that he raided anyway within the season and lost two men doing it, and never again troubled the Hall to bless what he had already decided to do without it. Eimhir died in the two hundred and ninetieth year of the age, some eighty years old, having kept the flame steadier through the widening quarrel than the quarrel's own principals kept their tempers, and the nine hearths chose after her a younger Keeper who would hold much the same course, the Hall's own indifference to the king's blood's private wars having become, by then, as settled a custom as the measure itself.

## V. Of the Deaths of the King's Children

The old children of Ailean Mòr, who had held their shares since before the strife had any name at all, went one after another into the ground during these same decades, each death loosed a little more of the discipline their long presence had kept over their own descendants, whatever quarrels those descendants ran beneath them. Fionnghal nic Ailein, who had held the western share since the earliest days of the age and had watched the wedding quarrel begin from her own hall without living to see where it led, died in the two hundred and thirteenth year at some two thousand eight hundred years of age, the mountain's own reckoning agreeing that no soul born of the grove before or since had held so western and quiet a share so long or so lightly. Her own funeral, held at Ros dhomhain within the same season as the wedding, was the last occasion on which Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair stood under one roof without a blow struck between them, and even that peace, Niall said, was kept only because Griogair mac Lachlainn had the sense, sober at his own great-grandmother's grave, to send word to Tormod's household that no man of the salt shore would be turned from the door that day whatever lay between them, a courtesy neither line troubled to repeat afterward.

Artair mac Ailein, whose salt-shore blood ran now through Tormod's own veins, died in the two hundred and ninety-eighth year at two thousand six hundred years old, at his own hall above Baile ghorm, the tellings agreeing only that his last years were harder than his first, the widening feud a weight he had not asked to carry into his own old age and could not, by then, set down. Cormac mac Ailein, whose eastern share at Caol shean had taken no direct part in the quarrel between west and salt shore but felt its cold in every market that dealt with both, died in the three hundred and thirty-first year at some two thousand four hundred and fifty years, the last of the king's sons to hold a share, and it is told that his final word to his own household was a plain wish that they keep clear of a quarrel that was, by his own long reckoning, no business of theirs, a wish his descendants honoured for rather less than a generation.

"A death among the king's own blood," Niall would say at this point in the telling, looking up from the fire the one time in the whole tale that he looked up at all, "is a thousand years of patience lost all at once, and a household that has just buried two thousand years of it does not, in my long experience, grow more patient for the burying." He had watched three such funerals within his own span by the time he told the tale this way, and would watch a good many more before his own turn came, and he counted each one, he said, a small defeat for whatever peace the island might otherwise have kept.

## VI. Of Niall's Peace at the Long Table

In the three hundred and fifty-second year, wearied at last of watching a quarrel he had first seen begin over spilled ale at a stranger's wedding grow, across well over a century, into raids that now cost real lives on both sides, Niall Òg did what he had done once before at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's own table and tried, on a larger and more deliberate stage, to bring the two lines to a peace. He sent word to the heads of both Sliochd Fhionnghail and Sliochd Artair, by then men two generations removed from Griogair and Tormod themselves, that he would host a meeting on ground that belonged to neither, a long table set up in the open beside the carriers' road at the crossing near Ros fhionn, and that he asked only that both sides come unarmed and hear each other out before the day was through.

Both sides came, which Niall counted afterward the meeting's one true success, though it proved the only one. He had chosen the crossing near Ros fhionn deliberately, remembering the bridge Ailean Clachair's masons had thrown there near two centuries before with a hearth-sign cut into the keystone for luck, and thought a place built to be crossed by everyone might carry something of its own purpose into the men who sat beside it. He set two benches facing each other across a single board laid on trestles, no lord's own hall to lend one side or the other the comfort of its own hearth, and had a single pot of plain stew set between them, enough for both tables and belonging, by his own design, to neither.

The head of the western line, a great-great-grandson of Griogair's named for a grandfather Niall had known and buried, spoke first and at length of every wrong the salt shore had done his household across fourteen decades: cattle lifted, a barn burned, a cousin's arm broken at a market and never answered for. "You count your dead," he said, when he had finished, looking across the board rather than at Niall, "and I will count mine, and we will see whose column runs the longer, and that will settle it as well as anything else has." The head of the salt-shore line answered with an accounting no shorter and no less bitter, matching burning for burning and broken arm for broken arm down a list he seemed, from the ease of his own telling, to have carried ready in his head for years against exactly this occasion, and finished it by saying that he had not come to apologise for what his own blood had done in answer to what the west had done first, and would not, whatever an old man's long memory of a widow's table led him to hope.

By the time both accountings were finished the sun had gone down and the pot of stew sat cold and largely untouched between them, neither man having troubled to eat from it, and neither had once, in all that speaking, offered the other anything that could fairly be called an apology, only a longer and more particular list of grievances than either had troubled to draw up before. Niall, who had hoped the mere act of speaking plainly to one another might loosen something the years had knotted, told the two men before they parted that he had sat at this same trick of a long table once already in his own life and watched it work between a widow's guests who owed each other nothing, and that he did not understand, and did not expect ever to understand, why it failed so completely between men who shared the very blood he shared himself. "Because," the salt-shore man told him, rising, "your widow's guests had a debt between them that ended at her door. Ours has no door it ends at." Neither man answered Niall again after that. They rose from the table at the same moment, an agreement neither side would ever plainly own to, and walked back to their own shares by the same road they had come by, leaving the cold stew for whoever wanted it, and the raids resumed within the season, if indeed they had ever truly stopped for it.

## VII. Of Eachann Ruadh's Bed

Not every death of the king's blood in these years came of the wedding quarrel or its like. Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh, who had killed Ìomhar Dearg at the ford in vengeance for his own brother a full four generations before and had lived the whole of the strife's long middle as an old man at the edge of the Hall's own ground, neither forgiven nor pursued, died in his bed in the three hundred and seventy-seventh year of the age, at seven hundred and twenty-nine years old, the last of his own generation of the king's kin and by some distance the quietest death among them. He had outlived the killing that made his name by longer than most men's whole lives run, and it is told that in his final seasons he spoke of it seldom and without pride, saying once to a grandchild who asked him of the ford that a man's youngest deed followed him further than any of his later ones, however small it had seemed at the time he did it, a lesson he offered, Niall said, with more weariness than wisdom, though the two are not always easily told apart in an old man's mouth.

His own line, unlike Fionnghal's and Artair's, took no fresh quarrel from his death, having settled, a generation before, into a peace with Dùghall Dearg's Red Share that neither side troubled to disturb, and it was remarked at the time, by those who kept account of such things, that the one death among the king's old blood in these years to pass without raising a single spear was the death of a man who had himself once raised one in earnest. Niall, telling this part of the tale, would let it sit a moment without comment, as though the fact spoke for itself better than any moral he could set beside it.

## VIII. Of the Households Going On

Through all of it, the wedding's small insult widening across nearly two centuries into a habit of raids the households themselves had long since stopped troubling to explain, the ordinary business of the island went on largely undisturbed beneath the quarrelling. The handful was measured out at the stone cup as it had been measured since Fionnlagh Dall's own day, the tallies kept, the carriers walked their roads with their baskets, and a household sworn to whichever lord's stewards reached its door first in a given season paid its dues to that lord and troubled itself no further with which side of which grudge he stood on, so long as the measure he asked for stayed within the Law.

A household of the fourth hearth at Cnoc leathan, midway between the two quarrelling shares and sworn to neither, kept through these same generations a single tally-stick hung above its own door, notched once for every season the western share's steward called first and once, on the stick's other face, for every season the salt shore's steward came first instead, a plain record kept for no reason grander than settling, at the year's turn, whose grain-store the household's own custom bound it to feed first at threshing. The stick, by the time of Niall's own telling, carried better than a hundred and fifty notches on each face, more marks by far than either quarrelling line's own reciters kept of the raids that had made the two households enemies, and it is told that the family who kept it could say, without hesitation, exactly which steward had called first in any given year of their own grandfathers' lives, while neither Sliochd Fhionnghail nor Sliochd Artair could any longer say with any certainty who had struck the first blow of the whole quarrel that had cost them both so dear.

Marriages continued to be made across the very lines that quarrelled, as marriages will, sons and daughters of Sliochd Fhionnghail wedding into households that owed nothing to either feud, the strife itself running always a little apart from the great slow ordinary current of ploughing and lambing and the mending of roofs that made up the greater part of any year for any household on the mountain, whatever its blood.

Niall Òg, closing the tale as he always closed it, would set down his bowl at this point, cold by then whatever hearth he told it beside, and say the one line that every listener across those centuries carried away with them whole, word for word, more surely than they carried any other part of the telling: that the island, in all his own long years of watching it, was never so well governed as when all its governors were too busy quarrelling with each other to trouble the rest of it. He meant it, those who knew him best agreed, only half in jest, and the other half of it, he would add if pressed, was the saddest thing he knew how to say about his own blood, three centuries deep into a grudge that had begun over nothing more than a boast and a drinking-horn at a stranger's wedding, and showed, in his own lifetime at least, no sign at all of ending.

# Part Three: The Long Strife and the Threshold

# Chapter Seventeen: Of Eilidh nic Ìomhair and the Four Houses

*FE 381 – 397*


## I. Of the Empty Threshold

The Keeper who had held the flame after Eimhir nic Mhuirich was an old woman of the hearth-line by the time Eilidh nic Ìomhair first came to Dùn ìseal to ask a season's grace on a debt of coal her household owed the Hall, and she remembered the meeting afterward only for the Keeper's hands, which shook badly by then pouring the measure, and for the patience with which the woman waited for them to steady before she would let anyone else pour it for her. That Keeper died in the winter of the three hundred and eighty-first year of the age, at an age nobody troubled to reckon exactly, having kept the flame quietly and without incident for longer than most people at Dùn ìseal could remember any other way of things being kept. She died on the low stool beside the cup, having sat down there after the evening measure was poured to rest her legs before the walk to her own bed, and the boy sent in at first light to relight her lamp from Brìde's own flame found her still sitting upright with her hands folded in her lap, so that he stood a long moment in the doorway unsure whether he had come upon a woman asleep or a woman dead, and only knew the second when he had gone close enough to see that the coal in the small lamp beside her had burned out in the night for want of any hand to feed it, the first time in living memory that any lamp in Talla na Lasrach had been let go dark. The nine hearths gathered at the Hall in the spring to choose whoever would keep it after her, as they had gathered eight times before since Beathag Bhàn first took the coal from the slab.

Eilidh was two-and-forty that spring, a granddaughter's granddaughter of Ìomhar Dearg through a line that had long since stopped naming itself anything grander than a household of Dùn dhearg, and she had spent the better part of her life doing exactly what any woman of that household did: keeping accounts for the Red Share's steward, walking the granary rolls at threshing, and raising three children on ground her own grandmother had walked before her. She had never asked to be considered for the flame, and said so plainly to the two hearth-elders who came to Dùn dhearg to sound her out, sitting her down at her own table and asking her, in the roundabout way such questions are always first asked, whether she thought a woman of her particular blood might be persuaded to sit a season with the coal.

"You mean the king's blood," Eilidh said, because she had never in her life found much use in letting another person finish a sentence she could see coming from three words off, and the elders admitted that yes, that was rather the difficulty they had come to discuss.

It was late in the evening when they came, the two of them having walked from Dùn ìseal since morning and eaten nothing since, and Eilidh's own household gave them bread and a bowl of the same broth her children were fed on before either elder was let say a further word about hearths or flames or blood. One of the two, a thin man with a cutter's scarred hands who had spent forty years in the galleries before the nine hearths thought his knees too poor for the climb and set him instead to walking their errands, watched Eilidh feed her youngest from her own bowl while the older two argued over whose turn it was to fetch water, and said afterward, to the other elder on the road home, that he had gone to Dùn dhearg half expecting a woman puffed up with her own blood and had found instead a woman who could not get a full sentence out of her own table without being asked twice for the salt.

The difficulty was old and plain enough that nobody at the table needed it explained twice. The Binding had sworn the flame to no one of the king's blood, and had been kept to that oath, without exception, since Beathag Bhàn herself had been chosen for no reason grander than that she was of nobody's blood at all. Muireach Liath, Gormshuil, Fionnlagh Dall, Eimhir, the woman just carried up to the slope: none of them had been able to claim so much as a great-grandmother among Ailean's own children, and the nine hearths had never, in all that time, needed to ask themselves whether the rule still held, because no candidate worth considering had ever forced the question. Eilidh forced it. She was, by every reckoning the hearth-elders could make sitting at her own table that afternoon, plainly the ablest of the three names put forward that spring, and just as plainly a great-great-granddaughter of the man who had burned the halls of Dùn dhearg and sent a king home on a bier of spears.

"Then choose one of the other two," Eilidh said, not unkindly, and meant it; she had said as much to her own husband the night before, and he had told her that a woman who did not want a thing badly enough to argue for it seldom got it, and seldom deserved to.

## II. Of the Season of Refusal

The nine hearths chose her anyway, in the spring of the three hundred and eighty-second year, by a count neither Sliochd Mhuirich nor anyone else who kept the tally troubled to say aloud, and word of the choosing reached Sliochd Mhuirich at Dùn ìseal before Eilidh herself had finished packing a single basket to travel there. The house that had held the flame since Muireach Liath's daughter first took the coal from her father's dying hand did not send word back that it welcomed the choice. It sent word that it did not accept it, and for the better part of a year afterward the cup at Talla na Lasrach sat under the care of the hearth-line's own eldest, unfilled by any new hand, while every household with an opinion on the matter found occasion to air it at every market and every threshing floor on the mountain.

The argument made loudest that year, and the one Eilidh herself was made to answer more times than she could count, was put to her first by a cousin of her own who meant it as comfort: that there was, by then, hardly a household left in the hills without some thread of the king's own blood run through it somewhere, a great-great-grandmother here, a disowned younger son there, so that the Binding's old rule against the blood had become, in practice, a rule against nearly everybody or nobody at all, and Eilidh's own blood was no different in kind from half the blood in the valley, only better remembered. Eilidh heard the argument out from more mouths than her cousin's, and found it no comfort whatever the number of times it was offered her, because it answered a question nobody at Dùn ìseal had actually asked. Nobody doubted that half the mountain carried a drop of Ailean's line by now, diluted past any household's power to name it. What Sliochd Mhuirich doubted, and said so without troubling to soften it, was whether a woman who could stand up at any gathering of the Red Share and be named, plainly and without dilution, as a granddaughter's granddaughter of Ìomhar Dearg, could be trusted to keep a flame the Binding had sworn against exactly that kind of naming.

"They are not wrong to ask it," Eilidh told her cousin, the third or fourth time he brought the argument to her door meaning to cheer her with it, and the flatness with which she said it left him with nothing further to offer. She did not, in that whole season of waiting, once send word to Dùn ìseal pressing her own claim, nor did she withdraw it; she went on keeping the Red Share's granary rolls as she had always kept them, and let the argument run its course among people who had more patience for arguing it than she did.

The waiting wore harder on her household than it did on her. Her husband, a cutter's son with no blood worth naming on either side, took to answering for her at the granary door whenever a steward's runner arrived with some fresh word from Dùn ìseal, saying only that his wife was at the rolls and had nothing to add to what she had said the last time, until the runners stopped troubling to knock and simply left whatever they carried with him instead. Her eldest daughter, a girl of nineteen who had grown up hearing her own great-great-grandfather's name spoken at markets the way other households spoke of weather, asked her once, straight out at the supper table, whether she wanted the flame at all or only refused to be told she could not have it, and Eilidh considered the question longer than she considered most, turning her spoon in the broth a while before she answered that she had stopped, some years back, being able to tell the two apart in her own mind, and did not think the difference mattered as much as her daughter seemed to.

## III. Of the Condition

What finally settled it was a condition offered rather than any argument won, and it came, as such things at Dùn ìseal generally did, from the hearth-line's own eldest rather than from any voice on Eilidh's side of the question. She was a woman named for no one now living to remember, old enough to have helped carry Fionnlagh Dall's own body south along the eleven days' road, and she came to the Hall's threshold on the morning appointed for the nine hearths to meet again and said, before any other business could be raised, that Sliochd Mhuirich would yield the flame to Eilidh nic Ìomhair on one condition and no other: that the stone cup Fionnlagh Dall had cut to the measure of two cupped hands should never, for any cause, for any lord's asking, for any war or famine or royal wedding the island might yet see, be carried out through the door of Talla na Lasrach.

It was not, on its face, much of a condition to ask, since no Keeper before Eilidh had ever once thought to carry the cup anywhere, and several of the hearth-elders who heard it said as much, wondering aloud what the house of Muireach thought it was guarding against that had not already been guarded a hundred times over by the Binding. But the eldest of Sliochd Mhuirich, when pressed to say plainly what she feared, answered only that a cup that never left a house could never be carried off by whoever next held the strongest claim to whatever else that house kept, and that she would rather ask for a small thing plainly than a large thing she could not name, and left it at that. Eilidh, told of the condition before she had even finished the walk up from Dùn dhearg to swear to it, said she would have sworn to it unasked, and did so before the nine hearths that same afternoon with her hand flat on the cup's rim, the coal poured level to her palm exactly as it had been poured for every Keeper before her, and the flame carried to her own lamp before nightfall.

It never did leave the Hall, not once in the whole of Eilidh's keeping nor in the reigns of any Keeper who came after her, and the tellers since, looking back on that single afternoon's bargain, would say that Sliochd Mhuirich had asked for the one thing it could be certain of getting and got, by the asking, a good deal more besides.

## IV. Of the Four Houses Sworn

Eilidh had been three years at the flame, and had by then heard the argument about her blood raised so many times by so many mouths that she had stopped troubling to answer it at all, when the shape of a settlement came to her less from any single voice than from the plain fact of who kept coming to Dùn ìseal to argue it. Four houses, and no more than four, had by then taken to sending their own elders to speak at every gathering of the nine hearths as though they alone had a right to be heard on the matter of the Keeper's office: Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the office by more than two hundred years of custom and now by Eilidh's own oath besides; Sliochd Ìomhair, claiming a voice through Eilidh's own blood and unwilling, now that the thing was done, to let anyone forget the connection; Sliochd Thormoid, whose eldest stood up at the third such gathering and named, for the first time in anyone's hearing, an ancestor called Tormod Liath who was said to have held the hill under the old king before ever a flame was bound to it; and Sliochd Raghnaill, whose claim ran through a man named Raghnall Ceannfhionn and rested less on any hill than on the plain fact that Sliochd Raghnaill's boats had carried more coal down the coast in a bad season than any other house's carriers had carried inland.

Eilidh, who had grown tired of hearing four houses argue a question the other five hearths had long since stopped troubling to weigh in on, put the settlement to the nine in the spring of the three hundred and eighty-fifth year in words plainer than any house had used to argue its own case: that the office of Keeper would be bound, from that season on, to these four houses of custody and no others, that the other hearths would keep their seats on the council as they always had but surrender any further claim on the flame, and that the four houses might settle among themselves, by whatever quarrel or marriage or patience the years gave them, which of their own would sit the flame when her own turn at it ended. Three of the four, she noted aloud before the nine hearths that same afternoon, claimed some thread of the king's blood or said they did, and only the house that had first raised the flame claimed none at all, which she thought, she said, a tidy enough shape for an office the Binding had meant to keep clear of blood and had somehow, across three centuries, filled with almost nothing else.

It was sworn that same spring, on the same threshold where the condition about the cup had been sworn three years before, four elders standing where one had stood alone, each with a hand laid flat in turn on the same stone rim Eilidh's own hand had rested on at her own swearing, and a fifth hand, the hearth-line eldest's, laid last of all and longest, as if to remind the other three whose custom it was they had come late to share in. Most of the great families known on the island now trace themselves, rightly or by their own telling, to one of the four, and it had already become, within two or three generations, a common enough boast at any market to claim descent from one house or another of the swearing, though Eilidh herself, asked once by a grandchild years later which of the four her own blood belonged to, said only that she supposed it belonged to whichever house wanted the claiming least, since that was the one nobody troubled to dispute with her.

## V. Of Seann Dunn and the Fullest Lamp

Sliochd Thormoid did not wait long to make its claim a visible one. Within the year its eldest had raised, at Seann Dunn on the river's northern bank, a hall and a shrine of squared timber facing the mountain across the water, with a coal-lamp set to burn at the Law's own measure day and night in a niche cut for it beside the door, so that any traveller on the road below could look up from the ford and see the house's light burning steadily whatever the season. The other three houses grumbled about it from the first, not because a lamp at the Law's measure was against any rule Eilidh had made, but because Seann Dunn's lamp, by every account that reached Dùn ìseal, always seemed to burn a shade fuller than anyone else's handful managed to, and no cutter sent to check the measure ever found so much as a grain over what the Law allowed.

"It is the same coal as everyone's," Eilidh told a steward of Sliochd Ìomhair who came to complain of it on his own house's behalf, turning the man's own grumble back on him with more patience than the complaint deserved, "and if Seann Dunn's hearth burns brighter on it than yours, I expect that says more for their draught than for their honesty." She did not trouble to have the lamp measured a second time, judging, as she told the hearth-elders privately, that a grievance a house could not prove was a grievance best left to wear out on its own, and it did, more or less, though Seann Dunn's neighbours went on saying it of the lamp for as long as the shrine stood.

Sliochd Raghnaill, meanwhile, made no shrine at all, having chosen for its own seat Seann Tarr on the north-eastern coast, the same town whose household had been the very first sentenced under Fionnlagh Dall's Small-Burning Law two centuries before, its name still carried on the Hall's own roll with the old offence beside it. The house that took its seat there kept no galleries and cut no coal of its own, choosing boats instead, and grew rich enough on the fishing within two generations that the other three houses stopped mentioning the old offence at all, which Eilidh privately thought a stranger silence than any grumble about a lamp.

## VI. Of Tormod Ruadh and the Coast That Was Only Looked At

It was a household of Sliochd Raghnaill's own boats, in the twelfth year of Eilidh's keeping, that did the one thing none of the other three houses had thought to try, and did it, by every later account, less from ambition than from an argument over a wager that had gone on rather longer at Seann Tarr's own quay than the ale served there could reasonably sustain. A steersman named Tormod Ruadh, no kin to Sliochd Thormoid whatever the shared name might suggest to a stranger, had spent the better part of a winter's evenings insisting to anyone who would listen that a boat built to weather the open water past the skerries could as easily be sailed clean round the black island the fishers called Eilean dhubh as fished within sight of it, as every boat out of Seann Tarr had always done before him, and by spring enough silver rings had changed hands on the wager that Tormod found himself with a crew of four and no honest way left to back out of the claim.

They put out at the first fair tide of an Cèitean in the three hundred and ninety-seventh year, provisioned for eight days though the crossing and back, by Tormod's own reckoning, ought to want no more than five, and the quay that saw them off did so with more laughter than blessing, a dozen wagers still being settled on the strand as the boat cleared the harbour mouth. The weather held fair the first two days, wind enough to spare the oars, and Tormod's own account, told afterward more times than any man should have patience to repeat a single tale, made much of the third night, when the boat lay becalmed under a headland none of the four crewmen could put a name to and a light rain came on that none of them troubled to shelter from, having by then long since given up any dryness worth keeping. The fourth day brought the cliffs of the island's far side into view, taller by half, Tormod said, than any cliff on the coast he had grown up fishing under, white with birds from the waterline to a height no stone could be thrown to, and the noise of them, he told the quay more than once, was a thing no teller before him had ever troubled to mention, a great ceaseless clamour that did not stop for the whole day they coasted under it, so that the crew found themselves shouting to be heard over birds rather than over any sea.

Eilidh heard nothing further of the voyage until word reached Dùn ìseal that the boat had been sighted rounding the island's far side by fishers of a strand that had never before had reason to look for any boat of Seann Tarr's coming from that particular quarter of the sea, and the word that reached her carried, along with the fact of the sighting, a good deal of alarm from a strand that had taken the strange boat, at first glimpse, for something worth lighting a warning fire over. They were nine days out before the boat came home, a day longer than provisioned and no worse for it, and the whole of Seann Tarr's quay turned out to meet them, less, by most accounts, out of any fear for their safety than out of an eagerness to settle the wager one way or the other.

What Tormod brought back, when pressed by half the quay at once to say what lay round the far side of Eilean dhubh, was rock, and birds enough to darken the sky over certain stretches of the northern cliff, and the plain fact of having gone there and come back, and nothing else that any teller since has been able to add to it however many times the tale has been told at Seann Tarr's own hearths. He had looked for a landing and found none worth the name; he had looked for any sign that another boat, of any coast, had gone that way before him, and found none of that either; and when a woman of the quay asked him outright whether the far side of the island was worth the wager he had won by seeing it, he is said to have answered only that a man does not sail nine days to bring home an answer to a question nobody but a drunk crowd at a quay had thought worth asking, and that he would do it again all the same, given the ale and the wager to make him.

Word of the voyage reached Eilidh at Dùn ìseal within the month, carried up by a carrier who had heard it fresh at Seann Tarr's own quay and told it, by his own account, rather better than Tormod himself ever troubled to tell it again. She asked the carrier only one question in return, whether any of the four houses had claimed the voyage as their own doing, and was told that Sliochd Raghnaill had certainly not discouraged the telling, whatever truth there was in a wager settled over too much ale being any house's doing at all.

## VII. Of the Watching from the Threshold

Eilidh kept the flame a further three-and-thirty years after that spring, long enough to see the argument about her own blood fade from something argued at every gathering into something an older generation remembered arguing and a younger one had simply always known to be settled, and long enough, too, to see boats out of all four coasts sail a little further past their own headlands than their grandfathers had thought worth the risk, though none again quite so far, nor quite so needlessly, as Tormod Ruadh's had gone.

She was at Seann Tarr herself in the last days of that same summer, come down from Dùn ìseal to see the new seat of the house her own settlement had sworn, and she stood on the quay on an evening with the tide making and watched the small dark shapes of the fishing boats come in past the headland in the last of the light, Tormod Ruadh's among them, each boat finding its own strand as it always had, none of them, that evening or any evening after, troubling to sail any further than the fishing required. It was, she thought, watching them come in, a smaller thing than the argument over her own blood had ever made it sound, and a larger one than any wager settled at a quay had any right to be, and she found, standing there with the flame two days' walk behind her and the cup that would never leave its house, that she could not have said with any certainty which of the two she believed the truer measure of what her own long season at the flame had actually kept.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of the Plunderers and the Thing under the Boat

*FE 398 – 421*

> *Cha do dh'fhaighnich a' mhuir cead.*
> The sea did not ask leave.
>
> — said still at the wake of Baile chrom, by whoever pours the first cup

## I. Of the Households Put Out to Sea

Anndra Cìobair was eighteen the year his uncle's household lost its right for the third time, and he remembered it less as a shame than as a leaving: three men going down to the strand at Baile chrom with what they could carry on their backs, a woman weeping without troubling to hide it, and his uncle Murchadh Ruadh saying nothing at all, which those who knew him thought the worse sign of the two. The Law took no pleasure in a third offence and no more trouble over it than over a first; it set the household's name on the roll that the waypoint-keepers cried at Samhain, and after that no hearth on the coast would give the household coal, nor grumble, nor discuss it, for the discussing had all been done at the first offence and the second. Anndra's father stood at his own door and watched his brother's household go down the path to the strand with their bundles on their backs, and said only, when Anndra asked him why he did not call out some word of parting, that a word said across a threshold the Law had shut could do the leaving household no good and the speaker a good deal of harm, and that he had five sons of his own still under that roof to think of.

What the Law did not do, and had never troubled to do, was ask where a household went once its name was on that roll. Some went inland to kin who would have them on sufferance and cold porridge. Some starved slowly and were counted among the reverent centuries' quiet dead, a household here and a household there that the rolls simply stopped naming, no cause given because none was asked. And some, that year and in the years after it, went down to the strand instead and put out in whatever hull would still float, and lived off the north-western waters the way a household with no coal and no grain and no roof lives: by raiding the strands of households luckier than themselves.

They were not the first to try it. Baile chrom's own grandfathers told of a leaner year, generations back, when two brothers had done the same thing for a single winter and come home again once their own cousins forgave them, and no one had troubled to give it a name. This time the name stuck, because there were more of them, and because most did not come home, and because within three years of the first household's leaving there were boats enough on those waters, out of half a dozen strands and not one household among them, to make a raid worth calling a raid rather than a theft worth calling a shame. Spùinneadairean, the strand called them, plunderers, and by the time Anndra was a man grown the word had settled onto the north-western waters as a whole, the whole grey width of them from the sea-monster's rocks to the point where no boat of Baile chrom cared to go unescorted, as if the sea out past the headland had always belonged to thieves and always would.

Anndra's own household kept its right. His father fished the near grounds and paid the Law its handful without complaint or love, and taught his sons that a man who lost his right had lost it fairly, whatever pity a body might feel watching the boats go out, and that pity spent on a man already gone to sea was pity wasted on the one man who could no longer use it. But Anndra had grown up beside boys whose cousins were now spùinneadairean, and he had sat at more than one hearth where a mother would not say the word for her own son, only "my boy that's on the water now," as if he had merely taken up fishing a little further out than most, and Anndra never once heard any of those mothers say where the fish he brought her came from, or ask.

## II. Of the Night the Southern Strand Burned

He was one-and-twenty, and two years wed, when the raid came near enough to his own coast that he stood in the smoke of it. It fell on a strand half a day's walk south along the shore, six households that kept goats on the machair above the tideline and dried more fish than they ate themselves, and it fell in the small hours of a night with no moon, which every teller after agreed was no accident, for a boat coming in dark and going out dark leaves little for a strand to swear to in the morning beyond smoke and empty racks.

Anndra was not there when the boats came in, only when the word came up the coast at first light, carried by a boy who had run the whole way and could barely stand by the time he reached Baile chrom's own hearths, and he went south with a dozen others of the fitter men, arriving to find two of the six houses burned to their stone footings, the drying-racks stripped bare to the last strip of fish, and a woman of that strand sitting on the ground before her own ruined door with a burned hand wrapped in her skirt, saying to whoever would listen and to no one in particular that she had known two of the men in the boats by their voices, though she would not, then or ever after, say the names aloud where the Law's own ears might carry them home to kin who still had a right to lose.

It was the first raid Anndra had seen the marks of rather than merely heard of, and it taught him a thing the tellings had never quite made plain, that the spùinneadairean did not raid as strangers raid, taking what they could carry and gone before a strand woke, but as men who knew exactly which houses kept the fullest racks and which dogs barked loudest and which men slept furthest from the door, because most of them had grown up on those same strands themselves and had cousins sleeping in half the houses they burned. He said as much to his father that same evening, and his father told him only that a man does not choose his kin. He chooses, every day of his life, which of his kin's roofs he will burn and which he will not, and a household on the wrong side of the Law's third offence had made that choice already, whatever pity it earned it afterward.

## III. Of the Calm Water

The year Anndra was five-and-twenty he crewed the boat of Cailean Buidhe, a broad-beamed hull that had brought in more herring than any other keel out of Baile chrom in a decade, with four men aboard besides himself: Cailean at the steering-oar, his two sons Murchadh Òg and Eachann, and Anndra's own second cousin, a quiet man named Torcall who talked to the nets more than to the crew and was thought lucky for it, though luck, as it turned out that year, is not a thing any man can lend another.

They went out past the headland on a morning so still that Anndra remembered afterward being able to hear, a mile from shore, a dog barking on the strand behind them as clearly as if it stood at his elbow. The water lay like poured metal, no swell in it at all, which the older men said was a thing to mistrust more than any storm, for a boat in a gale at least knows what it is fighting. Cailean himself said so that morning, easing the boat out past the point with the oar barely stirring, and Murchadh Òg laughed at him for it and said a calm sea had never yet drowned a careful man, to which Cailean answered nothing, only watched the water a while longer before he gave the word to shoot the nets.

They shot the nets in the flat calm and sat waiting on oars gone slack in their locks, the sea so smooth under the hull that a man could watch his own face in it if he leaned over the gunwale, which Torcall did, once, leaning far enough that Eachann told him to mind he didn't fall in and save the fish the trouble of being caught, and Torcall straightened without answering and said nothing about what he had seen there, if he had seen anything at all beyond his own reflection.

It came up without a wave to announce it. Anndra was watching the net-floats for the first tug of fish when the whole boat lifted: a slow, deliberate lift, the lift of something enormous passing beneath, as if the sea had drawn one long breath and held it. The floats went under. The boat tipped, righted, tipped again, and for three or four heartbeats every man aboard stood or crouched exactly where the lift had caught him, not one of them making a sound, for there was, in that silence and that stillness, nothing yet to cry out against: no shape breaking the surface, no fin, no eye, only the water gone taut and strange beneath the keel, as a drumskin goes taut under a hand laid flat on it before the hand strikes. Cailean said one word only, low, not a command and not quite a prayer either, and no man aboard remembered afterward what the word had been.

Then the boat went over.

Anndra never afterward could say, and would not for the rest of his life be made to say, whether the capsizing came from below or from the men's own scramble to the one side, which is the ordinary way boats are lost in a calm as much as in a storm, five men throwing their weight the same way at the same instant out of the same fear. He went into water colder than the still morning had promised, came up under the hull's shadow, and swam clear of it without deciding to, the way a man's body decides such things for him when the deciding mind has nothing yet to decide with. Close by, once, he heard a great slow displacement of water that was not a wave and was not any fish he had ever heard broach, a sound with weight in it, the sound a hillside makes settling rather than a sound the sea usually makes, and he did not look toward it. He swam and did not look, and has never in any telling since said which of the two took more from him.
