Of the five who had gone out on Cailean Buidhe's boat that morning, two came in: Anndra himself, and Torcall, who had somehow kept hold of an oar the whole way and gave it up to no one on the strand, not even when his hands had to be prised from it finger by finger once he was ashore and could no longer feel them. Cailean and his two sons were never found, not that day nor after, though the coast was walked for a week and the near rocks searched at every low tide, and the boat came ashore three days later a mile down the coast, upside down, its planking sound, not a mark on it that any man could point to and call a cause.

## IV. Of What Was Not Said

The strand asked Anndra what he had seen, in the way a strand always asks, gently at first and then less gently as the days passed and no bodies came ashore to answer for themselves, and Anndra told them what he had heard and what the boat had done, and no more. He did not say that the lift beneath the keel had felt, for the length of one held breath, like a hand cupping something too small for it. He did not say what size he had judged the displacement to be, out of the corner of an eye that had refused, in the moment, to turn and look directly at it, nor did he ever, in the forty years he lived after, describe the sound of it to anyone in words closer than "a hillside settling," which satisfied no one who asked and was, he always maintained, the truest account he had to give. Torcall said even less, and within a year had stopped fishing the near grounds at all and taken instead to mending nets ashore, a trade no one begrudged him and which he followed, in near total silence, for the rest of a long life.

It was not the first such loss the north-western waters had given the coast, nor, the old women said, would it be the last, and there were tellers enough at Baile chrom's own hearths who called the thing by a name before the year was out, the Sea-Watcher, and swore it had been seen off that same headland since before any hearth now standing had been raised, some thirty feet of it by the tellings that kept closest to modesty and a good deal more by the tellings that did not. Whether it was one beast or many, or the sea's own way of answering a calm too still to trust, no one at Baile chrom claimed to know, and those who claimed to know were, as a rule, men who had not been in the boat.

What the coast did agree on, without needing to discuss it the way the household's third offence had needed no discussing, was that the loss should be kept, and kept every year, on the day nearest the one it had happened, with a bowl set out for the three who did not come home and the boat's name spoken aloud once by whoever poured the first cup. Anndra poured it the first year, because he was the one who had come back with a story to tell and would not tell it, and by unspoken agreement he went on pouring it every year after, growing old at the task the way another man grows old at a trade he never chose and could not now set down.

## V. Of the Fire Relit

Four years after the loss, in a season when three more boats had gone missing off the same stretch of water, though none so strangely as Cailean Buidhe's, the fishers of Baile chrom climbed the headland and lit the old beacon on the point again, the one their grandfathers had let go dark once the Law's own coal-galleries made every hearth's fire a counted and measured thing and a fire kept for no household's own handful had come to seem, to a generation grown careful of the Law, a kind of waste no one wished to answer for. They fed it with driftwood, as the Law required of any fire kept outside a share's own handful, and a beacon fed with driftwood burns unevenly, now high and now guttering, so that a boat far out watching it learns to read its own danger in how steadily the point holds its light, and learns, too, that a fire which cannot be measured cannot be rationed, and will burn on whatever the tide happens to leave it, generous some nights and mean on others, exactly as the sea it watches over is generous or mean.

Anndra carried wood up that headland himself more nights than he later cared to count, in the years the beacon was young and its keeping still fell to whoever happened to be ashore and willing rather than to any household by right. It became, before long, a charge some households took in turn the way other coasts took turns at a granary door or a toll-stick, a season each, and the fire on the point came to be called, by fishers from other harbours who steered by it once Baile chrom's own people had stopped thinking of it as anything but the fire, the light of Baile chrom, kept for no coal the Law could measure and asked for by no one but the sea.

He stood the watch there the night word came up the coast, carried by a trader's boat out of the east that had put in for water and stayed the night for the company, that other households far off had found other uses for driftwood and silt and old stone, and Anndra, who by then thought of little beyond his own headland and his own three names in his own bowl, listened to the news the way a man listens to weather from a country he will never sail to: with interest, and no great sense that it touched him, and asked the trader, more from courtesy than curiosity, whether the coast he spoke of kept any beacon of its own, and was told that it did not yet, having found, in the stone it had dug up, a better inheritance than any fire a household could feed.

## VI. Of Seann Bhrenn and the Stone Quay

Far to the north-east, on a coast Anndra never saw and never expected to, fishers from the mountain's northern side had grown too many for the harbours they held and gone looking, as households on every coast of the island had gone looking before them, for a shore with room enough and water deep enough and no one already standing on it to say otherwise. They found such a shore at the old harbour the herders of that coast still called Seann Bhrenn, empty since some earlier age had emptied it, and settled there, and kept the name they found it under rather than giving it one of their own, the way the western settlers before them had kept Seann Warr's name and the road-builders before that had kept Seann Mhorn's, the whole island by then grown used to the notion that a place's old name outlasted whoever had first worn it out.

They found more than an empty harbour. Digging back the silt that had swallowed the old shoreline, the first families to break ground there struck stone: a quay, cut and laid by hands none of them could account for, buried deep enough that only the lowest tides had ever shown a hint of it, and sound enough, once cleared, to take a hull heavier than any their own boats yet built. They used it without asking who had laid it, the way a household uses a well it finds already dug, and the harbour prospered faster for the finding than it would have prospered digging its own quay from nothing, which is the kind of luck a coast does not question closely once it has taken hold of it, though more than one household there was heard to wonder, at its own hearth and no further, what manner of hands had cut stone so true before any hand now living had learned the trade.

Word of the stone quay travelled the coast the way word of any strange find travels, mouth to mouth and boat to boat, gathering a little in the telling at every hearth it passed through, so that by the time it reached Baile chrom, three seasons and the width of the island removed from the digging, the quay had grown in some tellings to a whole buried town and shrunk in others to a single worked stone no bigger than a door-lintel. Anndra heard it told both ways at his own hearth in the same winter, from two travellers who had never met each other and neither of whom had seen the quay themselves, and believed neither telling more than the other, which struck him, he said once to Torcall over the mending of a net, as very much how his own boat's story must sound by the time it reached a hearth as far off as Seann Bhrenn, grown to a whole drowned town in one mouth and shrunk to a man's own fright in another, and neither telling any truer than his own silence had been.

## VII. Of the Cairn at Cathair naomh

Further north still, at Cathair naomh, a smaller thing was begun in the same years that would grow, in its own way, larger than any stone quay: a cairn, raised on the hill above the town for its own dead, with a single stone brought to it at every burial by whichever household had lost the body being laid down. It was not the island's first ancestor-cairn, nor even the first at Cathair naomh, whose people had marked their dead with stones since before any hearth there could say why, but it was the one that took hold and did not stop growing, so that within Anndra's own lifetime travellers who had seen it once and passed that way again years later swore the hill looked changed, heavier at the crown, as if the mountain had grown a second, smaller mountain out of nothing but grief carried up one stone at a time, each stone no bigger than a fist and the whole of it, by the time word of it had travelled the length of the island twice over, taller than any hall the Hall had raised.

Anndra never climbed that hill. He knew of the cairn the way he knew of the quay at Seann Bhrenn, as a thing told at a hearth by someone who had it from someone else, and it would not have occurred to him, hearing it, that a coast so far off from his own headland kept its dead in much the way Baile chrom kept its own three names in a bowl once a year, a stone against a cup, the two of them sharing one refusal: that a loss should go unmarked merely because the sea, or the years, offered no better answer to it than silence. He thought of it once, hearing the tale a second time from a different mouth some years on, and said to his own wife by the fire that a coast a man had never seen and would never see kept its grief the same as his own coast kept its, which she took, rightly, for as close to a kind thought as her husband ever spoke aloud about a stranger.

## VIII. Of the Great Cats and the Southern Road

It was in the one-and-twentieth year after the boat went down that news came to Baile chrom of a ruling far to the south, carried up the coast the slow way such things travelled before any road ran the whole length of the island: that the carriers of the southern road had found the great cats' own crossing running straight over their own path, between the southern hills and the fens beyond them, at the same season every year without fail, the beasts coming down off the high passes in numbers no herder had troubled to count and crossing the road in a body rather than singly, so that a carrier caught on that stretch at the wrong hour might sit an hour or more waiting for the last of them to clear the road. Eilidh nic Ìomhair, Keeper of the flame these forty years and more, had ruled, on being asked what the Law made of it, that no panther might be killed on that road while the crossing lasted, whatever beast it cost a herd or a household to let pass, and that the carriers were to wait it out in the waypoint houses built along that stretch for exactly such waiting.

The carriers, the telling had it, had grumbled at first, as carriers grumble at any delay the Law lays on a basket already late, one waypoint-keeper of that road being quoted, by the time the tale had travelled as far as Baile chrom, as having asked Eilidh outright what a beast's road was worth set against a household's coal, to which she was said to have answered only that the beast's road had run there longer than the carriers' own, and that a Law which measured every handful to the grain could measure a few days' patience too, if it chose. They kept the rule, once it was made, the way the island had come to keep most rulings it did not much like: without gladness, and without the will to test what the Hall would do if they broke it, and it cost them, in the end, exactly what she had said it would, and no more.

Anndra, hearing the tale at his own hearth from a trader who had it third or fourth hand from the south, thought it a strange kind of law to trouble a ruling over, a beast's own road left alone for a season, and said so to Torcall, who by then mended more nets than he spoke words, and who answered, after turning the thought over a good while with his hands still busy at the mesh, that a coast which had learned to let its own dead go unnamed for the sea's sake could hardly grudge a road a few days for a beast's sake. Anndra had no answer to that, and turned the tale over again himself that night on the headland with the beacon guttering and flaring above him in its usual driftwood way, and it seemed to him, by the time the fire burned low, that a rule which cost carriers only time, to let something older than any road pass unhindered across it, was cheaper wisdom than most rulings he had heard of in his life, and dearer bought than most too, if a man reckoned rightly what it had taken to learn it.

## IX. Of the Bowl at the Wake

For near forty years after the boat went down, Anndra kept the beacon and poured the wake's first cup, growing from the young man who had swum clear of a lift in the water he could not name into an old fisher whom the younger households asked, when a strange calm came over the bay, whether it was the kind of stillness that wanted watching. He told them honestly what the water had done and what he had heard, the lift and the sound like a hillside settling, and never once, in all those years, what he had seen out of the corner of an eye he had refused to turn. The younger households learned, in time, not to press him further than that, the way a strand learns which questions a tide will answer and which it will only ever wash back unanswered.

He died in his sixtieth year, in his own bed above the strand, with Torcall's grandson keeping the beacon by then and the wake's bowl already passed to other hands some seasons before, Anndra having grown too stiff at the last to carry the cup up from his own door to the shore without a boy's arm to lean on. The coast buried him within sight of the headland, as he had asked, and the fire he had carried wood to on so many nights burned that same night as it always burned, unevenly, fed with whatever driftwood the tide had left, watched by no one who had been in the boat with him, and answering, as it had always answered, to no measure the Law had ever troubled to keep.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Reverent Centuries

*FE 422 – 542*

> *Chan eil fearann aig neach nach eil aig a shliochd.*
> No one holds land who does not hold it for those who come after.
>
> — said of the granaries at Dùn dhearg, in the reverent centuries

## I. Of the Granaries and the Debt of Bread

Coinneach Mòr mac Tormoid was two-and-twenty, and still counted among the young men of Seann Dunn who had not yet been asked to speak at a council, the year the storm season broke early on the lowland fields and Sliochd Ìomhair opened the doors of the new granaries at Dùn dhearg for the first time to households that were not its own. He rode down with his father to see it, more from curiosity than need, for the house of Tormod held grain enough of its own that season, and what he remembered after, more than the stone walls or the measured piles of barley within them, was the queue: three hundred people or more standing in a line that bent twice round the yard, each with a sack or a basket, each waiting a turn that the keepers of the granary gave out with no more ceremony than a nod and a mark scratched on a tally, and none of them saying much to the ones ahead or behind, as people do not talk much while they wait on a thing they are glad of and ashamed of both at once.

His father, Tormod Bàn, had held no love for the house of Ìomhar and said so plainly enough at his own hearth, but standing at the edge of that yard he only watched the queue a long while and said, at last, that a house which filled its granaries against the storm season and then opened them to whoever came short had done what the old custom of sharing always asked and no lord before it had troubled to do at this scale, and that a debt of bread was a debt like any other, save that it did not always feel like one to the man who owed it, not until the day his own field failed and he found he had nowhere else to go but Dùn dhearg's gate. Coinneach asked him whether that made the house of Ìomhar the better lord for it, and his father said only that it made the house of Ìomhar richer in people who owed it something, which is not the same question, and that a young man who could not tell the two questions apart yet would learn to before he was much older.

He did learn it, in time, though not from any single lesson. The granaries filled again the next storm season, and the one after, and within Coinneach's own lifetime it had become the ordinary shape of things along that stretch of the lowland, so ordinary that the households who came to the gate no longer thought of it as owing anything at all, only as the way grain was had in a bad year, the way water was had from a well that happened to stand on another man's land. Sliochd Ìomhair never called in the debt in words. It did not need to. A house that had filled every belly on the plain through three bad harvests running had no need to remind anyone of it at the fourth, and the households themselves, when the matter came up at all, spoke of Dùn dhearg the way a man speaks of the ford he crosses without paying it any particular gratitude, save that he would notice keenly enough if it were taken away.

At the foot of the high pass to the north, in those same years, a different debt was being built more quietly still. Carriers who took the Hall's baskets over the pass had long rested their beasts at the last flat ground before the climb began, a stretch of machair with a spring on it and little else to recommend it, and by the time Coinneach was a grown man there was a settled place there with byres and a smithy and an inn that never had an empty bed in the season the pass was open, called by the carriers themselves, before it had any other name, simply the resting-place, and afterward Baile Mòr dhomhain, the great deep town, though it stood on no deep water and had no claim to greatness beyond the beasts it fed and the rings it took for feeding them. It lived by the pass and little else, as the carriers said of it without unkindness, the way a man says of his own trade that it is what he has rather than what he chose.

## II. Of the Keeping of the Flame

Coinneach came to the flame in the month of Giblean, in his five-and-twentieth year, the first Keeper of Sliochd Thormoid, chosen by the four houses at Dùn ìseal on a morning cold enough that the breath of every man who spoke his name for the office hung visible in the air of the chamber before it reached the ears it was meant for. He had not sought the office with any great heat, being by his own account and everyone else's a young man of more patience than ambition, and it was that same patience, more than any gift for speech or arms, that the houses named when they chose him: a Keeper, they said, did not need to be clever, only steady, for the flame asked nothing of a man but that he keep it, and a man who kept it steadily for sixty years was worth ten who kept it brilliantly for five.

He kept it for two-and-sixty years, longer than any Keeper of any of the four houses before him, and it was said afterward, by those who lived to see the length of his keeping laid out whole, that he had changed nothing in all that time, which was meant, and taken, as the highest praise the office could earn rather than the smallest. The flame at Dùn ìseal burned the year he came to it exactly as it had burned the year before, and the year he died it burned the same still, fed the same measure, tended by the same order of hands, answering to no different rule than it had answered to when Sìne nan Snaidhm first tied the knots at Dùn ìseal, generations beyond counting before him. A visitor from a coast that changed its harbour-master every ten years and thought nothing of it once asked Coinneach, late in his keeping, whether it did not weary a man to hold one office so long without altering it, and Coinneach answered that a flame altered was a flame gone out under a different name, and that he had never yet met the man wise enough to alter a fire and be sure, afterward, that it was still the same fire he had lit. The visitor pressed him once more, asking whether he had never in sixty years wished to leave some mark of his own upon the office he had held so long, and Coinneach said that a Keeper's mark, if he left one worth leaving, was that no one after him could point to any year of his keeping and say the flame had burned differently in it than in the year before, and that he counted himself fortunate to have found, in his own nature, so little wish to be remembered any other way.

In those same generations, in words the rolls themselves used and Coinneach might have used of his own keeping without changing one of them, the people of the lowland fields neither grew greatly in number nor dwindled, mined the same small measure of coal and burned the same small measure, whichever lord's stones a household happened to live between, and the rolls called them the reverent centuries: not for any reverence the people themselves professed, which was ordinary enough, but for the stillness of the years themselves, laid one on another like courses of a wall that never rose any higher, a wall built, if it was built for anything, only to keep standing.

## III. Of the Headman of Achadh chaol

Not every household under Coinneach's keeping was so settled as the tellings of the reverent centuries made it sound, and the first council he sat through in the year after his choosing gave him a lesson in how much settling a household still had to do before the rolls would call it ordinary. Shepherds out of the eastern hills had taken up the upland fields at Achadh chaol some years before, sending their wool down to the harbours along tracks no cart had cut before them, and their headman, a broad, slow-spoken man named Griogair Ruadh who had never in his life sat under a roof he did not himself thatch, came down to the council at Dùn ìseal that season to ask, on behalf of the whole settlement, for a seat among the houses that governed the plain.

He asked it plainly and without much art, standing before the four Keepers with his hat in both hands and his feet planted the way a man plants them on a hillside rather than a hall floor, and said that his people had held the upland fields long enough now to be called a share like any other share, and that a share which paid its dues as faithfully as Achadh chaol paid its had earned some voice in how those dues were spent. The houses heard him out, as the custom required, and then asked him the one question the custom also required, which was whether any household of Achadh chaol held hearth-right under the old grant, the right knotted on the cord at the Roinn, without which no settlement, however long-standing, could claim a seat at the council rather than merely a place in its queue.

Griogair Ruadh had no answer to that question beyond the true one, which was that his people's grant was newer than the Roinn by some thousand years and carried no such right knotted anywhere. He did not pretend otherwise, nor try, as a lesser man might have, to talk the council past the question rather than answer it; he only stood a while longer with his hat still in his hands, looked once round the chamber at the four Keepers seated above him, and said that he had walked five days down off the hill to hear a thing he had half known before he set out, and would walk five days back up having heard it said plainly rather than merely feared, which was, in its own way, worth the walking. Having given that true answer he sat a single season on the council as courtesy allowed, said little in it that any teller thought worth keeping, and went home again to Achadh chaol at the season's end with no seat and no promise of one, only the courtesy he had been given and the dues he still owed. He bore it, by every account that reached Seann Dunn afterward, without bitterness, telling his own people only that a right knotted at the Roinn outlasted a right spoken aloud, however fair the speaking, and that a household wanting a seat at that council had best begin, if it could, by finding some old knot of its own to show. Coinneach remembered the sound of Griogair Ruadh's voice longer than he remembered the substance of what either side had said, a man asking plainly for a thing plainly refused, and thought, more than once in the years after when some newer household came asking the same question in gentler words, that the answer never changed because the cord never changed, and that a Keeper's whole use, in such a matter, was only to say so without pretending the saying cost the asker nothing.

## IV. Of the Walkers and the List of Ruins

It was in his own seven-and-twentieth year of keeping, when the flame had settled into him as thoroughly as he had settled into the flame, that Coinneach sent out the walkers, four men and two women chosen for legs that had carried them the length of the plain more than once and tongues that did not run ahead of what their eyes had actually seen, with instructions to list every ruin standing on ground the four houses claimed and to say, of each, only who did not own it, and never to guess who had built it or why. It was not a grand undertaking as the plain reckoned such things, and Coinneach himself, asked why he troubled with it at all, said only that a lord who did not know what stood on his own ground could not in honesty claim the ground, and that the plain had grown thick enough with old walls and older stones that no house any longer knew, without asking, which of them belonged to anyone living.

The walkers were gone the better part of two years, and came back with a list longer than any of them had expected to make. They brought Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, a walled outpost on a spur above Cathair mhòr with stones dressed smooth on the outward face only and a single gate blocked from within by rubble no living hand had put there; they brought Làrach an Dùin, three rings of broken wall and a cistern cut into the bedrock with room, by the walkers' own reckoning, for four hundred souls and their beasts, though what four hundred souls had ever sheltered there none of the households nearby could say; they brought Làrach an Teampaill, a stepped platform of fitted stone whose altar, they noted with the same flat honesty they gave to everything else, faced the central mountains and not the sea, as no altar raised in living memory ever faced; and they brought word, too, of standing stones scattered singly across the plain that answered to no name at all, only a description each, a long stone leaning east, three stones in a broken ring, one stone alone on a rise with a hollow worn at its foot by nothing the walkers could account for.

Of not one of these did the list say who had raised it. Coinneach ruled, when the walkers laid their tally before him, that it should not, and held to the ruling against more than one house that pressed him afterward for a guess dressed up as a finding, saying that a Keeper who let his walkers guess once would have to let them guess every time after, and that a list which told the plain only who did not own a ruin was worth more, in the end, than a list which told it a comforting lie about who had. The list stood, unaltered, for the whole length of his keeping and beyond it, and it was from that list, more than from any single ruin in it, that the plain first learned to speak of the builders of such places, whoever they had been, as simply the old people, with no house's name attached to the phrase and no house troubled, thereafter, to attach one.

## V. Of the Ring of Stakes at Cnoc bheag

The standing stone above Cnoc bheag was the one ruin on the walkers' list that did not stay untended once it was named. It stood alone on rising ground just outside the town, taller than a man and cut, on its upper face, with marks none living could read, the lines of them running in no order a household of the plain could follow. No one at Cnoc bheag claimed to know whose hands had cut them, nor when, only that the cutting was old enough that even the oldest woman in the town, asked about it at her own hearth, could say only that her grandmother had called it old already.

It was the cattle grazing the rise around it that moved the people of Cnoc bheag to act, in the year the walkers' list reached them, more than any thought for the stone's age: they had taken, over some seasons, to rubbing themselves against its lower face the way cattle rub against any standing thing in a field with few trees, until the lower cut signs had begun to wear soft at their edges under hide and horn. A household whose byre stood nearest the rise raised the first ring of stakes about the stone that same season, driving them by hand into ground too stony for a proper post-hole, and the ring held the cattle off well enough that the household beside it raised a second length the year after, and within Coinneach's own lifetime the whole rise had a fence about it that no single household could claim to have built, only to have added to, each generation renewing the stakes its own grandparents had first driven and never once moving the stone itself so much as a hand's breadth from where the old people, whoever they were, had set it. It stands so yet, ringed and unmoved, the fence renewed oftener than any hall on the plain has been rebuilt, which Coinneach, hearing of it in his own old age from a Cnoc bheag man come to Seann Dunn on other business, allowed was as fitting a monument as any stone the old people themselves had ever cut, for it asked nothing of the plain but that the plain go on doing, every generation, the one small thing it had already learned to do.

## VI. Of the Bath-House at Muileann ruadh

The warm springs below Muileann ruadh had been known to the plain longer than any hall now standing on it, a handful of pools where the ground ran hot enough to steam on a cold morning, and for as long as anyone could tell it they had been used the way a household uses any good thing it finds unclaimed, by whoever walked far enough to reach them and troubled to strip and wade in. It was in Coinneach's eightieth year, when a cousin of his own house fell sick of a wasting cough that the ordinary remedies had failed to touch and was carried the two days' journey to the springs on a litter more in desperation than in any settled hope, that the plain first saw what a roof over those pools might do that the open pools themselves had never managed, for the cousin lay in the steam of the covered spring through a hard winter that would have killed him lying anywhere colder, and came home in the spring thinner but breathing, and lived nine years more.

Coinneach, hearing the whole of it from the cousin's own mouth, gave the order that a proper bath-house be raised over the largest of the pools, roofed and walled well enough to hold the steam through a winter storm, with sleeping-places built along one side for the sick and rough benches along the other for whoever had carried them there and meant to wait out the cure with them. He named a keeper of the springs to tend the place, a task he gave, deliberately and against the grumbling of more than one house that thought the honour beneath a hearth-holder, to a widow of no great name who had nursed her own husband through a like wasting and knew, she said, more of steam and fever than any council was likely to teach her, and he set her office in the name of Dian Cècht, the healer, the first office the flame at Dùn ìseal had ever made that answered to no measure of coal at all. It was, by his own accounting late in life, the ruling he was proudest of among all he had made or left unmade in two-and-sixty years, not because it altered anything about the flame or the granaries or the reverent stillness of the plain's own years, but because it was the one thing in the whole of his keeping that had cost the house of Tormod nothing and given a sick man breath he would not otherwise have drawn, and a Keeper, he said once to the widow herself, might do worse with sixty years than to find, somewhere in the middle of them, one such ruling. She kept the springs for four-and-thirty years after, and trained, before she died, two of her own grandchildren to the same office, so that the keeping of Muileann ruadh's steam passed from hand to hand within one household long after the household that had first carried a dying man there had any other claim on the place at all; and Coinneach, who lived only a few years past the raising of the roof, said of that alone among his rulings that he hoped it would outgrow him.

## VII. Of the Weights of Muileann chiar

The silversmiths of Muileann chiar cast their set of weights in the same decade, though not at Coinneach's asking nor at any house's, being a matter the smiths took up among themselves after one too many disputes at their own market over whether a given lump of silver weighed what the seller claimed for it. They cut the least of the set to the weight of a single barley-corn and the greatest to the weight of a newborn lamb, with a dozen steps between carefully checked one against another until the smiths themselves would stake their own trade's name on the set's honesty, and set the whole of it out for any trader on the carriers' roads to use, asking nothing for the use beyond the courtesy of returning the weights to their proper rack when the weighing was done.

It spread the way an honest thing spreads among people grown weary of dishonest ones: no ruling of any house sent it abroad, only traders themselves carrying word of it from market to market, until within Coinneach's own lifetime a thing weighed at Muileann chiar was spoken of on every stretch of the carriers' roads as weighed fairly, a phrase that outlived, in the plain's own mouth, every other thing the smiths of that town were known for. Coinneach, who governed no market and claimed no credit for the weights, said of them only, when a visiting Keeper of another house asked him how his own flame had managed so useful a thing, that the flame had managed nothing, that the smiths of Muileann chiar had managed it themselves out of their own weariness with liars, and that the plain would do well to remember, watching the weights spread unbidden from market to market, that not every good thing on it had needed a Keeper's hand to make it good.

## VIII. Of the Marriage and the Double-Sworn Fields

The dark thread of Coinneach's own old age began, as such threads so often do, with a match that pleased everyone who arranged it. Torcall Donn, great-grandson of Eithne nic Ailein and a landed man of the lowland plain about Cathair mhòr, was five-and-eighty and long past the age most men on the plain married a second time, when he took to wife Muireall nic Ìomhair, a young kinswoman of the house of Ìomhar not yet four-and-twenty, in a match both houses spoke of afterward as having cost neither side anything and gained both a great deal: Torcall a young wife and heirs still to come of her, and Muireall's own kin a tie of blood into the line that held Cathair mhòr's great share, which no marriage before had managed. The wedding was held at Dùn dhearg, by Muireall's own family's wish, and Coinneach himself, though the match was no business of his flame, travelled down to bless it at the asking of both houses, and said afterward to no one in particular that he had rarely seen two houses so pleased with an arrangement that neither of them, strictly, needed.

Muireall died in her first winter as a wife, of a fever that took hold in the space of nine days and gave the physicians of Cathair mhòr no chance to do more than watch it run its course, and she left behind no child, only the lands that had come to her at her marriage and the lands she had brought into it, held under both a grant from the house of Ìomhar and a grant from the line of Eithne, as her marriage-portion had been sworn to satisfy both sides at once and had satisfied, in the drawing, no one's question of what should happen were she to die without an heir of her own body. Within the year, the house of Ìomhar claimed her lands as returning, on a childless death, to the kin that had granted them, and the line of Eithne claimed the same lands as passing, by the marriage, into the husband's holding and thence to his own kin at Cathair mhòr, and both claims were argued with equal heat and equal justice by men who had never troubled, while Muireall lived, to ask which grant would prevail should she die too soon, because no one had thought a woman not yet four-and-twenty would die too soon.

What began as an argument over a bride's portion did not stay an argument over a bride's portion. Within two years of Muireall's death, households on ground her marriage-portion had touched found themselves claimed by both houses at once, sworn, or made to swear, to Dùn dhearg on one hand and to Cathair mhòr on the other, and a holding sworn twice over was a holding neither side would leave standing for the other's use. The first of the double-sworn fields to burn belonged to a household that had held the same stretch of barley ground for four generations without either house troubling to ask it whose grant it lived under, and the burning, when it came, came in a single night from men its own household could name by voice if not by face, the byre fired first and the standing barley after, so that by morning there was nothing left on that stretch worth either house's claiming. The household that had held it went, as the plunderers' households had once gone, down to whatever kin would have them, and the ground lay unsown the season after, claimed loudly by both houses and worked by neither, which those who saw it called a stranger sight than the fire had been: land that a house of Ìomhar's blood and a house of Eithne's blood both wanted badly enough to burn a neighbour for, and neither wanted enough to plant. The men who fired it were no strangers to the household that lost it, but its own near neighbours, men who had shared a boundary stone with the burned household the season before and would share nothing with it now but the smoke. Coinneach, growing old by then and troubled more by the burnings than by anything else two-and-sixty years of keeping had shown him, called it, the one time he was heard to name it plainly, the war neither house had declared and both houses were fighting, and said that a plain which had gone three centuries scarcely changing had found, in one woman's early death, a wound that changing might not close again in his own lifetime nor in the lifetime of whoever kept the flame after him.

## IX. Of the Death of Coinneach Mòr

He died in his eighty-seventh year, in the month of the year's turning, in the small room off Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal where the Keepers slept, with the flame he had kept so steadily burning in its accustomed place not twenty paces from where he lay and the widow of the springs herself among those who sat the watch with him at the end. In his last days he asked after the walkers' list, whether it still said only who did not own each ruin and had not been made, in his absence, to say more, and was told that it stood as he had left it, and seemed satisfied with that answer beyond any other comfort offered him.

He asked, too, after the fields his own Keeping had failed to keep whole, and was told, because those who sat with him judged an old man's asking better answered than left to guess at, that three more holdings on the marriage lands had burned that same season, the smoke of the nearest of them visible, on a still day, from the rise where the fence still stood about the stone at Cnoc bheag. A long silence answered that news, such as those who had known him through his whole keeping recognised as his particular way of receiving a thing he had no ruling left to give against, and he died before the season turned again, leaving the flame to whoever the four houses would choose after him and leaving the plain, in the words the rolls kept afterward of his going, exactly as reverent and exactly as centuries-still as he had found it, save for the smoke that stood, some mornings, on the horizon south of Dùn dhearg, where no smoke of that kind had stood in living memory before Muireall nic Ìomhair died too young to settle which of two houses her lands belonged to.

# Chapter Twenty: Of Fearghas of the Two Oaths

*FE 543 – 556*

*The reapers of Achadh mhòr tell this at the end of harvest, when the last sheaf is cut, and they cut it high.*

## I. Of the House Sworn Twice

Achadh mhòr lay where the Red Share's stones ran out and Eithne's plain began, and no one now living could say which of the two had held it first, only that both had held it long enough to be sure of it. The fields ran flat and wide between the two boundary lines, the best grain ground on the island, and the house that farmed them had been sworn to both lords since before Fearghas's grandmother was a girl. It was Ciorstaidh who had made the double oath, not by any wish of her own: she had stood up at the Roinn among the seven hundred and twelve, had her knot cut through with the rest, and married after into a family already sworn to Dùn dhearg, so that her children answered to two halls at once and her grandson after them. Fearghas had heard the story of the cutting so many times as a boy, at so many hearths, that he could have told it himself in his grandmother's own words, down to the catch in her voice at the place where the knife went through.

By the year the reapers now reckon as the true beginning of his trouble, Fearghas was a hundred and seventy-one years old, which on the island of that century was old but not yet remarkable, and had held Achadh mhòr's granary fields alone for longer than most men then living had been alive. He was called, and had been called since he was young enough to find it funny, Fearghas Dà-Mhionn, Fearghas of the Two Oaths, and for the better part of a hundred and fifty years the name had been a joke told at his own hearth as readily as at anyone else's. Twice a year, at the two greater cuttings, he sent a sheaf to Dùn dhearg and a sheaf to Cathair mhòr, each a little short of the full measure, measured on his own threshing-floor before both stewards' men so that neither steward could say he had been cheated more than the other. He used to say, when a stranger asked him how a man served two lords without being torn between them, that he had never yet met the lord who begrudged a short sheaf so long as his neighbour got no more, and that this was the whole of statecraft as he understood it. It got a laugh at Dùn dhearg and a laugh at Cathair mhòr both, which he counted, privately, as proof that he had struck the balance right.

He had a wife once, Beathag, who died young of a fever the healers at Muileann ruadh could not put a name to, and no children who lived past their first winter, so that by the year the reapers mean, the house at Achadh mhòr held only himself, his steward, and whatever hands the harvest needed hired in from the granaries round about. He kept a stone knife of his grandmother's on the lintel of the hall, the one she had carried after the Roinn and given him in his turn, since the knife that had cut her cord that day no one had kept, and he touched it going in and out of his own door the way another man might touch a charm, without troubling to say why.

The fields ran a good half-day's walk from stone to stone, east to west, longer than any granary holding on either side of the two shares, and a carrier coming up the east road with his basket could reckon he had reached Achadh mhòr a full morning before he reached the hall, so wide was the grain before any roof showed over it. Fearghas had walked every rod of it on foot at one time or another in a hundred and seventy years, first at his father's heel and then alone and then, in the last decades, with whichever steward the years had left him, and there was no boundary stone on either side, the Red Share's or Eithne's, that he could not have found blind by the shape of the ground underfoot. He knew, better than either hall that claimed him, exactly where his own oath ran out and the other's began, which was one reason, though not the only one, that neither Dùn dhearg nor Cathair mhòr had ever managed to catch him short on either sheaf.

## II. Of the War Fought in Fits

The joke held for most of a hundred and fifty years because the two houses it named had no quarrel that Fearghas's short sheaves could not paper over. It stopped holding the year a great-grandson of Eithne's, Torcall Donn, took to wife Muireall nic Ìomhair, of the line that held the Red Share, meaning the marriage to heal what the island still called, out of old habit, the strife of the heirs, though the Roinn that had begun it was by then five centuries gone and half forgotten outside the Hall's own rolls. Muireall died in her first winter at Cathair mhòr, of nothing anyone could point to, only the ordinary cruelty of a cold season on a woman not raised to it, and the lands she had brought to the marriage, three granges and a fishing-right on the Abhainn fhionn, were claimed at once by both houses: Cathair mhòr's, because the widower held them; the Red Share's, because Muireall had never sworn them away from her own line. Neither claim was new in its kind. What was new was that there were, by then, some hundreds of holdings across the island sworn to two lords the way Achadh mhòr was, households that had married and been given land and taken oaths without troubling, in quieter years, to notice that the oaths might one day pull in different directions, and every one of those hundreds of holdings now had to choose.

Fearghas watched it happen to his neighbours before it came near his own gate. The household two valleys east of Achadh mhòr, sworn the same double way, chose the Red Share within the first season, on no better reason than that the Red Share's steward asked first and asked more civilly, and Cathair mhòr's men burned it to the field-walls before the following harvest, taking the cattle and leaving the house standing empty and black-eaved as a warning to the next household asked to choose. A holding to the south, sworn the same way, tried the opposite course and chose neither, sending word to both halls that it would keep faith with whichever kept faith with it, and was burned within the year by both, first the Red Share's riders in a night raid that took the barn, and then, before the roof could be mended, a company out of Cathair mhòr that finished what the first had started, each host telling its own men it was only punishing what the other had already begun. Refugees from both kinds of burning came through Achadh mhòr on the road to wherever they still had kin, and Fearghas fed what he could of them from his own stores and asked no oath of any of them, since he judged, and said so once to his steward, that a man burned out for choosing badly had paid enough already without being asked to choose again at another man's gate.

One family from the southern burning, a widow and three grown sons with nothing left to their name but a hand-barrow and a milking cow that had somehow been walked clear of the fire, stopped three nights at Achadh mhòr on their way to a sister's holding beyond Ceann leathan, and the widow, warming herself at Fearghas's own hearth on the second of those nights, asked him outright, with the bluntness of a woman who had already lost everything a lord could threaten to take, why a man sworn twice himself had never once been asked to choose the way her own household had. Fearghas told her, and it was the only time his steward ever heard him say it in so many words, that he supposed neither hall had yet reckoned Achadh mhòr's grain worth the burning, and that he had made his peace, long before she ever came to his door, with the year they finally did. The widow said nothing to that, only looked at him a while over the fire, and went on to Ceann leathan the next morning without asking him anything further.

Fearghas rode out himself, once, in the third year of the burnings, to the black-eaved holding two valleys east, not to claim it, for it was Cathair mhòr's men who had burned it and no lord of the Red Share's would have thanked him for standing on ground his own house had never held a right to, but only, as he told his steward before he went, to see with his own eyes what a double-sworn holding looked like once the choosing was done and paid for, since he judged a man ought to know the shape of the thing he might himself be asked to choose. He found the field-walls standing and the house gone to its foundations, the byre likewise, and an old dog still living about the ruin that would not be coaxed away from it though no one remained there to feed it, and he stood a long while at what had been the threshold, saying nothing to the steward who had ridden with him, before turning his horse back toward Achadh mhòr without once setting foot inside the walls themselves. It was after that ride, the steward said, that Fearghas stopped speaking of the war as something happening to other men's holdings, though it was three years more before anyone at either hall heard him speak of it as something that might happen to his own.

It went on that way in fits rather than as one war fought straight through, a burning in one valley followed by two quiet years and then a burning in another, because neither the Red Share nor Cathair mhòr had the strength any longer, five centuries and more after the Roinn had first cut the island into shares, to keep a host in the field for a whole season. The lines that had once stood up seven hundred and twelve strong were down, by then, to a scattering of great-grandchildren holding what their forefathers had held whole and parting it further at every burial, and only the two strongest, the Red Share that Ìomhar's blood had never let be broken and Eithne's own plain, still had spears enough to call a muster worth the name. The island came to call it Cogadh an Dà Mhionn, the War of the Two Oaths, for Fearghas's own house before any other, since his was the oldest and best known of all the double-sworn houses, the one every teller reached for when the war wanted a name, though he himself had done nothing yet to earn it beyond going on sending his short sheaves and hoping, as he told no one but his steward, that the two hosts would exhaust each other on smaller holdings before either thought to reckon what a granary the size of Achadh mhòr's might be worth to whichever side finally took it whole.

## III. Of Torcall Donn

Torcall Donn did not live to see how long the war he had made, without meaning to, would run. He was a hundred and eighteen years old, and had never in his life led men further than the boundary of his own fields, when the Red Share's riders caught his company on the road below Dùn thais in the fifth year of the burnings, going, by his own account afterward given to no one, only to see the granges his wife had brought him and judge for himself whether they were worth what both houses were spending to hold them. He was killed there, on the road and not in any hall, and his own steward, who survived it, said after that no one on either side had struck the first blow with any particular hatred, only that a company of the Red Share's riders had met a company of Cathair mhòr's on a narrow stretch of road neither would give way on, and that Torcall Donn had been in front when the pushing turned to something worse. Word of it reached Achadh mhòr within three days, carried by a granary carrier who had seen the bodies still on the road and would not eat at Fearghas's table until he had told it all, start to end, twice over.

Fearghas heard it out standing in his own doorway with his hand on his grandmother's knife, and said only, when the driver had finished, that a man dead on a road solved nothing that a man alive with a claim on land had not already made insoluble, since the lands Muireall had brought were no less claimed by both houses for her husband's death, and might now be claimed with less patience on either side, there being no one left living to argue that the marriage had ever been meant to end this way. He was right in it, as the years after bore out: the Red Share pressed its claim on the three granges harder once Torcall Donn was gone rather than less hard, judging, not wrongly, that Cathair mhòr's grip on lands it held only through a dead man's marriage was weaker than it had been while he lived, and Cathair mhòr held to its claim all the harder for the same reason, so that the war, which might have guttered out on Torcall Donn's death the way a fire sometimes dies with the man who lit it, instead burned on past it into holdings that had nothing to do with Muireall's dowry at all, Achadh mhòr's own among the number that both houses now began, for the first time in Fearghas's long life, to count aloud.

Torcall Donn's body was carried back to Cathair mhòr and buried there rather than sent to whatever Red Share ground his wife's people might have claimed for it, and it was said afterward, though Fearghas never repeated it as more than a saying he had heard, that Eithne's own hall kept his grave apart from the family ground for a season, as though even the dead of the marriage that had begun the war could not be let lie too near the living who still argued over what it had bought them. Fearghas sent no man to the burial, judging that a lord sworn to both houses had no honest place at a grave either side might read as taking sides merely by his standing near it, but he sent, by the same granary carrier who had first brought the news, a measure of Achadh mhòr's own barley to be burned at the graveside in Torcall Donn's name, the old rite for a man who had died before his harvest was in, and asked that no word go with it saying who had sent it. The carrier kept that silence rather less carefully than the mason later would keep his, so that within the season it too was known on both sides of the war, and read, as everything Fearghas did in those years came to be read, two different ways by two different hearths.

## IV. Of Ciorstaidh's Stone

It was in the second year after Torcall Donn's death that Fearghas had his grandmother's stone cut and set into the wall of his own hall, a plain grey slab cut on its two faces with the signs of the two shares and, between them, the sign of the knot, the same sign the eleven had worn who had their cords cut through at the Roinn. He had put off doing it for a hundred years and more, telling his steward, when the man asked why, that a stone in a wall could not be unsaid the way a story at a hearth could, and that he had never been sure, until that year, what he wanted said permanently about a woman who had been sworn twice before he himself was ever sworn to anything. What decided him was neither grief nor age but the plain reckoning that the house he had inherited from her, along with her double oath, was now spoken of on both sides of a war as a prize rather than a farm, and that whichever host eventually took it, he wanted it known, cut in stone and not merely told, that the man who had held it last had held it from a woman who had cut her own cord at the Roinn and answered for it all her life without once choosing a side to betray the other.

The stone-cutter who came up from Muileann chiar to do the work said afterward, to whoever would listen, that he had cut a hundred memorial stones in his time and never one where the man who ordered it stood over his shoulder the whole day watching every stroke of the chisel, as though he feared the mason might carve some sign into the grain of it that was not true. Fearghas paid him double the going rate and asked him to say nothing of the day's work at Dùn dhearg or at Cathair mhòr, a request the mason kept for exactly as long as it took him to reach the next market, where the setting of Ciorstaidh's stone became, within a season, one more thing the tellers on both sides of the war repeated of Fearghas Dà-Mhionn, some saying it proved he still meant to hold for both houses to the end, and others saying, more shrewdly, that a man who set his grandmother's memory in stone before deciding anything else was a man already reckoning how he wished to be remembered, which was not the same thing as reckoning how he meant to act.

## V. Of the Hosts Called Out

The word that both hosts were finally on the road for Achadh mhòr came to Fearghas in the heat of Lùnastal, six years after the stone was set, carried by two riders arriving within an hour of each other, one from the east swearing that the Red Share's council had that week resolved to take the granary whole rather than go on arguing its worth in councils that settled nothing, one from the west swearing the same of Cathair mhòr, each rider plainly astonished to find, on arrival, that his own lord's host was not the first to move. Fearghas was a hundred and eighty-four years old that Lùnastal, and had outlived his wife, both his children, his grandmother, and every steward who had served him before the one now standing at his shoulder, and he heard the two riders out in the yard, one after the other, with no more visible feeling than he had shown at any of the burnings two valleys off, though his steward, who had served him eleven years by then and thought he knew the shape of the man's silences, said afterward that this one had a different weight to it.

The steward had asked, when the second rider's dust was still settling in the yard, whether word should go to the granaries round about so that the smaller households might carry off what stores they could before either host arrived, a question any steward of thirty years' less service might have asked out of plain decency, and Fearghas had answered only that word had best go instead to the reapers still working the western strips, to finish the cutting they were on before they thought about anything else, an answer the steward found so strange coming from a man who had fed every burned-out household on the road for six years that he did not know, telling it afterward, whether to set it down to age, to grief he had not shown, or to some reckoning the old man had already made and not yet spoken.

The barley that year stood ripe to the edge of the sky, the best crop Achadh mhòr had raised in a decade of uneven summers, heavy-headed and dry after a summer with almost no rain in it, the kind of harvest a granary saw perhaps once in a generation and long remembered for it, and Fearghas walked out into it that evening with his steward a pace behind him, the way he had walked his fields every harvest evening of his long life, and ran his hand along the heads of grain as he went the way another man might run a hand along a horse's neck, an old habit he had never broken himself of, though his eyes could see well enough on their own by then what his hand was telling him. He looked east first, to where a low haze of dust hung over the road that came down from the Red Share, too far off yet to show men or spears but unmistakable to anyone who had watched such roads for six years running, and then west, to where a second haze, thicker and nearer, showed that Cathair mhòr's host had the shorter way to come and meant to use it. Neither haze had yet crossed a boundary stone, and by the steward's own reckoning there was the best part of a day left before either host could reach the fields at all, time enough, he thought, for the two of them to talk over what might yet be done, and he was already turning over in his mind which of the two halls a rider might be sent to first when Fearghas spoke.

"Whichever I feed, the other burns me," he said, not loudly, and not as a question, so that his steward, who had half expected to be asked which host stood the better chance, understood only afterward that the old man had not been asking anything at all. "I've sworn to both of them." He was quiet a moment, still looking west, where the dust was nearer than the east's. "Let them both have it."

The steward said afterward that he took the words at first for a bitter kind of surrender, a lord too old and too tired to fight either claim any longer allowing that whichever host arrived first might simply take what it liked, and he answered Fearghas in that understanding, saying that a rider sent now to Dùn dhearg, or failing that to Cathair mhòr, might yet buy the granary a season's grace while the two halls argued the matter between themselves as they had argued the three granges for forty years without once coming to blows over Achadh mhòr. Fearghas heard him out and shook his head, once, and said that forty years of argument over three granges had already cost more burned households than either hall would trouble to count, and that he did not mean to add Achadh mhòr's own people to that number waiting on a season's grace that would only be spent arguing the next season's instead. He asked, then, whether the last strip in the western field had been cut, and being told it had not, said that it should be, that evening, before dark, the same as any ordinary harvest evening the two of them had ever kept together.

## VI. Of the Last Sheaf and the Smoke

The reapers had already begun the last cutting that week, working the western fields first as the custom of Achadh mhòr had always run, and it was among them, not in the hall, that Fearghas walked next, asking which sheaf stood ready to be cut last and highest, the honour every harvest gave to whichever binder's hands were steadiest at the end of a long day, and telling the reapers, when they showed him, to cut it as they always had and carry it in to the hall as they always had, war or no war on the road. Some tellings since have made more of that evening than the steward himself ever claimed for it, saying Fearghas told the reapers plainly what he meant to do with their harvest before he did it, but the steward's own account, given many times over at hearths from Achadh mhòr to Muileann chiar, says only that the old man watched the last sheaf cut and bound, said nothing of fire to any reaper living, and walked back to the hall alone once the dark had properly come down, leaving the reapers to carry the last sheaf in behind him not knowing it would be the last thing carried into that hall whole.

He took the torch himself from the hearth inside, not sending steward or reaper to do it, and walked the bounds of his own fields lighting the standing barley from the eastern boundary stones, the Red Share's own markers, clear across to the western ones that marked Cathair mhòr's edge, so that by the time either host came over the rises that bordered the valley there was nothing left standing for a rider to see but smoke going up in one long sheet from stone to stone. He walked slowly, the steward said, not as a man in any haste to be done, stopping twice to catch his breath the way a man of a hundred and eighty-four years must, and laying the torch to each new stretch of standing grain with the same unhurried care he had once given to the reaping, as though a field fired badly might somehow be fired again more honestly. The barley took at once, dry as it was after a rainless summer, and ran ahead of him faster than an old man could walk, so that by the time he reached the western stones the eastern ones were already lost behind a wall of smoke he did not look back to see.

The fire took the field-walls and the drying-barns and, before any hand thought to stop it or any hand any longer wished to, the steadings themselves, running up from the fields to the hall on a wind that had stood fair for burning all that dry summer, so that the hall Ciorstaidh's stone stood in was already alight by the time the first riders of either host crested their rise and understood, each separately and each too late to matter, what the dust of the other host had been racing toward all along. The reapers who had cut the last sheaf that same evening carried it clear of the burning before the wind turned, and it was that sheaf, and not the granary it came from, that the households round about kept afterward and still keep, cutting a new one high at the end of every harvest since in the field-strips that grew back green the following spring, on ground that had been ash the autumn before.

Fearghas went back into the hall while it burned and shut the door behind him, and did not come out again, and no one who was there that night, reaper or steward, ever gave an account of trying to stop him or of being asked to. His steward said only that he had followed the old man as far as the threshold and been told, in the same voice that had said *let them both have it*, to go and see the reapers safe on the road to Muileann chiar, and that he had gone, and that by the time he judged it safe to look back the hall's roof had already fallen in on itself, and no door remained for anyone to have opened even had they wished to.

The Red Share's host came over the eastern rise first that evening and found the barley already ash to the middle distance; Cathair mhòr's host, coming over the western rise not an hour behind them, found the same, and both hosts, meeting at last on ground that had cost neither of them a spear thrown, stood on the black stubble in the last of that evening's light with nothing between them any longer worth fighting for, looking down at Achadh mhòr's smoke going up straight in the windless dusk, and finding, when each looked for the granary they had marched to take, only more of it. Neither host stayed the night on that ground. The Red Share's riders turned east again before full dark, and Cathair mhòr's before the last light was gone from the sky, each company going home to a hall that had spent six years and more arguing over a prize that had put itself beyond either of their reaching in a single evening, and it was said after, on both sides, that no rider of either host ever cared to say aloud which of the two hosts had arrived the first.

The reapers came back the following spring to strips gone black and then, within two seasons, green again, since fire does a granary field less lasting harm than it does a hall or a house, and they cut their harvest there for generations on ground that had once been sworn twice and was sworn, after that Lùnastal, to no one living. Fearghas Dà-Mhionn had lived a hundred and eighty-four years, sworn for a hundred and fifty of them to two lords at once, and was remembered on both sides of the shares he had refused, in the end, to choose between, though never, on either side, with quite the same story of why. It is the reapers' own telling, not the Hall's roll nor either lord's tellers, that has lasted longest: that a man who could not feed two masters honestly chose to feed neither, and that the last sheaf of Achadh mhòr is still cut high at every harvest's end for the sake of the one that was carried clear of the fire the year the fields answered, at last, to no oath but the reaping.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of the Peace of the Threshold

*FE 556*

*Niall Òg told this at more hearths than any other tale of his long life, and he always ended it the same way: "I have carried a great many things up that path. That was the heaviest, and she weighed nothing at all."*

## I. Of the Hungry Winter

The smoke of Achadh mhòr had not gone out of the sky before the middle of the island understood what it had lost. The two hosts that came home from the burned fields that Lùnastal brought back no grain, for there had been none to bring, and every granary between Dùn dhearg and Cathair mhòr that had counted on Fearghas's short sheaves to see it through the dark months now counted its own stores twice and found them wanting both times. The Red Share's granaries were full enough from the east, but the east had spent forty years feeding a war and had little to spare beyond its own households, and Cathair mhòr's plain, which grew less grain than it ate even in a fat year, had leaned on Achadh mhòr's harvest longer than anyone at either hall had cared to say aloud.

By the turn of the year the households of the middle plain were boiling bark with their oats to make the sacks last, and the waypoint-keepers on the road between the two shares had begun to ask carriers for news of grain before they asked for news of anything else. Old men said it was the worst want since the reverent centuries, when the same measure had been mined and burned generation after generation and nobody had thought to ask whether it was still enough for the mouths it fed. Younger men, who had grown up knowing nothing but the burnings, said only that a war fought over granary fields had done what neither side's spears could, and burned the granary itself.

The Hall's own rolls, kept on the knot-keepers' cords since Sìne nan Snaidhm's day, counted that winter's dead among the dead of the war, not apart from them, for the cold took the old and the very young in numbers no one troubled to count separately from the numbers the burnings had already cost, and there was no one left with the heart to draw so fine a line between a death by the sword and a death by an empty sack. Those who lived through it gave it a plain name and kept to it afterward: the hungry winter, said the same way in every hearth between Dùn dhearg and Cathair mhòr, and no other name was ever offered for it.

At the waypoint house on the road below Muileann chiar, where carriers had once asked first for news of the war, the keeper that season began asking first for news of grain, and kept a slate by his door on which he chalked, and rubbed out, and chalked again, which granaries along the road still had anything to sell and at what the toll-house on either side would let it pass for. A household two days' walk from Achadh mhòr's black fields sent its youngest son round every kinsman it had, near and distant, sworn or unsworn to either share, asking only for seed corn and not for grain to eat, on the reckoning that a family that ate its seed that winter would have nothing to sow when the ground opened again; and it is remembered, in that country, that the boy came home with less seed than he asked for but more than he had feared, gathered a handful at a time from households no better off than his own. It was the kind of winter, the old at Cathair mhòr said afterward, in which a neighbour's door mattered more than either lord's, and in which a good many people who had spent forty years choosing between two halls learned, in a single cold season, how little either hall could do for them once the choosing was over.

## II. Of the Call to the Threshold

It was Ruairidh Glas who sent the first word. He held the Red Share at Dùn dhearg by then, an old man himself, though nothing to the age of the woman he was sending to, and the word his runner carried to Cathair mhòr was short: that a war fought for a granary which no longer stood profited no one, that his own people were as hungry as hers, and that he would meet her to say so, if she would name a place neither hall need be ashamed to walk from.

Eithne sent back that she set foot in no hall of the Red Share's, as he set foot in none of hers, and that this had been true since before either of them held anything, and was not like to stop being true now. But she named a place all the same, by the same runner, who had to say it back to her twice before she would let him go. There was ground on the island that belonged to no share and never had, ground that every line of the old heirs had sworn to on the same day, before any of them had learned to hate the others: the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal, where the stone cup stood, and where seven hundred and twelve of them, in another age, had agreed on nothing except that the vein under the hill should belong to none of them. If the lords of the shares could not go under one another's roofs, she sent, let them stand under no roof at all.

Ruairidh Glas agreed to it, and so, in the weeks after, did every lord and lady left holding a share worth calling one: the Red Share out of Dùn dhearg; Cathair mhòr's plain under Eithne; the lesser holdings that had come through the burnings still whole, whose lords had watched the war from the edges and had no wish to be caught in the next one; and the double-sworn, those hundreds of households that had chosen a side, or refused to, and been burned by one or both for it, whose headmen came to Dùn ìseal with nothing left to lose by standing on ground that owed allegiance to neither of the powers that had ruined them.

Not every lord who was asked came willingly. The steward of one of the lesser holdings north of Achadh mhòr sent back word that his lord saw no profit in standing bareheaded before an old woman and an older man to be told what he already knew, that a burned field feeds nobody; and Eithne, when the answer was brought to her, said only that the man could stand at home then, and explain to his own hungry households why the peace that fed everyone else's had passed his door by. He came, in the end, with the rest, a season later than the first runners, and swore the same words as any other, and no one at the threshold troubled to remind him aloud that he had once thought better of it.

The day set was Samhain, the dark of the year, when every hearth on the island burned its own small handful and remembered the night the seven hundred and twelve had first sworn the Binding. It was the Keeper who pressed for that day above any other, arguing to both halls, by runners whose words Eithne and Ruairidh Glas each repeated afterward in much the same form, that a peace sworn on the one night every household on the island already kept the same rite would need no explaining to the households themselves; they would understand it the way they understood their own hearths, without a herald's telling. No one troubled to say aloud that this was also the night the Binding itself had first been sworn, on that same hill, by heirs who had agreed on nothing but that the vein should belong to none of them. It did not need saying, and by the time the runners had gone the length of the island and back, everyone who mattered to the swearing had worked it out for themselves.

## III. Of the Carrying of Eithne

She had ridden to Dùn ìseal once before, in the first year of the Roinn, on her own feet and at her own pace, quick and sharp and impatient of the ceremony that had kept seven hundred and twelve heirs sitting in a gathering-house through a whole winter and the summer after it. She did not ride there now. Her legs, which had carried her the length and breadth of the plain for the better part of two thousand years, had stopped carrying her some decades before, quietly, the way a well runs low before it runs dry, and she had accepted the chair the way she accepted most things by then, without complaint and without pretending it was anything other than what it was.

Two of her household carried the poles, one at the front and one at the behind, and the one at the front was Niall Òg. He had come to Cathair mhòr a season before, as he did most seasons by then, for he had outlived nearly everyone else who remembered the valley under Dùn ìseal in the days the tents stood there, and Eithne was one of the last who could still finish his own stories for him when his memory faltered on a name. He was some fourteen hundred and fifty years old that winter, a grandson of Ailean beside a daughter, and young enough beside her that she still called him the boy, as she had at the Roinn, though his own hair had long since gone the colour of hers.

"You could have sent a chair-man," she said to him, on the second day of the climb up from the plain, when the path had begun to steepen toward the hill. "You could have sent two chair-men and stayed by your own fire."

"I could have," Niall Òg said, and did not slow his pace, and did not answer the rest of it, because they both knew the rest of it, and neither of them had ever found much use in saying aloud what a silence already carried.

They went by the old carriers' road rather than the shorter track over the hill-shoulder, for a chair could keep the road where it could not keep the track, and the going was slow enough in any case that the second bearer, a grandson of one of Eithne's own household some three generations removed and young enough beside the other two that neither of them thought to ask his opinion of anything, had time to point out to her, at every mile, some boundary stone or byre or burned strip of ground he judged she might not have seen from a chair before. She had seen most of it a great many times, from a horse and from her own two feet, in centuries he had no memory of and no grandmother old enough to have told him of either, and she let him point it out to her all the same, because a young man's pleasure in showing an old woman his own country cost her nothing and seemed, on a road with so little else to recommend it, worth the having.

At the first night's stopping-place, a waypoint house on the old road where the keeper turned out half his own stores to feed a party he had not been told to expect, Niall Òg sat by her fire after the household had gone to their own beds and asked her, as he had not troubled to ask in some decades, whether she remembered the valley under Dùn ìseal the first time, when the tents had stood there and the cord had not yet been tied. She said that she remembered the smell of it before anything else, woodsmoke and wet canvas and something under both that she had never found a word for and had stopped trying to, and that she remembered Murchadh's voice before she remembered his face, a door on a cold hinge, he had, and had kept it to the end of his own long life. Niall Òg said that he remembered being called a boy for the first time in his life at that gathering, by men younger than his own father who had somehow contrived to be older than he was in years the island still counted, and that it had taken him the better part of nine hundred years to stop minding it and rather longer than that to be glad of it, since every one of the men who had called him it was dead now, and he was not.

"You are not a boy," Eithne said. "You are the last man on this island who remembers what I remember, and when I am gone you will be the only one, and there is nothing boyish left in that."

He said nothing to that for a while, and mended the fire instead, and when he spoke again it was only to ask whether she wanted another blanket against the cold, which she took as his own way of not saying aloud what her silence, in its turn, had already told him.

She watched the country go by from the chair, the burned black stretch where Achadh mhòr had stood still bare between the rebuilt eastern boundary and the rebuilt western, the boundary stones of a hundred small holdings along the road, cut with the marks of shares that were no longer as whole as they had been when the marks were first struck.
