Two thousand four hundred and fifty-five years she had lived by then, more than any soul then living on the island, and she had watched every one of those stones go up, and the wars that moved them, and she thought, watching the road unwind behind her, that she was tired in a way sleep did not answer, and that she meant this to be the last long road she asked her own legs, or anyone else's, to walk for her sake.

She said none of that to Niall Òg. She had never been a woman who told a man behind her what she was thinking before she had decided what to do about it, and she had not changed that habit for dying, any more than she meant to change it for living a while longer yet.

## IV. Of the Swearing

They came up to the hill of Dùn ìseal on the evening before Samhain, and found the stones before Talla na Lasrach already crowded, for word of the meeting had run ahead of every party that came to keep it, and no lord wished to be the last to arrive at a peace he had asked for himself. Ruairidh Glas was there before her, an old man in a plain cloak with no more men about him than courtesy required, and when her chair was set down he came across the stones himself, without waiting to be sent for, and gave her his arm to stand on, which she took, because her own legs by then needed it and there was no profit in pretending otherwise in front of the one man on the island old enough to remember why they had once been enemies.

"I have not stood this close to you since the ford," he said. He did not say which ford. There had been more than one in their two long lives, but she knew, because she had asked him once, decades before this, whether he still thought of the boy he had killed at Dùn thais, and he had said that he thought of little else on a cold morning, and had never asked her not to mention it again, which she had taken, from a man of his kind, for as near to an invitation as he was able to give.

"Nor I you," she said. "It has taken a burned granary to do it."

"Less than that, in the end," he said. "A winter with nothing in the sacks did it. I have buried more of my own people to this last hunger than to forty years of war, and I expect you can say the same of yours."

She could, and told him so, and they said nothing further to each other that evening, for there was a Keeper to greet, and lesser lords waiting their turn to be seen greeting the two eldest, and the ordinary business of a great meeting that neither of them, after so many centuries of great meetings, had any taste left for hurrying.

The Keeper that year was neither of the two names the Hall's own roll remembers best from either side of her, an office between offices, holding the flame in the years after Coinneach Mòr and before the woman who would take it from her; but she held the stone cup at her feet all the same, as every Keeper before and since had held it, and when the lords of the shares gathered on the stones the next morning, in the grey light before Samhain's dark truly closed on the day, it was she who set it down on the worn sill of Talla na Lasrach's threshold and stood back from it, so that no one might say the Hall itself had asked for anything from either side.

She had shaped the terms herself, at both halls' asking, for neither Eithne nor Ruairidh Glas had trusted the other's stewards to shape them and neither trusted his own stewards not to shape them a little in his own favour; and it was the Keeper who said them aloud to the gathered stones before any lord was asked to swear to a word of them, so that the crowd standing back beyond the lords themselves, headmen and stewards and a good many households who had walked up from the plain on no better claim than curiosity and hunger for news, might hear the whole of it plainly and carry it home in their own words rather than whatever a lord's own steward chose to tell them afterward. She said them slowly, in the flat voice the office asked of her rather than any voice of her own, and the crowd was quiet enough, in the cold of that morning, that a man at the back of it said afterward he had heard every word of it clear across the stones, though he stood further from the threshold than any lord standing to swear.

Eithne swore first. It had been agreed beforehand, by nobody's authority but the plain fact that she was the last living of the nine who had cut the cord at the Roinn, and no one at the gathering, not even Murchadh's own great-grandsons who still held the northern share in his name, thought to dispute it. She came forward on Niall Òg's arm rather than the chair, for she judged, and said so afterward to no one but him, that a peace sworn from a chair looked too much like an old woman being carried to her grave, and she meant this peace, if it held, to look like something a living woman had chosen. She laid her palm across the cup's mouth, as the custom asked, and said the words that had been agreed among the lords in the weeks before: that no share should be parted again at a lord's death, but pass whole to one heir named while the lord yet lived, or, failing a name, to whoever the Keeper judged nearest and fittest; that no household should hold an oath to two lords, and any that did should give up one of the two before the spring sowing; and that the boundary stones should stand where they stood that morning, on every share and every holding, and whoever moved one after should answer for it at Dùn ìseal.

Ruairidh Glas swore next, and where Eithne had said the words plainly and been done, he stood a moment longer with his hand still on the cup after the words were out, and said one thing more of his own, which no one had agreed beforehand and no one afterward thought to strike from the telling: "I shed the first blood of this at Dùn thais, over cattle on a wet slope, when I was young enough to think a stone worth a life. I am old enough now to know what I bought with it, and I would not buy it again for twice the grazing on the island." He took his hand from the cup, and no one answered him, for there was nothing owed in answer, and the lords who came after him to swear, one by one down the line of the shares, great and small, said only the words that had been agreed, until the sun that had barely cleared the eastern ridge when Eithne began was well up and warm on the stones by the time the last of the double-sworn headmen had sworn his own turn and stepped back.

So, on the day the island still calls Sìth an Stairsnich, the Peace of the Threshold, the lords of the shares ended Aimhreit nan Oighrean, the strife of the heirs, some five hundred and fifty years after Ruairidh Glas's spear had gone into Aonghas Bàn on the wet slope above Dùn thais. No one who stood on the stones that morning troubled to reckon the years aloud. It was Niall Òg, telling it afterward at his own hearth and at every other that would have him, who did the reckoning, and who first said the number to anyone who had not already worked it out for themselves.

## V. Of the Double-Sworn

The clause that had already remade the shape of the island, holding a share whole from one lord's death to the next heir's swearing, cost the shares themselves the least grief that winter. The clause that cost the most was the plainer one, that no household should answer to two lords, and that whoever did must choose before the spring. There were still some hundreds of such households scattered along the old boundary lines, most of them families who had married across a share's edge two or three generations back and never thought the double oath worth troubling over until the burnings taught them otherwise, and every one of them now had a winter to decide which hall it would keep faith with and which it would let go.

Some chose the way Achadh mhòr's neighbours had chosen years before, for the same reasons: nearness, an old debt of kindness, a steward who asked civilly rather than one who threatened. Others chose against their own nearest interest, out of a grief that was still raw enough to want no further dealing with whichever hall's riders had done the burning in their own valley, whatever the cost of refusing it. A few, it is told, chose by no reckoning at all, but by a knucklebone thrown at the hearth on the night before the deadline, judging, as one such headman is remembered saying, that a knucklebone at least bore no grudge and asked for no bribe, which was more than either hall's steward could truthfully claim.

One such household, a holding on the old boundary a half-day's walk east of Achadh mhòr's black fields, had been sworn twice since a grandmother's grandmother's marriage, and its headman that winter sat by his own hearth three nights running, saying nothing to his wife or his grown sons beyond that he was thinking, until the eldest son, who had lost a brother to the burnings and had no patience left for his father's thinking, asked him outright which hall had ever once sent grain to their door in the whole of the hungry winter just past. The old man said neither had, and the son said that this, then, was the whole of the answer, and by the son's own account, given many years after at his own hearth in his turn, that was the reckoning that decided it: the plain memory of which door nobody's carrier had knocked on when the sacks ran low. The household kept the oath that had cost it least, and let the other go before the first thaw, and was neither the first nor the last on the island to reckon its loyalty that way that winter.

What none of them did, that whole winter, was burn a neighbour's roof for choosing wrong. The Peace held that first test better than either the lords who had sworn it or the households bound by it had quite dared to expect, and by the time the spring sowing came the boundary lines that had shifted and blurred through forty years of burning had settled again into a shape that would hold, with only small mendings, for longer than any lord who swore that Samhain morning would live to see.

## VI. Of the First Market

In the spring after the Peace, the Hall at Dùn ìseal opened its ground under Talla na Lasrach to a market on the four quarter days, Samhain, Là Fhèill Brìde, Bealltainn and Lùnastal, when the households of the eastern hills came up to pay their dues and found, waiting for them under the Hall's own shadow, traders from both the shares that had so lately burned each other's granaries, laying out hides and venison and charcoal and the silversmiths' new weights from Muileann chiar side by side on the same trampled grass. The first of those markets was a thin one, for the hungry winter had left little enough to trade, and more than one household came up the hill with nothing to sell and stood about the edges only to watch whether a trader of the Red Share and a trader of Cathair mhòr's plain could truly stand at the same stall without a steward from either hall coming to part them. None came. The Keepers allowed no coal to be sold on the Hall's own ground, then or ever after, and none was; but everything else the island grew or made or dug changed hands there on the fair weights, and by the third quarter day the households who had only watched the first were bringing their own baskets, and within a few years no one thought it worth remarking that a trader of one share should haggle over the same measure of hides with a trader of the other within a spear's throw of the cup that had lately parted their two hosts.

Eithne lived to be carried up the hill to a great many more of those markets than her household thought wise; Ruairidh Glas did not, whose own years, long as they were beside any ordinary man's, ran out within two generations of the swearing. But the stones they had sworn to leave standing stood, boundary after boundary, along every road a carrier walked between the shares, cut with the marks of lines that had once counted their honour in spears and now counted it, more quietly, in whether a stone had moved. In time the carriers who passed them going to and from the quarter-day market stopped troubling to read the signs cut on their faces at all, for the stones had stood so long, and the peace they marked had held so plainly, that a boundary no longer needed reading to be believed.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Truce in the Galleries and the Walled Town

*FE 557 – 634*

## I. Of the Rolls that Fill

In the years after the Peace of the Threshold the rolls at Dùn ìseal began to fill the way a field fills with barley once the birds have had their share of it and stopped coming: slowly, unevenly, season on season, until a shelf that had held a handful of notched sticks and a coil or two of knotted cord held more than any one knot-keeper could carry in both arms. The knot-keepers of Sìne's line were still the ones who kept it, cord and notch and nothing else, as their mothers and grandmothers had kept it since the Roinn; and the cords themselves had begun to multiply past what any hand could hold at once, one for every share, one for every boundary stone the Peace had fixed, one for every household that came up the mountain at the quarter days to swear an oath or settle a debt or ask the Keeper's word on a matter no lord below would touch. The island was at peace, and a peace, it turned out, made more work for a clerk than a war ever had, for a war at least had the grace to burn its own tally along with everything else it touched.

Seonaid Chiar was born into this fatter, quieter island in the year the reapers of the low country still reckoned by the last burning, though by the time she was old enough to reckon anything herself the burned fields of Achadh mhòr had long since greened over and the boundary stones the Peace had fixed stood as unremarkable as any others. She came of the house of Muireach, Sliochd Mhuirich, the one house among the four of custody that held no drop of the king's blood and had never claimed to, and she grew up on the mountain's own ground, among the nine hearths, with the smell of the galleries in her clothes before she had any clear notion of what lay under the mountain or why her grandmother's hands were always faintly grey at the knuckle no matter how often they were washed.

She was some six-and-twenty years old, by her own house's reckoning, when the nine hearths raised her to the flame; a young Keeper by any measure the office had known since Muireach Liath's own day, and younger than several of the cutters she would spend her first years learning to judge fairly. In those first years she held the cup the way a new-married woman holds a house not yet her own, carefully, and with an eye always on how the last Keeper before her would have done a thing, until enough seasons had passed under her own hand that she stopped asking herself the question and simply did what seemed right, which is, by most tellings, the mark of a Keeper who has finally grown into the office rather than merely into the name of it.

Her own grandmother, who had cut coal at Dùn ìseal all her working life and never once expected to see a grandchild raised above the galleries she had spent her back on, told her, the night the nine hearths' word came down, that a young Keeper's first year was worth two of any other, because a young Keeper is watched by every hearth in the Hall to see whether she will bend to the first steward who flatters her or the first lord who frowns, and that a Keeper who bends once in her first year is asked to bend again for the rest of her keeping. Seonaid took the warning to heart, and it is said of her, by cutters old enough to have served under her from the first season, that she never once in six decades gave a different answer to the same question asked twice, however many years apart the asking fell, which her own knot-keepers came in time to reckon the surest mark of her rule.

## II. Of the Stag's People at Cnoc bhàn

It was in the third year of her keeping, some nine-and-twenty years old by the reckoning her own house kept for her, that the matter of the stag's people came to the door of Talla na Lasrach and would not be turned away by silence, as it had been turned away by every Keeper before her since Gormshuil nic Mhuirich first shut the galleries against them.

The stag's people, newly housed at Cnoc bhàn north of the mountain, had grown in the generations of the shutting-out rather than withered, as the Hall had perhaps hoped it would. Its teachers still kept the question Sìleas nic Coinnich had left them at the far-eastern grove, generations before, unanswered and unforgotten: why the coal answered its colours to one hand and not to another, and whether the vein knew the difference between a cutter born to the galleries and one merely trained to them. They had not found an answer the Hall would accept, nor, in truth, had they found one they were wholly satisfied with themselves; but they had gone on teaching all the same, and their own cutters, barred from Dùn ìseal, had found work at Cnoc bhàn's own small seams and at Muileann chiar's silver, and the school had not starved for it.

Seonaid received their asking through three old men who climbed the mountain road on foot, in autumn, with nothing in their hands but a single lamp, which they set down unlit on the stones before the Hall's door as a sign that they had come to ask a flame and not to bring one of their own to compare against it.

"We do not ask to be believed," the eldest of the three said, when she had come out to them herself rather than send a steward, which the Hall had not troubled to do for the school in living memory. "We ask only to be let back among the cutters who are already there. Let the question stay a question. We will not ask it of the vein aloud, if the Hall will only stop asking us, aloud, whether we have any right to stand near it at all."

She thought on it through that winter, and took counsel of no one but her own galleries, walking them at odd hours with a lamp of her own until she had satisfied herself that the objection she had inherited from every Keeper before her — that a cutter trained outside the nine hearths might work some harm on the vein that a cutter born to it would not — was an objection she had never once seen answered with anything better than the fact that it had always been made. On 26 an Gearran, FE 574, she let the school's cutters back into the galleries, sworn, every one of them, to ask nothing of the vein aloud in the Hall's own hearing, whatever they went on asking of it among themselves at Cnoc bhàn. The Hall's own roll, in the dry words of whichever knot-keeper was set to keep it that season, calls the day a reconciling. The school, from that day to this, has never called it anything but a truce, and Seonaid, hearing both words used of the same morning in the same week, said only that she did not much mind which word a man chose, so long as the cutters kept the oath under either one.

The first of them to cross the gallery door again was an old man of the school whose teachers' teachers had been shut out by Gormshuil, and had spent the better part of his own long working life at Muileann chiar's silver seams believing he would die there without ever seeing the vein his own teachers had spent three generations arguing over. He stood a long while in the mouth of the gallery before he went in, by every account that survives of that morning, and said nothing to the cutters of the nine hearths who stood back to let him pass, and they said nothing to him, and it was, in its way, as full a truce as any words could have made it.

## III. Of the Island Filling Out

The rolls that came up to Dùn ìseal in Seonaid's years told of an island growing steadier than it had been in the five centuries since the Roinn, though no single teller then living could have said, from any one report, quite how much the whole had changed.

Cathair mhòr, on the southern coast, raised a wall of fitted stone about its own headland in those years, the first wall of its kind the island had ever built, and would not say, then or afterward, what it had raised the wall against. The reapers of Achadh mhòr, when anyone asked them, said only that the town had not forgotten the smoke, and left it at that, for the burning of the great granary fields was still near enough in living memory that no one much doubted them, and far enough that no one troubled to ask Cathair mhòr's own people to confirm it. Ceann leathan, on the southern fishing grounds, grew fat on dried fish sent inland along the carriers' roads, and its harbour-master began keeping tallies on notched sticks, among the oldest counted things kept anywhere on the island; the man who cut the first of them, it is told, was no scholar and no clerk, only a fisherman's son who had grown tired of arguing with buyers over how many baskets a boat had brought in, and had found that a stick with a notch for every basket argued better than he could.

At Inis thais, on the western coast, a shrine was raised to the ancestors the sea had taken and never given back, and its keepers burned their season's handful on the open shore rather than under any roof, so that the drowned, gone west over the water, might see the flame from wherever the sea had carried them. Cuan shean, further up that same coast, dug salt-pans on the flats below the town and boiled the sea over peat fires that burned day and night through the drying months, and sent its salt inland on the western road until it kept the fish of half the island through the long storm season; and where the road from Cuan shean crossed the heath above Baile fhiadhaich, a scatter of salt-carriers settled by a stream that ran the summer through, on ground too poor for the plough, and kept goats there ever after, by every account that has come down of them.

On the eastern road, where the carriers out of Cnoc leathan met the southern coast path, a waypoint house was built on ground already known for its warmth, and took the name the ground had always had, An Taigh-òsta Grianach, the sunny house; its own builders, asked afterward why they had chosen that stretch of road over a dozen others no less convenient, said only that a house ought to be built where the sun already liked to stand, and that this was reason enough. Cnoc leathan itself, at the road's eastern end, grew into the market town of the whole south-eastern hill country, and its carriers bound themselves into a guild that held, by the Hall's own grant, the sole right to carry for the Hall on the stretch of road down to the coast, a right its members guarded, in the years that followed, with rather more jealousy than the road itself was worth to anyone who had not grown up walking it.

Seonaid heard all this, in her years at Dùn ìseal, from the tallies and the tellings the waypoint-keepers and the harbour-masters sent up the mountain each quarter day, more of them each year than the year before, until she found herself saying to her own knot-keepers, more than once, that she had come to know the shape of towns she had never set foot in better than she knew the shape of her own galleries' further reaches, which she had likewise never had cause to walk to their very end. It was, she said once, at her own hearth and not for any roll to record, a strange thing to rule an island chiefly through the reports of men who had never once seen her face; and stranger still, she added, that it seemed to trouble the island rather less than it troubled her.

The guild at Cnoc leathan brought its own quarrel to her door in the fourteenth year of her keeping, when two of its own carriers came up the mountain, each swearing the other had carried a load down to the coast road out of turn and taken the fee for it, and each demanding the Hall strip the other of his place in the guild altogether. Seonaid heard them both out on the stones before Talla na Lasrach, in the plain grey light the office asked of every hearing, and asked at the end of it only one question of either man: which of them had first offered to give the disputed load back rather than argue over who had carried it. Neither had. She told them then that the Hall's grant to the guild was a right to carry, not a right to quarrel, and that she would as soon strip the whole guild of its charter as decide between two men who had each thought a fee worth more than a friendship of twenty years' carrying together, and left them to settle it between themselves before she troubled to hear either man's case again. They came to an agreement on the road home, by their own later account, before they had gone a mile, which the Hall's knot-keeper that season kept as proof, if proof were wanted, that most quarrels brought up a mountain could have been settled at the bottom of it, had either party troubled to try.

## IV. Of Ruairidh Glas and the Ford He Never Returned To

Of the old blood that had stood up at the Roinn, few enough were left by the time Seonaid held the cup, and fewer still who had themselves shed blood in the long strife the Peace had ended. Ruairidh Glas, holder of the Red Share at Dùn dhearg, had come to the holding some hundred and eighty-five years before Seonaid's own birth, at an age, six hundred and fifty-eight years, that had seemed unremarkable enough among his own kin and would have seemed past belief to any household of the low country; and he had held it, by the time the Peace was thirty years old, longer than any other lord then living had held anything.

He had sworn the Peace himself, on the stone cup, with his own hand still upon it when he spoke the one thing beyond the agreed words that no one afterward thought to strike from the telling: that he had shed the first blood of the whole long strife at Dùn thais, over cattle on a wet slope, when he was young enough to think a stone worth a life, and that he would not buy such a peace again for twice the grazing on the island. He had never gone back to Dùn thais after that morning at Aonghas Bàn's body, not once in all the centuries between, though the road there from Dùn dhearg was no longer than a hard day's ride and he had ridden further, on lesser business, a hundred times over. His steward, in the last years, used to say that his lord knew every stone on every road on the island except the one road he could have walked blind, and had chosen, deliberately and for reasons he never once gave aloud, not to.

In his nine hundred and ninth year he sent to Dùn ìseal, unasked, for leave to come up and stand once more before the stone cup, which no lord of a share was required to do outside the quarter days and which none had troubled to ask for in Seonaid's own years of keeping. She granted it without asking his reason, and he came up the mountain road on foot rather than by any chair or litter, for his legs still carried him and he saw no cause to spare them for whatever years remained. He stood before the cup a long while, by the account of the knot-keeper who kept the door that day, and said nothing aloud that any living ear caught, and went back down the mountain the same evening to Dùn dhearg, and died there within the year, in his own bed, with his own household about him, having lived nine hundred and ten years and outlived every soul who had stood up in the gathering-house at the Roinn, save only Eithne nic Ailein.

His son took up the holding without any summons to the Hall, for the Peace by then required none where an heir was named and undisputed, and the rolls of that season, which had grown careful about naming every lord however small, are strangely thin about naming this one; a fault, Seonaid's own knot-keeper said drily, that lay with the household's own silence about him rather than with any failure of her cords. He held the Red Share after his father a very long time, by any ordinary reckoning, and a markedly shorter one than his father had, though neither he nor his own son after him would live to see the day when that shortening was spoken of, in the Hall's own rolls, as anything but the ordinary way of things.

## V. Of the Fall in the High Gallery

It was in the three-and-fortieth year of Seonaid's keeping, when she herself was close on seventy years old and had begun, though she said so to no one but her own hands on a cold morning, to feel the mountain's damp in her joints the way the older cutters had always sworn a person eventually did, that the roof of the highest gallery at Dùn ìseal came down.

It fell in the dark hour before the second watch, when the gallery held fewer cutters than it would have by daylight but not so few that the fall went unwitnessed. The lamps went out with the dust before anyone standing further down the gallery understood what had happened, and it was the coughing, by every account that survives, that told the cutters below which way to run, since no one could see anything at all for the better part of a minute, and no one who was there afterward found much to say about that minute beyond the coughing and the dark. Four men died under it, cutters of the nine hearths every one; the eldest of them, a man named Aonghas Crom who had cut coal at Dùn ìseal since before Seonaid herself was born and had trained half the younger cutters now working the lower galleries, was found still gripping his pick, which the men who carried him up remarked on afterward more than they remarked on anything else about that morning. A fifth man was pulled out with a crushed hand that never again closed fully round a pick, and worked the lighter galleries for the rest of his years cutting one-handed, which the rolls note without further comment, as if a one-handed cutter working on regardless were no more remarkable, in that Hall, than a wall standing where a wall had always stood.

Seonaid went down into the gallery herself before the dust had finished settling, against every counsel her own stewards gave her, and stood in the broken rock with a lamp held high enough to see the shape of what the mountain had done, and said, to the men working to clear the fallen stone, only that she wished to see it with her own eyes before anyone told her what to think of it. What she saw, by every account, was rock enough to have killed twice the number it had, held back only by a seam of harder stone that had happened, by no planning of any cutter living, to catch the worst of the fall before it reached the floor where the other men stood.

The four dead were carried up and buried on the Hall's own ground, the one ground on the island no feud had ever been let to follow a man, and Seonaid herself set the last stone over the last of them, which no Keeper before her, so far as the rolls remember, had troubled to do with her own hands rather than a steward's. She gave the season over to argument after that, not about whether the dead should be mourned, which no one disputed, but about what should be done so that no gallery should ever again be held up by nothing more than the luck of a harder seam catching a fall before it found a man. On 23 an Lùnastal, FE 614, she ordered timber props of oak set in every gallery the Hall worked, the first timber the Hall had ever spent on the mountain rather than on a road or a bridge or a waypoint house below it, and the first oak for the purpose was felled and cut within the season, so that by the following year's cutting no gallery at Dùn ìseal stood without a prop of its own between the roof and the men beneath it.

The walled-up mouth of the highest gallery, where the four had died and where the fall itself had been judged too dangerous to work again, stood sealed from that year on, and stands sealed still, by every telling that has come down since; and it is that walled door, more than any prop or any roll, that the cutters of Dùn ìseal point to, when a stranger asks them why every gallery below it now stands propped in oak that no earlier generation of cutters had thought to spend.

## VI. Of the Close of Seonaid's Keeping

Seonaid Chiar held the flame sixteen years more after the fall, and grew old in the office in a way none of the four houses of custody had troubled to record of any Keeper before her, for the simple reason that few Keepers had held the cup long enough for anyone to notice the greying of a hand that had once been young. She died in her own quarters above the galleries, eighty-five years old, having kept the flame the better part of six decades, and the nine hearths that had raised her young chose another after her without any dispute that the rolls thought worth setting down, which is, of every Keeper's ending, the kindest sort a Hall can give.

Word of her death went out along the same roads that had carried her own rolls up to her for sixty years, and came, among other places, to the school at Cnoc bhàn, whose teachers sent up the mountain no message of grief and no delegation to mourn her, only the single unlit lamp their own three old men had once set down before her door, carried back up now by cutters young enough to have known no Keeper but her, and left again on the same stones, still unlit, as they had left it the first time: which the Hall's knot-keeper that season understood well enough not to ask the school to explain, and did not.

Cathair dhomhain, on the western coast, was founded in the same years as her dying, by carriers who had settled at the western road's end above its harbour and raised a town on the rise there that they meant, from the first, to be known for keeping every measure strictly, in coal as in everything else a scale could weigh. Its own shrine, from 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634, held the Small-Burning Law to the very grain from its founding day onward, and the town grew, in the years that followed, a name for a kind of pride that no other town on the island quite shared: pride in how exactly it kept to what it was owed, whatever measure of its own it had to show for it. It stood, that year, still a place carriers passed through on their way to somewhere else, its harbour no more than a fishing quay and its wall not yet raised; but its shrine's own strictness outlasted every one of the carriers who founded it, and was spoken of, by lowland households who had never once set foot on its own rise above the sea, as a strange, stiff-necked kind of pride to hold a whole town by.

At Dùn ìseal the walled mouth of the high gallery stood as it had stood since the year of the fall, sealed in dry stone, with the oak props running down every working gallery below it into the dark the way a spine runs down a back; and the cutters who passed the sealed door on their way to their own lower galleries had, within a generation, stopped remarking on it at all, the way the carriers on the roads below had long since stopped reading the boundary stones the Peace had set. It had become, as the Hall's own oldest things so often did, no longer a thing anyone spoke of, but a thing that was simply there, propping up, in its own silent way, everything built above and around it since.

# Part Four: The Gathering of the Shares

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of Goraidh mac Ìomhair

*FE 635 – 753*


## I. Of the Red Share Whole

By the time the oak props at Dùn ìseal had stopped smelling of the axe, the island had begun to fill out again, the way a field fills with barley once the birds have had their share and stopped coming. Cathair mhòr had its wall now, and would not say what it had built the wall against, though the reapers of Achadh mhòr still said, whenever anyone asked, that the town had not forgotten the smoke. Ceann leathan had a harbour-master keeping notched sticks that were already the oldest counted things on the island, and the Keeper Seonaid Chiar, before she died, had let the stag's cutters back into the galleries of the Hall on oath to ask nothing of the vein aloud, which the Hall called a reconciling and the school still called a truce. The Peace of the Threshold was eighty years old and had not been broken once, not at a death, not at a boundary stone, not even at Cathair dhomhain, whose people were proud of keeping every measure to the grain and were forever finding some new law to keep strictly. The shares no longer shrank at every burial. Here and there, slowly, without anyone marking the day it began, they had started instead to grow.

Of no line was this truer than the line of Ìomhar.

Goraidh mac Ìomhair was born in the Red Share in the spring of the Hall's fifth century, the year his grandmother's roof at Dùn dhearg was new-thatched, and he grew up under a roof that had never in his father's memory, or his father's father's, been parted from a neighbour's spear. The Red Share had been won with a sword, not given at the Roinn, and it had never been cut since; whatever quarrels the rest of the island's heirs had over their boundary stones, the holders of Dùn dhearg had only to hold what they already had, and they had held it with a plainness that other lines, forever arguing a grazing-right through three generations of cousins, found almost insulting.

He came into it young, as his line reckoned youth. His father died at four hundred, a middling age by then for one of Ailean's blood and past belief for any other household, thrown from a horse on the low ground below Dùn dhearg in a spring so wet the ground never firmed under the beast's feet. Goraidh stood at the grave with his mother's people and his father's stewards, a hundred and twenty-six years old and taller than any man in either line, and he said nothing, because there was nothing that wanted saying. He took up the household the next morning. The granaries at Dùn dhearg were full that year, as they generally were; the Red Share paid its own way and had done since Ìomhar Dearg burned the halls within the double bank six centuries before, and Goraidh's first act as its head was no more than to walk the granaries with the steward and check the thatch.

In those years he thought of himself as no more than a holder of a hall. He married early, a woman of a small house on the coast whose name the Red Share's own reciters kept and no one else troubled to, and she gave him a daughter before the century was out, a quick, restless child who could not be got to sit still at a hearth and was forever down at the ford watching the carriers. Goraidh called her Mòrag, for his mother, and thought no more of the succession than any lord of a whole share needs to. The girl would have the hall when he was done with it, as her grandmother had had it before him, only smaller than most, because the Red Share had never been the kind of thing that grew.

Then, within the same ten years, both his mother's brother's sons died without children of their bodies.

They were cousins he had known well enough as a boy, before his own father's death and the long duties after it had cut down his visiting. Cailean had gone under a wall he was mending at his own hall on a night of high wind, and Donnchadh, the younger, had wasted two winters with a cough the hearth-women could not cut and died in the third with his hand in his sister's. Between them they had held two of the old counties east of Dùn dhearg, parted from the Roinn's great share of the north four centuries before and parted again at every death since, the way the north had gone on parting itself until, as the tellers of Dùn ìseal like to say, it could not raise twenty spears from the whole of it. There was no one of either dead man's body to take up what was left. By the custom that had held since the Peace, a share with no heir named went to the Keeper to give as she saw fit, unless some other of the blood could show a claim before her.

Goraidh could show one, through his mother, and so could three other households, more distantly. He did not go to Dùn ìseal to argue it. He went instead, the winter after Donnchadh's burial, to the third of his mother's kin who was still living unmarried and held the third of the three old counties in her own right, a widow some four hundred years old named Muirne nic Dhonnchaidh, whose county marched with both the dead men's and who had buried two husbands of her own without a child of either surviving her.

He did not pretend to himself, nor to her, that it was a love match. She was old enough to remember the War of the Two Oaths from its first burning, and he was not far behind her. But she had held her county alone for eighty years with no one to leave it to, and had watched her cousins' lands sit empty of a lord while three strangers' stewards argued over them at Dùn ìseal, and when Goraidh rode over in the worst of the winter with six men and no threat in him at all, she heard him out at her own hearth and told him she had been waiting for someone to ask her a sensible question, and that he was the first.

"You have not asked me what I want kept in the marrying," she said to him, the second evening he sat at her hearth, before he had so much as named the thing he had ridden over to ask.

"Tell me, then," said Goraidh, "and I'll swear to it before I swear to the rest."

She told him. Her own reciter would keep his place and his fire, whatever the Red Share's own reciters thought of sharing a hearth with a stranger's teller; the debts her two husbands had left the county's smiths were his to carry, and not her name's to carry after her; and she would be buried, when it came to that, among her own dead and not among his. He agreed to all three before she had finished the third, and she looked at him a while, the way a woman looks at a tally that has come out even for once, and said that he was the first of his line she had ever heard of who did not need a thing explained to him twice.

They were married at Dùn dhearg in the spring, before the roads had properly dried, with the Red Share's own reciters standing witness because no others could get there in time. By the terms she brought to it, her county came into the marriage whole, as the Peace allowed; and by the same terms, made before the Keeper's own knot-keeper so that no line could later say the marriage was got up only for the land, Goraidh took on himself the debts her two dead husbands had left the county's smiths, which were not small.

So it was that within a single winter's dealing, and by nothing more than two deaths he had not caused and one marriage he had gone looking for, Goraidh mac Ìomhair held in one hand the Red Share, whole as his fathers had kept it, and three of the old counties of the east besides, parted since the Roinn and gathered now, for the first time in four hundred years, into a single household's granaries.

## II. Of the Third County and What It Cost

The stewards of the three counties came to Dùn dhearg that first summer to be sworn, and they were not, on the whole, glad men. Two of the counties had been managed for a generation by men who had grown used to answering to no one nearer than a dead cousin's memory, and the third had been Muirne's alone, run her own close way, with her own notches on her own sticks, and she had never once in eighty years asked any of them to account to a husband. Now there was a hall at Dùn dhearg that wanted their tallies each autumn, and a lord in it younger than some of their own grandchildren, of the Red Share's blood but not, until that winter, of theirs.

Goraidh did not go about it the way his father would have. He rode the boundary of all three counties himself in the first year, on foot half the time, with Muirne beside him telling him which stream had moved its bed and which family had held a grazing since before the Roinn and would go to war over it if a new steward tried to measure it out again. He ate at the hearths and not the halls, and asked before he ruled. It cost him a full summer and most of the autumn, and it cost Muirne, who was not young even by the reckoning of her own line, more than she let him see; she died in the ninth year of the marriage, in her sleep, with the county's own reciter in the room, and Goraidh buried her among her own dead, not his, because she had asked it of him plainly the week before, and he had learned by then not to argue with her.

He did not marry again. He had his daughter, growing tall and impatient at Dùn dhearg, and he had four counties where his father had held one, and he found, in the years after Muirne's death, that the four together took more of his waking hours than the Red Share alone had ever asked of him, and that he did not mind it.

It was a hard decade for the low ground east of the mountain. Two summers running the rains came at the wrong end of the season and the barley stood in the field and rotted before the reapers could get to it, and in the second of those years three of the smaller households along the old boundary between Cailean's dead county and Donnchadh's went hungry enough that their children were sent to kin in the hills to be fed through the worst of the winter. Goraidh opened the granaries at Dùn dhearg that year, all four of them, the Red Share's own stores and the three counties' besides, and sold the grain at less than it had cost him to keep, and gave it outright to nine households that could not have paid even that.

It was not, by his own account of it, a generous act. He said so once to his daughter, late in his life, when she pressed him on it: that a lord who lets his own low ground starve has nothing left to be lord of, granary or no granary, and that he had done the arithmetic before he had done anything that could be mistaken for kindness. Mòrag did not believe him, and neither, in the end, did the households.

## III. Of the Granary Door

It began, as such things do, with no one meaning it.

A household at the eastern edge of what had been Donnchadh's county came to the granary door at Dùn dhearg in the third bad autumn to beg seed corn against the next year's sowing, and the steward at the door, new to the post and unsure of the forms for a thing that had never before crossed three counties' worth of custom at once, asked whose authority he should set against the debt.

"The rìgh's," said the old woman who had come for the corn, before the steward could finish the question, and went on into the yard as if she had said nothing remarkable at all.

The word went through the queue at the door faster than the corn did. No one on the island had been called that since Ailean Mòr fell at the ford six hundred years before; at the Roinn the seven hundred and twelve heirs had sworn, each with some private reservation, that none of them would take it, and in the centuries since, only the reciters of the Mason's line had troubled to remember that the gods had once given the word to Ailean in the grove, and even they had let it go mostly to dust. The heirs of Ailean's blood, all down every one of the nine great shares, had never once offered it to Goraidh, nor to any lord of the Red Share before him. It was the granaries that gave it to him, and the granaries did not ask anyone's leave.

Goraidh heard of it that same evening from the steward, half apologising, as though the man had let something get past him at the door that he should have stopped. Goraidh did not answer at once. He walked out to the granary himself, in the last of the light, and stood by the door a while looking at the grain-dust still hanging in the air of the yard, and when the steward asked him at last whether he wanted the word stopped at the door in future, Goraidh said only that he did not see how a man was to stop a word once nine households had already said it to each other on the road home.

It spread the way such words do among people who have use for them and none for the thing they properly name. By the fourth bad harvest it was not only the hungry who said it at the door; the smiths of the third county said it, and the carriers on the road to Cathair dhomhain said it of him without ever having stood in his hall, and within a generation the lowland households from the Abhainn dhomhain to the old bounds of Donnchadh's county called Dùn dhearg the rìgh's hall as plainly as they called Talla na Lasrach the Hall.

Goraidh never once used the word of himself. He gave his name at the granary door as he always had, Goraidh mac Ìomhair of the Red Share, and when the reciters of neighbouring counties tried it on him to his face, the way a man tries a new coat on another man to see how he wears it, he let it pass without either taking it up or putting it down, which some of his own stewards thought a kind of cunning and others thought a kind of honesty, and were probably both right.

## IV. Of the Climb

He was a hundred and ninety-nine years old, by the granaries' own count, though there were men half that age in the hill counties who looked older than he did, when word came down from Dùn ìseal that the council wished to speak with the lord the lowlands had taken to calling their king.

It was not a summons in the way the Keepers had ever summoned anyone before. The council did not raise its voice; it had never needed to, in six centuries of holding the one thing every share on the island had sworn to hold in common, and it did not raise it now. But the word went east plainly enough for all its quiet, and Goraidh, who had by then held four counties for the better part of a century and been called a king by lowland households for the better part of two generations, understood well enough what was being asked of him, and rode west that spring with six men, as far as the last waypoint house on the mountain road.

There he stopped, and gave his spear to the man riding beside him, and told him to wait with the horses.

He had thought about it for three nights before he set out, lying awake in the hall his father and his father's father had held without a stranger's spear ever crossing its threshold in peace, turning the thing over the way his stewards turned a tally-stick to catch the light on a notch. A man who came to the Hall armed had already said, before he opened his mouth, what he wanted; and Goraidh, walking up the last mile of the mountain road on his own two feet with the wind coming down cold off the passes and his breath going short in a way it had not gone short in eighty years, hoped that the council would read the other thing in his empty hands, because he did not entirely trust himself to say it as plainly as he meant it.

The grey roof of Talla na Lasrach came in sight over the shoulder of the hill while he was still catching that breath, and for a moment, an old man on a mountain road with his knees aching and his men and his spear left behind him at the last house, Goraidh mac Ìomhair looked very little like anyone's king at all.

The council sat outside on the stones before the door, for the day was fine, and the Keeper sat among them with the stone cup at her feet, the same cup that had stood on the threshold since Fionnlagh Dall's time, filled always to the two palms and no more. Goraidh stood before them in his travelling cloak with the wind in his beard, an old man by any low-ground reckoning and a young one by his own blood's, and he said the thing he had come up the mountain to say before any of them could ask it of him.

"I claim nothing under the mountain. Not a gallery, not a grain of coal. Let the Hall hear me say it."

The Hall heard him. Nobody answered at once; the wind took the words up over the roof and out along the ridge, and one of the council, an old woman of the Mason's line who had sat on that bench longer than Goraidh had been alive, looked at him a long while before she said anything at all, as if she were counting something on his face that he could not see himself.

"A man who holds four counties and is called a king by nine households in ten does not come up a mountain to tell us what he does not want," she said at last. "Tell us what you do."

So he told her, and the telling of it was most of the day. The roads he wanted plainly, because his granaries already fed the households that walked them, and it seemed to him a poor kind of ruling to feed a man and let some other hand toll him on the way home. The waypoint houses he wanted left to their own keepers, because he had learned enough from Muirne's eighty years of one county to know that a thing gathered by a stranger is gathered worse than a thing gathered by a neighbour with a share in it. Of the galleries, the flame and the cup he asked to have nothing said, in the swearing or out of it, because he had watched what four hundred years of the Roinn's quarrelling over the vein had done to every line that tried it, and he had no wish to be the fifth line remembered for trying again.

Then they bargained, and they bargained until the light went.

It was not a quarrel, though it had the shape of one at times, voices raised and let fall again, a councilman getting up to walk the length of the terrace and sit down somewhere else before he spoke his next piece. It was a dividing, done slowly and in the open air because neither side wanted it done any other way, each line of it turned over from every side before it was set down: what a rìgh might hold and what a Keeper must, what roads belonged to which of them and what happened at a boundary between a granary and a gallery, what was owed a household that answered, as so many did along the old bounds, to both halls at once. Goraidh gave up more than he had meant to when he set out, and got less, in the way of standing, than the lowland households already believed he had; the council gave him the roads and did not pretend, by the end of it, that the roads were a small thing to give.

They swore it the next morning, before the council had had time to sleep on second thoughts, on the stone cup itself: the Keeper to keep the flame and the galleries, the rìgh to keep the roads, the granaries and the peace of the lowlands; the rìgh never to set foot in a working gallery, the Keeper never to raise a spear. *Roinn a' Ghleidhidh*, the division of keeping, the council called it before the knots of the roll were tied, and by it, more than by any granary door or any word a hungry household chose to use of him, Goraidh mac Ìomhair became the first ruler since Ailean Mòr that the Hall itself would answer to as a ruler, on the one narrow ground the Hall had left him to be one.

He walked back down the mountain the way he had come, on his own feet, and took up his spear again at the last house without a word, and one of his own men said afterward that the old man had looked, coming down, twenty years younger than he had looked going up, though nobody could say for certain that it was the bargain and not simply the road being downhill.

## V. Of the Timber Hall and the Fish in Twenty

He built the hall the council had, in effect if not in any clause of the swearing, told him he had a right to build. It went up on the same rise at Dùn dhearg where his father's turf-and-timber house had stood, a long hall of squared oak with a granary set at each of its four corners, so that a man riding in from any of the four counties saw first, before he saw the door, the thing the hall was actually for. The Red Share's own carpenters cut it, and the three gathered counties' carpenters raised it, working side by side in a way their stewards would not have thought possible ten years before, and when it was roofed Goraidh had the granaries filled from all four counties at once, in the same season, so that no household along any boundary could say its grain had gone first into a stranger's store.

Within the next handful of years, with the roads under his keeping and the Keeper's word behind the division that had put them there, he set the first toll the island had ever known on the carriers who used them: one fish in twenty, or its worth in whatever a carrier's basket held, to pay the guards who kept the road-peace and to mend the bridges the floods still took every few years wherever a crossing had been built too near the water. He did not set the toll himself, at every crossing, with his own hand; he had learned that much from Muirne's eighty years of running one county alone. He gave the gathering of it to the keepers of the waypoint houses along each road, the same households that had kept a bed and a fire for carriers since before his grandfather's day, and let each of them keep a share of what they took, on the plain reckoning that a keeper with something of his own in the toll would gather it more honestly than one gathering only for a stranger at Dùn dhearg. The rolls said so themselves, in their dry way: that the waypoint-keepers kept their share, and the rest went to the guards and the bridges, and the sums, allowing for the ordinary dishonesty of the world, came out close enough to be believed.

At one of the waypoint houses on the northern road, a woman who had kept its fire for thirty years and her mother before her tallied her first season's toll before Goraidh's own steward, sack by sack, and when the count came out a full tenth short of what the steward's own reckoning of the traffic said it ought to, she did not flinch from it. "The carriers who go by night pay nothing," she said, "because there is no one at the door to ask them, and I am not walking a night road at my age to catch a man carrying salt fish." The steward carried it word for word to Dùn dhearg, and Goraidh, hearing it, laughed for the first time in some weeks and said only that a rìgh who wanted every fish in every twenty counted true had better learn to walk a night road himself, and let the matter drop. It was the kind of ruling the lowland households came, in time, to expect of him, and the kind the hill counties, who had never had a rìgh to expect anything of, found faintly ridiculous.

The years after that went the way years go for a man who has already done the one or two things his life was going to be remembered for. He grew old past two hundred and stayed hale a long while past it, the long years of his blood fading in him the way they had been fading in every line since the Roinn, century by century, so that where Murchadh Mòr had lived near three thousand years and Ìomhar Dearg fifteen hundred, Goraidh mac Ìomhair, seven generations on from the Roinn, counted himself old at two hundred and fifty and was right to. His daughter Mòrag, who had grown from the restless child at the ford into a woman who could not sit still in a hall any better than she had ever been able to sit still at a hearth, took over the walking of the roads long before he was willing to call it a handing-over, and he let her, because he had never much cared, himself, for the roads once they were built, only for the fact of their being kept.

He died in his own hall at Dùn dhearg in his two hundred and fifty-ninth year, in the granary month, with the smell of the new grain coming in through the door he had insisted be left open. Mòrag was with him, and two of the waypoint-keepers who had come in that week to render their tallies and stayed on when they saw how it was going, because a man does not like to walk out on a dying king over a fish in twenty. He said little at the end that the tellers thought worth the keeping; what they did keep was that he asked, the last evening, whether the toll-sticks for the western road had been notched that season, and was told that they had, and said that was well, and did not speak again.

Some days after, at the old waypoint house on the western road that had been Mòr nic Dhùghaill's in the Small-Burning Law's own time and was a waypoint-keeper's still, the keeper of that house sat at her door in the last of the light with a fresh-cut stick across her knees, and notched it once for a carrier's toll paid in fish and once for a toll paid in wool, exactly as she had notched it the week before, and would notch the next one the week after that, the granaries at Dùn dhearg being full or empty, a rìgh being alive in the timber hall or laid in the ground beside it, the road going on being a road either way.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Mòrag of the Roads

*FE 754 – 879*

## I. Of the Hall Left Standing Open

Goraidh Mòr had ruled at Dùn dhearg four-score years, from the granary door where the lowland households had first called him rìgh to the timber hall he raised over it with a granary at each corner, and when he died in his sleep in the seven hundred and fifty-third year of the Hall the hall stood a night and a day with its doors open, as the custom of the household was, before anyone was let in to take his chair.

Mòrag nic Ghoraidh was a hundred and thirty-five years old that night, and she had never once sat in it. She had stood beside it at feasts and at judgements, and had leaned on its arm once as a girl until her father lifted her off by the collar, laughing, and told her a rìgh's chair was not a thing to lean on; and now she stood in the doorway in the grey of the morning with the household behind her, and looked at the empty seat, and did not go in.

It was Tormod, her father's steward, who broke the silence, because someone had to and no one else would. He said that the toll-sticks were a season behind in the counting, and that the eastern granary wanted its roof seen to before the rains, and that three waypoint-keepers had sent word asking whether the road-toll still stood now the old rìgh was gone, as if a toll were a thing that might have died with a man.

"Tell them it stands," said Mòrag, "and tell them I'll be asking after it myself before the year is out."

She went in and sat down. The chair was warm from nothing; it had stood empty a night and a day, as the custom asked, and the wood was cold under her, and she sat in it a while without speaking, getting the feel of a thing she had watched other people sit in her whole life. Then she stood up again and did not sit in it for the better part of a year, because she had said a thing in the doorway that she meant to keep, and there is no keeping a road-toll from a chair.

She sent for a staff first. Not a sceptre; her father's steward brought her one of those, cut and banded for the purpose, and she looked at it and sent it back to the woodworker with word that she wanted something a woman could lean her whole weight on across the length of the island, and that if it looked well in a hall that was no fault of hers. What came back was a plain thing of black-thorn, taller than she was, worn smooth where a hand would fall on it before ever her own hand had touched it, because the woodworker had walked with it himself a week to be sure of the balance. She kept that staff the rest of her life, and it is the one thing of hers that is remembered by its own shape and not only by its name.

The roads her father had left her were his father's roads before that: tracks widened where a toll-house wanted widening and left as they were everywhere else, fords that a wet spring made impassable for a week at a stretch, one stone bridge at the western crossing that had not been touched since the masons of an earlier age set the last course. The waypoint-keepers sent word to Dùn dhearg twice a year with their tallies and their complaints, and Goraidh Mòr had answered the tallies and let the complaints lie, being a builder of halls and not, in his heart, a mender of roads. His daughter had three years of those complaints said over to her in a week, sitting up past the lamp's good hours with Tormod's tally-sticks stacked at her knee, and in the spring she called for her staff and a horse and went out to see the roads for herself, and she did not come back to sit in the chair again until the autumn.

## II. Of the Broken Stretch above the Ford

The first stretch she walked was the road up from the ford at Dùn dhearg, because it was the one nearest home and because a waypoint-keeper there had sent word three years running that the spring floods took the same twenty yards of it every year and that the carriers went round it through a farmer's barley until the farmer complained, and then round it through his neighbour's until that one complained too.

She found it exactly as told. The road dropped to the ford between two low banks that the water undercut every spring, so that by autumn there was a raw scar of red earth on either side and a soft place in the middle that swallowed a laden ox to the hocks. She stood on the near bank in her travelling boots with the staff planted beside her and watched a laden ox-sledge go through it while she was there, watched the carrier swear and the ox strain and the whole load lean sideways before it came free, and she said nothing until the sledge was past and the carrier had seen who was watching him.

"How long has it done that?" she said.

"Since before my father's father, my lady," said the carrier, "and the toll-house has sent word every year, and every year they send word back that it'll be seen to."

"It'll be seen to," said Mòrag, "because I'm standing in it."

She had the waypoint-keeper of that stretch bring her every man and ox-team within a day's walk, and she paid them out of the toll itself, which no one had thought to do before, since the toll went to Dùn dhearg and the roads were left to whatever labour a household owed its lord besides. In eleven days they had cut back both banks, laid a bed of stone under the soft place, and raised the road a hand's breadth above the water on either side of the ford. She stood in the finished stretch herself when the first loaded sledge went through it dry-footed, and said nothing at all that time, only watched it go, and then walked on to the next bad stretch, which a complaint three years old had also told her of and which no one had touched.

Not every waypoint-keeper welcomed her. At a stretch two days east of the ford, where the toll-house had gone unanswered longest of all, the keeper met her at his own door with his arms folded and said that the road had been bad since his grandfather's time and would be bad after his own grandchildren, and that a rìgh who came once with a staff and a season's labourers would be forgotten before the next flood took the bank again, as every rìgh before her had been forgotten. Mòrag heard him out, and then had her road-guards break open his own toll-chest before him, in his own doorway, and counted the silver herself onto a cloth on the ground: enough, by her own reckoning, to have paid for the mending three times over in the years he had let it lie. She did not shame him further than the counting. She left half the silver where it lay, for the household's own use, and took the other half for the work, and told him that she would be back in four years to see whether the bank had held, and that if it had not, the next counting would be done at Dùn dhearg and not at his door. It held. He sent word to her twice a year after that, of his own will, whether the road wanted mending or not, and his words are among the few from that stretch that the toll-rolls keep entire.

She walked the roads of the island that way for the better part of six years: every road a toll-house sat on, and every bad stretch the complaints named, though there was no time in one life for every mile of every road besides. She had them mended in the order the complaints had come in, oldest complaint first, a rule of her own devising that some of the older keepers called foolish, since a small hurt long borne got mended before a great one newly reported. It meant, all the same, that a waypoint-keeper who sent word and was ignored for ten years learned that sending word to Dùn dhearg was no longer wasted breath. Some of the mending was small: a culvert cleared, a gate hung where a farmer's beasts had been getting onto the road and fouling it. Some of it was not small. She had a whole stretch of the northern road moved a quarter-mile east, off a slope that slid every winter, and the farmers whose barley the new stretch crossed were paid out of the toll for the ground, which had likewise not been done before, and which some of the older waypoint-keepers said was no way to run a road and would beggar the toll inside a generation. It did not.

## III. Of Niall Òg on the Cold Road

She met Niall Òg on the northern road in the seventh year of her reign, in a wet spring, on a stretch she had not yet reached and had no plan of reaching for another two years. He was sitting on a boundary stone with his cloak over his head against the rain, an old man by then past his sixteen hundredth year, small and bent and grey, with a stick of his own across his knees that he had never had cut for a purpose the way she had had hers cut, only picked up somewhere along some road forty years before and kept because it was a good length. She did not know him. He knew her at once, by the staff and by the four road-guards behind her, and by something in the way she stood looking at a rut in the road as if it had done her a personal injury.

"You'll be Goraidh's daughter," he said.

"I am," said Mòrag.

"You look at a bad road the way your grandfather's brother used to look at a bad debt," said Niall Òg, "and I knew him, so I say it kindly. Sit down out of the wet a while. There's room on the stone."

She sat, because a man of sixteen hundred years asking a rìgh of a hundred and forty to sit is not easily refused, and because her feet were glad of it. He told her, without being asked, who he was, and she had heard the name from her father, who had heard it from his father, the way everyone on the island had heard the name Niall Òg by then, though fewer and fewer of them had ever sat beside him.

"I tied a knot once," he said, "at a door below Dùn ìseal, when the whole of what Ailean Mòr left was cut on a cord and laid on a floor for seven hundred and twelve of us to walk the length of and count. I found my own knot that night and sat by it a good while, the way a man does, looking for what he was owed. And do you know what I saw, sitting there?"

"No," said Mòrag.

"I saw that everyone else in the house was doing the same. Every one of the seven hundred and twelve of us walked that cord looking for his own knot, and having found it, stood up and went looking at everyone else's. I thought that a fine thing to have watched, at the time. I've had a long while since to think it a sadder one. We were all tied on the one cord and not one of us, that whole night, looked at the cord. Only at the knots."

Mòrag said nothing to that for a time, watching the rain come down the road ahead of them in grey sheets.

"And is that why you tell it to a woman mending a road?" she said at last.

"It is," said Niall Òg. "You're the first of the line I've met in a long life who looks at the cord and not the knot. A road doesn't ask whose share it crosses. It only asks to be walked on, by whoever's walking. Keep at that, and you'll have done something the seven hundred and twelve of us never managed among ourselves, and never will, being who we are."

He got up before she did, stiffly, with his stick, and went on down the road ahead of her household on foot, an old man alone in the wet, refusing the offer of a horse with a wave of his hand and a remark she did not catch over the rain. She never saw him again, though she heard of him twice more before her own death, both times at the funerals of people younger than himself, standing at the graveside with his stick, the last of the seven hundred and twelve who still came to such things.

## IV. Of the Golden House and the Sign Recut

She built the golden house in her ninth year, on the eastern road north of Seann Dunn, where the stage from the coast to the mountain had always been a hard day's carrying with no house to break it and a bad night's camping if the weather turned. It was not the first waypoint house on the island; there had been such houses since the carriers' roads themselves, built by whatever household held the ground and kept up out of what custom the ground's own people were owed. It was the first built at a rìgh's order and out of a rìgh's toll, and she meant it to be seen to be one, and had it built larger than the ground needed and roofed it with new-cut timber that stood pale and bright against the older grey houses about it, so that carriers coming up from the coast called it the golden house before the beams had so much as weathered, and the name held.

She opened it herself, on a night in the autumn, with every carrier who could be got word to in time asked to eat there free of the toll, and stood in the doorway of her own hall watching them come in wet and cold off the road and sit down to a fire and a full table that none of them had paid for, and she thought, watching it, that this was worth more of her father's granaries than anything he had built with them, and did not say so aloud, because he was three years dead and past hearing either the praise or the argument.

Five years after that she had the western crossing of the Abhainn dhomhain widened, where the old bridge below Cathair dhearg had stood narrow enough that two laden carriers could not pass on it, and where every spring saw a shouting match on the span between a string of carriers going up and a string coming down, neither willing to back off first. The new stone went up wide enough for two, and when the masons came to the keystone she had them find, among the older stones taken down, the hearth-sign that Ailean Clachair had cut there in an age before her grandfather's grandfather was born, worn nearly smooth by the years and the weather, and she had it cut fresh into the new stone, in the same hand as near as a mason four generations removed from Ailean Clachair could match it. It is there yet. From that year the small fishing town at the bridge-foot, that had shrunk to almost nothing after the old wars and grown slowly back since, began to grow in earnest, for a wide bridge draws trade the way a narrow one turns it aside, and within Mòrag's own lifetime it had outgrown three of the towns around it, though no one troubled yet to give it any name grander than the ground it stood on had always borne.

## V. Of Dòmhnall, Who Could Not Walk

Her son was called lame all his life, though he had not been born so; he came into the world with two sound legs and used them like any child until his sixteenth year, when he fell under a laden ox-sledge on the road above the ford at Dùn dhearg, the stretch his mother would mend in her first summer as rìgh. He had been riding the load, as boys do against every warning, and the sledge had struck a stone standing proud of the track and rolled, and taken his leg under it. The leg was set, and set again when it did not knit true, and in the end he walked with a stick for the rest of his life and could not do it far, and never rode a horse again without another man's hand at the bridle.

Mòrag never once, in all the years she outlived that day, ordered the stone taken up, though her masons mended the stretch round it and pointed out to her more than once that it still sat there. She had it left, and told no one why, though her own household guessed, and some of the older road-guards said among themselves that she went out of her way to walk past it whenever her road took her near, and stood by it a while before going on, as if it owed her an answer it never gave.

Dòmhnall could not do what his mother had done. He knew it before she did, and said so to her plainly, sitting in the golden house one evening in his thirtieth year with his bad leg stretched out before the fire, and told her that whatever she left him he would rule from a chair, and that she had better begin now teaching him how a chair could be made to reach as far as a staff had. She did not argue with him. That autumn he was carried the length of three road-stretches, in a covered chair on two men's shoulders, so that he should at least have seen with his own eyes the roads he could otherwise know only from a waypoint-keeper's word, and before the year was out she named him at Dùn dhearg as her heir, an old woman by then and past her hundred and eightieth, with the long years thinning fast in her line the way they had thinned in her father's and would thin further in her son's, so that where Ailean Mòr's own children had lived three thousand years and more, his great-great-granddaughter counted herself fortunate to see two hundred, and his great-great-grandson, sound of mind and short of leg, would not see even that.

## VI. Of the Last Circuit

She made her last circuit of the roads in her two hundred and eleventh year, against the advice of her household and her son both, who said a woman of that age had no business on a horse in the spring mud, and she told them that a road she had not walked in four years was a road she no longer knew, and that she would rather die on one of her own roads than in the chair she had spent a lifetime staying out of. She went the whole western circuit, from the wide crossing below Cathair dhearg round by the golden house and back, five weeks on the road with her staff worn now to a paler colour at the grip than anywhere else on its length, and she found, to her own satisfaction and to the surprise of the waypoint-keepers who had grown used to sending their complaints into a silence, that there was less to mend that year than in any year of her reign, and she said so at every waypoint house she stopped in, which the keepers took as high praise from a hard woman and repeated to their children after.

Four years later she died at Dùn dhearg, in the winter, of nothing anyone could name beyond her age, with her son beside her and the black-thorn staff standing in the corner of the room where she had had it set every night of her life since the woodworker gave it to her. She was two hundred and fifteen years old. There were people living on the island by then, of her own kin among the waypoint-keepers' houses, who had never known a rìgh but her, and who found it hard to picture the roads with anyone else's name attached to their mending.

They laid her out in the hall her father had built, and the household came in as it had for him, and stood a night and a day before the doors were shut. Word went out on the roads themselves, carried by the same waypoint system she had built up out of a ten-year-old complaint and a rutted ford, and it reached the far waypoint houses before the funeral could be held, so that carriers came in from three days' distance to stand outside the hall at Dùn dhearg, men and women who had eaten free at her opening feast or been paid out of her toll to cut back a riverbank, more of them than the household had thought to feed, and Dòmhnall, new in his chair and lame on his stick, had the golden house's own stores brought up to Dùn dhearg to feed them, which his mother would have counted, had she lived to see it, the rightest thing he ever did.

Niall Òg came, the last time anyone at Dùn dhearg saw him, older now than any living memory could measure him against, and stood at the grave a long while on his own stick, and when someone asked him, since he had known her, to say a word over her, he said only that he had told her once about a cord and seven hundred knots, and that she was the one heir of that whole gathering who had spent her life looking at the cord, and that the roads she had mended were the nearest thing the island had, after her, to that same cord laid honestly on the ground for anyone to walk. Then he went away down the road on foot, as he had come, and refused a horse again, and no one at Dùn dhearg saw him after that day, though word came, years later and from a great distance, that he was still living.
