The black-thorn staff was laid across her feet on the bier, whole and unbroken after forty years of every road on the island, worn smooth from end to end by a single hand; and that is the last thing the tellers give of Mòrag nan Rathad, before they go on, as the roads themselves went on, into the reign of her son.

## VII. Of the Keepers of Ceann mhin and the Grain That Came First

Dòmhnall Crùbach ruled four-score years from the same hall, carried where his mother had walked, and where she had gone herself to every bad stretch of road, he sent the keepers of the waypoint houses in his stead, and trusted them to bring him an honest tally. Round the harbour town of Ceann mhin, where the road-toll came in heaviest off the eastern shipping, the keepers took to gathering it into their own hands within thirty years of his rule beginning and paying the hall what they judged a fair remainder, and their judgement, the rolls note without further comment, was generous to themselves in every year the rolls survive. Dòmhnall knew it, by report if not by his own eyes, and let it stand, for he could not walk to Ceann mhin to argue it and had no wish to send road-guards against men who kept the roads his mother had built running. It was a bargain no one swore as a bargain, and it held, more or less, for longer than his own reign.

In the west that same generation, settlers out from Cathair dhomhain took up the wet heath by the coast, where the ground was thin and the reed-beds thick with a small yellow scorpion the older shires thought a plague and the new settlers, within a few years of living among them, had come to think a kind of luck. A woman of that settlement, stung on the hand at a trade of cattle for salt fish, held her swelling fingers up before the other party rather than draw back from the bargain, and finished the trade with her hand still burning, saying that a hurt taken in the open was worth more than a promise given behind a closed door. Others took up the way of it after her, keeping a scorpion's sting, dried in a box, at every trading and swearing an oath on the pain of it rather than on a name or a god, and the settlement that grew up there took the name Baile àrsaidh, and its neighbours, who swore on hearth-fire or on the flame itself as everyone else on the island did, thought the whole custom a strange and a hard one, and said so, and traded there anyway, because a woman who would finish a bargain stung was a woman whose word could be trusted after.

Sìleas Dhonn, Dòmhnall's sister's daughter, was a girl of fourteen at Dùn dhearg when her uncle first began asking her to sit in on the reckoning of the waypoint-keepers' tallies, because her eye for a tally that did not add was sharper than any tally-keeper's he kept, and she found, going back through ten years of the Ceann mhin rolls at his bidding, three separate years in which the keepers' own count of what they had gathered did not match the count of what had passed through their gates, though never by enough, in any single year, to be called outright theft before a council that had no proof to set against a keeper's word. She said nothing of it publicly while her uncle lived, being young and his niece and the ruler of nothing at all, and kept her own tally-sticks of the count, notched in her own hand and locked in the same chest as her mother's marriage-cloth, and told no one why she kept them, only that a tally that did not add was a thing worth keeping until someone asked to see it.

In the forty-fifth year of Dòmhnall's reign a storm out of the west drove the sea over the harbour at Seann Chwen and took the boats at their moorings and a third of the houses with them, and left the survivors on the high ground above the water with nothing but what they stood in. Word of it reached Dùn ìseal and Dùn dhearg within the same day, carried on the road Mòrag nan Rathad had raised above the flood, the same road that had once swallowed a laden ox to the hocks and now ran dry through worse rain than that storm brought; and it was the Keeper's grain, carried down from the Hall's own stores, that reached the ruined harbour first, a full day ahead of Dòmhnall's, though he had sent his the same hour the word came to him and grudged no bushel of it. The people of Seann Chwen ate from both that winter and were glad of both, and never afterward forgot, in all the tellings that followed, which grain had come up the road first; and it is told that the road itself, when the tale is given whole, is remembered as being no less part of the saving than the grain that was carried on it, being the very stretch above the ford that a rìgh's daughter had raised out of the mud in the first summer of her reign, a hundred and twenty-five years before the storm that proved it.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Stag-Letters

*FE 880 – 914*

## I. Of the Boy Who Counted Wrong

Rònat was ten years old the summer he was sent up from his father's holding to the stag's school in the holy wood east of Muileann chiar, and he arrived with a bundle of clothes, a knife his mother had cut too sharp for a boy his age, and a talent, already noticed by every adult who had ever set him to watch a flock, for losing count of anything past thirty. The teachers of the stag kept their reckonings on notched sticks, one stroke to a beast, a bundle, a day, and it was the first task of every new pupil to cut such a stick clean and true and bring it to the old cutter for judgement, and Rònat's first stick, judged by Aonghas Cam, came back to him with a groove scored clean through the middle of it and the single word: again.

Aonghas Cam had taught at the wood longer than any pupil then living could remember him not teaching, and he had a leg that had set crooked after a fall from the oak he still climbed every autumn to mark the mast, and a patience with a wrong stick that did not extend to a boy who argued with him about it. He set Rònat cutting sticks for two years before he let him near a beast to be counted at all, and told him, more than once and always in the same words, that a stick that lied was worse than no stick, because a man believed a stick the way he did not always believe another man, and a wrong count believed was a debt paid twice or a debt never paid at all.

It was slow work, the counting, and Rònat was not, by his own later account, ever quick at it; what he was, once he had it, was exact, and Aonghas Cam came in time to trust his sticks over the sticks of pupils twice as fast with the knife, and to say so where the boy could hear it, which from Aonghas Cam was a kind of praise that other teachers spent whole speeches failing to match. By the time Rònat was one and twenty he cut the wood's own tally of the mast harvest and the new lambs and the toll owed the road-guards for the year, and it was put about, by pupils younger than himself, that Aonghas Cam trusted Rònat's stick before he trusted his own eyes, which Aonghas Cam neither confirmed nor troubled to deny.

The teaching itself, beyond the counting, was carried the old way, by a mouth and an ear and a memory trained to hold what it was given: the names of the beasts of the wood and which were the stag's and which were common; the turns of the year and which rite belonged to which turn; the descent of the teachers themselves, one from another, back further than any pupil could hold without losing the thread somewhere in the middle. Aonghas Cam held that whole thread, and said it over at every year's turning to whichever pupils could sit still long enough to hear the whole of it, and Rònat, sitting through it a dozen times by his twentieth year, found that he could hold perhaps two-thirds of it after, and lost the rest within a season, the same as every pupil before him had lost some part and no pupil after him would keep whole.

He said as much to Aonghas Cam once, in his twenty-fourth year, more out of a wish to be told he was wrong than any real complaint, and the old cutter looked at him a long while before he answered, in the flat way he had of answering a thing he had thought about longer than the boy asking it.

"You will lose more of it than I did," he said, "because I lost less of what was said to me than you will lose of what is said to you, there being more of it said now than there was said to me. And whoever comes after you will lose more again. It has always gone that way and there is no stick cut yet that holds a word instead of a count, so there is no help for it."

Rònat did not forget that answer, though he could not, at four and twenty, have said why it stayed with him longer than most of what Aonghas Cam said that same year.

The school itself was no more than three low houses and a byre set among the oaks of the holy wood, a morning's walk east of Muileann chiar along a path the mast-gatherers kept clear with their own feet more than any road-guard troubled to clear it, and it had stood in that clearing, teacher after teacher, longer than the wood's own oldest trees, or so the pupils were told and had no cause to doubt, there being no mark on any tree to say otherwise and no stick cut yet that held such a mark if there had been. The pupils slept two and three to a pallet in the low house nearest the byre, rose before the light to feed what beasts the school kept for its own table, and spent the day between the counting and the beast-lore and, on the turning of the year, the rites that belonged to the stag's people alone, which Aonghas Cam taught with more patience than he ever showed a wrong stick, and which Rònat, of all that he was made to hold in memory those years, found came back to him whole and unbidden even in his old age, long after the thread of names had thinned past keeping.

## II. Of the Sign Made for a Sound

Aonghas Cam's leg, crooked since his fall, took a fever in the wet autumn of Rònat's thirty-first year that no poultice the wood's healers laid on it would draw out, and he did not climb the oak that year to mark the mast, sending Rònat up in his place for the first time, and spent the winter in the low house by the fire, teaching what he could sitting down and losing his breath over what he could not. Rònat sat with him most evenings of that winter, less as a pupil now than as the man who fetched wood and water for an old teacher too proud to ask a younger one for either, and it was in those evenings, watching Aonghas Cam search for a name or a line of the old thread and not always find it before his breath gave out, that the shape of the thing came to Rònat, slowly and in pieces, the way a knot comes undone by first one strand and then another and not all at once.

He had been cutting a tally-stick that same week, one groove to a fish counted at the smoke-house, and it struck him, watching Aonghas Cam grope after a name he had said clean a hundred times before, that a groove held a count exactly and forgot nothing of it, and a mouth held a name or a line of teaching only as well as the mouth's own memory served it on the day, which was not always well. If a groove could be made to stand for a count, he thought, there was no reason in wood or knife that it could not be made to stand for a sound instead, and a row of sounds was a name, and a row of names in their right order was the very thread Aonghas Cam was losing by the fire, held now on something that did not have a bad night or a failing breath.

He did not say any of this to Aonghas Cam that winter, fearing to be told it was foolishness, and fearing worse, though he owned to this only later, to be told it had been tried before and failed for a reason he had not thought of. So he worked at it alone, in the hours before the school woke, cutting the same length of straight-grained ash over and over, one edge to lay the strokes against, as a stick already carried for a plain count. The trick of it, when it came, lay in giving each sound of speech its own small mark against that edge: some short and to one side, some short and to the other, some crossing the edge clean through, some slanting, so that a hand running down it in the dark could tell one sound from the next by touch alone before the eye had even looked. The vowels he set apart from the rest, five short cuts standing clear of the long consonant-marks, for a school-child learning them first would want the vowels easiest to the hand, and he had been such a child himself not so many years before, and remembered which sounds had come hardest.

By the spring he had cut his own name on a stick, and could read it back cold, without the stick in front of him, three days after cutting it; and then Aonghas Cam's name, and read that back too; and then, on an evening when the old man's breath was better than it had been in a month, he set the stick in Aonghas Cam's own hand and told him what the marks were, and asked him to run his thumb down the edge and say what he found.

Aonghas Cam was a long time silent over it, turning the stick, running his thumb back along the strokes a second time and a third. "This is my name," he said at last, "cut on a stick as if it were a count of fish."

"It is a count," said Rònat. "A count of sounds, in their order, same as a count of fish is a count of fish in their order taken."

The old man laughed at that, a short laugh that cost him more breath than he had to spend, and said that a boy who had once cut a stick so wrong it had to be scored through the middle had come, in the end, to cutting a stick no one on the island had thought to cut before him, and that he did not know whether that was a joke on him or a joke on the wood's whole way of teaching, and thought, on the whole, it was likely both.

## III. Of the Stone That Answered Nothing

Word of the sound-marks went round the school before the summer was out, and round the other schools of the stag within two years more, carried by pupils moving between them the way any new trick of the knife was carried, and by the time Rònat was five and thirty he had taught the whole scheme, strokes and vowels and the order of cutting them, to every pupil under him and to two teachers of the western school who came east on purpose to see it and stayed a season learning it from a man twenty years their junior without any evident shame in the asking. Aonghas Cam did not live to see the western teachers come; he died in Rònat's thirty-third year, in his sleep, in the same low house by the fire where he had first read his own name off a stick, and it was Rònat who cut, at the old man's own asking made some months before, the tally of his years on a length of the same ash, one stroke for each, rather than the sounds of his name, because Aonghas Cam had said, hearing what the new marks could do, that he wanted his years counted the old way at the last, having spent his whole life trusting a count over a name.

It was Sìleas nic Ruairidh, eldest of the western teachers who had come to learn the scheme, who first asked the question that sent Rònat and two others west to Cnoc bheag in Rònat's four-and-fortieth year, in the season the mast was gathered. She had been told, as every pupil of the stag was told somewhere in the long thread of teaching, that there stood at Cnoc bheag an old grey stone cut with marks no living teacher could read, set up by hands no living teacher could name, and it came to her, turning the new sound-marks over in her mind as she fell asleep one night, to wonder whether the old marks on that stone might be sounds too, cut by some maker whose speech the marks would give back if only someone knew now how to look.

They walked the road west together, the three of them, five days on foot with a tally-stick from the wood's own steward to see them fed at the waypoint houses along the way, and slept the fourth night at a turf longhouse with a hearth at either end, where the keeper, an old woman who had never heard of the sound-marks nor asked to, fed them barley and dried fish and told them, unprompted, that the road that far west ran along ground her own grandmother's grandmother had walked before there was any toll on it at all, which Rònat wrote down nowhere, having as yet nothing to write it in beyond his own memory, and thought afterward that this too was a kind of thread that would thin and be lost the way every unwritten thread was lost, whether or not anyone standing by the fire that night troubled to mourn it. They came to the stone on a grey morning, the rain still holding off, and stood before it a long while before any of the three so much as touched it. The marks on the old stone ran in lines and crossings not unlike Rònat's own scheme, cut deep enough that centuries of weather had not worn them smooth, and for a morning and half an afternoon the three of them set every stroke of the old marks beside every stroke of the new, turning the stone, comparing angle to angle and count to count, hoping, none of them said aloud what they hoped, that some line of it would answer to some line of theirs and give back, after all that silence, a single sound they could name.

Nothing answered. The strokes on the stone kept no order that matched the order Rònat had given his own, no vowel stood apart the way his stood apart, no five-and-five grouping of the marks gave up anything a mouth could shape. By evening Sìleas nic Ruairidh sat down on the wet grass at the stone's foot and said, plainly, that whoever had cut it had not taught them, and had not been taught by anyone who had taught them either, and that the two schemes, hers and the stone's, shared nothing but the accident of being marks cut in rows on a hard surface, which was no kinship at all, being the only way marks can be cut on a hard surface whether the makers ever knew of one another or not.

Rònat cut that finding onto a fresh stick before they took the road home, the first time, so far as any of the three knew, that a whole thought and not a single name or a single count had been set down in the new marks: that the makers of the stone at Cnoc bheag had not taught the makers of the stag's marks, and were not known to them, and left nothing behind that answered anything the three of them had brought to ask it. It was a small thing to have crossed five days of road to learn, and a smaller thing still to have carved, a handful of strokes on a length of ash beside a stone that had stood mute for longer than any of them could reckon; but it was the first thing the Dia-thìrich ever set down of the makers of that stone, and what it said was only what they were not.

## IV. Of the Ancient Man Who Laughed

Niall Òg came through the far east twice in those years, once before Aonghas Cam's death and once after, walking as he always walked, on his own two feet with a stick worn pale at the grip and no household about him beyond whatever family happened, that season, to be minding the wood he passed through. He was old past any counting the school itself could put a number to with confidence, well past his eighteen hundredth year by the reckoning the teachers kept among themselves from the tales told of Ailean's own fall, and he had outlived, by that reckoning, every one of the seven hundred and twelve heirs who had stood beside him at the cord's cutting save Eithne nic Ailein alone, and most of the children of those heirs besides, and he walked the roads still as a man walks a road he means to keep walking, without any particular hurry to be somewhere he had not yet been.

He came to the school in Rònat's forty-third year, the second of his two passings, an old man greeting an old man's school with the easy familiarity of someone who had watched it built in his own lifetime and expected, without saying so, to watch a good deal more of it before he was done, and he sat by the fire in the low house two evenings running, telling the pupils tales of the night of the handful that not one of them had heard told by a man who had stood there, and asking, when the tales ran out, after the trick he had been told of on the road, the marks that were said to hold a name the way a stick held a count.

Rònat cut his name for him that second evening, Niall's own name in the strokes, and set it in his hand, and told him to run his thumb along it the way Aonghas Cam once had, and said what each stroke gave. Niall Òg was quicker at it than Aonghas Cam had been, or perhaps only less proud to be seen slow, and read his own name back within the hour, haltingly at first and then clean, and sat with the stick in his two hands a while after, turning it, before he began to laugh.

It was not a short laugh. It took him by the chest and would not let go for the better part of a minute, an old man's laugh that ended, as old men's laughs will, in a fit of coughing that brought two of the younger pupils half out of their seats before he waved them back down with the hand that was not holding the stick, and when he had his breath again he said that he had been called by his name more times than there were fish in the western sea, by mothers and by kings and by every heir of the seven hundred and twelve who had ever wanted a thing off him, and that not one of those tellings had ever held still on a piece of wood after the telling was done, waiting for him to come back and hear it again whenever he chose.

"A name that stays," he said, "when the mouth that gave it is gone home to its supper. I have wanted that trick my whole long life and never once thought to ask for it, because I did not know there was a trick to ask for." He gave the stick back to Rònat, though Rònat pressed it on him to keep, and said that a man who had outlived every stick anyone had ever cut of him so far had no need to start keeping the ones that came after; better it stayed at the school, where a pupil could learn from it that even a name as old as his own could be held on so small a thing.

He went on east the next morning, refusing, as he always refused, the offer of a horse, and word of him came to the school twice more in the years after, from travellers who had passed him on some other road entirely, walking still.

## V. Of the Keepers Who Would Not Write

Dòmhnall Crùbach died at Dùn dhearg in his hundred and eightieth year, the same season Rònat turned four and forty, and the household stood the customary night and day with his chair empty before Sìleas Dhonn, his sister's daughter, went in and sat down in it and did not get up again for the better part of a year. She had kept, through all the years of her uncle's reign, her own fair copy of the waypoint-keepers' tallies locked in a chest with her mother's marriage-cloth, three years of Ceann mhin's figures that did not match the count of what had passed through Ceann mhin's own gates, and she had told no one why she kept them beyond that a column that did not add was worth keeping until someone asked to see it. In the first winter of her own reign she had that chest brought up and opened before the whole household, and sent word to every waypoint house on the island that the keeper of it should come to Dùn dhearg within the year and render account of the tolls taken in his own hand or another's, in whatever manner he judged fit to render it, so long as it could be checked against what the road-guards themselves had counted passing the same gate.

Word of the sound-marks had reached Dùn dhearg by then, carried the length of the island the way any new trick travelled, on the tongues of carriers and the word of stewards, though no keeper of a waypoint house had yet troubled to learn the scheme himself, it being, as far as most of them were concerned, a schoolboy's trick of the stag's people and no business of a toll-house. It was the keeper of Muileann shean, an old man named Beathan mac Dhonnchaidh who had held that house since before Dòmhnall Crùbach's own accession, who came to Dùn dhearg in the second year of Sìleas Dhonn's reign with his tally recited from memory in the old way, name for name and count for count, the way every keeper before him had ever rendered an account to any ruler; and Sìleas Dhonn heard him through to the end without once interrupting, and then asked him, plainly, how she was to know that what he had just recited was the same tally he had recited to the road-guard who rode through his gate that same season, there being no way to set one telling against the other once both were three seasons gone and held only in two separate memories that might, without either man meaning to lie, have drifted from each other in the telling.

Beathan mac Dhonnchaidh had no answer to that beyond his own long honesty, which Sìleas Dhonn did not doubt and said so, and let him go home without penalty; but she sent, within the month, to the far-eastern school, asking whether a teacher of the stag might be spared to come to Dùn dhearg and teach her own clerks the sound-marks, so that a keeper's tally, cut once at the gate in the road-guard's presence, might be carried whole to the hall instead of trusted a second time to a memory that had crossed the whole island since.

It was Rònat himself who went, in his forty-sixth year, the last long road he walked before age began to slow him, and he taught Sìleas Dhonn's clerks the strokes and the vowels over a winter at Dùn dhearg much as he had once taught them to pupils half his own age in the holy wood, finding the ruler's clerks quicker with the knife than any pupil he had taught before, being grown men and women already trained to a column of figures and wanting only the new marks to set beside the old ones they already knew. Ailig mac Ruairidh, keeper of the toll at Ceann mhin, whose house had been named in Sìleas Dhonn's own three years of mismatched figures, was the first keeper summoned to render account after the clerks were taught, and the first ordered to bring his tally cut in the new marks rather than carried in his head, checked against a second cutting made by the road-guard at his own gate the same season; and when the two tallies were set side by side at Dùn dhearg before the whole hall, in the second winter of Sìleas Dhonn's reign, they did not match, by a sum neither honest forgetting nor an honest drift of memory could account for, and Ailig mac Ruairidh, who had judged, like every keeper of Ceann mhin before him, that his own word carried further than any road-guard's, found for the first time that a stick cut at his own gate had carried further than his word.

He was not the last keeper found out that way, nor even, in that first year, the worst of them; but he was the first, and word of it ran the length of the carriers' road faster than any letter could have carried it, so that keepers who had never troubled to learn the new marks sent, within the season, to ask whether a teacher might be spared them too, having heard it said, by carriers who had stood in the hall at Dùn dhearg and seen the two sticks set side by side, that a keeper caught out by his own gate's stick had no more room left to argue than a man caught with the stolen thing still in his hand. The clerks who set Ailig mac Ruairidh's two tallies side by side and read out the difference between them, plainly, before the hall, did it in the new marks, off two sticks that neither man's memory could soften afterward however either of them told the story elsewhere. Sìleas Dhonn took no more from him than the sum itself, made whole, and let him keep his house, saying that a keeper caught once and shamed before the whole hall commonly kept an honester tally after than a keeper hanged for it would have taught any other keeper to be, there being no other keeper left alive to learn the lesson from a hanging.

It was in the same winter, cutting the record of Ailig mac Ruairidh's shortfall for the hall's own keeping, that Rònat set down, for the clerks to copy and learn by, the first whole sentence any hand at the hall had yet cut in the new marks: that the toll of Ceann mhin, counted at the gate and counted again at the hall, had come short by a sum the gate's own count made plain, and that the keeper had answered for it before Sìleas Dhonn and her household. It was a plain thing to say and a plainer thing to have needed saying at all, after so many years of tallies rendered on trust and kept only as long as one old man's breath held out to repeat them; but it stood after, cut whole on its length of ash in the hall's own keeping, saying the same thing every time any clerk's thumb ran down it, in a season when the man who had spoken it first was already three days gone home on the eastern road, and would not himself have known, walking it, that his own words had outlasted the telling.

He walked that road a slower man than he had walked the road to Cnoc bheag two years before with Sìleas nic Ruairidh beside him and a question about an old stone still open between them, and he thought, somewhere on the third of those days, of Aonghas Cam by the fire in the last winter of his life, groping after a name he had said clean a hundred times before and not always finding it, and of the answer the old man had given a boy of four and twenty who had complained, once, of losing the thread of a teaching within a season of hearing it. There was no help for it, Aonghas Cam had said, there being no stick cut yet that held a word instead of a count. Rònat came home to the holy wood in the last light of the fifth day, an old man himself now by the school's own reckoning, and found the pupils waiting on him for the evening's counting the way pupils had always waited on a teacher, and cut that evening's tally as he had cut ten thousand tallies before it, one stroke to a beast, before he sat down by his own fire and, for the first time in all the years since he had first set his own name on a stick, cut nothing further that night at all, being content, for once, to let the day go unrecorded and trust it, as every day before the sound-marks had ever been trusted, to memory alone.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of the Basket of Fish-Bones

*FE 915 – 1,009*

## I. Of Sìleas Dhonn's Reckoning

Iain, son of Sìleas Dhonn, was born at Dùn dhearg in the fifteenth year of his mother's long watch over the waypoint-keepers' tallies, and he grew up under a roof where a column of figures was looked at with the same care other households gave a wound. His mother had found, going back through the Ceann mhin rolls in her girlhood, three years in which the keepers' own count did not match what had passed through their gates, and she had never afterward let a tally lie unchecked a season. By the time Iain could walk the length of the hall without a hand to steady him, she was ruler in all but the chair itself, her uncle Dòmhnall Crùbach old and content to let her carry what his leg would not, and the boy grew up at her knee hearing her read out a keeper's account the way other boys heard the old tales.

He was not a quick child with the reckoning itself. What he had, his mother said, laughing at him more than once across the ledgers, was a memory for a face that had lied to her once, and he never forgot one. She set him, from the age of ten, to sit beside her when the keepers came in from the road to give their tallies in person, watching the men who gave them rather than the columns they gave, and more than once it was Iain who said afterward, low, that the keeper of Muileann shean had not looked at her when he named his season's toll, and more than once his mother found, on going back through the man's figures with a harder eye, that he had been right.

He was not gentle with what he found. He had his father's build, broad through the shoulder before he was fifteen, and a laugh that carried the length of a hall and did not always come at the moment a laugh was looked for; the household called him Iain Garbh, Iain the Rough, half in fondness and half in caution, and the name stayed on him the rest of his life. His mother did not check the name. "A rough hand keeps a straight column as well as a soft one," she said, "and better, in a season when a keeper thinks a soft hand can be talked round."

Dòmhnall Crùbach died in the nine hundred and fourteenth year of the Hall, and the household stood the customary night and day with the chair empty before Sìleas Dhonn went in and sat in it, and did not get up again for the better part of a year. She was five-and-seventy and would rule four-score years more, and in all that reign, which the keepers came to call, among themselves and not to her face, the long counting, she broke not one column that she found honest and forgave not one that she found false. She widened the toll on nothing and lightened it on nothing; she only made certain that what was owed came in whole, and that what came in whole was written down where a later hand could not soften it. Under her the granaries at Dùn dhearg filled steadier than they had filled under any ruler since Goraidh Mòr first raised the timber hall over the granary door, and the roads Mòrag nan Rathad had cut through the mud two centuries before were kept, by Sìleas Dhonn's order and at her cost, in better repair than the old woman herself might have troubled to keep them once the far stretches stopped catching her eye.

She sent Iain out on the roads himself from his twentieth year, first with an older keeper to mind him and then alone, and he came back from those years with a sunburn that never wholly left his face and a habit, which stayed with him the rest of his days, of counting a granary's sacks with his own hands before he would take any steward's word for the number. He learned the shares that paid their tolls whole without being asked and the ones that paid only when a rider from Dùn dhearg stood at the gate to watch them do it, and among the second kind, in the years his mother still ruled, none was worse than the harbour town in the south-west called Caol leathan.

Caol leathan sat where the western fishing came in thickest and where the carriers' road that ran the length of the island met the sea, and it had grown fat on both, fatter than any town of its size on the coast, under the leading family of the place, whose head in Iain's young manhood was a broad, quiet man named Lachlann Ciar. The town's toll on the road's southern end had been Dùn dhearg's by right since the road-peace was first sworn, but it reached Dùn dhearg thinner every season Iain rode down to collect it, and thinner still the seasons he did not, and Lachlann Ciar's answers, when pressed, were always the same: a poor season on the boats, a poor season on the road, the toll-house roof wanting mending before the toll itself could be counted properly. Iain rode home from his third visit at twenty-six years old and told his mother, plainly, that the man was lying to her face and smiling while he did it, and that he had counted the boats in the harbour himself and there had been no poor season in it that any eye but a liar's could see.

"Then you know him," said Sìleas Dhonn, "and knowing a liar is worth more than catching him once. Wait. He is not the one who will answer for it; his account is not run out yet, and mine has years left in it either way."

Her account had near sixty more years in it, and Iain waited them out at her side, counting granaries and watching a man in the far south-west grow fatter on a toll that was not his, and he did not forget the man's face, nor the smiling poverty of his excuses, nor the boats that had not once, in all Iain's visits, been fewer than the harbour could hold.

There was one keeper, in those waiting years, whom Iain never forgot either, though for a gentler reason. The man kept the toll-house at Cnoc dhubh on the eastern stretch of the road, an old fellow with a stammer that grew worse the longer Iain sat across the table from him, and on Iain's second visit the tally came out a full third short of the traffic Iain had himself counted passing the gate that week. He said nothing while the man stammered through his reckoning, and said nothing after, only asked, mildly, whether the keeper's daughter was still down with the fever that had kept the household from the last two fairs. The keeper, startled into honesty by the question, said she was, and that the physician at Muileann shean wanted paying, and that he had thought, the gods forgive him, to make up the difference out of the toll and put it back before the reckoning was due. Iain rode home and told his mother the whole of it, expecting, he said afterward, to see the man's name struck from the rolls before the month was out. Sìleas Dhonn sent instead silver for the physician and word that named no theft at all, only a debt owed and now discharged, and told her son that a rough hand did well enough on a column that lied for greed, but wanted a softer one for a column that lied for love, and that he had best learn to tell the two apart before he sat in the chair himself. Iain kept that lesson beside the other; it was, he said in his own old age, the harder of the two to hold onto, and the one he was proudest of holding.

## II. Of the Basket of Fish-Bones

Sìleas Dhonn died in her hundred and fifty-fifth year, in the nine hundred and ninety-fourth year of the Hall, sitting upright in the chair with a keeper's tally still open on her knee, and the household found her there in the grey of the morning with the ink not yet dry on the line she had been reading. She had asked, near the end, that the chair stand its customary night and day and no longer, and that whoever came after her not waste a season getting the feel of it, having had, she said, sixty years to get the feel of it already at her side.

Iain Garbh was eighty-five years old the night the chair stood open, and he did not stand long in the doorway looking at it the way, it was told, his grandmother's grandmother once had. He went in at first light, sat down, and sent for the year's tallies before the household had finished the mourning-meal.

Caol leathan's account that year showed the same figure it had shown for a decade: a toll paid thin, and an excuse to cover the thinness. Iain read it once, set it down, and sent a rider south with a plain demand, in his own hand and no steward's: the toll owed in full, counted before Dùn dhearg's own man at the harbour, or an answer for why it should not be paid at all.

The rider was gone the better part of a month, longer than the road alone accounted for, and came back at last white about the mouth and would not meet Iain's eye when he set what he carried on the floor of the hall. It was a basket, covered, of a size a fisherman's wife might carry to market, and it had been carried the length of the island roped shut, and the household backed a step from it before Iain had so much as touched the lid.

He lifted it himself. The smell came up first, old and gone dry, and under the smell, packed in rows the way a careful hand packs herring for the keeping, was a basket entirely full of fish-bones, picked clean, not one scrap of flesh left on any of them, and no letter, no word, no answer at all beyond the basket itself and the silence of the man who had sent it.

Iain looked at it a long while. Then he laughed, once, short and hard, a sound that frightened the household a good deal more than shouting would have done, because they had heard him shout before and knew the shape of it, and had never heard this. He called for the road-guards to be summoned from every waypoint within three days' ride, and for the lowland households to be told their levy stood, and he did not raise his voice again the whole of that week, which those who had known him longest found harder to bear than any roaring would have been.

"He has sent me an answer," Iain said, to the steward who asked what the basket meant. "There is nothing left in Caol leathan worth the honesty of a letter, and I believe him."

## III. Of the Flame That Would Not Come

He marched west before the month was out, with the road-guards of the southern waypoints and the lowland levies behind him, and he took the toll-house at Muileann òg that Lachlann Ciar's people had seized from Dùn dhearg's own keeper two winters before, and burned it, standing with his arms folded to watch the thatch go up, in a silence the household about him found harder to read than any order he might have given. It was the first war fought by Dia-thìreach against Dia-thìreach since the Peace of the Threshold had been sworn, and the first, of all the wars the reciters could name before it, fought over a road and not a share; every quarrel before this one had been a quarrel over land, and this was a quarrel over the right to carry a thing across land that both sides agreed belonged to neither of them.

Before he marched further Iain sent to Dùn ìseal for the Hall's blessing on the warband's hearths, as every rìgh before him had done at the raising of a levy, asking no more than the customary handful to light the first night's fires on the road. The messengers came back on the third day with their hands empty and a message they had been made, by the Keeper himself, to repeat word for word before they were let go.

*Cha bhlàthaich an lasair fir a tha a' dol a mharbhadh.* The flame will not warm men who are going to kill.

Uisdean mac Ruairidh had held the flame at Dùn ìseal eleven years by then, a spare, grey-eyed man who had never once, in all that time, refused a rìgh's messenger anything the Hall was able to give, and Iain heard the answer read out twice before he was certain he had heard it whole. He did not send a second messenger to argue it. He stood a while with the strip of hide the first had carried, on which the Keeper's words had been set down in the stag-letters by a clerk at Dùn ìseal so there could be no mistaking them later, and then he folded it once and put it inside his coat, and it is told that he carried that same strip, worn soft at the folds, the rest of his life, and would show it, in his old age, to anyone fool enough to ask him why he never once, in forty years, set foot inside the Hall's own ground.

"Then we'll burn peat," he said, and the warband wintered on peat that year at Muileann òg, coughing through the cold months on smoke that lay low and sour over the camp and would not draw clean the way the Hall's flame drew, and men who had marched south whole came home in the spring with a cough that some of them carried the rest of their days, so that the older road-guards, decades on, could be told from the younger by the sound of a hard winter's night. Iain coughed with the rest of them and never once said, that whole winter or after, that he wished he had swallowed his pride and sent a gentler messenger; and it was in that camp, watching the sour smoke lie over his own men, that the division of keeping was first spoken aloud and understood for what it was: that the rìgh held the spears and the Keeper held the flame, and that neither, whatever the provocation, could any longer lay a hand on the other's.

The camp at Muileann òg was a poor thing to winter in, a scatter of turf shelters thrown up around the burned toll-house with the black timbers still standing over them like a warning nobody had asked for, and Iain walked it every evening of that season with a road-guard named Dùghall at his shoulder, a young man from the eastern waypoints who had never before been further from home than a day's ride and said so, more than once, in the flat voice of a man too cold to be ashamed of complaining. "The Hall would have kept us dry," Dùghall said one such evening, not quite meaning it as a challenge, and Iain, who had not expected to be answered for the choice by anyone under his own command, found he had no readier answer than the one he had already given the steward. "The Hall keeps whoever it likes dry," he said, "and it does not like us this season. Wrap the coat tighter and mind the peat doesn't smother; a smothered fire coughs worse than a good one." Dùghall did as he was told, and lived to be an old man himself, and told the story of that winter, in his own age, to grandchildren who found it hard to credit that a rìgh had once stood over a peat fire at midnight showing a common guardsman how to keep it drawing.

## IV. Of the Ford of the Forty

In the spring the men of Caol leathan met the levies of Iain Garbh at the ford of Àth fhiadhaich, where the road crossed the last river before the harbour town, and held the water against them a full day before they gave way. They had chosen the ground with more care than Iain expected of them, forming along the far bank where the current ran hardest and a man had to fight the water before he could fight anything else, and he heard, before ever he saw the far rank clearly, Lachlann Ciar's own voice carrying across the noise, hoarse already, telling his people to hold the deep water and let the river do half the work for them. It did. The first men across went down as much to the current as to any blade, and Iain, standing in reserve on the near bank with the second rank around him, watched the water take three before a single spear had crossed it, and understood, watching, why his mother had always said a fool fights the ground before he fights the man on it.

Iain went in with the second rank himself, when the first had thinned enough to want him, and he remembered it afterward, in the few tellings he ever gave of that day, less as a battle than as a string of particular things: the cold that took the legs at the first step into the current, worse than any cold he had felt on the winter roads; the noise of it, which was not the noise he had expected, less shouting than a kind of grunting labour, men working at killing the way other men worked at a stubborn stump; and one man of Caol leathan in particular, standing waist-deep with a shield split clean through and still holding it up before him with no sense left in the holding, until a spear thrown from somewhere behind Iain's own shoulder found him and he went down into the water and did not come up where Iain could see.

By evening the men of Caol leathan had given the ford, falling back toward the harbour in good order, and the carriers who came that way named it the ford of the forty, for the number of dead the two sides left in the shallows and on the near bank, and said, in the tellings that grew up around it in the waypoint houses, that the Morrìgan's own crows were down on the ford before the last light left the water, walking among the dead as if the field were theirs before either side had finished claiming it.

Iain crossed the water that night with the rest of the levy and did not look for the man with the split shield among the drowned, though it is told he asked, once, months later, whether any name had been kept for him, and was told none had.

## V. Of Baile ghlas and Baile chiar

Falling back on Caol leathan, Lachlann Ciar's men burned the granaries and the standing grain at Baile ghlas, a lowland town that had sent Iain neither men nor grudge in the whole of the war, so that the levies coming after would find nothing there to feed themselves on. Iain rode through the warm ash the next morning, the roofs still smoking, and found no one left in the place to ask where its people had gone; they had walked north to Cathair dhomhain in the night, most of them, and a good number of those, weakened on the road or taken by the cold that followed, never came home again to see what little was left standing.

South of the bridge-foot, the town of Baile chiar shut its gate against both hosts that same season and would let neither the levies of Dùn dhearg nor the men of Caol leathan inside its walls, and instead opened its own granaries to the burned-out people of Baile ghlas and fed them through the whole of that hard winter on grain the town had meant for its own year. Iain rode up to that gate himself, meaning to ask lodging for a night for no more than himself and a dozen men, and was met on the wall by the town's own reeve, a broad woman named Beathag who called down that the gate opened for the hungry and for no one carrying a spear, rìgh or otherwise, and that if he wanted a roof he could leave the spear on the road below and come up with empty hands like any other man asking shelter of a stranger. Iain looked at the wall a while, and at the smoke of Baile ghlas still faint behind him on the wind, and left the spear where she had told him to leave it, and slept that night on a floor among refugees from a town he had ridden through the ashes of two days before, and never afterward spoke a hard word of Baile chiar in any household where the tale might carry back to it. Neither side forgave the shut gate, each reading it as favour shown to the other, and neither, for all that, ever brought a spear against it; and in the years after, when the carriers spoke of the towns that had kept faith in the War of the Roads, they set Baile chiar's name beside no other town's, because it had kept faith with neither army and with every hungry mouth that came to its gate.

Iain closed Caol leathan by land before that winter was out, ringing the town on every road with his levies, but he could not close what the town's own boats still brought it from the sea. From the camp on the hill above the harbour he watched, night after night, the low dark shapes slip in past his lines at dusk, heavy in the water with fish, and there was nothing a road-guard on a hillside could do about a harbour that opened onto open sea. His levies, drawn from households that had their own harvest waiting, began going home first by ones and then by whole villages as the season turned, and the siege that could not close a harbour ended without an assault, dissolved by an army that simply was no longer there to press it.

## VI. Of the Peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's House

The war ended, as every long quarrel on the island's roads had come, in the end, to end, under the roof of a waypoint house bound by the road-peace, where no man might draw a blade on another whatever stood between them outside its door. Iain Garbh and Lachlann Ciar met that autumn at the house that had once been Mòr nic Dhùghaill's, on the western road where the road-peace had first been sworn generations before, and sat down at one board because the roof over them allowed nothing else.

Iain had thought, riding to it, that he would find the fat, smiling liar of his younger years, the man who had sent boats out full while he swore the season poor. He found instead an old man with a cough of his own, thinner than the harbour's wealth should have left him, who ate the jugged buffalo the house was known for without much appetite and did not, for a long while, say anything at all. It was Lachlann Ciar who broke the silence first, saying only that the fish-bones had been his son's notion and not his own, and that he had let it go out under his own name because a father does not send a son's foolishness back to be answered for by the son; and Iain, hearing it, found he no longer much wanted the argument he had ridden south to have.

They talked the rest of that evening as two old men talk who have spent thirty years disliking each other from a distance and find, sitting across one board, that the distance had done most of the disliking's work. Caol leathan kept half its road-toll after that and sent half to Dùn dhearg, and Lachlann Ciar swore to the Small-Burning Law before the witness of a keeper sent down from the Hall for the purpose, the first oath the Hall's own witness had taken from him in twenty years, though Uisdean mac Ruairidh did not come himself, and neither man asked him to.

It left three things behind it, that war fought over a road and ended in a house built to feed the carriers of one. Iain rode south the following spring, at Lachlann Ciar's own asking, to stand at the town gate of Caol leathan while the men who had fought the siege that could not close a harbour swore their new watch upon it: a white stone cut, by a mason of the town, in the rough shape of a wolf standing over what might have been a fish or might have been a lamb, no two tellers agreeing which, and set into the gatepost where every traveller on the road would pass under its eye. The men knelt to it one by one, a hand laid flat on the stone's cold flank, and swore to count a toll true and carry a warning fast and never again send a covered basket in place of an honest word, and called themselves, from that swearing on, the wolf-sworn; and Iain, watching from horseback with Lachlann Ciar's son at his stirrup, said to no one in particular that he would have given a fair sum, in his younger years, to see the day a road-guard of Caol leathan swore anything at all before an honest witness. No waypoint-keeper on the southern road ever again found reason to doubt a toll that a wolf-sworn guard had counted. The harbour town of Caol fhiadhaich, whose boats had fed the besieged town through the whole hard winter Iain could not starve it out, was given by Lachlann Ciar a share of the western tolls in payment, and built with it, in the years after, a harbour wall of its own. And Iain Garbh, riding home past Dùn ìseal for the last time in his life, did not turn in at the Hall's gate, nor ever would again; the folded strip of hide stayed inside his coat, and the flame that would not warm him stayed, by his own choosing, a flame he never again asked to be warmed by.

Lachlann Ciar died eleven years after the peace at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's house, in his ninetieth year, the cough that had sat with him at that last board having worn him down by slow degrees the way it had worn down half the men who wintered on peat smoke at Muileann òg; and word came to Dùn dhearg that his household had buried him within sight of the harbour he had grown fat and then thin defending, with his son standing where he had stood at the peace-board, ready, if the toll ever thinned again, to send an honester answer south than a basket of bones. Iain read the word of it at his own hearth, said nothing for a while, and then went out into a cold rain that had been falling since morning and walked the length of the road above the ford without his staff or his steward, in no hurry at all to come back in.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of the Last of the Nine

*FE 1,010 – 1,122*

> *Dh'fhairtlich air an fhèath fhèin fuireach.*
> Even the calm could not stay calm.
>
> — said of Eithne nic Ailein by the reciters of Cathair mhòr, after her

## I. Of the Hall at Cathair mhòr

Eithne nic Ailein kept her hall at Cathair mhòr in the hundredth generation of her own house, though she called none of them her house, since a woman who has buried her own great-great-grandchildren counts her kin by some longer measure than generations. She was the youngest of the nine who had cut the cord at the Roinn, and by the tenth century of the Hall she was also the last of them living, though she felt it first in the way a hall feels emptier before anyone tells you who has died, and knew it for a fact only later.

She was old past two thousand nine hundred years and did not look it, or rather looked it in a way that had stopped changing: the long years did that, her father's blood held its shape once it had settled into age, the way a stone settles into the bank of a river and is not moved again by any flood after the first hundred. Her hands were thin and quick still. Her hair had been white so long that no one living remembered it any other colour, not even her own stewards, whose grandfathers had died in service to her. She sat in the lowland hall she had sat in since before the Peace of the Threshold, and she heard the island's news the way a person hears weather come in from a long way off: felt before it was named.

Her household kept her days simple, by her own long-standing order: bread and fish and the wool of her own sheds, a fire lit whatever the season, and no one troubled to bring her the disputes of Cathair mhòr's own share, which she had handed to a council of stewards a hundred years before and had not once taken back. She had, in her time, cut a knot at a gathering-house, sworn an oath on a threshold beside a carried chair, and buried more kin than most halls on the island had ever held living at one time; and by the tenth century of the Hall she had settled, without meaning to settle anywhere, into the office of an old woman who is asked nothing and told everything, which she had come to think, on her better days, the most restful office a person of her blood could hold.

In the tenth century of the Hall the news that came to her hall was mostly of the west, where a rìgh she had never met, a son of Sìleas Dhonn called Iain Garbh, was fighting a war over a road-toll with a household at Caol leathan that would not send its share to Dùn dhearg. Eithne heard the first of it from a wool-merchant come up from the coast with a load for her own weaving-sheds, a man who told the tale the way traders tell any tale, for what it was worth in the telling.

"They say the Keeper sent his messengers home with nothing," the merchant said, "and the rìgh burned a toll-house for it, and the whole west is up in arms over a basket of fish-bones."

"A basket of fish-bones," said Eithne, who had heard stranger reasons for a war and started one or two herself, long before this merchant's grandmother was born. "Tell it me again from the beginning."

She heard it three times more before the war ended, each telling a little different, as tellings are, and she did not go to it and did not send to it. Cathair mhòr's own share had kept its tolls and its peace both, and she had long since given up riding to wars that were another share's business to end. The last of the nine, whoever she was, stayed by her own fire.

## II. Of the Harbour Wall at Caol fhiadhaich

It was told to her afterward, by the same wool-merchant on his next journey, how the town of Caol fhiadhaich on the south-western shore had sent its own boats out in the worst of the siege to feed the besieged town of Caol leathan by night, running fish past the rìgh's watch-fires on the hill, because the two towns had markets in each other's children and would not see either starve for a quarrel neither had made.

"Iain Garbh gave them a share of the tolls for it, after," the merchant said, "the western tolls, a good share, and they've put up a wall round the harbour with the silver of it, the first stone wall that coast has had."

Eithne had never seen Caol fhiadhaich and never would; it lay the width of the island from her own hall by the roads she no longer travelled, and she pictured it the way an old woman pictures a place from a stranger's words, as something both smaller and grander than it was, a wall of pale stone standing up out of grey water with boats drawn under it. She thought, hearing it, that it was a fair thing to do with a war's spoils, better than most she had heard of in her father's day, when spoils had meant the taking of a share and the burning of a hall. She said so to her steward, an old man himself by then, and the steward, who had heard her say such things before, only nodded and let her say it, the way a household lets an old woman have her thoughts undisturbed.

It was not her wall to build, and she sent nothing west. But she asked, in the years after, whenever a trader came up from that coast, whether the wall still stood, and was told each time that it did, a little higher each telling, as walls grow in the telling the way wars shrink.

## III. Of the Death of Iain Garbh

Iain Garbh lived long after the war he had made, and died at last an old man in his own hall at Dùn dhearg, in the thousand and forty-fourth year of the Hall, a hundred and thirty-five years old. He had ruled forty years past the war's end, and had never once, in all that time, gone up the mountain road to Dùn ìseal to stand before the cup, though every rìgh before him and every rìgh after would go at least once in a reign.

Eithne had this from a Keeper's messenger, one of the young men the Hall sent out now with the season's news, a young man of perhaps twenty who had never known a world without the Small-Burning Law and thought it as old as the vein itself.

"He would not have the flame at his own burying," the messenger told her, standing in her hall with the cold of the road still on him. "His daughter had him laid in the floor of the hall at Dùn dhearg, under the hearthstone where his own father used to sit, and not on the slope at Dùn ìseal where the kings before him lie. The Hall did not ask for him, and I do not think it would have been given him if it had asked."

"He never forgave the flame for the war," Eithne said. It was not a question, though the messenger answered it as one.

"They say he never forgave it for saying no to him," the young man said. "Not for the war itself. He'd have forgiven a war. He didn't forgive being refused."

Eithne sat with that a while after the young man had gone on his way, because she had known men like Iain Garbh, more of them than this messenger could guess from a name in a chronicle: men who would take any hurt from a fight but not from a flame that would not fight beside them. She had watched Ìomhar Dearg wash his hands at a ford in the very first year of the Hall and known even then that a man who takes a thing by the sword remembers the taking longer than he remembers the thing. Iain Garbh had wanted the flame's blessing on a war the flame would not bless, and had gone without it, and had died still wanting it, buried under his own hearthstone rather than under the mountain, because a man's grave is the last word he gets to have.

"He had a daughter," Eithne said to her steward, when the household had gone in to their supper and she sat on alone by her own low fire, which she kept lit even in summer now, more for the company of it than the warmth. "Wise, they tell me. Let us hear of her instead."

## IV. Of Catrìona Ghlic and the Breach Mended

Catrìona Ghlic ruled at Dùn dhearg from her father's death, and the name the island gave her within ten years of her crowning was Catrìona the Wise, which is not a name given lightly to a ruler by the people who pay her tolls, and Eithne, hearing it, thought it the kind of name a daughter earns by undoing what her father did rather than by doing anything grand of her own.

What Catrìona undid, first of all, was the coldness between the hall and the Hall. She sent her own son, a boy not yet come to his full growth, to sit a season with the flame at Dùn ìseal, to carry the baskets and learn the galleries the way any hearth's child might, and this had not been done by the royal house since the division of keeping in Goraidh Mòr's day, when the rìgh had taken the spears and the Keeper had kept the flame and the two had gone their separate ways for the better part of four centuries.

Eithne heard of it from a knot-keeper's granddaughter, one of the last of that dwindling trade, who still came to Cathair mhòr twice a year with the tallies the old way, on a cord, though the letters had come west out of the stag's schools by then, a thing Eithne had heard of and never troubled to see.

"They say the Keeper wept to see him come up the path," the woman said, "a boy of the royal blood carrying a basket like any hearth's son, and asking no more of the Hall than any other boy would ask. And when his season was out he did not want to go home."

"Did they let him stay?"

"They sent him home. A rìgh's son belongs at the rìgh's hall, whatever he wants for himself. But he goes back every year since, at the turn of the season, and they say the Keeper keeps a place for him at the long table without being asked."

Eithne thought of the flame kept once in a keepers' hut of turf and stone, before the Hall was built at all, and of the long quarrel of spears and flame that had run under every reign since Ìomhar Dearg first won a share with the sword before any was given him. It seemed to her, sitting in her own hall so long a time on, that the quarrel had never once been about the flame itself, which asked nothing of anyone, but about which of the island's two powers would be seen to bow first, and that a boy carrying a basket without being asked to had done what four hundred years of rulers and Keepers, careful of each other's pride, had not managed between them.

"Tell them at Cathair mhòr," she said to her own steward, "that when the boy is a man and rules at Dùn dhearg, this hall will send its own tithe to the Hall's handful without waiting to be asked, the way it has not done since the Roinn."

It was done, and it held, a small thing set beside a war and a wall and a king's grave, but Eithne, who had seen a great many large things come to nothing, had learned by then to trust the small ones that held. She thought, sending the order, of Aodh Crom standing on the hill in the first year of the Hall and asking that the vein be in no share. He had meant the flame for every hand equally, and it had taken the island's two powers four hundred years to learn the meaning of it, a rìgh's pride and a Keeper's pride each finding it harder to swallow than any war.

## V. Of the Two Houses and the Wool of Inis mhòr

Catrìona built two houses on the northern road in the years after, and Eithne heard of both from carriers before she heard of them from anyone at court, which was the way of it now: the carriers' roads carried news faster than any messenger the halls could send, because a carrier told his tale at every waypoint house between one end of the island and the other, and a messenger told his only at the end of his riding.

The first house stood above the river port in the north where the wool trade gathered, on ground that had held nothing before but a burned foundation and a bad name; Catrìona had it built fresh and gave it to the carriers of the northern baskets, who took the Hall's grain up to the wool country and brought wool back for it. The second stood further on, out on the open moor between the port and the northern coast, a plain stone house built for no other purpose than to be there when the snow came down early and caught a string of carriers between one hearth and the next with nowhere to shelter. The Hall paid its keepers in grain and the crown paid them in cloth, and the keepers, being carriers' people themselves and used to complaint as a form of thanks, grumbled at both payments and stayed at their post through every winter all the same.

"The wool town has grown past every other town in the north," a carrier told Eithne, an old man himself, near the end of his last run before his knees gave out the trade for good. "They've asked the crown for a road-guard of their own, the way the wolf-sworn keep the west, and the crown has given them one. There's more silver moves through that port in a season now than moves through Dùn dhearg in a year, they say, though I'd not swear to the saying, only the telling of it."

Eithne had seen the wool herself once, in bales brought south along the very road the carrier spoke of, soft grey fleece from the northern flocks that her own weavers turned into cloth finer than anything the lowland sheep gave. She held a handful of it in her hand, that last winter she was strong enough to walk her own sheds, and turned it over between her fingers the way her own weavers did when they were judging a fleece's worth, though she had no craft in the judging and only liked the feel of it, soft and slightly greasy with the lanolin still in it, smelling of a country she would never see. She thought that she had outlived the four rules and the nine shares and the double oaths and a war fought over fish-bones, and here at the end of it all was a town she had never seen growing rich on wool, asking the crown for a guard the way a child asks a parent for a coat, and being given it without argument, as if the asking and the giving were the most ordinary thing in the world.

It seemed to her a good sign of the age, though she said so to no one, having learned that an old woman's good signs are mostly taken for an old woman's fancies. She thought, too, though she kept this thought closer still, that a town could grow that rich and that fast only in an age when no lord's household needed to fear another's spears across its own boundary stone, which had not always been true of the island and had been true for less than half the years of her own life; and she set the fleece down and went back into her hall a little comforted by a thing she could not have explained to her own steward without sounding, to her own ear, like an old woman talking to herself.

## VI. Of Niall Òg on the Last Road

Niall Òg came to Cathair mhòr in the hundred and ninth year of that century of the Hall, unannounced, on foot, with a single household man behind him carrying nothing but a blanket and a skin of water, and Eithne's steward came to her chamber before the sun was well up to say that an old man was asking at the gate who gave his name as Niall, grandson of Ailean, and would not be turned away though he looked in no state to be let stand in the yard.

She had not seen him in over four hundred years. She went down to the gate herself rather than have him brought up, because some meetings are owed the courtesy of going to them, and found him leaning on a stick worn smooth by a use far longer than the making of it, a small bent man with a face gone the colour and texture of old bark, and eyes that had not dimmed at all, which was, she thought, the cruellest part of what the long years did to a person: the eyes went on seeing everything clearly long after the rest had begun to fail.

"You've taken your time," she said, "coming to see me."

"I've been coming for four hundred years," said Niall Òg. "I kept getting distracted by roads. There was always one more stretch of it I hadn't walked, and a man doesn't like to die owing the island a road he never saw."

"And have you seen them all now?"

"Most," he said. "Enough. I met a rìgh's daughter on one of them once, mending a broken stretch with her own staff, and told her a thing about a knotted cord that I don't think she's forgotten, and I've been glad of that meeting ever since, more than of most things I did with a spear in my hand in the early days, which were more than I'd care to count now."

She had him brought in and fed and given the best chair by her own low fire, and he sat in it the whole of that day and would not be moved to a bed until the light was long gone, because, he said, he had slept in enough beds in four centuries and would rather sit up a night talking to the only other person alive who remembered the smoke in the gathering-house on the night of the handful.

They talked of it. Eithne had not spoken of that night to anyone in a hundred years or more, because everyone she might have spoken to about it was long dead, and a memory kept alone in one head begins to feel less like a memory and more like a thing one dreamed; and it was, she found, a relief beyond anything she had felt in a long while to say to another living person, "I knelt by Ciorstaidh's knot a long while before I cut it," and have that other person say, "I remember. You were the only one who knelt. The rest of us just cut and walked on."

"I've thought since," Eithne said, "that kneeling changed nothing. She still lost her share to mine that night."

"It changed you," said Niall Òg. "I watched it. You were never quite so quick to cut anything again, all the years after, not a knot and not much else. I don't think anyone else in that house noticed. I noticed, because I was watching you instead of my own knot, which is a poor way to conduct yourself at a gathering of seven hundred and twelve heirs, but I was young and you were the one worth watching."

He told her the night of the handful once more before he slept, the whole of it, every hearth burning its measure at once and the smoke lying in the rafters and the nine knives going round the cord, and she saw that he told it now the way a teller tells a tale rather than the way a man remembers a thing that happened to him, smoothed by four hundred years of telling into its final shape, every pause in the right place; and she understood, hearing it told that way for what she guessed rightly would be the last time, that this had become his life's whole use in his last years, the carrying of that one night down through every year since, so that when the last of the nine who had lived it was gone, someone would still be able to say how it had truly been, in the smoke, with the lamps.

He died in her own hall three days later, in the chair by her fire, in his sleep, without pain that anyone could see on his face after. The evening before, he had told her that he had walked the road to her gate on purpose, the last road he meant to walk, because he did not want to die on some empty stretch between waypoint houses with no one by to hear the story out, and would rather it were told once more, to her, than carried into the ground with him half-spoken.

She sat with him the night after he died, alone, because she found she did not want her household in the room, and thought that of the seven hundred and twelve who had walked that cord with their lamps, she was now the only one who could say she had been there, in body and in memory both, and that a night no longer walked by a living foot begins, from the moment of the last such walker's death, to belong entirely to the tellers, who had not been there, and would tell it their own way from then on, well or badly, as tellers do.

She had him carried up the mountain road herself, at her own cost, though he was no kin of her own share and she owed his line no such honour by any rule the Roinn had made; she had him laid near the old graves at the slope below Dùn ìseal, among the first heirs, because she judged, and no one troubled to argue her judgement, that a man who had spent four hundred years walking every road on the island back to that one house had earned the right to lie near it at the last.

## VII. Of the Last of the Nine

Eithne outlived him thirteen years, and in those years she felt, for the first time since her father's death at Àth na Fala, entirely alone in a way that was not loneliness so much as a kind of clear sight, the sight of a woman standing at the top of a stair and looking down and finding no one else on any step of it. She had outlived Murchadh, who had cut first at the Roinn; she had outlived Ìomhar, whose blood had thinned in his own line faster than any of the others'; she had outlived Fionnghal and Artair and Cormac and the four whose shares the tellers named in different orders; and now, with Niall Òg gone, she had outlived every one of the seven hundred and twelve who had walked that cord with a lamp on the night of the handful, and every child of Ailean Mòr who had stood weeping in the valley when word came of his falling.

Loud grief, she had learned long before, was mostly for the living to hear, and there was no one left of her own generation to hear hers, so she grieved the way she had grieved for the others: quietly, at her own low fire, in the evenings, when the household had gone to its supper and left her the room. Her hall went on as it always had. She heard the island's news as it came to her, of a market that had begun at the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain, where the lords of the deep river gathered cattle and sheep and horses and hides and the white stone of the hills for sale on the day after each new moon, and took one fleece in forty from every seller for the privilege of the ground; a small thing, a market like a hundred others the island had grown since the Peace, but it pleased her to hear of it, a new thing built on old ground by people who had never heard her name and would not have known it if they had.

Her steward, in those last months, thought her mind had begun to wander, because she asked him more than once what the day was, and made him say the year over twice to be sure he had it right. It had not wandered at all. She wanted, at the end, to know exactly how long the count had run: three thousand years and then some, a number that had stopped meaning anything to her decades before and had become, in her last year, a thing she wanted fixed precisely, the way a weaver wants to know the exact length of a cloth before she cuts it. When he told her the tale of it, one last winter evening, he found himself weeping before he had finished the sum, though she herself only nodded, as if he had confirmed a measurement she had already taken by her own hand and only wanted checked against another's.

She died in her hall at Cathair mhòr on a quiet morning with no illness anyone could name, simply not waking when her women came to her at the hour she always rose, and the reciters who kept the rolls of that hall wrote of her afterward in the old formula they gave to the children of the first king, so that the tale should be told the same way it had always been told of Ailean's line: and all the days of Eithne were three thousand and twenty-one years, and she died.

After her, none of the nine who had cut the cord at the Roinn was living, and the great shares that had once been carried in seven hundred and twelve living memories became names cut into boundary stones, read by carriers who did not know whose hand had first claimed the ground they walked, or why. The long years went on thinning in the king's kin after her, generation by generation, the way a river thins as it runs from the mountain to the sea, until there would come a day, though no one then could have named it, when no one on the island could be told from anyone else by the length of the life allotted him.

At the fords of Baile Mòr dhomhain that same season, on the day after the new moon, the market ran as it always ran: cattle lowing, a fleece in forty going into the lords' baskets, a boy haggling over a length of the white hill-stone with a trader who would not come down on his price, none of them sparing a thought for an old woman who had died a few days' walk off in a hall most of them would never see, whose knife, eleven hundred years before any of them were born, had cut the last knot on a cord that no longer existed, in a house that no longer stood, for a kingdom that had long since forgotten it had ever been undivided.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Eleven Names and Tormod the Writer

*FE 1,123 – 1,320*

> *Chan eil dà chuimhne aig dithis air aon oidhche.*
> No two people keep one night the same way in memory.
>
> — said of the reciters of Dùn dhearg, after Tormod Scrìobhaiche

## I. Of the Mill on the Northern Road

A mill was raised at Muileann shean in the year after Eithne died, on the northern road where the carriers' baskets came down off the pass heavy with grain and went back up light. It was built for no grander purpose than to save every household along that stretch of road the day's walk to the next stone, and it did that well enough that a town grew round it inside two generations, the way a town will grow round anything that saves a day's walk often enough. The miller paid the Hall in grain for his stone and his water-right, and paid the rìgh's toll in flour, and between the two payments he was left, most years, enough to feed his own house and complain that he was left nothing at all, which the carriers who stopped there took as a sign of a well-run mill rather than a poor one, since a miller who is not complaining is a miller counting a loss he has not yet found.

It was an unremarkable town in an unremarkable stretch of years, and the years themselves, for once, had little in them worth a teller's breath.
