Catrìona Ghlic, who had buried Iain Garbh in his own hall floor and mended what she could of the breach his war had opened, died at Dùn dhearg an old woman by the ordinary count and a young one by the count her blood had once kept, a hundred and twenty-two years old, which would have seemed to Ìomhar Dearg, had he lived to hear it, no age at all for a ruler of his line. Her son took the hall at ninety-two and held it eighteen years and died at a hundred and ten, and after him came another, and after that one another, and the king-list, when at last someone thought to make one, gave eleven names for the hall at Dùn dhearg between Catrìona Ghlic and the queen who came after them, and nothing more than the names and the order they sat in.

It is not that nothing happened in those years. Roads were kept, tolls were gathered, a harbour wall went up somewhere and a granary went up somewhere else, and every one of the eleven, no doubt, believed his own reign the equal in incident of any that the tellers still told whole. But the reciters who carried the hall's memory from one generation to the next carried it the way a river carries silt, taking up what a flood brings down and letting the rest settle unseen, and by the time anyone asked them for those years entire they had already settled into eleven names and a rough count of the winters each ruler held, and no reciter living could give back what had never been asked of them in time.

The Hall on the mountain kept its own roll for the same years, spoken, not written, and it gave five Keepers where the hall at Dùn dhearg gave eleven rulers, which any teller of the Hall's years will tell you is no more than the ordinary difference between a mountain's years, which are long, and a lowland's, which are not.

Somewhere in the middle of those eleven reigns, in a year no reciter troubled to fix more closely than "before Ealasaid Chiar and some while after Catrìona Ghlic," the last ruler of the house of Ìomhar and Goraidh who carried any of the long years in his blood died at a hundred years old, which had once, in his grandmother's grandmother's day, been a boy's age and was now, without anyone marking the day it happened, an old man's. The long years had been going out of that line since the ford at Àth na Fala, thinning a little in every child the way a dye thins with every washing of the cloth, and by the time the thinning reached its end there was no one left who remembered the blood as it had been, and so no one to mourn it going. The rulers after him lived and died at the pace of any household on the island, and the numbering of their years, wherever it is set down, reads no differently from the roll of any carrier's family kept beside it.

Of the eleven themselves, the roll, once it was made, gave little beyond their names and the years they sat, and this telling, which owes the roll its facts, follows it in that restraint. No one, in their own day, thought a written hand would ever be asked to remember them, and by the time a written hand was, the deeds were gone and only the names were left standing, the way boundary stones stand long after the fence between them has rotted into the ground.

## II. Of Tormod mac Iain

Tormod was born at Dùn dhearg in the reign of the tenth of the eleven, a younger son of the house of Tormod, which had held no great office in the hall for three generations and was not expected, by anyone in it, to hold one again soon. His father Iain kept a modest stretch of the granaries on the crown's account, an honest post and a dull one, and Tormod grew up among grain-tallies and the smell of dust and mice, learning to count sacks by the age of six and to hate counting them by the age of eight, a hatred that would have surprised, later in his life, everyone who came to know him only as a man bent over a roll with a stylus in his hand.

He was fifteen, by his own later reckoning, when a stag-teacher passed through Dùn dhearg on his way east and stayed the night in his father's granary-loft, out of the rain, and told the household over supper of the letters kept at Muileann chiar, marks that could hold a teaching in a line cut on hide or bark without a teacher standing over it to keep the teaching straight. Tormod had never in his life heard of a thing that could remember without a person to do the remembering, and it struck him, he said afterward more than once, the way lightning is said to strike a man who has spent his whole life indoors and steps out at the wrong hour: a thing that happened to him and left him changed, whether he had chosen it or not.

His father thought little of it, a boy's fancy caught by a traveller's tale, and would likely have let it pass had the boy not gone on asking after it, at meals and in the fields and once, to his father's lasting embarrassment, in front of the granary-reeve who had come to check the tallies. In the end simple arithmetic sent Tormod east: a younger son of a house with no office to give him was a mouth the granary could feed more cheaply at Muileann chiar, learning a trade no one else in Dùn dhearg troubled to learn, than kept idle at home waiting for a post that would never come. His father called it practical sense and told the neighbours so. Tormod, walking the northern road with a carrier's basket-string for company and his own feet blistering inside a fortnight, called it, privately, the first stroke of luck his life had given him, and never after changed his mind on the matter.

## III. Of the Stag-Letters at Muileann chiar

The teachers at Muileann chiar took him in without much ceremony, as they took in most who came asking, on the reckoning that a mind willing to sit through the tedium of the marks was worth more to them than a mind merely quick, and tedium there was: weeks of nothing but the shapes themselves, the strokes for breath and the strokes for stop, drilled on a slate until the hand knew them without the eye's help, before any teacher would let a pupil near a real telling. Tormod was neither the quickest of that season's intake nor the slowest, but he was, by his teachers' own account, the one who complained least at the drilling, which they took for the better sign, and rightly.

He wrote his first whole leaf in the second summer, a tally of a household's grain-debt over three seasons, copied from a spoken account an old woman gave him twice over to be sure he had it right, and it survived, folded small and much handled, among the leaves of his own house long after his death, the oldest thing in his own hand that the world still has. He kept it, his teachers said, tucked inside his shirt for a full year after the writing of it, the way a young cutter is said to keep the first coal his own hand brings up out of the vein, for the plain fact of having made a thing that had not existed the day before.

The better part of four years he stayed at Muileann chiar, longer than most who came only to learn the marks and go home to some clerk's post that wanted them and nothing more, and read what the teachers there kept, which was mostly grain-tallies and toll-counts and the odd letter between one waypoint house and another, and he found, reading it, that he wanted more than tallies: he wanted, though he could not have said so plainly even to himself at nineteen, to write down a thing that would still be readable when every mouth that had ever spoken it was dead, the way the mountain's own coal, once cut and burned, gives its light to hands that never touched the vein it came from. It was a want with no post attached to it and no household waiting to pay for its satisfying, and he carried it home to Dùn dhearg unspoken, because a young man who says aloud that he means to outlast every reciter in the hall is a young man inviting every reciter in the hall to make sure he does not.

## IV. Of Ealasaid Chiar

He served forty years at Dùn dhearg as a clerk of the granaries, his father's trade after all, before the chance came that his four years at Muileann chiar had been, without his knowing it, preparing him for the whole while. Ealasaid Chiar took the hall in the year Tormod turned fifty-nine, the granddaughter of the ninth of the eleven, a woman who had grown up hearing the reciters give the roll of her own house in a different order at every telling and had come, by the time she was crowned, thoroughly out of patience with it.

She had heard, from her own granary-reeve, that there was a clerk in her stores who could set a thing down in marks and have it read back the same way twice, which struck her, she said afterward, as either the most useful thing she had ever heard of a clerk or the strangest, and she sent for him to find out which. Tormod came before her in his working clothes with flour still in the seams of them, an old man by then in everything but the eye, and she asked him, without preamble, whether he could write down the names of every ruler who had held the hall before her, in the right order, so that her own grandchildren need not learn it eleven different ways from eleven different mouths.

He told her, honestly, that he did not know, since no one had ever asked such a thing of the marks before; the marks had been made, at Muileann chiar, for grain and debts and the odd letter, not for the memory of a house. But he said he would try, and Ealasaid Chiar, who had learned by then to value a clerk who said "I will try" over one who promised more than he could give, told him to begin that week and gave him a room off her own hall to work in, with a standing order that no reeve was to call him back to the granaries while the roll was unfinished, which his father, had he lived to see it, would have found the strangest turn of all: that his son's idleness, once the family's shame, should end as the crown's own business.

## V. Of the Reciters

Tormod began, sensibly enough, with the reciters, the old men and women whose whole office in the hall was to carry the ruler's line in their heads and give it out at feasts and namings, generation folded into generation the way a story-teller folds a long tale for a short evening. He sat with each of them in turn through the autumn and winter, asking the same questions of each and writing down what each one gave him, and it was in this work, more than in any drilling at Muileann chiar, that he learned the true use of the marks: to hold still, on a leaf, exactly what one mouth had said on one day, so that it could afterward be set beside what another mouth had said and the difference between them looked at plainly instead of argued over in the air.

The differences, when he set them beside one another, troubled him more than he let Ealasaid Chiar see at first. Two reciters gave the ninth ruler's mother a different name. One gave the seventh reign nine years and another gave it eleven, and neither would yield the point, each citing a teacher long dead who had told it so and could not now be asked. A reciter from the southern households, brought up before Ealasaid Chiar on some other matter and questioned by Tormod almost as an afterthought, gave an order for three of the eleven that put none of them where the hall's own reciters put them, and defended it with as much certainty as any of the others had defended theirs.

"They cannot all be remembering the same thing," Tormod said to Ealasaid Chiar, the first time he brought her his doubts rather than his progress, "and yet each of them is certain."

"Then which is right?" she asked him.

"I do not know," he said, "and I have come to think that not knowing may be the truest thing I can write down."

She was silent a moment at that, turning it over the way a woman turns over a ring she is not sure is good silver. "Write down the doubt, then," she said at last, "where you have it, and the sure thing where you have that, and let the two stand together on the leaf. A roll that hides its own uncertainty is a roll that will be believed too well by people who have no way of knowing better, and I would rather my grandchildren doubted rightly than believed wrongly."

It was not, in the end, an order many clerks after him chose to follow, since a roll with gaps in it looks, to most eyes, less finished than one without; but Tormod took her at her word, and in three places where his reciters' account disagreed with what he later learned the Hall's own roll gave, he set both readings down side by side and chose neither, a habit that earned him, among the few scholars who ever came to read his leaves entire, more honour than any of the names he did manage to fix beyond doubt.

## VI. Of the Roll's Making

The writing of the first roll took the better part of a year, since Tormod would not set a name down until he had heard it from more than one mouth, or marked plainly that he had not; and because Ealasaid Chiar, once the habit of asking had been started in her hall, found she wanted more than the eleven names that had first sent her to him. She had him go back further, into the reigns the earlier reciters still just remembered whole, Goraidh Mòr and the war of the roads and the peace under Mòr nic Dhùghaill's roof, setting down in the same careful hand what until then had lived only in the telling.

He worked at a low table by the window of the room she had given him, a room that had been a store for undyed wool before it was a clerk's room and still smelled faintly of lanolin on a damp day, and he kept, through that year and the years of going back that followed it, the two-summer boy's habit of the first leaf he had ever written: he read each finished page over to whoever had given it to him, reciter or steward or Ealasaid Chiar herself, before he counted it done, so that no name went into the roll that its own source had not heard back and owned. It was slow work, and it made him few friends among the reciters, who did not care to be read back to like children learning a lesson. It made the roll, when it was finished, a thing no one at Dùn dhearg could afterward call a single clerk's fancy, since every name in it had been sworn to twice, once in the giving and once in the hearing.

The finished roll ran from Goraidh Mòr to Ealasaid Chiar herself, the eleven names set at last in an order Tormod judged, after weighing every reciter's account, the least contradicted rather than the most certain, with the three doubtful places marked as doubtful and left so. He brought it to Ealasaid Chiar on a winter evening with the wool-smell of the room still on his sleeves, an old man of sixty with a stylus-callus on his first finger that would not soften now for the rest of his life, and set it in her two hands the way a steward sets a harvest tally before a lord, though what he had brought her weighed nothing at all and had cost him a year of his life.

She read it through by her own fire without speaking, and when she had finished she said only, "Now no one at Dùn dhearg need learn it eleven different ways again," which was, from a queen not given to open praise, as much praise as Tormod Scrìobhaiche ever had for his life's whole work, and by every account he asked for none.

He died ten years after, at seventy, in the same room off the hall where he had written the roll, with the finished leaves stacked beside his bed and a half-begun copy of the disputed reign still under his hand. Ealasaid Chiar had the room's wool-smell scrubbed out of it afterward and gave it a proper clerk's floor, and named it, in the hall's own speech, no more than "Tormod's room."

## VII. Of the Shamed Hall

Word of the written roll reached the Hall on the mountain the following spring, carried up by a carrier who had heard it told at a waypoint house and thought it worth the telling twice, and it reached the Keeper of that year, Fionnlagh Dall's line by four generations though the years had by then taken his sight as they had taken his forebear's, in words that stung more than the carrier had meant them to: that the rìgh's clerk had set down in marks a memory the Hall had only ever kept in the mouth.

The Keeper heard it out and said nothing for three days, which those who knew him took for a bad sign, since a blind man's silence has nowhere to look and so settles, when it settles at all, on whatever is nearest. On the fourth day he called the reciters of the Hall before him, the old men and women who kept the Keepers' line the way Dùn dhearg's reciters had once kept the rulers', and told them, in words the reciters afterward repeated more often than any other he ever spoke, that a Hall shamed by a rìgh's clerk into writing down what it should have written down of its own accord a century before had no one to blame for the shame but itself, and that he would not sit blind at the head of a Hall that let a lowland granary-clerk out-remember it.

The writing of the Hall's own roll fell, in the end, less to any one hand than to a company of hands, since no clerk among the Hall's own people had Tormod's years of practice at the marks; a young cutter who had spent a season at Muileann chiar himself was set to the actual writing, while the reciters gave their account and the Keeper, sightless, listened to every leaf read back to him twice before he let it stand, a slower and stranger method than Tormod's but one that suited a blind man's hall as well as sight had suited Tormod's own working. It began, as the Hall's spoken roll had always begun, with Beathag Bhàn, and it ran longer than Tormod's roll by several centuries, since the Hall's own line reached back past the eleven rulers and past Goraidh Mòr both, into years the rìgh's own reciters had never troubled to keep at all.

## VIII. Of the Cord Untied

It was in the last summer of that writing, some thirteen hundred years since the cord of the heirs had been cut at the Roinn, that Cairistìona nan Snaidhm came down from her own house to the Hall with the cord carried before her on a cushion of undyed wool, the last of Sìne nan Snaidhm's line still living who could read a knot the old way, without letters, by the shape and the tightness and the place of it along the length.

She was an old woman herself by then, the knot-keeping long since fallen from any real use in the Hall's business, since the Hall had kept its accounts by tally-stick and now by the marks for longer than she had been alive; but the old cord itself, the whole cord Sìne nan Snaidhm had tied a second time in the year after the Roinn so that the Hall should keep entire what the nine had carried away in pieces, had never been untied, seven hundred and twelve knots still holding the shape she had given them, and no one at the Hall could read what they held save Cairistìona, and after Cairistìona no one at all.

She sat with the young scribe two full days, the cord across both their laps, and untied it knot by knot from the first end, naming aloud, for each knot, the heir it had been tied for and the share that heir had taken, while the scribe set each name down in the new marks as she gave it. It was slow work, slower even than Tormod's had been, since a knot untied cannot be tied again to check the reading, and Cairistìona would not have a knot loosed until she had named it twice to her own satisfaction, turning it under her fingers the way her mother had taught her mother's mother to turn them, feeling for the small differences of tightness that thirteen hundred years of handling had not quite smoothed away.

"My mother could read this cord blind," she told the scribe, on the second day, when her own eyes had begun to tire of the light in the low room, "and her mother before her, and neither of them ever wrote a single name of it down, because the cord did the remembering and a Snaidhm's fingers did the reading, and between the two of them nothing was ever lost in thirteen hundred years. I am the last who can do both. After me the cord will still exist, coiled in whatever chest you set it in, but it will not be able to speak, because there will be no hand left that knows its language, only these marks of yours, which speak a different way and cannot be unmade back into a knot if anyone should ever doubt them."

The scribe, a young man with no reply ready for so plain a grief, said only that the marks would keep what she gave them for longer than any hand could keep a cord, hers or her daughter's or any daughter after.

"That may be true," Cairistìona said, "and it is no comfort at all," and went back to the untying.

When the last knot came free, the seven hundred and twelfth, tied for a claimant so far down the great division that no reciter of either roll had carried the name whole into living memory, she held the loose cord a while in both hands before she gave it over, feeling its slackness the way a person feels the absence of a weight they have carried so long they no longer notice carrying it. Then she coiled it herself, in the old way, the way her mother had taught her to coil it for storage between one Roinn business and the next, and laid it in the chest the Hall had made for it, and did not ask to see it again.

In the three places where the rìgh's roll and the Hall's roll disagreed, as Tormod had marked they would, no one at either hall in that season thought it worth another six years of arguing to settle which was right, and both readings were let stand side by side, the one habit of Tormod's that the Hall's own scribes had, without quite meaning to, taken up as their own.

In the year the last knot came free it was only a cord, coiled small, going into a chest built for it by a hall that had learned, in the space of two clerks' careful lifetimes, to trust marks on a leaf over the memory of any single mouth or any single pair of hands, however faithful either had been. The chest was set in the Hall's own gallery, and the lid was closed on it, and no one that season thought to open it again.

## IX. Of the Names That Are Left

Eleven names stand now on Tormod's roll where before there had been eleven shapes in a reciter's memory, some clearer than others, none of them fixed. Five names stand on the Hall's roll for the same span of years, and neither roll, for all the care its makers gave it, can now be checked against the mouths that first carried the memory, since every one of those mouths is generations in its grave. What is left is marks on a leaf and a coiled cord that no living hand can read, and a room off a hall that still smells, faintly, on a damp day, of the wool it once stored, though no one now remembers why a clerk's room should smell of wool at all.

It is a small thing, set beside a war fought over fish-bones or a bier made of a host's own spears, eleven names written where eleven shapes had stood before; but it is the thing this telling has to set down of those years, since the years themselves, for all the width of them, chiefly held themselves and did not choose, in their own day, to be remembered further than that. The next hand that comes to the roll, wherever it comes from, will read Tormod's doubt in the three disputed places exactly as he left it, neither resolved nor hidden, and will know, from that alone, more of how the roll was made than either roll's makers thought, at the time, they were troubling to tell it.

# Part Five: The Written Roll and the Red Hall

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Wood-Watchers

*FE 1,321 – 1,595*


> *Cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann.*
> We did not come; we were here.
>
> — said by both companies of the dark wood, each of its own wood, and neither meaning the other

## I. Of the Years the List Does Not Count

Ealasaid Chiar died in the thirtieth year of her writing, having lived sixty years and reigned thirty-one of them, and was carried to the graves of the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg. It is told that the clerk Tormod had trained stood at the grave with the roll his master had made her, the first written king-list on Dia-thìr, and read her own name out of it last, in its right place, because she had once asked Tormod whether a written name could feel it was written, and Tormod had not been able to answer her and had thought of the question every day he had left.

After Ealasaid Chiar the list falters. For a space the reciters cannot close, the roll Tormod began gives no ruler at all, only a silence where a name should stand, because in those years no household strong enough to hold the hall at Dùn dhearg troubled to have its claim written down, or because the writing lapsed with the clerk who alone knew how to keep it, or for some third reason no one living now can give. The Keepers' roll at Dùn ìseal keeps its own count through the same years. It was begun later than Tormod's and kept by a different hand, and where the king-list is silent the Keepers' roll goes on naming its own Keepers one after another, each dying and each replaced, so that a person wishing to know how many years passed in the gap must count them there instead, by the flame's own succession rather than by the hall's.

It was in this gap, some fifty years into it by the Keepers' count, that the Hall at Dùn ìseal first set its own hand to teaching. Until then the stag-letters had been the stag's people's alone, taught in their own schools to their own novices, and any at Dùn ìseal who wished to read sent a son or a daughter east to learn it as a guest. In the fiftieth year of the gap the Keeper of that day judged that a Hall which could not read its own roll without borrowing another order's letters was a Hall too dependent on goodwill it had not earned, and set two of his own clerks to learn the stag-letters at Dùn ìseal, taught by a stag-teacher paid in coal for the winter of his teaching. It is remembered now as a small thing, though it did not feel small to the clerks who first sat down to a stranger's alphabet at their own Keeper's order. From that year the Hall kept its roll in its own hand, and the roll it kept, once begun, did not stop, through every year of the silence that followed in the king-list, so that when at last a ruler's name returns to the record it is the Keepers' roll, not the king-list, that can say with any certainty how many years had passed.

Seventy years further into the gap a Keeper was named of whom the roll gives only the years of her reign, twenty-two, and the year of her death. It is the fate of a quiet age that most of what happens in it happens to no one the tellers thought worth naming, and a hundred small keepings, harvests neither good nor bad, coal cut and burned and cut again, children born and old people buried in the ordinary way, pass without a single teller troubling to set them down, because a teller tells what changes, and in those years, on the whole, nothing changed. The households burned their handful at dawn as their grandparents had burned it. The carriers walked the roads their grandparents had walked. The Hall's clerks, in their new letters, wrote the Keepers' names into the roll as each died and each was chosen, and nothing in the writing asked to be read twice.

It is not that the island slept through those years, only that it did what an island does when no one is fighting for it and no god has spoken and no famine has come: it went on, quietly, at the pace of a life rather than the pace of a telling, and the tellers, who love a fire or a war or a birth of note, left it mostly alone.

## II. Of the Black Horned Beast

Near the far end of that quiet a woman of the households of the north-west gave birth to a son she named Conall, and called him Dubh for the black hair he came into the world with and kept all his life, thick and unfading even in his last years, when every other hair he had gone grey turned white instead of thinning. He was the fourth of five children in a household that kept sheep on the high ground above Cnoc bheag, in sight of the wood the island had never cleared, a stand of old oak and thorn that ran back from the moor's edge further than any household's memory, and that no one, in all the generations since Aodh Crom had first divided the vein from the shares, had ever put an axe to.

Conall grew up half afraid of that wood and half in love with it, the way a child is of any dark place close enough to walk to and far enough that its parents forbid the walking. He heard from his grandmother, who had heard it from hers, that something walked in the uncleared wood that was not a stag and was not a wolf and was not any beast a hunter's dog would follow, a thing horned and black that let only those it chose come upon it, and that the wood was left uncleared on its account rather than on any rule of the Hall's, because the first households to try clearing it had lost cattle in it and never gone back to try again. His grandmother told it as an old woman tells a thing she half believes and wholly enjoys telling, with a shiver in the voice at the right places, and Conall, who was a serious child even at six years old, asked her each time whether she herself had seen it, and each time she said no, but that her own grandmother had, once, at dusk, at the wood's edge, and had never afterward walked past it without making the old sign against ill luck, faith or no faith.

He was twenty years old, in the household's own reckoning, when he saw it himself.

He had gone up to the high pasture before first light to bring down two ewes that had strayed the night before, and came along the wood's edge in the grey hour when the birds have not yet begun and the light is more a lessening of dark than a beginning of day, and there, at the treeline, not thirty paces off and standing quite still, was a beast the size of a large hind but built heavier through the shoulder, black from nose to hoof but for two pale horns that caught what little light there was and held it, so that Conall, who told the tale only twice in his life and both times to people he trusted absolutely, said afterward that the horns seemed lit from within rather than by the sky. It looked at him. He did not move, and it did not move, for what he judged afterward to have been the space of ten or twelve breaths, though it might have been less, fear being a poor clock. Then it turned, without hurry, and walked back into the trees, and was gone before he had drawn a full breath to call out, though he had no one near enough to call to and would not, in any case, have known what to call.

He told his mother that night. She did not laugh at him, which surprised him more than the beast had. She said only that her own grandmother's grandmother, by the family's count, had seen the same thing in the same place, or something enough like it that the tellings could not be told apart, and that a household that farmed this close to the wood had best let it keep its own council and not go looking for it a second time.

Conall did not let it keep its own council. He went back.

## III. Of the Watch

He went back first alone, then, within a year, with his younger sister, who did not believe him until she saw the beast herself from the same spot at the same grey hour, and after her with two cousins, and within five years there were nine of them, none older than thirty, who kept a watch at the wood's edge by turns, not to hunt the beast and not, at first, for any reason any of them could have set down in words beyond a wish to be there when it came again, which it did, not often, perhaps once in a season, always at the grey hour, always at a little distance, always turning back into the trees before anyone had gathered courage or wit enough to follow.

The people of Cathair dhearg, hearing of it from carriers who stopped at the household on the northern road, called them the wood-watchers, a name none of the nine had chosen for themselves and all of them, in time, came to answer to. Conall, being the first and the steadiest, and having by then given up shepherding to his brothers so that he might keep the watch through every season rather than the seasons his flock could spare him, became without any choosing on anyone's part the one the others looked to. He did not call himself a teacher of anything. He said, when the carriers asked him what the watchers believed, that they believed a beast walked in the wood and that a wood a beast walks in ought to have someone by it who is paying attention, which was not, he knew, an answer that satisfied a person looking for a faith with rules and a name, but it was the only answer he had, and he gave the same one for the rest of his life whenever the question was put to him.

By his thirtieth year, when Conall was already greying a little at the temples though his hair kept its black, the watchers numbered near thirty and had built themselves a low turf hut at the wood's edge where two or three of them slept in every season, keeping the watch through the night as well as the grey hour, because the beast, once, had been seen at full dark by a watcher out later than she meant to be. It was in that year that Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the uncleared wood, was first called sacred by anyone outside the watchers' own company, when a Hall clerk travelling the northern road to count the season's coal wrote the word down in his own report, more from habit than from any judgement of his own, having heard the watchers speak of the wood in that way and having no better word to hand.

## IV. Of the Tree in the Stag's Grove

It was Conall's own doing, and he never afterward denied it or claimed it was other than his own doing, that brought the wood-watchers into their first quarrel with any other company on the island.

In the dark of a winter some seven years after the clerk's report, the beast came right up to the watch-fire, closer than it had ever come before, and stood at the very edge of the firelight while five watchers sat frozen and silent around the flame, and then walked a slow circle about the fire, and stopped, and looked long at one particular tree at the wood's edge, a black-barked oak no different to the eye from a hundred others near it, before it turned and was gone into the dark. Conall lay asleep in the turf hut that night, and heard it told before the fire had burned down, by watchers too shaken to sleep, and he went out himself before first light and stood a long while before the tree the beast had looked at, and decided, in the way a man decides a thing he has been circling toward for years without knowing it, that the beast had shown it to him.

He cut the limb himself, with his own axe, the only cutting the wood-watchers had made in all their years of keeping their watch without cutting anything, and he did not cut it from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag at all. The beast, when it turned from the fire, had turned east, and gone east into the dark; and Conall, who had once as a young man driven sheep the length of the island and seen, at the western edge of the stag's grove at Muileann chiar, a stand of black-barked oaks like the one the beast had stood beside, took it into his head that the beast had been showing him the way. He walked east six days with the axe at his belt and one watcher for company, and at dawn on the seventh he cut a limb from the first black-barked oak at the edge of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, believing, once the thought had taken him, that a sign shown to the watchers belonged to the watchers wherever it stood. He carried the limb home to the turf hut and set it above the door, and the watchers kept a small fire under it that spring, calling it the beast's own wood, given by the beast's own choosing.

The teachers of the grove found the wound in the tree that same morning. The teachers at Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, who kept their own long watch over their own wood far to the east and had heard of the wood-watchers only as a strange household custom on the far side of the island, not as any rival order, sent two of their eldest west with the word that a tree had been cut from the stag's own ground, a theft of a teaching-place rather than merely of wood, for the black-barked oaks at the grove's western edge had for longer than any of the wood-watchers' memory been used by the stag's teachers for lessons, and the tree Conall had cut was one three generations of teachers had taught beneath.

Conall met the two elders at the wood's edge himself. He did not deny the cutting; he never in his life denied a thing he had done. He told them what the beast had done, circling the fire and looking long at the one tree, and said that he had read it as a sign meant for the watchers, and the elder who spoke for the pair, a woman old enough to have taught three generations of her own order's novices, heard him out in full and then said, not unkindly, that a sign was a hard thing to read from outside another order's own understanding, and that the stag's people had their own long history of signs read wrongly by those who wanted them read a certain way, and that a man who read a sign as leave to walk six days into another order's wood with an axe had read it, at the least, very much to his own advantage.

## V. Of the Teachers in the Dark Wood

The stag's people did not let the matter rest with words at the wood's edge. Within the season they sent teachers of their own west, straight into Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, the wood-watchers' own uncleared wood, and set up a teaching-circle at its western edge, saying that the first stag any teller could name had come from that wood before it came to any grove in the east, and that the stag's people therefore held as good a claim to the uncleared wood as the wood-watchers held to any border tree.

Conall would not have it that the teachers had come to steal his own ground in answer, though several of the younger watchers said so plainly and said it to the teachers' faces. He thought, and said so to any watcher who would listen, that the stag's people had done exactly what he himself had done at the border tree: taken a grievance and answered it the only way either order knew how, by claiming ground. He did not think it made either side wrong, only that it made both sides the same kind of wrong, which he found, when he had turned it over long enough in his own mind, oddly steadying, since a quarrel between two sides equally wrong is at least a quarrel that can be settled without either side needing to be told it alone was at fault.

For the better part of two years the two companies kept to their two ends of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, each claiming both woods, and it is told, and Conall himself told it so in the one full account he ever gave of those years, that the watchers and the teachers met often enough in the wood between their two camps, gathering the same fallen wood for the same small fires, drawing water from the same spring, and that in all that time neither side spoke a word to the other beyond what courtesy required to pass on a narrow path, each nodding to the other and going on, as if an old agreement neither had ever made held them apart more surely than any boundary stone could have. It is the first quarrel remembered on Dia-thìr between two holy claims, and it was fought, if fought is the word for it, in silence, by two companies that shared a wood, a spring, and firewood, and would not share a sentence.

Word of it went to Dùn dhearg and to Dùn ìseal both, carried by the same carriers who had first named the wood-watchers, and both halls, hearing that neither company had raised a hand against the other and that the quarrel, such as it was, threatened no household's grain and no road's peace, judged it a matter for the two orders to settle between themselves, and sent no one to settle it for them. It was, in the end, a death that moved the matter, though not a death either side caused. In the second winter of the silence one of the teaching elders, the same woman who had spoken for the two who first came west, died of an ordinary winter cough in the teaching-circle's own camp, an old woman whose years had simply run their course, and Conall, hearing of it from a watcher who had heard it from a teacher too grieved to keep the old silence, walked alone to the teachers' camp and stood at its edge until he was noticed, and said, when he was asked what he wanted, only that he had come to say he was sorry for their loss, and that he thought, whatever else stood between the two companies, an old woman's death was not a thing either side should keep silent over.

## VI. Of Fearchar Òg, a Boy of Seven

The two companies kept the wood between them in their changed silence for fifteen years more, meeting at the spring, gathering the same fallen wood, nodding and passing on, and it is told that in all that span not one further word was cut in anger nor one further branch taken without leave, so that the quarrel, such as it remained, had by then worn itself down to a habit of politeness neither side troubled to explain to the other.

It was in the fifteenth of those years, though the wood-watchers did not hear of it for some months, that a boy of seven years old was brought to the Keepers' hall at Dùn ìseal by his own mother's hand, a great-grandson, by a line the reciters had kept with more care than most, of the house that had once held Dùn dhearg before the gap swallowed its record. He was named Fearchar, and called Òg, the young, from the day he first stood before the Keeper to be looked over, because there had been, within living memory of the hall, no ruler young enough to need the naming.

The Keeper of that year judged the boy's claim as carefully as the gap-worn records allowed, weighing the line the reciters gave him against what little the Keepers' own roll could confirm of it, and found nothing in it she could set aside. She did not crown him that day, a boy of seven being no ruler by any measure the island kept, but she had his name entered in the roll as heir acknowledged, and sent word to Dùn dhearg that a claim had at last been found worth the hall's confidence, the first such word in longer than the Keepers' own count could say with certainty.

Fearchar Òg was raised after that within sight of the hall, in a household the Keeper trusted, and grew, as boys of seven do, slowly and without any teller's notice, learning the roads and the halls and, in time, the names of the two companies quarrelling in silence in the wood his own great-grandmother's line had once held authority over, a quarrel that by the time he was old enough to be told of it at all had already run near twenty years without a blow struck on either side and showed no sign, to anyone watching from Dùn ìseal, of ever settling.

## VII. Of the Shared Keeping

It was Calum Liath, made Keeper in the boy's ninth year, a man of forty-five summers when he took the flame and known already for a patience the roll credits him with more than once, who judged at once that the wood-watchers and the stag's people would go on sharing a wood and a spring and a silence forever unless someone with authority over neither order set a boundary between them that both could keep without either being told it had lost. He did not summon the two companies to Dùn ìseal, judging rightly that neither would come at the summons of a hall it did not answer to. He went to the wood himself, that same spring, and brought the boy-king with him, a boy still by any measure but for the office now laid on him, not yet crowned in any full sense the roll would call a reign.

They walked the wood's whole length together, Keeper and heir, from the western turf hut to the eastern teaching-circle, and spoke first with Conall, who was by then a man past fifty with more grey than black left in his hair though it had not, even then, whitened through, and then with the eldest of the teachers, a man who had come west in the first year of the quarrel and stayed every year since. Calum Liath asked each company the same question: what would you keep, if you kept only your own claim and gave up any claim to the other's ground. Conall answered that the watchers wanted only the western wood, where the beast had first shown itself and had gone on showing itself in all the years since, and would give up any claim to the eastern grove if the eastern grove gave up its claim to the western wood. The teacher answered much the same of the eastern grove, and it was Calum Liath, hearing both answers land so near the same ground, who proposed what neither company had thought to ask for on its own: that the black-barked stand be left to the stag's people who had taught beneath it, with the watchers free to keep a watch there at their pleasure so long as they cut no branch of it again, and that each wood, western and eastern both, stay in the keeping of the company that had first claimed it, with each free to walk the other's wood unarmed and without cutting, as a guest walks a neighbour's ground.

Fearchar Òg, standing by, said little through the whole of it, being young and new to matters he had been raised to understand only in outline, but it is told that when Calum Liath had finished setting out the terms, the young king asked the two elders whether either side had, in near twenty years of silence, ever once wished the other gone from the wood entirely, and that both Conall and the teacher, after a long pause, said no, each in their own words, and that Calum Liath took the two no's as the surest sign yet that the terms would hold.

They held. Stones were cut that same season, at the boy-king's own order and the Keeper's, and set at the edges of both woods, with the terms cut into them in stag-letters, so that any who could read might know, walking that ground, what was kept and by whom. No side was named the victor of the quarrel, because the roll that recorded it, kept in the Hall's own hand as it had been since the Keeper who first set his clerks to their letters two centuries before, judged there had been no victory to name, only a boundary two companies had at last agreed to keep.

## VIII. Of Conall in the Eastern Wood

Conall walked into the eastern grove for the first time in his life the day after the last stone was set, alone, without the axe he had carried at his belt for thirty years out of habit rather than any need of it, and without any of the younger watchers who would have gone with him gladly had he asked. He wanted, he told the one watcher he did tell, to walk it once as the stones now allowed, a guest in another order's wood, before he grew too old to walk it at all.

The teachers let him pass without a word raised against him, as the stones now bound them to, and he walked the length of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar in the slow hour before dusk, under oaks no different to look at from the oaks of his own wood, and came at last to the black-barked stand at its western edge, where the stump of the limb he had cut had long since healed over, and stood there a while in the failing light, an old man by then in all but the roll's reckoning, thinking, as he told it afterward, of nothing in particular, only that the wood was quiet, and that it had taken him thirty years and a stranger's death and a boy-king's question to learn that a company could keep a watch without needing the whole wood for its own.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Knotted Cords in the Galleries

*FE 1,596 – 1,641*

## I. Of the Keeper's Cutters

Calum Liath had kept the flame no more than a season when the last stone was set between the two woods, and in the years after, the reciters of Dùn ìseal say, he asked for nothing that a Keeper had not already asked for before him. He fed the flame, he weighed the coloured coal against no man's claim, he judged the small quarrels the Small-Burning Law was made to settle, and beyond that he wanted little, a want so plain that people remarked on it, for the Keepers before him had mostly wanted a great deal in one direction or another. What he wanted, when he came at last to want something for himself, was to know how much coal the mountain held.

He put the question first to old Aonghas nan Uaimh, a cutter grown grey in the lower galleries who had followed the vein by touch since before Calum Liath was born, and Aonghas laughed at him, not unkindly, and said that a man might as well ask how deep the sea ran under a boat. The vein went where it went. It thickened under one gallery and pinched to a thread under the next, and no cutter living had ever cut to the end of it, because no cutter had ever needed to. You cut your measure, you filled your basket, you went home. Calum Liath heard him out and said that he had not asked whether the thing could be known, only whether anyone had tried to know it, and when Aonghas allowed that nobody had, the Keeper said that was answer enough for him.

He sent for cutters from every gallery at Dùn ìseal in the turn of that year, 9 an Giblean, FE 1,602, and gave each of them a cord knotted at the length of a man's forearm and a lamp that burned longer than the Law allowed a household's, being the Hall's own oil and not a hearth's handful, and told them to walk every gallery the mountain had, counting the knots as they went, and to mark on a slate where the coal ran thick under their feet and where it ran thin, and where it ran out altogether into blind rock. He did not tell them why, beyond what he had told Aonghas, and most of them did not ask, because a Keeper's asking passed for an answer in the Hall, and had done since Beathag Bhàn's silence was first counted a virtue.

It was slower work than any of them had reckoned. A cutter's hand knows a rich vein from a poor one at a touch and does not trouble to measure the poor one; Calum Liath's cutters had to measure both alike, poor and rich, dead rock and running coal, cord-length by cord-length, in galleries that had never been walked from end to end by anyone living, because no one had ever had reason to walk them so. Aonghas, who took the lowest galleries for his own share of the work, being too old by his own reckoning to be sent to the high cold ones, came up some evenings with his hands shaking from more than the cold, and said to anyone who would listen that a man's whole life passed differently when he was counting instead of cutting; that a cutter felt the mountain giving to him, handful by handful, the way a household feels a harvest coming in, but a counter only felt how much of the mountain he had not yet counted, which was, every evening, nearly all of it.

## II. Of the Three Lean Seasons

The counting cost what counting costs. A cutter set to measuring the vein was a cutter not filling a basket, and the baskets of Dùn ìseal's own galleries, which fed the nine hearths and, through them, more households than any other seam on the island, ran short through three seasons running while the cords were walked. The Small-Burning Law did not bend for it. The measure stayed the measure, a household's handful was still a household's handful, but there were fewer hands filling the store the handfuls were drawn from, and by the second of the three lean seasons the waypoint-keepers who kept the Hall's own tallies were sending less than the Law's full measure to households a full day's carry from the mountain, with a mark against each short delivery so that it might be made good later, though nobody could say when later would come.

At the household of Beitris nic Ruairidh, three days' carry north on the road to Baile Mòr mhòr, the winter of the second lean season was cold enough that her husband's father, an old man who had outlived two Keepers and three of his own sons, sat by a fire built half of driftwood and half of the coal they had, and said, more than once and to anyone in the house who would sit still for it, that he did not remember the mountain ever asking a household to wait on it before. Beitris, who had six mouths at her own hearth besides his, told him each time that the mountain was not asking anything, the Hall was asking, and the Hall had told them plainly enough why, if he cared to have the reason read to him again from the waypoint-keeper's mark. He did not care to. He had lived, he said, under the Binding his whole life and under no other law, and the Binding had never before told him to burn driftwood in his own hearth while the mountain kept its coal for counting.

It is told, and the reciters of Dùn ìseal tell it against themselves as often as for themselves, that in that second lean season three households of the northern road sent a steward to Dùn ìseal to ask the Keeper directly whether the counting would end before the grain in their own stores did, and that Calum Liath received the steward himself, at the door of the Hall and not within it, and answered only that he could not yet say, because he did not yet know the answer himself, which was true and satisfied nobody. The steward, a stooped man called Uisdean who had walked three days to ask a question and would walk three days home with the same one unanswered, said before he turned to go that a household could live on a true answer no better than on a false one if neither filled a basket, and Calum Liath, the reciters say, had no reply to that either, and let him go with only the one truth to carry. The households of the northern road burned what driftwood and dried dung they could find that winter, and kept their grudge, as households do, longer than the Keeper who had given them cause for it.

Even at the mountain's own foot the short seasons were felt, though less sharply, for the nine hearths ate first from what the galleries gave and felt the pinch last. The waypoint-keepers, whose own tally sticks recorded every short delivery against the day it might be made good, found that the marks piled faster than any later plenty could clear them, and more than one keeper of a northern house, going over her sticks by firelight, wondered aloud whether a debt owed by the mountain to a household was a debt at all, or only a Keeper's word that a household must take on trust, the way it had always been made to take the weather on trust, and the vein's own moods, and everything else that no household had ever been asked to agree to and every household had always had to live inside.

## III. Of the Cords in the Dark

Through all three seasons the cutters went on knotting their way through the mountain's galleries, and by the second summer even Aonghas, who had begun the work half in scorn of it, had come round to a kind of pride in the doing, though he would not have called it that himself. He had walked, by his own count, further under the mountain than any cutter before him, further than any hunter had walked above it, and he had begun, without meaning to, to know the mountain's shape as a blind man knows a familiar room, by the cords and the echo of his own lamp and the way the air moved or did not move in a gallery that ran true or one that had been abandoned for a reason nobody living remembered.

The young cutters set to the high galleries fared worse. Two of them were lost a full day in a working that had been cut and abandoned in Fionnlagh Dall's time and forgotten since, and came out half starved and swearing they had heard something moving in the dark beyond their lamp's reach that was not the mountain settling, though neither of them would say more of it afterward, and the tellers of Dùn ìseal, who love a mystery no better than they love a plain answer, leave it exactly as the two cutters left it: unfinished.

Calum Liath walked the counted galleries himself when the cords came back to him. He had no skill to check a cutter's work and did not pretend to it; he went because he had said, from the first, that he would not ask a cutter to walk ground he had not walked, and he kept to it even in the last winter of the counting, when his own knees had begun to trouble him on the steep pitches and Aonghas, twenty years his elder, went ahead of him with a hand held back to steady him over the worst of the rubble, an old cutter steadying a Keeper, which the reciters say pleased Aonghas more than anything else that happened in those three years.

## IV. Of the Slab and the Silence

When the last cord came back and the last slate was read against the others, it fell to a clerk of the Hall, a woman named Mòr nic Aonghais who had learned her letters from a wanderer of the stag's school and kept the Hall's small store of writing ever since, to set the sum down where any who could read the stag-letters might see it. At Calum Liath's own word she cut it on a slab of the grey stone the Hall's masons kept for its own building, a slate being too easily lost or broken for what it would carry, and set the slab upright inside the Hall's door, where the light from the doorway fell on it in the morning.

The sum said that the mountain, giving out no more than the Small-Burning Law already allowed and no less, could give every household on the island its handful for more generations of households than there were grains of barley in the granaries of Dùn dhearg at full harvest, a comparison Mòr nic Aonghais had chosen herself, having counted grain for the Hall before she counted anything else and knowing no larger number that a household could hold in its own hand and believe.

It was read out at the council that autumn, 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,607, with the great shares' stewards and the waypoint-keepers and as many of the nine hearths as could be spared from the flame all crowded into the Hall to hear it, and Calum Liath read it himself, plainly, without adding to it, and when he had finished there was a silence in the Hall long enough that the reciters who were there, and told it after to their own daughters, remembered the silence better than they remembered the sum. Nobody stood to speak against it, and nobody stood to praise it either. The stewards of the northern road, who had burned driftwood three winters running to pay for the counting, said nothing at all, and it was that silence above every other in the Hall that the Keeper, and the Hall after him, chose to take for assent, though Mòr nic Aonghais herself said once, late in her life, to a niece who pressed her on it, that a silence could mean a great many things besides yes, and that she had never been sure, cutting the sum into that slab, whether she was cutting the Hall's proof or the Hall's excuse.

## V. Of the Lower Gallery

The lean seasons ended with the counting, and the galleries filled again, and it might have been no more than a hard three years remembered afterward the way households remember any hard three years, if it had not been for what came in the fourteenth year after the slab was set, when two youths of the nine hearths, neither of them a full season in the galleries, were sent down into the lower working at Dùn ìseal, the same working the two cutters had once lost a day in, to bring up a basket the evening's cutters had left behind.

Their names were Griogair mac Dhonnchaidh and a girl called Sìne Bheag, cousins of the same hearth, sent together because the lower gallery frightened Griogair on his own and Sìne Bheag had gone down it twice before and told him there was nothing in it worse than the dark. They went without a Keeper's cutter to walk ahead of them, because none was to spare that evening and the errand seemed a small one, a basket and back, and in the dark beyond the last lamp-mark they broke, by whatever mischance the tellers can no longer reconstruct, a face of rock that Aonghas's own cords had marked as unsound years before, a mark that had gone into the Hall's slates but never, it was found after, into any warning a cutter carried down with him in his own head. The rock came down across them both. It was Aonghas himself, roused from his own hearth near midnight when the two did not come up, who went down with three others and dug them free, and found Griogair already gone and Sìne Bheag alive but not for long past the digging.

The Hall keened them as it keened its own, which it had never before had cause to do for two so young, and buried them on the slope above the vein where the Keepers' own dead were laid. Aonghas, who had marked the unsound face himself years before and lived to dig the two of them out of what it had done, kept his own silence about that winter for the rest of his life, and spoke of it only once, in his own old age, to Oighrig Bhàn, telling her that he had gone down into the lower gallery that night thinking of nothing but the digging, and had only understood, climbing back up into the grey of the morning with Sìne Bheag's weight failing in his arms before he reached the air, that his own mark on his own slate had done this as surely as the rock had, a mark he had cut and trusted a slate to carry when it should have been carried, he said, in the head of every cutter who went down after him.

It might have ended there, in grief alone, as such things mostly did, but Griogair's mother, a woman named Ealasaid Rìoghach of no particular note before that winter, stood up at the council that followed and asked the Hall, before every steward and hearth-holder gathered there, what it owed her son.

## VI. Of What the Hall Owed

It was not a question the council had an answer ready for, and the reciters of Dùn ìseal, who are fond of Calum Liath and slow to fault him, admit plainly that he had none either, not that day. The Small-Burning Law set the measure a household might burn and the peace of the Hall's own ground; it had never set down what a household was owed for a child sent into the dark on the Hall's own errand and lost there. Ealasaid Rìoghach did not ask for silver, having none to spend and no custom to spend it in; she asked only, and asked it twice more before the council found an answer, why a boy of one season in the galleries had been sent down a working two cutters had already lost a day in and a slate had already marked unsound, and why no one had told him so before he went.

The council sat three days on it, which was longer than it had sat on anything since the Small-Burning Law itself, and the first day was spent, by the reciters' account, on little more than stewards of the nine great shares each saying, in their own words, that the fault lay elsewhere: with the errand's giver, who had not thought a basket worth a Keeper's cutter; with the slates, which had kept a warning no one had thought to carry down in memory; with the two youths themselves, who ought, said one steward and was shouted down for it, to have known a lower gallery's dangers without being told. Ealasaid Rìoghach sat through all of it on the floor by the door, and it was only on the second day, when she stood a second time and asked again, in fewer words than before, what the Hall owed her son, that the council turned from fault to custom, which the reciters count the true turning of those three days, more than anything said in them.

The Hall had no payment to offer that would not have looked like a coal-price set on a life, and offered none. What came out of the three days was a custom instead: that no young Dia-thìrich would go into any gallery of the vein's custody again, on any errand however small, until they had spent seven years bound to a cutter of proven years, learning the mountain's marks and its unsound faces and its moods before they were trusted alone in its dark. It was not called a payment, and Ealasaid Rìoghach, when it was told to her, said only that it came seven years too late for her own son, which was true and which nobody in the council disputed.

Calum Liath himself did not live to see the custom much beyond its first winter. He had failed through the last of the counting years, a failing the reciters put down more to age than to any single grief, though they note, as reciters will, that he was never quite the same Keeper after Griogair and Sìne Bheag as he had been before, readier to sit long over a small dispute than he had once been, as if he had learned, late, that a Keeper's silence could cost more than his own dignity. He died in the eighteenth year after the slab was set, in the Hall itself, by the door he had had the slab set beside, and was carried up to lie among the Keepers' own dead near the two he had buried before him, a resting he had asked for himself and been given without argument.

## VII. Of Oighrig Bhàn

The nine hearths chose Oighrig Bhàn to follow him, a woman of six and thirty years who had come to the Hall as a girl of the northern road, one of the very households that had burned driftwood through the lean seasons, though she never once, in all her years at the flame, spoke of that against the Keeper who had caused it. She had sat with Calum Liath in his last winter more than any other of the nine hearths, and she had no wish to be chosen after him; she had a gift the reciters call patience and a plainer name calls stubbornness, and she had stayed at his side through the failing when younger hands found reasons to be elsewhere.

She took the flame in a season thin on ceremony, the Hall still close in its grief for the old Keeper, and one of her first acts, before she had worn the office a full year, was to send for the custom the council had made after Griogair and Sìne Bheag and ask why, three years on, it still stood only as a thing agreed and not a thing done. Nobody in the Hall could give her a good reason, beyond the plain one that grief cools and custom is easier sworn than kept, and Oighrig Bhàn, who had buried nobody of her own in the galleries but had grown up on short seasons all the same, said that a custom not kept was worse than none, because it let a household believe itself answered when it was not. She had it declared a custom of every gallery in the vein's custody within three years of her choosing, on 24 am Faoilleach, FE 1,628, though six years more passed before she found twelve youths and twelve masters she judged fit to begin it.

## VIII. Of the Twelve on the Stone Cup

She bound the first twelve herself, at Dùn ìseal, in the Hall's own doorway where the light fell on the reckoning-slab still, each of the twelve sworn by name to a master cutter of her own choosing, most of them the very cutters who had walked Calum Liath's cords through the lean seasons and knew the mountain's unsound faces better than any slate could tell it. Aonghas nan Uaimh, old now past any gallery-work of his own, took the youngest of the twelve, a boy called Tormod Beag who had been born the same winter Griogair and Sìne Bheag died, and taught him, in his first season, more of where not to cut than of where to cut, which Aonghas said, to anyone who asked, was the whole of the teaching that mattered.

The twelve swore on the stone cup, each in turn, to serve seven years at a master's side before the coal was theirs to touch alone, 21 an Giblean, FE 1,634, and Oighrig Bhàn stood by the cup for every one of the twelve oaths and did not sit down until the last was sworn, a small stubbornness the reciters note because it cost her a long morning on her feet in a doorway open to the winter air, and because it was, in its way, the same stubbornness that had first brought her to Calum Liath's bedside and kept her there. Four of the twelve, grown old in their own turn, came in time to hold the flame themselves, which the reciters of Dùn ìseal count the best proof the custom ever had, better than any words the council could have found for Ealasaid Rìoghach, though none of it, they are careful to say, ever answered her question in full, for no custom made after a death answers the death that made it, only the deaths that might have followed and did not.

## IX. Of Cnoc bhàn and the First Entry

Word of the binding travelled north in the years of the twelve's service, carried by the same carriers who carried most things between the mountain and the far side of the island, and came at last to the stag's house at Cnoc bhàn, where the teachers who kept their own long watch over their own grove heard it and judged, after the manner of that school, that a custom worth a Keeper's keeping was worth their own testing. They took up the seven years for their own cutters, binding each apprentice to a master of the school as the Hall bound its own, and added to it a rule the Hall itself had never thought to make: that every apprentice keep, in their own hand once the stag-letters were learned, a written account of every stroke made in a season's cutting, so that a master might read back, at the season's turn, exactly what the apprentice's hand had done and where it had gone wrong.

It was a small rule when it was made, meant, by the teacher who first set it down, only to give a master something firmer than memory to correct an apprentice by, but the accounts grew, season on season, into a store the school kept and consulted the way the Hall kept its slates, and in time the teachers of Cnoc bhàn came to call them by a plainer name than any the stag-letters gave them: the strike-books, for the strokes they recorded, one stroke and one line at a time.

The first of them was begun by a girl called Rìoghnach, no kin that any reciter can trace to Ealasaid Rìoghach of the northern road though the two names are near enough that more than one teller has made the mistake, a novice of that first bound company at Cnoc bhàn, in the winter after her binding, at her master's own bidding. She wrote her first line by lamp-light in a hand still stiff from the letters' learning, three words and no more, set down as plainly as a stag-letter allows: *chuir mi buille*, I struck a stroke, and under it the day, and under the day nothing else, because there was, in that first season, nothing else yet to say. It was the least of anything written on the island in that age, and it is kept still among the strike-books of Cnoc bhàn, the school's own reciters say, because a beginning ought to be kept exactly as small as it was.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of Fearchar Òg and the Silver Rings

*FE 1,642 – 1,685*

> *Cha b'e an aois a rinn an rìgh; ach dh'fhàg i sinn ga chuimhneachadh.*
> It was not his age that made the king; but it left us remembering him by it.
>
> — a saying of the road-guards of Dùn dhearg, said of no other rìgh before or since

## I. Of the King Who Went On

In the year the first strike-book entry was set down at Cnoc bhàn, three words scratched by a novice's stiff new hand, Fearchar Òg had sat at Dùn dhearg for nine-and-forty years, and was still called Òg by everyone who had known him as the boy of seven the Keeper had entered on her roll. He had stopped correcting them some twenty years before. A name given at seven, he told his own steward once, is a debt a man pays the rest of his life whether he likes the price or not, and Fearchar Òg, six-and-fifty years old that year, greying at the temples but not yet stooped, had long since made his peace with it.

He was not a builder of walls, as Cathair mhòr's rìghrean before him had been, nor a maker of laws remembered by their sentences, as Fionnlagh Dall was remembered for the stone cup and the Small-Burning Law two centuries before him. What he built, in the main, he built out of the plain fact that he did not die. Ealasaid Chiar's own line had run thin in the years before him, a ruler here and a long gap there that the reciters could not close, and every household on the roads between Dùn dhearg and Dùn ìseal had grown used to hearing, every few years, that the hall was empty again and the succession in question. Fearchar Òg ended that simply by staying. He crowned no wars, quelled no strife the Peace of the Threshold had not already quelled a hundred years before him, and is remembered by the roll, in the end, for very little beyond the plain number of his years and a handful of small things his clerks did in his name that outlasted every one of them.

The first of these small things began twelve years after, in the sixty-first year of his reign. His steward, an old man named Griogal who had served Fearchar's mother's house before him, came to the hall one evening with a complaint he had carried three days from the southern road: that the road-guards of the southern ford, who kept the crossings and the waypoint houses against thieves and floods both, had gone two seasons without their due from the hall, because the granary-clerks who paid them in grain and cloth could not always find carriers spare to send south when the grain was wanted nearer home.

"Pay them in coal, then," said Fearchar Òg, who had heard the same complaint in different words every winter of his reign and had grown tired of answering it the same way each time.

"The hall has no coal to spare either, lord. The mountain gives what the mountain gives, and the guards do not sit near enough the Hall's galleries to be paid from them even if it had."

Fearchar Òg sat a long while with that, turning a ring on his own hand, a plain band of silver his mother had worn before him and her mother before her, the kind every household of any standing kept a few of against a daughter's marrying or a debt too proud to pay in grain. It is told that he looked at it longer than a man looks at a thing he has worn every day of his life without once considering it, and that when he spoke again it was to ask Griogal how much silver the hall's own smiths could spare from a season's ordinary work without troubling any household for more.

Griogal did not understand him at first, and said so plainly, being an old man too tired of the road to pretend to a cleverness he did not feel. Fearchar Òg explained it slowly, as a man explains a thing he is still working out himself as he speaks it: that a guard paid in grain must carry his own pay home on his own back, and a guard paid in cloth must find a buyer for what he does not need. A small stamped ring of silver, known at a glance to every smith on the island from the Muileann chiar trade, could be carried in a fist, spent at any market that knew silver at all, and would travel, once spent, far past wherever the guard himself ever walked.

"It is not grain," said Griogal, who did not think much of the idea and said so.

"No," said Fearchar Òg. "It will keep longer."

## II. Of the First Rings and Aonghas Ruadh

The first rings were struck that winter, small and plain, no thicker than a woman's finger and stamped on one face with the hearth-sign of Dùn dhearg, and there were not many of them: forty, by the steward's own count, enough for one season's pay to the road-guards of the southern crossings and no more. Among the men who took one that winter was Aonghas Ruadh of Cnoc mhòr, a guard of the ford below Ceann leathan these eleven years, a broad, quiet man who had buried one wife of the coughing sickness and married a second, Sìne, the year before the rings were struck, and who had, that same year, a daughter he and Sìne named Mòrag, for no one in either house could afterward agree whose grandmother it was for.

Aonghas Ruadh did not think much of the ring when it was first put into his hand at the ford, a small cold weight he turned over twice before he understood it was meant to be his whole winter's due and not some token toward it. He had carried grain home from the hall's granary every winter of his service and had grown used to the weight of a full sack on his shoulder as the shape his labour took. A ring the size of a barleycorn's shadow felt, at first handling, like being paid in nothing at all.

He carried it home anyway, because a guard does not argue with the hand that pays him, and it was Sìne who saw the good of it before he did. She walked it to the market at Ceann leathan the next week, where a cloth-seller from the eastern road, who had never in his life had reason to travel as far west as Dùn dhearg and would not have known a grain-measure of that hall's stamp from any other, weighed the ring on his own scale, found it good silver of the Muileann chiar weight he already dealt in, and gave her cloth for it without a question asked beyond the weighing. Sìne came home with more cloth for the ring than Aonghas could have carried home in grain in the same day's walk, and told him so at the hearth that night while Mòrag slept in the basket by the fire, not yet a year old and already, though neither of them could have said it then, growing up in a household that had begun, without quite meaning to, to think in silver.

Word of the southern crossings' new pay went east before the spring was out, carried the way all such things were carried, by carriers who had nothing better to talk of on a long road and travellers who liked a curious thing to tell at the next hearth. By the time Fearchar Òg's clerks struck a second batch of rings, the following winter, waypoint-keepers from three roads he had never troubled to pay in silver before sent word asking whether the hall meant to go on with it, and whether their own guards might be included. Fearchar Òg, who had meant the rings as no more than a fix for one season's short grain, found within five years that every road-guard on the roads out of Dùn dhearg was paid, in whole or in part, in the small stamped silver, and that the rings themselves had begun to turn up in markets the guards had never walked to, carried on by hands the hall's clerks would never trouble to count.

"They travel further than the men do," Griogal said to him once, some years into it, in the tone of a man admitting he had been wrong without quite saying so.

"That was the whole of the thought," said Fearchar Òg, and did not say more, because there was not much more to say of a thing that had, by then, said itself.

## III. Of the Toll-House at Àth ghlas

The southern road crossed the river at Àth ghlas on its way toward Ceann leathan, a shallow ford between two low banks where a laden beast sank to the hock in a wet spring and a child could wade it dry-shod in a dry summer, and it was there, within five years of the first rings, that the hall built its first toll-house.

There had been a toll at Àth ghlas long before the house was built, kept as most such tolls were kept, by whichever household of the ford's own bank had the standing and the patience to sit by the crossing and collect it, a portion going to the household and a portion carried up to Dùn dhearg twice a year with the rest of the road's due. It had worked well enough for longer than anyone at the ford could say, and the household that kept it, a family called the Griogaraich after some ancestor no one living remembered, had grown used to thinking of the toll as theirs by a kind of standing that felt, to the family, near enough a right to be worth defending.

Fearchar Òg's clerks judged, reasonably enough by the hall's own reckoning, that a toll paid in the new silver wanted a keeper who could be trusted to weigh a ring honestly and not merely to eye a purse and guess, and sent a man of their own from Dùn dhearg to keep the new toll-house: a clerk named Dòmhnall Beag, careful with a scale and careless, by his own later admission, of the ford's own feelings, who arrived at Àth ghlas in the spring with the hall's own commission in his hand and no kin at the ford at all.

The Griogaraich took it hard. It is told, and told still at Cnoc mhòr, where Aonghas Ruadh's own household heard it from the ford folk themselves, that the family's eldest stood in the toll-house door the morning Dòmhnall Beag arrived and asked him, plainly enough that the whole crossing heard it, what right a man with no kin at the ford had to weigh a ford-family's own toll.
