Dòmhnall Beag, who had been told to expect trouble and had, in his own quiet way, prepared an answer for it, said only that the commission in his hand was the rìgh's, and that he had not asked to come, and would go again the day the rìgh sent for him and not a day before, and that in the meantime he meant to weigh every ring honestly, the Griogaraich's tolls along with everyone else's, and would be glad of their help if they cared to give it and would manage without it if they did not.

They did not help him, not for the better part of a year. But a toll-house wants firewood in winter and a hand at the gate when the spring floods run high, and Dòmhnall Beag, being alone at it and no fool, hired what help he needed from whoever at the ford would take his silver, most of the Griogaraich in time, one at a time and never all admitting it to one another. By the year the rings had been struck for a decade, the toll-house at Àth ghlas stood as the first on any road of Dia-thìr whose keeper had been sent from a hall and not chosen by the ford, and the Griogaraich had made their peace with the fact of it, because the toll ran honester under Dòmhnall Beag's scale than under any of their own.

Aonghas Ruadh crossed that ford twice a season for the rest of his working years, and it was there, waiting his turn at Dòmhnall Beag's scale with his daughter riding his shoulders one summer when she was too small yet to walk the whole way, that Mòrag Dhubh first saw the games.

## IV. Of Mòrag Dhubh

She was called Dhubh from the day she could stand, for hair black enough that her mother's own people, fair to a woman for three generations, took to saying she must have got it from the ford's own water. She grew up at Cnoc mhòr in a household that kept sheep on the low ground and sent its men, when the roads wanted guarding, down to the crossings her father had walked all his life, and she grew up, too, in the particular way a road-guard's daughter grows, hearing more of tolls and thieves and the weight of a season's silver at her own hearth than most children of Cnoc mhòr heard of anything.

Her father taught her the staff before he taught her much else. It was no wish of his to make a fighter of her; a road-guard's household simply kept staves the way a fisher's kept nets, hung by the door and taken down as often for mending a gap in a fence as for anything else, and a girl underfoot at a hearth full of staves will sooner or later be given one to stop her taking someone else's. Aonghas Ruadh, whose own father had taught him the ford-guards' old bout-play with a stick no thicker than a thumb, more a way of keeping a man's balance and his temper both than any true fighting art, taught it to Mòrag the same way, in the yard behind the house, first for the game of it and then, as she grew and would not be turned from it, because she asked him to and would not be put off.

She was quick rather than strong, small for her years until she was not, and it is told of her, by those who trained beside her, that she never once in all her years at it struck the first blow of a bout, preferring to let an opponent spend himself against her guard before she answered, a patience her father said came from her mother's side and Sìne always swore came from his. By the time she was fifteen she had outgrown every staff her father owned and cut one of her own from a young ash at the wood's edge, straight-grained and a hand's breadth taller than she was, and carried it everywhere a girl of that country could carry a staff without remark, which in a road-guard's household was nearly everywhere.

It was at Àth ghlas, riding her father's shoulders as a small child and, later, walking beside him as a girl grown tall enough to carry her own bundle, that she first heard the talk that would shape the rest of her young life: that the guards of the southern crossings, paid now in silver they had somewhere to spend and nowhere in particular to spend it on any given day, had begun meeting once a year at Ceann leathan, where the ford-market already drew traders from three roads, to fight bout after bout with blunted staves for the newest and best-struck ring the hall's smiths had sent south that season.

## V. Of the Meeting at Ceann leathan

The meeting had begun small, as such things do, a handful of guards from the nearest crossings settling an old argument over whose bout-play was the surer with a match fought in the market square on the day of the autumn trading, the loser buying the winner a cup and the whole thing forgotten by the next year's trading, except that it was not forgotten. The next year there were more of them, guards from crossings two days' walk distant who had heard the tale and wanted a bout of their own, and the year after that the market began setting aside a corner of the square for it, because a crowd that gathers to watch two men trade blows with staves is a crowd that buys cloth and cups and cooked meat while it waits its turn to watch, and Ceann leathan's traders were not slow to see the good of that.

By the time Mòrag Dhubh was old enough to be let compete, some ten years after the meeting first began, it had grown into a full day's contest, guards from every southern crossing entering by turns through the morning and the afternoon both, the losers of each bout dropping away and the winners meeting again until, by evening, two stood who had beaten every man put in front of them, and fought the last bout by torchlight for the season's finest ring, struck that year and never worn by anyone until it was won.

Her father did not want her to enter, the first year she was old enough by the meeting's own loose custom, which asked only that a fighter be grown and be a guard or a guard's kin trained to it, and said so plainly at the hearth the week before the autumn trading. It was not, he told her, that he doubted her staff-work, which he had watched grow past his own teaching some years before and had stopped correcting, out of a kind of pride he did not often show her, when she was seventeen. No woman had ever entered the meeting in all its years, and he did not want his daughter's first bout to be one fought, as he put it, against the whole square's opinion before ever a staff was raised.

"Then I'll fight the square's opinion first," said Mòrag Dhubh, "and my bouts after, and see which tires me more."

She lost that first year, in the second round, to a guard of the eastern ford twice her age and near twice her size, who beat her guard down by main strength rather than by any skill she could not have answered in a longer bout, and who told her afterward, not unkindly, that she had the surest staff of anyone he had fought that day and the worst luck of drawing him for it. The second year took her further and still ended in a loss, to a younger man whose reach she had not yet learned to read. The third year and the fourth she did not lose, and by the fifth, the year she turned twenty-five, she had beaten every man put in front of her through a long grey morning and a longer afternoon, standing at dusk across the torchlit ground from the last guard left to beat, a broad-shouldered man of Muileann chrom named Ruairidh Fada who had won the meeting twice before and meant, by every sign he gave before the bout began, to win it a third time without much trouble from a woman half his size.

## VI. Of the Last Bout

It is told at Cnoc mhòr, in the telling the household kept for three generations after her and no doubt shaped a little in the keeping, that Mòrag Dhubh said nothing at all before that bout, where every other fighter of the day had traded some word or some grin with his opponent across the torchlight, and that Ruairidh Fada, finding no word offered him to answer, said his own anyway, loud enough for the square to hear, that he would go easy on her for her father's sake, who he knew by the crossing where they had both served a season together some years before.

She did not answer that either. She let him come first, as she let every man come first, and took the weight of his opening strike on a guard raised so quietly that half the square, watching for a woman's nerve to fail her, missed the moment it did not. He was strong and he was quick for a man his size, and for the better part of the bout he pressed her back a pace at a time across the torchlit ground, striking hard and often, spending, as her father had taught her every man eventually spends, more strength than the bout wanted from him because he had not yet learned, three strikes in, that she meant to let him.

She turned him on the ninth strike, catching his staff high and driving it wide with a twist of her own that owed more, by her own telling, to a morning spent freeing a gate-post from a stuck hinge than to any bout-play her father had ever named for her, and in the gap that twist opened she struck once, low and short, across the back of his knee, and he went down in the dust of the square with the crowd's noise breaking over both of them at once, a noise, it is told, louder than the square had made for any bout in the meeting's history, because no one there, Ruairidh Fada least of all, had thought to see a woman standing at the end of it.

The ring given her that night was the finest struck that season, heavier than most, cut with the hearth-sign of Dùn dhearg on one face and, new that year, a small mark of Ceann leathan's own on the other, the market having asked the hall's smiths, now that the meeting had grown into something the whole square profited by, for a ring that carried the ford's name along with the crown's. Mòrag Dhubh is the first winner of that meeting whose name the reciters of the southern crossings kept, and it is not lost on any who tell it that the first name kept was a woman's, in a contest no woman had fought before her.

Her father wept at it, which he had not done at either of her losses nor, so far as the household ever knew, at very much else in his life, and told her afterward, walking home in the dark with the new ring cold in her own fist for the first time, that he had been wrong to try to keep her from the square, and that he would not try again.

## VII. Of Muileann òg and the Lùnastal Fair

The ring Mòrag Dhubh won that autumn stayed in her own keeping the rest of her life and passed, after her, into her household's, worn on high days and shown to travellers who asked after the mark on it and told the tale, in shorter and shorter tellings as the generations went, of the woman of Cnoc mhòr who had beaten every man in the meeting the year the ring was cut. But the silver itself, the rings struck each winter in their dozens and scores now, went on doing what Fearchar Òg had first hoped a small hard thing might do, travelling further than any guard who ever carried one, into markets and hands the hall's own clerks would never trouble to trace.

Nowhere did that travelling show plainer than at Muileann òg, a market town on the ford where the old Stone Kings and the holders of the Red Hill had once agreed salt for wool, burned in the War of the Roads six centuries before and left, since, little more than a scattering of rebuilt hearths around the old ford-stones. In the same years the meeting at Ceann leathan was growing from a handful of guards to a whole day's contest, traders drifting west along the southern road with silver rings in their purses had begun stopping at Muileann òg's ford rather than pressing on, finding there, in the ruin of a town too poor to charge them anything for the privilege, goods and prices neither Ceann leathan's crowded market nor Dùn dhearg's own could match.

It was traders' own custom, at first, and not the hall's doing, that fixed the meeting at Muileann òg to the feast of Lùnastal, when the first of the harvest came in and the roads were driest and best for travelling; but within a few years of the custom taking hold, the households resettling the town, seeing what a season's fair might bring them, asked Fearchar Òg's clerks for a charter of their own, and were given it gladly, the hall by then having long since learned that a market well fed brought more silver home in tolls than a market starved of custom ever would. The fair of Muileann òg, held that first chartered year and every year after at the turn from summer into harvest, grew within Mòrag Dhubh's own lifetime into the largest gathering of goods and craft on the southern half of the island, its ford lined three days running with stalls that sold, by the end of her years, near everything the roads of Dia-thìr could carry to it.

She went there herself, once, some years after her own win. Muileann òg kept no meeting of staves; she went there only to trade a season's wool for cloth her own household could not weave as fine, and it is told, though the household's own telling grows uncertain on this point with every generation that passes it on, that a trader of the eastern road, seeing the mark on the ring she still wore, asked her outright whether the tale of the woman of Ceann leathan was true, and that she answered only that it was, and let him tell the rest of it to whoever asked him after, because a tale told by a stranger travels further, she said, than one told by the person it happened to, and she had already seen how far a small hard thing could travel once it left a person's own hand.

## VIII. Of Cidhe Beag and the River-Men

Not every road the silver opened ran so smoothly. Some twenty miles north-east of Muileann òg, where the Abhainn uaine ran broad and slow enough for a laden boat to sit steady in it, an old landing had stood since Ailean's own age, a place called Cidhe Beag, the little quay, where a fisherman or a ferryman had put a boat into the river time out of mind without ever troubling to make more of it than a scramble of flat stones at the water's edge.

The carriers of the eastern road, who had walked grain and salt fish overland from the lowland granaries to the market towns for longer than any of them could count generations, had never had reason to think much of Cidhe Beag at all, until the year Fearchar Òg's clerks, weighing the cost of paying carriers' wages against the cost of building a proper landing there, judged that a river running near empty of traffic beside a road worn to ruts under sack after sack of the same grain was a waste neither the hall's granaries nor its silver could afford to go on making. They built the landing that same year, timbered piers driven into the old scramble of stones and a shed raised above it for the goods waiting passage, and put out word to every boatbuilder on the lower river that the hall would pay well for flat-bottomed craft of hide over withy frame, built to sit shallow enough for the Abhainn uaine's own shifting bars.

The carriers of the eastern road sent word to Dùn dhearg within the month, three of their eldest walking the whole distance to say to Fearchar Òg's own face what they had already said to every clerk who would listen, that the granaries' grain had gone on their backs for generations and ought to go on going there, and that a river-boat, once it took up the trade, would leave half their households without the wages that had fed them since before the hall was built.

Fearchar Òg heard them out fully, in the same unhurried way he had heard every complaint of his reign, and answered them, in the end, much as he had answered Griogal over the rings some years before: that a sack of grain carried on a man's back for two days' walk cost the hall, in wages and in spoiled grain both, more than the same sack floated down in an afternoon cost it in the wear of a boat and the pay of two boatmen, and that he could not, weighing the granaries' own good against the carriers' own comfort, choose the dearer road when a cheaper one lay open beside it.

"Then what becomes of us?" asked the eldest of the three, a woman named Ciorstaidh who had carried grain on that road herself for sixty years before her knees gave out and left her to the walking rather than the carrying.

"The road does not close," said Fearchar Òg. "Only the river opens beside it. There is grain enough on this island, and will be more each year the granaries fill, for a road and a river both to carry, and neither to starve of work while the other eats." It was not, by the carriers' own reckoning, an answer that mended what they had walked so far to mend, and they went home saying so plainly to anyone who would hear it; but it proved, in the years that followed, truer than they had believed it could be, for the river carried the heaviest and least urgent of the grain, the loads that could wait a boat's slow pace, while the roads kept the carrying trade in everything that could not wait, cloth and tools and the small urgent parcels no boatman would trouble himself over, and both trades, in time, grew rather than starved.

## IX. Of Muileann chrom and the Paddle-Oath

The boats themselves, once the landing was built and the first of them launched, drew their builders and their crews from Muileann chrom, a small town up the valley from Cidhe Beag whose men had fished the river's slower reaches for longer than anyone at the landing could say, and whose skill with hide over withy, learned first for coracles no bigger than a single man could carry, proved, once it was set to the larger work, exactly what the hall's clerks had hoped to find.

The first crews to take up the trade were young men of Muileann chrom with more nerve than standing, sons of fishing households too many to divide a single boat's catch among, and it was among themselves, not at any hall's asking, that they settled the custom that came, in time, to mark every boatman of that river after them: that no man might call himself one of their fellowship, nor be trusted at another boatman's back on a laden crossing, until he had sworn on his own paddle, held flat across both palms before the others of his crew, to answer any fellow boatman's need on the water before his own household's, a river being no place, as the eldest of them put it, for a man who would let another drown to save his own cargo.

The swearing was a small thing, no priest's rite and no hall's law, a custom made among working men who wanted a way to know, before they trusted a stranger's hand on a crossing, that the stranger had sworn the same oath they had. But it held, year on year, more surely than many a law the hall itself had made with far greater ceremony, and by the time Mòrag Dhubh was grown old enough to have grandchildren of her own at Cnoc mhòr, the boatmen's fellowship of Muileann chrom was building flat river-boats not only for the Abhainn uaine but for every river of the island wide enough to float one, each boat leaving the yards with a paddle laid across its bow until the crew that took it had sworn their own oath upon it.

Her own younger brother, Dòmhnall, who had never taken to the staff the way she had and had spent his boyhood down at Cidhe Beag watching the first boats loaded rather than at Àth ghlas watching the toll weighed, was among the second crews to take up the river trade, and swore his paddle-oath the same year Mòrag Dhubh's own daughter was born, so that the household at Cnoc mhòr came, within one generation, to hold both a silver ring won on land and a paddle sworn on water, and told both tales at the same hearth without ever quite agreeing which of the two mattered more.

## X. Of the King Who Died Old

Fearchar Òg lived to see all of it: the rings spreading past every road his clerks had first meant them for, the meeting at Ceann leathan grown from a handful of guards to a whole day's contest, Muileann òg's fair drawing traders from three roads at once, the river opened beside the roads and neither one starved by it. He did not live to see much beyond it. His reign, remembered by the roll for very little else, is remembered above all for its length, and in his last years, when he had sat at Dùn dhearg longer than any ruler the reciters could name before him, it became a kind of custom among the households of the southern roads to reckon their own years by his, a child born in the year of the toll-house at Àth ghlas, a marriage made in the year the fair was chartered, a death in the year the river-boats first sailed, so that Fearchar Òg's long sitting became, without his ever asking for it, the measure other lives were told against.

He died in the winter of his ninety-fourth year, at Dùn dhearg, in the same hall his clerks had struck the first rings in more than fifty years before, and it is told that Griogal's own grandson, steward by then in his grandfather's place, found him in his chair by the hearth one morning, gone as quietly as a man goes who has simply, after so very long, stopped going on. He was buried among the house of Ìomhar with the state a reign of eighty-seven years was owed, and the roll that recorded him, which had made much of other rulers for their wars or their laws or their buildings, could find little to say of him beyond the plain fact the whole island had already learned to measure by: that he had come to the hall a boy of seven and left it, eighty-seven years later, an old man who had simply gone on, season after season, longer than anyone then living had thought to expect of him.

Word of it reached Cnoc mhòr the way all such word travelled, carried down the southern road by guards who had themselves been paid, most of their working lives, in the dead king's silver, and it found Mòrag Dhubh in the winter after her own win, sitting by her own hearth with the ring still bright from the smith, kept where her household could see it on high days. She is said to have turned it once in her fingers when she heard the news, the same slow turning her father had given it the winter he first carried it home, and to have said only that the king had done one thing right in a long reign of small quiet things, which was to make a thing worth keeping that did not need his own hand on it to go on travelling after he was gone.

She lived on herself many years more at Cnoc mhòr, and the ring lived longer than she did, passed down through a household that never afterward forgot, whatever else it forgot with the passing of the generations that first won it, whose hand had held it first and why.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Red Hall and the Census of Hands

*FE 1,685 – 1,735*

## I. Of the Twenty-Year-Old Queen

Beathag Mhòr took the hall at Dùn dhearg five years after Fearchar Òg died at ninety-four, and she took it at twenty, which the reeve Lachlann Dubh, who had kept the granary accounts under three rulers of her line and meant to keep them under a fourth, thought a poor age for anyone to begin anything. He said so to no one but his wife, and even to her only once, for Beathag Mhòr's great-grandfather had died old and easy and his own father before him the same, and a house that buried its rulers gently was not a house a careful man complained of.

She was brought up through the granary yard on the morning of her crowning, past the sacks that had fed the Red Share since Ìomhar Dearg burned the old halls within the double bank, and Lachlann Dubh walked at her stirrup with the tallies under his arm because it was his office to walk there, whoever rode above him. He had expected a girl's questions, the kind Fearchar Òg's own heir had once asked him, about the weight of a full sack and how many the granary held. Beathag Mhòr asked him instead how many of the sacks were owed elsewhere before the winter was out, and when he told her, she asked him to whom, by name, and wrote nothing down, because she had not yet learned her letters past her own name and the count to a hundred, but she remembered every name he gave her, and asked after three of them again a year later, by which time he had stopped thinking her age a fault in her.

It was the list-keepers at Dùn ìseal, and not Beathag Mhòr herself, who first wrote her down as ban-rìgh, queen, rather than rìgh with a woman's name set after it as the rolls had always done for Eithne and Catrìona and the rest. Nobody asked her leave for the change, and she gave none, for it seemed to her, when Lachlann Dubh told her of it, a small matter beside the sacks, though she noticed, in the years after, that the word travelled ahead of her wherever she rode, spoken first by strangers who had never called any ruler anything but rìgh in their lives and found the new word came easier to them than she would have guessed.

Her crowning was held at Dùn dhearg in the last cold week of am Faoilleach, 6 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,685, with snow lying thin on the double bank and the wind coming down off the granary roofs in a way that made the household's fires gutter every time a door was opened. Fearchar Òg's own line filled the hall three deep, cousins she had met perhaps twice in her life come to stand for a great-grandfather most of them remembered only as an old man too tired at the end to be much afraid of, and Lachlann Dubh, watching from his usual place by the grain-stores' door, thought the girl looked smaller under the household's old crown than any ruler he could remember crowning, and said as much to his wife, who told him that every crown looked too large on whoever first wore it and grew no smaller for the wearing.

There was a moment, before the crown was set, when the eldest of the cousins, a woman near six hundred years old who had outlived two rulers of her own generation and buried a granddaughter besides, stood up unasked and said to the hall at large that a twenty-year-old girl who had never sat a council nor ridden a boundary was no fit head for a line that had held its ground unbroken since the ford. Beathag Mhòr had no leave yet to speak from the chair, and held her tongue; she looked at the woman long enough that the hall grew quiet waiting to see what would come of the look, and what came of it, in the end, was nothing at all: the crown was set, the woman sat down, and no one in that hall ever heard Beathag Mhòr mention the challenge again, though Lachlann Dubh's own accounts show that the woman's household received, every winter after, its full measure of grain and never a sack more.

## II. Of the Fleece at Baile Mòr fhionn

In her third year she rode west to the fair at Baile Mòr fhionn, where the lords of the plain held their market each autumn and had lately taken to pricing everything in fleeces, a grown ewe's fleece the measure against which grain and wine and the plain's own horses were weighed. Beathag Mhòr had never seen a market run on wool before and stood a long while at the edge of it watching a horse-trader and a grain-factor argue a bargain down to the quarter-fleece, each of them naming a different ewe in his head and neither troubling to say so.

The silver rings of Muileann chiar were sold there too, though the plain's traders would not call a price in rings outright and reckoned every ring against its fleece-worth first, as if the silver were a foreign thing that needed a native measure to stand beside it before an honest man would touch it. Beathag Mhòr bought nothing at Baile Mòr fhionn that year but a length of the plain's own wool cloth, dyed the red the western dye-houses were known for, and had it made into a cloak she wore at her own crowning-feast the following spring, so that the two colours of her reign, the red of the Share she was born to and the wool-red of the plain she had gone to see, were the same colour before anyone thought to remark on it.

She rode home by the northern road rather than the way she had come, three days longer, because Lachlann Dubh's own accounts had shown her that the northern waypoint houses saw less of the queen's custom than the western ones did, and she wished, she told her household, to know what a keeper's face looked like when a queen's own party filled his hearth for the first time in a generation. It looked, at the house called An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, like a man who had killed his last fowl for a stranger's supper and was already wondering how to feed his own children through the week that followed, and Beathag Mhòr, seeing it, sent a carrier's load of grain back to him from Dùn dhearg before the month was out, though she never told him it was hers.

The keeper of that house was a thin, quick-spoken man called Fearchar Iar, no kin to the line of kings that shared his first name, and he served the queen's party the same steamed carp and heather ale his house had served the carriers every winter since the road was first cut, apologising for it twice over supper as though a queen's own stomach might want better than a carrier's. Beathag Mhòr told him, the second time he apologised, that she had eaten worse at her own hearth as a girl and would eat worse again before she died. It was a small enough lie, and her own household knew it for one, yet Fearchar Iar took it for kindness rather than flattery and repeated it to every traveller who lodged under his roof for years afterward, so that the saying outlived the visit that made it by a good deal longer than the visit deserved.

She asked him, before she rode on, how many households the house served in a hard winter and how many turned away for want of room, and he answered her plainly, having nothing to hide and no reason yet to think a queen's questions worth measuring his answers against. It was that plain answering, more than anything seen at Baile Mòr fhionn, that stayed with her longest of everything from that journey, and she said once, years later, to Dùghall mac Raghnaill, that she had learned more of her own island from one night at a road-house's hearth than from every steward's letter that had ever reached her at Dùn dhearg.

## III. Of the Bridge-Foot

The hall at Dùn dhearg had stood on its hill since before the shares were cut, and Beathag Mhòr's own line had held it whole and unquestioned longer than any other line on the island had held anything. It was Lachlann Dubh, oddly, who first said aloud what she had already begun to think: that a hall at the island's eastern end, days' ride from the western harbours, could rule a boundary quarrel in the west only at second hand, through a steward's letter that was a season old by the time it was answered, and that a queen who wished to see her own island rather than hear it reported to her would do better to sit where the roads and the river and the western harbours all came together.

He meant it, he said afterward, as an old man's grumble and nothing more, having no wish himself to leave the granary he had counted for forty years, but Beathag Mhòr rode down to the bridge-foot town the winter after he said it and stood on the rise above the harbour a long while in a wind that had her household's cloaks snapping about them, and said only that the ground was good building ground, and asked no one's leave before she began.

Dùn dhearg's people took the news as they took most things touching their own pride, at first with a flat refusal to believe it, and then, when the masons' ox-sledges began to pass through on the western road, with a silence Lachlann Dubh recognised from the winter of the counting slab four generations before, the silence a household keeps when it has decided a thing cannot be argued and will not therefore be forgiven either. He himself said nothing against the move in the queen's hearing, but he kept, from that year on, a second set of accounts beside the Hall's own, a private tally of every sack that left Dùn dhearg's granaries for the new hall at the bridge-foot, and showed it to no one, not even his son, who found it among his tally-sticks after he died and could not say what his father had meant to do with a count kept for no eye but his own.

The new hall was built of the red stone the town was already named for, on foundations laid deep enough that no age after would need to dig them again, and the masons cut the hearth-sign into its lintel as if the whole building were no more than a threshold, which in a sense, Beathag Mhòr said once to the master mason, it was. The building took four years, through two wet winters that flooded the harbour road and a third summer so dry the masons carried water up from the river in relays of carriers to keep their mortar workable, and Beathag Mhòr rode down from Dùn dhearg to stand on the scaffolding herself more often than her own household thought fitting for a ruler, saying, when Lachlann Dubh's own steward asked her why, that a hall built without its ruler watching was a hall built for someone else's reign, not hers.

The master mason, a broad-shouldered woman of Cathair dhomhain named Sìleas nan Clach, had never before been asked to raise a building meant to outlast every hall on the island, and she told the queen plainly, at the laying of the last course, that she could promise the stone would hold and nothing else, for a hall's worth was made by whoever sat in it after the masons had gone home, and that was no mason's business to answer for. Beathag Mhòr took the answer for the honest one it was and paid Sìleas nan Clach in full before the hearth-sign was even cut, against the custom of paying a mason only on the building's finishing, which Sìleas nan Clach remembered, she told her own apprentices in her old age, as the first time in her working life anyone had trusted her hand before they had seen the whole of what it made.

From that year the hall at the bridge-foot was where a ruler of Dia-thìr kept court, whatever else about the reign might change, though Dùn dhearg kept its granaries and its graves and went on calling itself, in every reeve's own letters home, the rìgh's hill, long after the rìgh had stopped living on it.

## IV. Of the Harbour's Grudge

Cathair dhomhain lay near enough to the new hall to smell the masons' dust, and its people, who had built their own harbour into the largest on that coast while Dùn dhearg's rulers were still five days' ride away and easily flattered by a gift of fish, did not care for a queen's toll-gatherers appearing at their own quays as though the harbour had been waiting all along for someone to come and own it.

The harbour-master, a broad woman named Iseabail nic Fhearchair who had run the quays longer than Beathag Mhòr had been alive, brought the matter to the new hall herself rather than send a steward, and stood in front of the queen's own chair with her arms folded and said that Cathair dhomhain had weighed its own fish, mended its own nets and buried its own drowned for longer than the Red Share had held a single stone of Dùn dhearg, and had no memory of asking the Red Share's leave to do any of it. Beathag Mhòr heard her out to the end, which Iseabail nic Fhearchair said afterward she had not expected, having come ready to be interrupted, and answered that she asked no toll of a harbour older than her own hall's foundations, and that Cathair dhomhain might keep its own tolls under its own charter if it kept its own peace with the new town beside it.

The charter was written that same season, in the clerks' own hand and not the knot-keepers', for Beathag Mhòr had by then set two of the Hall's young stag-scholars to write down what had once only been recited, and Iseabail nic Fhearchair carried it home rolled inside her own cloak rather than trust it to any steward's saddlebag. It settled nothing between the two towns beyond the letter of the tolls themselves. Cathair dhomhain's harbour-masters went on for the rest of the age finding some new law of their own to keep more strictly than the new town beside them kept it, a rivalry that cost neither town anything worse than pride, and pride, as Iseabail nic Fhearchair told her own successor before she died, is a cheap enough thing for two towns a few miles apart to spend on each other instead of spears.

The rivalry came out first, and most plainly, in the matter of the winter storm the third year after the charter, when a grain-ship out of the western islands broke its mast off Cathair dhomhain's own harbour mouth and drifted, helpless, toward the shoals below the new hall's rise. Cathair dhomhain's boats reached it first, being the nearer and the more practised at a lee shore in weather, and towed it in to their own quays rather than the new town's, and though the grain itself went, in the end, to whichever granary the queen's own clerks directed it, Cathair dhomhain's harbour-master let it be known, in every telling of the rescue after, that the ship had been saved by an older skill than any charter could grant a younger town, and the new town's own boatmen, stung, spent the better part of that winter refitting two hulls of their own against the day a ship might drift the other way instead.

None ever did, in Beathag Mhòr's reign or after it, but the two towns kept their boats the sharper for the waiting, and a visitor to either quay had only to ask after the weather to hear some version of the same story, told from whichever side he happened to be standing on.

## V. Of the Quarrels over the Handful

At Dùn ìseal, in those same years, the council that judged the small disputes the Small-Burning Law had always settled found itself judging fewer boundary quarrels and more of a kind it had barely troubled with before: households whose right to the handful was disputed outright, a new hearth claiming descent from one of the nine without proof, two households sworn to the same waypoint-keeper each saying the other had no standing at all.

The Keeper who held the flame in those years, an old man who had come to it late from a hearth in the far north and left it again after a short season none of the reciters of Dùn ìseal cared to dwell on, had let the disputes pile against each other without settling more than the loudest, and it fell to his successor, a man named Dùghall mac Raghnaill, chosen by the nine hearths in his twenty-ninth year, to find the council's floor at his own first sitting so crowded with claimants that he could not walk from the door to the cup without a hand catching at his sleeve.

Dùghall mac Raghnaill was of Sliochd Raghnaill, one of the Four Houses sworn at Dùn ìseal, though he had left his own house's hall as a boy to learn the vein's reckoning and had not gone back to it since, and he judged, in that first crowded season, with a plainness his own house was not much known for, ruling three claims for and eleven against inside a single afternoon, until an old woman of the eastern road stood up before him and asked, not unkindly, how a Keeper meant to judge eleven claims a season for the rest of his life without ever once knowing, for certain, which of the eleven he had judged rightly.

He had no answer ready for her, and he told her so, which the reciters of Dùn ìseal count the beginning of what came after, for a lesser Keeper, they say, would have found some answer rather than admit he lacked one, and Dùghall mac Raghnaill rode to Cathair dhearg within the month to ask the queen for a count.

The old woman who had asked him the question, a widow of the eastern road named Beitris nic Ailein, lived long enough, a very old woman by then, to see the first counters ride out from Dùn ìseal six-and-thirty years later, and she told her own grandchildren, more than once before she died, that she had put the question to the Keeper meaning only to shame him a little for the crowded council floor, and had never once expected an island's worth of households to be walked and written down because of it. Dùghall mac Raghnaill himself, when the reciters asked him in his own old age whether he remembered her question word for word, said only that he remembered her face better than her words, and that a Keeper who forgot the faces that had unsettled him was no Keeper worth the flame he kept.

## VI. Of the Count Agreed

Beathag Mhòr received him in the new hall's smaller chamber, the one that still smelled of fresh-cut stone, and heard him through without once interrupting, a habit Lachlann Dubh, watching from the doorway, recognised from the granary yard fourteen years before and thought, not for the first time, that a queen who listened whole before she answered was rarer than her own age's reeves ever gave her credit for.

What Dùghall mac Raghnaill asked was simple to say and hard to do: that every household on the island claiming the old right to the handful be counted once, in its own place, its right proved or refused before a clerk who wrote it down, so that no council afterward need judge the same claim twice from memory alone. Beathag Mhòr agreed to it before he had finished asking; it was six-and-thirty years before she found clerks enough and grain enough to begin it, in the last year of her reign, and when the two of them came at last to the doing she asked only where the counting should be done, since neither the Hall's own clerks nor the queen's own stewards could reach every household on the island inside a single lifetime without some fixed ground to work from.

It was Dùghall mac Raghnaill who thought of the waypoint houses, for every household on Dia-thìr lay within a day's walk of one, and the queen agreed to feed the counters at her own cost out of each house's own stores, which the waypoint-keepers, more used to feeding travellers who never paid enough to cover a night's fire, remembered afterward as the best year their own hearths had ever had. At the house called An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the same house Beathag Mhòr had ridden three days out of her way to see filled once, a counter named Sorcha nic Ruairidh sat six months with a household's own grandmother going back four generations by name and by story until the old woman's claim, thin as it had looked on the council's own doubtful roll, stood proved beyond any argument the council could have raised against it, and Sorcha nic Ruairidh wrote the four names down in a hand the old woman could not read and would not have trusted if she could, and told her, when she asked what was to become of the leaf, that it would outlast them both, which was the plain truth and no more comfort to the old woman than the plain truth generally is.

## VII. Of the Refused Roll

The count ran the length of the island and took the better part of that year, and when the last waypoint house had sent its tally in to the clerks at Cathair dhearg, the rolls gave eleven thousand four hundred households holding the right by clear descent and near two thousand whose claims the counters had been unable to prove by any account, old or new, that the council would accept.

The refused were written on a roll of their own, kept separate from the rest, and it was that separate roll, more than the larger one, that the island remembered afterward, for a family with a clear right had nothing to think about it and a family without one had a roll to search for the rest of its life. Most of the refused lay along the north-eastern coast about Seann Tarr, fisher-families who had never burned coal at all in living memory and now found, when the counters came to their doors expecting to write down a right already held, that no such right had ever been theirs to begin with. A fisherman there named Ruairidh Cam told the counter plainly, when she asked whether his house meant to appeal the ruling, that his house had burned peat before the Small-Burning Law was thought of and would go on burning it after, and that peat, in his own experience of both, was the warmer fire besides, a saying the counters carried back to Cathair dhearg and that spread, in the years after, further along that coast than the census roll itself ever did.

Sliochd Raghnaill, Dùghall mac Raghnaill's own house, took up the fisher-families' cause at the council the following spring, arguing that a right so long unclaimed ought to be granted rather than refused, since a household that had never burned coal could hardly be said to have forfeited a habit it had never had. The council heard the argument through and ruled against it, on the plain ground that the Small-Burning Law had never promised a right to a household that had not held it, only protected the right of a household that had, and Dùghall mac Raghnaill, sitting the ruling out from the Keeper's own place beside the cup, did not speak for his own house's argument nor against it, a silence the reciters of Dùn ìseal note without troubling to explain, since a Keeper's silence in his own house's cause was, by then, the kind of thing the Hall had learned to take for something, though never for the same thing twice.

Three of the old sea-lights, fallen to ash and unkept along stretches of coast the census had newly walked from end to end, were rebuilt in those same years, at Baile ìseal on the eastern cape, at Muileann bheag on the northern point, and at Àth dhearg on the north-eastern headland that marked the passage in toward Seann Tarr, each kept afterward with driftwood and seal fat as the Law required, by households who had counted their own coasts, in the walking of the census, for the first time in longer than any of them could say.

Ruairidh Cam himself never troubled the council again after the ruling, and lived to see his own grandson keep the driftwood fire at Baile ìseal's rebuilt light two winters running, a duty owed to no coal-right at all but to the plain fact that his family had always lived nearest the point and knew its rocks in the dark better than any counter's roll could teach a stranger. He was asked once, by a traveller who had heard the saying about peat repeated as far south as Cathair dhearg, whether he still held to it, and he answered that he did, and that a fire a man had tended with his own hands since boyhood was always the warmer one, whatever its ash was made of, which the traveller wrote down as a fisherman's stubbornness and the fisher-families of that coast kept, afterward, as something nearer the truth.

## VIII. Of the Long Road Home

Beathag Mhòr's son Ruairidh was born at the new hall in its first year, grey-headed almost from his cradle, which his own household took for an ill sign and his mother, when she was told of it, took for nothing at all, having by then buried enough of her own line's short-lived cousins to know that a child's colouring foretold no more than a child's colouring ever does.

She lived only months past the count's finishing, long enough to see the refused roll consulted for the first time by a family proving an old claim through a cousin's cousin, and to see Dùghall mac Raghnaill, grey now in his own turn at the cup, still Keeper, still hearing the same handful of claims that the census had not quite managed to end.

In her last years she sat less at the harbour rise and more at the small chamber's own window, which looked east, back the way the bridge-foot road ran toward Dùn dhearg, and her household came to know that a queen sitting at that window in the last hour of daylight was a queen who wished to be left with her own thoughts rather than her own council. Her son Ruairidh, grown into a tall, grey-headed man who had long since stopped minding the colour that had once been called an ill sign, sat with her there more often than his own stewards thought fitting for an heir with a hall's business waiting on him, and it was to him alone, in the last winter, that she gave the command about her carrying, speaking it plainly and only once, as though a thing worth doing at all was not worth the saying twice.

She died at Cathair dhearg in her seventieth year, in the same small chamber where she had first heard Dùghall mac Raghnaill ask her for a count, and by her own command, given years before to her son and never once changed, she was carried back to Dùn dhearg to lie among the house of Ìomhar, the granaries she had grown up counting and the hill her own great-grandfather had died old and easy upon.

No royal journey before it had been so long. The road ran east the whole width of the island, five days at a walking bier's pace, and it was carried by relays of bearers drawn from every waypoint house along the way, twelve to a stage, so that the same road that had once counted the island's households now carried its queen home along the ground her own counters had walked. Ruairidh rode at the bier's head the whole distance and would let no one take his place, though his own stewards offered more than once to spell him on the harder stretches, and at each waypoint house where the bearers changed he stood by while the new twelve took up the poles and said nothing, having, his own household remembered, very little left to say by the second day.

Dùghall mac Raghnaill rode with it the last stretch from Dùn ìseal, an old man himself by then, remembering, as the bier passed the waypoint house at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr where a counter had once sat six months over one grandmother's claim, that the queen he was burying had asked him, the very first time he stood before her, only where the counting should be done, and had never once, in all the years after, asked him whether it had been worth the doing. He thought, riding behind her bier into the granary yard at Dùn dhearg where Lachlann Dubh's grandson stood waiting with the household's own tallies under his arm, that he might have told her, had she asked: that the roll of the refused, thin and worn as it already was, would go on being searched long after that, when every hand that had written it was dust, and that this, of everything a reign could leave behind it, was no small thing to have made.

They laid her among the house of Ìomhar on the slope above the double bank, within sight of the granaries Lachlann Dubh had walked her through as a girl of twenty who had asked a steward the name of every household a sack was owed to, and no sack's weight besides. The roll of the refused was carried up from Cathair dhearg in its own worn chest the following season, kept for the living rather than laid with the dead, and read aloud once at Dùn dhearg before the household of Ìomhar, so that the hill that had given up its own hall might hear, at least once, what the giving had bought.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of the Silver Feud

*FE 1,736 – 1,781*

> *Cha do bhris an t-airgead a dhath riamh; carson a bhristeadh e a chumhachd?*
> Silver never broke its colour; why should it break its word?
>
> — said still at the smiths' hearth of Muileann chiar, of no ruler in particular

## I. Of the Grey Rìgh

Ruairidh Liath took the red hall at Cathair dhearg in his thirty-sixth year, five days after they had carried his mother the length of the island to lie among the house of Ìomhar, and the reeves who set the crown on him did it quietly, for a household still in its year of mourning is not a household that wants a feast made of a crowning. He had been grey since his cradle, as his mother's own household had first taken for an ill sign and then, watching him grow tall and steady and no sicklier than any other child, for nothing more than the colour a man is born with, and the byname stuck to him the way a byname sticks to a family that has run out of new ones: Ruairidh Liath, Ruairidh the Grey, the one jest the king-list ever allowed among its years of names.

He kept his mother's clerks, her stewards, her reeve at Dùn dhearg, and for the first years of his reign changed little that she had set in order, being, his own household said of him, a man who mistrusted a thing done only because it was new. The old reeve who had walked at Beathag Mhòr's stirrup was long dead by then, but his grandson kept the same tallies in much the same hand, and it was to him, in his first winter, that Ruairidh Liath said the one thing of his own that the granary household remembered afterward: that he had watched his mother spend her reign finding out what the island held, and meant to spend his own reign finding out only what it needed, which he judged the smaller and the harder task of the two.

What he did change, in his fourth year, was the guard he kept on the eastern road, doubling it against the toll-cheats who had grown bold in the years the census had kept every clerk in the island walking from house to house rather than watching the roads, and it was the guard's own pay, more than anything else in his reign, that brought him at last to the silver.

The silver of the island came from one place only, the workings at Muileann chiar, a small town of a few hundred souls a short ride north of Dùn ìseal, where the seam ran shallow enough to be worked with pick and fire-setting and had done, by Ruairidh Liath's day, for longer than any family there could count in generations rather than reigns. It was Muireach Liath himself, second Keeper of the flame, who had ruled in the age's first years that silver showed no colour when it broke and so was not the mountain's, and Muileann chiar had dug as deep as it liked ever since on the strength of those words, paying no toll to the Hall and none, until Ruairidh Liath's reign, to the crown either.

## II. Of Sliochd Fhearchair

The house that held the workings by that time, and had held them for sixty generations without any other house troubling to dispute it, was Sliochd Fhearchair, the line of Fearchar Airgeadach, the basket-carrier who had first hammered the ore into rings in the Hall's first century, and it was an old woman of that house, Màiri nic Fhearchair, who spoke for it in the years that followed, having outlived two husbands, three of her own children, and every other smith of her own generation who might have spoken instead.

She had been born in the first years of Beathag Mhòr's reign, and had lived to see her own grandmother's claim to the handful proved before the counters when the census came at last to Muileann chiar, so that Màiri nic Fhearchair knew, before she knew much else, what it cost a house to have its right questioned and what it was worth to have it settled beyond argument afterward. She came to speak for Sliochd Fhearchair the ordinary way a smith's house chooses its voice, by being the one whose word the others trusted furthest, and she held the place for twenty years before Ruairidh Liath ever asked anything of her that was hard to give.

Neither large nor loud, she was known to the traders who came up from Dùn ìseal to buy rings by the basket only for weighing a ring twice before she named its price and never once, in all the years they dealt with her, weighed it wrong. Her own hands, by the time Ruairidh Liath's reign was ten years old, had thickened at the knuckle from forty years at the fire, and she wore, summer and winter both, a single ring of her own house's silver on a cord at her throat rather than on her finger, saying, when anyone asked her why, that a ring worn where it could be seen was a ring a smith remembered making rather than a ring she had forgotten she owned.

Her own house kept, in those years, some thirty smiths and apprentices at the workings and the forge-yard beside them, a small enough number beside the shepherds and cutters of the greater shares but the only hands on the island that drew silver at all, and Muileann chiar had grown up around them a town of a few hundred souls who owed their bread, one way or another, to the ore beneath their own feet. Màiri knew every one of the thirty by name and by trade, the fire-setters who cracked the rock with heat and water before the pick ever touched it, the smelters who read a flame's colour the way a reciter read a knotted cord, the smiths proper who drew the wire and struck the rings, and she judged each of their disputes herself rather than let them go before the town's own reeve, saying that a smith's quarrel was a family matter until the day it was not, and she meant, by that, to keep it a family matter as long as she was able.

## III. Of the Ring in Five

The demand came in Ruairidh Liath's ninth year, carried up from Dùn dhearg by a steward who had ridden three days to deliver it and plainly wished, from the look of him, that someone else had been sent instead: that Sliochd Fhearchair should render one ring in every five it drew from the ore, the silver going to pay the guard whose doubling had emptied the crown's own purse faster than the eastern tolls could fill it again.

Màiri nic Fhearchair heard the steward out in the yard before her own forge, with the fire banked low behind her and her apprentices standing well back, and the steward, who had expected an old smith to hear a rìgh's asking with some show of trouble at least, said afterward that she heard it the way a woman hears news of weather she has already dressed against. She asked him only one question before she answered him at all: whether he had been told to wait for her answer or only to carry it away with him whatever it was, and when he said he had been told to wait, she told him he need not, for the answer would take her no longer to give than it had taken him to ask.

She answered him, then, with words she had not troubled to soften: that the tokens which paid a queen's guards were the queen's own business, but the silver that made them had never once, in sixty generations, been anybody's business but the hands that dug it and the fire that shaped it, and that Muireach Liath himself, second Keeper of the flame, had said as much before any road-guard on the island carried a spear. The steward asked her, before he left, whether she wished him to soften the words on the road back to Cathair dhearg, and she told him no, that a message softened in the carrying was a message that lied twice over, once to the one who sent it and once to the one who received it, and she would rather Ruairidh Liath heard her exact meaning and be angry at it than a kinder one and be satisfied with less than the truth.

She sent the steward home with no other answer, and within the month, before the crown's own clerks had finished drawing up the toll roll they meant to collect it by, the workings at Muileann chiar stood shut, the fires out, the ore left in the ground.

It was not a thing any house on the island had done before, to close a working rather than pay what its ruler asked, and Sliochd Fhearchair did not do it lightly: the shutting cost the house its own trade as surely as it cost the crown its silver, and more than one of Màiri's own kin asked her, in the first weeks, whether a ring in five paid quietly would not have been the cheaper course in the end. Tormod himself, then a young man newly come into his own place at the forge, put the question to her most plainly of any of them, standing in the cooling yard with the last of the fire's light on his face, and asked whether a house that had never once been troubled for a toll in sixty generations might not simply pay the one toll and go back to being untroubled the generation after.

She told him that a house which paid the first asking without argument would be asked again within the year, and a third time within two, until it had nothing left to argue with, for a right unused, she said, was no different in the end from a right given away, only slower in the losing of it; and she told him besides that she had not shut the fires to save the house a single ring, since the house could well have spared the silver, but to make certain that whatever it paid afterward, it paid because a Keeper had judged it owed and not because a rìgh had asked for it once and found no one troubled to say him no. Her own certainty in the matter, Tormod said years afterward, was the only certain thing in Muileann chiar that whole first season, for even her own household went to their beds most nights that winter no surer than the rìgh himself how long a smith's house could go without its fires before it stopped being a smith's house at all.

## IV. Of the Three Seasons

The shutting held three seasons entire, the longest quiet the workings at Muileann chiar had known since they were first opened, and the island felt it before the year was out. The fair at Muileann òg, which had traded half its custom in silver rings for as long as the smiths of Sliochd Fhearchair had carried them there, went back to weighing its bargains in grain and cloth as it had done before the workings were dug at all, and the traders who had grown rich carrying rings down the eastern road found their own baskets empty and their own trade gone to whoever still had grain to sell.

## V. Of the Toll-House at Àth ghlas

The road-guards themselves, whose pay had begun the whole quarrel, went unpaid through the second season and the third, and it was at the toll-house of Àth ghlas, the first keeper the rìgh's hall had ever sent to stand a road, that the wanting was felt worst. Two of the four guards posted there left their spears against the toll-house wall in the same week of the second winter and walked home to their own villages rather than stand a further watch for wages that were themselves standing, unpaid, on a silver toll no one had yet agreed to gather, and the keeper who held the house, a woman named Oighrig nic Ailein who had kept it eleven years without missing a season's watch before that winter, sent no word of the desertion to Cathair dhearg at all, judging, she told the two who stayed, that a rìgh already short of silver had no need of a letter telling him he was short of guards as well.

She stood the toll-house herself through the worst of that season with the two guards who remained, turning back no traveller and collecting no toll from any of them either, for a toll-house with half its watch was no toll-house at all in her own reckoning, only a roof with a fire under it, and she told travellers who asked after the toll that the crown's business with the silversmiths was the crown's own to settle and none of theirs, an answer more than one carrier carried onward down the road and repeated at hearths from Àth ghlas to the western harbours until it had travelled, by the third season, further than the quarrel itself had yet been heard of in some quarters. The tolls of the eastern road went ungathered the whole three seasons through, for want of anyone willing to stand the road and collect them, and it was the emptiest the crown's own purse had stood since Beathag Mhòr's own reign, before the census had ever begun to fill it.

Ruairidh Liath, for his own part, did not send soldiers to the workings, though more than one of his own reeves urged it on him; his mother's household remembered him saying once, in those years, that a mine could be broken open by force but a smith's hand could not, and a crown that had only broken hands to show for its silver had made a poor bargain of it. He sent, instead, a second steward to Àth ghlas with grain enough to feed the toll-house through what remained of the winter, unasked and unannounced, much as his own mother had once sent grain to a hungry waypoint house without naming herself the sender, and Oighrig nic Ailein, who guessed well enough whose grain it was, never once told a traveller the story of it, though she kept, for the rest of her life, a fuller hearth at Àth ghlas than the crown's own wages alone would have bought her.

## VI. Of the Third Winter

He held to the toll, and waited, through the whole of that hungry season, and it was Màiri nic Fhearchair, in the end, who moved first, not because her own house's will had bent but because of what she saw, in the third winter, in her own forge-yard: two of her youngest apprentices, a brother and sister taken on the year the shutting began, going thinner at the wrist than any apprentice she had trained in forty years at the fire, their own family having nothing to send them from Muileann chiar's own thin fields, and no wage from the silver to buy what the fields could not give. She fed them from her own table rather than send them home, and told no one of it beyond her own household, but she judged, watching the boy's hands shake over a task that should not have troubled hands half so young, that a right worth keeping was not worth keeping at the cost of the hands that would keep it after her.

She said as much to her own kin, plainly, the same week she sent word to Dùn ìseal: that Sliochd Fhearchair had shut its fires to keep a principle and very nearly starved two children doing it, and a principle that cost a smith's own apprentices their strength before it cost the crown a single ring was a principle she had begun to hold for her own pride's sake rather than the house's, which was, she told them, the one thing she had sworn, on taking up her place at the forge twenty years before, that she would never let herself do.

## VII. Of the Journey to Dùn ìseal

She made the ride to Dùn ìseal herself, in the last month of the third season, in a rain that had not let up in four days and turned the road below Muileann chiar to a soup the horses baulked at twice before she got them through it, taking with her only her grandnephew Tormod and a single strongbox holding every ring Sliochd Fhearchair had struck in the reign of Fearchar Òg, that the Keeper might see, she said, exactly what silver looked like before anyone had thought to argue over who owned it.

She had never before asked the Hall for anything, her own house having stood, since Muireach Liath's ruling, entirely outside the Hall's reckoning of what belonged to the mountain and what did not, and it cost her something, Tormod said years afterward, to ride up to the Keeper's own door and ask a judgment of a man whose office existed to weigh coal, not silver. Dùghall mac Raghnaill received her all the same, being by then an old man of seventy-nine who had judged every manner of claim the island could bring him and had long since stopped thinking any of them beneath his hearing, and he sent word to Cathair dhearg the same week asking that Ruairidh Liath meet her there, at Dùn ìseal, on ground that belonged to neither of them outright.

## VIII. Of the Rain-Shut Hearing

The hearing was held in the Hall at Dùn ìseal on a day the rain shut every door in the town and kept the roof-gutters running loud enough that Dùghall mac Raghnaill twice had to ask both sides to speak again, and it was there, before the cup and the Keeper and Ruairidh Liath, grey and forty-nine and no longer young enough to think a quarrel would settle on its own, that Màiri nic Fhearchair said Muireach Liath's sentence for the first time: that silver showed no colour when it broke, and so was not the mountain's.

She said it standing, her strongbox open on the floor before the cup so that any who wished might look into it and see the rings themselves, struck before the crown had ever thought to ask anything of them, and she added to Muireach Liath's own words only a handful of her own: that she had not come to Dùn ìseal to ask whether the crown might be poor, for every house on the island had known a poor season and none begrudged its ruler one, but to ask whether a right sixty generations old could be unmade by a single asking from a man who had held the hall thirteen years, and if it could, she wished to be told so plainly, that Sliochd Fhearchair might know from that day what its rights were worth.

Ruairidh Liath answered that he did not dispute the mountain's claim or lack of one; he disputed only whether a crown might ask a toll of a trade that used its roads, wore its peace and sold its wares under laws his own house had written, silver or no silver, mountain's or no mountain's. He said, further, that he had not shut her workings; she had shut them herself rather than argue the matter with him first, and a house that answered an asking with a closed door had made the quarrel larger than the asking ever was, a charge Màiri nic Fhearchair did not trouble to deny, saying only that a door closed in argument was easier to open again than a right given away was to take back.

Dùghall mac Raghnaill let them argue it the better part of a day, the rain never once slackening, and when he judged at last he had Màiri nic Fhearchair say the sentence a second time, word for word as she had said it the first, before he gave his own ruling on it.

He ruled that the words of Muireach Liath stood as they had always stood: silver was not the mountain's, and no Keeper after him would say otherwise. But he ruled, in the same breath, that the crown kept the roads the silver travelled whether the silver itself was the crown's or not, and that a house which used those roads owed something toward their keeping, though nothing toward the ore beneath its own feet. Each of them was right, he said, and each of them had asked the wrong question first, Ruairidh Liath for reaching past the silver to the roads without saying so and Màiri nic Fhearchair for reaching past the roads to the silver in her own defence of it, and a ring in five had never been the toll he would have set had either of them asked him the plainer question at the start.

He set it, in the end, at one ring in ten, owed not on the ore drawn from the ground but on every ring that left Muileann chiar by the roads the crown kept, and both sides, Tormod said afterward, rode home from Dùn ìseal calling it a victory, though neither, in truth, had won anything but the certainty of knowing what it would cost them from that year on.

## IX. Of the Weight Made Law

The workings opened again within the month, the fires lit and the ore drawn as it had been for sixty generations, but the settlement left one thing behind it that outlasted the quarrel's own memory: for the toll to be reckoned fairly, ring against ring, the weights of Muileann chiar, kept by Sliochd Fhearchair's own hand since the Peace of the Threshold and trusted nowhere beyond the workings themselves, were declared by the Keeper's own judgment the only lawful weights on the roads of the island, and copies in bronze were ordered sent to every waypoint house between Dùn ìseal and the western harbours, that a ring weighed at one hearth might be trusted at the next without argument.

Màiri nic Fhearchair was paid, by the crown's own clerks, for every copy cast from her house's own weights, the first silver Sliochd Fhearchair had ever taken from Cathair dhearg rather than given it, and she remarked once to Tormod, counting the payment into the strongbox that had ridden to Dùn ìseal and back, that she had gone to the Hall meaning to keep the crown's hand off her house's silver and had come home, instead, with the crown's own silver in her own strongbox, a different victory than the one she had set out to win, and, she judged, no poor one to settle for.

## X. Of the Bronze-Casters

The copies themselves were cast at Muileann dhearg, a market town roughly midway along the road between Cathair dhearg and Dùn ìseal, by a family of casters named Sliochd Aonghais who had learned the trade from the smiths of Muileann chiar two generations before and had never yet found a market for it beyond a few pins and buckles a season. The weight-copies gave them, for the first time, a craft the whole island wanted, and they went on, in the years after, to cast bells for the waypoint houses and lamp-bowls for the Hall's own use, each lamp-bowl holding, by the founder's own boast, exactly the measure the Small-Burning Law required and not a hair's breadth more or less.

The founder of that trade, a broad woman named Beitris nic Aonghais, kept for the rest of her life the first weight-copy she had ever cast, a poor one, cracked along its rim from cooling too fast, and showed it to every apprentice she took on afterward before she let them near the good bronze, telling them that a caster who forgot her own worst work was a caster likely to repeat it.

She sent word to Màiri nic Fhearchair, the season the good copies first went out along the road, asking leave to cast the smiths' own hearth-sign into each weight's underside, that any waypoint keeper who turned one over might know at a glance whose measure it stood for, and Màiri gave the leave gladly, saying it cost Sliochd Fhearchair nothing and might, in some quarrel neither of them could yet foresee, save a keeper an argument over whether the weight in his own hand was the true one. It was a small mark, cut no bigger than a thumbnail, and the two houses that had never traded more than a few pins between them before the settlement went on trading weights and bells and lamp-bowls for years after both women who had first agreed to it were dead, every weight cast at Muileann dhearg still carrying, to the close of Ruairidh Liath's reign and past it, the same small sign struck at Muileann chiar and cast at Muileann dhearg together.

## XI. Of Màiri's Last Years

Màiri nic Fhearchair lived eleven years past the settlement, long enough to see the bronze weights reach every waypoint house from Dùn ìseal to the western harbours and long enough to see her own grandnephew Tormod take up her place at the forge-yard, speaking for Sliochd Fhearchair in his turn with a plainness she had taught him without ever once calling it teaching. She wore the same ring on its cord at her throat to the end of her days, and when she died, in the eightieth year of her life, the household of Sliochd Fhearchair buried her, at her own long-standing word, with the strongbox itself rather than the ring on the cord, empty by then of everything but the single weight-copy she had carried to Dùn ìseal in the rain, saying she had carried enough silver in her life without needing to carry any of it into the ground.

Dùghall mac Raghnaill died the same year, in his ninetieth, an old man who had held the flame near as long as Coinneach Mòr before him and had judged, by his own late count, more disputes over the handful and over the silver both than he could any longer put a number to; the reciters of Dùn ìseal remembered him afterward less for the census that had made his name than for the rain-shut hearing at which he had told two sides they were each right and each wrong, a saying more than one Keeper after him borrowed without troubling to say whose it had first been.

## XII. Of Seonag Chrom and the List Kept Yearly

Ruairidh Liath reigned one-and-thirty years more, growing no greyer than he had been at his crowning, for a man born grey has little further to grow into, and died in the red hall at Cathair dhearg in his eightieth year, in the same small chamber where his mother had died before him, mourned by a household that remembered him, in the reeve's own words to his successor, as a rìgh who had waited where waiting served and moved where nothing else would.

His granddaughter Seonag Chrom took the hall the year after, in her twenty-first year, the crown set on her without argument from any of the houses that might once have disputed a young ruler's age, for the island had by then buried enough young rulers grown old in office to have stopped counting a crowned head's years against her. She had grown up, her own household said, on stories of her grandfather's silver quarrel told at the granary fire by clerks who still kept, among the hall's own rolls, the roll of weights sent out that year to every waypoint house, and she asked, in the first month of her reign, to see that roll for herself before she asked to see any other roll in the hall's keeping.

What she found, turning it over by lamplight with the reeve who had kept it since his own father's day, was a record set down on whatever scrap of hide or bark had come to hand at the time, one clerk's tally crossed through and corrected in another clerk's hand, a third page missing its corner where damp had eaten it, and she judged, closing it at last, that a crown which meant to keep such a roll at all owed the keeping of it more care than a corner of the granary stores had ever given it. She gave the Hall's clerks, in her first season, a room of their own within the red hall, the first they had ever had that was not a corner of the granary stores or a table borrowed from the kitchens, and a wage in silver besides, the same silver the settlement at Dùn ìseal had first taught the crown to reckon by the ring rather than by the sack.

It was from her reign, the clerks of Cathair dhearg said afterward, that the king-list ceased to be kept reign by reign, as it had been kept since Tormod first set it down, and began instead to be kept year by year, so that no year of the island's telling, however quiet, would ever again go unwritten for want of a reign large enough to hold it.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of Peigi's Hand and the Dawn-Hawk

*FE 1,782 – 2,217*

> *Chan eil fuil aig an fhìrinn; tha i mar a chithear i.*
> Truth has no blood in it; it is as it is seen.
>
> — a saying of the clerks' room at Cathair dhearg

## I. Of Fish that Do Not Need Reading

At Inis bheag, where the Abhainn bheag comes down brown with peat-water into the sea and the fisher-houses stand along the one street with their backs to the wind, a teacher of the stag's people took a boat north a century after the Silver Feud was settled and stayed. He had been a cutter's son himself before he was a teacher, and had come to letters the way the stag's people came to most of what they taught, sideways, from a lesson meant for something else; but he found at Inis bheag a village of children who would never in their lives cut a handful of coal, whose fathers measured their year by the herring and not by the Hall's roll, and he taught them the marks anyway, on slate and on the smoothed bark of driftwood, because it seemed to him a poor thing that a mark should belong only to the vein.

The Hall's roll took note of it, as the Hall's roll took note of most things done anywhere on the island that year, and set down beside the notice, in the dry hand of whichever clerk kept the roll that season, a line to the effect that fish had no need of reading. Most who copied the line took it, in the years after, for nothing crueller than a clerk's small joke, the kind a tired hand makes at the foot of a long entry, and for two generations at Inis bheag it was told against the reading fisher-children themselves, at the boat-mending in winter, a jest the letters had as yet done nothing to earn: they had lightened no net and stilled no wave. The children the teacher taught grew old and taught their own in turn, and the marks he had begun on driftwood were still, by the time his grandchildren's grandchildren were grown, marks for counting a catch and naming a boat, no stranger in the eyes of the rest of the island than a knot on a cord, only harder on the eye to read at a distance.

The teacher himself did not live to see the marks travel further than his own street. He died an old man at Inis bheag, having taught three generations of the same dozen families and never once been asked by the Hall what use the teaching served, and his own grave-marker, cut by a pupil's hand, carries his name in the fisher-marks rather than in the Hall's own hand, the first stone on the island so cut, though no teller thought, at the time it was raised, to set the day down.

What the fisher-houses did not know, because no one troubled to tell them and they had no way of finding it out on their own, was that a boy of their own street, sent inland in his youth to serve at Cathair dhearg because his mother's cousin kept horses in the red hall's own stables, carried the marks with him into the red hall's own household, where no one before him had thought to teach them to anyone who was not already a clerk.
