He taught them badly and by accident, scratching a fisher's tally on a granary door for his own amusement while he waited on a groom who was slow to his work, and a clerk's daughter watching him at it asked what the marks meant and would not be put off with an answer that they were nothing, being a child who had already, by nine years old, formed the habit of believing that a thing written down meant something, or it would not have been written at all.

## II. Of Peigi's Hand

The clerk's daughter was Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, who had first set a ruler's name on a leaf of oiled hide more than six hundred years before her, and by the time she came to the clerks' room herself, grown, the room Seonag Chrom had given the clerks five generations before had four benches in it instead of one, and a chest for the rolls that would not shut for the fullness of it. She learned the fisher-marks from the stable-boy before she learned the Hall's own hand from her mother, and kept both all her life, though she used the second far oftener. Clerks two generations after her own said that a document in Peigi nic Tormoid's hand could be told from any other in the chest without a name beside it at all: the letters were set close and upright, and never once trailed off at the foot of a page the way a tired hand trails, whoever holds the pen.

She was given the clerk's stool in her twenty-sixth year for a plainer reason than her own family cared to admit afterward: the elder cousin who had held it before her had died of a fever the winter past, and no one else in the room wanted the work. Peigi herself, told the plain truth of it years later by the reeve who had made the choice, thought it a better reason to be given anything than most reasons rulers give. She kept the roll of the red hall for four-and-forty years from that day, through a reign and the half of another, and left behind her, when she died in her own bed at seventy, entries enough that the clerks who came after her learned to date a leaf by nothing more than whether her hand lay on it. More than one of them called it a truer clock than the reign it was written under.

Her days ran, for most of those four-and-forty years, on a pattern so unbroken that later clerks who read her own account of an ordinary week found it stranger, in its way, than any single ruling she made. She rose before the household woke, kept her own small fire until the granary bell rang, and walked the length of the clerks' room twice before touching a single leaf, to see, she told a young clerk once who asked her the use of it, whether anything had been moved in the night that oughtn't have been. Nothing ever had been, in all the years she kept the habit, but she never gave it up, on the reasoning that a habit which cost nothing and caught nothing was still worth keeping against the one year it might catch something.

She never gave a reason where a fact would serve, and it was this above her hand that the clerks who followed her remembered longest. A lord of the plain came to her once, in her middle years, to have a boundary dispute set down in his own favour, and pressed her at length for her opinion of the case's justice before she would write a word of it. Peigi told him she kept no opinions in the roll, only what was said and by whom, and that if he wanted an opinion set down he should say his own aloud and she would write that too, word for word, with his name beside it. He did not ask her again. What she wrote instead, plainly and at his own asking once he saw there was no other way to have it set down at all, was the boundary as both sides had described it, the disagreement between the two descriptions, and the day the two sides had last agreed on anything, which turned out, when a Keeper's clerk went looking for it two centuries later in a dispute grown far larger than the first, to be the one fact in the whole roll that settled the matter.

## III. Of the Grey Hawk of the Northern Skell

While Peigi kept her roll at Cathair dhearg, far to the north at Seann Skell on the cold coast the fowler families had begun a custom the Hall's roll would not hear of for years yet, being a custom kept entirely among themselves, on a shore few clerks ever troubled to visit. Every household there kept a hawk, as fowlers along that coast had always kept hawks, for the wild geese and the duck that came down onto the flats in their season; but somewhere in the years after the letters reached Inis bheag, without any teacher coming north to bring them, the fowler households of Seann Skell took to feeding the hawk before the household ate, on the reasoning, as one of them put it to a trader who asked, that a hunger fed first was a hunger that did not turn on the house that kept it waiting.

Raghnaid nic Chaluim was born into one of those households in the same generation that Peigi's roll, far south, was already growing thick with her successor's hand, and her own household came to say of her, in the tellings that followed, that she was the first of her line to carry the custom the whole distance it would go. Her hawk was a grey bird her father had flown before her and called Mòd, as the old households of that coast called their hawks Mòd, after the grey hawk of time that had lived down every age as a salmon and an eagle and a hawk by turns and remembered, between its shapes, more than any single creature could remember alone. At every dawn of the season when the handful was due she stood at her own threshold, unhooded the bird herself rather than leave it to a servant, and burned her household's measure with Mòd on her wrist, so that its eye was on the flame the whole time it burned, the smoke going up past its head into a sky still more grey than light.

A clerk sent up from Cathair dhearg to write the custom down for the Hall's own roll found her at that threshold one such dawn, in the last winter of her middle years, and asked her plainly, once the burning was done, why the bird had to watch it rather than wait fed in its mews until the handful was ash. She did not answer him at once. She looked at the hawk a while, working a loose feather straight with two fingers, and then said only that the flame was a hunger too, as the hawk on her wrist was a hunger, and ought to be fed the way a hunger is fed, in the sight of the thing that hungers; a household that burned its handful with the bird shut away would be doing the whole business by halves, the way a man does a kindness by halves when he does it where no eye can find him out. The clerk wrote the answer down as she gave it, without a word of his own beside it, for the Hall's roll had learned, at some cost, what came of setting a joke beside a keeping it did not yet understand, and meant, this time, to make no such mistake twice.

## IV. Of "No Concern of Ours"

The custom spread from Seann Skell up the Abhainn ìseal within Raghnaid's own lifetime, carried by traders who had seen it kept and thought it a fair thing to keep, until households at Inis ìseal and at Cnoc bheag were feeding a hawk before themselves and burning their dawn handful on the wrist as the Skell fowlers did, though none of them fowled for a living and more than one household, in the first years, kept a bird they had bought at no small cost from a Skell trader and fed better than they fed their own children, which their neighbours who kept no hawk at all were not slow to remark on.

Word of it reached Dùn ìseal in its own season, as word of every rite kept anywhere on the island reached Dùn ìseal sooner or later, and the Keeper who held the cup that year, whose name the Hall's roll set down plainly enough but whose face no teller troubled afterward to remember, was pressed by a household of the lowland plain to say whether the Hall meant to rule on the hawk-rite as Fionnlagh Dall had once ruled on a household's burning of its own measure. The household was uneasy less at the burning itself than at a keeping it did not understand spreading past its own coast into ground it thought its own to watch. The Keeper sent a clerk north to Cnoc bheag to see the dawn kept before answering rather than trust a report carried three times over by mouths that had not seen it, and the clerk came back and said plainly that the hawk-households burned no more of their handful than any other household on the island, to the grain, no later in the day and no earlier, only in the sight of a bird where other hearths kept no such sight at all.

On the strength of that report the Keeper wrote to the lowland household, and to every household after it that raised the same question in the years that followed, four words that were copied afterward into more than one household's own chest as a ruling in their own right: the rite kept the measure, and was no concern of the Hall's. It was, as it turned out, the last time in the whole age that the Hall answered any rite so simply. No one at Dùn ìseal that season, occupied wholly with the hawk-households and nothing beyond them, reckoned how many other keepings the island held that a household might one day put the same question to, nor how much harder each answer after the first would grow, once the first had been given away so freely and for so little in return.

## V. Of the Sting and the Western Harbours

Down the western coast, at Ros bheag where the harbour court had kept its own customs of trade since before any hawk was fed on that shore, a different swearing had begun to travel up from Baile àrsaidh among the yellow scorpions of the dry hill country, where a sting shut living in a box had been sworn on for longer than any teller could say why. A merchant of Ros bheag named Coll Ruadh, trading salt fish for the dry country's dyed wool, came home from his first journey south with the box and the custom both, and swore his next bargain on the sting before the harbour court had ever seen such a thing done, more from habit picked up on the road, he said afterward, than from any belief that a sting in a box bound a man tighter than his own word.

It bound the western harbours tighter than anything else had, within a few short years, for reasons Coll Ruadh himself was the first to admit he had not foreseen. A trader of the plain came to Ros bheag the following season, meaning to buy a season's fish on credit against a debt he swore would be paid by midwinter, and would not swear it on the sting when the harbour court, having by then grown fond of the custom, asked him to; he gave his reasons plainly enough, that a box of scorpions was no fit thing to swear a grown man's debt on and he would swear it on his own name or not at all. The harbour court let him swear on his own name, as he asked, and sold him no fish, on the reasoning, given him by the court's own eldest without much softening, that a man who would not swear on the sting when every other trader on that coast did was a man telling the court something about his debt that his own name alone did not say.

He came back within the season, paid double what the fish would have cost him at midwinter, and swore on the sting the second time without being asked, and it was remembered afterward at Ros bheag, by those who told the tale against traders of the plain generally, that he had learned in one dear lesson what the harbour had known for a generation: a custom trusted by everyone costs a stranger far more to refuse than to keep. He was not the last to learn it the hard way. A wool-factor of Cathair mhòr, a few years later, made the same refusal on the same grounds and got the same answer, and left Ros bheag that season, the harbour's own tellers say, with a string of pack-beasts still laden with the fleeces he had meant to sell against fish he never bought.

By the time Coll Ruadh himself died, an old man still keeping his own scorpion in its box behind the harbour-master's door, no merchant travelled the western coast without learning the swearing before he learned the prices, and the harbour courts from Ros bheag to Baile àrsaidh had come to hold, without any of them writing it down as a law, that a bargain sworn any other way was a bargain a careful man watched closely. His own box, kept after him by his daughter and her daughter after her, outlived three generations of the family that first brought it north, the scorpion within it renewed from the dry hill country each time the old one died, so that the box itself, the harbour-master's clerks noted once in an idle entry, had by then held more scorpions than any single trader who swore upon it would live to count.

## VI. Of the Second Wolf-Stone

Inland and to the south, where the roads Ailean Clachair's masons had first bridged now carried more carriers than ever, the wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan kept a watch the island's peace had come, by slow degrees, to lean on more than it once needed to, feuds being rarer on the roads with every generation that forgot what the stones at Dùn thais had once marked. The guards swore their own oath on a white stone at their founding, and it had stood alone for so long that most travellers who passed it took it for no more than a boundary marker of the guild's own ground, until the shrine-keepers of Inis thais, hearing of the guard's stone and its keeping, asked whether a second might be set at their own shrine, where the drowned were already prayed to and a guard's oath, they thought, would sit well beside an older prayer.

The guards agreed, being flattered more than they let on to be asked, and set about the dragging of it themselves rather than trust the work to any mason who had not sworn their own oath. The stone they chose was white quartz from high on the mountain, heavier by half than the guard's own first stone, and it cost them, by the account their captain Calum Mòr gave afterward to a teller who asked him plainly what a shrine-stone was worth, more oxen than the guild could easily spare and the better part of a season's toll besides, the sledge breaking twice on the lower slopes and one ox dying under the strain of the second breaking before it ever reached the road proper.

Calum Mòr stood at Inis thais himself when the stone was finally raised beside the shrine, and it was noted by more than one of the shrine-keepers present, and set down afterward in their own thin roll, that the road-guard's captain, asked by the eldest keeper whether he wished to pray before the stone himself now that it stood, answered only that he had sworn on it once at his own founding and saw no cause to swear on it twice in one lifetime, but that his guards were welcome to pray there as often as the drowned welcomed a stranger's prayer, which was a longer answer, the keeper thought, than the question had strictly asked for, and she let it stand in the roll unaltered, since a captain's own words, once given, were no clerk's business to shorten.

The eldest keeper herself, who had asked leave to set the second stone in the first place, lived to see it stand thirty years and more, long enough to watch travellers who had never known the shrine without it take the second stone for as old as the first, and older pilgrims correct them without much patience. She said once, to a younger keeper who asked her why the guard's white quartz sat so close beside the shrine's own darker stone rather than at a more respectful distance, that a shrine which could not stand a guard's oath at its elbow had no business calling itself a shrine to the drowned, who had never in any teller's memory asked to be prayed to alone.

## VII. Of the Roll Filed Without Comment

None of these keepings, taken alone, seemed to the red hall at Cathair dhearg a thing worth troubling a ruler's own attention with, and for a long while none of them troubled it much. The clerks who kept Peigi nic Tormoid's roll after her, and their own successors after them, entered each report as it came up from the coasts and the western harbours and the road-guards' ground, in the same dry hand the roll had always been kept in, without a word beside any of them to say which, if any, mattered more than the rest. A trader passing through Cathair dhearg in those years, asked by a clerk what he had seen kept on his travels that season, might name the hawk fed before its household at Seann Skell, the sting sworn on at Ros bheag, the wolf-stone prayed to at Inis thais, and the fisher-marks still taught at Inis bheag though no fisher's child who learned them any longer remembered the joke once made about them, all in the one breath, as though they were pieces of the same custom rather than four keepings that had grown up a hundred miles apart from one another without ever once being planned together.

The red hall's own roll, by the year the last of these reports was entered, ran to more chests than the room Seonag Chrom had first given the clerks could hold, and a later generation of them had long since given up trying to read every leaf of it at once. They worked instead from summaries their own predecessors had made of it, summaries of summaries by then in places, the original hands beneath them known to the clerks who copied them only by name and reputation, never by sight. What no clerk at Cathair dhearg thought to write, because it was not the kind of thing the roll had ever been kept to say, was that the Hall which had once answered a hawk-household's rite with four words and no more had found, in all the years since, no occasion to answer any other rite so simply again. Each of the coasts and the harbours and the road-guards' ground had, by slow and separate degrees, grown a keeping too much its own to be dismissed any longer in a clerk's single line, the way the first of them had once been dismissed and never troubled again.

The report on the second wolf-stone, the last of that season's news to reach Cathair dhearg, was filed in its turn behind the sting-oath and the hawk-rite and the fisher-marks, in a hand none of the four keepings would have known from any other. No ruler of the red hall that year, and no clerk who filed the report, thought to ask what it might mean that the island now held so many ways of keeping faith with what it could not fully explain, each sworn and fed and prayed to in its own corner, none of them counted among the rest, nor asked to be.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Strike-Books

*FE 2,218 – 2,391*

> *Cha do dh'iarr an fhèith oirnn breith a thoirt.*
> The vein never asked us to give judgement.
>
> — the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh, at Dùn ìseal

## I. Of the Strike-Books Compared

At Cnoc bhàn, in the stag's house among the pines north of the mountain, the strike-books that a novice called Rìoghnach had begun with three words and a day, near six hundred years before, had grown by then into a store no single shelf could hold: chests of oiled hide leaves in the long room behind the grove, each leaf a season's account of one apprentice's hand, kept by masters who had themselves once been the apprentices of masters long dead, so that the room smelled, winter and summer both, of oil and old smoke and the particular dryness of hide that has been read too many times by too many lamps. No one at Cnoc bhàn any longer thought the keeping strange. It had become, in those six centuries, simply what the school did, the way a smith banks a fire or a fisher mends a net, a habit so worn into the place that a child born there took the sight of the chests for granted before it could read what was written in them.

Donnchadh mac Iain was born into that house in the Hall's twenty-third century, the second son of a cutter's widow who had brought him to the teachers herself rather than send him down to the vein at ten years old as his elder brother had gone, on the reasoning, given plainly enough to the master who took him in, that one son owed to the coal was as much as her house could spare and the other might as well learn what use could be made of the marks. He grew up among the chests before he grew up among the seams, and by his twelfth year could find, faster than any master then living, the leaf of any apprentice whose name he was given, a skill that earned him no particular honour at Cnoc bhàn, where finding a leaf was reckoned a small thing beside cutting a fair day's coal, but that stayed with him after the honour of cutting had long ceased to interest him.

He came to his own reading of the chests in his thirtieth year, in the dead of a winter when the vein ran thin and the school's own cutting fell behind its measure, so that the masters set him, for want of better work to give an idle hand, to going through the older leaves and striking out any apprentice long since dead whose account no longer served any purpose but to take up room. It was a task given him as a punishment more than a trust, Donnchadh said himself, once he was old, to more than one of his own pupils, and he did it at first the way a man does a punishment, without much thought beyond finishing it; but somewhere in the second month of that winter, with the strike-books stacked higher than his own head on the table before him and the lamp burned low at his elbow more nights than he afterward cared to count, he began setting a private tally of his own beside the school's: a count, leaf by leaf, of when in a cutter's years the coal had come brightest from the vein.

The answer, when he had it, was plainer than he had looked for. It made no difference whose house a cutter had been born to, the son of a master's line or a cutter with no line worth naming; every hand, without exception among the hundred and more he had gone through, cut its brightest and truest coal well on in its own years at the seam, seldom or never in its first, the vein answering, leaf after leaf, to years spent at it however little blood had been carried to it. Some nights the tally would not come out even, a leaf or two running against the grain of all the rest, and he set those aside in their own small stack rather than force them, on the reasoning, which he kept to all his life afterward, that a count a man has to bend to make it agree with him is no count at all. He brought the whole of it before the elders of the house on the night nearest midwinter, the whole school gathered as it gathered every year for the turning, and read it out plainly, leaf and year and hand, until the room had gone quiet enough that the lamp's own guttering was the loudest thing in it, and a cutter near the door, a young woman with no schooling in the chests at all, said afterward that she had understood, for the first time in her life, why the teachers made so much of a thing so small as a mark on hide.

The elders did not deny his count. They answered him instead, through the eldest of them, a teacher named Aonghas Cam who had held the chests longer than Donnchadh had been alive, that the vein answered what a cutter was born with, and that the years only showed what had been there from the first, the way a seed shows, in its ripening, no more than what it was planted as. "A seed planted poor does not ripen rich," Aonghas Cam said, "whatever the season does for it." It was an old answer, older than Cnoc bhàn's own strike-books, and Donnchadh had heard it given to lesser questions than his own more times than he could count; but he asked, that night, the one thing no apprentice before him had thought, or dared, to ask back: if the coal answered only to blood and the years showed nothing new, why did every hand in the chests, without one single exception among a hundred and more, show more with every year that passed than it had shown the year before. Aonghas Cam was quiet a while at that, turning it over, and said at last that a seed might ripen slowly and still be no richer a seed for the slowness, which struck more than one in the room as an answer to a question Donnchadh had not asked; and the school let the matter close there for that winter, as the school had let harder matters close before it on nights when no one present had the heart to press further.

## II. Of the Twenty-Two Hearers

Donnchadh did not let it close in his own mind, and for ten years he kept his count, adding to it every leaf that came into the chests in that decade and reading his tally aloud at every midwinter gathering, until the masters of Cnoc bhàn came to expect it of him the way they expected the turning of the year, some listening each time with more patience than the last and some with less. He gathered, over those years, a following among the younger teachers and the older apprentices that the house never troubled to give a name to until the followers had a name of their own choosing: those who heard Donnchadh out to the end of his tally before they answered him, as against those who answered before he had finished, and by the eighth year of it the two groups sat, at the midwinter gathering, on opposite sides of the same long room without any master having told them to.

What broke the house at last was smaller than the tally. In the tenth winter of his counting Donnchadh brought before the whole school not his count alone, which by then most of the house had heard often enough to recite along with him, but a plain question set beside it: if the vein answered practice and not blood, as his own hundred leaves and more showed it did, why did the house still write a cutter's parentage at the head of every leaf, before a single stroke of the cutter's own hand was set down. Aonghas Cam, older now and greyer, gave the same answer he had given ten years before, that the vein answered what a cutter was born with and the years only showed it; and Donnchadh, who had by then heard the answer so many times he could have spoken it himself in the old teacher's own voice, said only that a school which wrote a cutter's blood before it wrote a single stroke of the cutter's work had already answered its own question before the question was asked, and that he, for his own part, would keep no more books that way.

He did not leave that night, nor that winter. It took him the better part of a year to gather what he meant to take, twenty-two of the house's own hearers, apprentices and younger teachers both, who had sat on his side of the long room long enough that the choice, when it came, cost most of them less than it might have cost a stranger to the quarrel. Not all who had once sat on his side came with him in the end; three stayed at Cnoc bhàn on the plain grounds, given to Donnchadh himself without much softening, that a house was still a house whatever it wrote at the head of a leaf, and that they had no wish to spend the rest of their own years proving a point at the cost of the roof they had grown up under. Donnchadh took the refusal, by his own later word, harder than he let any of the twenty-two see at the time. They left Cnoc bhàn on 30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300, ten years to the season after Donnchadh's own question had first split the room, carrying between them copies of the strike-books they judged their own, made in their own hands over that last year from the chests that still stood, as they always had, in the long room behind the grove. The elders who watched them go called it theft, and said so plainly to the twenty-two as they loaded what they carried onto two ox-sledges borrowed from a carrier of the river for the day; Donnchadh, standing at the second sledge with the last of the leaves in his own arms, answered only that a copy taken from a book left whole behind it was no theft that any court on the island would know how to try, whatever a grieved house chose to call it, and that the leaves themselves, every one, still stood where they had always stood, for any hand at Cnoc bhàn that cared to read them.

They walked the half-day south and east to Muileann chaol, a mill-town on the same river the school at Cnoc bhàn stood beside, further down where the water ran slower and the banks stood wide enough for a settlement to spread without crowding the mill it was named for. Donnchadh had chosen the place himself, in the year of the gathering, for no reason he ever gave the twenty-two beyond that it lay far enough from Cnoc bhàn that the two houses would not trip over each other's grounds within a single season, and near enough that a letter could still cross between them inside a day. He was forty years old the day the sledges came into Muileann chaol's own square, grey already at the temple though no greyer than his father had been at the same age, and it was there, in a millwright's storehouse the town's own reeve let them at a rent none of the twenty-two could then have paid in silver and did pay, that first winter, in mended roofs and re-hung doors for half the town, that the second school of the stag began.

The storehouse itself had stood empty three years before Donnchadh's people came to it, a long low building of river stone the miller's own grandfather had raised for grain and never filled past its first floor, and the twenty-two spent that first autumn clearing out the old sacking and the damp before a single leaf of the strike-books was so much as unwrapped from the oiled hide it had travelled south in. One of the younger among them, a girl not yet twenty who had left a mother and two brothers still at Cnoc bhàn and never went back to see them, said afterward that she remembered the storehouse's own smell before she remembered anything Donnchadh ever taught her in it, mildew and river damp giving way, over that first winter's work, to the oil and old smoke the chests themselves would come, in their turn, to fill the place with. The town took to calling them, in that first season and for some years after, the river-house teachers, a name none of the twenty-two much minded, having no other name yet of their own choosing to set against it.

## III. Of the School Without Parentage

The rule Donnchadh set for the new school's own strike-books, once the storehouse had a proper chest to hold them and a proper roof to keep the damp from the leaves, was the one his ten years of asking had led him to and Cnoc bhàn had never once been willing to grant him: that a cutter's parentage should not be written in the book at all, not the father's name nor the mother's, not the house nor the line, only the cutter's own name, the day, and the stroke. An apprentice's leaf at Muileann chaol carried, from its very first line, nothing that a stranger reading it could use to say whose child had cut it, and more than one of the twenty-two, in those first years, found the omission harder to keep to than they had expected, a hand's habit of thirty years being slower to unlearn than a rule was to set down. One of the elder teachers among them, who had kept the Cnoc bhàn chests longer than any of the other twenty-two, was caught out at it three winters running, writing a father's name from long habit and scraping it out again before the ink had dried; she said of herself, to any apprentice who asked, that she had unlearned worse habits in her time and expected the fourth winter to serve where the first three had not, which it did. Donnchadh himself kept to the rule without exception, in his own leaves and in every leaf he checked over another's shoulder, and by the fourth or fifth year of the school's own keeping the omission had stopped feeling, even to the oldest of the twenty-two, like an omission at all.

Word of the new house reached Cnoc bhàn within the season, as word of anything done on that river reached the other bank soon enough, and for some years the two schools kept apart entirely, each teaching its own apprentices from its own chests and answering questions about the other, when a trader or a carrier asked, with no more than a dry word and a shrug. It was the school at Muileann chaol that broke the silence first, in FE 2,330, when Donnchadh, seventy years old by then and less able to travel even that short road himself than he once had been, sent a letter north by a carrier bound that way regardless, addressed to no one master of Cnoc bhàn by name but to the house at large, asking only whether the elder school's own count, kept now for near seven centuries, showed the same rise in a cutter's years that his own hundred leaves had shown thirty years before, or whether the years at Cnoc bhàn told some other tale entirely.

The answer came back within the month, in the hand of a teacher none at Muileann chaol had heard of before that winter, and said, in fewer words than Donnchadh's own letter had asked its question in, that the count was the same at Cnoc bhàn as he said it was at Muileann chaol, and had been the same for as long as any leaf in either house's chests could show it, and that this changed nothing whatever in what the elder school believed the coal answered to. Donnchadh read the letter twice at his own table, by his own account given to a pupil who asked him of it years later, and laughed once, without much humour in it, at a house that could grant him every fact he had spent forty years gathering and refuse him, in the same breath, the single conclusion he had built the facts to carry. He wrote back once more, a shorter letter than his first, saying only that the two houses, having agreed at last on what the vein showed, need not agree on what it meant to go on writing to each other about it; and it was that second letter, the reeve of Muileann chaol's own clerk noted years afterward in a private hand at the foot of a copy he kept for himself, that began the correspondence the two schools would keep for the rest of the age, neither house ever again letting a full season pass without some word crossing the river between them, whether the word carried agreement or its plain refusal.

Donnchadh mac Iain did not live to see the correspondence outlast its own quarrel. He died at Muileann chaol in his eightieth year, in the same storehouse-turned-schoolhouse the twenty-two had first taken shelter in forty years before, having taught, by the school's own later reckoning, some six generations of apprentices whose leaves, true to his own rule to the last, carried no name of father or mother anywhere upon them. He was buried, at his own asking given some years before his death to the pupils who would carry it out, not under any stone cut with his own house's mark, which by then none at Muileann chaol troubled to keep any longer, but under a plain leaf of oiled hide set in the ground above him and left to weather away in its own time, a grave-marker that told, within a season of rain, nothing of who lay beneath it but the one word he had asked cut upon it before it went into the ground: *scrìobhaiche*, one who writes.

## IV. Of the Vein That Asked No Judgement

In the same year that Donnchadh mac Iain died at Muileann chaol, a girl was born at Dùn ìseal, in the household of a clerk of the Hall's own roll, and given the name Raonaid Dhubh for the black hair she kept, unusually, from her first day, when most children of that household had been born fair. She grew up nearer the mountain's own vein than either school on the river had ever stood, in the long galleries the strike-books of the elder generation had first been born to keep account of, and came to the Hall's own service in her twentieth year as a clerk of the Keeper's own chest, the roll the Hall had kept in its own hand since the Keepers first wrote it down, which had passed, in the generations since, through more hands than any single leaf of it now bore a name for.

Her rise in that service came on a plainer reason than her own house cared to admit, an elder cousin's death leaving the Keeper's own stool empty at a season when no one else in the room wanted the sitting of it, much as the red hall's own clerk's stool had once been given to Peigi nic Tormoid for the same reason four centuries before her; and when the Keeper she served died, the nine hearths and the Four Houses gave the flame into Raonaid Dhubh's own hands, at six-and-twenty years old, the youngest to hold it in three generations. Word of the giving reached the granary households before the ink of the roll's own entry had dried, one reeve remarking to another, as the story was told afterward, that a Keeper young enough to be his own daughter would want watching the first year or two, a remark the reeve himself was said to have taken back within the season.

Raonaid Dhubh had known of the two schools' quarrel long before she came to the cup, as any clerk at Dùn ìseal knew of it, the letters between Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol having by then grown into a small archive of their own that more than one idle clerk had read through for want of livelier business on a slow afternoon. It came, by her own later account, as no great surprise to her when both houses, within her first year in office, sent word asking the same thing of the new Keeper that they had once asked, without much hope of an answer, of every Keeper before her: that the Hall say, once and plainly, which school's reading of the vein was the truer one, so that a matter forty years unsettled might at last be settled by a voice neither house could answer back to.

She heard them both at Dùn ìseal, in the same hall her own predecessors had heard lesser disputes in for longer than the mountain's own chests could number, a delegation from each school standing on either side of the same floor as the two halves of Cnoc bhàn's old long room had once sat on either side of a single table. The elder school's own delegation spoke first, an old teacher naming leaf after leaf of near seven hundred years to show how long the house's own reading had stood unshaken; the younger school answered with Donnchadh's own tally, carried north in a hand not his own, since none of the twenty-two who had first walked it south still lived to carry it themselves. Raonaid Dhubh let each speak its full case before she answered either, asking no question of her own beyond a plain point of date now and again, which one of the clerks with her noted afterward she had asked chiefly, he thought, to be certain both delegations knew she had listened to every word.

What she said, when both had finished, was fewer words than either delegation had spent making its case, and the Hall's own roll set it down that same evening in the plain hand of the clerk who had once been, before her own rise, no more than one voice among many reading old letters for want of livelier business: that the vein had never asked the Hall to give judgement on what a cutter was born with, and she saw no cause to give one now that it had not asked for, either school being free to keep its books as it judged best so long as neither book claimed for itself an authority the mountain had never granted to any book at all.

It was, the roll's own later summary noted, the plainest refusal any Keeper of that century had given, and for that reason, more than any ruling could have been, the one most often cited afterward by clerks weary of a dispute they had no wish to settle themselves: a Keeper's own words, once given, standing thereafter as a kind of ruling in everything but the name, though Raonaid Dhubh, asked years later by a younger clerk whether she had meant her answer to stand as one, said only that she had meant it as what it said and nothing further, and that a clerk who read more into four sentences than the four sentences carried was doing the roll no favour by it.

## V. Of Cnoc ghorm's Stone and the Diggers' Road

The two schools kept their letters after that hearing as they had kept them before it, neither claiming the Keeper's refusal for its own side though each, in its own private correspondence with its own house, read the silence somewhat to its own advantage; and it was scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol, ten years on from the hearing, who made the journey west to Cnoc ghorm in the autumn of FE 2,376 to look at a standing stone the town had kept at its own centre longer than any teller there could say, cut in a hand no school on the river, elder or younger, could make out a single letter of. The scholars stood before it the better part of a day, turning its worn face to the low autumn light from every angle a careful reading asks, tracing a finger along grooves that might have been letters once and might, as one of the younger scholars said, be nothing more than what any stone standing that long in that weather comes to wear on its own account. They left it, by evening, no nearer an answer than they had come with.

It was the people of Cnoc ghorm themselves, who read no more of the stone's own cutting than the scholars had, who gave the visitors what the stone would not give up on its own: that the stone said, as it had always been told in that town from mother to child longer than any single house there could trace its own line back, *cha do thàinig sinn; bha sinn ann*, we did not come; we were here. The scholars wrote the saying down exactly as the town gave it to them, together with the plain fact that neither they nor any hand before them had read the stone itself to confirm it, and left the matter there, in a hand as careful of what it did not know as of what it did; and no scholar of either school, nor any teller after them, ever explained the stone or the saying further, the one being, as the elder among the visiting party put it to the younger on the road home, no poorer a thing for having no explanation than a great many older things on the island that had gone unexplained a good deal longer.

Ten years after that again, in the summer of FE 2,386, a company of men from Baile ghorm to the south, hearing a tale grown old in their own district that the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin held riches enough to buy a poor man's house twice over, went up under cover of a single night and broke into the ruin's lower ground with picks and torches. The oldest of them, a mason's son named for no history now troubles to keep, had heard the tale from his own grandfather, who had heard it in turn from a grandfather of his own, so that none of the company digging that night could have said with any certainty how old the promise of riches was, only that it had never once, in all the tellings, been said to be false. They found, when the dawn came up on their digging, nothing beneath the fallen stone but ash, cold and undisturbed, that no fire any of them could name had left there.

The Keeper, word of the digging having reached Dùn ìseal within the fortnight, had the diggers brought before her and sentenced them as though they had broken the Law, though no law then written covered a ruin no living hand had built or owned; and it was that sentence, given for a wrong the roll admitted no statute named, that stood from that summer on as the rule for every old place the island held, that a thing standing from before any house now living could claim it was a thing no living hand had leave to break into, riches or no riches beneath it.

The families of the diggers did their penance, as the Keeper set it, by keeping in repair, at their own house's cost and their own house's labour, the road that ran from Baile ghorm south to the tomb-ground at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, a stretch of track that had gone to mud and broken stone in more winters than any reeve had troubled to count before that summer; and they kept it, the families and their children after them, long past the years any sentence could properly have bound them to, until the road, within a generation, had gone by no other name in all the southern hills but the one the penance had given it, the diggers' road, a name that told, to anyone who asked why an ordinary stretch of track between an ordinary town and an ordinary tomb-ground should carry so plain a title, the whole of the story in the two words alone.

By that same year the letters between Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol had crossed the river between them for near sixty years without a season's gap, two chests of correspondence standing now in each house beside the chests of strike-books that had begun the whole quarrel, neither school any nearer agreeing with the other on what the vein truly answered to than Donnchadh mac Iain and Aonghas Cam had been on the night the question was first asked aloud, and neither house, for all that, willing to let a single season pass without writing to say so.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Shared Meal

*FE 2,392 – 2,474*

> *Chan eil aran aig aon taigh a dh'easbhaidh aig taigh eile.*
> No house lacks bread while another has it.
>
> — still said at Àth dhìreach, of the extra bowl set out at the turn of the year

## I. Of the Carriers' Road

The coal road out of Muileann chiar ran high before it ran anywhere else, up out of the galleries by a track no cart could keep to, so that everything the mountain sent down to the lowlands and everything the lowlands sent up in trade went on a back or a pony's load, carried by families who had carried for their fathers and would carry for their sons, and who owned, most of them, nothing else worth the naming. Calum Ruadh of Àth dhìreach was such a man, broad through the shoulder from thirty years of it, and in a hard year in the middle of Lachlann Bàn's reign, before any granary law was thought of, he carried down more coal than his own household ate grain in trade for, a plain enough arithmetic that needed no clerk to read it. He was not the only one. Àth dhìreach that year, and Muileann gheal beside it, and the smaller houses of Doire uaine strung along the same track, all carried more than they were given back, because the lowland households they traded with had, in a poor season of their own, less to spare than the mountain had coal to sell, and no custom on the island yet bound one district to feed another when the trade between them ran short.

The small halting-house below the pass, where every carrier of that road broke his journey whether the day was fair or foul, kept in those years a rough tally of loads carried and grain owed, scratched on a board by the fire, and it was there, as Calum Ruadh was fond of saying, that a man first saw the whole shape of the trouble rather than only his own household's corner of it: mark after mark for coal going down and next to nothing coming up, in every hand that had cut a line on it that winter. The keeper of the house, an old woman named Mòr who asked no man his business before she fed him, told the carriers who stopped there that she had seen three such winters in her own life and buried a husband in the second of them, of a chest that a thinly fed winter had never let mend; she said it plainly, over the fire, to men too tired to answer her, and let the silence after do the rest of the telling.

Nothing came of that year worse than short commons and a hard winter got through on less than anyone would have chosen, and no teller troubled to set it down at the time, there being nothing in an ordinary hungry season that the island's rolls thought worth a line. But Calum Ruadh remembered it all his life, and told it after to his son, when the boy was old enough to understand why his father counted a full granary the way another man might count silver: that a mountain which lived by carrying could carry its own households into want as easily as any other house, and that no strength of back had ever yet fed a family through a winter when there was nothing at the bottom of the road to carry home.

It was in the years before, at Cathair dhearg on the plain below, that the red hall had passed by a road only the king-list itself troubles to keep whole, from Seonag Chrom's line to a house that traced its own line back to Goraidh Mòr, the rìgh who had first climbed to Dùn ìseal on foot with his spear left at the last house. Of the years between, the island's own rolls say little, and this telling has no better to add to them; but the line held, as lines on Dia-thìr mostly did, quietly, one reeve's book handed to the next, until a young man of six-and-twenty took the crown in his own right and gave his name, before his reign was very old, to a law that outlasted every other thing he did.

## II. Of Lachlann Bàn and the Granaries

Lachlann Bàn came to the red hall in his twenty-sixth year, and the household that raised him said of him afterward, when he was long past caring what was said, that he had been from a boy the kind who counted a room before he sat down in it: how many benches, how many at each bench, how much bread would need to be cut before the meal was called. It was not a gift that made him quick company, and it made him none at all with the reeves who had grown used to a looser hand at the granary door, but it served him, once he held the hall himself, in the one matter he is chiefly remembered for.

He found, in his first years, a hall whose granaries filled and emptied by no rule but the harvest and the whim of whichever steward kept the key that season, so that one province seat might sit on grain enough for three winters while another, a hard week's carry away, went short in the same year for no reason but that its own harvest had failed and nobody's business but its own to mend it. Lachlann Bàn thought this a poor way to keep a household, whether the household was his own kitchen or the whole island, and he set about building a granary in every province seat that would agree to keep one, of stone where stone could be had and of timber banked with turf where it could not, each one built to the same plan so that a steward moved from one to another would know, on the first morning, where the grain lay and how it was kept.

Cnoc mhòr, close under Cathair mhòr on the plain, built the first of them before any other seat on the island, and sent word of it to Cathair dhearg within the same season the roof went on, its reeve plainly hoping to be first noticed as well as first built. Lachlann Bàn sent back a silver ring for the reeve's own hand, a small enough thing beside the cost of the granary, but it did what he meant it to do, for within two years every province seat on the plain had a granary of its own or was building one, none of them wishing to be named last where Cnoc mhòr had been named first.

## III. Of the Law of the Common Granary

A granary built and never filled is a shed, and Lachlann Bàn knew it, so that the building was only the half of what he meant to do. He went himself to Dùn ìseal, in the fourth year of his reign, to put the other half to the Keeper who then held the cup, Raonaid Dhubh, a woman of the north country who had come to the flame at six-and-twenty herself and held it, by the time Lachlann Bàn climbed the last path to her door, for the better part of forty years.

What he asked her for was not new. Every household on the island already kept, as an unwritten custom older than any king-list, the habit of giving a neighbour grain in a hard year on the understanding that the neighbour would do the same when the turn came round; it was a kindness owed and repaid the way a fire was banked and relit, without anyone troubling to write down the terms of it. Lachlann Bàn wanted only to set that same custom under the granaries he had built, so that it ran district to district, at the pace of a full granary and an empty one, rather than house to house at the slower pace of one neighbour's memory: a household with grain above its winter's need would give the surplus to its district's common granary before the storm season closed the roads, and the granary would feed, in turn, any household of the district that ran short, without asking first whether the shortfall was the household's own fault or the year's.

Raonaid Dhubh heard him out at her own hearth, and it is told that she asked him only one question in return, whether he meant the law for his own reign or for every reign after his: and when he answered that a law worth the writing was worth writing for longer than one life, she set the cup down between them and said the custom was old enough already, and needed only a king willing to be bound by it as much as any carrier, before she would put her own hand to it. She asked him further, being a woman who had heard kings promise things before, whether he meant his own hall's own granary bound by the same terms as any household's, or held apart as a king's granary is so often held apart; and when he answered that the red hall's surplus would go in on the same terms and be drawn on the same terms, no household's need weighed heavier for being poorer than the crown's, she told him that was the answer she had been waiting to hear rather than the one she had asked for, and put her hand to the writing.

Lachlann Bàn swore, before her and before the flame, that his own hall's surplus would go into the granary at Cathair dhearg on the same terms as any household's, and the successors of Peigi nic Tormoid wrote the law into the rolls in full that same year, the first ever made by rìgh and Keeper together rather than by the hall alone.

Under the new law the granaries went up faster than before, and none faster than in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households lived wholly by cutting and carrying and grew almost nothing of their own, so that a common granary there was less a convenience than the difference, in a bad year, between a hard winter and a starved one. The lowland districts that were asked to fill those granaries grumbled at it more than once, being asked, as they saw it, to feed households that grew no grain of their own to put in return, and more than one reeve of the plain wrote to Cathair dhearg to say so plainly. Lachlann Bàn's own answer to one such letter is kept in the rolls yet: that a household which carried the plain's coal down every winter of its life had already paid, in the coin of its own back, for whatever grain the plain sent up in return, and he would hear no more of the matter unless the letter's writer wished to carry a season's coal himself before he judged what it was worth.

At Cathair mhòr, whose fishing towns grew no grain either, a granary was raised within the old town wall, the first anywhere to stand behind one, and the southern strands that fed it sent dried fish rather than barley for their own share, packed in baskets the same way the toll fish had once been packed for the Hall at Dùn ìseal, so that in a hard winter a mountain household might find itself, without knowing it, eating the same salt herring a fisher's wife had gutted a season before on a strand two days' walk from the nearest coal seam.

## IV. Of the Eastern Raiders and the Childless Queen

Not every trouble of those years bent to a granary's cure. Out beyond the eastern strands, where the fishing boats of Seann Tarr worked the shallows, outlaws in low black boats had begun raiding from the offshore islets, taking nets and dried fish from any strand too small to keep a watch, and running before any boat large enough to give chase could be launched after them. Sliochd Raghnaill, whose own house had held the boats of that coast since the reign of Eilidh nic Ìomhair, armed three of its own craft at Seann Tarr in answer, and caught the raiders at their own anchorage one grey morning with the tide against them, burning two of the low boats where they lay and losing, in the burning, more of the raiders' plunder than they recovered whole. The rest of the raiders' boats slipped the harbour mouth before the fire had well caught, and were not seen again on that stretch of coast for the length of the telling, though the strands kept a closer watch after, and Seann Tarr's own boys grew up knowing the shapes of the low black hulls the way other boys knew the shapes of gulls. The captain who led that morning's chase, a grandson of the house's own line named Ruairidh mac Nèill, was asked afterward by a trader why he had not pressed on and taken the rest of the raiders while the tide still ran against them; he answered only that a boat burned at its own anchorage was a lesson the strand's own watch would remember longer than a raider hanged at Seann Tarr, and that he had come out that morning to end a season's raiding, not to fill a gallows he had no order to fill.

Lachlann Bàn's own household, meanwhile, grew by one child only, a daughter, Oighrig nic Lachlainn, born in the four-and-thirtieth year of his reign and raised, from what the rolls of her own household say of her upbringing, with more of her father's habit of counting a room than any softness to balance it. She married, in her turn, a lord of no great house who died young of a fever some years before her father, and she bore him no children before his death nor after it, a plain fact that the hall's own clerks noted without comment at the time and that the island's greater houses, who noted everything touching a childless heir, did not let pass so quietly.

In the fourteenth year of Lachlann Bàn's reign, Raonaid Dhubh, who had kept the flame at Dùn ìseal since before he was crowned, died at last in her own eightieth year, having seen the law she had sworn to stand unbroken through its first years. The Keeper who followed her is named in the Hall's own rolls, but nowhere in the mountain's telling of what came after, the mountain households having troubled themselves, in the years that mattered most to them, far less with who held the cup at Dùn ìseal than with who kept the granary key at Muileann gheal.

Lachlann Bàn held the red hall five-and-fifty years from his crowning, longer than most of the reigns before or after his, and died in his own bed at one-and-eighty, mourned, the rolls say, chiefly by the reeves whose granaries he had built and by the carriers of the mountain roads, who had never once, in all his reign, gone the whole distance of a winter without knowing where the next grain was coming from. Oighrig nic Lachlainn took the hall in her own one-and-twentieth year, the same year her father was laid among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, and it was remarked at the time, by more than one house with an eye already on the succession after hers, that a queen with no child of her own body was a queen whose reign would be watched more closely at its end than at its beginning. The houses did not press the matter while she was young and the hall still full of her father's own men, but they began, before her reign was very old, the slow business of counting what each of them might claim should she die without an heir, a counting that went on quietly under the ordinary business of the hall for the whole of her reign and longer. Sliochd Ìomhair counted its claim by blood, being of the same house that had held Dùn dhearg since Ìomhar Dearg's own day; Sliochd Thormoid counted its claim by the clerks who had kept the hall's own rolls since Tormod Scrìobhaiche first set a ruler's name on oiled hide; Sliochd Raghnaill counted its claim by the boats it had armed at Seann Tarr and every strand its own captains had kept safe since; and Sliochd Mhuirich, which held the Keeper's own office and had held it since the Binding, counted nothing at all, being of the one house on the island that had never once, in all the age, put its hand to the cup for itself.

None of the four houses spoke its counting aloud in Oighrig's own hearing, and she gave no sign, in all the years of her reign, that she had heard of it; but a clerk of that room, copying a routine grant of land some years into her reign, noted in the margin of his own copy, in a hand meant for no eye but his own successor's, that the hall's business went on as it always had, and that a hall which goes on as it always has is a hall whose ruler has begun to be watched for the day it will not.

## V. Of the Late Snow

The trouble that came was weather, and it came the way weather on Dia-thìr had always come to the mountain, without asking leave of any reign. The watchers who kept the cairns above Cnoc ghlas, whose whole office was watching the high passes for the sign that told the Hall when the galleries might safely open, looked up one spring in Oighrig's eleventh year and saw snow lying white on the passes long past the day it should have gone, and looked again a month later, and saw it lying still. The Hall, on their word, kept the galleries shut a full season longer than the custom of the mountain expected, for a cutter caught by a late fall on those slopes was a cutter not coming home, and no reeve at Dùn ìseal was minded to weigh a season's coal against a company of cutters buried under it.

When the galleries did at last open, they opened late and closed early at the first sign of the passes closing again, and the coal that came down that whole season was not a third of what a common year gave. For the mountain households, who had nothing of their own to fall back on but the coal they carried and the grain they carried it for, the shortfall was not a hardship to be borne so much as a debt with no way to pay it: Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach alike found themselves, by the season's end, with nothing left to trade for grain at all, their own granaries already thin from the two poor years before, and by the following autumn the households of all three were eating, one careful handful at a time, the very seed they would need in spring if the next planting was to be anything at all.

Calum Ruadh, old now and past the heaviest carrying himself, sat that autumn at his own hearth with his son Iain Caol, a boy of some fifteen years grown already near his father's own height, and told him plainly, the way he had never troubled to soften a hard fact for the boy before, that this was the very want he had carried through as a young man, come round again in his own old age, and that neither of them would live to see it not come round a third time unless something below the mountain had changed since the last. Iain Caol asked him, being at the age when a boy first begins to ask his father questions the father cannot easily answer, whether the new law the old king had made would hold any better than the old custom had. Calum Ruadh told him he did not know, never having seen a law tried by a true want before, only by grumbling reeves with grain enough to spare in the end whatever they wrote to Cathair dhearg about it.

## VI. Of the Granaries Opened

The law was tried, and it held. Word went down from Cnoc ghlas to Cathair dhearg of the mountain's want before the worst of the winter, and Oighrig nic Lachlainn, whose own household had never once gone hungry in her life, gave the order the same week the word reached her: the common granaries of the mountain were to be opened at Muileann gheal, the largest of the three seats, and every household of the three settlements was to draw on it as its own need asked, without a steward standing over the door to weigh whether the need was proved.

The granary at Muileann gheal ran low again within the month, the three settlements together holding more mouths than one granary had ever been built to feed through a whole winter, and it was here that the law was tried a second time, in a matter the writing had never troubled to say in so many words. The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had for generations kept their own granaries close and their own accounts closer, apart even from the rest of the plain, opened the old stores of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain the same week word of the shortfall reached them, and sent the grain up the carriers' roads before any order came down from Cathair dhearg telling them to. Oighrig nic Lachlainn wrote afterward, in a letter the Hall's own clerks kept, that she would have given the order herself had Dùn dhearg only waited for it; the clerk who copied her words into the roll added beneath them, in the same dry hand every clerk of that room seemed to inherit from the one before, that Dùn dhearg had not waited.

Calum Ruadh was among the carriers who went down for that grain, too old by his own reckoning for the full weight of a load but unwilling, he told his son, to sit at his own hearth while younger men carried what his own life's work had once carried in a leaner year with no granary at the bottom of the road to catch it. Iain Caol went with him, not yet old enough by the town's own reckoning to carry a man's load but old enough to carry half of one, and it was the boy, walking the last mile into Àth dhìreach behind his father with the light going and the first sacks of Dùn dhearg's grain on both their backs, who first heard what the town meant to do for the men who had brought it.

The carriers took no fee for that winter's carrying, no household on the mountain having anything to pay them with, and in the town's own account of what came after, it was this refusal, more than the grain, that Àth dhìreach chose to answer. The reeve of the settlement called the whole town together before the spring thaw, in the same hall the households used for weighing tolls and settling boundary disputes, and asked the carriers who had walked the road that winter to stand forward where all could see them; Calum Ruadh, being the eldest of them and the one whose own hunger the town remembered longest, was asked to stand first, and stood with his son beside him though the boy had carried, by his own honest word to the reeve, no more than half a man's share of it.

The reeve granted, before the whole gathering, that every carrier who had stood forward that day should have the right to rest, for the whole of his life after, in any house of Àth dhìreach without payment asked or expected, and asked the town's own households, one by one round the hall, whether each would keep the grant as its own word rather than as any order out of Cathair dhearg. Every household answered that it would, Mòr of the halting-house loudest of any of them, being the one among the town's own who had fed the coldest of that winter's carriers longest before the grain ever came. It was kept, from that day, as a right the town's own households owed rather than any the Hall recorded, on the reasoning, as one of the elders present put it, that a kindness owed to a neighbour was the neighbour's business to keep, not the Hall's to write down. Not one soul of the three settlements is known to have died of hunger that whole winter, a fact the mountain's own tellers set beside the granting of the right whenever the tale is told, as though the one could not be properly understood without the other.

## VII. Of the First Load and the Bowl Still Set

Iain Caol grew to a man's full height and strength in the years after, and it was known of him, by those who remembered his father's own carrying, that he walked the coal road with much of Calum Ruadh's own steadiness, though the two men rarely put their loads down at the same waypoint house any longer, Calum Ruadh's back having given out at last, past sixty, to more years of the road than most carriers' backs were asked to bear. Iain Caol took up his own first load as a carrier proper in his three-and-twentieth year, in the autumn of Oighrig nic Lachlainn's nineteenth year in the hall, walking the same track his father had walked before him with a company of four other young men of Àth dhìreach, none of whom had carried a working load before that season.

He was not one of the carriers the town had named in the granting after the famine winter, being too young then by the settlement's own reckoning to have carried a full share, and it was a plain fact he never once, in all his life, tried to claim otherwise. But the men the town had named grew old through the years of his own carrying, one by one, and as each of them died the town found itself, without ever quite deciding to, extending the same rest to whichever carrier of that road was oldest living at the time, on the reasoning that a custom kept for the men who had walked the famine's road was a custom that belonged, in the end, to the road and not only to the particular feet that had first walked it hungry. Iain Caol, by the time he was old himself, had carried that road the better part of fifty years, through easy seasons and two lean ones after, and had buried, along the way, every man who had carried grain up to Muileann gheal in the year he was a boy of fifteen at his father's hearth.

In his own last years, when his legs would carry him no further than the halting-house and back, Iain Caol took to telling the whole of it himself, at the turn of every year, to whatever children of the town would sit still long enough to hear an old man out: his father's own hungry youth, the late snow above Cnoc ghlas, the granaries opening at Muileann gheal, and the night the reeve had called the whole town together and asked every household, one by one, whether it would keep the grant as its own word. He never once, in the telling, put himself among the carriers the town had named that day, being as careful an old man about the plain truth of it as he had been a young one; but he set out, every year he told it, a bowl at his own hearth all the same, for whichever carrier might be on the road that night, and let the children carry that habit home with them the way he had once carried grain, without troubling to explain to them why a boy too young to have earned a right should be the one keeping it.

He died at Àth dhìreach an old man, in the ninetieth year of his own life, the last then living of any who could say he had carried on that road in the years the famine and the right to rest were both still new, and the right the town had kept for its carriers died with him, there being none left of that particular reckoning to extend it to. It is told, and the town does not trouble to soften the telling, that no carrier's back has since been asked to bear a winter's want the way that mountain once bore it, the coal roads having grown wider and the granaries fuller with every reign since Lachlann Bàn's; and so the right was never renewed for want of the hunger that had first earned it, though what remains of it is kept all the same, at the turn of every year, in the one bowl still set out at Àth dhìreach's own hearths for whatever carrier is on the road that night, whether he has any claim to it by the old reckoning or none at all.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Shut Hall and the Choosing of Gilleasbuig

*FE 2,475 – 2,558*

> *Cha do rugadh rìgh; chaidh e a shuidhe air an stòl a bh' ann.*
> No king was born; he came and sat on the stool that was there.
>
> — a saying of the clerks of Seann Dunn, kept in no other house

## I. Of the Boy at the Rolls

At Seann Dunn the hall and the shrine stood on the near bank of the Abhainn chaol, and the mountain stood across the water, and between them the ford ran shallow enough in summer that a boy of five could wade it holding his father's hand. Gilleasbuig's father was Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid, and his trade was the same trade Peigi nic Tormoid's line had kept since her own hand was first proved worth telling from another's: he sat at a bench under the shrine's north window with a knife and a scraped hide and put down, in the small square hand the house had taught for six generations, whatever the red hall sent him to copy. Gilleasbuig grew up under that bench before he grew up beside it. He knew the smell of the scraping-knife's grease before he knew the sound of his own name in any mouth but his mother's, and by the time he was old enough to be sent for water he could tell, without being told, which of his father's rolls was the king-list and which was only a province's tithe.

He asked once, small enough still to be answered rather than sent off, why the king-list needed six copies where the tithe needed one. His father said the tithe would be true for a year and then thrown out, and a king-list had to be true for longer than any man who wrote it, so it went into six hands at once, that if fire took one house or flood another, the rest would still agree. Gilleasbuig turned that over for the length of a whole winter and came back to it in the spring with a second question, whether a king-list could be wrong if all six copies agreed and were wrong the same way. His father put down the knife at that one and looked at him a while before he answered, and what he answered the boy did not think worth remembering until he was an old man himself and had cause to remember it very well.

The temple across the river was Sliochd Thormoid's own, raised in Eilidh nic Ìomhair's day when the Four Houses were first bound, and its lamp burned the Small-Burning Law's measure like every other lamp on the island, or was supposed to; the other three houses said, in the flat voice houses use for an old grievance they no longer trouble to prove, that Seann Dunn's lamp burned fuller than its neighbours'. Gilleasbuig heard that said at his own hearth more than once before he was ten, always by a stranger and always denied at once by whoever in his own house was nearest, and he learned early that a thing repeated and denied in the same breath, in every house on the island, was probably not worth losing sleep over either way.

He learned his letters at that bench, and then the shapes of the Roinn's old shares, and then, because his father's hand was wanted at Cathair dhearg two summers out of three, the road between Seann Dunn and the red hall, first riding behind Tormod Beag and later, at fourteen, riding alone with the rolls in a satchel across his back and a hearth-sign token that let him sleep free at any waypoint house on the way. The road ran a day and a half in fair weather, down through the mountain districts and onto the lowland plain, and he came to know every waypoint keeper on it by name before he knew half the great families whose shares those waypoints stood in, which his father said was the proper order for a clerk to know a road in, whatever order a lord might prefer.

He was set once, at eleven, to copy out a short roll of a province's tithe under his father's eye, and made in it a single error, a stroke too many in a number that turned a modest year into a plentiful one, and did not himself catch it. His father caught it before it left the bench, scraped the hide clean to the one line, and made him write the whole roll again from the beginning rather than mend the single stroke, though the mending would have taken a tenth of the time. Gilleasbuig asked, aggrieved as a boy of eleven is entitled to be, why the whole roll needed doing over for one wrong stroke. His father told him that a roll with one mended stroke in it taught a boy that a mistake could be quietly put right, and a roll done over from the beginning taught him it could not, and that of the two lessons only one was worth having in a clerk who might one day be trusted with a roll no one stood over to check. Gilleasbuig did the roll over, and never again, by his own later account, let a wrong stroke stand unscraped in anything that left his own bench.

He was, by every account that troubles to say anything of him at all before his fortieth year, an unremarkable clerk's son doing an unremarkable clerk's work, and there is no sign that he thought of himself as anything else, or that anyone else thought of him as anything else, until the year the line of Goraidh Mòr ran out.

## II. Of the Failing of a Line

The failing had been long in coming and was no secret to anyone who read the rolls Gilleasbuig's own house kept. Lachlann Bàn had built his granaries and set his shared-meal law with the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh, and had a daughter, Oighrig nic Lachlainn, who took the red hall at one-and-twenty and held it the better part of fifty years without ever bearing a child of her own body. The houses had begun their counting early, before her reign was even half spent; Gilleasbuig heard it done at his own father's bench, in the careful unhurried voices men use when they are reckoning something they hope not to need. Sliochd Ìomhair reckoned its blood, which ran thin by then but ran; Sliochd Thormoid reckoned the clerks who had kept every roll the red hall owned since Tormod Scrìobhaiche's own day; Sliochd Raghnaill reckoned its boats and its silver and the seat at Seann Tarr the Small-Burning Law had first named. Only Sliochd Mhuirich, which held the Keeper's own office and answered to no share at all, took no part in the reckoning, and said, when asked, that the vein had not asked it to give judgement on the matter.

Oighrig herself, whom Gilleasbuig saw only once in his life, on a summer he came to Cathair dhearg at sixteen with his father's rolls, was by then a spare grey woman who signed what was put before her and asked few questions of it; the famine that was never allowed to become a famine had happened under her reign and under her name, though it was Lachlann Bàn's law and the reeves of Dùn dhearg's own quick hands that had turned it back, and she is remembered, where she is remembered at all, for having been present at a good thing rather than for having done it. She asked him, that one summer, whose son he was, and when he told her, said only that his father's hand was known to her and left it there; it was the whole of the speech any ruler of the island ever made to him before he came to sit where she had sat, and he remembered it, he said later, chiefly for how little either of them had thought to make of it at the time.

She died at Cathair dhearg in her one-and-seventieth year, without an heir of her body and with the line of Goraidh Mòr ending in the same breath as her own life did, and the red hall was shut behind her, its doors barred and its clerks — Gilleasbuig's own house among them — set to keep it, there being no other hand to give it to.

Gilleasbuig was one-and-forty that year, a clerk of thirty years' standing and no more remarkable than he had ever been. He was at Seann Dunn when the word came up the river road, and what he remembered of the day, when he was old and told it, was the small practical scramble that followed it at his own hearth: which rolls to send down to Cathair dhearg and which to keep, and whether the shrine's own lamp should be let burn on as before or banked against a season nobody yet knew the shape of. He said the news of it, oddly, went out of his head almost at once, crowded out by the tally of rolls he had to sort before nightfall.

## III. Of the Shut Hall

The clerks kept the shut hall the better part of two years before the Four Houses so much as agreed to sit in the same room together, and Gilleasbuig's own hand was among the hands that kept it: he rode down to Cathair dhearg the winter after Oighrig's death and stayed the better part of a season, sealing rolls and answering, as best a clerk could answer for a hall with no one in it, the reeves who came asking whom they were to render their accounts to now. He told them, truthfully, that he did not know, and that the tallies were to be kept all the same, on the plain reasoning that whoever came to the red hall next would want them true and would not thank a clerk for having let a good year go unrecorded for want of a name to put at its head.

The queen's own chambers were shut with the rest of the hall, the fires in them let go cold, and Gilleasbuig slept that whole season in the rolls-chamber among the boxes of hide, with the other clerks of the house of Tormod turning the lock in the great door themselves each night, since no steward remained whose office it was to do it for them. He wrote to his father once that winter that a red hall with no one in it was, for all that anyone outside it could tell, exactly the same red hall it had always been, the rolls being kept, the rents being reckoned, the granaries opening and shutting to the same seasons; only the men who kept it knew how strange it felt to hand a reeve his own tally and have no name to put after the word *sworn to*.
