His father's answer, kept among the house's own letters, said that a clerk who found that stranger than he found the years before it, when the tallies were kept for a queen he never once saw sign her own name to them, had not yet understood what a clerk's work had always been.

The Four Houses met at last at Dùn ìseal, in the second year of the shut hall, because no custom on the island covered a red hall with no one to fill it and the Hall's own ground was the one place none of the four could be told they had no right to stand. Sliochd Ìomhair claimed by blood, thin as that blood now ran; Sliochd Thormoid claimed through the clerks who alone among the four houses had never once let the rolls fall silent in fifty years of an ageing queen; Sliochd Raghnaill claimed through its boats and its silver, which by then paid for more of the island's carrying than any two of the other shares together. Sliochd Mhuirich, whose own house held the Keeper's office and so stood outside every reckoning of blood or trade, made no claim at all, and said again what it had said at Oighrig's death, that the vein had not asked it to give judgement on the matter of a stool it had never sat in and had no wish to.

How long the three houses argued, and whether they argued in good faith or only long enough to be seen to have argued, is not a thing the rolls of any of them agree on; Sliochd Ìomhair's own account, kept at Dùn dhearg, makes more of the sitting than Sliochd Raghnaill's does, and Sliochd Thormoid's account, kept by the same clerks' bench Gilleasbuig had grown up under, says least of all, which a man might read either as modesty or as the plain fact that the clerks had the least to gain from making the quarrel sound weighty. What is agreed by all three is that no blow was struck and no word was said that could not be unsaid over the same table the next morning, and that the sitting dragged three years past the meeting itself before any name was put forward that all four houses could be brought to sit still for.

Gilleasbuig himself sat through most of that sitting at the edge of the room rather than in it, called down from Cathair dhearg twice a year to lay the hall's own rolls before whichever house asked to see them, and so he heard more of the three years' arguing, from the doorway and the side bench, than any of the four houses' own principals ever troubled to say to his face. He heard Sliochd Ìomhair's eldest ask, more than once, what blood was worth if it were passed over for a boat or a bench; he heard Sliochd Raghnaill answer that the island's silver did not care whose grandfather had held a hill, only whose hand could be trusted to reckon it truly; and he heard, oftenest of all, the long patient silences of Sliochd Mhuirich's own man, who came to every sitting, said the same few words at the start of it and the end of it, and otherwise let the other three talk themselves hoarse over a stool his own house had no wish to sit in. Of himself, in all that time, nobody asked anything at all, beyond whether the year's tallies balanced, and he answered that question, each time it was put, exactly as truly as he had ever answered it for Oighrig.

## IV. Of the Cup Set in His Hands

The name that was put forward, in the end, was Gilleasbuig's own, and by every account it was Sliochd Raghnaill that first said it aloud, on the reasoning that a clerk who had kept the shut hall's rolls straight for three years without once putting his own house's claim ahead of the work had shown, whether he meant to or not, exactly the kind of hand a red hall wanted at its head. Sliochd Ìomhair, whose blood claim would have cost the other three houses more to refuse outright than any of them wished to pay, consented on one condition only, which it had been readying since the first year of the shut hall and did not trouble to soften in the asking: that whoever took the red hall, the graves at Dùn dhearg would remain the kings' own burying-place, as they had been since Ìomhar Dearg first washed his hands at the ford. Gilleasbuig, when the condition was put to him, is said to have answered that he had never in his life expected to be buried anywhere else, which was true in a plainer sense than the house that heard it understood, and the condition was sworn to on the spot.

He was summoned to Dùn ìseal in the sixth year of the shut hall, in his six-and-fortieth year, and told nothing of why beyond that his own presence was wanted before the council; he rode down from Cathair dhearg expecting, by his own account, to be asked some further question about the tallies, and packed no better cloak than he wore for any ordinary sitting. He stood before the council of the Four Houses in that same plain cloak while Sliochd Raghnaill's own elder named him, and Sliochd Ìomhair, having already had its condition of the graves sworn to beforehand, consented without argument, and Sliochd Mhuirich's man said the same few words he had said at every sitting for three years, which this time were enough.

The Keeper set the stone cup in his hands, filled to the fill of two palms as it had been filled for every household's dues since Fionnlagh Dall's own day, and for the first time in the whole of the age a ruler was made under the mountain rather than crowned or chosen anywhere else on the island. Gilleasbuig held the cup a long moment before he drank from it, and what struck him then, by his own later telling, was the plain foolishness of a clerk's son from Seann Dunn holding in his two hands the very measure his own father had spent a lifetime copying onto hide for other men to swear by. He asked the Keeper, before he drank, whether a clerk's hands were the right shape for it; the Keeper answered that the cup had no opinion of the hands that held it, only of whether they spilled it, and Gilleasbuig did not spill it. It looked, more than one chronicler has since said dryly, very much as though the Hall had made the king, there being no blood in the choosing and no boat and no old grievance settled, only a hand the Hall had come to trust with its own rolls.

He rode to Cathair dhearg that same season to take the red hall, by the lowland road his father had ridden twice a year for thirty years, and slept his first night in it, by his own account, in the small room off the rolls-chamber where the clerks kept their own beds, because the queen's own chambers had stood empty five years and nobody had thought yet to air them.

## V. Of the Line Drawn and the Temple Enlarged

His first act of any weight, the year after the cup was set in his hands, was to have the king-list copied again from its beginning, in his own house's careful square hand, with a single line drawn beneath the name of Oighrig nic Lachlainn. He drew it, or had it drawn, not to mark her death, which every copy of the list already marked well enough in its own way, but to mark the ending of a whole line of names running back to Goraidh Mòr, so that no clerk after him would waste an afternoon hunting a kinship that no longer existed. The line is in every copy of the king-list made since, and it is the first mark in the whole record that a clerk's own hand put there for a reason the clerk himself troubled to explain in the margin, which some later readers have taken as the surest sign of all that a clerk, and not a warrior or a boat-captain, had at last come to sit in the red hall.

He kept the clerks' office in his own house's hands for the whole of his reign, which cost him nothing, since no other house had ever much wanted the work of it, and he sent for his son Tormod, a boy of sixteen already taught the bench at Seann Dunn as Gilleasbuig himself had been taught it, to sit beside him at Cathair dhearg and learn the red hall's own rolls before he was taught anything else of ruling, on the same reasoning his own father had given him and never troubled to improve upon. He enlarged his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a full temple in the one-and-twentieth year of his reign, with a court where pilgrims from as far as Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chiar could stand under a roof while they waited their turn at the lamp, and the other three houses said, as they had always said, that its measure burned fuller than the Law allowed; a Keeper's cutter was sent every season after to try it by the same weights used everywhere else on the island, and every season the cutter found the measure kept, which satisfied nobody who had not already believed it and changed the mind of nobody who had not already doubted it, and so the saying outlived the doubt by a good many years, as sayings will.

By the plain evidence of the rolls his own house kept of him, he was neither a great king nor a poor one. He raised no new law that outlasted him and lost no old right that had not already been half lost before he came to the cup; the granaries Lachlann Bàn had built stood full or empty by the same seasons as before him, and the roads his mason predecessors had cut were mended by the same waypoint-keepers as before him. The island under his hand was, by every account, neither better nor worse governed than it had been under Oighrig's, only governed by a man who had grown up knowing exactly how the rolls that governed it were kept, which is not nothing, though it is not much to set beside the deeds of the men the earlier tellings of this age remember.

He heard, in his eighth year, the one dispute of his reign the rolls trouble to set down whole: a household of Muileann àrsaidh and a household of Ceann àrsaidh both claiming a single water-meadow their grandfathers had shared without a stone between them, each holding a notched stick that named the whole meadow theirs and neither stick agreeing with the other. Gilleasbuig sent a clerk of his own house, rather than a steward, to copy both sticks stroke for stroke before he judged anything, and found that the two tallies agreed exactly up to a season forty years back and disagreed only after it; this told him less about the meadow than about the year a notch had been cut wrong by someone long dead on one side or the other. He gave the meadow to neither household outright and to both together, with a boundary stone cut down its centre for the first time in living memory, on the plain reasoning that a stick a man could not check against another man's stick was worth exactly as much as the two men trusted each other, which by then was not much. The households of Muileann àrsaidh and Ceann àrsaidh have shared the meadow by that stone ever since, and grumbled at it about equally, which a clerk of Seann Dunn once told his own son was the surest sign a judgement had been fair.

## VI. Of His Death and the Son Who Followed

He died at Cathair dhearg in his one-and-seventieth year, in the small room off the rolls-chamber he had never troubled to leave for the queen's own empty chambers, having kept, to the end, the habit of rising before his own household to check the night's tally against the day's before either was sent on to a steward. He was carried to Dùn dhearg to be buried among the house of Ìomhar, as had been sworn at his choosing, over five days on the lowland road his own father had ridden twice a year for thirty years, the bier stopping each night at a waypoint house whose keeper had known him first as a boy with a satchel of rolls and last as the man whose seal was on every tally in the house. Sliochd Ìomhair kept its own oath to the letter: the grave was dug beside Ìomhar Dearg's own kin, and no voice was raised against a clerk's son lying there, the condition having been the graves' and not the blood's.

His son Tormod succeeded him at Cathair dhearg in his one-and-fortieth year without any meeting of the Four Houses at all, and none of the four asked for one; whatever quarrel over the red hall the island had once thought worth three years of sitting at Dùn ìseal for, it had by then settled itself so thoroughly into a single house's keeping that a son following a father seemed to every house the plainer course, and the plainer course, once taken, was never afterward questioned. Between that quiet handing-on and the coming of a queen from the same house long years later, the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives nine rulers their names and their years and very little else, the clerks of Gilleasbuig's own line having proved, in the reigns that followed his son's, as diligent in the keeping of the rolls as they were brief in the writing of anything beyond a harvest, a toll and the mending of a bridge. It is a sign, the tellers of Seann Dunn still say, of an island doing tolerably well; a shut hall had been filled without a blow struck over it, and a clerk's own careful hand had proved, in the end, as sound a measure of a king as blood or a boat or an old grievance nursed three centuries long.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of the Bridges, the Riders and the North-West

*FE 2,559 – 2,791*

> *Chan eil clach gun neach a chuir ann i.*
> No stone stands without a hand that set it there.
>
> — the fourth hearth's own saying, said over every keystone since Ros fhionn

## I. Of the Carts on the Lowland Roads

The list at Dùn ìseal keeps no ruler's name between Tormod Òg, who died in the seventieth year of his own life without ever walking the whole circuit his father had been chosen to walk, and Anna Ruadh, who came to the red hall two hundred and thirty-six years after him and walked it twice. Of the reigns that filled those years the rolls say only that the red hall passed from hand to hand at Cathair dhearg as it had passed since Gilleasbuig, without war and without a name any teller troubled to keep past its own generation; and where the red hall has so little to say, this telling turns, as it has turned before, to the roads, the bridges and the shore, whose keeping fell to no single house and so was never once let lapse for the want of one.

The lowland roads in those years carried more than they had ever carried before, for the cart had come onto them at last in numbers, where for the whole of the age before it a back or a pony's load had done most of a household's carrying between one waypoint house and the next. A cart asked more of a road than a back ever had: it asked a level bed where a foot could climb a rut without complaint, and it asked, above all, a bridge wide enough to take it, where the narrow footbridges of the earlier reigns had answered a walking man and nothing wider. The bridge at Cathair dhearg, first thrown by Ailean Clachair's own fellowship in the reign before Mòrag nan Rathad and widened once already in her own time, was widened a third time in these years, its old piers kept and a new span laid across them broad enough for two carts to pass abreast without either driver giving way to the other. The hearth-sign was cut again into the new keystone, the same small mark the fourth hearth had cut into every crossing since Ros fhionn, and the masons who cut it left, beside it, the old stone that had carried the sign before, set into the parapet where any hand might touch it, rather than break it for rubble as an easier fellowship might have done.

It was in this same stretch of years that the road-guards of Dùn dhearg first took to riding the lowland roads rather than walking them, mounted on the small tough horses of the southern grass country, bred for a light rider and a long day rather than for weight or war. A guard on foot had answered a quarrel at a waypoint house only after it had cooled into a grievance nursed over a night's telling and retelling; a guard on a horse could be at the same house before the first blow had properly landed, and it changed, within a few years, the whole temper of the road-guard's own trade, from a company that judged what had happened to one that could, on a fast enough horse, sometimes stop it happening at all. The riders of that first company are the earliest whose names the road-guard's own roll troubles to keep, and for a long while after they were the only ones so kept, every rider before them having ridden nothing faster than his own two feet and so left no mark on a roll built to record a particular kind of speed.

## II. Of the Mending at Ros fhionn

The flood that took the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's own span above Ros fhionn came in a wet spring some way into this stretch of years, a season of rain on rain that swelled every river of the western shares past any bank built to hold it, and it carried off, along with a good stretch of the road on the eastern bank, three households built too near the water on the strength of a hundred quiet years. The masons of the fellowship, called down from Cathair dhearg within the same season, found the span standing where Ailean had left it, its piers untouched by a flood that had taken lesser work on every side of it, and set about mending only the washed-out approach, laying a new causeway on stone footings deep enough, this time, that no flood within living memory of the mending was ever expected to trouble it again.

It was in clearing the old approach for the new footings that the masons came, at last, to the keystone Ailean had cut with his own hand in the hundred and sixtieth year of the age, the small mark of the fourth hearth that said, to any mason's eye that knew to look for it, that living hands and not chance had raised the stone above it. The sign was as sharp as the day it was cut, the grey stone of that quarry having proved, as Ailean himself had judged it would when he chose the face near Ros fhionn over an easier one closer to hand, harder wearing than most that went into a bridge on Dia-thìr; and the masons who found it, none of them born when Ailean cut it, left it exactly as they found it, cutting their own new work a full course below rather than disturb a sign that had already outlasted the man who set it and looked fit to outlast a good many masons after. It became, from that mending onward, a small custom among the fellowship, never written into any rule of theirs but kept all the same, that a mason sent to mend an older crossing left the old signs standing wherever the stone beneath them still stood, and cut his own work apart from them rather than over them, so that a bridge mended twice might carry, in its own stones, the mark of every hand that had answered for it.

## III. Of Dùn chrom and Ceann àrsaidh

Two crossings went up in those same years that the fellowship built new rather than mended, and neither answered quite the same want as Ros fhionn's had.

The first spanned the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western by a route that saved a full day's cart-journey over the long way round through Cathair dhearg, and the fellowship set its toll, by a custom of its own that no rule of the red hall had ever told it to keep, at half of what the road-toll asked at the capital's own crossing, the mason who led that building holding it no fair thing to charge a full toll for half the road. Cathair dhearg's own reeves complained of it loudly and at length, in letters the rolls still keep, arguing that a toll set anywhere on the island by anyone but the crown's own reckoning was a toll that would, in time, be set anywhere by anyone, and calling the fellowship's half-measure at Dùn chrom the year the red hall's own word on tolls first went unanswered. The fellowship answered, through the mason who had set the toll, that a bridge built by its own hands on its own stone might be priced by its own reckoning until the red hall chose to build one of its own beside it, and offered, should Cathair dhearg wish it otherwise, to hand the whole crossing over to the crown's own keeping, tolls and upkeep together. No reeve of Cathair dhearg ever took up that offer, the upkeep of a bridge proving, as it generally does, a less welcome inheritance than the toll alone, and the half-toll at Dùn chrom stood unaltered for as long as the fellowship stood.

The second crossing, at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, was the fourth stone bridge raised across the lowlands, and it was built, from the first stone laid to the last, by forty of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill rather than by cutters bred to the trade, men and women who had learned the mason's craft in a season when their own boats lay idle after the burning at Seann Tarr had thinned the raiders from that coast and left, for a while, more hands on the strand than there was fish to occupy them. The fellowship's own roll at Cathair dhearg names all forty, a courtesy it did not always trouble to extend to a crew of borrowed hands, and the reason given in the same roll is plain enough in its own way: that forty people who had learned a new trade rather than sit idle through a season deserved, whatever their birth, to be named among the masons who had spent a life at it. The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh stood a little rougher in its coursing than Ros fhionn or Dùn chrom, the fisher-kin's hands being surer, that first winter, with a net than with a chisel, but it stood, and it carried, within the year, more cart-traffic between the river towns of the eastern lowlands than any crossing before it had carried in three.

## IV. Of Beathag Clachair

Among the households that settled, in these same generations, along the fellowship's own roads rather than at any single hearth, was a family of Doire mhin on the southern road, cutters of ordinary boundary-stones and byre-lintels for three generations before a daughter of that house was born, one whose fellowship remembers her still for a single small mark on a bridge no grander than a dozen others of its own age, though every boundary-stone her grandfather ever cut has weathered past reading.

Beathag Clachair came to her family's own trade the way most of that trade's daughters and sons came to it, at an age too young to remember choosing it, her first task no harder than sweeping chips from beneath her father's chisel and her first lesson no deeper than which face of a stone would split true and which would shatter if a hand did not first read the grain of it. She was quicker at the reading than most of her father's own apprentices, a fact her father noticed early and said aloud often, in the plain way of that house; and by the time she had seen twenty summers she was cutting boundary-stones of her own, sound work that stood where it was set and troubled no household with a crooked line, though nothing in it yet asked more of her than the trade had asked of her grandfather.

The bridge that made her name was a small one, built to carry the southern road over a stream at Doire mhin that flooded each spring past any ford a cart could safely trust, no grander in its span than the footbridges of an earlier age and no harder, by the fellowship's own reckoning, than a dozen others its masons had thrown in those same years without any one of them being remembered for it after. Beathag was three-and-thirty when the fellowship set her to lead the cutting, the first time a woman of that house had been given a crossing of her own to answer for rather than a stretch of some other mason's work to finish, and she led it, by every account the fellowship kept, exactly as her father and his father before him would have led it: a sound bed, a true arch, the fourth hearth's own sign cut into the keystone where every crossing since Ros fhionn had carried it.

What she added, beside the hearth's own sign and beneath it, was her own name, cut in her own hand in letters no larger than the sign: *Beathag Clachair a chuir seo*, Beathag the mason set this. No mason of the fellowship, in all the generations since Ailean Clachair first cut the fourth hearth's mark at Ros fhionn, had ever cut a name of his own beside it, the hearth-sign having been understood, from the very first crossing, to speak for every hand that had answered to it rather than for any one hand alone; and when the fellowship's elder masons came down from Cathair dhearg, as they did each season, to look over the year's work, more than one of them stood a long while at the small bridge at Doire mhin before they said anything of it at all.

It is told that the eldest among them, a woman near seventy who had cut stone since before Beathag's own father was born, asked her plainly why she had done it, whether she held her own hand a better one than the hearth's, or thought her own work owed more remembering than the forty who had died, over the generations, cutting crossings no less sound than hers and left no name behind them. Beathag answered, by the fellowship's own telling of it, that she held her hand no better than any hearth-mark ever cut, and had cut her own name to stand beside the hearth's sign rather than above it, so that whoever stood at that stream a hundred years on and asked who had set the stone might, for once, be given an answer rather than only a sign that said hands had done it, without saying whose. The eldest mason gave no answer of her own that day; within two seasons masons of every hearth on the island had begun cutting their own names beside the fourth hearth's sign wherever a fellowship crew finished a crossing, a custom that held for as long as the fellowship held, and the island's own masons still call it, to this day, by no other name than Beathag's mark.

Beathag Clachair lived to see her own mark cut on four further crossings before her hands grew too stiff for the finer work of a keystone, and died at Doire mhin in the seventieth year of her own life, an ordinary age for a mason's death by then, no age on Dia-thìr since Fearchar Òg's own generation having asked a life to run much longer; she was buried, at her own asking, at the foot of the bridge she had cut her name into rather than among the household's own dead, and the fellowship's own masons passing that road are told to have kept, for a long while after, the habit of laying a chip of good grey stone on the grave whenever their own work carried them by it.

## V. Of the Far-Off House and the Fire-Water

The waypoint house on the site the carriers called, half in earnest and half in the plain joke of the road, the far-off house, having stood so long from any town that a traveller was never nearer to reaching it than halfway, was rebuilt in stone in these same years, the old timber and turf of its earlier building having at last given out under one too many storms off the western sea. It kept, in its rebuilding, the same name the carriers had always known it by, the fellowship's own masons holding that a name earned by a hundred years of true telling was not a thing to improve upon, whatever a stone building might otherwise have suggested to a prouder hand.

Further north, at a waypoint house on the northern road, a keeper new to that house began, in the same generation, to serve a spirit distilled from barley rather than the small beer every waypoint house on the northern road had always kept, a stronger drink than any the carriers had trade with before, that warmed a man through on a cold night in a way small beer never troubled to and left him, more than once, warmer still the next morning than the night's own cold could account for. The carriers took to calling it fire-water, for the way of it going down and the way of it sitting after, and the name held faster than any other the drink was ever given. Word of it reached Dùn ìseal before two winters were out, more than one household of that road having found its own hearth's peace disturbed by a carrier who had taken more fire-water than sense the night before, and the Keeper of that generation was asked, by more than one reeve troubled at the change in her own district's roads, to rule whether the drink fell under the Small-Burning Law that governed every other burning on the island.

The ruling, when it came, was as plain as most of that Hall's rulings had always been: that a fire kept in a man's own belly, however hot it burned there, was no burning the Law had ever been written to answer for, the Small-Burning Law having concerned itself, since Fionnlagh's own day, with what a hearth or a forge sent up into the air rather than with what any household chose to swallow of its own free will, and that the Hall would rule on drink the day it began ruling on food, and not a day before. The keeper of that house took the ruling for the leave it plainly was, and the house's trade doubled within the season, carriers of the whole northern road coming to hear of a house where a cold night's journey might be answered with more than small beer and a hard bench. What quarrels the fire-water caused after, the rolls of that road are content to let the waypoint houses settle, as they had always settled a carrier's own excesses without troubling Dùn ìseal for a ruling on every one of them.

## VI. Of Caol mhòr, Ceann mhòr and the Edge of Things

Of the north-west in these years the island's own rolls have little to say, and what little they keep is mostly complaint, the north-west having always sat at the far edge of whatever reach the red hall's own writ carried, and further still from whatever reach its own attention troubled to follow. The fisher-families of Caol mhòr, on that coast, had by these generations gathered themselves under a headman of their own choosing rather than any reeve sent out from Cathair dhearg, and sent their tolls to the red hall only in the years a road-guard actually came so far to collect them, which by the fisher-families' own telling was not every year, nor even most of them. A reeve of Ros dhomhain, whose own district lay nearest the north-west of any that troubled to keep a written roll, wrote to the red hall more than once in these years to say that Caol mhòr paid what it pleased and answered to whom it pleased, and that a coast so far from the capital's own eye might as well keep its own law for all the crown's writ reached it; the red hall's own answer, where the rolls keep one at all, is generally no answer, the north-west's tolls having never yet amounted to a sum the red hall thought worth a road-guard's whole season to collect.

Ceann mhòr, further up that same coast, found in these years a trade that the rest of the island came, in time, to depend on more than it ever troubled to thank Ceann mhòr for: seal-oil, rendered from the seals of the northern rocks and carried down the western coast to Ros bheag in exchange for silver rings, burned in the beacons of every western harbour from Ros bheag to Cuan shean. The seal-oil lamps of the western harbours have burned, since, the brightest light on the whole of Dia-thìr, a fact every sailor of that coast came to know before he knew much else of the trade that fed him, and Ceann mhòr grew, on the strength of a trade in nothing grander than rendered fat, into a town of some standing on a coast where standing of any kind was otherwise hard come by.

In the high country above Muileann leathan, further north again, herding families took to the summer pastures for the wool of the mountain sheep that grazed there, sheep whose fleece the weavers of Inis mhòr had long prized above any other on the island; the herders held no right to the handful that the census of hands had reckoned two generations before, having never held one, their pastures lying too high and too far from any waypoint house for a road-guard to trouble counting them, and they were not written into that census nor into any that followed it, a people the island's own rolls knew existed without ever quite troubling to know how many of them there were.

Inis mhin, a small fishing harbour on the northern shore further east again, came into the rolls for the first and, in this stretch of years, the only time, when its own headman walked the whole distance to the wool-fair at Inis mhòr to lay a complaint against the road-guard's toll before whichever reeve would hear it. The complaint is kept in full in the rolls of that fair, a longer telling by far than the harbour otherwise earned in the whole of this age, and it is the plain truth of that coast, as one clerk of Inis mhòr noted in the margin of his own copy without troubling to soften it, that a small harbour's whole history on the written page might amount to nothing more than the one grievance it once walked far enough to voice.

## VII. Of the Raid, the Second Sighting and the Round of the Islands

The western strands, in these same generations, suffered a season of raiding out of the north-western waters, low boats coming in at first light to take a night's catch of dried fish from any strand too small to keep its own watch and running before any boat large enough to give chase could be launched after them, much as an earlier generation of raiders had once troubled the eastern islets in Lachlann Bàn's own day. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag, whose own trade in seal-oil and silver rings ran along that whole coast, paid from their own purses for two boats armed and crewed to watch the strands through the worst of that season, a cost none of them welcomed but every one of them judged cheaper, in the end, than a season's fish lost to raiders with no watch to answer them. The raiders moved north before the two boats ever caught one at open sea, the western strands having grown, within a season, too well watched to be worth the risk, and the coast north of Ros bheag kept, for a good while after, a wariness it had not troubled to keep before.

It was off that same coast, in the north-western water, that two boats of Baile chrom told of something vast moving beneath them one grey morning, neither crew able to say more of it than that the sea had seemed, for the length of a held breath, to breathe under their own keels, and that whatever it was had passed beneath them without touching either hull and was gone before either crew could properly say they had seen anything at all. It was the second such telling the coast remembered, an earlier crew of the same harbour having told a like tale some generations before in Ruairidh Liath's own reign, and the second telling was believed more readily for the first having gone before it, the way one strange thing believed makes the next easier to credit. One of the two boats that morning did not come home, its own crew never found nor any wreck of it either, and Baile chrom, which had kept a wake for the earlier loss out of the first telling, kept the same wake after for both losses together, the harbour holding, as its own elders put it, that a sea capable of taking two boats a generation apart owed no household an explanation before it was owed a proper mourning.

Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill, in a calmer season of these same years, sailed out from Seann Tarr round the whole ring of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and came home again within the one season, the first crew of the age known to have made the whole round rather than only visiting one island at a time as the fishing or the grazing asked. No crew of that whole stretch of years is known to have gone further from the coast than those islands, nor is any told to have wished to, the open water beyond them holding, for every sailor of that generation, the same plain want of anything worth the sailing to that it had held for every generation before. Families of that same coast took, in these years, to carrying sheep over to Eilean ruadh each summer for its grazing, building turf shelters there against the worst of the weather and bringing the flocks home again before the autumn storms closed the crossing, a custom the coast's herders keep up still, using the same shelters the first families built, patched season by season rather than rebuilt, so that a herder of any later summer shelters, without knowing it, under turf his own great-grandmother first cut and laid.

## VIII. Of the Mark That Held

Of the two hundred and thirty-six years between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, this telling has told what the roads and the shore troubled to keep, and left, as the red hall's own rolls left, whatever passed at Cathair dhearg in those same years to a silence no teller has since thought worth disturbing. It is not a silence this telling judges a loss. A road bridged, a coast watched, a mark cut once and copied after by every hearth on the island: these are not lesser things for having no king's name fixed beside them, and the fellowship of masons that carried the fourth hearth's sign from Ros fhionn to Doire mhin and on to every crossing after asked no ruler's leave to keep its own trade, nor any ruler's remembering to make the keeping worth the labour.

The bridge at Doire mhin stands yet, by every account kept of it, its stream no less given to spring flooding than it ever was and its span no grander than the day Beathag Clachair set the last stone of it; and it is told that a mason passing that way, whatever hearth he answers to and whatever crossing he is bound for next, still stops, before he passes on, to read the small cut letters beneath the fourth hearth's own sign, and to set, if his own errand allows him the moment, a fresh chip of grey stone at the bridge's foot before he takes the road again.

# Chapter Thirty-nine: Of Anna Ruadh's Two Circuits and the Parting of the Rites

*FE 2,792 – 2,863*

> *Aon lasair, iomadh ainm.*
> One flame, many names.
>
> — said of the companies at Dùn ìseal, after Seumas Bàn had done his counting

## I. Of Anna Ruadh's First Circuit

Between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh's own father the house of Tormod had sat the red hall nine reigns running, and the rolls of those years hold little beyond harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges, which the tellers of Cathair dhearg took, not unreasonably, for a sign that the island had been doing well. Anna Ruadh's father was the ninth and quietest of them, a man remembered for having asked, in thirty years, no question of the provinces that a reeve could not answer sitting down.

Anna Ruadh took the red hall at Cathair dhearg in her six-and-twentieth year, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806, and the clerks who had known her father's quiet reign found her a restless kind of ruler from the first council she sat. She asked the reeves who came up from the provinces how the roads stood between one seat and the next, and when none of them could tell her past the borders of his own district, she said she would go and see for herself, as Mòrag nan Rathad had gone before any road-guard rode it and before any bridge stood at Cathair dhearg to be widened. No ruler had walked the whole circuit since. Cathair dhomhain's own reeve, who kept the Law by the letter and had little patience for a queen's whims, told her plainly that a hall was better kept from a hall. Anna Ruadh answered that a hall built by a woman who had walked every mile of it might be worth the keeping, and left the following spring with a dozen of her household and no more baggage than a carrier takes. She took no litter and no guard beyond what any well-off traveller kept on the road, and told the household she left behind that a queen who could not be spared from her own hall for a season was no queen worth the keeping either, a saying more than one later ruler of her house repeated without ever once acting on it.

She came, on the mountain road, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,809, to the house that carriers still called Am Buabhall Fortanach, the Auspicious Buffalo, where the War of the Roads had been ended so long before that its own keepers no longer troubled to say in which reign. The house had passed by then through five generations of a line that still called itself Mòr nic Dhùghaill's own, though none living had known her, and its hearth had not gone cold since. The keeper of the house, a broad, unhurried woman who had heard a queen was coming and set nothing extra on the table for it, gave Anna Ruadh the same jugged buffalo she gave any carrier who stopped there, in the same wooden bowl, with the same crust of bread beside it. Anna Ruadh ate it at the long table among the household's own carriers, asked for a second helping, and got it without ceremony. It is the keepers of that house who tell the tale still, not the rolls, and they tell it exactly so: that the queen ate what was put in front of her and did not ask for better.

Further east, on the road that climbed toward Cnoc leathan, she came to the turf longhouse the carriers called the sunny house for the way its south wall caught the morning, 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813. Its keepers had mended the worst of that road themselves for three generations, out of their own stores and their own backs, because no province seat claimed the stretch as its own to mend. Anna Ruadh heard the whole of it from the youngest of them, a woman missing two fingers from a rockfall on that same road, and before she left she granted the house a toll of its own for the road's keeping, Slighe Cnoc leathan, the first and only charter any waypoint house on the island holds. She is said to have told the woman, when she thanked her, that a road mended by a stranger's charity for three generations had earned the right to be mended by its own money instead, and that this was no great gift but only a debt the hall had been slow to notice. The woman, whose name the rolls never troubled to keep though the toll they keep to this day, asked only that the charter be cut in stone rather than skin, since skin could be lost in a house fire and a road could not; Anna Ruadh had it cut in stone before she left the district.

At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast, 12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816, she found a quarrel old enough that neither side troubled any longer to be civil about it: the fishers of the strand and the carriers of the mountain road, both claiming the right to carry the dried fish up-country, each accusing the other of spoiling a trade that had fed them both for generations. Anna Ruadh heard the fishers first, in the low stone shed where they dried their catch, and then the carriers, at the halting-house above the strand, and gave her ruling under the open sky between the two, where both households could hear it together: that either might carry, and the trade would go to whichever kept the fish drier and the road shorter, and no household of either kind was to be turned back at the other's door. The fish going inland doubled within two years, and its price at Dùn ìseal fell by half, and both households, it is told, claimed the doubling as proof they had been in the right all along. An old fisher of the strand, asked years after whether the queen had favoured his own side in the end, is remembered to have said only that she had favoured the fish, which was more than either side had thought to do.

## II. Of the Contest Field and the Wood-Watcher

At Ceann leathan the road-guards had kept a staves-contest on an open green since before living memory, the kind of match where a young man made his name and an old one kept it a season longer, and Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr was still spoken of there for a win two centuries gone; her ring, or one so old it was taken for hers, still hung by the green's own well, and every fighter who came to try the green touched it before he took up a staff, whether he had heard her name told rightly or garbled past all knowing. Anna Ruadh watched a match fought in the mud of a wet spring and thought it a poor return for the skill on show. She gave the green a wall of dressed stone and a drained floor, 11 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,819, and set a silver ring from the red hall's own store as the prize, and ruled besides that whoever lost a match at her contest should eat at the crown's cost before going home, win or lose being no reason, she said, for a man to go home hungry. Fighters came after that from every province of the south to try the stone field, and the year Fearchar Ruadh of Doire mhin took the ring, he was carried on the shoulders of men who had lost to him not an hour before. He had come to the green as a mason's apprentice with nothing to his name but a borrowed staff, and he ate, by Anna Ruadh's own new law, the same crown's meal as every man he had beaten, at the same board, before the ring was ever put in his hand; it is remembered of him that he never afterward sat down to eat without asking who else was at the table.

It was on the same circuit that Anna Ruadh took into her household a wood-watcher out of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, a spare, sun-browned man who read the fall of a dropped stick or the turn of a bird's flight the way a clerk read a slate, and asked him to read the omens of the hall at Cathair dhearg as he had read them under the trees. It was the first time the rite of the wood-watchers, which held Macha for its goddess, sovereignty and horses both, had come so far east, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822. Anna Ruadh's own household saw him first read the hall on a morning when three geese crossed the yard from the north before the queen had broken her fast, and the wood-watcher told her, without being asked, that a message she had given up waiting for would come before the week was out; a rider from the southern coast rode in on the sixth day with an answer to a letter she had sent a full year before and thought lost on the road, and after that no one in the household troubled him with questions he had not been asked first. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal sent a protest up by the same road Anna Ruadh had walked, asking by what right a hall built on the Binding kept an omen-reader who answered to no measure of the vein at all. The rolls give no answer to it, and none is remembered as having been sent.

Cathair dhomhain took the matter harder than Dùn ìseal had. Its own shrine had kept the Law strictly since the town's founding, its Keeper's cutter tried every season without complaint, and its people said openly, where Anna Ruadh's messengers could hear it, that the capital had handed its omens to folk who sat in trees, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826. Cathair dhomhain and the capital had quarrelled before over tolls and over precedence at the council bench; from that year the quarrel carried a weight of faith as well; and it never again lost it. A generation later a Cathair dhomhain reeve, asked why his town still would take no wood-watcher of its own, is said to have answered only that a bird did not judge a king, and left it at that. Cathair dhomhain's own shrine, in the same season, doubled its cutter's visits to the Keeper's measure without being asked, as though the strictness alone might answer an insult that no letter to Cathair dhearg had ever troubled to make plain, and for a hundred years after, a Cathair dhomhain man swearing an oath was known on the roads by how exactly he kept to the letter of it.

Anna Ruadh walked the circuit a second time some years on, in her middle years, slower than the first, stopping longer at each house and asking after names she remembered from the first walking; more than one keeper who had fed her as a young queen fed her again white-haired, and told their own children afterward which meal it had been. At Am Buabhall Fortanach the same broad-handed keeper who had served her the jugged buffalo unceremoniously the first time set the bowl down before her a second, with grey in her own hair by then, and this time asked, since the queen had come so far twice over, whether she would not sit a while longer than the meal took. Anna Ruadh stayed the night, the only night of either circuit she is known to have slept two together under one roof that was not her own.

She came home from that second circuit already tiring, though she said nothing of it to her household, and she held the red hall four years more before she died of no sickness anyone could name, in the way that a candle goes out at the end of its wick rather than by any wind, 26 an Cèitean, FE 2,829, in her nine-and-fortieth year. In her last winter she had the household read her the toll rolls of the sunny house and of Slighe Cnoc leathan aloud at her own bedside, twice, as though to be sure the charter still stood as she had cut it, and asked after no other matter of state before she died. She was carried to Dùn dhearg and laid among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house together, as her line had been promised at its choosing.

The council kept the hall three years in her son's name, and Coinneach Bàn took it in his own, 27 an Giblean, FE 2,832, seven-and-twenty years old and already known to the reeves for asking the same close questions of a slate that his mother had asked of a road. He did not walk the circuit as she had. He said, when a councillor asked him whether he meant to, that his mother had already walked it twice and left him little to see that she had not seen first, and that he would rather have every province seat send him a true copy of its own rolls than walk out to read them himself. It was the beginning of the work that filled the better part of his reign: seat after seat sent its clerk down to Cathair dhearg over the following years with the district's laws copied fresh, and Coinneach Bàn read every copy through himself before it was shelved, so that within a decade a province seat's own clerks, wanting to settle a point of law, more often sent to the capital for a copy of their own rolls than trusted the skins in their own keeping, which the damp of a mountain winter had usually got to first.

## III. Of Seumas Bàn and the Roll

Sliochd Mhuirich had held the Keeper's office, without ever once claiming the red hall in its own name, since long before Oighrig nic Lachlainn's death, and through the shut hall that followed it, when the house had stood back from the choosing at Dùn ìseal while three other houses quarrelled over the red hall; and it was said of Sliochd Mhuirich, half in respect and half in the way a rival house says such things, that it had learned early to want the keeping of a thing rather than the owning of it. Seumas Bàn was the youngest son of that house's youngest branch, raised at Dùn ìseal within sound of the flame, and no one who had known him as a boy running the Hall's own passages was greatly surprised when the flame came to his keeping in his turn.

Seumas Bàn came to the flame at five-and-thirty, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835, and did what every new Keeper before him had done, and sat down with the Keepers' roll to learn the names of those who had kept the flame before him. He read it by the light of Brìde's own flame, in the stone room below Talla na Lasrach where the roll was kept, with a jug of small beer going flat at his elbow and no company but the clerk who had shown him where the oldest skins were stored. The names ran down the page in the old stag-letters, a hundred years and more to a skin, some hands cramped and some sprawling, a few so faded with age that he had to tilt the whole page to the firelight to read them at all. He had meant, when he sat down, only an evening's reading, the way a man learns the names of his own grandfather's brothers before a feast; the roll ran to nine skins by the time it reached him, and he was still at the fourth when the clerk came in to tell him the fire in the outer room had gone out and been relit twice without his noticing either time.

He read for the better part of two nights before he noticed the pattern, and a third before he stopped reading and began instead to count, going back to the beginning and setting a mark on a scrap of hide for every name of his own house, and counting the whole roll through twice to be sure of himself. When he had finished he sat a long while looking at the two rows of marks, which agreed with each other exactly. More than half the Keepers of the age, from Beathag Bhàn down to himself, had been of Sliochd Mhuirich. He went further, though the roll gave him no cause to and no one afterward thanked him for it, and reckoned how many of the rest had married into the house or fostered a child of it, and found the true number nearer to two in every three.

He told no one at once, sending the clerk to his bed and sitting alone with the roll until the fire burned low, and it is the clerk's own account, given in his old age and kept unstruck in a hand not his master's, that Seumas Bàn said only one thing aloud that night, to no one: that a Hall built so that no heir might hold the flame had, without anybody meaning it so, let one house hold the watching of it instead. In the morning he sent for the same clerk and a knife, and had the count struck from the roll's preface where he had written it the night before in a heat that had not survived till daylight, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835. The clerk did as he was bid and said nothing of the copy he had already made for his own hand before the knife came near the page, and it is that copy, not the scraped one, that answers for the fact today.

That winter, done with counting his own house, Seumas Bàn turned to counting everyone else's. He had the clerks of the Hall set down every rite on the island that burned a handful at dawn or laid any claim at all to the vein, so that the council should know, he said, what it was that it kept, 18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,838. The list, when it was finished, ran longer than he had expected: the Hall's own rite of the flame and the stone; the old keeping of the ancestors, which asked nothing of the vein and troubled no one; the dawn-hawk of the northern coast; the wood-watchers of the western wood; the wolf-sworn of the road-guards; the sting-oath of the harbour courts; and both schools of the stag, the elders' and Donnchadh mac Iain's, still trading their letters after three generations of disagreement. The clerk who wrote the list added, at its foot, that a thousand years before no such list would have been needed, since there had been, in the memory the roll kept, only the one flame and the one measure. Seumas Bàn read the note and let it stand.

## IV. Of the Rites Counted

In the spring he sent a cutter named Ruairidh Òg north to Seann Skell, to try the hawk-keepers' dawn-burning against the Hall's own measure, as every rite on the list was tried in its turn. He came back within the month, 19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840, wind-burned about the face and short in his answers, with a strip of tanned hide folded inside his coat. He had put the Hall's question to the household of Ealasaid Bhàn, eldest of the fowlers, who fed her hawk before her own table was laid, as the rite required, and who heard him out at her own door without asking him in. She had told him, he said, standing in her own doorway with the hawk hooded on her wrist and the dawn fire already lit behind her, that the measure he had come to try was the hawk's own, not the Keeper's, that her people burned exactly what the Law required and had done so every dawn of her life, and that they had put it in writing so that no cutter after him could mistake the matter again. When Ruairidh Òg asked whether he might at least see the handful weighed, she answered that he might watch from the yard as any neighbour was welcome to, but that watching was not trying, and the two were not the same thing however he chose to name them to the Keeper. The strip of hide he carried was that writing. It was the first time any rite on the list had turned the Hall's own trial away outright, and Seumas Bàn read it twice by the fire before he put it in the chest with the roll rather than answering it.

From Caol leathan came word, a few years on, that the wolf-sworn had raised a hall of their own about the white stone at the town gate, the second such stone the order had ever set, and that the oaths sworn there now were no longer the plain guards' oaths of the road but something graver, 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,843. The stone, its keepers said, watched the whole island as any guard watched his own stretch of road, and would cry out under a rightful king as under no other; men had begun to call it Lia Fàil, the Stone, and the wolf-sworn who kept it An Fhianna, though the road-guards among them still rode the same roads they had always ridden. A young guard swore the new oath that same season with his hand flat on the stone in a hall still smelling of its own fresh mortar, and told his own household after that the stone had felt warm under his palm on a cold morning, though the mason who had set it swore he had cut and laid nothing but plain grey rock out of the same quarry that built half the town's walls. Seumas Bàn had known most of those men by their given names before they were anything of the kind, and it troubled him more, he told the clerk, that a name could change a man's oath than that the oath itself had changed.

At the western Seann Skell the harbour court's old sting-oath, sworn on a scorpion carved for the purpose since before anyone living could say why, had by then become a settled creed, 3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,846. Its keepers held that one power alone stung the liar wherever he stood, naming him Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion was no more than his sign; and it was the first teaching on the island to claim, in so many words, that it alone was true, where every other rite on the list had been content to be its own. From that court's founding the oath was sworn thereafter over a cup marked with the scorpion, called Manannan's Cup of Truth, which was said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole again by three truths, though no clerk of the Hall ever saw it broken, and a merchant of the harbour town who was once heard to wonder aloud what would happen if it were tested found no one willing to lend him a boat that season. Seann Vell, below Cuan shean on the same coast, took up the oath from its neighbour within the year and carved its own scorpion in yellow stone, 4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849, the first image of the creature cut for worship rather than for swearing on, so that a child of that town grew up knowing the scorpion's shape before it ever heard the oath explained. The stonecutter who carved it, a woman better known for gravestones than for shrines, is said to have complained that no one had ever shown her a living scorpion to work from, and to have carved it in the end from a fisherman's telling of one washed up dead on the strand, so that the image every child of Seann Vell learned to fear owed at least as much to a fisherman's memory as to the god it was meant to serve.

The wood-watchers went furthest of all. They stopped sending their quarrels to the Hall for judgement and began to settle them instead under the trees of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, where no clerk of Dùn ìseal had ever sat in council, 13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852. They held that the black beast of the wood had two natures, one that kept and one that devoured, and that the vein under the mountain had the very same two, though it showed only one face to any cutter who had never gone hungry a winter for want of it. Some among them told it further, in a telling the order took up afterward as its own, of two horses harnessed to a single chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha, pulling one load between them and neither able to run without the other. A cutter of Cnoc bhàn and a fowler of the Abhainn ìseal brought a boundary quarrel to the wood-watchers that same year rather than to Dùn ìseal, over a stretch of scrub neither the Hall nor any province seat had ever troubled to survey, and came away with a judgement neither had asked for and both, it is told, accepted: that the ground belonged to whoever kept it fed through a hard winter, and to no one in a good one. Seumas Bàn heard the tale from the same wood-watcher who still read the omens of Anna Ruadh's old household, now grown old himself in Coinneach Bàn's service, and said only that he had heard stranger doctrines argue less sense.

## V. Of the Parting

By the time the last of these reports had reached Dùn ìseal, the one practice the island had kept since the Binding had plainly come apart into as many pieces as it had reasons to, 11 an Gearran, FE 2,855. Men had begun to call the whole scattering of rites An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and set beside it, standing a little apart as it always had, the older reverence of the hearths, which asked nothing of the vein and was known by its own name, Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits; and it was no longer possible, Seumas Bàn told the council plainly, to speak of the belief of the Dia-thìrich as though it were one thing, whatever the roll of the Hall had once assumed.

The council gave up the pretence a few years on, in its own turn. It had sat, since the days of the Roinn, by hearth and by house, a man beside whoever his neighbour happened to be; that year it began instead to sit in companies by rite, each on benches of its own, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858, and the seating held for the rest of the age without anyone troubling to reverse it. The carpenters who built the new benches were given no instruction beyond a count of heads for each company, and it is remembered that they set the hawk-keepers' bench nearest the door, for no reason any clerk ever wrote down, so that latecomers to every council after sat longest among strangers before they reached their own.

Seumas Bàn stood at the door on the first morning they sat so and watched the benches fill, knot by knot, none of them so much as glancing at the bench beside it, and said to the clerk at his shoulder, loud enough, by his own wish, to be set down: that he kept the one flame now for eight peoples, and each of the eight was certain it was the only one that kept it truly.

Two things alone stayed outside the companies, and Seumas Bàn is said to have taken more comfort from them than from anything else that year. Pilgrims of every rite still walked to Allt an Àigh at the proper turn of the moon, as they always had, and asked no one's company or leave to do it; the Hall's own list, drawn up to set every rite in its place, had found no place to set that one and left it out of the reckoning entirely, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860. That same season pilgrims of four rites, meeting on the path from Caol shean by no arrangement anyone could afterward account for, fell to mending its worn stones together, hawk-keeper beside wolf-sworn beside a stag scholar of the elders' school, and finished the work before any of them thought to ask whether the others belonged there.

And at Muileann ruadh, where the warm springs still ran from under the mountain as they had before the Binding was ever sworn, the keeper of the bath-house, a broad, plain-spoken woman named Beathag Fhionn, ruled that year that the sick of every rite should be carried up and bathed at dawn without being asked first which company they kept, 19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863. Her ruling was copied that same season into the rolls of every province seat that had a copy of anything at all, and it is remembered as the last ruling of the whole age that every company of the council accepted without a single voice raised against it, coming as it did from the one office in the Hall's whole keeping that had never had anything to do with the coal.

Seumas Bàn kept the flame five-and-forty years in all after that winter of the roll and the roll's scraping. What is chiefly told of him is one morning, standing again at the door of the council as he had the first day the benches were parted, and looking down the length of the Hall at knot after knot of his own eight peoples, none looking at any other, when he said nothing further to the clerk beside him. He had come to the flame meaning only to learn the names of the dead who had held it before him, and had found instead, by the same reading, the shape of the thing he now kept: no longer the one measure the Binding had set over every hearth alike, but eight measures each certain it alone answered to the vein, sitting as far from one another as the carpenters' benches would allow and closer, in the end, than either the hawk-keepers or the wolf-sworn much cared to be told. None of the eight companies, from that day to the last day the rolls of the age were kept, ever sat together again by hearth and house as one; and the flame on the threshold at Dùn ìseal burned on regardless, keeping, as it had always kept, the one measure no company of the eight had yet found cause to dispute.

# Chapter Forty: Of the Last Quiet Years

*FE 2,864 – 5 am Faoilleach FE 2,960*

> *Chan eil bliadhna aig aon nach eil aig càch.*
> No one has years that the rest do not.
>
> — said at Dùn ìseal, of the roll's last count

## I. Of the Provincial Rolls

The clerks of the red hall kept, in these last generations of the Holy Age, a roll of the provinces that no single teller has ever set down whole, for the plain reason that no single year of it held anything a teller would trouble to carry from house to house; and yet it is out of that same roll, dry province by dry province, that the shape of these last quiet years is best read, since the red hall has, for most of that stretch, next to nothing else to say.

At Cnoc dhìreach in the east, on the carriers' road south of the springs, the weavers turned out in these years a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers came to wear on the high passes and nowhere else, a cloth coarse enough to turn a wind that finer weaving let through, 18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,866. It is not, the roll is careful to say, the same Cnoc dhìreach that keeps the old tombs and the grave-keepers' silence; the two towns share a name and nothing further, and the roll tells them apart, where a stranger could not, by that one cloth. The dyers of Muileann bhàn, in the eastern hills not far off, learned in the same years to fix a pale blue out of a hill plant that grew nowhere lower, and the mountain country's cloth was dyed there ever after, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,869; the Keepers alone, of everyone who wore the cloth, kept theirs undyed, and said so to any who asked, holding, as they had always held, that a flame kept for no one's blood needed no colour to mark whose it was.

A water-mill was raised in those same years at Muileann dhomhain, further into the hills, to grind the grain of the common granaries that the mountain districts had kept since Lachlann Bàn's own day, 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,872. The miller took one measure in sixteen for his own trade and no more, and the roll calls it fair, a word the roll uses of few enough millers in the whole of it. It was at Àth chiar, not two valleys off, that the same rains which had watered Muileann bhàn's blue plant and Cnoc dhìreach's cloth-wool that generation came down instead as a flood, carrying the river clean over its ford and taking with it the carriers' shelter and six of the town's own people, 26 an Cèitean, FE 2,875. The common granary of that district stood on a rise the flood never reached, and it fed the town through the winter that followed on nothing but its own stores, so that the roll, having told the drowning plainly, tells the granary's answer just as plainly and leaves the two to stand together without further comment, as the roll's own custom was.

On the south-eastern coast the people of Seann Bhral began, in this same stretch, to lay oyster-beds in the shallows below their own town, a craft they held had come with their town's own name, though the clerks who keep the provincial roll set the claim down and mark it doubtful, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,878, the roll's own custom being to doubt a claim it had not itself walked out and seen made good. Further down that coast Seann Vell grew, on the strength of its own fishing and the silver of Muileann chiar carried down the eastern road, into a town large enough to raise the first stone quay any harbour on the island had ever built, 20 an Gearran, FE 2,880, its timber jetties having rotted out from under one too many seasons of the tide. On the southern cape the old beacon at Tobar dhearg was built up in stone in the same years, a tower now rather than a heap of driftwood, with its fire kept burning above the ground for the first time on any coast of Dia-thìr, 22 am Faoilleach, FE 2,883; it burned seal-oil carried the whole length of the island from the northern rocks, the same trade that had made Ceann mhòr's name a generation before, and every sailor of that southern water learned to look for its light before he learned much else his trade required of him.

At Muileann naomh, on the same southern coast, a mill and a shrine came in these years to share one roof, the miller keeping the shrine's own handful of grain beside his millstones as faithfully as he kept his sixteenth measure, 19 an Giblean, FE 2,886; the Keeper's cutter who came out to try it, as the Hall's cutters tried every rite's measure in its turn, found the handful kept and the flour good, and wrote as much in the roll and no more. Dùn thais, in the eastern hills, was walled in the same generation, and within its new wall the stag's people raised the first temple of their own ever built in stone rather than kept in a grove, 21 am Màrt, FE 2,889, the elder school at Cnoc bhàn sending teachers down to see it properly served. Inis mhòr, on the northern coast, held by now a wool-fair at every shearing that drew buyers from the whole of that coast and some from Cathair dhearg itself, its silver weighed on the same weights Muileann chiar had sent to the northern road two generations before, 16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,892; and further along that same coast, west of Seann Toll, the fishing town of Baile Mòr mhòr grew great enough to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal, a seat the Four Houses mislike to this day and gave, when they could no longer refuse it outright, at the foot of the hall rather than beside their own benches, 18 an Cèitean, FE 2,895. Seann Toll had by then become the home of the whole northern fishing fleet, its boatbuilders shaping the longest craft the island knew, built for a single day's run along the coast and never meant for anything further out, 13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,898.

In the east a dry summer burned the pastures round Achadh shean and left the district's common granary empty by the following spring, 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,900; grain came up from Baile chaol and from Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law that Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh had made together three generations before, and the district repaid it, harvest by harvest, over the years after, the rolls of Baile chaol setting the repayment down measure by measure to the very last, with a clerk's own note added that no such debt in the whole of that roll had ever before been repaid in full, 10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,903. The panthers crossed the southern road late that same autumn, and fewer of them than the carriers remembered crossing in any year before; the weather-watchers read it for a hard winter and were not wrong, 11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,906, and the Keepers of that generation, whose own reckonings answered to the vein and not to the beasts of the south road, noted the crossing in their own roll without troubling to remark on it further. On the north-eastern coast a timber watch-tower went up at Baile ruadh against raiders out of the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, the only tower built for war in the whole of this age, 13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,909; and further south, at Cuan ruadh, the fishers gave boats and men to that same watch and were given, in return, a place on the council beside Sliochd Raghnaill's own seat, 11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,912, a bargain both sides of it were still keeping at the close of the age.

At Inis chrom, on the western coast, the families of the drowned took up the custom of holding a feast on the shore each year with an empty place set for each of the lost, a custom that spread northward in these same years as far as Seann Warr, 10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,915. Potters at Baile ghorm, on the south-western coast, learned to fire a hard red ware of their own clay in the same stretch, and their jars carried oil and grain the length of the western road, sherds of them lying, by a reeve's own count, on every waypoint-house site a rider had troubled to walk, 8 an t-Samhain, FE 2,918; the same potters set up new kilns before long at Cnoc àrsaidh, where the clay ran better and the wood nearer, and the red ware of the western road was made there for the rest of the age, 19 an Giblean, FE 2,920. On the southern coast, families crowded out of the harbours about Cathair dhearg settled at Cathair fhada and raised its long street along the ridge above the water, bringing with them a wood-watcher of their own rite and a copy of the laws, and the town grew, 18 an Cèitean, FE 2,923. At Cnoc naomh the people kept, in the old folk way, a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of their own hill, with no hawk in it, no wolf, no sting, no stag, 16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926; and the Hall's own list of rites, drawn up not long before in Seumas Bàn's day, named them among the keepers of the old reverence, a company by now as settled and as separate as any of the eight.

It is out of this same weave of small and settled things, and out of very little else, that the last generations of the Holy Age must be read, for the red hall in these years kept, for the most part, only the red hall passing from hand to hand as it had passed since Gilleasbuig Mòr's day, and troubled the roll with little more than that.

## II. Of Coinneach Bàn's Last Years

Coinneach Bàn, son of Anna Ruadh, who had copied the laws for every province in his own strong years and had them read at every waypoint house from the northern road to the southern cape, held the hall a long while after that work was done, growing old at Cathair dhearg the way a man grows old who has already done the one thing his own name will be kept for and finds himself, past it, with nothing further asked of him but to keep on living. He died in the ninety-first year of his own life, in his own bed at the red hall and not on any road, and the roll gives him no more than that, holding, as the roll had held of every rìgh since the long years went out of the line, that a death in a man's own bed at ninety-one years was a death like any other and owed no further telling than the fact of it.

His son, Coinneach Donn, took up the red hall in the way sons of that house had always taken it up, without any meeting of the Four Houses troubling to be called, the hall by then passing so quietly from father to son at Cathair dhearg that a reeve of some outlying district might learn of one rìgh's death and the next rìgh's holding both from the same single line of a single roll, sent up months after the fact and answered with no more surprise than any other item of provincial business. Coinneach Donn held it thirty years and more, long enough that the carriers' road-guards of his own generation knew no other name to give the red hall, and long enough, too, that when he died in his turn, in the eighty-seventh year of his own life, it seemed to more than one reeve that the hall's passing that year ought to be as quiet as every passing before it had been.

It was not so quiet, this once, for Coinneach Donn left, besides his own daughter Mòr, a younger brother, Tormod Donn, who had held no hall of his own and wanted, now that his elder brother's line stood at a girl not yet twenty-three years old, to hold this one.

## III. Of Mòr's Claim Against Her Uncle

Mòr nic Coinnich had grown up, by her own later telling, expecting nothing of the red hall beyond the ordinary daughter's portion of a house that already held the red hall, her father having never once, in the whole of her girlhood, spoken of the succession as a thing that might be contested rather than simply continued; and it was a hard schooling to her, in the first winter after his death, to learn from her own household's own steward that her father's brother had gone to the Four Houses at Dùn ìseal with a claim of his own, arguing before them that a girl of not yet twenty-three had no more right to a hall her own line had held three generations than any other daughter of any other house on the island, and that a man grown, of the same blood and twice her years, stood the plainer heir.

The Four Houses heard Tormod Donn's claim in the same hall where they had heard Gilleasbuig Mòr's claim and old Oighrig's line's claims before him, four centuries and more back, and found themselves, as their own predecessors had found themselves then, arguing a question the roll had never troubled to settle in words because no one had ever before troubled to ask it in words: whether the hall passed by blood alone, or by blood and by the house's own custom together, and whether a woman's blood ran thinner in the reckoning than a man's when both stood equally close to the line. Sliochd Mhuirich's own bench, silent as it had been silent at every such reckoning since the shut hall of Oighrig's own day, gave no voice either way; the bench that had once sat for the clerks' line spoke for Mòr, holding that a house's custom, once kept three generations running without challenge, was a kind of blood in its own right; and the two remaining benches split evenly between them, so that the matter stood, at the winter's end, exactly where it had stood at the winter's beginning, decided by no vote the Four Houses could agree to call a decision.

It was Catrìona nic Mhuirich, Keeper of the flame in those years and the last of her office the Holy Age was to know, who ended it, though the ending was none of the Hall's own business by the Small-Burning Law's own letter, and Catrìona said as much to the Four Houses before she said anything else. She had known Coinneach Donn her own self, she told them, in the years before either of them held the office each now held, and she had known his daughter as a child brought once a year to see the flame kept, wide-eyed at a burning no larger than a man's two hands cupped together; and she had watched Tormod Donn, in the same years, come to the Hall himself not once, holding, by his own account to anyone who asked him, that a younger son's business lay in his own house's lands and not in a flame he would never be called on to answer for. A red hall, she told the Four Houses, was no business of the Hall's to give. She had watched, all the same, enough hands over enough years to have formed her own opinion of which hands a house's custom had shaped for the holding and which had not; and she said, plainly, that she would set the stone cup in Mòr's hands, as it had been set once before in Gilleasbuig Mòr's, should the Four Houses ask her to, and in no one else's.

Tormod Donn yielded within the season, quietly, in his own house at Cuan ruadh rather than before the Four Houses, sending word by his own steward that he withdrew a claim he had never, in his own telling afterward, much wanted to press so far as it had gone, and had pressed it chiefly, he said, because no one else of his own house had troubled to ask him whether a girl not yet twenty-three could hold a hall her own father had held without any man standing behind her to hold it for her. It was, by the roll's own later reckoning, the last such claim the house of Tormod was ever to see contested, and the reason given for that, by more than one clerk who wrote of it after, was Mòr nic Coinnich's own long and plain holding of the hall, which left no younger brother of her own generation any reason to think a girl's hand unfit for it.
