Catrìona nic Mhuirich set the stone cup in Mòr's hands at Dùn ìseal in the spring of her own twenty-fourth year, as a Keeper had set it in Gilleasbuig Mòr's hands four centuries before and in no rìgh's hands since, 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929, and it is told that Mòr, taking the cup, asked Catrìona only one question of her own, low enough that the Four Houses standing by did not hear it: whether her uncle's claim had been, in Catrìona's own honest judgement, a wicked thing or only a foolish one. Catrìona is said to have answered that she had known few enough claims in her own long keeping of the flame that were purely one or the other, and that Mòr would do better, holding the hall twenty years or more as Catrìona judged she might, to spend her own reckoning on the hall's proper keeping than on her uncle's proper punishing; and Mòr took the answer, by every account that has come down of that day, for the whole of the counsel it plainly was, and never once, in the years after, brought any charge against her uncle beyond the one the Four Houses had already let lapse of their own accord.

## IV. Of Mòr's Reign

Mòr nic Coinnich wed, within two years of taking the cup, a man of Sliochd Raghnaill named Dòmhnall Dubh, whose own kin had kept the watch-tower at Baile ruadh and given boats to the coast's own defence in her father's time, and whose own reckoning of the sea, she is said to have told her household, sat easier beside her own reckoning of the hall than any lowland house's reckoning of grain and silver would have sat. Dòmhnall Dubh held no office at the red hall and asked none, keeping, through the whole of Mòr's reign, to the same trade his own house had always kept, boats and the watch of the north-eastern coast, and coming to Cathair dhearg only as a husband comes to his wife's own hall rather than as any rìgh's consort claiming a hand in her own business; and it is remembered of him, by the one or two tellers who troubled to remember him at all, chiefly that he never once, in twenty years at Cathair dhearg, learned to sit easy through a full council sitting of the eight companies by rite, finding the benches' own silence toward one another harder to bear, he is said to have said, than any storm his own boats had ever ridden out.

The reign these two years opened ran, for the better part of thirty years, very much as Coinneach Bàn's and Coinneach Donn's reigns before it had run: the red hall at Cathair dhearg, the provinces sending their rolls up each year with little in them a teller would trouble to keep, the eight companies of the council sitting their own benches without disorder and without, so far as the rolls show, any of them troubling to speak across the gap between one bench and the next. Mòr herself is remembered as a rìgh who read every roll that came up to her rather than leaving the reading to a clerk, a habit her own steward is said to have found tiresome when she was young to the office and to have come, as his own service under her lengthened, to value above any other habit a rìgh had ever kept; and it was Mòr, reading the Hall's own roll one winter evening not many years before her death, who first had the count made that the roll's later keepers were afterward to set at its foot: one hundred and forty names of Keepers from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and better than ninety names of rìghrean from Goraidh Mòr to her own, 2 an Giblean, FE 2,939, a reckoning she is said to have sat with a long while by her own lamp before she troubled anyone else with it.

It was in that same reckoning, brought to her by a clerk who had made it chiefly to answer her own asking, that Mòr found the fact these tellings have made most of already, though she herself, by her steward's own account, made rather less of it at the time: that no family on the whole of the island, her own included, now lived any longer than any other, the long years that had once carried Ìomhar Dearg to fifteen hundred summers and Eithne past three thousand having gone, generation by generation, clean out of every line that had ever carried them, so that a rìgh of Cathair dhearg in that year could expect, by the plain arithmetic the roll now showed, very much the same span of years as a potter of Baile ghorm or a weaver of Cnoc dhìreach. Mòr is said to have remarked to her steward only that it seemed to her a fitting enough thing, a cup meant from its first swearing for no one's blood having taken, in the end, the better part of three thousand years to make every blood on the island answer to the same measure; and the steward, setting the remark down afterward at Ruairidh Clèireach's own asking, added nothing of his own beside it, judging it needed none.

Dòmhnall Dubh died in the fiftieth year of his own life, at Baile ruadh among his own kin rather than at Cathair dhearg, and Mòr, who had kept the hall by then the better part of twenty years, is told to have gone north herself to see him buried beside the watch-tower his own house had kept three generations, a journey no rìgh of Cathair dhearg had troubled to make in living memory for a husband's burying rather than a province's own business. She held the hall three years more after that, alone in her own hall in a way she had not been alone in it since her uncle's claim was first brought against her, and it is of those three years that the least is told of the whole of her reign, the roll of that stretch holding nothing beyond the provinces' own small business and a single note, written in Ruairidh Clèireach's own hand, that the rìgh kept her own counsel more than she had kept it in any year before.

## V. Of Mòr's Death and Beathag's Crowning

Mòr nic Coinnich died on the one-and-twentieth day of an t-Iuchar, in the eight-and-fortieth year of her own life, at Cathair dhearg, in the same hall her father and her father's father had died in before her. She left two daughters, Beathag, not yet sixteen, and Mòrag, younger still, and no brother, no uncle, no cousin near enough in blood to raise the question her own reign had opened with; and it is told, by more than one hand that wrote of that year afterward, that the Four Houses, summoned in haste to Dùn ìseal within days of the rìgh's death, found themselves for the first time in living memory with a succession that raised no claim at all, Tormod Donn's own line having died with him some thirteen years before and left no son of an age or a temper to trouble a girl of sixteen for a hall her own mother and grandfather and great-grandfather had all three held before her.

Beathag was crowned at Cathair dhearg within the month, by her own house's word and the Four Houses' own assent, rather than by any journey to Dùn ìseal to have the stone cup set in her hands as her mother had had it set in hers; and it is this, of all the small departures the last years of the Holy Age made from the years before them, that the chroniclers who came after troubled most to remark on, some holding it a plain matter of a girl of sixteen being crowned in haste at her own hall rather than made to journey the fifty-five miles east to Dùn ìseal in the heat of the harvest, and others holding it the first sign of a distance opening between the red hall's own crowning and the Hall's own flame that no teller of that year, watching it happen, yet had words to name. Catrìona nic Mhuirich, by then past threescore years, sent word to Cathair dhearg that she stood ready to travel to Dùn ìseal and receive the young rìgh there whenever the roads and the season allowed it, as the Hall's own custom asked; and it is recorded, without further comment from the roll, that the journey was never made in Mòr's own daughter's first year, nor troubled over again in the years the roll of this age had left to keep.

It fell to Ruairidh Clèireach, clerk of the red hall these twenty years and more, to find, in the same weeks, that the skin on which the king-list and the Keepers' roll together had been kept since Coinneach Bàn's own day was filled to its last line with Mòr's own name and the count her own reading had asked for, and no room left on it for any name after hers. He began a new skin that same winter, ruling its first lines himself by lamplight at his own table rather than waiting on any clerk under him, and set at its head, in the same plain hand he had kept the old roll in for twenty years, the name of Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, crowned rìgh at Cathair dhearg in the year of her mother's death; so that the old roll, closed that winter and laid away in the same chest that held every roll of the Hall before it, carries to this hour no name later than Mòr's, and it is Mòr's name, not her daughter's, that stands last of all the names the Holy Age was to write down.

## VI. Of the Winter Morning

The fifth day of Faoilleach, by the almanac the red hall kept, in the year the roll had by then run to two thousand nine hundred and threescore, found the young rìgh Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill down at the harbour below her own hall at Cathair dhearg, her younger sister Mòrag beside her, both of them come down in the dark and the cold ahead of any steward's asking to see the last of the season's boats brought in before the weather the watchers had promised broke over the coast in earnest.

The boats came in by ones and twos through the last of the dark, the crews calling to each other across the water in the plain short words men keep for a cold morning's work, and were made fast along the same stone quay Seann Vell's own masons had raised the pattern for the better part of a hundred years before and every southern harbour since had copied; and Beathag stood at the harbour's edge in a cloak too thin for the hour, by her sister's own later telling, and counted the boats in against some tally of her own that she never troubled to share with anyone standing near her, whether it was the whole season's fleet she was counting or only the boats she had watched go out the evening before.

Mòrag, younger by four years and not yet crowned with any business of her own beyond a girl's ordinary place at her sister's side, asked her, standing there in the cold with the last boat still some way off the quay, whether she was afraid of the storm the watchers had promised; and Beathag answered, after a while long enough that Mòrag is said to have thought she would not answer at all, that she was not afraid of a storm that every fisherman on that coast had ridden out a hundred times before her, but that she found herself thinking, more mornings than not since her own crowning, of the stone cup sitting on its threshold at Dùn ìseal, waiting on a journey neither she nor the old Keeper who had asked for it had yet troubled to make, and wondering whether a rìgh who had never held that cup in her own two hands could rightly call herself the last name of an age that had begun with heirs quarrelling over who might hold a flame no hand was ever meant to keep.

The last boat came in as the light began, thin and grey, over the water east of the harbour, and the crews went up to their own hearths with the night's catch, and the two sisters stood a while longer at the quay's edge with nothing further asked of either of them that morning beyond the ordinary business of a cold season's turning. The sea beyond the harbour mouth lay open and empty to the edge of what the morning's grey light let them see, as it had lain empty of any wished-for shore through every one of the two thousand nine hundred and threescore years the roll behind them had troubled to keep; and it is on that sea, and on that morning, and on the stone cup standing yet on its own threshold a day's hard ride to the east, that the last roll of the Holy Age closes, with no name written after Mòr's, and no shore in sight from any coast the island's own boats had ever thought worth the sailing to.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years FE 1 – 200

- <a id="ev-I-0098a"></a>**2 an t-Sultain, FE 1** — *Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala* (Dùn dhearg). The host of Dùn dhearg and the eastern households who never bowed come against the king at the ford below Dùn dhearg. Ailean Mòr holds the ford alone three days and three nights, and the dead of the host dam the river. On the third night he falls, worn down by the whole host; no one man overcame him, and age had not touched him. His kin, quarrelling already over the shares of the kingdom, did not come. He was four thousand six hundred and twenty-six years old, and had been king since the grove. The ford is called Àth na Fala after.
- <a id="ev-II-0001"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, FE 1** — *The Binding of the First Flame*. Custody is declared over the vein, and the first flame is bound at Dùn ìseal: the undying flame of Brìde, kept over the stone of Crom Cruaich. The heirs of Ailean Mòr, gathered to part his kingdom, cannot part the vein, and swear it to no one of the blood. Its keepers, Òrd Bhrìde, are the first order on Dia-thìr to govern both rite and people, and they are older by centuries than any rìgh after Ailean.
- <a id="ev-EIII-1001"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, FE 1** — *Runners to every coast* (Dùn ìseal). The kin in the valley send runners in pairs from fires that do not trust each other to every coast of the island, to call in the king's blood who had not come.
- <a id="ev-EIII-1002"></a>**5 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *Aodh Crom asks for a cord of the heirs* (Dùn ìseal). The eldest keeper of the slab, Aodh Crom, comes to the house of the knot-keeper Sìne nan Snaidhm by night and asks her for a new cord, to count the heirs, since none of them will believe another's count.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1001"><em>Runners to every coast</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1003"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The knotting of the heirs begins* (Dùn ìseal). Sìne nan Snaidhm sits down at the door of the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal with a new cord of flax and wool of many colours, one colour for each child of the king with living heirs. No heir is to be heard on the shares who has not first been knotted at the door.
- <a id="ev-II-0001a"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). The kin of Ailean Mòr, come too late to the ford, stay on at Dùn ìseal after the Binding to part his kingdom. The knot-keeper Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a knot on a cord for every heir who stands up to claim: seven hundred and twelve. The eldest of them, Murchadh Mòr, is near two thousand nine hundred years old; the youngest who claims is a child in arms.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1001"><em>Runners to every coast</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1002"><em>Aodh Crom asks for a cord of the heirs</em>, 5 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1003"><em>The knotting of the heirs begins</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1004"></a>**19 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *Ìomhar Dearg comes to the ford* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar Dearg, a son of Ailean Mòr, who had stayed three days in the valley under Dùn ìseal arguing for river-grazing, comes down out of the heather to Àth na Fala on the morning after the king fell, and finds the river dammed by the dead and his father on the west bank.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1005"></a>**20 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The spent host broken at the ford* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar Dearg's household crosses the ford and falls on the host of the east where it lies spent in the heather. Many are killed, many run, and some sit down and cover their heads. By evening Ìomhar holds the ford.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1004"><em>Ìomhar Dearg comes to the ford</em>, 19 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1006"></a>**21 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The greybeard found in the ford* (Dùn dhearg). The greybeard of the eastern households who gave the counsel of the third day is found at dawn face down in the shallows below the king's stone. Whether he fell or went in of his own will, nobody on the east bank will say.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1007"></a>**25 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *Dùn dhearg taken and its halls burned* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar Dearg walks in through both gates of Dùn dhearg, where the households of the east had sworn they owed nothing to Dùn ìseal. No one will own the blow that felled the king. He has the halls within the double bank burned, and takes the people under his own hand.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1008"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The bier of spears* (Dùn ìseal). On the fifth day after the ford the king's body is laid on a bier lashed from the host's spears and carried up the valley road by twelve men of Dùn dhearg who had been in the river. Two grey sons of the king meet it at the lip of the valley and walk behind it. Ìomhar Dearg does not go with it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1007"><em>Dùn dhearg taken and its halls burned</em>, 25 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1009"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The dead of the ford buried on the meadow* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar Dearg has the dead of the host drawn out of the river and buried in long trenches on the meadow, all together, since none can be told apart. The king's stone at the head of the ford is left standing, and he forbids anyone to move it.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1008"><em>The bier of spears</em>, 26 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1010"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, FE 1** — *The twelve bearers given cattle* (Dùn dhearg). The twelve bearers come back to Dùn dhearg with the poles of the bier. Ìomhar Dearg gives each a cow and a place within the bank, and sets the poles up at the inner gate.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1009"><em>The dead of the ford buried on the meadow</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1011"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The grey stone at the ford left standing* (Dùn dhearg). In his nine days at Dùn dhearg Ìomhar Dearg has the bank of the ford cleared but the grey stone left where it stands, and forbids anyone to move it.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1010"><em>The twelve bearers given cattle</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1012"></a>**3 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The eastern households called down from the hills* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar sends riders round the eastern hills to the households who fled with their cattle: if they come down to him and to nobody else they keep their cattle and their lives. Most come. Those who do not are hunted.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1011"><em>The grey stone at the ford left standing</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1013"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The tidings at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Donnan, a herd-boy of the eastern hills who watched the ford from the ridge, comes over the tops to the spring below Dùn ìseal on the fourth evening after the battle. The first word said in the camps of the kin is a question: who holds the hill now?<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1002"><em>Aodh Crom asks for a cord of the heirs</em>, 5 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1014"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The keening in the valley* (Dùn ìseal). Mairsile, an aged daughter of the king, begins to keen alone at her fire in the upper valley, and the whole valley of the kin takes it up fire by fire.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1015"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The bier at the gathering-house* (Dùn ìseal). The bier of spears comes up the valley road with two grey sons of the king behind it. Sìne nan Snaidhm gives the twelve bearers water at the spring. The keepers of the slab take the king from them at the door of the gathering-house.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1016"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The king laid in the earth* (Dùn ìseal). After three nights in the gathering-house Ailean Mòr is carried out before dawn and laid in the earth under a mound. The tellers of Dùn ìseal show a mound on the slope facing the vein; the reciters of the Mason's line, following Seathan Crom of Clann na Ceiste, show another. The two have never been reconciled.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1015"><em>The bier at the gathering-house</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1017"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *Ìomhar Dearg comes up as lord of Dùn dhearg* (Dùn ìseal). Ìomhar Dearg rides up the valley road with his household in the cloaks of the east and stands in the door of the gathering-house as lord of Dùn dhearg. Aodh Crom bids him sit.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1018"></a>**13 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *Two mounds shown for the king's grave* (Dùn ìseal). The knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal show a long low mound on the slope facing the vein as Ailean Mòr's grave; the reciters of the Mason's line tell of another, and of the lame reciter Seathan Crom who spoke to the grey sons on the third night. Sìne did not follow the bier and will not say.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-I-0098a"><em>Ailean Mòr falls at Àth na Fala</em>, 2 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1019"></a>**14 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The keepers bring down their fire* (Tobar dhìreach). The nine keepers of the slab come down from Tobar dhìreach to Dùn ìseal with the fire of their hut in a covered pot. The reciters of the Mason's line hold that it came down from the mason's fire; the keepers say only that it is old and must not go out.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1020"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The heirs' first quarrel over the hill* (Dùn ìseal). The kin of Ailean Mòr meet in the gathering-house below Dùn ìseal and quarrel three days over the hill, which stands over the vein: by the eldest, by the living, by the dead, and by a gallery to each line. Eithne nic Ailein and Murchadh Mòr nearly come to blood on the first day.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1021"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *Aodh Crom's asking* (Dùn ìseal). Aodh Crom, eldest of the keepers of the slab, asks the heirs to declare the keepers' charge, as the keepers had asked of Catrìona Mhòr, and to put the vein and the hill over it into no share, held by no one of the king's blood. Each line would sooner nobody had it than a cousin.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ✦ Fulfils <em>The keepers ask to be named</em> <a href="era-pdf:../age_II/The_Diathir_Legendarium_Age_of_Ailean.pdf#ev-I-0255">→ An Aois Ailein, GE 4,376</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1020"><em>The heirs' first quarrel over the hill</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1022"></a>**19 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *Gille-Brìde carries a coal of the First Flame home* (Dùn ìseal). Gille-Brìde of the line of Somhairle comes down from the high valleys, swears the Binding last of the king's blood, and asks for a coal of the flame. He carries it home in a clay pot and asks for nothing more, and no knot is tied for him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1021"><em>Aodh Crom's asking</em>, 18 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1023"></a>**22 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The flame kept in the keepers' hut* (Dùn ìseal). After the Binding the First Flame is kept in the keepers' hut on the slope above the gathering-house at Dùn ìseal, fed with a little of the coloured coal each night.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1022"><em>Gille-Brìde carries a coal of the First Flame home</em>, 19 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1024"></a>**25 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *Murchadh Mòr comes alone to the keepers' hut* (Dùn ìseal). On the night before the swearing Murchadh Mòr climbs alone to the keepers' hut and sits across the fire from Aodh Crom like a carrier, knees up, to tell him the hill will go to the fire and not to the man who feeds it, and to ask what the keepers want.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1023"><em>The flame kept in the keepers' hut</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1025"></a>**28 an t-Samhain, FE 1** — *The youngest keeper asks who will hold the flame* (Dùn ìseal). On the night after the Binding, while the heirs drink in the valley, the youngest of the nine keepers sits down across the flame from Aodh Crom and asks who will hold it when he and the rest of them are gone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1024"><em>Murchadh Mòr comes alone to the keepers' hut</em>, 25 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1026"></a>**1 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Murchadh Mòr knotted first* (Dùn ìseal). Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king, gives his line in two words, 'Ailean's son', and stands over the knot-keeper while she ties it. The knotting of his line takes the whole first day.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1003"><em>The knotting of the heirs begins</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1027"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Fionn Beag sent home* (Dùn ìseal). Eithne nic Ailein sets her own knot-keeper, Fionn Beag of the lowlands, on the step to count after Sìne nan Snaidhm. After four days he tells her that the knot-keeper of Dùn ìseal has made no mistake, and Eithne sends him home.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1026"><em>Murchadh Mòr knotted first</em>, 1 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1028"></a>**6 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Niall Òg's knot tied once* (Dùn ìseal). Niall Òg, a grandson of the king, gives his line through his mother and again through his father and says that he is owed twice. Sìne nan Snaidhm ties his knot once.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1027"><em>Fionn Beag sent home</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1029"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The knot-keeper refuses a cow* (Dùn ìseal). A steward of one of the lines of the dead brings Sìne nan Snaidhm a cow in milk to have doubtful cousins tied close to his lord's line. She sends him away, and two more after him, and the stewards begin to watch one another's lines at the door.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1028"><em>Niall Òg's knot tied once</em>, 6 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1030"></a>**8 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The knots of the dead* (Dùn ìseal). For the lines of the king's children who died before him, Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a hollow knot of black wool round nothing, and ties their heirs after it. By the end there are more hollow knots in the cord than knots for the king's living children.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1029"><em>The knot-keeper refuses a cow</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1031"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Four lines protest Ìomhar's knot* (Dùn ìseal). When Ìomhar Dearg is knotted as a son of the king, four lines send their stewards to Aodh Crom to say they will not agree to Dùn dhearg being counted as one share when the shares are cut.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1030"><em>The knots of the dead</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1032"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The youngest heir knotted* (Dùn ìseal). A great-great-grandchild of the king of the salt-shore line, a child in arms, is held up at the door and knotted, the youngest of all the heirs.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1033"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The cord laid on the floor* (Dùn ìseal). On the eleventh evening the cord of the heirs, Sreang nan Oighrean, is laid along the floor of the gathering-house from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set beside it, and the heirs walk it looking at their own knots and counting their neighbours'.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1032"><em>The youngest heir knotted</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1034"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The four rules put before the valley* (Dùn ìseal). As the sitting settles in for the winter, the heirs' quarrel sorts itself into four rival rules for the parting of the kingdom: the eldest to hold and feed the rest, the living to hold by nearness of blood, the dead's children to stand in their fathers' places, and the shares to be thrown for by lot.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1035"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Murchadh Mòr argues the eldest's rule* (Dùn ìseal). Murchadh Mòr holds, before the assembled heirs, that the eldest of the king's children should take the whole kingdom and feed the rest of the blood from his own hand, as a household divides no differently at a father's death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1034"><em>The four rules put before the valley</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1036"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Eithne argues the rule of the living* (Dùn ìseal). Eithne nic Ailein argues that the living should hold in the order of their nearness to the king's blood and no further back, so that the youngest living child stands level with the eldest.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1035"><em>Murchadh Mòr argues the eldest's rule</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1037"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The dead's children ask a place in the reckoning* (Dùn ìseal). The lines of the king's dead children, gathered behind an old man who had felt the hollow knot at the door, argue that a line does not end because its head died before the king, and ask a rule that does not forget them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1036"><em>Eithne argues the rule of the living</em>, 20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1038"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The youngest heirs ask the lot* (Dùn ìseal). Among the youngest and least-landed of the heirs a fourth rule is heard, that the shares be thrown for by lot and left to the ancestors to judge, since none of the other three rules gives them much to hope for.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1037"><em>The dead's children ask a place in the reckoning</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1039"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *Niall Òg carries words between the two fires* (Dùn ìseal). Niall Òg, owed twice over and feared by nobody's steward, begins carrying words straight between Murchadh Mòr's fire and Eithne nic Ailein's, each of them trusting him, of all the valley, to repeat the meaning and not soften it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1038"><em>The youngest heirs ask the lot</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-1040"><em>The grass of the valley fails to come back</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1040"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1** — *The grass of the valley fails to come back* (Dùn ìseal). The riverside grass, grazed to the earth by two winters of the sitting's horses and households, does not come green again with the spring, and does not for three years after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1039"><em>Niall Òg carries words between the two fires</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1041"></a>**21 an Gearran, FE 2** — *Mairsile nic Ailein dies in the cold* (Dùn ìseal). Mairsile nic Ailein, the white-haired daughter who began the keening at the ford, dies in the valley in the second month of the year, when the short winter ration leaves her brazier low overnight; she is laid by the river as she had asked before her death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1040"><em>The grass of the valley fails to come back</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1042"></a>**15 am Màrt, FE 2** — *Four lines protest the Red Share* (Dùn dhearg). Four lines with no claim on Dùn dhearg argue that Ìomhar Dearg's hold on it, won by the sword and not by any of the four rules, ought to be parted into whatever settlement the rest of the kingdom comes into; Eithne answers that no rule written after the fact can take back what is already held.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001a"><em>The heirs sit at Dùn ìseal</em>, 13 an Dàmhair, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1041"><em>Mairsile nic Ailein dies in the cold</em>, 21 an Gearran, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1043"></a>**6 an Giblean, FE 2** — *The clause against the name of rìgh* (Dùn ìseal). Through the summer the strongest lines come, fire by fire, to swear that none of the nine shall be called rìgh or take the word for a share, since the kingdom ended with Ailean Mòr; Murchadh Mòr swears it hardest, having watched what the word cost his father.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1042"><em>Four lines protest the Red Share</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1044"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, FE 2** — *Aodh Crom proposes the four rules together* (Dùn ìseal). Aodh Crom, asked his mind though he holds no share, tells the heads of the strongest lines that no one of the four rules can be sworn alone, and sets out a settlement that gives each rule something: nine great shares for the eldest living lines, a portion out of all nine for the dead, and the lot within each share where an equal claim cannot be told apart.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1043"><em>The clause against the name of rìgh</em>, 6 an Giblean, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1045"></a>**3 an Lùnastal, FE 2** — *The nine eldest lines agree to the settlement* (Dùn ìseal). The nine strongest lines of the king's blood, among them Murchadh Mòr, Eithne nic Ailein, Fionnghal nic Ailein of the western shore, Artair mac Ailein of the salt shore and Cormac mac Ailein of the east, agree to hold the nine great shares, with the portion of the dead set out of all nine and the Red Share of Ìomhar Dearg let stand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1044"><em>Aodh Crom proposes the four rules together</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1046"></a>**25 an Lùnastal, FE 2** — *The agreement to cut the cord at the handful* (Dùn ìseal). The nine lines agree that the cord of the heirs shall be laid on the gathering-house floor again and cut into nine lengths at the night of the handful, with the clause against the name of rìgh and the peace of the Hall's ground sworn once before the whole valley as it is cut.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1045"><em>The nine eldest lines agree to the settlement</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1047"></a>**16 an t-Sultain, FE 2** — *The cord of the heirs laid twice round the gathering-house floor* (Dùn ìseal). On Oidhche an Dòrlaich the keepers bring the cord of the heirs down from its chest and lay it from the hearth to the door and back, with lamps set along its length. Nine plain, unmarked knives are laid out for the nine lines that will cut it.
- <a id="ev-II-0001b"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, FE 2** — *Roinn na Rìoghachd* (Dùn ìseal). On the night of the handful the heirs swear the parting of the kingdom, Roinn na Rìoghachd. The island below the mountain is cut into nine great shares, earrannan mòra, for the nine eldest lines of the king's blood, and the lines of his dead children are given the portion of the dead, cuid nam marbh, out of all nine. No heir is to be called rìgh. The ground of the Hall is in no share. Dùn dhearg, which Ìomhar Dearg had taken with the sword after the ford, is let stand as his share, over the protest of four lines.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1030"><em>The knots of the dead</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1031"><em>Four lines protest Ìomhar's knot</em>, 12 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1034"><em>The four rules put before the valley</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1041"><em>Mairsile nic Ailein dies in the cold</em>, 21 an Gearran, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1042"><em>Four lines protest the Red Share</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1043"><em>The clause against the name of rìgh</em>, 6 an Giblean, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1044"><em>Aodh Crom proposes the four rules together</em>, 12 an t-Iuchar, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1045"><em>The nine eldest lines agree to the settlement</em>, 3 an Lùnastal, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1046"><em>The agreement to cut the cord at the handful</em>, 25 an Lùnastal, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1047"><em>The cord of the heirs laid twice round the gathering-house floor</em>, 16 an t-Sultain, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1048"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, FE 2** — *Murchadh Mòr cuts the cord first* (Dùn ìseal). Murchadh Mòr, eldest living son of the king and near two thousand nine hundred years old, cuts the cord in one stroke exactly where he had long meant to, and takes up the great share of the north, from Baile Mòr mhòr to the high passes.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1047"><em>The cord of the heirs laid twice round the gathering-house floor</em>, 16 an t-Sultain, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1049"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2** — *Eithne nic Ailein's knife cuts through a knot* (Dùn ìseal). Eithne nic Ailein, youngest of the nine eldest lines, kneels long over her place on the cord and cuts through a knot rather than between two, leaving one heir's line divided between her share and the next.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1048"><em>Murchadh Mòr cuts the cord first</em>, 15 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1050"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *Ciorstaidh cut through and claimed by two shares* (Dùn ìseal). Ciorstaidh of the salt shore, whose knot is cut through by Eithne's knife, answers the two lords quarrelling over her with "I'll take both." It is let stand: the first of the double oaths sworn that night.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1049"><em>Eithne nic Ailein's knife cuts through a knot</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1051"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *Eleven knots cut through in one night* (Dùn ìseal). Where the nine knives cross the cord's thickest stretches, eleven knots in all are cut through rather than between. Eleven households find themselves sworn to two lords at once; most pay both oaths rather than contest them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1050"><em>Ciorstaidh cut through and claimed by two shares</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1052"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The western share sworn to Fionnghal nic Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). Fionnghal nic Ailein cuts her length of the cord clean and takes the western share, with its seat on the harbour at Ros dhomhain.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1051"><em>Eleven knots cut through in one night</em>, 16 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1053"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The salt shore sworn to Artair mac Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). Artair mac Ailein, who had argued least of the nine that summer, takes the share of the salt shore, seated at the western Baile ghorm.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1052"><em>The western share sworn to Fionnghal nic Ailein</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1054"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The eastern share sworn to Cormac mac Ailein* (Dùn ìseal). Cormac mac Ailein takes the eastern share, seated at Caol shean, in which the silver of Muileann chiar will one day be found.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1053"><em>The salt shore sworn to Artair mac Ailein</em>, 22 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1055"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The four lesser shares sworn to Ùna, Coll, Gormlaith and Tadhg* (Dùn ìseal). The last four of the nine cut their lengths in quick succession: Ùna nic Ailein takes the north-west at Muileann àrsaidh, Coll mac Ailein the hills of the Abhainn fhionn at Ceann àrsaidh, Gormlaith nic Ailein the south-east at Tobar dhearg, and Tadhg mac Ailein the Abhainn ìseal and the Hawk bay at Cnoc bheag.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1054"><em>The eastern share sworn to Cormac mac Ailein</em>, 23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1056"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The cord of the heirs lies in nine pieces* (Dùn ìseal). With the ninth cut made, the cord no longer runs the floor of the gathering-house whole. It lies in nine lengths, one over each lord's arm, with the loose ends of the eleven double knots hanging free between them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1055"><em>The four lesser shares sworn to Ùna, Coll, Gormlaith and Tadhg</em>, 24 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1057"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The Red Hill declares itself sworn to nobody* (Dùn ìseal). The holder of the Red Hill, whose line had sworn to Ailean Mòr alone and to no lord of a share, stands up on the night of the handful and says his oath died with the king, and that the Red Hill is that night sworn to nobody at all.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1056"><em>The cord of the heirs lies in nine pieces</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1058"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *Three great shares claim the Red Hill* (Dùn ìseal). Murchadh Mòr and two other lords of the nine cross the floor at once to claim the ownerless Red Hill. None yields, and none of the three can make the claim stand, that night or in the years that follow.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1057"><em>The Red Hill declares itself sworn to nobody</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1059"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The Hall's ground confirmed in no share* (Dùn ìseal). Aodh Crom reminds the nine, on the night of the handful, that the hill of the slab and the gathering-house and the valley about it, as walked by the keepers, lie in no share, as sworn at the Binding, and are not to be argued afresh.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-II-0001"><em>The Binding of the First Flame</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, FE 1</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1058"><em>Three great shares claim the Red Hill</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1060"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The lengths of cord carried out of the gathering-house* (Dùn ìseal). At dawn the nine lords go out through the door of the gathering-house one after another, each with his length of the cord folded or coiled over his arm, and their households follow, so that the valley empties along nine roads at once.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001b"><em>Roinn na Rìoghachd</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 2</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1059"><em>The Hall's ground confirmed in no share</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1061"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *The boundary stones cut and set along the Roinn*. Through the winter after the handful the stewards of the nine lines ride the boundaries with the reciters, agreeing what they can, and masons cut and set the clachan-crìche, each stone bearing the sign of the share it faces. Some are moved in the night and set again by morning.
- <a id="ev-EIII-1062"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2** — *A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). No steward of the north or of the Red Share will yield Dùn thais to the other, so the masons of both lines set a stone on the north bank of the burn below the old fort, cut with Murchadh's sign, and another on the south bank, cut with the sign of the Red Share, and leave the hill itself between the two.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1061"><em>The boundary stones cut and set along the Roinn</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-1063"></a>**24 an Gearran, FE 3** — *Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais* (Dùn dhearg). At his own supper-table Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that the grazing on the northern slope above Dùn thais belongs to the Red Share, stone or no stone, and that it is time the cattle grazing there under the northern share's sign were driven off it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1062"><em>A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0001c"></a>**17 an Giblean, FE 3** — *First blood among the heirs* (Dùn thais). At Dùn thais, on the line between the great share of the north and the Red Share, the men of Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh and of Ruairidh Glas of the line of Ìomhar come to blows over which share the fort lies in. Aonghas Bàn is killed. With his death begins Aimhreit nan Oighrean, the strife of the heirs, between the line of Murchadh and the line of Ìomhar and then between many lines.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1062"><em>A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais</em>, 31 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1063"><em>Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais</em>, 24 an Gearran, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2001"></a>**21 an Giblean, FE 3** — *Aonghas Bàn carried home to his brother's hall* (Dùn thais). Ruairidh Glas's men carry Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh down off the hill of Dùn thais in a cloak between two spear-shafts, in the rain, and word runs ahead of them to his own household, where his brother Eachann Ruadh is already waiting at the gate.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001c"><em>First blood among the heirs</em>, 17 an Giblean, FE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-1063"><em>Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais</em>, 24 an Gearran, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2002"></a>**7 an Cèitean, FE 3** — *Eachann Ruadh's oath over his brother's body*. Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh kneels by his brother's body in the yard of their own hall and swears that the blood spilt at Dùn thais will be answered, blood for blood, by his own hand or his sons' after him, without naming the man he means, which by the old custom of the households leaves the quarrel open to a settling short of a second death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001c"><em>First blood among the heirs</em>, 17 an Giblean, FE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2001"><em>Aonghas Bàn carried home to his brother's hall</em>, 21 an Giblean, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2003"></a>**23 an Cèitean, FE 3** — *Ìomhar Dearg refuses to answer for the killing* (Dùn dhearg). Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that he did no more than a man does when his own are threatened, and that he is not to trouble himself with an oath sworn by a boy over his brother's body. The line of Ìomhar makes no answer to Eachann Ruadh's oath.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001c"><em>First blood among the heirs</em>, 17 an Giblean, FE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2002"><em>Eachann Ruadh's oath over his brother's body</em>, 7 an Cèitean, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2004"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, FE 3** — *The shares parted into countries and provinces*. Under each of the nine great shares the households sworn to it are parted again into countries, and the countries into provinces, as the lines of the king's dead children are fitted in among the living heirs' claims.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2003"><em>Ìomhar Dearg refuses to answer for the killing</em>, 23 an Cèitean, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2005"></a>**20 an Lùnastal, FE 3** — *Provinces parted again into counties and holdings*. Below the provinces the land is cut finer still, into counties and, under the counties, holdings no larger than a single steading, sworn by whichever household holds them to whatever county's steward stands nearest and troubles to ride out and take the oath.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2004"><em>The shares parted into countries and provinces</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2006"></a>**5 an t-Sultain, FE 3** — *Holdings sworn to two counties and to three*. A stream that shifts its bed in a wet winter leaves more than one holding claimed by two counties at once, and some households, rather than fight for the difference, swear to both and pay both, and the two counties are slow to compare their rolls.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2005"><em>Provinces parted again into counties and holdings</em>, 20 an Lùnastal, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2007"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, FE 3** — *The three lords of the mill on the Abhainn dhomhain*. Three counties meeting at a bend of the Abhainn dhomhain each claim the eel-catch of an old mill's pond, and the miller, who built the wheel before the Roinn was thought of, takes to paying each lord a third of the autumn catch unasked, and the quarrel goes no further.
- <a id="ev-II-0001d"></a>**25 am Màrt, FE 4** — *Shares of shares*. The great shares are parted again among their holders' children and grandchildren, into countries, provinces, counties and holdings, until the lesser blood of the portion of the dead is fitted in. Many holdings owe oaths to two lords, and some to three. The boundary stones of the Roinn are set up, and moved, and set up again.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1061"><em>The boundary stones cut and set along the Roinn</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2004"><em>The shares parted into countries and provinces</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, FE 3</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-2005"><em>Provinces parted again into counties and holdings</em>, 20 an Lùnastal, FE 3</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-2006"><em>Holdings sworn to two counties and to three</em>, 5 an t-Sultain, FE 3</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-2007"><em>The three lords of the mill on the Abhainn dhomhain</em>, 21 an t-Sultain, FE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2008"></a>**21 an Cèitean, FE 4** — *Aodh Crom's charge to the new Keeper* (Dùn ìseal). At the choosing on the slope below the slab, Aodh Crom, eldest of the keepers, holds out a lit rush to Beathag Bhàn and charges her to hold it for Brìde and answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. She says nothing, and the keepers count her silence in her favour.
- <a id="ev-II-0002"></a>**28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4** — *Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame* (Dùn ìseal). At Dùn ìseal under the central mountains the keepers of the slab and the households sworn to the Binding choose Beathag Bhàn to hold the first flame for Brìde and to answer to Crom for what is taken from the vein. She is of no heir's blood and holds no share, and the heirs let her be chosen for that. The spoken roll of the Keepers begins with her name. Of her life before it nothing is remembered.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2008"><em>Aodh Crom's charge to the new Keeper</em>, 21 an Cèitean, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2009"></a>**4 an Lùnastal, FE 4** — *The knot-keepers count forty-four countries* (Dùn ìseal). Riding the boundaries themselves with cords of their own, the knot-keepers of Dùn ìseal come to a count of forty-four countries under the nine great shares, a count that holds for a season before two countries are found to have quietly divided themselves into three apiece.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001d"><em>Shares of shares</em>, 25 am Màrt, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2010"></a>**20 an t-Sultain, FE 4** — *The count of a hundred and thirty-one provinces*. The knot-keepers count a hundred and thirty-one provinces under the countries, and hold the number the better part of a year, though even as it is counted two provinces of the eastern share split into three over a fishing-weir.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001d"><em>Shares of shares</em>, 25 am Màrt, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2009"><em>The knot-keepers count forty-four countries</em>, 4 an Lùnastal, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2011"></a>**4 an Dàmhair, FE 4** — *The knot-keepers give up the count at the counties* (Dùn ìseal). Cairistìona, Sìne's eldest daughter, tells Aodh Crom that the counties change their own boundaries faster than any cord can be tied to hold them, and that a knot-keeper who tries to count them all will chase a number that is never the same twice. The count of counties is given up unfinished.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001d"><em>Shares of shares</em>, 25 am Màrt, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2010"><em>The count of a hundred and thirty-one provinces</em>, 20 an t-Sultain, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2012"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, FE 4** — *A boundary quarrel brought to the Hall's ground* (Dùn ìseal). Stewards of the Red Share and the great share of the north, come to lay a raid and a cattle-theft before the keepers, nearly bring their quarrel armed onto the ground under the mountain. Aodh Crom stands between them and says again that no spear may come onto that ground in anger.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001c"><em>First blood among the heirs</em>, 17 an Giblean, FE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2011"><em>The knot-keepers give up the count at the counties</em>, 4 an Dàmhair, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2013"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 4** — *The heirs go home from the valley* (Dùn ìseal). In the second summer after the stones went up at Dùn thais, the heirs and their households go home from the valley below Dùn ìseal, most of them for the first time in nearly two years without a boundary still openly disputed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0001d"><em>Shares of shares</em>, 25 am Màrt, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2012"><em>A boundary quarrel brought to the Hall's ground</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2014"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 4** — *The flame kept in a turf hut* (Dùn ìseal). With no hall yet raised, the households build Beathag Bhàn a one-room hut of turf at the mountain's foot, and she carries the newly given flame into it and sits up with it through the first night, having found no words to answer the keepers with.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0002"><em>Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame</em>, 28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2008"><em>Aodh Crom's charge to the new Keeper</em>, 21 an Cèitean, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2015"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, FE 5** — *Beathag Bhàn learns the galleries* (Dùn ìseal). Aodh Crom leads Beathag Bhàn down into the low galleries under Dùn ìseal and names them for her one by one, though he will not let her cut the coal herself, telling her that the hand which holds the flame does not also cut the vein.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0002"><em>Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame</em>, 28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2014"><em>The flame kept in a turf hut</em>, 23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2016"></a>**7 an Gearran, FE 6** — *The watch set on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas* (Cnoc ghlas). Beitris, an old keeper of the slab, teaches Beathag Bhàn to read the cloud on the high passes from the cairns above Cnoc ghlas, the sign by which the Hall judges when a gallery may safely be opened for the season.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0002"><em>Beathag Bhàn keeps the first flame</em>, 28 an t-Ògmhios, FE 4</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2015"><em>Beathag Bhàn learns the galleries</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, FE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2017"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, FE 9** — *The nine districts argue the turn of the hearths* (Dùn ìseal). Before the first season is set, two of the nine districts about the mountain's foot claim the tending of the flame for themselves alone, on the ground that their people sat nearest the old slab the longest, and are outvoted by the other seven.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2016"><em>The watch set on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas</em>, 7 an Gearran, FE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0003"></a>**27 an t-Iuchar, FE 10** — *The nine hearths* (Dùn ìseal). Nine households about the mountain's foot, one for each district of the old keepers of the slab, take the tending of the flame in turn, each sending a son or daughter to sit with it through a season. The later houses of custody all claim descent from one or another of the nine. Not all the claims can be true.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2017"><em>The nine districts argue the turn of the hearths</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, FE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2018"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, FE 10** — *Cailean of the northern hearth sits the first season* (Dùn ìseal). Cailean, a boy of the northern district, is the first of the nine hearths sent up to sit a season with Beathag Bhàn and the flame, arriving expecting a shrine and finding a cold hut with one keeper barely older than himself.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0003"><em>The nine hearths</em>, 27 an t-Iuchar, FE 10</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2017"><em>The nine districts argue the turn of the hearths</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, FE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2019"></a>**21 an Dàmhair, FE 10** — *The first cairns raised above Cnoc ghlas*. Before fixed cairns marked the ridge, watchers of the weather climbed wherever their own eye judged best each morning. An eastern woman, Sorcha, first piles stone at the three places she finds she reads the sky truest, so that watchers after her need not guess afresh each dawn where to stand.
- <a id="ev-EIII-2020"></a>**10 am Faoilleach, FE 12** — *Niall Òg offers Beathag Bhàn a silver cup* (Dùn ìseal). Niall Òg climbs to the Hall's ground alone and offers Beathag Bhàn a cup of worked silver beaten with running deer, so that she might have one thing of her own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2018"><em>Cailean of the northern hearth sits the first season</em>, 22 an t-Sultain, FE 10</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2021"></a>**8 an Gearran, FE 12** — *Beathag Bhàn refuses the gift* (Dùn ìseal). Beathag Bhàn gives the silver cup back to Niall Òg, saying that whatever she holds she holds for every hand in the valley, and that taking a gift from one heir would oblige her to answer for refusing every other.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2020"><em>Niall Òg offers Beathag Bhàn a silver cup</em>, 10 am Faoilleach, FE 12</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2022"></a>**9 am Màrt, FE 13** — *Mòrag nan Càrn named watcher of the ridge*. A child of the fifth hearth who could tell one grey sky from another better than watchers grown old at the work is named, at not yet twenty, to keep the cairns above Cnoc ghlas in her own right, the youngest the mountain has yet trusted with the reading of its weather.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2019"><em>The first cairns raised above Cnoc ghlas</em>, 21 an Dàmhair, FE 10</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2023"></a>**7 an Giblean, FE 14** — *The door of Talla na Lasrach set toward the vein* (Dùn ìseal). Aodh Crom walks the ground of the new hall with Beathag Bhàn before the first stone is laid and marks where its one door must stand, facing the vein and turned from the sea, giving no reason he will afterward repeat the same way twice.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2021"><em>Beathag Bhàn refuses the gift</em>, 8 an Gearran, FE 12</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0004"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *Talla na Lasrach raised* (Dùn ìseal). A long hall of dry stone and turf is raised over the flame at Dùn ìseal, with one door toward the vein and none toward the sea. It is rebuilt many times on the same footings, and the footings are all of it that anyone can now swear to.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-1023"><em>The flame kept in the keepers' hut</em>, 22 an t-Samhain, FE 1</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2023"><em>The door of Talla na Lasrach set toward the vein</em>, 7 an Giblean, FE 14</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2024"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *The nine hearths raise the hall's walls* (Dùn ìseal). Sons and daughters of the nine households build Talla na Lasrach's walls of dry stone and turf under Beathag Bhàn's eye, each household's work known afterward by the set of its stones, straight where the ninth hearth laid it and less so where the second did.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0004"><em>Talla na Lasrach raised</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2023"><em>The door of Talla na Lasrach set toward the vein</em>, 7 an Giblean, FE 14</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2025"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *Ruairidh Glas and Eachann Ruadh stand at one fire* (Dùn ìseal). At Samhain on the Hall's ground, Ruairidh Glas, who killed Aonghas Bàn at Dùn thais, and Eachann Ruadh, the dead man's brother, stand at opposite sides of the same fire the whole night and speak no word to one another, but neither draws.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-II-0001c"><em>First blood among the heirs</em>, 17 an Giblean, FE 3</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2024"><em>The nine hearths raise the hall's walls</em>, 25 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2026"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a knot for good news* (Dùn ìseal). Sìne nan Snaidhm comes up to Dùn ìseal for the carrying of the flame into the finished hall and ties a plain unmarked length into her long cord-record, the first knot she has ever tied for good news alone rather than for a claim or a grief.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0004"><em>Talla na Lasrach raised</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2025"><em>Ruairidh Glas and Eachann Ruadh stand at one fire</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2027"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15** — *The flame carried into Talla na Lasrach* (Dùn ìseal). On the shortest day of the year Beathag Bhàn lifts the flame from the hearth-stone of the turf hut that had held it eleven years and carries it into the finished hall, where it burns that evening for the first time under a roof built to hold it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0004"><em>Talla na Lasrach raised</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2026"><em>Sìne nan Snaidhm ties a knot for good news</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 15</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2028"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, FE 18** — *The reverence about the mountain given a name*. Asked by a walker of the eastern share what the households call the milk left on the sill and the silence kept on the ridge, old Beitris of the Hall answers for them: Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach, the ancestors, the sìth, the vein and the weather held together, owed remembering and courtesy and watching, and needing no priest to speak for any of them.
- <a id="ev-II-0005"></a>**17 am Faoilleach, FE 21** — *Seann Spioradan nan Dia-thìreach established*. At the hearths the eldest of the island's folk-ways takes shape: reverence for the ancestors, for the vein, for the weather that rules the mining season, and for the sìth of the hills and mounds. It keeps no priests, and it has never ceased.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2028"><em>The reverence about the mountain given a name</em>, 30 an Lùnastal, FE 18</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0006"></a>**22 an Dàmhair, FE 27** — *The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas* (Cnoc ghlas). Watchers build cairns on the ridge above Cnoc ghlas and read the cloud on the high passes from them, to tell the Hall when the galleries may be opened for the season. A wrong reading costs the whole mountain its season, and the watchers are chosen with more care than the Keeper.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2019"><em>The first cairns raised above Cnoc ghlas</em>, 21 an Dàmhair, FE 10</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2022"><em>Mòrag nan Càrn named watcher of the ridge</em>, 9 am Màrt, FE 13</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2029"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, FE 29** — *Fearchar Glas reads the cloud wrong*. A watcher of six years' standing judges a low grey sky wind only and sends the galleries open; the rain that follows floods the low gallery past saving and costs the households the whole autumn's cutting. Fearchar comes down off the ridge unbidden to tell the keepers of the slab what he did.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-II-0006"><em>The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas</em>, 22 an Dàmhair, FE 27</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2030"></a>**3 an t-Iuchar, FE 30** — *The cairns given a stricter choosing*. After the season lost to a wrong reading, the keepers of the slab rule that no one may watch the cairns alone who has not first stood a full season under an elder watcher's eye and been judged fit by more than one. Mòrag nan Càrn sits among those who judge the youths who come after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0006"><em>The weather-cairns of Cnoc ghlas</em>, 22 an Dàmhair, FE 27</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2029"><em>Fearchar Glas reads the cloud wrong</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, FE 29</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2031"></a>**17 an t-Sultain, FE 33** — *A boy of Doire uaine chooses the cold over the flint*. In the hardest winter the slopes have seen, a boy sent to bring in a ewe is caught by the wind and found two days later, alive, having refused to strike a fire within sight of the forbidden hills though he carried flint enough. His mother carries him down to the Hall herself rather than risk the road past the standing stones.
- <a id="ev-II-0007"></a>**20 an t-Samhain, FE 33** — *The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). In obedience to the old inscriptions the Keepers forbid any fire, of wood or of coal, to be lit in sight of the Doire uaine hills. Herders who winter on those slopes eat cold for the season. The ban is never lifted, and none is known to have owned to breaking it.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2031"><em>A boy of Doire uaine chooses the cold over the flint</em>, 17 an t-Sultain, FE 33</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2032"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 33** — *The Hall's hearth opened to the Doire uaine households*. Beathag Bhàn sends word that any household of the forbidden slopes may bring a sick child or a frost-bitten hand to the Keeper's own hearth at Dùn ìseal, the ban forbidding only a fire lit within sight of those hills. Few households make the long journey, but the offer is remembered longer than it is used.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0007"><em>The ban on fires in sight of Doire uaine</em>, 20 an t-Samhain, FE 33</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2031"><em>A boy of Doire uaine chooses the cold over the flint</em>, 17 an t-Sultain, FE 33</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2033"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, FE 34** — *Beathag Bhàn walks alone to the temple ruin*. Telling no one where she goes, Beathag Bhàn crosses broken ground to Làrach an Teampaill and finds its altar-slab, worn by hands no one living can name, turned toward her own mountain. She returns and tells the keepers of the slab plainly that she cannot say whose place it is, only that it is neither Brìde's nor Crom's.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2032"><em>The Hall's hearth opened to the Doire uaine households</em>, 20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 33</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0008"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, FE 34** — *Làrach an Teampaill left unentered* (Làrach an Teampaill). Beathag Bhàn walks to Làrach an Teampaill, finds its altar already turned toward the mountain, and declares the place not the Hall's to keep. The Keepers set no foot in it for the rest of the age. Whose it was they did not say, and it seems they did not know.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2033"><em>Beathag Bhàn walks alone to the temple ruin</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, FE 34</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2034"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, FE 34** — *The keepers swear never to enter the ruin*. After argument over whether the temple ruin should be cleared and watched like the cairns or left untouched, Beathag Bhàn ends it: no keeper of the slab, and no Keeper of the flame after her, will set foot inside it again, a reverence built on courtesy to what it cannot read being no reverence at all if it tramples the ground.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0008"><em>Làrach an Teampaill left unentered</em>, 5 am Faoilleach, FE 34</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2033"><em>Beathag Bhàn walks alone to the temple ruin</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, FE 34</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2035"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, FE 44** — *Death of Beathag Bhàn*. After a winter's slow failing, Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal without ever having risen ill from her bed. She is laid on the slope facing the vein with her back to the sea, at Beitris's word, since she never once turned from the mountain living and none will have her do it the one day she cannot choose.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2034"><em>The keepers swear never to enter the ruin</em>, 23 an Lùnastal, FE 34</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0009"></a>**3 an Gearran, FE 44** — *Death of Beathag Bhàn* (Dùn ìseal). Beathag Bhàn dies at Dùn ìseal and is laid on the slope facing the vein, with her back to the sea. The nine hearths choose Muireach Liath, her sister's son, to keep the flame after her.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2035"><em>Death of Beathag Bhàn</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, FE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2036"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, FE 44** — *Muireach Liath chosen to hold the flame*. The nine hearths gather within the week and name Muireach Liath, Beathag Bhàn's sister's son, faster than any choosing the mountain has seen. Old Beitris puts the rush into his hands with words close to Aodh Crom's own, and he carries the flame into the Hall that same evening.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0009"><em>Death of Beathag Bhàn</em>, 3 an Gearran, FE 44</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2035"><em>Death of Beathag Bhàn</em>, 3 am Faoilleach, FE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2037"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, FE 45** — *The basket argued to one size*. Muireach Liath asks the nine hearths for a common measure, a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. The households argue the size of it until they have argued themselves into agreeing on one.
- <a id="ev-EIII-2038"></a>**20 an Gearran, FE 46** — *The weavers of the third hearth take the basket's making*. The plaiting that holds the measured basket's shape under a full load proves particular enough that the weavers of the third hearth keep the craft for their own. Baskets of that weave outlast a season's use before any other household's do.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2037"><em>The basket argued to one size</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, FE 45</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2039"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, FE 47** — *A second and third sinking answered* (Caol shean). Two more households of Caol shean come forward with tales like the first woman's, of boats kept whole after a drink of the stream in what each judges the right quarter of the moon. The laughing that met her first telling thins.
- <a id="ev-II-0010"></a>**15 an Gearran, FE 48** — *Coal by the basket* (Dùn ìseal). Muireach Liath fixes the first common measure for coal carried down from the galleries: a lidded basket of plaited heather, one to a household, filled once a season. Baskets of that weave are made at Dùn ìseal still, for no purpose but the making.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2037"><em>The basket argued to one size</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, FE 45</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-2038"><em>The weavers of the third hearth take the basket's making</em>, 20 an Gearran, FE 46</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2040"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 49** — *Muireach walks up to Muileann ruadh* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). In his fourth year Muireach Liath goes up to the warm springs himself rather than let the households' carrying run past him unquestioned, and finds an old woman keeping her granddaughter's ill-set arm a season longer in the water before anyone speaks of breaking it again.
- <a id="ev-EIII-2041"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, FE 52** — *A hearth-elder puts the stream to Muireach* (Allt an Àigh). One of the hearth-elders who kept the ancestors' watch before Beathag Bhàn's own choosing asks Muireach Liath directly whether a stream running off the vein's own mountain belongs to the Hall's reckoning. His answer, given plainly in a few sentences, is repeated by every Keeper who follows him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2040"><em>Muireach walks up to Muileann ruadh</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 49</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0011"></a>**17 am Faoilleach, FE 53** — *Allt an Àigh named* (Allt an Àigh). A stream is held to bring good fortune to any who drink of it in a certain quarter of the moon. Pilgrims come to it, and have never wholly ceased to come.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-2039"><em>A second and third sinking answered</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, FE 47</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2042"></a>**2 an Giblean, FE 53** — *Gille-Brìde dies in the high valleys*. Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line, who carried a coal of the First Flame home from the Binding and asked for nothing since, dies among his own people at two hundred and twenty-four, in an early winter hard on the hill-folk of Coille naomh.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-II-0010"><em>Coal by the basket</em>, 15 an Gearran, FE 48</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2043"></a>**30 an t-Ògmhios, FE 53** — *Ceallach keeps the coal*. Ceallach mac Ghille-Bhrìde takes up his father's hearth and the coal of the First Flame kept on it, changing nothing the hill-folk who sit by that fire can name, since he had been feeding it quietly on his father's behalf for years before.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0010"><em>Coal by the basket</em>, 15 an Gearran, FE 48</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2042"><em>Gille-Brìde dies in the high valleys</em>, 2 an Giblean, FE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-2044"></a>**4 an Dùbhlachd, FE 53** — *Niall Òg sits an evening at Ceallach's hearth*. Niall Òg goes up alone to the high valleys on hearing of Gille-Brìde's death, and finds, for the first time in sixty years of burying his father's kin, a death that leaves him nothing to feel bitter about.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0010"><em>Coal by the basket</em>, 15 an Gearran, FE 48</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-2043"><em>Ceallach keeps the coal</em>, 30 an t-Ògmhios, FE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0012"></a>**14 an Giblean, FE 57** — *The pilgrims' path from Caol shean* (Caol shean). A path is worn from the river landing at Caol shean up the valley to Allt an Àigh. It is walked by night, so that pilgrims reach the water in the right quarter of the moon. Fishermen who walk it are said to lose fewer boats; no count was kept either way.
