The teacher who first brought letters to Inis bheag dies an old man, having taught three generations of the same dozen families. A pupil cuts his grave-marker in the fisher-marks rather than in the Hall's own hand, the first stone on the island so cut.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0156"><em>Inis bheag's school of letters</em>, 22 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,854</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7050"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,908** — *A stable-boy's tally teaches a clerk's daughter her letters* (Cathair dhearg). At Cathair dhearg a boy of Inis bheag, sent inland to serve in the red hall's stables, scratches a fisher's tally on a granary door. A clerk's daughter, Peigi nic Tormoid, asks what the marks mean and will not be told they are nothing, and so learns the fisher-marks before she learns the Hall's own hand.
- <a id="ev-II-0157"></a>**21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926** — *Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi nic Tormoid, of the line of Tormod Scrìobhaiche, is clerk of the hall at Cathair dhearg, the first whose own hand can be told from the others in the copies that survive. Her entries are short, and she never gives a reason where a fact will serve. Much of what is known of the middle of the age is in her hand, or copied from it.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7050"><em>A stable-boy's tally teaches a clerk's daughter her letters</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,908</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7051"></a>**21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,926** — *Peigi nic Tormoid takes the clerk's stool* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi nic Tormoid is given the clerk's stool at Cathair dhearg in her twenty-sixth year, after the death of an elder cousin from fever and for want of anyone else willing to take the work. She keeps the roll of the red hall for four-and-forty years after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0157"><em>Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall</em>, 21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7050"><em>A stable-boy's tally teaches a clerk's daughter her letters</em>, 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,908</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7052"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,948** — *Peigi's ruling on the boundary of two descriptions* (Cathair dhearg). A lord of the plain presses Peigi nic Tormoid to set a boundary dispute down in his own favour. She refuses to keep opinions in the roll and writes instead both sides' own words and the last day they had agreed on anything, a plain record a Keeper's clerk consults to settle a far larger dispute two centuries later.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0157"><em>Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall</em>, 21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7051"><em>Peigi nic Tormoid takes the clerk's stool</em>, 21 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,926</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7053"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, FE 1,970** — *Death of Peigi nic Tormoid* (Cathair dhearg). Peigi nic Tormoid dies in her own bed at seventy, having kept the roll of the red hall through a reign and the half of another. The clerks who follow her learn to date a leaf by whether her hand lies on it, a truer clock, some say, than the reign it was written under.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0157"><em>Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall</em>, 21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7052"><em>Peigi's ruling on the boundary of two descriptions</em>, 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,948</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7054"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, FE 1,975** — *The fowler households of Seann Skell feed the hawk first* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families begin feeding their hawks before the household eats, on the reasoning that a hunger fed first turns less readily on the house that keeps it waiting. The custom spreads from household to household along the one street.
- <a id="ev-II-0158"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999** — *The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families keep a hawk in every household and feed it before the household eats. They burn their season's handful at dawn with the hawk on the wrist, for the flame, they say, is a hunger and should be fed as a hunger is fed. They call the hawk Mòd, the Hawk of Acaill, the grey hawk of time, as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who lived down the ages as a salmon, an eagle and a hawk; between them the two remember all things. From them Òrd an t-Seabhaig counts its beginning.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7054"><em>The fowler households of Seann Skell feed the hawk first</em>, 4 an t-Sultain, FE 1,975</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7055"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, FE 2,000** — *Raghnaid nic Chaluim burns her handful with the hawk unhooded* (Seann Skell). Raghnaid nic Chaluim of Seann Skell burns her household's dawn handful with her hawk Mòd unhooded on her wrist, its eye on the flame the whole time it burns. Her own household says of her afterward that she carried the custom the whole distance it would go.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0158"><em>The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7054"><em>The fowler households of Seann Skell feed the hawk first</em>, 4 an t-Sultain, FE 1,975</a>.</span>

## The Years FE 2,001 – 2,200

- <a id="ev-EIII-7056"></a>**8 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,019** — *A clerk questions Raghnaid on the hawk's watching* (Seann Skell). A clerk sent from Cathair dhearg to set the dawn-hawk custom in the Hall's roll asks Raghnaid nic Chaluim why the bird must watch the burning. She answers that the flame is a hunger too and should be fed in the sight of the thing that hungers, and the clerk writes her words down unaltered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0158"><em>The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,999</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7055"><em>Raghnaid nic Chaluim burns her handful with the hawk unhooded</em>, 3 an Dàmhair, FE 2,000</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7057"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, FE 2,035** — *The dawn-hawk kept at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). Households at Cnoc bheag, none of them fowlers by trade, buy hawks at cost from Skell traders and take up the dawn burning with the bird on the wrist. Their neighbours, keeping no hawk, remark that the birds are fed better than the households' own children.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7056"><em>A clerk questions Raghnaid on the hawk's watching</em>, 8 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,019</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7058"></a>**11 an Cèitean, FE 2,041** — *The Keeper sends a clerk to see the dawn kept* (Cnoc bheag). Pressed by an uneasy household of the lowland plain, the Keeper of that season sends a clerk north to Cnoc bheag to see the dawn-hawk rite kept before ruling on it. The clerk reports the hawk-households burn no more of their measure than any other hearth, only in a bird's sight rather than none.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7057"><em>The dawn-hawk kept at Cnoc bheag</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, FE 2,035</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7059"></a>**9 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,042** — *The Hall answers that the rite is no concern of its own* (Inis ìseal). The Keeper writes to the lowland household, and to every household after it that raises the question, that the dawn-hawk rite keeps the measure exactly and is no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time in the age the Hall answers any rite so simply.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7058"><em>The Keeper sends a clerk to see the dawn kept</em>, 11 an Cèitean, FE 2,041</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0159"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, FE 2,072** — *The hawk-rite spreads up the Abhainn ìseal* (Inis ìseal). The dawn burning with the hawk spreads from Seann Skell on the northern shore up the Abhainn ìseal to Inis ìseal and Cnoc bheag. The Keeper at Dùn ìseal writes that the rite keeps the measure exactly and is therefore no concern of the Hall. Never again does the Hall say so of any rite.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7057"><em>The dawn-hawk kept at Cnoc bheag</em>, 6 an Lùnastal, FE 2,035</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7058"><em>The Keeper sends a clerk to see the dawn kept</em>, 11 an Cèitean, FE 2,041</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7059"><em>The Hall answers that the rite is no concern of its own</em>, 9 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,042</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-7060"></a>**7 an Cèitean, FE 2,098** — *Aonghas Ruadh brings the sting-oath north to Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). Aonghas Ruadh, a merchant of Ros bheag trading salt fish for the dry country's dyed wool, returns from Baile àrsaidh with a boxed scorpion and swears his next bargain on its sting before the harbour court has seen the custom done. The court takes to the swearing within the year.
- <a id="ev-EIII-7061"></a>**8 an Giblean, FE 2,099** — *A trader of the plain is refused for want of the sting-oath* (Ros bheag). A trader of the plain who will not swear his debt on Ros bheag's sting, calling a boxed scorpion no fit thing to bind a man, is sold no fish by the harbour court, which holds that a man unwilling to swear as every other trader swears is telling the court something his own name does not.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7060"><em>Aonghas Ruadh brings the sting-oath north to Ros bheag</em>, 7 an Cèitean, FE 2,098</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0160"></a>**1 am Faoilleach, FE 2,145** — *The sting-oath at Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). The swearing on a scorpion's sting spreads from Baile àrsaidh up the western coast to Ros bheag, and the harbour court there takes it for every oath of trade. For the rest of the age a merchant who will not swear on the sting is not trusted in the western harbours.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7060"><em>Aonghas Ruadh brings the sting-oath north to Ros bheag</em>, 7 an Cèitean, FE 2,098</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-7061"><em>A trader of the plain is refused for want of the sting-oath</em>, 8 an Giblean, FE 2,099</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8001"></a>**12 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,146** — *Death of Aonghas Ruadh* (Ros bheag). Aonghas Ruadh dies an old man at Ros bheag, still keeper of his own scorpion in its box behind the harbour-master's door. By then no merchant travels the western coast without learning the sting-oath before the prices, from Ros bheag to Baile àrsaidh alike.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0160"><em>The sting-oath at Ros bheag</em>, 1 am Faoilleach, FE 2,145</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-7061"><em>A trader of the plain is refused for want of the sting-oath</em>, 8 an Giblean, FE 2,099</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8002"></a>**10 an Lùnastal, FE 2,180** — *The shrine-keepers of Inis thais ask for a second stone* (Inis thais). The shrine-keepers of Inis thais, hearing of the wolf-sworn road-guards' oath-stone at Caol leathan, ask the guild whether a second might stand at their own shrine beside the drowned, where a guard's oath, they judge, would sit well beside an older prayer. The guards, flattered more than they admit, agree to drag one themselves rather than trust any mason unsworn to their own oath.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8003"></a>**8 an t-Sultain, FE 2,181** — *The dragging of the second wolf-stone* (Inis thais). The road-guards of Caol leathan drag a block of white quartz from the mountain to Inis thais at the cost of more oxen than the guild can easily spare, the sledge breaking twice on the lower slopes and one ox dying under the second breaking.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8004"></a>**7 an Dàmhair, FE 2,181** — *Calum Mòr declines to swear twice at Inis thais* (Inis thais). Asked by the eldest shrine-keeper whether he wishes to pray before the new stone, the road-guards' captain Calum Mòr answers that he swore on it once at his founding and sees no cause to swear twice, though his guards may pray there as the drowned welcome any stranger's prayer.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8003"><em>The dragging of the second wolf-stone</em>, 8 an t-Sultain, FE 2,181</a>.</span>

## The Years FE 2,201 – 2,400

- <a id="ev-EIII-8005"></a>**5 an t-Samhain, FE 2,205** — *The Hall's roll outgrows the clerks' room* (Cathair dhearg). The roll kept at Cathair dhearg since Seonag Chrom first gave the clerks a room runs by now to more chests than the room can hold. A later generation of clerks works from summaries of summaries, the original hands known to them by name and reputation and not by sight.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0157"><em>Peigi nic Tormoid, clerk of the hall</em>, 21 an t-Iuchar, FE 1,926</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0161"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217** — *The wolf-stone at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The wolf-sworn road-guards of Caol leathan set a second wolf-stone at the shrine of Inis thais, and the keepers of the shrine begin to pray before it as well as to the drowned. The stone is white quartz, dragged from the mountain on a sledge at a cost greater than the shrine's.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8002"><em>The shrine-keepers of Inis thais ask for a second stone</em>, 10 an Lùnastal, FE 2,180</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8003"><em>The dragging of the second wolf-stone</em>, 8 an t-Sultain, FE 2,181</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8004"><em>Calum Mòr declines to swear twice at Inis thais</em>, 7 an Dàmhair, FE 2,181</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8006"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217** — *Four keepings named in one breath at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). A trader passing through Cathair dhearg names the hawk fed at Seann Skell, the sting sworn at Ros bheag, the wolf-stone prayed to at Inis thais and the fisher-marks taught at Inis bheag all together, as though of one custom, though none were ever planned as such.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0161"><em>The wolf-stone at Inis thais</em>, 3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,217</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8007"></a>**2 am Faoilleach, FE 2,260** — *Donnchadh mac Iain is born at Cnoc bhàn* (Cnoc bhàn). A cutter's widow of Cnoc bhàn brings her second son to the stag's teachers rather than send him to the vein at ten years old, judging one son owed to the coal enough for her house. He grows up among the school's chests of strike-books before he grows up among the seams.
- <a id="ev-II-0162"></a>**28 an Gearran, FE 2,290** — *The strike-books compared* (Cnoc bhàn). Donnchadh mac Iain, a teacher of the stag's people at Cnoc bhàn, reads through the strike-books of many generations of apprentices. He finds that the coal breaks brighter in its colours for cutters in their later years than in their first, whatever their house, and argues that the vein answers practice. The elders answer that it answers what a cutter was born with, and that practice only shows it.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8007"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain is born at Cnoc bhàn</em>, 2 am Faoilleach, FE 2,260</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8008"></a>**4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,290** — *Donnchadh mac Iain is set to the old leaves* (Cnoc bhàn). In a thin winter Cnoc bhàn's masters set the young teacher Donnchadh mac Iain to clearing dead apprentices' leaves from the school's chests, a task given him more as punishment than trust. He begins, instead, a private tally of when in a cutter's years the coal comes brightest.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0162"><em>The strike-books compared</em>, 28 an Gearran, FE 2,290</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8007"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain is born at Cnoc bhàn</em>, 2 am Faoilleach, FE 2,260</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8009"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,290** — *Aonghas Cam answers the tally* (Cnoc bhàn). The eldest teacher of Cnoc bhàn, Aonghas Cam, hears Donnchadh mac Iain's tally at the midwinter gathering and answers, as the house had always answered, that the vein knows a cutter's blood and the years only show what was already there. The two teachings begin to divide the room.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0162"><em>The strike-books compared</em>, 28 an Gearran, FE 2,290</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8008"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain is set to the old leaves</em>, 4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8010"></a>**29 an Cèitean, FE 2,296** — *The house at Cnoc bhàn sits in two halves* (Cnoc bhàn). By the eighth year of Donnchadh mac Iain's yearly tally, those who hear him to the end of it and those who answer him before he finishes have come, without any master's ordering, to sit on opposite sides of the long room at every midwinter gathering.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0162"><em>The strike-books compared</em>, 28 an Gearran, FE 2,290</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8009"><em>Aonghas Cam answers the tally</em>, 29 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,290</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0163"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300** — *Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two of his hearers leave the house at Cnoc bhàn and settle at Muileann chaol, taking copies of the strike-books with them. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft of the books. Donnchadh calls it copying, which it is.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8011"></a>**31 am Màrt, FE 2,300** — *The twenty-two leave Cnoc bhàn* (Cnoc bhàn). Donnchadh mac Iain and twenty-two hearers load copies of the strike-books they judge their own onto two borrowed carts and walk south to Muileann chaol. The elders of Cnoc bhàn call it theft; Donnchadh calls it copying, since every leaf they made a copy of stands where it always stood.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0163"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8010"><em>The house at Cnoc bhàn sits in two halves</em>, 29 an Cèitean, FE 2,296</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8012"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, FE 2,300** — *Muileann chaol's reeve houses the school* (Muileann chaol). The reeve of Muileann chaol lets Donnchadh mac Iain's twenty-two hearers a millwright's storehouse for a rent none of them can pay in coin, taken instead that first winter in mended roofs and re-hung doors for half the town.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0163"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain leaves Cnoc bhàn</em>, 30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,300</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8011"><em>The twenty-two leave Cnoc bhàn</em>, 31 am Màrt, FE 2,300</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8013"></a>**3 am Màrt, FE 2,301** — *Muileann chaol's books are ruled to keep no parentage* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain sets the rule for the new school's strike-books: no cutter's father, mother or house is written on a leaf, only the name, the day and the stroke. More than one of the twenty-two finds the old habit slower to unlearn than the rule was to set down.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8012"><em>Muileann chaol's reeve houses the school</em>, 3 an Dàmhair, FE 2,300</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0164"></a>**7 an t-Sultain, FE 2,317** — *The founding of the rival druid school*. A school of druids breaks away, holding that the vein answers labour and not birth.
- <a id="ev-II-0165"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330** — *The school at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). The school of Donnchadh mac Iain at Muileann chaol keeps strike-books of its own under a rule the elder school never had: a cutter's parentage is not written in the book at all. The two schools of the stag dispute by letter for the rest of the age, and both keep the letters.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8013"><em>Muileann chaol's books are ruled to keep no parentage</em>, 3 am Màrt, FE 2,301</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8014"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,330** — *Donnchadh mac Iain writes north* (Muileann chaol). Seventy years old and less able to travel, Donnchadh mac Iain sends the first letter to Cnoc bhàn, addressed to the house rather than to any one master, asking whether its own century-and-a-half of leaves shows the same rise with a cutter's years that his own count once showed.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0165"><em>The school at Muileann chaol</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8013"><em>Muileann chaol's books are ruled to keep no parentage</em>, 3 am Màrt, FE 2,301</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8015"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,340** — *Donnchadh mac Iain dies at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). Donnchadh mac Iain dies at eighty in the storehouse-schoolhouse his twenty-two hearers first took shelter in forty years before, having taught six generations whose leaves carry no father's or mother's name. He is buried under a leaf of oiled hide cut with one word: one who writes.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0165"><em>The school at Muileann chaol</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, FE 2,330</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8014"><em>Donnchadh mac Iain writes north</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,330</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8016"></a>**24 an Lùnastal, FE 2,340** — *Raonaid Dhubh is born at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). A clerk's daughter is born at Dùn ìseal in the same year Donnchadh mac Iain dies, given the name Raonaid Dhubh for the black hair she keeps unusually from her first day.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8017"></a>**27 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,360** — *Raonaid Dhubh takes the Keeper's stool* (Dùn ìseal). Raonaid Dhubh comes to the Keeper's own chest of clerks at twenty, an elder cousin's death leaving the stool empty at a season when no one else in the room wants the sitting of it, and reads there, among other papers, the growing archive of letters between Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8016"><em>Raonaid Dhubh is born at Dùn ìseal</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, FE 2,340</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0166"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366** — *The Hall hears the two schools* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper Raonaid Dhubh hears both schools of the stag at Dùn ìseal and gives no ruling, saying that the vein has not asked the Hall to decide. The Hall's roll sets down the hearing and the refusal. No refusal of the Hall is more often cited.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8017"><em>Raonaid Dhubh takes the Keeper's stool</em>, 27 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,360</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8018"></a>**28 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366** — *Both schools ask the new Keeper for a ruling* (Dùn ìseal). Within her first year holding the cup, Raonaid Dhubh receives word from both Cnoc bhàn and Muileann chaol asking her to say, once and plainly, which school's reading of the vein is the truer, as every Keeper before her has been asked and never once has answered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0166"><em>The Hall hears the two schools</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,366</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8017"><em>Raonaid Dhubh takes the Keeper's stool</em>, 27 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,360</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0167"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376** — *What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). Scholars of the stag from Muileann chaol come to Calbh Cnoc ghorm and cannot read it. The people of Cnoc ghorm tell them the stone says: we did not come; we were here. The scholars write that the people say so. No later hand explains either the stone or the saying.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8019"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,376** — *The scholars of Muileann chaol cannot read Cnoc ghorm's stone* (Calbh Cnoc ghorm). Scholars of the second school travel east to Cnoc ghorm to read the standing stone at the town's centre, and spend the better part of a day turning its worn face to the light without making out a single letter of its cutting.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0167"><em>What the people of Cnoc ghorm say of their stone</em>, 6 an Dàmhair, FE 2,376</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0168"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,386** — *The digging at Làrach an Dùin* (Làrach an Dùin). Men of Baile ghorm dig under the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin for the riches the ruin was said to hold, and find ash and nothing else. The Keeper has them sentenced as if they had broken the Law, though no law covered it, and the sentence stands as the rule for all the old places after.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8020"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,386** — *Baile ghorm's diggers find only ash* (Làrach an Dùin). A company from Baile ghorm breaks into the fallen walls of Làrach an Dùin by night on the strength of an old tale of riches, and finds at dawn nothing beneath the stone but cold, undisturbed ash that no fire any of them can name had left.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0168"><em>The digging at Làrach an Dùin</em>, 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,386</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0169"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,391** — *Baile ghorm's penance* (Baile ghorm). The families of the diggers at Baile ghorm do penance by keeping in repair the road from their town to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach. In the southern hills it is called the diggers' road still.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8021"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, FE 2,391** — *The diggers' road earns its name* (Baile ghorm). The road the families of Baile ghorm keep in repair as their penance, from their own town south to Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, is by this year known in the southern hills by no other name than the diggers' road, kept long past any term the Keeper's sentence set.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0169"><em>Baile ghorm's penance</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,391</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8022"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, FE 2,400** — *The hungry season at the halting-house below the pass* (Àth dhìreach). Calum Ruadh of Àth dhìreach and the other carriers of the mountain road read, on the tally board of a small halting-house, the shape of a poor year no custom yet mends: coal going down the road and next to no grain coming up. The house's keeper, an old woman named Mòr, tells them she has buried a husband to just such a winter before.

## The Years FE 2,401 – 2,600

- <a id="ev-II-0170"></a>**16 am Faoilleach, FE 2,406** — *Lachlann Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. He builds granaries in every province seat that will have one, and makes a law about them, and for these he is remembered.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8022"><em>The hungry season at the halting-house below the pass</em>, 22 an t-Sultain, FE 2,400</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8023"></a>**29 an Dàmhair, FE 2,406** — *Lachlann Bàn's vow at his crowning* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn, come to the red hall in his twenty-sixth year, finds granaries that fill and empty by no rule but a steward's whim, and resolves to build a common granary in every province seat that will keep one, to the same plan, so that no district need go hungry beside another's plenty.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0170"><em>Lachlann Bàn</em>, 16 am Faoilleach, FE 2,406</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8024"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,408** — *The reeve of Cnoc mhòr's silver ring* (Cnoc mhòr). Cnoc mhòr raises its common granary before any other province seat and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg the same season. Lachlann Bàn sends the reeve a silver ring for his own hand, and within two years no province seat on the plain is willing to be named last where Cnoc mhòr was named first.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8023"><em>Lachlann Bàn's vow at his crowning</em>, 29 an Dàmhair, FE 2,406</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8025"></a>**24 an Lùnastal, FE 2,410** — *Lachlann Bàn's journey to Dùn ìseal* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn climbs to Dùn ìseal to ask the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh to set the island's old neighbour-custom of shared grain under his new granaries as law. She asks whether he means his own hall's granary bound by the same terms as any household's; he swears it will be, and she puts her hand to the writing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8024"><em>The reeve of Cnoc mhòr's silver ring</em>, 26 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,408</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0171"></a>**14 an Gearran, FE 2,411** — *The shared-meal law written* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn and the Keeper Raonaid Dhubh make the old unwritten custom law at Cathair dhearg: a household with grain above its winter's need gives the surplus to the common granary of its district before the storm season, and the granary feeds any household of the district that runs short. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid write it into the rolls in full. It is the first law made by rìgh and Keeper together.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8025"><em>Lachlann Bàn's journey to Dùn ìseal</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, FE 2,410</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8026"></a>**29 an Cèitean, FE 2,412** — *Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh swear the shared-meal law* (Cathair dhearg). The rìgh at Cathair dhearg and the Keeper at Dùn ìseal set their names together to the law of the common granary: that no district's store be kept from a neighbour's hunger, and that what is lent in a hard year be repaid harvest by harvest.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0171"><em>The shared-meal law written</em>, 14 an Gearran, FE 2,411</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8025"><em>Lachlann Bàn's journey to Dùn ìseal</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, FE 2,410</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8027"></a>**27 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,415** — *A reeve of the plain protests the mountain's granaries* (Cathair dhearg). A reeve of the lowland plain writes to Cathair dhearg that his district is asked to fill granaries for mountain households that grow no grain of their own. Lachlann Bàn answers that a household which carries the plain's coal all winter has already paid, in the coin of its own back, for whatever grain comes up in return.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8026"><em>Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh swear the shared-meal law</em>, 29 an Cèitean, FE 2,412</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8028"></a>**1 an Giblean, FE 2,418** — *Cathair mhòr's fisher-towns pay their share in fish* (Cathair mhòr). The granary raised within Cathair mhòr's old wall, the first anywhere behind a town wall, draws its share from the southern fishing strands in dried fish rather than grain, packed in baskets as the old toll fish once were packed for the Hall at Dùn ìseal.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8029"></a>**30 an Giblean, FE 2,420** — *Death of Raonaid Dhubh* (Cathair dhearg). Raonaid Dhubh, Keeper of the flame at Dùn ìseal for the better part of forty years and the woman who set the shared-meal law beside Lachlann Bàn, dies in her own eightieth year, having seen the law hold unbroken through two poor seasons.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0171"><em>The shared-meal law written</em>, 14 an Gearran, FE 2,411</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8030"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, FE 2,422** — *Ruairidh mac Nèill burns the raiders' boats at Seann Tarr* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Ruairidh mac Nèill of Sliochd Raghnaill catches the eastern raiders at their own anchorage with the tide against them and burns two of their low black boats. Asked why he let the rest escape, he says a boat burned at its own anchorage teaches the strand's watch more than a raider hanged at Seann Tarr.
- <a id="ev-II-0172"></a>**19 an t-Samhain, FE 2,425** — *The granary of Cnoc mhòr* (Cnoc mhòr). Cnoc mhòr builds its common granary under the new law before any other district, and sends word of it to Cathair dhearg. Lachlann Bàn sends back a silver ring for the reeve.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8024"><em>The reeve of Cnoc mhòr's silver ring</em>, 26 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,408</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0173"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,435** — *The common granaries of the mountain* (Muileann chiar). Common granaries are raised under the new law in the mountain districts round Muileann chiar, where the households live by cutting and carrying and grow little of their own. The lowland districts grumble at filling them.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8027"><em>A reeve of the plain protests the mountain's granaries</em>, 27 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,415</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8031"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, FE 2,444** — *The Four Houses begin their quiet counting* (Cathair dhearg). With Oighrig nic Lachlainn newly widowed and childless, Sliochd Ìomhair, Sliochd Thormoid and Sliochd Raghnaill each begin, without speaking of it before her, to reckon what it might claim of the red hall should she die without an heir; Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's own office, makes no claim at all.
- <a id="ev-II-0174"></a>**12 an Cèitean, FE 2,445** — *The granary at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). A common granary is built within the old wall at Cathair mhòr, the first behind a town wall. The southern fishing towns, having no grain, send dried fish to it for their share.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8028"><em>Cathair mhòr's fisher-towns pay their share in fish</em>, 1 an Giblean, FE 2,418</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0175"></a>**10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,455** — *Raiders in the eastern waters* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Outlaws in boats raid the eastern fishing strands from the islets offshore, taking dried fish and nets. Sliochd Raghnaill arms its boats at Seann Tarr and burns two of the raiders' boats. The rest escape.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8030"><em>Ruairidh mac Nèill burns the raiders' boats at Seann Tarr</em>, 26 an Dàmhair, FE 2,422</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0176"></a>**15 am Màrt, FE 2,461** — *Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn, daughter of Lachlann Bàn, takes the hall at Cathair dhearg. She has no children, and before her reign is half done the houses begin to count their claims.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8031"><em>The Four Houses begin their quiet counting</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, FE 2,444</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8032"></a>**17 an t-Sultain, FE 2,461** — *Death of Lachlann Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Lachlann Bàn dies in his own bed at one-and-eighty, five-and-fifty years after his crowning, mourned chiefly by the reeves whose granaries he built and the carriers of the mountain roads, who never once in his reign went a whole winter without knowing where the next grain was coming from.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0176"><em>Oighrig nic Lachlainn</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2,461</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8033"></a>**1 an Dàmhair, FE 2,461** — *Oighrig nic Lachlainn takes the hall at one-and-twenty* (Cathair dhearg). On her father's death Oighrig nic Lachlainn takes the red hall in her one-and-twentieth year. She will hold it the better part of fifty years and bear no child.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0176"><em>Oighrig nic Lachlainn</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2,461</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8034"></a>**19 an Gearran, FE 2,465** — *Calum Ruadh tells his son of the old want* (Àth dhìreach). With the passes above Cnoc ghlas still white with late snow and the mountain households eating their seed, Calum Ruadh tells his son Iain Caol, a boy of fifteen, of the very want he carried through as a young man, and doubts aloud whether the new law will hold where the old custom never had to be tried.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8035"></a>**21 am Faoilleach, FE 2,466** — *Calum Ruadh and Iain Caol carry grain to Àth dhìreach* (Dùn dhearg). Calum Ruadh, past his own heaviest carrying, walks down for the grain Dùn dhearg has sent unasked, and his son Iain Caol, too young by the town's reckoning to carry a full load, carries half of one beside him, the boy's first sight of what the shared-meal law meant in a true want.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8034"><em>Calum Ruadh tells his son of the old want</em>, 19 an Gearran, FE 2,465</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8036"></a>**18 an Giblean, FE 2,466** — *Àth dhìreach grants the carriers the right to rest* (Àth dhìreach). The reeve of Àth dhìreach calls the town together and grants every carrier who walked the famine road that winter the right to rest, for life, in any house of the town without payment; the households swear to keep it as their own word rather than write it into any roll at Cathair dhearg.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8035"><em>Calum Ruadh and Iain Caol carry grain to Àth dhìreach</em>, 21 am Faoilleach, FE 2,466</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8037"></a>**20 am Màrt, FE 2,470** — *Gilleasbuig born to a copying clerk of Seann Dunn* (Seann Dunn). Gilleasbuig is born at Seann Dunn to Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid who puts down on scraped hide, in the house's small square hand, whatever the red hall sends him to copy. The boy grows up under his father's bench.
- <a id="ev-II-0177"></a>**13 an Giblean, FE 2,472** — *The late snow on the high passes* (Cnoc ghlas). The weather-watchers on the cairns above Cnoc ghlas see snow lying on the high passes long past the opening of the galleries. The Hall keeps the galleries shut for the cutters' safety, and the mountain households wait.
- <a id="ev-II-0178"></a>**5 an t-Sultain, FE 2,472** — *The poor season in the mountain* (Muileann chiar). The galleries open late and close early, and the coal carried down is a third of a common season's. The mountain households of Muileann gheal, Doire uaine and Àth dhìreach, who trade their carrying for grain, have nothing to trade, and by the season's end they are eating their seed.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8034"><em>Calum Ruadh tells his son of the old want</em>, 19 an Gearran, FE 2,465</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0179"></a>**4 an Dàmhair, FE 2,473** — *The first recorded famine averted*. A poor mining season brings three settlements near to starving. The shared-meal law, made in the reign before, holds and saves them. It is the first true trial of the custom.
- <a id="ev-II-0180"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473** — *The granaries opened* (Muileann gheal). Under the shared-meal law the common granaries of the mountain districts are opened at Muileann gheal. When they run low the granaries of Dùn dhearg and the southern coast send grain up the carriers' roads without being asked twice, and the carriers bear it for no fee. None in the three settlements is known to die of hunger that winter.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8035"><em>Calum Ruadh and Iain Caol carry grain to Àth dhìreach</em>, 21 am Faoilleach, FE 2,466</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8038"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473** — *Iain Caol's first load up* (Àth dhìreach). Iain Caol, grown to a man's height, takes up his first load as a carrier proper, walking the same track his father Calum Ruadh had walked before him, with a company of four other young men of Àth dhìreach carrying their first working loads that same season.
- <a id="ev-II-0181"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,474** — *Àth dhìreach after the poor season* (Àth dhìreach). At Àth dhìreach, one of the three settlements the granaries fed, the carriers who brought up the grain are given the right to rest in any house of the town without payment for as long as they live. The last of them dies old, and the right with him.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8036"><em>Àth dhìreach grants the carriers the right to rest</em>, 18 an Giblean, FE 2,466</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8038"><em>Iain Caol's first load up</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0182"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,474** — *The reeves of Dùn dhearg send the grain* (Dùn dhearg). The reeves of Dùn dhearg, who had withheld their accounts from Cathair dhearg for generations, open the old granaries of the house of Ìomhar to the mountain without waiting for an order. Oighrig nic Lachlainn writes that she would have given the order had they waited. The successor of Peigi nic Tormoid notes that they did not.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8035"><em>Calum Ruadh and Iain Caol carry grain to Àth dhìreach</em>, 21 am Faoilleach, FE 2,466</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8039"></a>**17 an Cèitean, FE 2,475** — *Why the king-list is kept in six copies* (Seann Dunn). Asked by his small son why the king-list needs six copies where a tithe needs one, Tormod Beag answers that a tithe is true for a year and a king-list must be true for longer than any man who writes it, so that if fire takes one house the rest will still agree.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8037"><em>Gilleasbuig born to a copying clerk of Seann Dunn</em>, 20 am Màrt, FE 2,470</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8040"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,481** — *A tithe-roll scraped clean for one wrong stroke* (Seann Dunn). Tormod Beag, a copying clerk of Sliochd Thormoid at Seann Dunn, scrapes clean a province's tithe-roll his young son Gilleasbuig has copied with a single stroke too many in it, and makes the boy write the whole roll again from the beginning rather than mend the one line, so that he learns early a mistake quietly mended teaches a clerk less than a roll done wholly over.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0176"><em>Oighrig nic Lachlainn</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2,461</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8039"><em>Why the king-list is kept in six copies</em>, 17 an Cèitean, FE 2,475</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8041"></a>**18 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,484** — *Gilleasbuig rides alone to Cathair dhearg with the rolls* (Seann Dunn). At fourteen Gilleasbuig first rides the day and a half from Seann Dunn to the red hall alone, the rolls in a satchel on his back and a hearth-sign token that lets him sleep free at any waypoint house. He learns every waypoint keeper's name before he knows half the great families.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8040"><em>A tithe-roll scraped clean for one wrong stroke</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,481</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8042"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, FE 2,486** — *Oighrig nic Lachlainn's word to a clerk's son* (Cathair dhearg). A young Gilleasbuig, carrying his father's rolls to Cathair dhearg at sixteen, is asked by Oighrig nic Lachlainn whose son he is; told his father's name, she says only that the hand is known to her, the one exchange of the whole reign between the woman who holds the red hall and the clerk who will one day fill it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0176"><em>Oighrig nic Lachlainn</em>, 15 am Màrt, FE 2,461</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8041"><em>Gilleasbuig rides alone to Cathair dhearg with the rolls</em>, 18 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,484</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0183"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,511** — *Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg with no heir of her body, and with her ends the line of Goraidh Mòr, as the list reckons it. The red hall is shut, and its clerks keep it.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8043"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, FE 2,512** — *The clerks keep the shut hall's tallies* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr, sent down from Seann Dunn the winter after Oighrig nic Lachlainn's death, spends a season sealing rolls and answering reeves at the shut red hall who no longer know whose name to render account to, keeping every tally true on the plain reasoning that whoever fills the hall next will want them so.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0183"><em>Death of Oighrig nic Lachlainn</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,511</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8042"><em>Oighrig nic Lachlainn's word to a clerk's son</em>, 16 an Lùnastal, FE 2,486</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0184"></a>**10 an Giblean, FE 2,513** — *The four houses meet* (Dùn ìseal). The Four Houses of custody meet at Dùn ìseal to choose a ruler, for no custom covers a hall without an heir. Sliochd Ìomhair claims it by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the clerks, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats. Sliochd Mhuirich, holding the Keeper's office, makes no claim.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8044"></a>**4 an Cèitean, FE 2,513** — *Sliochd Mhuirich makes no claim to the empty hall* (Dùn ìseal). At the Four Houses' meeting at Dùn ìseal, Sliochd Ìomhair claims the red hall by blood, Sliochd Thormoid by the unbroken rolls, Sliochd Raghnaill by its boats and silver. Sliochd Mhuirich, which holds the Keeper's office, makes no claim and says the vein has not asked it to judge.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0184"><em>The four houses meet</em>, 10 an Giblean, FE 2,513</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8043"><em>The clerks keep the shut hall's tallies</em>, 14 an t-Sultain, FE 2,512</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8045"></a>**24 am Màrt, FE 2,514** — *Gilleasbuig watches the Four Houses argue* (Dùn ìseal). Called down from Cathair dhearg twice a year to lay the shut hall's own rolls before whichever house asks to see them, Gilleasbuig Mòr sits at the edge of the Four Houses' long sitting at Dùn ìseal, and hears blood, boats and silence argued past each other for three years without once being asked his own mind on the matter.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0184"><em>The four houses meet</em>, 10 an Giblean, FE 2,513</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8046"></a>**26 an Gearran, FE 2,516** — *Sliochd Ìomhair's condition of the graves* (Dùn ìseal). Sliochd Ìomhair consents to the clerk's choosing on one condition: that whoever takes the red hall, the graves at Dùn dhearg remain the kings' burying-place. Gilleasbuig answers that he never expected to be buried anywhere else, and the condition is sworn on the spot.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8045"><em>Gilleasbuig watches the Four Houses argue</em>, 24 am Màrt, FE 2,514</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0185"></a>**12 am Màrt, FE 2,516** — *The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Seann Dunn). The houses choose Gilleasbuig Mòr mac Tormoid of Seann Dunn, a grandson of the clerks' line, to hold the red hall. The Keeper sets the stone cup in his hands before the council, and so for the first time a ruler is made at Dùn ìseal. Sliochd Ìomhair consents, on condition that its graves at Dùn dhearg remain the burying-place of the kings.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-8046"><em>Sliochd Ìomhair's condition of the graves</em>, 26 an Gearran, FE 2,516</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8047"></a>**16 an Cèitean, FE 2,516** — *Sliochd Raghnaill first names the clerk of the shut hall* (Dùn ìseal). Sliochd Raghnaill is the first of the Four Houses to put Gilleasbuig Mòr's own name forward for the red hall, on the reasoning that a clerk who kept the shut hall's rolls straight three years running, favouring no house's claim over the work, has already shown the hand a red hall wants at its head.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0185"><em>The election of Gilleasbuig Mòr</em>, 12 am Màrt, FE 2,516</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8046"><em>Sliochd Ìomhair's condition of the graves</em>, 26 an Gearran, FE 2,516</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8048"></a>**16 an t-Sultain, FE 2,516** — *Tormod mac Gilleasbuig sits at the rolls* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr sends for his son Tormod, already taught the clerks' bench at Seann Dunn at sixteen, to sit beside him at Cathair dhearg and learn the red hall's own rolls before he is taught anything else of ruling, the same order his own father once taught him a road in.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8047"><em>Sliochd Raghnaill first names the clerk of the shut hall</em>, 16 an Cèitean, FE 2,516</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0186"></a>**11 an Gearran, FE 2,517** — *Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr takes the red hall. He keeps the clerks' office in the hands of his own house and has the king-list copied again from the beginning, with a line drawn beneath Oighrig nic Lachlainn. The line is in every later copy.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8048"><em>Tormod mac Gilleasbuig sits at the rolls</em>, 16 an t-Sultain, FE 2,516</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8049"></a>**21 an Giblean, FE 2,517** — *The line drawn beneath a queen's name* (Cathair dhearg). In the year after the cup is set in his hands, Gilleasbuig Mòr has the king-list copied again from its beginning in his own house's hand, with a single line drawn beneath the name of Oighrig nic Lachlainn to mark the ending of Goraidh Mòr's whole line, so that no clerk after him need hunt a kinship no longer there.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0186"><em>Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg</em>, 11 an Gearran, FE 2,517</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8048"><em>Tormod mac Gilleasbuig sits at the rolls</em>, 16 an t-Sultain, FE 2,516</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8050"></a>**31 an Cèitean, FE 2,517** — *Gilleasbuig sleeps in the clerks' room of the red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Coming to Cathair dhearg by the lowland road, the new rìgh sleeps his first night in the small room off the rolls-chamber where the clerks keep their beds, the queen's chambers having stood empty five years and no one having thought to air them. He keeps that room to his death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0186"><em>Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg</em>, 11 an Gearran, FE 2,517</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8049"><em>The line drawn beneath a queen's name</em>, 21 an Giblean, FE 2,517</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8051"></a>**11 an t-Samhain, FE 2,524** — *The meadow of Muileann àrsaidh and Ceann àrsaidh* (Muileann àrsaidh). Gilleasbuig Mòr judges the one dispute of his reign the rolls set down whole, a water-meadow claimed whole by two households on notched sticks that agree for forty years and then part company; he sends a clerk to copy both sticks stroke for stroke and gives the meadow to both households at once, with a boundary stone cut down its centre for the first time in living memory.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0186"><em>Gilleasbuig Mòr at Cathair dhearg</em>, 11 an Gearran, FE 2,517</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8050"><em>Gilleasbuig sleeps in the clerks' room of the red hall</em>, 31 an Cèitean, FE 2,517</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0187"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,537** — *The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged* (Seann Dunn). Gilleasbuig Mòr enlarges his house's shrine at Seann Dunn into a temple with a court for pilgrims. The other houses say still that its coal-lamp burns fuller than the measure, and every season a Keeper's cutter is sent to try it.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8052"></a>**13 an Dàmhair, FE 2,538** — *The Keeper's cutter tries Seann Dunn's lamp* (Seann Dunn). The other three houses say the enlarged temple at Seann Dunn burns fuller than the Law allows. A Keeper's cutter is sent every season to try its measure by the island's common weights, and every season finds the measure kept, which changes nobody's mind.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0187"><em>The shrine at Seann Dunn enlarged</em>, 13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,537</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8053"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, FE 2,540** — *Death of Iain Caol, the last of the grain-carriers* (Àth dhìreach). Iain Caol dies at Àth dhìreach in his ninetieth year, the last living of any who could say he had carried the road when the famine and the right to rest were both still new. The right the town kept for its carriers dies with him, though the town still sets out, at the turn of every year, the one bowl he had kept for whichever carrier walked the road that night.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0181"><em>Àth dhìreach after the poor season</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,474</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8038"><em>Iain Caol's first load up</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,473</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0188"></a>**27 an Giblean, FE 2,541** — *Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr* (Dùn dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried among the house of Ìomhar at Dùn dhearg, as was agreed. His son Tormod Òg follows him without a meeting of the houses, and none asks for one.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8054"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,541** — *Gilleasbuig Mòr carried five days to Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). Gilleasbuig Mòr's bier is carried the five days' road from Cathair dhearg to Dùn dhearg, stopping each night at a waypoint house whose keeper had known him first as a boy with a satchel of rolls, to be buried among the house of Ìomhar as Sliochd Ìomhair had sworn at his choosing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0188"><em>Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr</em>, 27 an Giblean, FE 2,541</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8055"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,541** — *Tormod Òg follows his father without a meeting of the houses* (Cathair dhearg). Gilleasbuig's son Tormod takes the red hall in his one-and-fortieth year without any meeting of the Four Houses, and none asks for one; a son following a father now seems to every house the plainer course.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0188"><em>Death of Gilleasbuig Mòr</em>, 27 an Giblean, FE 2,541</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0189"></a>**29 am Màrt, FE 2,558** — *The gap in the list* (Cathair dhearg). Nine rulers of the house of Tormod reign between Tormod Òg and Anna Ruadh, and the king-list at Cathair dhearg gives their names and years and little else. The successors of Peigi nic Tormoid were diligent and brief; for these reigns the rolls tell mostly of harvests, tolls and the mending of bridges.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8056"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,559** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg is widened a third time* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The masons' fellowship widens the old bridge at Cathair dhearg a third time on Mòrag nan Rathad's own piers, broad enough now for two carts to pass abreast. The old keystone, carrying the fourth hearth's sign, is set into the new parapet rather than broken for rubble.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8057"></a>**21 an Cèitean, FE 2,561** — *The road-guards first ride the lowland roads* (Dùn dhearg). The road-guards of Dùn dhearg take to the small tough horses of the southern grass country rather than walking their circuits, and can reach a waypoint house before a night's quarrel has cooled into a grievance. Theirs are the first riders' names the road-guard's own roll keeps.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8058"></a>**30 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,562** — *The road-guards' roll first names its riders* (Dùn dhearg). The first mounted company of the road-guards of Dùn dhearg, riding the small tough horses of the southern grass country, are the earliest guards whose names the road-guards' own roll troubles to keep.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8059"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,567** — *The flood takes the eastern approach at Ros fhionn* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). A wet spring swells the river at Ros fhionn past every bank built to hold it, carrying off the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span and three households built too near the water. The span itself, and Ailean's own hearth-sign in its keystone, stand untouched.
- <a id="ev-EIII-8060"></a>**2 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,568** — *The fellowship mends Ros fhionn on deeper footings* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). Masons called down from Cathair dhearg lay a new causeway on stone footings deep enough to outlast the flood that took the old one, and leave Ailean Clachair's hearth-sign untouched, cutting their own new work a course below it rather than over it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8059"><em>The flood takes the eastern approach at Ros fhionn</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,567</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-8061"></a>**1 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,569** — *The masons leave Ailean's sign standing at Ros fhionn* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). Clearing the old approach at Ros fhionn, the masons find the keystone Ailean Clachair cut with the fourth hearth's sign and leave it as it is, cutting their own work a course below. The fellowship keeps the custom after: old signs are left standing wherever the stone beneath them stands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8060"><em>The fellowship mends Ros fhionn on deeper footings</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,568</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0190"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,571** — *The bridge at Cathair dhearg widened* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). The bridge at Cathair dhearg is rebuilt a third time, wide enough now for a cart, for carts have come onto the lowland roads. The hearth-sign is cut again in the keystone. The span stands on the piers of Mòrag nan Rathad.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8056"><em>The bridge at Cathair dhearg is widened a third time</em>, 19 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,559</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9001"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,578** — *The bridge at Dùn chrom is built at half toll* (Dùn chrom). The fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg, and sets its own toll at half the capital's. Cathair dhearg's reeves complain in letters the rolls still keep; none takes up the fellowship's offer to hand the crossing to the crown.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-8061"><em>The masons leave Ailean's sign standing at Ros fhionn</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,569</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9002"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,580** — *Cathair dhearg's reeves complain of the half-toll at Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). The reeves of Cathair dhearg protest that a toll set by anyone but the crown will in time be set anywhere by anyone. The fellowship offers to hand the crossing to the crown, tolls and upkeep together. No reeve takes up the offer, and the half-toll stands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9001"><em>The bridge at Dùn chrom is built at half toll</em>, 19 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,578</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0190a"></a>**24 an Giblean, FE 2,583** — *Riders on the lowland roads* (Dùn dhearg). The road-guards of Dùn dhearg begin to ride the lowland roads on the small horses of the southern grass country, and a guard can now reach a waypoint house before a quarrel there has cooled. They are the first riders whose names are kept, and for long the only ones.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8057"><em>The road-guards first ride the lowland roads</em>, 21 an Cèitean, FE 2,561</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9003"></a>**22 an Cèitean, FE 2,591** — *The fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill bridge Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). Forty of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, taught the mason's craft in an idle season after the burning at Seann Tarr, build the fourth stone bridge of the lowlands at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh. The fellowship's roll names all forty, a courtesy not always given to borrowed hands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9002"><em>Cathair dhearg's reeves complain of the half-toll at Dùn chrom</em>, 20 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,580</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9004"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,592** — *The forty fisher-masons named on the fellowship's roll* (Ceann àrsaidh). The masons' roll at Cathair dhearg names all forty fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill who built the bridge at Ceann àrsaidh, on the reasoning that people who learned a new trade rather than sit idle deserve to be named among the masons.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9003"><em>The fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill bridge Ceann àrsaidh</em>, 22 an Cèitean, FE 2,591</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0191"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,598** — *The crossing at Ros fhionn repaired* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). A flood takes the eastern approach of Ailean Clachair's span above Ros fhionn, and it is mended. The masons find their founder's hearth-sign still sharp in the keystone, and leave it untouched.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8059"><em>The flood takes the eastern approach at Ros fhionn</em>, 1 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,567</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-8060"><em>The fellowship mends Ros fhionn on deeper footings</em>, 2 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,568</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9005"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, FE 2,600** — *Caol mhòr gathers under its own headman* (Caol mhòr). The fisher-families of Caol mhòr on the north-western coast gather under a headman of their own choosing and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years a road-guard comes so far to collect them. A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes that the coast might as well keep its own law for all the crown's writ reaches it.

## The Years FE 2,601 – 2,800

- <a id="ev-EIII-9006"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, FE 2,605** — *A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes of Caol mhòr* (Ros dhomhain). A reeve of Ros dhomhain writes more than once to the red hall that Caol mhòr pays what it pleases and answers to whom it pleases. The red hall mostly sends no answer; the north-west's tolls are not worth a road-guard's season.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9007"></a>**15 an t-Sultain, FE 2,610** — *Beathag Clachair is born at Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). Beathag Clachair is born to a family of cutters at Doire mhin on the southern road, three generations deep in boundary-stones and byre-lintels, and is quicker than her father's other apprentices at reading a stone's grain before she has seen twenty summers.
- <a id="ev-II-0192"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,613** — *The bridge at Dùn chrom* (Dùn chrom). The masons' fellowship bridges the river below Dùn chrom, joining the southern road to the western without the long way round by Cathair dhearg. The toll is set at half the road-toll, and Cathair dhearg complains.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9001"><em>The bridge at Dùn chrom is built at half toll</em>, 19 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,578</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9008"></a>**6 an Giblean, FE 2,615** — *Ceann mhòr begins the seal-oil trade* (Ceann mhòr). Ceann mhòr on the north-western coast begins rendering seal-oil from the northern rocks and carrying it down to Ros bheag for silver rings. From then on the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours burn the brightest light on Dia-thìr.
- <a id="ev-II-0193"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,628** — *The bridge at Ceann àrsaidh* (Ceann àrsaidh). A bridge is built at the river town of Ceann àrsaidh, the fourth stone crossing of the lowlands. The masons' roll names the forty who built it, all of the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill, who had learned the craft while the boats lay idle.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9003"><em>The fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill bridge Ceann àrsaidh</em>, 22 an Cèitean, FE 2,591</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9009"></a>**8 am Màrt, FE 2,630** — *Herders take the high pastures above Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Herding families take the summer pastures above Muileann leathan for the wool the weavers of Inis mhòr prize above any other, holding no right to the handful and never counted in any census, their pastures too high and too far for a road-guard to trouble reckoning them.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9010"></a>**1 an t-Sultain, FE 2,635** — *Inis mhin's headman walks to the wool-fair with a complaint* (Inis mhin). The headman of the small northern harbour of Inis mhin walks the whole distance to the wool-fair at Inis mhòr to lay a complaint against the road-guard's toll, the only time the harbour comes into the rolls this age, and the complaint kept in fuller telling than the harbour otherwise earns.
- <a id="ev-II-0194"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,643** — *The bridge at Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). The masons' fellowship builds a small bridge at Doire mhin to carry the southern road over a stream that floods each spring. Beside the hearth-sign in the keystone is cut the name of Beathag Clachair, who cut it: the first mason's mark known.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9007"><em>Beathag Clachair is born at Doire mhin</em>, 15 an t-Sultain, FE 2,610</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9011"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,643** — *Beathag Clachair cuts the first mason's mark* (Doire mhin). Leading her own crossing for the first time, Beathag Clachair cuts her own name beneath the fourth hearth's sign at the small bridge over the stream at Doire mhin: Beathag the mason set this. No mason before her had ever cut a name of his own beside the hearth's, and within two seasons every hearth on the island follows her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0194"><em>The bridge at Doire mhin</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,643</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9012"></a>**29 an Dàmhair, FE 2,645** — *Masons of every hearth cut their names beside the sign* (Doire mhin). Within two seasons of Beathag Clachair's bridge at Doire mhin, masons of every hearth begin cutting their own names beside the fourth hearth's sign wherever a fellowship crew finishes a crossing. The masons call it Beathag's mark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9011"><em>Beathag Clachair cuts the first mason's mark</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,643</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9013"></a>**27 an t-Samhain, FE 2,650** — *The far-off house is rebuilt in stone* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The waypoint house the carriers call the far-off house, so distant from any town that a traveller is never nearer to it than halfway, is rebuilt in stone after its old timber and turf give out to a western storm, keeping the name a hundred years of true telling had earned it.
- <a id="ev-II-0195"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,658** — *The far-off house* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The waypoint house on the site of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the oldest house under the road-peace, is rebuilt in stone. It lies so far from any town that the carriers say one is never nearer to it than halfway, and from the saying it takes its name.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9013"><em>The far-off house is rebuilt in stone</em>, 27 an t-Samhain, FE 2,650</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9014"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,660** — *A waypoint keeper of the northern road begins serving fire-water* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). A new keeper of the waypoint house the carriers call a waypoint house on the northern road, on the northern road, begins serving a spirit distilled from barley stronger than any small beer sold on that road before. The carriers name it fire-water for the way of it going down and the way of it sitting after.
- <a id="ev-II-0196"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,672** — *Fire-water on the northern road* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). The house on the northern road, on the site of An Leòmhann Buidhe, begins to serve a spirit distilled from barley that the carriers call fire-water. The Keepers rule that it is not a burning and no concern of theirs. The house's trade doubles.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9014"><em>A waypoint keeper of the northern road begins serving fire-water</em>, 26 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,660</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9015"></a>**24 am Faoilleach, FE 2,673** — *The Keeper rules fire-water no burning of the Law* (An Leòmhann Buidhe). Asked by troubled reeves of the northern road to rule on fire-water under the Small-Burning Law, the Keeper of that generation answers that a fire kept in a man's own belly is no burning the Law was written to answer for, and that the Hall will rule on drink the day it rules on food. The waypoint house's trade doubles within the season.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0196"><em>Fire-water on the northern road</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,672</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9016"></a>**22 an Gearran, FE 2,680** — *Beathag Clachair dies at Doire mhin* (Doire mhin). Beathag Clachair dies at seventy at Doire mhin, having cut her mark on four further crossings, and is buried at her own asking at the foot of the bridge that carries her name. Masons of the fellowship keep, for a long while after, the habit of laying a chip of grey stone on her grave in passing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0194"><em>The bridge at Doire mhin</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,643</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0197"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,687** — *Caol mhòr in the north-west* (Caol mhòr). The fisher-families of the north-west gather at Caol mhòr under a headman of their own, and send tolls to Cathair dhearg only in the years the road-guard comes to take them. Little is written of the north-west in this age, and most of it is complaint of that.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9005"><em>Caol mhòr gathers under its own headman</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, FE 2,600</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9017"></a>**23 am Màrt, FE 2,695** — *Ros bheag's merchants arm two boats against raiders* (Spùinneadairean-mara). The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay from their own purses to arm and crew two boats against raiders taking dried fish from the western strands. The raiders move north before either boat catches one at sea, and the coast keeps a wariness it had not kept before.
- <a id="ev-II-0198"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,702** — *Seal-oil from Ceann mhòr* (Ceann mhòr). Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast begins to trade seal-oil down the western coast to Ros bheag for silver rings, and its beacons burn it. For many generations the seal-oil lamps of the western harbours are the brightest light on Dia-thìr.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9008"><em>Ceann mhòr begins the seal-oil trade</em>, 6 an Giblean, FE 2,615</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0199"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,717** — *The high pastures of Muileann leathan* (Muileann leathan). Herding families take the high pastures above Muileann leathan in the north and keep sheep there for the wool of Inis mhòr. They hold no right to the handful, have never held one, and are not counted in the census of hands.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9009"><em>Herders take the high pastures above Muileann leathan</em>, 8 am Màrt, FE 2,630</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9018"></a>**21 an Giblean, FE 2,720** — *The second sighting off Baile chrom* (Uilebheist na Mara). Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath their keels in the north-western water, the second such telling the coast remembers since Ruairidh Liath's reign. One boat does not come home, and Baile chrom keeps its old wake for both losses together.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9019"></a>**20 an Cèitean, FE 2,721** — *Baile chrom keeps one wake for both lost boats* (Baile chrom). One of the two boats of Baile chrom that felt the sea breathe under them does not come home, nor is any wreck found. The harbour keeps the wake it kept for the earlier loss for both losses together.
- <a id="ev-II-0200"></a>**30 am Faoilleach, FE 2,732** — *Inis mhin on the northern shore* (Inis mhin). Inis mhin, a fishing harbour on the northern shore, comes into the rolls for the first time when its headman goes to the wool-fair of Inis mhòr to complain of the road-guard's toll. The complaint is written down in full, and it is all that is written of the town in this age.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9010"><em>Inis mhin's headman walks to the wool-fair with a complaint</em>, 1 an t-Sultain, FE 2,635</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9020"></a>**31 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,735** — *Sliochd Raghnaill sails the round of the offshore islands* (Seann Tarr). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the whole ring of the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home within one season, the first crew of the age known to have made the whole round.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9021"></a>**2 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,740** — *Families take sheep to summer on Eilean ruadh* (Eilean ruadh). Coastal families begin carrying sheep over to Eilean ruadh each summer for its grazing, building turf shelters against the weather and bringing the flocks home before the autumn storms. Later herders keep patching the same shelters rather than building anew.
- <a id="ev-II-0201"></a>**28 an Gearran, FE 2,747** — *The raid on the western strands* (Spùinneadairean-mara). Raiders from the north-western waters take a season's dried fish from the strands of the north-western coast. The sting-sworn merchants of Ros bheag pay for two armed boats to watch the strands, and the raiders move north.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9017"><em>Ros bheag's merchants arm two boats against raiders</em>, 23 am Màrt, FE 2,695</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0202"></a>**29 am Màrt, FE 2,761** — *The second sighting* (Uilebheist na Mara). Two boats of Baile chrom tell of something vast moving beneath them in the north-western water, the second such sighting remembered. One boat does not come home. The wake that Baile chrom keeps for the first loss is kept now for both.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9018"><em>The second sighting off Baile chrom</em>, 21 an Giblean, FE 2,720</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0203"></a>**27 an Giblean, FE 2,776** — *Round the islands* (Seann Tarr). Boats of Sliochd Raghnaill sail from Seann Tarr round the offshore islands, Eilean ruadh, Eilean dhearg and Eilean fhada among them, and come home in one season. No crew of the age goes further from the coast than the islands, and none is known to have wished to.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9020"><em>Sliochd Raghnaill sails the round of the offshore islands</em>, 31 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,735</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0204"></a>**26 an Cèitean, FE 2,791** — *Summer herders on Eilean ruadh* (Eilean ruadh). Families from the coast take sheep over to Eilean ruadh for the summer grazing and bring them back before the storms. They build turf shelters there, which later herders use again.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9021"><em>Families take sheep to summer on Eilean ruadh</em>, 2 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,740</a>.</span>

## The Years FE 2,801 – 2,960

- <a id="ev-II-0205"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806** — *Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh of the house of Tormod takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. She walks the whole circuit of the roads, the first ruler to do so since Mòrag nan Rathad, and she walks it twice.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9022"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, FE 2,807** — *Anna Ruadh asks the reeves how the roads stand* (Cathair dhearg). At her first councils Anna Ruadh asks the reeves how the roads stand between one seat and the next. When none can tell her past his own district, she says she will go and see. The reeve of Cathair dhomhain tells her a hall is better kept from a hall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0205"><em>Anna Ruadh</em>, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9023"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, FE 2,808** — *Anna Ruadh sets out with a dozen of her household* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh leaves the red hall in spring with a dozen of her household and no more baggage than a carrier takes, no litter and no guard beyond a well-off traveller's, the first ruler to walk the whole circuit since Mòrag nan Rathad.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9022"><em>Anna Ruadh asks the reeves how the roads stand</em>, 27 an t-Sultain, FE 2,807</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0206"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,809** — *Anna Ruadh at Am Buabhall Fortanach* (Am Buabhall Fortanach). On her first circuit Anna Ruadh stops at the house on the site of Am Buabhall Fortanach, where the War of the Roads was ended, and eats the jugged buffalo like a carrier. The keepers of the house tell of it still.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-9023"><em>Anna Ruadh sets out with a dozen of her household</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, FE 2,808</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9024"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, FE 2,811** — *Anna Ruadh's second circuit*. Anna Ruadh walks the whole road circuit a second time in her middle years, slower than her first walking, stopping longest where keepers who fed her as a young queen feed her again grey-haired; at Am Buabhall Fortanach she sleeps a night under the same roof for the only time in either circuit.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0205"><em>Anna Ruadh</em>, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,806</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9023"><em>Anna Ruadh sets out with a dozen of her household</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, FE 2,808</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0207"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813** — *Anna Ruadh at the sunny house* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). On the eastern road Anna Ruadh lodges at the house on the site of An Taigh-òsta Grianach and grants its keepers a toll of their own for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan. No other waypoint house on the island holds a royal charter.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9025"></a>**22 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813** — *Anna Ruadh takes the sunny house's charter to stone* (Cathair dhearg). The keeper of the sunny house on the road to Cnoc leathan, who has mended the stretch out of her own household's stores for three generations, asks Anna Ruadh that the new charter be cut in stone rather than skin, since a fire can lose a skin but never a stone, and the queen has it cut before she leaves the district.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0207"><em>Anna Ruadh at the sunny house</em>, 21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,813</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0208"></a>**12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816** — *Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). At Ceann mhin on the south-eastern coast Anna Ruadh hears the quarrel of the fishers and the carriers over who may carry dried fish up to the mountain, and rules that both may. The fish going inland is doubled, and its price at Dùn ìseal halved.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9026"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,816** — *An old fisher of Ceann mhin judges the queen fair to the fish* (Ceann mhin). Years after Anna Ruadh's ruling that both fishers and carriers might carry the dried catch inland, an old fisher of the strand, asked which side the queen had truly favoured, answers that she had favoured the fish, which was more than either household carrying it had thought to do.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0208"><em>Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin</em>, 12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9027"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,818** — *Dried fish doubles inland after the ruling at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). Two years after Anna Ruadh ruled that fishers and carriers alike might carry dried fish up-country, the fish going inland has doubled and its price at Dùn ìseal has fallen by half. Both sides claim the doubling as proof they were right.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0208"><em>Anna Ruadh at Ceann mhin</em>, 12 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,816</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0209"></a>**11 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,819** — *The contest at Ceann leathan in stone* (Ceann leathan). Anna Ruadh gives the road-guards' contest at Ceann leathan a stone-walled field, and for its prize a silver ring from the red hall. Fighters come to it from all the south, and the losers are fed at the crown's cost.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9028"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, FE 2,819** — *Fearchar Ruadh wins the stone field at Ceann leathan* (Ceann leathan). A mason's apprentice named Fearchar Ruadh of Doire mhin takes the silver ring at Anna Ruadh's new stone-walled contest field, and eats the crown's meal at the same board as every man he beat under the queen's own new law, a custom he is said never afterward to have forgotten at any table.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0209"><em>The contest at Ceann leathan in stone</em>, 11 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,819</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0210"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822** — *A wood-watcher in the red hall* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh keeps a wood-watcher from Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag in her household at Cathair dhearg to read the omens of the hall. So the rite of the wood-watchers, the rite of Macha, goddess of sovereignty and of horses, first comes to the capital. The Keeper sends a protest from Dùn ìseal, and the rolls give no answer.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9029"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,822** — *The wood-watcher reads a message home before it comes* (Cathair dhearg).
