In Anna Ruadh's household at Cathair dhearg the wood-watcher out of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag reads the crossing of three geese and tells the queen, unasked, that a message she had given up waiting for will come within the week; an answer to a year-old letter reaches her on the sixth day, and no one in the household troubles him with idle questions after.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0210"><em>A wood-watcher in the red hall</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9030"></a>**7 an Gearran, FE 2,823** — *The Keeper protests the wood-watcher in the red hall* (Dùn ìseal). The Keeper at Dùn ìseal sends a protest up the road Anna Ruadh walked, asking by what right a hall built on the Binding keeps an omen-reader who answers to no measure of the vein. No answer is remembered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0210"><em>A wood-watcher in the red hall</em>, 23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,822</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9029"><em>The wood-watcher reads a message home before it comes</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,822</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0211"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826** — *Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers* (Cathair dhomhain). The shrine at Cathair dhomhain, proud of its strict keeping of the Law, will take no wood-watcher, and its people say that the capital has given its omens to folk who sit in trees. From this the rivalry of the two towns takes a turn in matters of faith that it never loses.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9031"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, FE 2,826** — *Cathair dhomhain doubles its own strictness in answer* (Cathair dhomhain). Cathair dhomhain's shrine, stung by the capital's wood-watcher, doubles its own cutter's visits to the Keeper's measure without being asked, and for a hundred years after a Cathair dhomhain man swearing an oath is known on the roads by how exactly he keeps to its letter.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0211"><em>Cathair dhomhain and the wood-watchers</em>, 24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,826</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9030"><em>The Keeper protests the wood-watcher in the red hall</em>, 7 an Gearran, FE 2,823</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9032"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,828** — *Anna Ruadh has the toll rolls read at her bedside* (Cathair dhearg). In her last winter Anna Ruadh has the toll rolls of the sunny house and of Slighe Cnoc leathan read aloud to her twice, as if to be sure the charter still stands as she had it cut, and asks after no other matter of state.
- <a id="ev-II-0212"></a>**26 an Cèitean, FE 2,829** — *Death of Anna Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Anna Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Dùn dhearg among the house of Ìomhar and the kings of her own house. Her son Coinneach Bàn takes the hall.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-9032"><em>Anna Ruadh has the toll rolls read at her bedside</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,828</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9033"></a>**4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,829** — *The council keeps the hall in Coinneach Bàn's name* (Cathair dhearg). After Anna Ruadh's death the council at Cathair dhearg keeps the red hall three years in her son's name before Coinneach Bàn, at seven-and-twenty, takes it in his own.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0212"><em>Death of Anna Ruadh</em>, 26 an Cèitean, FE 2,829</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0213"></a>**27 an Giblean, FE 2,832** — *Coinneach Bàn* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn rules long and quietly from Cathair dhearg. In his reign the clerks of the hall begin to copy the rolls for the provinces, so that each province seat has its own copy of the laws. Several of those copies survive where the first writings are lost.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-9033"><em>The council keeps the hall in Coinneach Bàn's name</em>, 4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,829</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9034"></a>**23 an Cèitean, FE 2,832** — *Coinneach Bàn begins the copying of the provincial rolls* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn, choosing a clerk's work over his mother's roads, has every province seat send its own laws to Cathair dhearg to be copied fresh, and reads each copy through himself before it is shelved, so that within a decade a province's own clerks trust the capital's copy of their rolls sooner than the damp-spoiled skins in their own keeping.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0213"><em>Coinneach Bàn</em>, 27 an Giblean, FE 2,832</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9033"><em>The council keeps the hall in Coinneach Bàn's name</em>, 4 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,829</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9035"></a>**8 an Lùnastal, FE 2,832** — *A second clerk keeps the unstruck preface* (Dùn ìseal). Before the knife reaches the Keepers' roll, the clerk Seumas Bàn sends for has already made a copy of the count of his own house for his own hand; it is that unstruck copy, kept quietly through the rest of the age, and not the scraped preface, that answers for the fact today.
- <a id="ev-II-0214"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835** — *Seumas Bàn keeps the flame* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn of Sliochd Mhuirich is chosen Keeper. Reading the Hall's roll at Dùn ìseal he finds that more than half the Keepers of the age were of his own house, and has the fact struck from the preface. The unstruck copy survives.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9035"><em>A second clerk keeps the unstruck preface</em>, 8 an Lùnastal, FE 2,832</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9036"></a>**17 an Lùnastal, FE 2,836** — *Seumas Bàn reckons two Keepers in three of his house* (Dùn ìseal). Going beyond the count of names, Seumas Bàn reckons how many of the remaining Keepers married into Sliochd Mhuirich or fostered a child of it, and finds the true share near two in every three.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0214"><em>Seumas Bàn keeps the flame</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,835</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9035"><em>A second clerk keeps the unstruck preface</em>, 8 an Lùnastal, FE 2,832</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0215"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,838** — *The rites counted at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn has the clerks of the Hall list every rite on the island that burns the handful and every one that lays claim to the vein, that the council may know what it keeps. The list holds the Hall's own rite, the ancestor-keeping of the old folk, the dawn-hawk of the north coast, the wood-watchers of the west, the wolf-sworn, the sting-oath, and both schools of the stag. The clerks write that a thousand years before no such list would have been needed.
- <a id="ev-II-0216"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840** — *The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter* (Seann Skell). The hawk-keepers of Seann Skell turn away the Hall's cutter who comes to try their measure, saying their measure is the hawk's, and the hawk is not the Keeper's. The cutter goes home with the refusal in writing. No rite had refused the trial of the measure outright before.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9037"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, FE 2,840** — *Ealasaid Bhàn writes the hawk-keepers' refusal into hide* (Seann Skell). Ealasaid Bhàn, eldest of the fowler households of Seann Skell, meets the Hall's cutter Ruairidh Òg at her own door and tells him the dawn measure is the hawk's and not the Keeper's, allowing him only to watch from the yard as any neighbour might, and setting the answer down in a strip of hide so that no cutter after him could mistake it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0216"><em>The hawk-keepers refuse the Hall's cutter</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,840</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9038"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,840** — *A guard swears the Fianna's new oath at Caol leathan* (Caol leathan). A young road-guard swears the first of the graver oaths at Caol leathan's new hall, hand flat on the white stone in a room still smelling of fresh mortar, and tells his own household after that the stone had felt warm under his palm, though the mason who set it swears he cut and laid nothing but plain grey rock from the town's own quarry.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9037"><em>Ealasaid Bhàn writes the hawk-keepers' refusal into hide</em>, 17 an Dàmhair, FE 2,840</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9039"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, FE 2,842** — *The province seats send their laws to Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Seat after seat sends its clerk down to Cathair dhearg with the district's laws copied fresh, and Coinneach Bàn reads every copy himself before it is shelved. Within a decade the seats send to the capital for copies of their own rolls, their own skins having gone to the damp.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0213"><em>Coinneach Bàn</em>, 27 an Giblean, FE 2,832</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0217"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,843** — *The wolf-sworn build a hall* (Caol leathan). The wolf-sworn of Caol leathan build a hall of their own about the white wolf-stone at the town gate, and swear oaths there that are no longer road-guards' oaths. The stone, they say, watches the whole island as the guard watches the road, and will cry out beneath the rightful king. From this hall comes Òrd na Cloiche, the order of the Stone, and the wolf-sworn begin to be called the Fianna.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9038"><em>A guard swears the Fianna's new oath at Caol leathan</em>, 14 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,840</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0218"></a>**3 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,846** — *The sting-oath at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). At Seann Skell in the west the sting-oath of the harbour court becomes a creed. Its keepers hold that one power stings the liar wherever he may be, Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, and that the scorpion is but his sign; theirs is the first teaching on the island to call itself the only true one, and the Hall's roll sets it down as new. Thereafter the oath is sworn over a cup marked with the scorpion, Manannan's Cup of Truth, which is said to break in three at three lies spoken over it and to be made whole by three truths. Òrd Mhanannain dates itself from this court.
- <a id="ev-II-0219"></a>**4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849** — *Seann Vell swears on the sting* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell, on the western coast below Cuan shean, takes up the sting-oath of its neighbours. Its shrine keeps a scorpion carved in yellow stone, the first image of the creature made for worship and not for swearing on.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9040"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,849** — *A gravestone-cutter carves Seann Vell's scorpion from a fisherman's telling* (Seann Vell). The stonecutter who carves Seann Vell's yellow scorpion, better known till then for gravestones than for shrines, works from a fisherman's account of one washed up dead on the strand, having no living creature shown to her, so that the image every child of the town learns to fear owes as much to a fisher's memory as to the god it serves.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0219"><em>Seann Vell swears on the sting</em>, 4 an t-Samhain, FE 2,849</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0220"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852** — *The dark wood keeps its own rite* (Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag). The wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag cease to send to the Hall for judgement of their quarrels, and judge them under the trees. They hold that the black beast has two natures, one that keeps and one that devours, and that the vein has the same. The order of Macha afterwards tells of the two horses that drew one chariot, the black Dubh Sainglenn and the grey Liath Macha: two horses, one yoke.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9041"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,852** — *The wood-watchers judge a boundary quarrel under the trees*. A cutter of Cnoc bhàn and a fowler of the Abhainn ìseal bring a boundary quarrel to the wood-watchers of Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag rather than to Dùn ìseal, and both accept a judgement neither asked for: that the disputed scrub belongs to whoever feeds it through a hard winter, and to no one in an easy one.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0220"><em>The dark wood keeps its own rite</em>, 13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,852</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9040"><em>A gravestone-cutter carves Seann Vell's scorpion from a fisherman's telling</em>, 19 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,849</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9042"></a>**5 an t-Samhain, FE 2,852** — *The council's carpenters set the hawk-keepers nearest the door* (Dùn ìseal). The carpenters who build the council's new benches at Dùn ìseal, told only the number of heads for each company, set the hawk-keepers' bench nearest the door for no reason any clerk troubles to record, so that latecomers of every company after sit longest among strangers before reaching their own.
- <a id="ev-II-0221"></a>**11 an Gearran, FE 2,855** — *The common root of the orders*. The one folk-faith of the island begins plainly to divide into the several ways that later ages name apart: the orders of An Creideamh Sean, the Old Faith, and the hearth-keeping of Na Seann Spioradan, the Old Spirits. From this time the belief of the Dia-thìrich is no longer one.
- <a id="ev-II-0222"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858** — *The council divided by rite* (Dùn ìseal). The council at Dùn ìseal, which had sat by hearth and by house, begins to sit in companies by rite. Seumas Bàn complains that he keeps the flame now for eight peoples, each of whom thinks itself its only keeper. The seating holds for the rest of the age.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIII-9042"><em>The council's carpenters set the hawk-keepers nearest the door</em>, 5 an t-Samhain, FE 2,852</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0223"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860** — *Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims* (Allt an Àigh). Pilgrims of every rite go on walking to Allt an Àigh in the right quarter of the moon; it is the one custom of the island that the Hall's list sets under no company. In one season the path from Caol shean is paved anew by pilgrims of four rites.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9043"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860** — *Pilgrims of four rites mend the path to Allt an Àigh* (Allt an Àigh). Pilgrims of four rites, meeting on the path from Caol shean by no arrangement, fall to mending its worn stones together, hawk-keeper beside wolf-sworn beside a stag scholar, and finish the work before any asks whether the others belong there.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0223"><em>Allt an Àigh keeps its pilgrims</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0224"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863** — *The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). The keeper of the springs at Muileann ruadh rules that the sick of every rite shall be bathed without asking which. Her ruling is copied into the rolls of the provinces. It is the last ruling of the age on which every company of the council agrees.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9044"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,863** — *Beathag Fhionn rules the springs open to every company* (Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh). Beathag Fhionn, keeper of the bath-house over the warm springs at Muileann ruadh, rules that the sick of every rite shall be carried up and bathed at dawn without being asked first which company they keep, and every province seat with a copy of anything at all copies her ruling into its own rolls that same season.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0224"><em>The springs at Muileann ruadh common to all</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, FE 2,863</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9043"><em>Pilgrims of four rites mend the path to Allt an Àigh</em>, 20 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,860</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0225"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, FE 2,866** — *Cnoc dhìreach's weavers* (Cnoc dhìreach). The town of Cnoc dhìreach in the east, on the carriers' road south of the springs, becomes known for a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers wear on the high passes. It is not the grave-keepers' village by the old tombs, and the rolls tell the two Cnoc dhìreachs apart by that cloth.
- <a id="ev-II-0226"></a>**23 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,869** — *The dyers of Muileann bhàn* (Muileann bhàn). The dyers of Muileann bhàn in the eastern hills learn to fix a pale blue from a hill plant, and the carriers' cloth of all the mountain country is dyed there. The Keepers wear it undyed, and say so.
- <a id="ev-II-0227"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, FE 2,872** — *Muileann dhomhain's mill* (Muileann dhomhain). A water-mill is built at Muileann dhomhain in the eastern hills to grind the grain of the common granaries of the mountain districts. The miller keeps one measure in sixteen, and the rolls call it fair.
- <a id="ev-II-0228"></a>**26 an Cèitean, FE 2,875** — *The flood at Àth chiar* (Àth chiar). Rain on the eastern hills brings the river over the ford at Àth chiar, and it carries off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The common granary of the district stands on a rise, is untouched, and feeds the town through the winter.
- <a id="ev-II-0229"></a>**24 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,878** — *The oyster-beds of Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The people of Seann Bhral on the south-eastern coast begin to lay oyster-beds in the shallows, a craft that came, they say, with the name of their town. The Library's copy of the provincial roll sets down the claim and marks it doubtful.
- <a id="ev-II-0230"></a>**20 an Gearran, FE 2,880** — *Seann Vell's harbour* (Seann Vell). Seann Vell on the south-eastern coast grows into a city on the southern fishing and the silver of Muileann chiar brought down the eastern road. Its harbour is the first on the island with a stone quay.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9045"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,880** — *Death of Seumas Bàn* (Dùn ìseal). Seumas Bàn dies at Dùn ìseal in his eightieth year, having kept the flame five-and-forty years, and in all that time seen none of the eight companies sit again by hearth and house.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0222"><em>The council divided by rite</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, FE 2,858</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9044"><em>Beathag Fhionn rules the springs open to every company</em>, 11 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,863</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0231"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, FE 2,883** — *The light at Tobar dhearg rebuilt* (Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg). The old beacon at Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is rebuilt as a stone tower with the fire on its top, the first sea-light raised above the ground. It burns seal-oil of the north-west, carried the whole length of the island.
- <a id="ev-II-0232"></a>**19 an Giblean, FE 2,886** — *Muileann naomh's mill-shrine* (Muileann naomh). At Muileann naomh on the southern coast a mill and a shrine share one roof, and the miller keeps the shrine's handful beside his millstones. The Keeper's cutter who comes to try it finds the measure kept and the flour good.
- <a id="ev-II-0233"></a>**21 am Màrt, FE 2,889** — *Dùn thais walled* (Dùn thais). Dùn thais in the eastern hills is walled, and a temple of the stag's people is raised within it, the first of theirs built in stone and not kept in a grove. The elder school at Cnoc bhàn sends it teachers.
- <a id="ev-II-0234"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,892** — *The wool-fair of Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Inis mhòr holds a wool-fair at every shearing, and buyers come to it from all the northern coast and some from Cathair dhearg. Its silver is weighed on the Muileann chiar weights sent to the northern road.
- <a id="ev-II-0235"></a>**18 an Cèitean, FE 2,895** — *Baile Mòr mhòr on the northern coast* (Baile Mòr mhòr). Baile Mòr mhòr, on the northern coast west of Seann Toll, grows great enough on the fishing to send its own member to the council at Dùn ìseal. The Four Houses mislike it, and seat its member at the foot of the hall.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9046"></a>**23 an Gearran, FE 2,896** — *Coinneach Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn, who had copied the laws for every province, dies in his own bed at the red hall in the ninety-first year of his life. His son Coinneach Donn takes up the cup without any meeting of the Four Houses being called.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9047"></a>**24 am Màrt, FE 2,896** — *Coinneach Donn takes the red hall without a meeting* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Bàn's son Coinneach Donn takes the red hall as sons of that house always have, with no meeting of the Four Houses; outlying reeves learn of one rìgh's death and the next rìgh's holding from the same line of a roll.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9046"><em>Coinneach Bàn dies at Cathair dhearg</em>, 23 an Gearran, FE 2,896</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0236"></a>**13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,898** — *The northern boats at Seann Toll* (Seann Toll). The harbour at Seann Toll becomes the home of the northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders make the longest craft on the island, built for a day's run along the coast and never for open water.
- <a id="ev-II-0237"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,900** — *Drought at Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). A dry summer burns the pastures round Achadh shean in the east, and by spring the district's common granary is empty. Grain is sent from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under the shared-meal law, and the district repays it over the harvests after.
- <a id="ev-II-0238"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,903** — *Baile chaol's repayment* (Baile chaol). The rolls at Baile chaol set down the repayment of the drought grain by Achadh shean, measure by measure, to the last. The clerk adds that no such debt in the rolls was repaid in full before.
- <a id="ev-II-0239"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,906** — *The panthers late* (Imrich nam Pantar). The great cats cross the southern road late, and fewer than the carriers remember. The weather-watchers read it for a hard winter, and are right. The Keepers note it without remark.
- <a id="ev-II-0240"></a>**13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,909** — *The watch-tower at Baile ruadh* (Baile ruadh). A timber watch-tower is raised at Baile ruadh on the north-eastern coast to look out for raiders from the islands, manned by turns by the fisher-kin of Sliochd Raghnaill. It is the only tower of war the age builds.
- <a id="ev-II-0241"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, FE 2,912** — *Cuan ruadh's boats* (Cuan ruadh). The fishers of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast give boats and men to the watch against the island raiders. In return Sliochd Raghnaill gives the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat.
- <a id="ev-II-0242"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, FE 2,915** — *The drowned-feast at Inis chrom* (Inis chrom). At Inis chrom on the western coast the families of the drowned hold a feast on the shore each year and set an empty place for each of the lost. The custom spreads to the harbours northward as far as Seann Warr.
- <a id="ev-II-0243"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, FE 2,918** — *The potters of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). Potters at Baile ghorm on the south-western coast begin to fire a hard red ware of the local clay, and their jars carry the oil and grain of the western road. Sherds of it lie on every waypoint-house site the Library's surveyors have walked.
- <a id="ev-II-0244"></a>**19 an Giblean, FE 2,920** — *Cnoc àrsaidh's kilns* (Cnoc àrsaidh). Potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns at Cnoc àrsaidh in the south-west, where the clay is better and the wood nearer. There the red ware of the western road is made for the rest of the age.
- <a id="ev-II-0245"></a>**18 an Cèitean, FE 2,923** — *Cathair fhada grows* (Cathair fhada). Families leaving the crowded harbours about Cathair dhearg settle at Cathair fhada on the southern coast and raise its long street along the ridge. They bring a wood-watcher with them, and a copy of the laws.
- <a id="ev-II-0246"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,926** — *Cnoc naomh's ancestor-shrine* (Cnoc naomh). The people of Cnoc naomh keep a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of the hill in the old folk way, with no hawk, wolf, sting or stag in it. The Hall's list of rites names them among the keepers of the old reverence, which by now is a company of its own.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9048"></a>**25 am Faoilleach, FE 2,927** — *Coinneach Donn dies* (Cathair dhearg). Coinneach Donn, who has held the cup thirty years and more since his father's death, dies in the eighty-seventh year of his own life at Cathair dhearg, leaving a daughter, Mòr, not yet twenty-three, and a younger brother, Tormod Donn.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9047"><em>Coinneach Donn takes the red hall without a meeting</em>, 24 am Màrt, FE 2,896</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9049"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,928** — *Tormod Donn's claim before the Four Houses* (Dùn ìseal). Tormod Donn brings a claim to the Four Houses at Dùn ìseal against his niece Mòr, arguing that a man of the same blood and twice her years stands the plainer heir. The Houses split, two benches for Mòr and two for neither.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9048"><em>Coinneach Donn dies</em>, 25 am Faoilleach, FE 2,927</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9050"></a>**5 an Gearran, FE 2,929** — *Catrìona nic Mhuirich speaks for Mòr before the Four Houses* (Dùn ìseal). With the houses split and the winter spent, the Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich tells them the red hall is no business of the Hall's to give, but that she will set the stone cup in Mòr's hands, as once in Gilleasbuig Mòr's, if they ask it, and in no one else's.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9049"><em>Tormod Donn's claim before the Four Houses</em>, 27 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,928</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0247"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929** — *Mòr nic Coinnich crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mòr nic Coinnich, granddaughter of Coinneach Bàn, takes the red hall at Cathair dhearg. The Keeper Catrìona nic Mhuirich sets the stone cup in her hands at Dùn ìseal, as the houses had done for Gilleasbuig Mòr. Hers is the last name written in the king-list of the Holy Age.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIII-9050"><em>Catrìona nic Mhuirich speaks for Mòr before the Four Houses</em>, 5 an Gearran, FE 2,929</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9051"></a>**8 an Lùnastal, FE 2,929** — *Tormod Donn yields* (Cuan ruadh). Tormod Donn withdraws his claim by his own steward's word, sent from his house at Cuan ruadh, after Catrìona nic Mhuirich tells the Four Houses she will set the cup in no hand but Mòr's. It is the last such claim the house of Tormod contests.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0247"><em>Mòr nic Coinnich crowned</em>, 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9050"><em>Catrìona nic Mhuirich speaks for Mòr before the Four Houses</em>, 5 an Gearran, FE 2,929</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9052"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,929** — *Mòr asks the Keeper whether her uncle's claim was wicked* (Dùn ìseal). Taking the cup at Dùn ìseal, Mòr asks Catrìona low whether her uncle's claim was wicked or only foolish. The Keeper answers that few claims are purely either, and that Mòr should spend her reckoning on the hall's keeping, not her uncle's punishing. Mòr brings no charge.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0247"><em>Mòr nic Coinnich crowned</em>, 15 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,929</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9051"><em>Tormod Donn yields</em>, 8 an Lùnastal, FE 2,929</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9053"></a>**18 an Giblean, FE 2,931** — *Mòr weds Dòmhnall Dubh* (Cathair dhearg). Mòr nic Coinnich weds Dòmhnall Dubh of Sliochd Raghnaill, whose kin keep the watch-tower at Baile ruadh. He holds no office at the red hall and keeps, through her reign, to his own house's trade of boats and coastwatch.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9052"><em>Mòr asks the Keeper whether her uncle's claim was wicked</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,929</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-II-0248"></a>**2 an Giblean, FE 2,939** — *The Hall's roll at the close of the age* (Dùn ìseal). At the close of the age the Keepers' roll holds one hundred and forty names, from Beathag Bhàn to Catrìona nic Mhuirich, and the king-list more than ninety, from Goraidh Mòr to Mòr nic Coinnich. The Small-Burning Law is unchanged in any word since the stone cup of Fionnlagh Dall, and the cup stands yet on the threshold of Talla na Lasrach at Dùn ìseal.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9054"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, FE 2,940** — *Death of Tormod Donn* (Cuan ruadh). Tormod Donn, who once claimed the red hall against his niece, dies at Cuan ruadh, and his line ends with him, leaving no son to trouble the succession after.
- <a id="ev-II-0249"></a>**1 an Cèitean, FE 2,949** — *The last age of even population*. So ends the Holy Age. The long years had gone out of the king's kin many generations before its end, and the chroniclers of after days look back on its later centuries with some unease: they are the last time in the history of Dia-thìr that no family's lives ran longer than any other's.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9055"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, FE 2,950** — *Dòmhnall Dubh dies at Baile ruadh* (Baile ruadh). Dòmhnall Dubh dies in the fiftieth year of his own life among his own kin at Baile ruadh rather than at Cathair dhearg. Mòr goes north herself to see him buried beside the watch-tower his house has kept three generations.
- <a id="ev-EIII-9056"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, FE 2,950** — *Mòr goes north to bury Dòmhnall Dubh* (Baile ruadh). Mòr nic Coinnich goes north herself to see her husband buried beside the watch-tower at Baile ruadh that his house has kept three generations, a journey no rìgh has made in living memory for a husband's burying.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-II-0240"><em>The watch-tower at Baile ruadh</em>, 13 an Lùnastal, FE 2,909</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9055"><em>Dòmhnall Dubh dies at Baile ruadh</em>, 26 an Dàmhair, FE 2,950</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9057"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,953** — *Mòr nic Coinnich dies* (Cathair dhearg). Mòr nic Coinnich dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two daughters, Beathag and Mòrag, and no brother, uncle or cousin near enough in blood to raise a claim. Hers is the last name the Holy Age itself sets down in the king-list.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0248"><em>The Hall's roll at the close of the age</em>, 2 an Giblean, FE 2,939</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9056"><em>Mòr goes north to bury Dòmhnall Dubh</em>, 24 an t-Samhain, FE 2,950</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9058"></a>**11 an Gearran, FE 2,953** — *Beathag crowned at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, not yet sixteen, is crowned at Cathair dhearg within the month of her mother's death, by her own house's word and the Four Houses' assent, rather than by a winter journey to Dùn ìseal for the stone cup.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9057"><em>Mòr nic Coinnich dies</em>, 13 am Faoilleach, FE 2,953</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9059"></a>**3 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,953** — *Ruairidh Clèireach begins the new roll* (Cathair dhearg). Finding the old skin of the king-list and the Keepers' roll filled to its last line with Mòr's name, the clerk Ruairidh Clèireach begins a new skin and sets Beathag's name at its head, so that no name later than Mòr's stands in the old roll.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0248"><em>The Hall's roll at the close of the age</em>, 2 an Giblean, FE 2,939</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9058"><em>Beathag crowned at Cathair dhearg</em>, 11 an Gearran, FE 2,953</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9060"></a>**2 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,953** — *Catrìona offers to receive the young rìgh at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Catrìona nic Mhuirich, past threescore, sends word that she stands ready to receive the young Beathag at Dùn ìseal whenever the roads and season allow. The journey is not made in Beathag's first year, nor troubled over again while the roll of the age is kept.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9059"><em>Ruairidh Clèireach begins the new roll</em>, 3 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,953</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIII-9061"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, FE 2,953** — *The old roll closed on Mòr's name* (Cathair dhearg). The skin of the king-list and the Keepers' roll kept since Coinneach Bàn's day is full to its last line with Mòr's name and her count. Ruairidh Clèireach closes it and lays it in the chest with every roll of the Hall before it, so that no name later than Mòr's stands on it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-II-0248"><em>The Hall's roll at the close of the age</em>, 2 an Giblean, FE 2,939</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-EIII-9060"><em>Catrìona offers to receive the young rìgh at Dùn ìseal</em>, 2 an t-Iuchar, FE 2,953</a>.</span>
